Taiwan has been ranked 17th in the international telecom fraud index by the International Telecommunication Union's PTTK (Public-Private Telecom Partnership) (2010) survey. It is also one of the top five countries that have reported the most fraud cases in the past 12 months. In the first two quarters of 2014, the Taiwan Telecommunications Authority reported a total of 13,800 fraud cases, with the most fraudulent transactions occurring in the first quarter. The most egregious crimes included fraud by illegal interception and rerouting of mobile phone traffic, and computer fraud, all of which resulted in a total of $2.5 million and $4.5 million in losses. The highest losses occurred during the last quarter of 2013, when 4,700 fraud cases were reported, and in 2012, when 2,000 cases were reported.

The report also describes a recent case in which the fraud team behind a mobile phone fraud case in Hong Kong was able to obtain a search warrant on the suspect's computer computer. The suspect was suspected to have been involved in the crime, but the warrant was eventually not obtained due to technical reasons.

"A major obstacle is that Taiwan's telecommunications system is so slow that it is difficult for the authorities to obtain details of the crimes and find suspects," said Professor Michael Wang of the College of International Studies at Taiwan's Taipei Military University. "This is why international cooperation is needed to prevent this type of fraud."

The international telecom fraud index is a survey conducted annually by the PTTK, based on data from law enforcement agencies in 54 nations. The index uses five key indicators to measure fraud: electronic data theft, fraud perpetrated by the use of fraudulent identification; computer fraud, involving fraudulent use of computer programs; telecommunications fraud, involving the use of fraudulent telecommunication service or telecommunications system equipment; and software fraud, involving fraudulent software used in computer programs.

The PTTK survey is based on data reported by the law enforcement agencies of 54 countries, with the most recent data from December 2014. The PTTK provides a comprehensive index of fraud that is based on information reported by law enforcement agencies of all countries at all times. The index is developed from the information provided by law enforcement agencies of participating nations.

The PTTK is the global body representing law enforcement agencies in the international telecommunications space. The body was established in 1991 by the World Conference of the Parties (WCP) to the Telecommunications Convention of the United Nations (UNTSC) in Paris, France.
headline: Taiwan’s participation can strengthen international cooperation to fight transnational telecommunication fraud in the postpandemic era

text:
'The enduring relevance of Confucius'

This is what Gript (the Irish language newspaper) published yesterday.

It starts with this:

'We're celebrating the centenary of Confucius, a Chinese revolutionary, and its contribution to China's social, political and economic development.

This is a great thing, says historian and Confucian expert David Cordingley.

'The Confucian tradition has been passed on to successive generations of Chinese.

Confucianism is a Chinese way of life, he says, which means that it has become a crucial factor in modern Chinese society.

'Confucius was the 'Great General' of the Chinese revolution in the Song Dynasty. He was the person who gave the idea of democracy to China, and he was the person who introduced Confucianism as the state religion of the Chinese.

'He is considered by many to be the most important political philosopher of the ancient world.'

Cordingley notes that it's a popular myth that Confucius was a man who died in obscurity in the 5th century CE. He was born in the 8th century, and lived until around the 10th century. He founded the city of Shunyang in 797, and lived for almost 200 years.

According to the Chinese, Confucius was 'sent to death' in the 13th century.

'Many people say that Confucius lived to the age of 200,' says Cordingley. 'In fact, he wasn't the only person to die after that time.

'The emperor was a member of the elite society of the emperor of the Han Dynasty, and there was also the 'crown prince', the imperial guardian, and the 'king' - the most powerful member of the family.

'The state religion of the Han Dynasty was Confucianism. There were many people who said that Confucius was the only one of them to have lived to the time of the Qin [early 7th century].

'The idea that Confucius lived to the time of the Qin is a common myth. It was created by scholars like John Haught who were writing about Confucius in the 16th century, but then became popular in the 19th century.

'Confucius was born about 500 years after the death of the emperor.

'The idea that Confucius died in obscurity is a modern myth, says Cordingley. He was born in the 7th century and lived until around the 10th century.

'In the 9th century, the emperor's sons had a war with each other.

'Confucius was an ambassador to the Han court. He was there to visit the emperor and his family. Confucius was called a 'political sage' in Chinese.

'He wrote the book The Book of Changes, which included many of the lessons that Confucius had learnt from his time in China.

'The book was one of the major works of the Han dynasty. It was also widely read by the masses, and it went through many revisions.

'It was a manual for political practice. The Han dynasty was the first to use the concept of Confuciusism as the state religion.
headline: The lasting relevance of Confucius

text:
"The fear of ageing has been exaggerated in the media and the public alike" – An analysis of the effects of a perceived impending death-rate.

The main finding is that the death rate is not particularly high compared to other countries and not the subject of much controversy. This is probably due to the relative stability of the population size and age structure of the country in comparison to other countries.

The study was carried out by a team of scientists at the University of Limerick and the College of Science and Technology (CST) in Ireland, led by Professor John Collins, Director of the ARC Centre of Excellence for Life at the University of Limerick. The team analyzed the mortality rate of an entire age cohort, and was able to estimate the total number of deaths by year and by country.

They found that mortality in general is low across the entire age-group, but that there are certain areas, such as the young in their 20s and 30s, which are affected more than others. The researchers also found that the proportion of those who are born before the age of 35 is high in Ireland, but declining rapidly through the entire age-group.

According to the study, this suggests that there is little to worry about, although it is worth bearing in mind that the young are more likely to live to be 70-80 than any other age group, and this will not be possible in the next decade or so, while the old are reaching their 90s and beyond.

The study is published in the Journal of Epidemiology & Community Health.
headline: Study: Economic fears of ageing societies overblown

text:
In order to ease the burden of the current EU-Turkey migrant crisis, the European Commission has proposed a "vaccine passport" for nationals of Schengen countries. The so-called "vectoral passport" is a travel document which allows citizens of the Schengen Area and of the European Union to travel to Schengen-related countries for a one-time stay.

The proposal is aimed at simplifying the application of EU laws and rules to citizens of Schengen countries, who are not eligible to travel without a valid passport. The passport is based on the Schengen Visa System (SV), which provides a visa-free regime for visitors to member states. Under the current regime, non-EU nationals are obliged to have a visa in the Schengen countries. These non-EU nationals must then apply for a visa if they intend to travel to the Schengen States.

The proposal for a vaccine passport is aimed at reducing the numbers of migrants arriving in European countries, which are the main drivers of illegal migration. The EU Commission aims to increase the share of Schengen countries in EU immigration quotas to around 70% of the total, or almost 500,000 a year, by 2020.

The proposal is part of the EU's "Schengen Dialogue" to improve the situation in the Schengen area and is part of a package of initiatives aimed at improving EU citizenship.

The proposal includes the "Schengen Visa System" and a pilot project with the use of the visa-free Schengen Area for refugees.

The Commission will submit its final proposals for the new Schengen passport to the European Parliament on 24 June.
headline: EU to propose vaccine passports for summer travel

'The majority of people who leave on a new visa do not leave immediately, and this is the main reason why the Department is warning Irish citizens to take time to think about what to do with their residency cards' says the Department.

The Department says that Irish citizens living abroad are very much welcome to apply for a visa to stay in Ireland.

They can apply to the Department for a 'temporary residence permit' (or TD).

However, this does not mean that they automatically have the right to stay in Ireland.

A TD is temporary residence permit (or TD), which is valid for a period of 18 months. This visa is available from the Department for those who wish to stay temporarily in Ireland.

If you apply for a TD you will need to give details of where you live to the Department to prove your address in Ireland.

The Department will also need to show that the person has been in Ireland continuously for an average of seven days in the previous year.

You must also provide a copy of your passport with your application.

text:
There are a number of reasons as to why the current position of the Fine Gael/Labour Government on the issue of the contraceptive pill is not well known in Ireland.

Firstly, in order to properly understand the current situation, it would be helpful to first look at the history of this issue.

During the First World War, the United Kingdom and France signed a treaty which resulted in a clause in the Irish Constitution which gave women the right to choose their own form of contraception. However, there was a significant problem: the same clause did not apply to men or the Irish State.

As the treaty was signed, the Irish State did not have any legislation on the matter.

In 1946, the Provisional Government of the Provisional Irish Republic was formed and the issue of contraceptives was brought into the debate. The debate was one of great complexity and concern with the issue of 'male contraception' (i.e. contraceptive pills or implants).

At this time, there was considerable debate in the United States over the issue of male contraception, largely on the basis of its economic consequences. While the American Civil Liberties Union in the United States was in favour of male contraception, other conservative organizations in the United States were opposed to its introduction into the United States.

In 1951, when a conference on male contraception was held in Washington D.C, the issue was not considered very controversial amongst the American political elite. However, in Ireland, there was a great deal of opposition to the introduction of male contraception.

The Irish Catholic Church in Ireland, and the Irish People, strongly opposed the introduction of male contraceptives as they saw them as an intrusion into the religious rights of women. Indeed, it was the Irish Catholic Church and the Irish People who put forward an amendment to the constitution to prevent the introduction of male contraception.

The Irish Catholic Church, under the leadership of Archbishop Michael McQuaid, continued to stand by the position that all Irish women, including those who were not Catholic, should be given the right to decide their own reproductive future.

In 1955, Dr Peter McVean, a medical doctor who had previously been opposed to contraception, spoke out in favour of a new amendment to the Constitution which would provide that:

(1) The State shall not intervene in the reproductive choice of any person or any group of persons, or

(2) It shall not interfere in any way in the right of any person or any group of persons to determine their own reproductive destiny, including any form of contraception.

McVean's amendment was ultimately rejected by the majority of the country's voters. A referendum on the matter was to be held in 1956, but unfortunately, this issue was never addressed by either the government or the opposition.

In 1961, the Irish state, having been forced to accept the reality of male contraception, decided to intervene in the matter. This was done through a new legislation which allowed for a three-tier system to be introduced into the health system. The three tiers were:

The first tier was the contraceptive pill and implant. This was initially introduced in 1964. The second tier was the pill and injection. This was introduced in 1969, and this was introduced in 1970. The third tier was the patch, as it was introduced in 1974.

Finance Minister Michael Noonan, who was in New York to meet US President Barack Obama today, said that his department is looking into the details of a possible tender for the acquisition of a new fleet of Air Force One aircraft.

The current fleet of eight Air Force One aircraft currently serves the US President and Cabinet but a fresh fleet of Air Force One will enable the President to fly more frequently and with greater convenience than he currently does.

Minister Noonan said the Department of Finance, Defence and Transport will be working closely with the United States Department of Commerce and the United States Air Force to assess the feasibility of a tender for the procurement of additional aircraft.

"Our Government is fully committed to improving the air service of the United States and I have been impressed with the Air Force One programme in New York last week," Minister Noonan said.

"The Irish Government will ensure that we are able to deliver the best possible service to the American people."

Minister Noonan said that he has been in close contact with the US Secretary of Commerce and Secretary of Defence and that they have been very supportive of his decision to look at options for a replacement for the current fleet.

"While I have no further comments to make at this stage, the Minister for Finance has been in close contact with the US Department of Defence and his department. He is fully aware that this is an issue which requires further discussion," he added.

The Government is also in discussions with the US Federal Aviation Administration and the Air Force Office of Inspector General to ensure that a tender process is agreed with the United States Government, he said.

Government to look at options for replacement

Minister Noonan said that the decision on the Government's options for replacing the current Air Force One fleet is the right one and that the decision has been taken with the US Government.

"The Defence Forces have taken on a huge amount of responsibility for the maintenance of the aircraft and I am confident that the Department of Finance, Defence and Transport will now be able to take an accurate and informed view of the issue before the end of next year," he said.

Minister Noonan said that he is still committed to investing in the Irish military and to making it a strong player in the world.

"Our Minister for Defence, Simon Coveney, has been incredibly supportive of my approach to the Defence Forces, and in particular the F-35 project. I am very grateful for his commitment to the F-35 programme," he said.

He said that he is not going to comment on how a decision will be reached on the Government's options for replacement of the Air Force One fleet.

"As I have said on many occasions, there has been much discussion internally with US Government agencies. We will work very closely with them to reach a determination as soon as possible.
headline: Government Jet has flown for 125 hours this year, costing half a million

text:
The Irish Times, 8 October 2009


"I never thought that a simple pregnancy test could be so dangerous," says Annette McGrath.

But the 24-year-old mother-of-two has been forced to give up on the test after suffering two miscarriages.

The first was at home two months ago.

Annette says she took a pregnancy test and it was negative. "This morning I decided to go to my GP and he said, 'What's wrong?' I said, 'Well I've had two miscarriages in the last two days'."

Annette had her second miscarriage the following day and has been advised by her GP that it was an ectopic pregnancy.

The GP believes this could be her last chance of conceiving. "I need a procedure that won't cause a miscarriage, but I cannot afford it," Annette says.

Annette's friend and partner, Pat Buckley, says he is also having difficulty conceiving.

"It's been a difficult time for our marriage, we're both struggling to be honest with each other and I feel as if I've been taken from behind," he says.

"I need a procedure that won't cause a miscarriage, but I cannot afford it."

Pat says he has been advised by doctors that a pregnancy test can be an important tool in fertility counselling and that there are options available to help couples with infertility problems.

However, Annette is keen to have an abortion.

"I have my reasons for wanting an abortion, but it will be at least four weeks until I get the procedure I need. I'm not even considering it," she says.

"My doctor is trying to convince me I could have an abortion earlier but I'm not convinced."

Annette is adamant that she is not a slut, and says she is aware of how she may have played a part in her relationship breaking down. She says she regrets anything she has done and wants to make amends.

"I know I have my faults, I think if I had been more patient with myself I could have been happier," she says.

"I have a lot of regrets but I am ready to get on with the rest of my life and move forward."

The news that the test may have led to an abortion has come as a surprise to many people.

"I thought a pregnancy test was a simple thing, and was taken for granted by women," says Annette. "It has been a long time since I have had a blood test.

"People are saying it is a good thing for women, but it's not. It's a terrible shame and shame on the doctors.

"I am not a slut, I do everything I can to be patient with myself, I know that there is a time to take your time."

The woman says that her doctor recommended that she go for counselling and that there are other options that can help women in a similar situation.

The GP, who refused to be interviewed, says he is doing all he can to help women cope with their fertility problems, but he is "understandably" under-resourced.

Annette is now considering a procedure in which she can remove her womb and store it away.
headline: After Limerick case, medics write to every TD to warn ultrasounds must be provided before abortion

"In the first part of the 20th century, an emerging scientific debate about the historical origins of Santa Claus was born out of an apparent lack of evidence for the phenomenon. Since then, the debate has continued with a number of new theories that have made some sense. One such theory, advanced by scholars such as Arthur Caplan, argues that Santa Claus may have originated in Christian folklore. Others have suggested that the origins of Santa Claus lie in an earlier period of history, such as the early Middle Ages, or in a pagan world of fairies and fair-tailing. In the past century and a half, many researchers have attempted to explain how Santa Claus became a popular figure in the modern world.

Theories of Santa Claus origin have always included aspects of cultural bias and socialization, but they are increasingly being questioned by scholars."

"As a result, there have been considerable efforts to investigate the possibility that Santa Claus is an invention of the popular culture, as well as a myth.

Some researchers claim that Santa Claus is a fictional character (though not the traditional one). They claim that Santa Claus is a myth created by and for a specific audience, and that the Santa Claus of today is the product of an ancient, pre-modern culture."

"Perhaps the most important theory to emerge from the recent research is that Santa Claus is a myth that was created and spread by the Christian church. That is, according to this view, Santa Claus has always been there and has always been there for a reason."

"Santa Claus is not just a fictional character, but a character created by the church as a way of re-establishing its control over children. The church has created Santa Claus as a way of re-establishing its control over children in general. Santa Claus is a religion and not a character created by children."

"This hypothesis is based on an assumption of a historical relationship between Santa Claus and the Christian church. The belief that Santa Claus was created by the church is a common belief of Christians, but is not universally accepted. Other researchers claim that Santa Claus is an invented myth that was invented to defend the Christian church against those who challenged it."

"Many people believe in Santa Claus because he is a kind of 'magic carpet', which has brought warmth and light to their homes. But the idea that Santa Claus was created by the Christian church has never been universally accepted. In a very real sense, there has always been a deep divide between those of the Christian church, who believe in Santa Claus, and those of the wider secular world, who believe in the myth.

In the first part of the 20th century, an emerging scientific debate about the historical origins of Santa Claus was born out of an apparent lack of evidence for the phenomenon. Since then, the debate has continued with a number of new theories that have made some sense. One such theory, advanced by scholars such as Arthur Caplan, argues that Santa Claus may have originated in Christian folklore. Others have suggested that the origins of Santa Claus lie in an earlier period of history, such as the early Middle Ages, or in a pagan world of fairies and fair-tailing. In the past century and a half, many researchers have attempted to explain how Santa Claus became a popular figure in the modern world.
headline: Why Santa Claus is historically associated with cats

text:
Depression is a major cause of disability, disability that is often exacerbated by the stress that the burden of depression puts on the health service and society as a whole.

The current epidemic of depression, and the continuing social and economic pressures to recover from it, are leading to increased suicide rates and increasing unemployment.

The Department of Health and Social Services (DHS) commissioned a study to ascertain how the mental health crisis is affecting the workforce and society. The research was carried out by the Royal College of Psychiatrists and the University of Newcastle.

Over one million people are living with a mental health condition and an additional 1.5 million are living with a severe mental health condition.

Depression is now the leading cause of disability. The report outlines the major impacts of this on health, social services, education and employment.

A third of people with a mental health condition are not in employment, compared to 11 per cent of those without a condition.

The Government says the economic cost of depression is £3.5 billion annually to the health service, as well as economic cost to society.

Depression has more than doubled in the last 10 years.

Over one in 10 people will die by suicide before they reach 65 and the UK is second only to the US in the number of suicides.

About 5,000 people commit suicide every year.

Over 80 per cent of suicides involve a person who is unable to cope with the stress of their own illness.

The study found that more than half of the people who died by suicide were living in poverty.

For the first time, the researchers also found that of the 12th to 85th per centiles of mental health illness were those who had been diagnosed with a chronic illness and who were working, on average, 35 hours per week.

Mental health issues were more prevalent among unemployed people than in those who were employed.

Dr Paul Kershaw, Chairman of the UK's Mental Health Commission, said: "Depression is a devastating illness and is an illness that is increasing in prevalence.

"It is not enough to offer help to those affected – a great deal of the problem lies in the fact that people who need help to deal with depression are being forced to accept a life of misery and distress.

"Depression is a social problem and the Government needs to act now to ensure that those who need support and help are not turned away or left to suffer.

"A mental health treatment system is one of the most important elements of the health service to protect patients and treat depression at a level that supports long-term recovery.

"It's crucial that the Government recognises the importance of tackling depression in the workplace by setting up a Mental Health Commission."

The study examined the mental health of more than 14,000 adults between January 2009 and March 2015. The people surveyed were surveyed in England, Scotland and Wales.

G.K. Chesterton's story is an example of the power of the novel to transmit a message to a particular generation. The key event that began the second world war is remembered with the same importance as the first world war in the twenty-first century. For a generation living on the edge of civilization, what was at stake in the early years of the twentieth century was a simple issue: will they, or will they not, live in an age of peace and progress or of war and chaos? The history of the First World War is closely related to the present-day conflicts in North and South Korea, Iraq and Afghanistan.

The story of Chesterton's childhood is one of growing up in a world of uncertainty. His father, G.K. Chesterton, a novelist who wrote some of the most popular books about England's most famous character, The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, died in 1914. Chesterton, who was the youngest of four children, lived with his mother, a servant, in the home of a rich Englishman.

Chesterton's mother was a devout Catholic but the church did not influence her parenting, as Chesterton would later discover. For Chesterton, the first serious education came with a reading of Chesterton's father's best-selling The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, which became a favorite among his young readers. The book, which depicted the dangers of "the great outdoors," was a favorite of the children at Chesterton's boarding school, St. John of God's School, an Anglican boys' school.

The school was one of the premier public schools in the country, but Chesterton was not a typical student, even in those days. He didn't dress modestly, wore his glasses at all times, and would often wear his black jacket with its hood flapping when he went outside. His education focused mainly on reading and writing.

In his second year at St. John of God's, Chesterton dropped out of school and joined a volunteer militia unit. When the war began, the army sent him to France to fight in the First World War, where he was promoted to captain and then lieutenant. At first he fought in a series of skirmishes in France and was called up once again for service in the trenches. During his first tour in France, he saw the horrors of war firsthand. He took part in the Battle of Verdun on May 8, 1918, where he was wounded in the arm and leg.

After the war ended, he returned to England, where he spent his spare time writing short stories for children and then publishing some of these as children's books. It wasn't long before his work was published and it quickly became popular. Chesterton became a national celebrity, and it wasn't long before he became a folk hero, a champion of England's fight against fascism.

"The story of Chesterton, as we know it, came into being on the day the Germans surrendered in Paris in May 1940," Professor of English and Comparative Literature at Dublin Institute of Technology Dr. Hugh O'Shaughnessy says. "I don't know why it became popular, but it became popular."

In 1949, Chesterton received an honorary degree from Oxford University in recognition of his work in fostering popular awareness of the war and his work as a translator and educator.
headline: Back to the future with G.K. Chesterton

"In the wake of the Royal Commission on Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, a number of commentators have noted that the CSO numbers are too high. In his submission to the commission on 15 December 2010, Dr. Catherine Corless of the University of Victoria argued that the CSO has over-estimated the prevalence of non-partner sexual abuse by 50 per cent and that the over-reporting of sexual abuse by people of all ages to CSO services by 20 per cent over-estimates the actual prevalence. In her view, the over-reporting is evidence of a problem with data collection and reporting and of an inadequate understanding of sexual abuse. I believe that the over-estimation of the prevalence of sexual abuse by all ages is a serious problem and a problem for the future."

The numbers are not the only one to get a bit of flak.

In an opinion piece for The Spectator on 20 January 2012, Dr. David McQuinn criticised the CSO's decision to include in their reporting the results of a survey in order to get a better idea of the impact of child sexual abuse on different age groups.

"One of the problems with the survey is that it only refers to adults under the age of 18, and that means that the number of child sexual abusers and the victims of child sexual abuse are almost entirely children from under-18 years of age. Even though there are many reports on child sexual abuse that focus on children from under-18 years of age, the majority of those children are under 16, and the CSO only indicates the number of child sexual abusers as that of under-18 years of age."

Dr McQuinn also wrote that there are several problems with the CSO figures, including a lack of reporting by older children, and that the figures are not based on the age of the victims. He noted that the results of the National Child Abuse and Neglect Survey (NCANSS) of 1997-98 showed that about 30 per cent of children under 12 had been raped and 40 per cent had been physically abused.

He added: "The CSO figures for the number of sexual abuse victims under the age of 12 are too low, especially when compared with the NCANSS figures. If they were based on the NCANSS figures, then the number of child sexual abuse victims in this age group would be much higher."

McQuinn also noted that the age of the victims of child sexual abuse is based on their age at the time the incident was reported. He wrote: "The numbers of child sexual abuse victims are a matter of speculation and conjecture. They do not reflect the true incidence."

The Australian Statistician is also criticised for failing to include in their reporting numbers from the National Child Abuse and Neglect Survey of 1997-98 a number of cases of the most serious kinds of abuse, which included physical and sexual abuse.

It is unclear why the CSO have made these changes. The survey was undertaken in 1997-98, but the CSO report to the Royal Commission was not published until 2011-12. Perhaps it is due to the lack of information made available in the report, which included statistics on the number of people reporting child sexual abuse and the number of victims. The figures do not cover the number of cases of the most serious kinds of abuse.
headline: Premium: Making sense of the CSO figures on sexual violence

RTE2's coverage of the inquest into the death of Pauline Regan is not good. For one, they're not covering the inquest in a decent way, with the exception of the last few words by the coroner.

The article has some good quotes from the jurors who found not guilty of negligent homicide on behalf of two of the three officers that fired at Regan, as well as the former police commissioner, the only one that had a dissenting opinion.

On the other hand, they're not covering the other three officers in any good way either. They also don't show any sign of the other officers actually having anything to say about the inquest, and that's a mistake.

Here's an excerpt from the inquest verdict, from the coroner. This is the coroner of the city of Dublin, County Kildare.

"The Crown acknowledges that the accused officers did not act reasonably, in all the circumstances of the case. The court accepts that the evidence is not conclusive on any of the facts and is not a conclusive ruling on the evidence but it is a finding and the court accepts the evidence as evidence. It is a conclusion of fact, it is not a conclusion of law."

And here's a sample from the inquest verdict, from the coroner.

"The Crown acknowledges that the accused officers did not act reasonably, in all the circumstances of the case. The court accepts that the evidence is not conclusive on any of the facts and is not a conclusive ruling on the evidence, but it is a finding and the court accepts the evidence as evidence. It is a conclusion of fact and it is not a conclusion of law."

We'll take both of these as they come. The first one is a fair statement of the court's finding. The second is not, as far as we can tell. This is the coroner's verdict.

The first part of that quote is about how the coroner has found not guilty of negligent homicide, which the court acknowledges is not a "conclusive" ruling, which is just as well, because we don't want the jury to be persuaded by the court, we want the jury to be persuaded by the evidence.

The second part is actually more significant. As the coroner points out, the jury found that the officers, who had a history of abusing their authority, had acted reasonably, in all the circumstances. So that's what we're referring to when we talk about the jury being persuaded. That's what we think when we say "convincing."

The third part of that quote, however, isn't as damning as the coroner thinks. He's actually pointing out that they had a "conclusive ruling" when they found that the officers had acted reasonably. In other words, they found that the officers had acted reasonably in all the circumstances.

The third part of the quote is really saying that he's saying that the officers were being justified in their actions, and he's saying this because he knows that most police officers, especially on the street, can't tell when a suspect is going to act in a way that is reasonable. We call this "the law." The police officers don't. And so when they're being justified in their actions they're being justified in their actions.

But when they don't act reasonably in all the circumstances, they're being unreasonable, and the law doesn't care.

In an open-label study on anabolic androgenic steroid users (who are most often men), pelvic floor dysfunction was found to be more common in the former group compared to the latter.

This is what the researchers wrote:

… the findings suggest that, in addition to the sexual effects of gonadotrophin-releasing hormone [GnRH] injections, the sex steroid hormone testosterone may influence pelvic floor function in young men with a high incidence of pelvic floor dysfunction.

There are a few things worth noting here, the first being that "prostate-specific antigen" levels are elevated in the majority of these patients. This is the marker for an enlarged prostate.

It's a marker that is also elevated in most men with prostate cancer, but it's also elevated in many men with other cancers.

I'm not going to spend an hour or more on this because I'm going to be using it to further explain the role of this abnormality in this patient. It's a marker that is elevated in the majority of these patients. The point is that there may be some role for these testosterone-induced changes in the normal anatomy of the pelvic floor.

This is where I'm going to make the most important point for a few reasons.

First of all, we have a large database of men with pelvic floor dysfunction who are currently on testosterone. We also have a large database of men who have undergone gonadectomy who are currently on testosterone.

We need to see if the testosterone-induced changes in the pelvic floor is associated with these outcomes in both groups.

The second point is that we know the role of the prostate in regulating the prostate, so we can use testosterone as a marker to determine the effect of gonadectomy on this function.

In this case, we know that in many of these patients, a significant amount of the change in the level of PSA is due to the gonadectomy, and it's also likely that this is a marker that is elevated in the majority of these patients.

If we extrapolate this to other men with pelvic floor dysfunction who have gonadectomy, it would be likely that a significant proportion of these patients will have a change in the amount of PSA due to the gonadectomy.

The other thing to note here is that this is an open label study with an unknown number of men who were followed for an average of 4 years. There may be other things going on that are not reflected in this data. There are studies that look at the prostate in those who have undergone the procedure, but we don't know what that study looked like.

If the effect on the sex organs is due to testosterone, the problem is not going to be as obvious as in this particular case.

Bottom Line

It is not unusual for women who want to be on anabolic steroids to develop pelvic floor dysfunction.

This is because the testosterone can stimulate a growth of tissue in the upper half of the body, and this leads to the development of a problem known as "pancreas insufficiency."

There is an article on the subject from the Mayo Clinic that talks about how testosterone therapy can be a good option for some women who have had pelvic floor dysfunction and want to improve their quality of life.

A team of scientists at the University of Cambridge and the Wellcome Trust Centre for AIDS Research (ICAR) have developed a protein based HIV vaccine that can be used in the developing world to prevent the virus from spreading. The research is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Using a method similar to that used in the development of the polio vaccine, the scientists in this study designed the vaccines to target the Gag protein, which is associated with the progression of HIV. The researchers believe they are on the verge of developing an effective anti-HIV vaccine that is more effective and cheaper than current treatments.

Dr. James Kornell, an assistant professor of medicine at Cambridge University, who worked on the work with Professor James Eade, a professor of molecular microbiology and immunology at the University of Cambridge, said:

"This has been a major breakthrough in the understanding of HIV. We have shown that HIV has a protein called Gag, which is responsible for HIV replication, and we now believe that Gag is a critical component of HIV vaccines. We are now focusing on using this approach to develop an effective vaccine. As well as being an innovative approach to developing vaccines for HIV, this method could be used to develop a number of other proteins, including HIV protease inhibitors. We are already working with researchers at the Wellcome Trust Centre for AIDS Research (ICAR) and the World Health Organization (WHO) to examine this vaccine concept."

Dr. Kornell added:

"Our approach to developing HIV vaccines has two important advantages over most existing treatments. First, by targeting the Gag protein, we have developed a vaccine which is less likely to cause adverse effects and that therefore may be more appealing to the poor countries in which the virus has spread. And second, by using a protein that is not currently available to treat HIV patients, we have significantly reduced the cost of the vaccine – potentially allowing poorer countries access to it. We hope that this will lead to an effective and cheaper HIV vaccine. "

"Gag" refers to the protein that forms part of the viral genome. In order to study this protein, researchers have to take advantage of the unique properties of HIV. The current best known method to study this protein is to use a virus that has been altered in some way, so that the virus has a more pronounced viral genome. When researchers take this approach, it is not possible to study the whole viral genome because it is impossible to get all the DNA out of the infected virus. Therefore, scientists have to study individual genes which are different to the standard virus and then use those genes to develop an understanding of the protein. The researchers in this study, however, have taken this approach in a different way. They have developed a 'recombinant' gene from HIV, which is used to create the Gag protein – the same protein that is used in other HIV vaccines. This method allows them to study different proteins in the virus and has the potential to develop a vaccine which is more effective, cheaper and more likely to be used in poor countries.

Dr.

The EU statistics, the European Commission's annual report on the European Union, show that illegal immigration is at an all-time high. The data published today also show that the number of asylum applications in the EU (mostly from EU member states) has risen by more than tenfold in the last seven years.

It should be noted that the EU Statistics report itself is not necessarily indicative of illegal immigration in Ireland.

What is the significance of illegal immigration in Ireland?

The EU's annual report is the biggest and most comprehensive of its kind in the world. It provides detailed information on illegal immigration at the national level and at the EU level and has been the subject of several highly-publicised reports. In the wake of the refugee crisis in 2015, the European Commission launched the Global Policing Agenda (GPAP), a strategy of tackling illegal migration across all 28 EU member states. The GPAP programme aims to improve the management of illegal migration and crime, improve the integration of irregular migrants and refugees in the EU, and support the EU member states in tackling crime.

The statistics reported in the EU's annual report are based on national statistics on crime, immigration, asylum and citizenship. Illegal immigration is not recorded separately by each EU member state, with the exception of Spain, which has taken steps to record it.

The EU statistics, however, show that illegal immigration in the EU is rising. The overall increase is significantly greater in Ireland than in all EU member states combined.

In 2014, more than 1.8 million people were living in the EU who did not have any passport or national identity card. There were 1.9 million EU citizens living in Ireland who were not citizens of any EU country, but with permanent residence or citizenship. The number of illegal immigrants, on the other hand, was much smaller.

This is a result of a number of factors. Many illegal immigrants are coming to Ireland to work or study, while others come to take advantage of generous benefits, such as free healthcare, child benefits, pensions and unemployment benefits.

The reason for this is that many EU countries also make it very difficult for illegal immigrants to apply for a passport or citizenship. If they try to do so, they face a long and drawn-out process that can take years. In Ireland, however, it can take no more than a couple of days.

There are further reasons for illegal immigration in Ireland. The majority of illegal immigrants come from countries with poor human rights records, such as Syria and Afghanistan. Illegal immigrants are often people who have been persecuted by their own governments, such as those who fled Afghanistan after the 9/11 terrorist attacks in 2001.

The most common reasons for illegal immigration in Ireland are the lack of work and education opportunities and the poverty in which many people find themselves. Most illegal immigrants come to Ireland from the most deprived countries in the world, with many coming from India and Bangladesh.

A second significant reason for illegal immigration in Ireland is that Ireland is not a member of the European Economic Area (EEA). As a result, illegal immigration from the EEA is not counted in the EU statistics, but is recorded in Ireland. It is estimated that approximately 8% of the people in Ireland are illegally in the EEA.

What are the illegal immigrants like?
headline: EU statistics reflect vastly increased levels of illegal immigration

A recent survey published in the Irish Times (17 February 2012) shows that the number of homes in the Dublin City Council has decreased by 2,821. This is due to a fall in the number of homes under construction, and a reduction in the number of new homes under construction.

The same survey, which asked households about their current dwelling and whether they were planning to buy a new one, also found that the number of single-family homes under construction (which includes houses built under the old "social housing" scheme) has increased by 3,000. This means that the number of homes under construction has increased by 9,000 homes between July 2011 and July 2012, according to the Irish Times.

The percentage of households that were planning to buy a home increased from 49.5% to 51.7% between July 2011 and July 2012. The percentage of households who are planning to buy a home will rise further as the housing crisis continues.

The current housing crisis

The Irish Times (17 February 2012) reports that a number of factors have contributed to the housing crisis. Firstly, a large number of homes have been built on sites with limited accessibility, and some of these sites are located outside of Dublin city, as we have seen, with sites outside Dublin city having a high concentration of vacant dwellings.

Second, a large number of homes have been built for families who do not live in the area. This is because the Irish State has been unable to create affordable housing. As a result, the number of households with children living in Dublin city and other areas that have a lack of affordable housing has increased. This has caused the number of households with children living in these areas to increase.

The lack of affordable housing has resulted in a shortage of affordable housing in the cities. It has also increased the number of families with children living in the cities.

In order to assist people who are in need, the Government provides a number of grants that provide housing for the under-18s, who are often the first to suffer when the local housing crisis is aggravated by the rising cost of housing.

The Department of the Environment (DoE) provides housing grants to the private sector, including private builders. This is a temporary measure and will be discontinued in 2014. The DoE also provides rent subsidies to help people pay for their housing costs.

In 2012, the DoE provided €2.5 million in funding to the construction of new homes. This funding includes grants to build new homes, as well as a number of rent subsidies.

Housing supply and demand

The Irish Times (17 February 2012) reports that, in general, the supply of new homes has increased with the fall in the number of new homes under construction. The number of existing homes under construction has also increased.

The DoE reports that, in general, the number of dwellings being built per year is higher now than in 2012, because the number of new dwellings under construction is higher. The DoE also reports that there is an increased level of demand for housing, as there are higher levels of demand for rental accommodation.

There is increased demand for housing in some areas of the country. The Irish Times (17 February 2012) reports that, according to the latest census figures, in Dublin city, the population increased by 4,000 between 2001 and 2011.
headline: The housing crisis threatening An Ghaeltacht

In a motion passed by the Dáil on Wednesday evening, the bill was passed with only one vote against, that of Seanad Éireann member Mary Lou McDonald who voted against the bill.

It passed by a vote of 59 for and 47 against with two abstentions.

Mr McDonald was the only one of the TDs present at the debate to vote against the bill, with his support coming from Fine Gael, Labour, Fianna Fáil and Sinn Féin.

"I am a very strong supporter of this bill and I hope that the House will pass it so that it can be brought to the House for a debate and hopefully to be voted upon in the Dáil as soon as possible," said Mr McDonald.

He also said he did not consider the law "unlawful" but called for further research into assisted suicide, saying the State was not equipped to deal with this case.

"The law can and has been used to help terminally ill people. People like me and those I know, who are dying, can't go through with it.

"I have not been allowed to assist anyone in the last five years and I will not be allowed to do so again," he said.

Deputy Martin McGuinness of Sinn Féin said Mr McDonald's decision to vote against the bill was "unacceptable".

He said it showed that "in this day and age of terrorism and the awful consequences of the IRA's violence" "when people in your position could say to their friends, 'you know, we'd just as soon not talk about it to anyone else because it might cause us to be labelled as terrorists'".

Mr McGuinness was speaking in the Dáil following a debate on the bill by Sinn Féin MP Eoghan Murphy, who called on the Government to make the bill an Act of Parliament, as the legal aspects of the act would be made clear.

Speaking after the debate, Mr McGuinness said it was a "mild and reasonable" act to allow a person to end their life with a doctor's prescription in Ireland, but said it did not go far enough and that the Government should act to make it an Act of Parliament.

"If the Government were to agree to this bill, they could take the legal aspects of it, such as the definition of assisted suicide out of the act," he said.

"I am not happy with it but it is a reasonable approach that is under discussion. If the Government are serious about making sure that every dying person in Ireland has the right to die with the doctor's prescription, it will be an Act of Parliament."

He added: "The Government should be willing to take this matter to an act of Parliament, whether it be in the next Dáil or in the next assembly. We need a change in the law because the people of Ireland don't want suicide to happen."

The debate, which was led by Mr Murphy, saw calls from Fine Gael deputy leader Mary Lou McDonald, and Sinn Féin's Catherine Murphy for a debate on the issue in the Seanad.

A decision on whether the bill will become law is likely to be taken within weeks.
headline: Dáil votes to accept report recommending legislating for assisted suicide

On 22nd of September 2009, a government-commissioned report was presented to Parliament in Stockholm. According to the report, the Government had adopted "a clear strategy to curb the potential threat of computer terrorism". The government has been forced to adopt a position that was "hard to square" with the report's conclusions.

The report was produced by the Swedish Security Council, a highly controversial panel. Its findings are expected to cause a stir across the country due to the political sensitivity surrounding the topic. This will be the first major political decision taken in the wake of the report.

The report was written by members of the Government Security Council. The main figure appointed to lead the Swedish Security Council is Peter Nyström, a member of the Moderate Party in the Swedish Parliament.

The report says that Sweden is at great risk of "an attack from abroad" and that its own security services are "incapable of dealing with the problem".

It is important to realise that the Government was forced to adopt a position against the report because they have to do so in response to a massive media backlash.

This issue has been under discussion in the Swedish Parliament since 2010. The Government was forced to adopt a position in order to secure support in Parliament.

What the Government report said

The Government's position:

The Government has made it clear that there is a need for a more comprehensive approach to the issue of computer-related terrorism. It has therefore commissioned a report by an organisation of highly respected academics to examine this issue. It is the belief of the Government that the report will be more than able to inform the debate in Sweden.

The key words of the report's first paragraph is:

The Swedish Security Council, the National Security Agency (Försvarets Högskolan), the Sweden Security Agency (Säpo) and the Swedish National Center for Combating Terrorism (Förenska Dagbladet) have been investigating computer-related terrorism for some time, and have concluded that the threat is high. The Government is thus not convinced that the current system is adequate, especially in terms of information sharing, or that information sharing between agencies is adequate.

It appears to be the first time the Government has directly denied that the Government, which is responsible for the current surveillance system, has any role in the assessment of whether the threat is real or not. In order to avoid any controversy, and so avoid being forced to address the report, the Government has instead released a statement. It says:

The Government is aware of the media reports, but we did not make this decision because we did not want to be accused of political interference or of interfering in the internal affairs of other Member States. In contrast, we are aware of the fact that some media reports have incorrectly characterized the findings of the security council report. We respect the democratic process. We must take into account the conclusions of the security council in Sweden. We cannot confirm or deny if the government has any part in the contents of the report.

This response is not good enough. The Government has had the opportunity to correct their position. The government is required to address this issue, or they risk being forced to admit that they were wrong about computer terrorism, which could lead to an increase in public concern.
headline: Does Sweden show we need a lockdown against the spread of government over-reach?

The Taoiseach has been very clear in his remarks about the need to ensure that these parties are in the coalition to deliver the budget.

He has made it clear that the Fianna Fáil Party cannot be part of a government which puts the economic recovery at risk.

The Taoiseach wants to ensure that the support of the Fianna Fáil Party is secured.

The Fianna Fáil leader has indicated that he would have more flexibility if the coalition agreement allows him to be part of the coalition.

The Fianna Fáil leader has also indicated that he would prefer to have his own party in coalition with Fine Gael.

But the Tánaiste has reiterated what she said in the Dáil the other day.

She is not willing to work with the Fianna Fáil Party on a deal that puts the recovery at risk.

The Fianna Fáil leader is not the only one who would be disappointed if the government fails to pass the budget.

Fine Gael's deputy leader Michael McGrath has been clear that if the coalition does not pass the budget, they will not support it in the Dáil.

McGrath has reiterated this position when asked if he would be happy with Fine Gael being in a government which does not pass the budget.

He said: "I would expect them to deliver on all their campaign promises, but it doesn't mean they can do it if they cannot do it.

"I'm very clear that I would not support a Fine Gael government which did not have the support of Fine Gael and the Labour Party."

Mr McGrath said the Government will be able to make its budget and debt resolution commitments when it is in government.
headline: Eamon O’Cuiv says: I am against this proposed coalition

The social scientists have had their day in court over their refusal to reveal their work.

The High Court has handed down a ruling that the ESRI, the Irish government and the Department of Arts, Heritage, and Gaeltacht (DAG) have to reveal any and all research that is carried out in the public interest.

This ruling was brought by a group of social scientists, led by James D. McCaffrey, a professor in the School of Government and International Studies at the University of Limerick, which has been involved in several public interest reviews and has received a total of €500,000 from ESRI and the Department of Arts, Heritage and Gaeltacht over the past 10 years.

The case was brought by Prof. McCaffrey, together with members of the Committee on Research Ethics of the Association of Research and Technology Unions (ARTDU) and members of the Irish Society of Research Ethics.

It was argued that the ESRI should release the information on all of its research into the social and economic impacts of the Common Travel Area which they have held since 2006.

The ESRI have argued that releasing the information would jeopardise their commercial relationship with the Department of Arts, Heritage and Gaeltacht and that releasing it would give the public "unacceptable" information which would not be subject to the Freedom of Information Act and which would be a "direct breach of the law".

The ESRI has also argued that releasing the information would violate the public interest and that disclosure of the information would be likely to "cause damage to the ESRI's commercial interests".

The ESRI have argued that the public interest in the release of the information would have been served by publishing the ESRI's report into the impact of the Common Travel Area on social and economic outcomes in Ireland, as well as information about their findings, including the results of the review of the Common Travel Area.

The ESRI has contended that disclosure of the report would be "unlawful" as the public interest would be served by publication of the report.

The case has been brought by the committee, the ARTDU and members of the Society of Research and Technology Unions which have raised the issue of the public interest in the release of the ESRI report.

Prof. McCaffrey and members of his group have argued that the report contains "significant and specific information" which could be used to "sabotage" their business dealings with the Department of Arts, Heritage and Gaeltacht.

The report was published in 2011, and its findings have been extensively published by the Department of Arts, Heritage and Gaeltacht, in response to public interest submissions on the Common Travel Area.

In their decision, the judges accepted that the report has "important implications" for ESRI's business interests, and concluded that the ESRI's decision to withhold the report is "not in the public interest".

Their ruling also stated that the release of the report would provide an "unacceptable" insight into the ESRI's work, and they also noted that they were not happy with the "inadequate" response from the Department of Arts, Heritage and Gaeltacht (DAG) on the issue of the report.

headline: The social scientists are doing alright: ESRI get €10 million for report

U.K. police have charged a 33-year-old Ukrainian man with assault after he allegedly attacked a man in an asylum centre.

It is alleged that the man was attacked on February 7, 2015, by Alexander Kuzmin, who was working in an accommodation centre for asylum seekers in south London.

Kuzmin was arrested by Scotland Yard's Homicide and Major Crime Command and remains in custody awaiting trial.

The man was in a critical condition when he arrived at St Thomas' Hospital, but he died two days later.

The incident is not being treated as terrorism.

The Home Office said Kuzmin was arrested in London on Thursday after the death of a man suffering from "unexplained abdominal pain".

The force's Northern Regional Organised Crime Command said the incident was reported to police in January.

The man had been sleeping on a mattress in a communal room at the centre.

He was taken by ambulance to hospital where he was treated for non-life threatening injuries.

Police said Kuzmin was an ex-Kiev employee who had worked for the Ukrainian embassy before he began working for the Home Office.

His next of kin have been informed and the man's family has been advised to make contact with police.

Det Insp Andy Blowers said: "This was a shocking incident that has left the family deeply shocked, and we have since spoken with both Mr Kuzmin and his victim to reassure them of the safety of both."

He went on: "We would like to reassure the public that if anyone has any concerns for anyone else, we encourage them to contact us."
headline: Ukrainian charged in connection with fatal assault on man in asylum centre

In a move that will impact thousands of travelers and their families travelling to the United States, the United States Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) announced today that the Canadian government will no longer require foreign travelers to be vaccinated against human papillomavirus (HPV) by the time they arrive at Canadian ports of entry.

"This is a significant step towards reducing the number of people who travel to the U.S. and Canada by not vaccinating against diseases that are easily acquired and spread at foreign ports of entry. This policy change also helps to protect the U.S. from the threat of additional outbreaks of disease like whooping cough and hepatitis B, which are often spread from infected travelers to Americans abroad. In fact, this change ensures that Americans traveling to Canada can continue to go through the same customs screening procedures as other foreign travelers, without fear of being diagnosed with a disease that can be easily prevented by the vaccination of the traveler's child," said Dr. Robert L. Siegel, MD, President of the American Academy of Pediatrics.

"It is vital to vaccinate travelers against serious diseases that can be transmitted from person to person, and prevent them from getting infected with an infectious disease in the first place. With the increase in travel to the U.S., and the increase in vaccine-preventable disease, travel is the most effective way to prevent those diseases from spreading throughout the country."

Since its introduction in 2007, when the HPV vaccine was first introduced in the United States, it has been estimated that as many as 500,000 females have been exposed to HPV. Approximately 12,000 new cases of HPV-related diseases are diagnosed in the U.S. each year, and HPV infections cause more than 1,000 deaths in the U.S. each year.

In January, CDC announced it would no longer recommend the HPV vaccine for women ages 9-26 who are not married or currently sexually active.

However, the National HPV Vaccine Advisory Committee (NVAC) of the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Academy of Family Physicians, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the American Cancer Society continue to recommend the HPV vaccine for women ages 9-26.

If a child is traveling to the United States, they are required by law to be vaccinated against HPV.

The announcement by the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) follows a recommendation by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), a panel of experts from the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA). The IDSA recommended last year that parents, students and workers travel in groups so that everyone can be vaccinated.

"The vaccination of travelers at airports is not a solution, but is an important component to reducing the risk of illness at the border," said Dr. Joseph W. Rose, MD, a professor in the division of Pediatric Infectious Diseases at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and an author of the ACIP recommendation.

"There are very few cases of infection that are not preventable with vaccination. A child infected in the United States cannot travel abroad for an unvaccinated child, but a traveler who is not immunized can have a serious reaction to the vaccine, or develop the disease, and then be vulnerable to spread."
headline: Canada finally drops Covid vaccine requirement for entry at border

It has been revealed that Fianna Fáil's Cllr Seán Kelly has resigned from his position after he wrote an article criticising immigration policy.

"I want to thank the party for the opportunity I've had to serve as a Member of the Seanad for the past two and a half years. I will be retiring from the Seanad in the coming weeks," Kelly wrote in his resignation letter on Friday.

"I have had the great privilege of representing the people of Dublin on the Seanad. It has been an honour and a privilege to have served the people of this area and the party has given me this opportunity."

"However, given that my time on the Seanad is coming to a close, I have a personal and professional responsibility to resign from the Seanad," he wrote.

In his resignation letter, the former Fianna Fáil minister said he had decided to resign from the Seanad "in order to allow for more time to address my personal and professional obligations".

He added that it was also "due to the fact that I have made a personal decision regarding my future and am unable to continue the work I have undertaken on behalf of the party and its members for more than two and a half years.

"It is also on this basis that I have decided to resign from the Seanad".

In his resignation letter, Kelly said he did not consider the recent criticism from Fine Gael leader Micheál Martin that the party could never have a policy that was similar to the Coalition Government's as an opportunity to speak out.

"I do not believe that this is an opportunity for a politician to speak out on a policy that does not exist in any of the parties," he said.

"I do believe that what the members of the party want to see in this country and they want to see in this government is a government that works for them. In order to be able to work for the people of this country, the people of this country want to see a government that makes the decisions, that gets the country back on the track it should be on in terms of economic growth and jobs and prosperity," he said.

"I believe that it is my duty to speak out on this point. I do not believe this is an opportunity for me to speak out on anything that I believe to be a personal decision that I have taken in the best interests of the party and its members, but I would say that on this one thing, the party leadership has shown an utter lack of accountability to the party."

Kelly said he believed that his comments in the article were unfair and "unfortunate". He said he was not being "political" but it was still a personal decision to step down.

"I have a responsibility to the party and to my colleagues at Fianna Fáil, the people of Ireland and to the country as a whole. I want to be able to spend time with my family and do other things," he said.
headline: Fianna Fáil Cllr who criticised immigration policy resigns, says party “detached from ordinary person”

The European Commission has published a recommendation to use the COVID Pass Sequel for online censorship on the Internet. The Commission has submitted a technical report to the EU Parliament, the Council and the European Commission on the use of COVID in European Union (EU) legislation.

The Commission's technical report makes clear that, if adopted, the COVID Pass Sequel would have a significant impact on online freedom of expression and the ability to monitor and regulate content in a timely manner. The Commission has noted that some EU Member States currently require sites to obtain access to legal content through legally binding legal obligations. If the COVID Pass Sequel is adopted, this would mean EU Member States would have the legal authority to order online censorship on the grounds of criminal liability, as defined in the EU Treaties.

The COVID Pass Sequel would also affect the ability of European courts to regulate the right to privacy and to protect freedom of expression.

The European Commission is also asking for more information about the specific legal framework for the COVID Pass Sequel.

The Commission is also seeking comments from stakeholders on the potential impact of COVID on EU lawmaking.

Background

The Commission is in the process of preparing the European Communications Directive. The Commission has consulted civil society in an effort to gain expert advice on how a COVID Pass Sequel might be implemented.

The Commission is seeking views from stakeholders before publishing the COVID Pass Sequel Technical Report.

What is COVID?

COVID stands for "Cross-border Internet Copyright Transparency". The COVID Pass Sequel is a framework for online censorship that would prevent sites from receiving access to legally-binding legal content (such as copyright) or requiring access to lawfully-owned content (such as personal data). The COVID Pass Sequel would only apply if a site is determined to be in breach of the law or is in danger of becoming so. This means that sites that are in breach of the law, are in danger of becoming so, or are in danger of becoming so through illegal activities, will not be able to access legal content or need to obtain access through legal means.

The COVID Pass Sequel would only apply if a site is determined to be in breach of the law or is in danger of becoming so.

Under the COVID Pass Sequel, a site would need to obtain access to the legally-binding content or legal content would need to be made available on an open source basis from a publicly accessible source (such as the COVID Open Source Repository).

The COVID Pass Sequel would not apply if:

The site is the subject of a legal case, such as an infringement or criminal conviction.

The site is the subject of a decision by a court, such as a preliminary injunction, a preliminary injunction application or a judicial review.

The site has the same content rights as other websites.

The site is the subject of a request from a third party.

The site is a recipient of EU funding.

The site is in the public interest, for example as a journalism outlet, a media partner of a non-profit organization or an educational institution.

The site is in the public interest as a news website or a discussion forum.

The site is in the public interest as a source of information about information security.
headline: EU to Use COVID Pass Sequel for Online Censorship

Irish Department of Justice and Equality has been working with airlines to reduce the problem of false documents, it has been revealed.

In a meeting at the end of March, the department agreed to work with airlines to deal with the situation.

The department, which is responsible for the regulation and enforcement of consumer law, had a long-standing complaint in relation to the issue of falsified documents which had arisen by airline passengers.

It was confirmed that airline passengers had filed complaints with the department, but was unable to determine how many of these had subsequently been resolved and how many had not.

"We are pleased that they will now be referred to the airline and we have agreed to work with them to address these problems and ensure that no more false documents are presented to passengers," said Minister for Equality Mary Mitchell O'Connor in a statement.

"I would encourage all airline passengers to contact their airline directly as there is no legal obligation on airlines to remove passengers from their aircraft for non-payment of tax.

"We are also delighted that airlines will be working with us to ensure that any such documents are not presented to passengers, as such a practice can cause harm to airline passengers, their families, staff and the general public," said Minister for Justice and Equality Mary Mitchell O'Connor in a statement.

Airlines are known to change their procedures to make sure that passengers can be satisfied in order for them to continue travelling.

However, Irish Independent columnist Eoin O'Donoghue was disappointed that the department had agreed to a deal with the airlines.

"I don't think it was done on the basis that we should be able to get more money out of the airline industry, but the airlines will be working to ensure that it is not possible, especially in case they are making passengers pay for the additional services," he said.

However, the airlines have not been able to confirm that their procedures have changed.

"It is the department's role to deal with the problem, and we have an obligation to work with the airlines in such a way that we do not create additional expense for the state, or that the airlines are taking away any other services they might otherwise provide to passengers," said Air Ireland spokesperson John Mullin.

The Department for Social Protection said it had not responded to a request for comment at this stage.
headline: Dept engaging with 19 airlines to address false documents scandal

China has allegedly been preparing to betray the Vatican deal signed with Pope Francis, according to the leading Italian news outlet, Gript (gript.ie). The article, which was first translated by the author (Lorenzo S. Pinto) and published by Gript (gript.ie) was written by the journalist Marco Zingaretti, who first discovered the document and later took a screenshot of it.

Article:

A report published on Sunday claimed that the Vatican is planning to cut off its support to the Vatican's "new initiative" for the development of a common religious and spiritual space.

The report claims that Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Tarcisio Bertone and Bishop Marcelo Sánchez Sorondo, the Vatican's representative for the initiative, are facing criticism from conservative cardinals who are upset about the deal between the two.

It is now being speculated that the Vatican could abandon its efforts to build a common religious and spiritual space in China, which is believed to have been the Vatican's second biggest diplomatic asset after the United States.

According to Gript (gript.ie), Bertone and Sorondo have been pressured by the Vatican's "new initiative" advisors to drop their previous plans to build a new spiritual center in Tibet, and to stop building a hospital in the village of Dali-Lah in China's Gansu province.

The plan was announced by Cardinal Tarcisio Bertone in February this year, with the intention to create a "new spiritual center" in the remote village of Dali-Lah. It was hoped that the project would bring the Holy See closer to the Tibetan diaspora, in addition to providing a spiritual space to promote the Catholic Church abroad.

It should be noted that the Vatican has been trying to bring Tibet to closer union with the Vatican since at least 2009, when Bertone initiated negotiations for the establishment of a "Catholic Dialogue Centre" to coordinate the Vatican's activities in Tibet.

However, the Dalai Lama has stated that the Vatican has always been a distant second to him and has always treated the Vatican as a "strategic partner".

Since 2009, the Vatican has been in negotiations with the Tibetans for the establishment of a new religious center, though there have not been any concrete developments in this field since.

However, a report in Italian newspaper, La Stampa (www.stampa.it), has stated that the Vatican has decided to abandon its plans for the creation of a new religious center in Dali-Lah.

It is reported that Vatican diplomats in Rome have made contact with Tibetan officials, expressing a desire to make a new agreement, which would "allow the Vatican to work in a more cooperative manner with the Dalai Lama's Chinese counterparts, in particular in the area of Tibetan culture."

This new agreement "is to be concluded within two years," reports La Stampa, and it is hoped that the Vatican will resume its previous efforts to establish a spiritual center in China.

The Chinese embassy in Rome did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.
headline: “Slap in the face”: China to reportedly betray Vatican deal

"Russian air-launched cruise missile Sakhalin (P-800) has hit a residential building in Romania. The owner of the building was not injured.

The missile hit the building at around 9:00 pm on Thursday, March 8 in the town of Cercin-Caiul, located in the southeast of the country."

Background:

On June 4, 2015, Russia's RIA Novosti news agency reported that "a Russian plane flying from Romania to Syria [was] shot down by Turkey." The report stated:

"The aircraft was flying at an altitude of 2,000 meters (7,300 feet) over a Syrian territory that is under the control of the Syrian regime. According to a military source, the aircraft was downed by a surface-to-air missile fired by a Syrian government fighter. In accordance with international law, such a strike by Turkey would be a flagrant violation of the Syrian sovereignty. Moreover, this incident follows another Turkish air force strike on the Syrian territory that killed more than 40 people."

In response to the RIA Novosti report, the US State Department stated:

"We strongly condemn this attack on a civilian aircraft."

The US Embassy in Bucharest, Bucharest, Romania stated:

"The Embassy strongly condemns this unacceptable attack on a civilian aircraft and we express our condolences to the family and friends of those killed and injured. We are actively working with our NATO allies and partners to determine the facts surrounding this incident."

In the same statement, NATO stated:

"NATO strongly condemns this unacceptable attack on a civilian aircraft. This attack is a clear violation of Turkish and international law and a flagrant violation of the sovereignty of Turkey, as well as a violation of the principles of international humanitarian law. Turkey's continued violations of these principles have nothing to do with international law."

This incident comes on the heels of a series of strikes by Russian aircraft on military targets in Syria. Russia claims that its warplanes are targeting Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL) terrorists.
