It's a big day for Hillary Clinton in Belfast.

As she addressed the American Jewish Committee's conference in Belfast on Wednesday, the former Democratic presidential nominee was heckled during an interview about Trump.

In her address to the AICC, Mrs Clinton was greeted with a standing ovation.

"No other candidate for the presidency or the US presidency is going to make me prouder than Hillary Clinton," said AICC President Steven Goldstein.

"She'll be just as determined and she'll be just as prepared, in fact she's already made history in her own right."

Mrs Clinton said that since the election she has been "in hiding".

"I have had to stop and look at what I need to do to be prepared for the work ahead. I have been in hiding for a couple of weeks. I'm going to be a strong president."

She said that the first order of business was to try to help US allies.

"I have a tremendous respect for the UK and its great people," Mrs Clinton added.

"I wish them well. I have no illusions about the challenge they face, but I also have no illusions about the opportunities that lie ahead."

The audience at the conference applauded Mrs Clinton's optimism.

"I'll be working with them as I have to work with everybody," she said.

"I hope we can make progress on every issue, but I also know that we've got to make sure that we're all on the same page as we make progress."

She said that her opponent, Donald Trump, and his rhetoric would divide the country.

"Our country will heal, we will heal together and we will be stronger together."

Image: The former Democratic presidential nominee will be addressing the American Jewish Committee conference

She said that while there will be differences, there are also lessons to learn from past mistakes.

"I do think it is important that we learn lessons from the past, especially on the most divisive issue of the last year."

"I think it is important that we learn that we are all people, and we have to look forward to the future together."

Mrs Clinton's speech came after Trump warned that "we will stop this madness" of immigration and "get our country back".

His comments came in an interview with the Washington Post, which quoted him as saying: "We have to have a much tougher immigration policy."

But he told the newspaper that while he might soften his hardline stance on immigration, he would deport "bad dudes".

He added: "The problem is that people come from all over and they do bad things."

It is not the first time Mrs Clinton has been heckled.

Last year, during a rally in the state of New Hampshire, a demonstrator interrupted her speech and was escorted out by police.

The Irish Health Service Executive has confirmed it has started an external review into the treatment of women who had abortions in Ireland.

The review was initiated by HSE earlier this year following media reports of a woman who had misdiagnosed as having a severe brain tumour after having an abortion in Ireland.

The HSE said it will work closely with the Department of Health and the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority to ensure the outcome of the review is positive.

"This review is the first step towards ensuring that women have the best possible care when they seek medical intervention to terminate their pregnancy. Our approach will be focused on the most appropriate treatment of the woman, and not on the circumstances of the abortion," said Dr Peter McLoughlin, senior health services executive at the HSE.

"It is unacceptable that women in Ireland are having to endure unnecessarily long and intrusive consultations with professionals in order to make the most of their choices. This review is one part of our ongoing effort to ensure women and their partners have a good experience with our medical services."

Source: Gript.ie

What is the HSE's position on abortions and miscarriages in Ireland?

The Irish Health Service Executive (HSE) has taken a very robust stance on abortion issues. HSE policy is clear: women who have an abortion or miscarriage must be supported to carry their pregnancy to term in a health facility and receive full health care.

Under the Abortion Act 1968, the HSE provides support for abortions and provides full medical support for all women who have been diagnosed with a pregnancy that could be affected by fatal abnormalities. The Act also requires that, if a woman wishes to end her pregnancy, she is able to do so in a health facility that is licensed by the Health Services Executive.

The HSE's position on abortion in Ireland is as follows:

"The position of the HSE in regard to the termination of pregnancy is that it is a matter for the woman who has the pregnancy, who has informed her health care provider, her partner or the courts, or the medical professional, to decide whether or not she wishes to continue with the pregnancy."

What is the HSE's position on abortion cases and abortion in general?

The HSE is not in a position to comment on individual cases. The HSE strongly believes that abortions should be a personal decision between a woman and her medical provider, who is responsible for her health.

The HSE has taken the position that when a woman seeks an abortion, she should be provided with full and accurate information and assistance in making this decision. In particular, women in Ireland who have been diagnosed with a severe genetic abnormality, for example, are advised that the decision to continue with pregnancy should be made by the woman's own health care provider, who is her own health care provider.

In order to facilitate full and accurate assessment and diagnosis of the woman's condition, we strongly recommend that she receive the services of a qualified medical professional. This is important for the woman to consider carefully, to ensure that the best outcome is achieved for her.

The HSE does not believe that the termination of pregnancy is an individual and personal decision, but it is a medical treatment to which all women, regardless of the type of abortion procedure they have had, should be subjected.
headline: HSE confirms external review into abortion misdiagnosis case

Irish girl who was brutally raped will be released from prison this week

By Glynis McShane

Irish Independent (Dublin) 29 Jan 2010

After years in prison, the girl who was brutally raped at 14 will walk out of prison in the coming weeks.

The girl, who had been in and out of the Dublin Children's Court for 15 years, was cleared at a hearing yesterday of rape at the time.

She was also cleared of the attempted rape of another girl who is 14 years younger.

Her lawyers argued the girl was being falsely accused by her former family, who were also the accused in other cases.

The rape trial of a 14-year-old girl in Dublin's Drogheda District Court has been adjourned for the weekend after the girl's mother, in tears, appeared outside court today.

"We are delighted with the acquittal today, but there are still some details to be settled", said the mother, who cannot be named for legal reasons.

The case began with the girl appearing before the Drogheda District Court in May, accused of the attempted rape of a girl of 14 years.

The girl was accused of two counts of rape, one count of the attempted rape and one count of the unlawful wounding of a person.

The girl was granted bail and the case was adjourned.

The court heard the girl was 14 when she was first assaulted.

The girl's father was initially involved in the case.

He has since been identified as Joseph Connolly, 58, from Waterford, who lives in Co Galway.

The prosecution says the father was charged with the attempted rape in March 2005.

The girl was charged with the rape on the same date.

The trial resumed last May after the father agreed to undergo a psychiatric assessment following a mental health assessment.

However, the girl's mother intervened and the case was adjourned to Friday to allow for the mother to attend the evaluation.

Her solicitor said the girl was distraught following the adjournment.

"She's absolutely devastated. This has been the hardest thing she's ever done.

"She has been treated in a very hostile environment and she's been subjected to violence and threats of violence.

"They were told she wouldn't be allowed to see anyone for a number of months after the trial and they kept making threats to her".

The mother said she was told that a statement would be taken on the 12th of December.

However, she said she never received any information about the matter.

"The mother went to court because she felt she was treated in a very unfair way by the courts".

The mother said she has yet to receive any information about the case.

"She's been under the impression it was all being dropped, that they were dropping the charges, that the charges were going to be dropped, but in fact nothing has been dropped at all."

However, there was a change of heart yesterday when the DPP and a number of police officers attended the Drogheda District Court to observe the case.

An announcement on the court's website yesterday said the court had accepted the family's plea to dismiss the charges and that the girl would be released on Monday.

Grenfell has become a "giant social media-storm", with the suicide toll rising, while the Department of Social Protection (DoSP) has launched a massive media campaign to warn the public about the dangers of self-harm and suicidal behaviour.

The Department of Social Protection, and the Irish Police, have been inundated with calls from concerned members of the public with concerns about the safety of themselves and their loved ones in the city.

Last night, the Department's suicide prevention helpline recorded 476 calls over the last 24 hours, with a further 12 calls received in the first 24 hours after the tragedy took place.

The highest number of calls recorded by the DoSP suicide prevention helpline was from a young girl in Dublin 11, while the number of calls received by the emergency call centre was significantly lower in Dublin 8 and Dublin 12.

The most recent figures show that 476 calls were received by the suicide prevention helpline in the period from 1pm to 3pm.

Some of the most popular calls were from women and men who said they had been worried about their safety following the tragedy.

One caller to the Suicide Prevention Helpline said:

"I'm so worried and worried… I'm afraid my friend is going to kill herself and I don't know what I'm going to do. I'm just going to stay in the house until the police come, then I'm going to call the emergency number and try to get help."

Another caller said:

"I've just had a conversation with my brother, he asked me if I know anything about this because he said he heard the news from the radio and said he heard my sister is seriously depressed. He said he was at the station and he heard a woman screaming and said 'I'll kill myself'. I said, 'Yeah but can I call you in case it's an emergency?'"

At 3am, the DoSP sent out a tweet urging people not to call the suicide helpline if they felt frightened, but to call the ambulance in case of emergency.

A statement from the Department of Social Protection said the "great outpouring of support and sympathy" for the deceased in Grenfell Tower showed that they were doing everything they could to help.

The department confirmed that it had launched a major media campaign to encourage people to stay safe in the city, where people are often at risk of being confronted by their own emotions.

"The Department is actively engaging the public in the issue of suicide and we are reminding people to remain calm and avoid contact with those with suicidal thoughts," said the statement. "We have also launched a new social media campaign to help people stay safe in the city. We hope the campaign will provide a wake-up call to people living and working in the city and we encourage anyone with concerns to contact their local police or social welfare department."

A Department of Social Protection spokesperson said that, as part of its work with the Department of Health, it has launched a "Safe Communities Program" to provide a safer place for people in Dublin.

"People experiencing suicidal thoughts should contact their GP or another healthcare provider and seek immediate help," she said. "When you call our suicide prevention helpline you can talk to a trained trained support worker, who can give you a range of helpful support.

"I was shocked, the man was lying there with his hands raised. He was quite pale, his trousers were open. His legs were in the air and he appeared to have been shot in the chest and it looked like he had just suffered an injury to his stomach."

"I've lived in the area for 30 years and this is the first time I've heard of something like this happening," he said.

text:
The author of this article (and the author of all of the blog posts above) is a Professor at the University of Limerick.

Background

In 2006, a report (pdf) released by the Office for National Statistics showed that the wages of women in their first year of employment, after controlling for experience, was 2.9% higher than the wages of men. The report was met with considerable criticism as a result, and the OBR (2005) examined the reasons for this discrepancy.

The following is a quotation from the report.

While there may be small variations between industries and occupations, there is a large difference in the wage distribution in relation to experience. For example, in the first year of employment, women on average earn 1.6% less than men who have the same experience. The higher average is not only explained by differences in the number of years since graduation from school, or the gender composition of the workforce, but by the fact that women tend to start their careers at lower rates of wage growth than men.

The OBR analysed over 16 years of data, and looked at whether there was a link between higher salaries and higher experience, which the authors stated was "clearly true".

The conclusion that the OBR came to is that the higher the number of years since graduation from school, the higher the wage gap in that first year. It concluded that the link between higher wages and higher experience was a problem in the UK.

However, this is not at all clear from this study, which uses one small set of data. There are over 5.8 million people in the UK working, of whom 1.8 million have more than five years of experience, 1.2 million have fewer than five years of experience, and 672,000 have no experience at all.

The authors state that "the gap between the wages of men and women for this data set is quite large, in the range of 10.1% – 17.4% of wage differences."

However, they then compare the experience of different groups, and in doing so use numbers from just one year of data. This is not a valid comparison, as the OBR themselves state:

We found no link between gender and experience in the most recent year, which is a major limitation of using data on graduates to compare men and women. For example, as Figure 1 shows, women in our sample have a much higher earnings growth rate than men who have the same experience. However, the difference in the difference between men and women is not large, and the data set only covers the first year of employment. These large differences could also be explained by differential skills and experience across occupations. It is possible that experience and skills are not directly related to pay, and that one's skills could have an effect but is not enough to explain the earnings differences.

(The OBR 2005 report also used data from one year, which may be the best comparison, but it fails to address the issue of gender bias in the data used. In particular, women may work more in certain occupations than men, but the wage gap could have been smaller if there was a much more equal distribution of experience across occupations).

The OBR concluded:

Our study does not support the conclusion that women have a lower wage growth rate.
headline: Regina Doherty revives feminist pay gap myth

The European Commission has today announced the launch of its Democracy Shield initiative to promote the protection of the rights of individuals in the EU member states to a wide range of critical online information and culture.

The initiative is based on the 'European Framework of Rights' (EURO), and includes both citizens' rights and democratic structures.

With the launch of the initiative, the Commission will help citizens, companies and civil society organisations in each member state to take more effective steps to protect and promote their rights online.

It will also help them to develop and implement digital strategies, in particular to promote the 'Right to be Forgotten' (RIP) where they are required to remove information they no longer need.

The EU is currently implementing a range of rights-respecting and effective measures to protect the rights of citizens online. This includes the Right to be Forgotten (RIP), and a range of measures in relation to the protection of personal data.

The EURO Directive on data protection and the Right to be Forgotten (RIP) will be implemented in 2014.

The Commission will continue to work closely with Member States to further enhance the protection of the online information and culture.

The Commission hopes that the launch of the Democracy Shield initiative will help the citizens and civil society organisations to raise awareness of the online rights they have.

Background

The Democracy Shield initiative was initiated by the EC in March 2013. The objective of the initiative is to encourage and facilitate the promotion of the protection of rights online.

The EU launched a European Framework of Rights in January 2014 under the title 'European Framework of Rights' (EDR), which includes both citizens' rights and democratic structures. The framework builds upon the existing 'Right to be Forgotten', 'Right to be Forgotten' and 'Right to have my private data erased' schemes.

In addition, the EDR provides for the right to be forgotten, as well as the right to have your personal data erased without your knowledge.

The Commission has also released a consultation on the use of 'memorandum of understanding' (MOU) between the Commission and the European Parliament in relation to the implementation of the EDR. The MOU outlines a number of important steps to be taken to support online rights protection and promote their implementation.

The Commission has also launched a consultation on the implementation of the EDR with member states on an even higher level, asking them to develop a digital strategy for online rights protection. The EU will consider all relevant proposals from member states on this initiative to be developed and implemented in accordance with their national law and the EU law on data protection.

The EU Charter of Fundamental Rights provides for the right of free expression, association and privacy, as well as the protection of freedom of peaceful assembly.
headline: European Commission announces ‘Democracy Shield’

An Irish abortion provider has been left angry after his account was included in a news article about an online harassment campaign that targeted a GP.

Dr Peter Kelleher, who runs the abortion services at Monaghan's Mona Point Clinic, was one of a number of prominent figures targeted by a group of anonymous internet users over the weekend, following the controversial decision by the Irish High Court to uphold the termination of a 17-year-old girl's pregnancy.

In what has been described as a "heinous abuse", the girl's parents were also included in the article, with the letter "I love you and your baby" read out in their names.

The website The Daily Mail published the article on Sunday night.

"I was shocked when it was published and felt compelled to write to clarify the circumstances," Dr Kelleher told the Irish Independent.

"The article is inaccurate and doesn't accurately represent the situation. I feel it should not have been published."

He added that he had been in contact with the newspaper since the article was published.

"I have also spoken to The Irish Independent and the paper has confirmed that the details of my account have been fully verified," he said.

The article refers to Dr Kelleher as "Dr H", a reference to the name of the clinic. The Daily Mail, in its article, is also claiming that it has verified details of the girl's account.

Dr Kelleher said that his first instinct was to contact the newspaper to say that they had misrepresented his account.

"I felt very much in shock that the article had been published," he said. "It's an obvious mistake. It's been edited out."

"But after speaking with the Irish Independent and the paper, we have come to the same conclusion as the journalist of how it happened," he added.

The Daily Mail has refused to comment on Dr Kelleher's allegations.

Online harassment campaign

The online harassment campaign against the abortion doctor, which is still ongoing, has continued on Monday morning.

The woman who began the online campaign, Claire Heneghan, posted a picture of Dr Kelleher with a quote from the "Auschwitz code" online, in which it states that "never mind whether we're in Auschwitz, no-one can change the truth".

The internet user, who went by the online handle "Omgiwr" - a reference to the acronym "On Her Back", was quoted by the Irish Independent as having said: "He has not been harassed at all. She is not a liar. Her story is false. There is no one on earth who is capable of anything but lies."

"I've had quite a bit of threatening phone calls. I'm still dealing with it," Dr Kelleher said.

Online abuse campaign

Online abuse has continued, with a number of prominent figures including actress Tilda Swinton, musician Lady Gaga, and actor Matt LeBlanc, among others, having their personal details published.

Other people have been targeted by the online campaign, with the Daily Mail using a post containing an address as part of the article.

The publication has also been contacted by Dr Kelleher's client, who is now considering whether to press charges.
headline: Abortion doctor provides no tangible evidence of harassment claim

The head of the Disability Rights Association (DRA) says they will file a suit on behalf of terminally ill people against the California State Department of Corrections (CDOC), which, they claim, is not helping them.

In an exclusive interview with Disability Rights Today (DRT), Stephen Smith, a senior research fellow, said the group believes that the California Department of Corrections (CDOC) is "doing nothing" to help people with disabilities when it comes to assisted suicide.

"I can understand the motivation for having the assisted suicide law – to help people who are so far away from being able to do it. However, it's not a good fit with the rights of terminally ill people who are on the verge of death," Smith said.

"You don't need a licence to kill someone," he added. "A lot of people may be in a desperate situation and they will use whatever means necessary to get the end of their suffering, rather than be able to end it when they get the end of their suffering."

The DRT is the national organisation representing persons with disabilities, and is responsible for developing and promoting the rights of those with disabilities. The DRT claims that the CDOC is "not taking an active role in the care of the terminally ill", and says that the CDOC is "far more interested in collecting money from the very wealthy" than helping terminally ill people.

"We don't need to get lawyers and we don't need to be expensive lawyers, but that is exactly what the CDOC is doing," Smith said. "They are collecting huge amounts of money from the very wealthy for the state, and they are doing this in a way that is not only illegal, but in a way that doesn't help people," he said.

"The problem with this whole situation is that the CDOC is being so out of touch with their role in society," Smith explained.

He said that the CDOC is not only out of touch with the lives of terminally ill people, it is also failing to provide sufficient support for those who need it the most.

"The state is using its money to help people who are struggling, not to help those who are suffering from a terminal disease," Smith said.

The DRT's lawsuit states that the CDOC is "not meeting its statutory responsibilities" in "helping the severely ill with access to life-ending treatment". The lawsuit also alleges that the CDOC has failed to "provide sufficient access to all terminally ill prisoners to ensure the right to assisted suicide".

A spokesman for the CDOC said in an emailed statement:

"The CDOC has consistently maintained a commitment to assisting people with disabilities, including assisted suicide. We continue to work hard on this issue and are committed to ensuring that all terminally ill people receive the care and support they need."

The CDOC says that the lawsuit is without merit and is without legal effect.

Smith says that the DRT "won't put up with this crap any longer".

"The state has a responsibility to help the terminally ill, but they aren't doing it," he said. "And they're not doing it for people who need it the most."

The DRT is seeking damages of €2.5 million.
headline: Disability rights groups launch lawsuit to quash California’s assisted suicide law

Sunday, January 18th, 2005

The European Commission has revealed that it has been told by oil companies that EU regulations would force them to cut consumption of natural gas for the next ten years.

The report states that companies such as BP, Shell and Total are already feeling the pinch, as the companies have already been told by regulators that if they do not cut gas consumption by 30% by 2020, they will have to pay a fine of up to €150m, or about €1bn.

The Commission has been unable to respond to the Commission's investigation and a decision on further action was not possible yesterday.

A majority of EU Member States are moving further to the right, according to a new survey, according to the findings of a recent poll.

The study by Ipsos-Mori showed that 49 percent of those surveyed, and 59 percent of those in the UK (35 percent of those surveyed) considered the EU to be "going in the right direction".

Among those in the US, the majority (62 percent) consider that the EU has moved to the right, while 61 percent of those surveyed in Germany and 62 percent in France considered the EU to be going in the wrong direction.

In the UK, the poll also showed that the majority (56 percent) think that the British Government is in favour of the EU.

The survey showed that the right-wing Conservative Party has increased its vote share in the EU referendums in France and in the UK since the 2012 referendum on EU membership.

On the contrary, the Eurosceptic anti-EU UKIP has seen its vote share fall after the UK vote to leave the EU. In 2014, UKIP secured only 15 percent of the vote and in the 2015 referendum it received 16.5 percent.
headline: Is Europe really shifting to the right?

The Minister for Justice said yesterday that he has "absolutely no doubt" that three persons are responsible for the deaths of two children and the wounding of three others in the Glenanne incident in Dublin this morning.

The Department of Justice has today released a report in the Dáil concerning the Glenanne gang incident which took place this morning. The report is the result of an investigation into the events of this morning following the police presence at the scene for several hours.

Minister of State for Justice Frances Fitzgerald said that she has "absolutely no doubt" that three persons are responsible for the deaths of two children and the wounding of three others in the Glenanne incident in Dublin this morning.

In the statement to Dáil Éireann, Minister Fitzgerald said the DPP has taken the matter very seriously and has asked that the investigation be widened by the gardaí and the Department of Justice to cover the circumstances surrounding the deaths and injuries of two children and the wounding of three others on Saturday, May 21st in the Glenanne area of Dublin.

The Department of Justice is cooperating with the gardaí in the matter, she said.

In a statement issued yesterday, the Taoiseach made reference to the "disturbing reports of an Garda investigation into the Glenanne gang attack and a number of arrests."

Mr Kenny said that he was "deeply concerned" about the reports made in the Dáil and the "grave consequences this may have for the lives of the victims and their families and the health and wellbeing of the community".

He said that the Government is now taking steps to ensure that the Gardaí are provided with the resources they need and that the Minister for Justice is given the authority to continue investigating the matters raised by the Taoiseach.

He said that the Government is "seeking to ascertain whether any further criminal proceedings should be brought in relation to the attack", but stressed that "the Taoiseach has asked Minister Fitzgerald to provide him with all the necessary resources to ensure that any further criminal proceedings are brought".

The Taoiseach said that the Taoiseach has asked to speak with the Minister for Children and Youth Affairs Brendan Howlin about the matters raised in the Dáil and is awaiting a response.

Mr Kenny said that he was also awaiting an answer from the Minister for Health James Reilly, as he is currently under a Dáil privilege order.

The Minister for Health said that he had had a positive meeting with Minister Fitzgerald today at which they discussed the matter.

Speaking at a press conference at the department of justice, Mr Howlin said that he had been told that the Minister for Children and Youth Affairs was not aware of any investigation into the attack.

He said he had also been told that he was not requested to attend a meeting at the department of justice where the Minister for Justice was informed of the incident.

"At no time was any request made to any member of the DPP's or the Garda Síochána's office by the Department of Justice in relation to this matter or any other investigation regarding any aspect of the incident," he said.

Mr Howlin said that he had been told that he was not informed of the matter because he had been advised to remain in his home in the Dáil.

'Tractors are here to stay', says Dublin farmer

A group of farmers and local residents are calling for thousands of tractors to be imported into Ireland after a new survey shows that more than half of them will not be used by consumers in the next three years.

The Irish Farmers' Union (IFAU), which is representing the majority of farmers, is calling on the government to act to ensure that farmers' produce is processed into products to be consumed within the EU.

The EU is the world's largest producer of foods and beverages. It is the dominant producer of agricultural and forestry products in the world.

An estimated 90 per cent of the food produced by Ireland is exported.

The EPCAT report, which surveyed 10,000 farmers, also found that 50 per cent of the tractors in use within the EU were imported, with the largest numbers coming from Bulgaria, Croatia and Slovenia.

In addition, a quarter of the tractors surveyed would not be used for the next three years.

"This is a real threat to the future of our farmers and the future of the Irish countryside," said IFAU chairman John MacQuaid.

"We have to protect our farmers. We have to protect our food production, and the Irish economy too. We will not be able to produce the food that is required to feed our citizens in the future without our farmers."

The EPCAT report says that one in three of the tractors surveyed in Ireland would not be used for the next three years.

"We need to ensure the future of our food production. We have to protect our farmers," said IFAU representative Frank Breen.

"We are in a global competition, we are all competing for the world's supply of food. It is important that we secure the future of our food production."

The IFAU has been lobbying hard to secure the export of large tractors to Ireland.

"The international transport of agriculture equipment is crucial to the global food supply chain," said Mr Breen.

"If we export our tractors, we will benefit from the growing use of low cost vehicles and engines in low-cost countries, making them more competitive with other countries in global markets.

"In addition, these tractors are highly dependable, and are also an efficient use of our scarce water. The European Union has already legislated that these tractors should not be used for more than two years.

"IFAU will continue to lobby for the export of large tractors to Ireland."

The EPCAT report also found that of the 7,500 farms surveyed, 1,200 were not in use. The remaining 6,000 were in use but with no vehicles.

The survey has raised questions about the adequacy of the national infrastructure for the transport of agricultural equipment. It also revealed that around half of farmers were planning to increase the number of tractors used in the next three years.

The research was carried out for the EPCAT report, which is expected to be released next week.

EPCAT reported earlier this year that the agriculture sector is facing a potential supply shortage in the coming years due to a lack of mechanisation.

This is likely to have an impact on food security.
headline: Call for thousands of tractors in Dublin: farmers’ protest escalates

"Housing crisis: Government's position may be at odds with the facts"

By David Grafton

Gript

"Government's position may be at odds with the facts"

A Department of Social Protection report on Ireland's housing crisis has cast doubt on the Government's previous claims that it was trying to ease the housing crisis by getting more people into homes.

The Department of Social Protection (DSP) released a report entitled "Towards a Housing Solution for the Irish Economy" (PDF), which concluded that, despite its aggressive measures of stamp duty relief, the Government's housing policy had failed to reduce the number of people who were living in rented accommodation.

Grafton told TheJournal.ie that the report's conclusion appeared to be "tantamount to a rejection" of the Government's claim that it was trying to reduce housing costs.

The report notes that the level of rent relief was the highest in Europe and that, in 2011, the lowest annual rents in Europe were in Germany.

However, the DSP report also noted that, according to the government's own figures, the number of people in rented accommodation fell from 10.8 million in 2010 to 9.9 million in 2011.

"That's a reduction of about 7,000 people in the last four years," Grafton said.

The DSP report noted that the number of people who were in rented accommodation had remained fairly stable over the last four years. However, it notes that in 2011 the number of people renting for less than €750 per month, the level of rent relief that the Government was imposing, declined by about 1,000 people.

In response to TheJournal.ie's questions, the DSP's media unit pointed to an April statement by Minister for Finance Michael Noonan saying that, in fact, the number of people in rented accommodation had risen in the last year.

Grafton said this would have been "unprecedented" if the DSP report had found that the number of people in rented accommodation had fallen, and noted that the report in fact found that the number of people in rented accommodation had risen.

"I have a fundamental problem with this report, the notion that the Government was trying to alleviate the housing crisis by getting people more housing – no amount of stamp duty relief – was going to bring down rents," Grafton said.

Asked if he agreed with the DSP report's conclusion that the number of people living in rented accommodation had fallen, Grafton said that a further question might be whether people were now renting houses that were either too big or too small.

Grafton noted that, over the last year, the number of people in rent arrears has fallen by about 500 people.

"Are we getting the number of people in rented accommodation down at the rate that the DSP report says it has?" he said.

"That's my biggest problem with the report: the report points to rent arrears but it doesn't say what's causing the rent arrears to fall, and I think that's an area where we need more information."

Grafton said he suspected that, if he had had access to the Department of Social Protection's report, it would have highlighted a number of issues and issues that he was calling for an independent investigation into.
headline: MCGUIRK: Want more houses? Get the Government out of housing.

Irish men under 25 are more likely to kill themselves than any other age group in the country, according to a new report.

The study, commissioned by the Irish Men's Health Alliance (IMHA), found that among all those who took their own lives in 2011, an Irish man under the age of 25 was the highest rate.

The highest rate of suicide for the group was seen amongst men under the age of 30 (12.4 per cent).

The highest rate of alcohol-related deaths was seen amongst men aged 35-44 (9.8 per cent), while the highest rate of drug-related deaths was seen amongst men aged 25-29 (9.1 per cent).

The study found that men were also at a higher risk of dying in the first 10 years of their life, and men were more likely to die in the first 5 years than women.

The study also found that men were more likely to be unemployed in Ireland than women, and the study's authors say a lack of employment opportunities, and the impact of the recession on employment opportunities, will continue to put pressure on the gender divide in suicide rates.

The research was conducted among over 1,000 men aged 17-85, and the average age was between 50 and 60.
headline: Suicide the biggest killer of Irish men under the age of 25

Journalists and politicians are being targeted by a "dire" media environment, with the potential to seriously damage their reputation, according to a new report.

The report, published by Gript, a technology innovation and education company, was commissioned by the Department of Communications and Arts (DCAA) and the Department of Justice (DOJ).

The report warns the media has been given too much latitude to distort the truth and take advantage of people's uncertainty about the future.

The authors, a number of former media industry professionals, outline three main problems in today's media environment, which they say are leading to a "dire" media environment.

One, the internet has changed the role of the traditional print media, and now gives people unprecedented access to information.

Two, people are more aware of the risks of certain media content, such as the dangers of climate change.

And three, people have the ability to access information and opinions that no longer come from newspapers or television stations.

Gript's analysis finds the number of journalists in print and broadcast media has declined dramatically in recent years, as digital media has become the leading form of news consumption.

At the same time, the report finds that fewer people are reading the mainstream news outlets, because many have moved online to get their news.

"A significant share of people in their late 20s, early 30s and early 40s are now consuming media content on the internet without having the luxury of a print publication or a broadcast one," says the report.

"In the UK, the proportion of people who don't read a daily newspaper or a daily broadcast TV channel has fallen from 50% in 2009 to 37% in 2012. That's a massive change in the UK – something we're seeing elsewhere in Europe as well.

"We're in a period of transition, and I think we're seeing the first signs of that in the way that people are consuming media in the digital world."

While there are many factors at play, the report argues that the main thing people care about is the quality of content, and is therefore increasingly driven by the popularity of the digital version of the news.

"If you're a journalist and you're not doing your job, then that's not what you care about," says Dr Brian Farrell, co-author of the report and CEO of Gript.

"People are increasingly concerned about how you make sense of all of the information that's coming at them."

The research was carried out by Gript, a technology innovation and education company, with its head of research and communications, Dr Brian Farrell.

Dr Farrell says the findings have been released to help media organisations deal with a "dire media environment" and encourage them to better understand how they're contributing to the problem.

"I think it's important that media organisations reflect on what they need to do to make sure they're contributing to the right kind of environment," he says.

"The key point that we've come to is that the majority of people still prefer traditional print media.

"That's not going to change anytime soon, and when people aren't consuming all of the information that's being produced, then we're going to see a really severe impact on the way that people consume information."
headline: A black day for media misinformation

A new study from the University of Exeter and Bristol University has revealed a link between viral infection and Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's and other neurological disorders.

Researchers analyzed 1,938 cases of Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and related neurodegenerative disorders across the globe from around 2003-2012. These included 1,938 individuals with dementia, 4,567 with parkinsonism, 3,938 with Alzheimer's, 1,813 with dementia and 1,853 with other neurological disorders.

The researchers found that those with the highest level of viral infection – for example, one that carries the hepatitis C virus – were four times more likely to develop Alzheimer's, parkinsonism or dementia.

The researchers said the findings also support the view that viral infections may play a role in the development of Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and other neurodegenerative disorders. The study was published in the Lancet Neurology, the medical journal of the American Medical Association.

The study also found that men with high viral load had twice the risk of developing Alzheimer's compared to men with low viral load.

Further research has found that there are three different strains of hepatitis C virus in the blood of individuals with Alzheimer's disease. The researchers said they can't explain why these viruses are associated with neurological disorders. However, they speculate that the viruses are potentially a causal factor in the development of Alzheimer's, parkinsonism and other neurological disorders.

The researchers said it is important to note that their findings are based on individuals and not necessarily of a community. In the United Kingdom, for example, they discovered that individuals with Alzheimer's disease who contracted hepatitis C virus were six times more likely to develop dementia than those who did not.

Dr. Christopher Walker, Head of Research at the Alzheimer's Association UK, said: "These findings are of huge significance because they provide a link between an infectious agent and a neurodegenerative condition in which the brain cannot communicate properly."

"There is no cure for Alzheimer's disease and a cure may be a long way off, so the identification of viruses as potential causes of neurological disorders is a vital step in the research agenda."

The researchers said there is also no vaccine to prevent Alzheimer's disease, although there is a promising treatment for the symptoms of the disease.

This study was funded by the National Institute for Health Research. The National Institute of Health is the largest supporter of biomedical research in the world, and is working to address some of the most pressing challenges of our time. For more information, visit www.nia.nih.gov.
headline: New Study: link between Alzheimer’s/Parkinson’s and viral infection

What would you do if you heard that a large number of people from your community were being brought into Dublin airport overnight?

This is a question that we are hearing more and more often over recent months as a result of the arrival of thousands of migrants into the country from the Republic of Ireland.

In particular, we hear about a large number of asylum seekers who have been housed at the airport. But what do we know about the people who have been housed at the airport? What does it mean to be a "minimal person", and how do they relate to the migrant crisis?

These questions need to be addressed and answered now to understand the implications for the lives of people and their families.

The Minimal Person

What does it mean to be a "minimal person"? This is a term that is used to describe anyone without a traditional job, as well as those with a lack of savings or a low income. It is also a term used to refer to those who are homeless, or those who have been in need of services, but are unable to access them.

At the beginning of 2012, it was widely known that migrants were being housed in Dublin Airport. On January 29th 2012, this was reported by the Irish Times with the following headline:

Migrants are housed at Dublin airport in protest at the "harsh conditions" they face in the airport.

The migrants were being housed in a former Department of Health, Department of Social Protection and Department of Transport parking lot on the eastern side of the airport. The facility was opened on April 6th 2010 and it remains open as of February 2013. It is called a "minimal person" facility and is for those without a "traditional job" and with low savings.

The purpose of the facility was to provide shelter for refugees and asylum seekers, as well as provide social services and support to refugees and asylum seekers. It was a temporary shelter, which was also used for family reunification.

What we are seeing now is the impact of the "harsh conditions" that are being described as being experienced by people who were housed at the airport, in the form of a lack of social services, lack of job opportunities and a lack of housing. It is a result of the policy of the government, the Central Government, in relation to the integration of migrants into our society and a number of other policies.

What has happened since that day?

Since the opening of the airport facility, the number of people receiving assistance in Dublin from the Irish State has declined. However, those who have been provided with accommodation in the airport facility have been found to be unemployed or underemployed. In fact, on February 27th 2013, it was reported by the Irish Times with the following headline:

The Government is giving aid to a small group of those in need of social support in Dublin airport.

This story has been reported again by the Irish Times with the headline:

The Government is making social payments to migrants, in a bid to help them find accommodation.

This story has been reported by the Irish Times with the headline:

The Government is also making grants to migrants who are living in the airport who are in need of housing assistance.

As well as receiving assistance in terms of social security payments, the migrants are also being offered accommodation in the airport facility.
headline: The migrant, the cost rental house, and the Willy Wonka Government

"The Perrin Group (one of Ireland's largest companies) today announced its support for a non-specific legislation amendment (Bill) which seeks to establish a child-free zone in the State. In this area of legislation, the majority of TDs in the Dáil agreed with the views of the Perrin Group, as expressed in the Bill. The Bill, which will come before the Dáil in January, will define a zone for persons under 18 years of age. The zone will be a part of the State and will be open to those who wish to live in the area, including those who are not in a relationship with a child. This will provide a space where young people can have relationships with parents and other adults without the need for them to have contact with a child.

"The Bill will include a legal definition of childfree. The Bill will also give a legal right to the State to provide this space for its citizens.

"The Perrin Group's view is that this is a positive step forward for child-free living. As the majority of the TDs in the Dáil agree, this Bill will protect child-free individuals and their families.

"The Bill will now head to the Seanad for consideration, and then to the President and the Government for consent."

In an update to the public, a spokesperson for the Perrin Group said:

"The Bill was agreed on by the Dáil in December 2015. The Dáil has a clear majority in favour of it. In the Seanad on 31 December it was approved by the Dáil unanimously."

The Dáil has also agreed to set up a committee on child-free living to review the Bill before it reaches the Senate for debate.

You can also get in touch with your MP or Taoiseach to discuss how the Bill will affect you.

What is a childfree zone?

In Ireland, a childfree zone is the legal area of a municipality or country, outside the jurisdiction of a child-rearing agency or local authority, that does not require a child to live with them or interact with them in any way. The area is often a "zone of exclusion" rather than a "zone of protection".

In Ireland, the legal definition of a childfree zone is "a space which is open to children but does not provide an area for a child to live."

It is a legal definition. It is not a legal prohibition on living in certain parts of the state that are childfree zones. A childfree zone is a legal definition and not a legal prohibition.

If you live in a zone of exclusion, you must adhere to the regulations of the zone. This is because a childfree zone does not extend to every area of the State, but merely areas of the State that are not childfree zones.

In a childfree zone, all legal obligations for the protection and maintenance of children rest with the local authority, not with the local authority or child-rearing agency.

This is one area that Ireland does not require the State or local authorities to intervene in. Local authorities, like the local authority and child-rearing agencies, can set up their own zones of exclusion, as long as they maintain appropriate services in place for children.
headline: PERRINS: No to childfree zones for the child-free

There are no survivors of the Cherry Orchard, a community of mostly Irish residents and some English speakers, who were killed by a killer in 1981.

The two Irish men who died in the derelict community, and whose bodies were left on the ground, were Michael O'Higgins and John McGarry.

But there are only one other families left who call Cherry Orchard home. In a community of some 8,000 people, it is the second largest community in Dublin and only a few hundred yards from the National Cemetery.

But the community has been derelict for about a century, and is littered with rubbish. The first time that anyone was found dead in Cherry Orchard was in 1854.

In the past, there have been a number of serious murders in the community. The first, in the summer of 1981, was that of the local historian, Thomas O'Gorman. He was murdered in a hotel room while out on a trip to England to see relatives.

In the years that followed, two other Irish men, John McGarry and Michael O'Higgins, were murdered. In the latter case, the bodies were found in a derelict house in Cherry Orchard.

In 1993, McGarry's body was discovered in the garden of a building in the Cherry Orchard that had been previously used for the housing of former Irish police officers.

The community of Cherry Orchard has long been blighted by the high crime rate. Many families have been robbed and even murdered.

While the houses in Cherry Orchard have had plenty of changes, the community is still populated with one of the city's greatest challenges - a small number of houses have been sitting empty for years, without being occupied.

Some of the houses are vacant for up to six years.

Many of the families in the community are from Cork, many of them settled on the north side of Dublin during the 1920s and '30s.

It is difficult to imagine any Irish city which has had such a long spell without a family house.

The houses and gardens are rotting, the walls are cracked, the windows are boarded up and the paint is peeling and falling off. But the houses themselves have remained a permanent feature.

In the 1950s, the original buildings had been moved into a new complex of five houses in the main street, along with an orphanage.

A major renovation was begun in the mid-1980s, but in recent years, some families have found themselves forced out of their homes.

Over the years, the community has seen changes such as the addition of a garda station, shops, cinemas, schools and a new council-run centre for the elderly and disabled.

But the community has also had its ups and downs.

One community leader, who did not want to be named, said the number of family houses had increased in recent years, but many of them had been empty for so long that there were few residents left to do much for the residents of the communities.

"The people in the community, if they knew they were not going to be able to continue to pay their bills, they would leave," he said.

"The families that do stay will have to cope with the new environment, with all of the new families, with the new cars.
headline: Falling down in Cherry Orchard: lots of amenities but few intact families

A long-term study of the medicalisation of emotions has found that, despite the increasing use of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), the majority of cases of post-traumatic stress disorder in the general population continue to be non-specific and non-clinical.

The study by Dr. Martin Bélanger at McGill University, based on an analysis of the Canadian Community Health Survey, found that of the 10,000 people assessed, about 2,100 (1.7%) showed signs of an anxiety disorder. Of these, about 1,500 were women and the most common form of anxiety was social phobia.

"We have a very conservative medical model in Canada and our approach is based on the idea that you don't have a problem with anxiety if it's not related to your body", Dr. Bélanger said in a press release.

He also said that while the study does not explain why the anxiety is unrelated to their bodies, it's an assumption, so further research is needed to see if anxiety is a marker for something deeper that doesn't have to do with the body.

He also believes that ECT is a valid treatment. "ECT is very effective, it's very safe and it's the same as a lot of other treatments. It seems to be very effective for some patients, but some people don't respond as well."

The findings will be published in the American Journal of Psychiatry, to be published in 2014.

Source:

There was an "unwarranted and unacceptable" breach of trust between three parties involved in the investigation of the late NAMA chief Brian Lenihan, an Irish judge has heard.

The case of the NAMA investigation, which resulted in the death of businessman Brian Lenihan, was before the Court of Criminal Appeal this morning, with the case continuing until September.

In the Court of Criminal Appeal in Dublin, Mr Justice Seán McNally, sitting with Mr Justice John O'Mahony, heard how the NAMA investigation of Mr Lenihan, who died in 2012 after being attacked by his own family, was "fundamentally flawed".

A number of witnesses had not been properly heard and they were not informed of the scope of the investigation.

The appeal court has to hear the case within 12 months.

Mr Justice McNally said that the issue was "profound".

The judge said that the issue of "compensation" for the "tragedy and suffering" caused by Mr Lenihan's death, had arisen, despite a number of witnesses having been consulted.

He said that there was no "good deed gone unpunished" and that the NAMA investigation was "fundamentally flawed".

It is the first time in recent times that a judge has heard a case on the NAMA case.

The NAMA inquiry, which concluded in September 2012, found that Mr Lenihan had been subjected to "inappropriate" treatment at the hands of a number of his family members.

It had investigated how Mr Lenihan had become the subject of a "suspected extortion", with the probe looking into how Mr Lenihan had become the target of his family's "extortion".

But Mr Justice McNally said that the case was not the most complex.

The appeal court decision was "more like a game of Whac-A-Mole than a real investigation", he said.

Mr Justice McNally said the key issue was that "nobody had been told the extent of the NAMA investigation and no one had been able to hear the witness statements.

"That is how serious the issue of 'compensation' is", he said.

The case was not about the money, he said, but was about ensuring that the interests of Mr Lenihan's estate "are not disregarded and that no one who suffered from the tragedy is left without any redress".

Mr Justice McNally said that the NAMA investigation was a "tragedy and suffering" and that he would have to take into account the "widespread and deep national concern" about a problem of "an unacceptable nature".

In his judgement, Mr Justice McNally said that the NAMA investigation of Mr Lenihan was "fundamentally flawed".

He said that they had been unable to get proper evidence before the court that had been given to them in November 2009 by the then chief executive of NAMA and that evidence about the "intriguing allegations" made by the estate had not been properly considered.

He said that in addition, the inquiry was "unnecessary".

Mr Justice McNally said that if Mr Lenihan had been "a rich man, perhaps in the billions", the investigation would have been done "in a different way".

Tadgh Farrell was one of the most brilliant musicians in Ireland. An award-winning composer, arranger and multi-instrumentalist, he was also an influential organist and arranger, and a great lyricist.

Today, he is remembered not only for his musical achievements but also as a gentle and caring human being.

Tadgh lived at the centre of the Irish music world, and is often seen in the music history of the 20th century, as a leader in the development of Irish music.

His work was largely instrumental, with he is considered to be one of the very best Irish instrumentalists to have ever lived.

In 2010, he was awarded the Order of the British Empire, the highest award given in Ireland, as well as the Dublin Opera Medal for his contributions to Irish opera.

His life, and his musical career, will be remembered by Irish music lovers, both those who knew him personally and those who did not.

She went on to appear in the TV series The Practice and was the star of ABC's hit series My Name is Earl, which aired from 1990 to 1992.

She also had an illustrious career in theatre, appearing in a number of roles as well as starring in television series and feature films.

Scarlett died peacefully in her bed at St. Luke's Hospital in Dublin, with husband John Faulkner, the brother of actress Sarah, saying: 'I am heartbroken, shocked and shocked.'

Scarlett was previously married to the actor Richard Burton, who died in 1997, and was a daughter of Irish film star James Faulkner.

The actress's family said: 'Her family would like to thank everyone for their thoughts and their respect.

'We ask that everyone respect their privacy during this time of great loss.'

They added: 'The family is currently working on family matters and the family wishes for privacy at this difficult time'.

text:
Poland will no longer supply Ukraine with weapons after a conflict with Russia that erupted in 2014.

The Polish parliament has voted in favour of ending a deal with Ukraine which had been criticised by the European Union, but that decision was taken before the current unrest erupted.

The decision means that the only military hardware Ukraine will receive from Poland will be combat helicopters.

The decision was approved by a vote of 565 to 46, with 513 voting against and 1 abstaining.

The decision was also supported by the Government.

Last week, President Bronislaw Komorowski said Poland would stop providing arms to Ukraine as it had already been asked to do by the EU.

Ukraine said on Thursday that it would not abide by the decision and would not stop supplying weapons.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko said on Thursday that his country would not stop supplying weapons to the pro-Russian rebels in his country's east.

"If there is such a demand from the Ukrainian government, it would be useless to stop it," he told reporters in the city of Donetsk. "The problem is that the Ukrainian government does not recognise the sovereignty of the Russian Federation."

On Tuesday, Ukrainian president Petro Poroshenko, backed by French president Emmanuel Macron, called on Russia to do more to aid his country in its fight against the rebels.

"We are ready to work with Russia if it acts as soon as possible," Mr Poroshenko said in a video message released to reporters on Tuesday.

Russia on Thursday denied providing weapons to the separatists in eastern Ukraine, the Associated Press reported.

It said that the Kremlin's statement was "an effort to justify its own actions".

In January, President Putin ordered troops in the country's eastern and southern regions to stand down in the face of mounting international pressure to show they could defend their country from what he said was an attempted coup.

Russia later accused Ukrainian troops of carrying out a coup, and Russia's ambassador to the UN has called for an "immediate ceasefire and a withdrawal of heavy weapons".

In Brussels, a spokesman for the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) said that a senior member of the organization's staff, a medical doctor, had been killed in an attack in Donetsk.

The ICRC said that both its medical staff and its medical staff working in Russia had been injured.
headline: Poland will no longer supply weapons to Ukraine after grain row

Irish Examiner (22-Oct-14)

Gormley's sister, Eileen, died at the age of 26 on 17-Oct-12, aged 14. The next day her parents, Michael and Margaret, were found hanged, strangled and their son, James Gormley, 17, arrested on suspicion of the killings.

The story is based on newspaper accounts of two weeks after Eileen's murder. The Irish Examiner reported:

At 10.30am last Saturday, a man drove up to the family home on Castle Street, in the North West, and opened fire on the Gormley's home. Mrs Gormley was shot in the head, and her husband was shot in the arm. Mr Gormley was struck on the head with a small piece of glass and died the next morning.

On Monday, a witness at the scene reported hearing a thud and looking out of a window at the back of the house as the man drove away. The man, who was not known to police, was never identified.

The family home was gutted. The remains of Mrs Gormley, her husband and their two children were found on the back of a tractor.

James Gormley was arrested the next day and brought to the police station.

James, the father of three, was arrested on suspicion of murder, but it is understood that he denied any knowledge of his family's deaths.

His father's brother, Michael, was detained on suspicion of manslaughter. His condition is not known at the moment.

James has been remanded in custody and is due to appear before Clonmel District Court on Wednesday. He has been charged with murder of his parents, his brother and their two-year-old son and the shooting of his mother.

The Irish Examiner reports that a post mortem examination indicated that Mrs Gormley's death had been caused by a single gunshot wound to the head.

James Gormley is due to appear before Clonmel District Court on Wednesday.

The Gormley's four children, aged 12 to 18, are now living with his sister in Donegal.
headline: BREAKING: Son charged with murder of parents, brother

New Government in Iran has launched a programme to improve the water supply system to enable the country's farmers to produce more grain and wheat. A project which aims to improve the quality of the water supply system in Iran will be launched in the coming days, according to a new announcement by Iran's Minister of Water Resources Ali Tayyeb Ahmadiyeh.

Iran's Minister of Water Resources Ali Tayyeb Ahmadiyeh said on Monday that the government will invest in improving the water supply system in Iran for the future to enable farmers to produce more grain and wheat and increase its production.

Tayyeb Ahmadiyeh said that the government will invest approximately 50 billion rial in improving the water supply system in Iran.

The minister said that the investment will be made on a local, regional and national basis.

In 2011, the government of Iran announced plans to introduce a water tax, in order to improve water quality in the country. The government said that the water tax was intended to pay for a number of projects, including the implementation of the Clean Water Law and other water projects.

Iran is the world's sixth largest producer of wheat, the country's second largest producer of rice, the country's fourth largest producer of livestock feed, the country's biggest producer of vegetables and fruits, and the second largest producer of livestock meat.

text:
The Kildare Asylum Centre will be bulldozed this morning. It was granted a permit yesterday but will now be bulldozed. It was granted last year but the Local Government Committee in Tipperary and the Minister for the Department of Justice has refused it. It was a local protest, a demonstration against the fact that asylum seekers were being sent to the centre as opposed to the Irish mainland and it was deemed by this committee to be inhumane, to be a significant breach of human rights and therefore unacceptable. It was a very popular protest and there was a significant turnout yesterday and many people are very angry about it.

The local councillors in Tipperary are furious at this. I spoke to one yesterday, who said he does not want any political political party to have their name or logo on the building and he is not happy about this.

We are trying to reach out to the Department of Justice and they have referred us to the Minister for the State. We are also speaking to representatives of the local area councillors. We are trying to get the Department of Justice to allow us to re-apply for a permit.

Our local representatives have been informed that we will not be allowed a permit from next week so we are going to need to go back to the local government committee for permission to re-apply. We will also need to get the support of the local community and I am asking them to stand up against this and to have a discussion about it. We are trying to reach out to the public but they have refused us.

Some people are upset about the way the process is going. We are trying to make a public spectacle of the bulldozing but it is a political move by the government. This will be the last of the Asylum Centres in the North East. This will mean they will be bulldozed all the way to the coast and they will not have any other sites left. It is very sad because they had good reception at the Kildare Centre. This is a major blow for the asylum seeker community in this part of Ireland. The minister has not consulted anyone in the local government committee in Tipperary, Tipperary County Council or the local community.

It is important that we are able to carry on, that we have these centers, that we have the resources and support that we need to help people in crisis. We need to continue to stand up for those in crisis.

We are really in a state of emergency in Ireland. We need to go back to local democracy. We need to get some answers to these questions. It is time for local people to have some say.

This morning we published the story of the first time a woman has used Facebook to post a picture of herself naked on the internet.

And her photo was of the young man who murdered her.

The photo was posted by the mother of a 17-year-old girl who had just become involved with a 16-year-old boy.

The picture was posted on Facebook, apparently by someone who was "shocked" to see it on the internet.

The caption for the photo read: "I woke up this morning and just received this phone call from my daughter, She was crying at the other end of the phone. She told me she was going to break up with her boyfriend and her dad was going to go to the police.

"She said she was going to tell the police she was in love with a 16-year-old boy she knew.

"She said that her family had not helped her as much as they should have. She wanted out. She was getting ready to leave. I can barely talk to her now.

"Her dad is trying to talk to her, to let her know it's OK and to reassure her that it won't happen again, but she doesn't seem to understand. I need her to understand what's happening. She needs to be clear with me as well. She said she could see my face on the news. She told me that she didn't care, that she had no one. She said it was the best thing for her.

"She asked if it hurt, if she was sad, she said no, it just made her feel happier to be naked. She said she was proud she was wearing her boyfriend's clothes. She said that she wanted to move on."

The photograph was taken in the grounds of the Royal Melbourne Hospital.

Ms O’Neill's Facebook page, the full caption of which can be viewed on the Gript site, features a photo of a smiling, smiling young woman sitting on a bench.

The woman was wearing a white tank top with her hair up in a braid and no make-up.

In addition to her profile picture, there is a photo of her with two of her children, ages six and 11.

The photo also shows a group of people, including her children and the two male friends she posted the photo with.

The man in the photograph is wearing a bright green hooded top.

He is holding his phone in one hand and a large gun in the other.

The woman's two friends are also wearing hoodies.

The four men are standing side-by-side, with their arms at their sides.

The woman holds up one hand as if she is trying to cover her face and the man in the picture is looking at the camera with a raised brow.

One of the men is in the foreground while the woman is in the background.

In a text message exchange, Ms O’Neill wrote: "This is me. I'm not going to do it. I've done it so many times before I can't even remember what it feels like anymore.

"I'm so tired of this."

Her message was also sent to the two other teenage friends she sent the photo to.

The girl's father, Hans-Christian Knutsen, 40, is a retired police inspector, who lives on a farm in the town. Knutsen was married with two children at the time of his daughter's disappearance.

But authorities are still searching for the killer, who is described as having dark skin, short blond hair, a medium build and a beard. He is about 5-feet-4-inches tall with blond, light brown eyes.

Lissendag police said the girl was discovered with several cuts in her back and face. She was dressed in a bright pink and blue dress.

Police do not know how she died.

Gardaí on duty at the scene of a suspected road rage incident in Westmeath are under pressure from the Garda Commissioner.

Speaking in Bandon, Co. Cork yesterday, the Garda Commissioner told the Independent: "The media and the public should be aware that the gardaí are under scrutiny and under increased pressure in relation to the case of [Nicolás O'Sullivan].

"I am pleased to say that our work with the press has been excellent. This has been an exceptionally difficult situation. I have repeatedly reiterated that there will be no leaks and nothing will be published. However, there have been some very worrying and distressing stories in the media, particularly that of the arrest of the Garda whistleblower Mr O'Sullivan in connection with Operation Conifer.

"I have spoken to the media and public, who should know this is not a case where there is any serious and pressing threat to public safety. We are dealing with a very serious and serious incident. The gardaí were confronted with an attempted road rage incident. It is the right of the gardaí to deal with these situations, as with any other case. I am concerned and disappointed that the media in this case have been the ones to make these reports. I am determined that this has to be brought to an end as quickly as possible."

The gardaí have not yet received any complaints about the incident.
headline: CITYWEST: news team accuse Gardaí of ‘attack’

According to Eurostat data released on 8 April, the number of asylum seekers from the European Union has fallen, but the number of people arriving in Ireland has remained steady over the last twelve months, at about 3,000.

However, there is a rise in the number of people arriving in Ireland. Figures published on 14 April indicated that a total of 1,895 people arrived in Ireland in the first month of 2017, an increase of about 45% compared to the same period in 2016.

"These figures show a continued increase in the number of people coming to Ireland, but these figures also show an increase in the number arriving in Ireland in the first month of 2017, compared to the same period in 2016. That's what we call an increase in the Irish community," said Ms Dermot O'Leary, Deputy Minister for Public Expenditure and Reform.

"The Irish community is still increasing. There is an increase in the number of people coming to Ireland, but we are also seeing a significant increase in people arriving here. This is the case from any EU member state as the country with the highest number of people coming to Ireland," she said.

However, Ms O'Leary said the increase in the number of people arriving in Ireland is a result of the country having a large number of refugees. The Department of Public Expenditure and Reform (DPR) estimated that in 2016 over 3,000 of the total 3,895 asylum seekers from Europe arrived in Ireland, while an additional 4,000 arrived in the first seven months of 2017.

She added: "The increase in the number of people coming into the country over the last 12 months can be attributed to the number of refugees coming to Ireland. They are coming to support families that have already arrived in Ireland. We have to look at whether we are increasing the number of refugees, or decreasing the number coming here."

The Department said in response that it is not the responsibility of the Irish government to reduce the number of refugees coming to the country. "These figures are from the European Union and reflect the volume of asylum seekers coming to Ireland," said the Department's Acting Commissioner for Asylum, Vassiliki Zekes.

The latest figures show that the number of asylum seekers arriving in Ireland has decreased from 3,971 in 2016 to 3,805 in 2017. However, a total of 1,895 asylum seekers arrived in Ireland in the first seven months of 2017, up from 1,831 in the same period in 2016.

Ms O'Leary said that the increases in the number of asylum seekers arriving in Ireland can be attributed to both the number of refugees coming to Ireland and the number of people coming here to visit family and friends.

She added that the increase in the number of asylum seekers arriving in Ireland in the first three months of 2017 is "the same as the number of people coming to Ireland from the EU" and she said that this is the same number as the number of asylum seekers coming from Europe.

Ms O'Leary said that the Department is not in favour of increasing the number of refugees coming to Ireland, adding that the numbers of refugees coming from the EU are increasing rapidly. "We have a fair number of refugees coming from the EU, but a fair number of people coming to the country from the EU.
headline: Numbers claiming asylum across EU fall, but rise in Ireland

Hundreds of people have taken to the Irish news website www.gript.ie to sign a petition to save an Irish Wolfhound.

The pet was found in a field in Cork City, Co Clare, on November 23.

The dog had to be put down following the owner's complaints that the dog "lacked common sense" and was "aggressive to all people".

"I have to admit he was a bit of an animal – he had a bad habit of getting in my eyes," said the owner, who only wanted to be identified as a local woman.

"He would bite, sometimes even through a glass window, but he was also very friendly. I just had to put him down."

The owner, who says the dog has been with her since she was seven years old, has been battling with the Irish Wolfhound Club (IWKC) to get the dog put down.

The IWKC's rules say, in part: "Wolves are not fit for human consumption and should never be left in the same home as any human."

However, in the dog's case, the owners were unaware they were allowed to keep her.

"The owners of these dogs are allowed to keep the animal and it is their choice as to whether or not they want to," said the IWKC.

"It is not our intention to make any claims regarding the welfare of the animals, only that they are in a situation where there are no alternatives to the animal's removal."

Grits and Guts

The owner, who did not want to be named, said she had a few issues with the dog, which she could not quite put her finger on.

"He was pretty, he was a little bit tough. I just didn't think I could keep him as I have no experience and I was quite scared, but I had to do it," she said.

"It was a rough beginning, he was quite aggressive to me, I thought if I tried to scare him back, he would get off me."

However, despite the problems the dog had at first, she decided the dog was perfect for her as she could not bear to see him going.

She bought a dog and started grooming him herself.

"He was pretty grunty. He wouldn't eat, he wouldn't drink, he was just kind of a tough dog. I liked the way he was," she said.

"I took him to the vet and they gave him a course of antibiotics. He got better, but he was still a bit grouchy. I was worried he'd get away, but he didn't get away for four days. He wasn't the kind of animal to get away.

"I knew I was going to get him back. I couldn't just give him up. I'd never give up a dog, and I was just so scared that he'd get away."

She paid the vet to put the dog on steroids to boost his stamina so he could be kept in the same situation for longer.

As well as the vet treatment, the owner also took him to a puppy rehabilitation centre and bought an expensive dog food, which he says has helped him with his health.
headline: Thousands sign petition to Save Dog from Being Put Down
