Police have confirmed the husband of a woman killed in the front of a police car in Bangor has been charged with her murder.

Jim Moore (85), who was arrested on suspicion of murder following the shooting of Patricia Aust (81) in Bangor yesterday, is being held on €1,000 bail.

Mrs Aust (81) died at the scene in Bangor.

Mr Moore was arrested at his home at 5.30pm yesterday following his wife's death.

He has been charged with first degree murder.

Police say the case is currently being investigated as a double homicide.

A spokesman for the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) said they have received a number of calls from members of the public regarding the death of Patricia Aust, 81.

The murder is now being treated as a double homicide with the officer injured.

Mrs Aust had recently travelled to the Republic of Ireland to visit a relative and did not return to the UK on Thursday night, police said.

The shooting incident occurred at 4.30am on Thursday morning when a patrol car stopped in the town of Bangor after seeing a man matching the description of a man arrested on suspicion of murdering Mrs Aust.

"The patrol car driver saw the man run across the road from the car park and towards the officers," the PSNI spokesman said.

"It is believed that the man shot at the officers and missed.

"The officers immediately stopped their car and entered the patrol car and called for an ambulance.

"The officer injured man is now being treated at the scene for non-life-threatening injuries.

"The PSNI are investigating the shooting incident as a murder."

The man arrested is still at large and no one else was injured in the shooting incident.

Mrs Aust lived in a house which she sold to her husband.

The woman worked as a nurse and had just returned to work following a brief holiday.

She was described by neighbours as a dedicated family man who loved his job.

One neighbour said: "It was a shock for everyone in the street. He was just a normal person. He never got upset or anything like that."

Last night, relatives of Mrs Aust expressed their relief at news of his arrest.

A family friend, who is a relative of the couple, said: "I feel for the whole family but at the same time, it is a bit of a relief."

Mrs Aust's daughter, Katie Moore, 21, who lives nearby, said: "It is good to hear about this because it is a horrible thing to happen."

The couple married in 1991 and lived in the town in the 1960s.
headline: Jim Moore (85) charged with murder of Patricia Aust (81) in Bangor

text:
The Irish Government will spend €50 million between 2016 and 2024 in order to develop the model of the HSE Refugee and Migration Health Care Service (MRMHC).

The service is to offer both an integrated integrated service providing integrated care for all asylum seekers and migrants in the State, and a more focused service focused specifically on vulnerable groups within Ireland.

The service will be funded from the HSE's budget and will be run in partnership with the Refugee Council of Ireland and other stakeholders.

This will include the establishment of a service that includes all the services currently available within the HSE – including a more focused service designed to treat all health issues and provide the following care options:

• acute, acute mental health services;

• health education, and

• health support.

The provision of these services will be integrated with the services available within the HSE Refugee and Migration Health Care Service. This will include provision of a comprehensive health and social care plan for each refugee and migrant.

Asylum seekers and migrants who have been resident in Ireland for a total of three years or less will be eligible to receive care from the MRMHC.

The service is expected to be operational by the middle of next year.

'This programme will provide a more focused service, providing specialist healthcare for a specific group of people in Ireland,' said Minister for Health Simon Harris.

'There will be a robust integrated service providing a range of options to suit the needs of each individual client and ensuring they are well cared for.'
headline: €50 million will be spent in 2024 to develop model of HSE refugee and migrant health care

The head of a dog welfare organisation has revealed the extent to which animal welfare groups are "using charity to cover up cruelty and murder".

Cullen Kilcoyne, CEO of the Dogs Trust, said the charity sector was suffering from "the same problem as other industries, where some of the problems are hidden behind an argument of charity".

Speaking to Newstalk ZB, Mr Kilcoyne said "it's an excuse not to do the right thing".

Speaking about a recent case of the Irish Livestock Association selling a puppy to a Chinese family for €3,000, Mr Kilcoyne said: "This is what they do, this is what they are doing with the poor dogs and the homeless dogs, as well as the dead dogs and the abandoned dogs."

Speaking about the killing of dogs by a dog trainer, Mr Kilcoyne said the training, including that which involves the handling of dogs without a leash, was "horrific".

"If it was not for the dogs' welfare organisations, there would be no dogs in this country," he said.

Speaking about the deaths of hundreds of dogs and cats being shipped into Europe by a company called The Irish Sheep Dog Company, Mr Kilcoyne said: "They were not humanely slaughtered. It was a deliberate act of violence.

"They were given a false bill of health and then killed."

Talking about the case of the dogs who were shot and killed by a farmer in Co Sligo last year, Mr Kilcoyne said he believed he had found a person who had "done some pretty awful things".

"I think it could be some kind of animal cruelty, but I am not quite sure of the circumstances," he said.

"I want to know what exactly happened, because it's going to be a challenge. We can't let this go on."

'We cannot allow this to go on'

Mr Kilcoyne said the Dogs Trust was working with the Department of Justice on an investigation into the killings, and said it would be "saddening" to the families of those killed if the investigations continue to "lose momentum".

"We have to have the courage to come forward and say who did it," he said.

"When it comes to the welfare of animals we can't allow this to go on."

Mr Kilcoyne said he believed the slaughter of the dogs on behalf of a company in China was "inhumane" and an act of violence.

"This has absolutely no place in Ireland, and it's not going to go on. I can't believe they have been allowed to go on for so long," he said.

He said the DSPCA had been "terribly busy" with the deaths of hundreds of dogs over a two-year period.

"We have to know who is responsible for the killing, the abuse that is happening," he said.

"If they are going to have an excuse for it, then it's time we did the right thing."
headline: Cruelty Cloaked in Compassion

How to get the best out of the New Economic Policy?

John Henry Newman, one of the great Irish economists of the last century, once wrote a prescient book called The Great Transformation: The Great Depression and the Great Awakening.

In the book he explained how the New Economic Policy (NEP) that was introduced in Ireland in 1982 was part of a plan to create jobs. The plan was to make Ireland a "European economic powerhouse" through the use of a range of policies such as a new national income accounting system, a new exchange rate, public-private partnerships, a banking union and so on.

In this article I would like to go through Newman's work and suggest the key areas of the NEP that have contributed most significantly to the Irish success story of the last few decades.

The importance of public ownership

For the first time ever, the government owned all of the economy. This was a huge change from the pre-NEP situation in the UK, where the major financial institutions were privately owned. The new NEP was an example of how to move from the ownership of the economy through the institutions to ownership of the economy through the individuals.

Many of the benefits from the NEP include the creation of the new National Insurance Agency, the creation of a new National Asset Management Agency, the opening of the state bank and the transfer of its shares to the State.

These key elements have contributed to the enormous success of the Irish economy and have resulted in a strong and flexible public sector. A good example of this is the Irish Bank Resolution Corporation (IBRC).

Ireland was the first country in the world to introduce a statutory bank resolution organisation. The IBRC was the first non-government institution in the world to be declared solvent, a milestone that contributed to Ireland becoming a leading banking union country. It is not a coincidence that the country is one of the fastest growing economies in the world.

The creation of the IBRC allowed the government to take control of the country's financial problems, and as a result, in 2011 Ireland became the only country in Europe to meet all of the IMF lending criteria.

The creation of the National Assets Management Agency

In the 1980s Ireland had a debt of over €30 billion. This was an increase from the previous year's debt of just over €2 billion. The situation was not improving.

In response to the increase in debt, the government decided to take action. It decided to create the National Asset Management Agency (NAMA) as an independent body to manage and manage public assets. In the context of the NEP, the NAMA is the body in charge of the implementation of the NEP.

NAMA was set up and appointed on 2nd January, 1982, by the previous government as part of the plan to create jobs and to reduce the size of the public sector.

The NAMA set out a number of reforms. They included:

Creating an Irish equivalent of the National Pension Fund (NPF).

Allocating money from the NPF to the banks.

Eliminating a tax break for the Irish Bank Resolution Corporation (IBRC).

The NAMA also set up the Irish Pension Fund, which had the same objectives as the NAMA.
headline: Holding liberalism to account: the prescience of John Henry Newman

Great Barrier Reef: record coral levels, survey finds

A team of scientists from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS) have recorded a record level of coral cover on the reef in the last two years, and say they are seeing a new level of ecological resilience.

The survey, conducted by the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS) and the Australian Research Council, examined the status of coral on the Great Barrier Reef in the northern Great Barrier Reef Marine Park, located off the Queensland coast. The survey covered the period from July 2013 to July 2014, and found coral cover covering a greater area and depth than ever recorded in the Great Barrier Reef.

The study also found that the rate of coral death is increasing, with a record-low coral death rate of 0.05 per cent recorded in the last three years.

The research team said they were not surprised by the trend, saying that coral is generally resilient to bleaching events in the region.

The researchers said: "The Great Barrier Reef has experienced record mortality in the past two years of around 0.05 per cent, which is less than one per cent of previous mortality rates for the reef.

"The rate of mortality on the reef is expected to increase further this year due to the continued occurrence of a low coral bleaching event in the eastern part of the Reef, which is thought to be the primary cause of mortality on the reef."

However, they acknowledged that some reefs are more sensitive than others and could still be in danger. The research team pointed out that some reefs in the northern Great Barrier Reef are particularly vulnerable, particularly in the western part of the Reef, where coral cover was at record low levels.

The research team said they have published their report, which they say will inform the ongoing research on the reef.
headline: Great Barrier Reef has record levels of coral, says survey

A group of children's authors have called for a ban on all policy-making that involves children.

The children's group, Parents of Children With Autism (POCA), said it believes that government needs to have "the courage to listen to all sides of the debate, rather than just one" before making decisions.

The group said it supports a universal child allowance (UA) and believes that such a policy should be introduced as soon as possible to provide an opportunity for families to move on from any issues that may be affecting their child.

Although the group did not provide further details of its proposed policy, it said that families should have the ability to choose what is best for their child.

"Our children don't need to be the first priority in government policy, and children with autism shouldn't be the last," said POCA.

"They should be a major part of policy-making and our children should have a say in what is best for their health and wellbeing."

However, the group said that its stance was not meant to detract from the well-intentioned efforts made by the Minister for Children, Children with Special Educational Needs and Children's Minister for Social Services.

"All parents want their children to be well-treated and their children to have an opportunity to have a positive influence on their communities. Our children shouldn't be ignored," said POCA.

"We support the universal child allowance as a step towards providing an opportunity for parents to have a say in their children's welfare."

The group called for greater emphasis on the inclusion of parents in policies, particularly in areas such as health, education and social assistance, so that they would feel an "assessment of their contribution" to policy-making could be undertaken.

The statement was released after a meeting between its members and the minister for children, children with special educational needs and children's minister for social services, Mary Mitchell O'Connor.

The group held the meeting in the Dóchas district in Co Tipperary in order to lobby the Government for a complete ban on all policy-making involving children.

The meeting was closed to the media.

POCA said its current policy was that it would support any effort to make the policy-making process more inclusive.

"The story of an Irish woman who had a baby with a Russian man is coming to light. The mother of the baby was born in Russia in July, 2015. The mother was married to a Russian man and she had no intention of adopting the baby. However, she decided to take the baby to the United States where she planned to get her husband back.

When the baby was born the baby boy and his mother decided to travel to Ireland to get back the child.

The mother told reporters about the trip, saying 'I felt happy and comfortable here because there are so many people who love me here and love me here. They were really nice.'

The parents took the baby back to Russia and after a few days they decided to give the baby back to the Russian father. The mother said: 'I'm very happy with how it turned out. I was really happy and I know that the boy was a blessing.'

The baby had been born with a defect in his heart and lungs. He was only two and a half weeks old when he was born and the mother was not able to take him home with her and was forced to give him up for adoption.

When the Russian couple returned to Russia, the mother said 'it was very hard to meet the father and the boy because they are different people. They were completely different.'

In December 2015 the couple decided to take the baby back to Ireland where they planned to get their son back.

In an interview with the local Irish paper, The Herald, the Russian man who adopted the baby said: 'We wanted to be in a family. I'm a very happy man, married and having children. The woman has been very good to us. We would like to have children. We did not know that this might be a possibility and that we might have some problems. But I think it was a good choice. We met some good people here, some families and we want to be a family.'

However, when the couple returned to Ireland they discovered that a child protection agency had registered their son with the Department of Social Protection. This meant that the mother was immediately forced to go back to Russia. She did not want to leave her son behind but the department said that the child must be returned.

The country's National Infrastructure Commission (CNI) has warned it could cost €375 billion to achieve the target of 100% renewable energy by 2035.

The Government is seeking to protect Irish-owned mining companies by requiring them to have a right of veto in all discussions about the future of Mercosur, the trade bloc that is one of the most controversial aspects of the EU-Canada trade deal. The Cabinet this afternoon signed the government's proposed amendment to the EU-Mercosur Agreement. The amendment, which passed by the Senate and the Dáil on Thursday, will require all parties to the trade deal to guarantee Irish interests on Mercosur's future. The amendment is expected to be tabled in the coming days.

Background

On 18 July 2016, Ireland became the third country after Chile and the UK to ratify the EU-Canada free trade agreement (Ceta). Ireland's Minister for Foreign Affairs Simon Coveney also made a speech at the signing ceremony in Brussels.

The EU-Mercosur Agreement (Ceta) will make the European single market an inclusive, global market, with a strong voice for workers' rights and fair rules, but also a new foundation for economic and monetary union, the Prime Minister of Ireland said yesterday.

The EU-Canada agreement, known as Ceta, will provide a new basis for the EU and Canada to develop a new economic and monetary union. The agreement will create a single market in goods and services, where trade rules will apply to all Member States and will cover all goods and services, including investment and financial services. This will be the first such agreement between the EU and Canada in over 50 years, since the FTA that was signed in 1984. Ceta will establish a new economic and monetary union, the Government of Ireland said.

The Government has published a paper on the details of the Ceta agreement. This document has been obtained under the Official Secrets Act, which was enacted in 1995 to protect certain government information.

The Government of Ireland's amended amendment to the EU-Mercosur Agreement will require all parties to the EU-Canada trade deal to guarantee Irish interests in Mercosur's future, Minister of Foreign Affairs Simon Coveney said. The amendment will provide for a minimum of 12 months' advance notice to EU Members State, which will enable Ireland's interests to be protected.

The Minister said that he hopes this amendment will secure the EU-Mercosur agreement. He said that Ireland's ratification will ensure that, in the event of a breach of the Ceta provisions, the Irish state will have the right to intervene in the dispute resolution process, through the European Court of Justice.

Ireland has one of the highest profile sectors within the EU economy. Approximately 30,000 people are employed in the mining industry in Ireland.

The minister said that Ireland will continue to engage with its international partners to enhance the future of Ireland's mining sector, and that the Government of Ireland intends to pursue a range of policies to support the Irish mining industry in the future.

The War

There was a great deal of speculation about the true origins of the Russia-Ukraine War and what happened to the USSR as a result of this conflict. I was interested in both of these questions so, following the GDI in the UK, I researched the war and its consequences.

How did the USSR end up fighting a war with Ukraine?

The Soviet Union lost over 40 million people between 1941-1944, according to the United Nations. It had also suffered a similar amount of economic losses as well as a large amount of military losses. The Soviet economy was in a terrible state, largely due to the Great Depression. In this context, Stalin decided to take drastic measures to prevent the Soviet Union from falling into bankruptcy.

The plan was to "liberate" Ukraine – a region between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, which was under Russian control. Under Stalin's plan, the Soviet Union invaded Ukraine in March 1941 and the war came to an end with a negotiated peace at the Yalta Conference in late February 1942.

What happened in Ukraine and what changed?

After the Soviet invasion, the USSR created its own army and began to develop its military capabilities. It also began to build up its economy, especially in the fields of agricultural production and trade. The Soviet Union had always been considered a communist country but, on the eve of war with the United States, it came to be seen as a very powerful, prosperous, modern, and technologically advanced country.

In 1943 the new Soviet Union began to build a large amount of new weapons and began to move toward a doctrine of mass production as well. This, combined with Stalin's aggressive actions in the east, led to the USSR's defeat in the war.

Why does this conflict still exist?

While the USSR's defeat at the end of World War II has been a part of the history of the Soviet Union, the war continues to be remembered with great importance and significance by many Russians. There is still a strong sense of Russian nationalism, a desire to protect the nation and its traditions, and a need to rebuild and maintain the nation's military capabilities.

The move was announced on 28 June 2012. The Irish government said it wanted to "restore order and fiscal stability" and ensure there was a "responsible fiscal balance". The tax, as reported by the Irish Times on 24 June, is "an income tax to pay for social welfare".

Irish Prime Minister Enda Kenny said: "The new law will address the very serious financial challenges that have developed in Ireland over the past year, with a total deficit in the budget of €40bn.

Ireland is not like other countries

A group of Irish activists has called for the country to plant native trees, including native Irish oak trees, to combat the negative effects of Ireland's heavily planted foreign oak and pine trees.

The group, which is called IOReoTrees, has been pushing for Ireland to plant native trees for more than a year.

The group has been supported by the Irish Forestry Authority, which has had meetings with representatives of Irish growers to discuss their concerns.

The group's leader, Jim Kelly, said the group wants to see "a big shift in the way we manage Ireland's native oak and pine forests."

A spokesperson for IOReoTrees, Colin Kelly, said: "The fact is that Ireland has a very large number of native oak trees which are threatened by the rapid growth in the number of foreign trees being planted.

"We're not suggesting the country should be planting too many foreign trees - but the fact that more than 1,000 new trees a year are being planted in Ireland means we must look at new ways to manage them."

He pointed out that "most native trees are planted in the autumn. The next time IOReoTrees have a meeting we will invite the Minister for the Environment to speak in favour of protecting native trees."

Last month, the IOReoTrees committee held an international meeting to discuss the topic.

It produced a report, which argued that Ireland should be planting more native trees rather than a greater reliance on imported European species.

The report recommended using native species instead of foreign species in a number of ways.

One of the recommendations was to develop "native oak management plans" for Ireland, which include the planting of native trees.

The group has also lobbied the Irish Forestry Authority, which is responsible for managing the Irish trees, to consider native oak planting on its behalf.

The group also wants the Irish government to consider the development of a scheme for "non-native" trees - such as native oak and native birches, which are not grown commercially and which provide an important service to the country.

Mr Kelly said that native trees are "very important for Ireland's economic viability" and that "nobody in Ireland wants an Irish oak".

"If you want to create a green Ireland, you have to look at your native trees," he said.

Hull schoolchildren are getting more school lunch than many in the country would like to know.

Last year, nearly 12% of all primary students were given a free school meal, up from 8% in 2004.

But last month a study by the National Children's Centre at the University of Hull has found a much higher rate of eating takeaway food than schools typically offer.

In the study, students were given an hour to prepare the lunch that the school served, including bread, soup, butter, jam and salad.

The students could eat a variety of foods, including takeaway sandwiches, salad and crisps and many chose not to buy them.

But not all the food was prepared by the school.

Just 3.4% of all students chose takeaway and this was followed by cheese, cakes, and ice cream, 3.7%, juice, 3.4% and chocolate, 2.5%.

The food also varied according to socio-economic status.

Most students were offered bread, soup, butter and crisps in a single serving. But some students, particularly those from more affluent backgrounds, were offered more than one serving.

The study of the pupils' choices shows that when a child's family income is higher, the children are more likely to have the option of a free school lunch, which can be beneficial to their health, the report says.

The study also revealed that students from more privileged families were more likely to have their school offer takeaway.

The researchers say that the increase in food choices could be due to better-off families paying more attention to the food quality and choosing healthier food for their children.

They are working on a follow-up study on students' school lunch choices in 2014 to see how they have changed since the last time the report was published.
headline: Top 8: Supermarket cheddars put to the taste test for school lunches

The letter from Mrs Keaveney states that the minister should take "immediate steps to ensure that an Army career would suit my family".

"I have come to a point in my life where the decision not to serve in the army, after 25 years of serving my country, has left me extremely disappointed," she writes in the letter to the Defence Minister.

"If your office can intervene and help resolve this issue for us all, it would be deeply appreciated."

Mr Coveney said he would not comment on Mrs Keaveney's letter.

In a letter to the Irish Examiner, Mr Keaveney says that he will not be making any decision on whether or not to serve in the Army for a year.

He adds that his family's decision to not go to the Army has been "extremely difficult" and has left him "extremely angry".

"It is my duty to put aside personal feelings and take what is right for the people of the North West.

"I believe that the Government is right to set the precedent that I should serve my country, but I am not prepared to serve a second term in the North West as a member of the House of Commons."

Mr Coveney added that he has the same position as Mr Keaveney on the issue of a career for a member of the Army.

However he said he would make a decision about whether Mr Keaveney should go to the Army in the next few weeks.

The Taoiseach stressed that it is the Irish Defence Forces' job to offer jobs to people who want to be in the Defence Forces.

"There is no suggestion that he should not do that," he said.

Mr Coveney said he was satisfied that Defence Forces bosses had listened to his advice.

He added that he has received no such response from Defence Forces bosses about Mr Keaveney's letter.

However he said he was satisfied that Mr Keaveney's letter was sent to the right person.

The Taoiseach said: "I have spoken to Colm Keaveney and his wife Colm has been in touch with Simon Coveney.

"I think the right person to talk to about this is Colm Keaveney.

"I think that it is a very serious issue and he will be talking with Simon Coveney.

"Colm Keaveney will be speaking to Simon Coveney and I think Colm is very much interested in having an answer to this issue."

Mr Coveney said he had spoken with Mr Keaveney on Monday.
headline: Officers would not recommend Defence Forces career to friends or relatives, survey shows

text:
A knife attack on an off-duty garda in Dublin has the authorities in a tizzy after it is claimed a member of the country's Muslim community carried out the brutal attack.

The armed, hooded assailant is said to have been a member of the Islamic State group and a member of a group called the "Dublin Brigade", it has been claimed.

The victim, a garda from the Garda National Immigration Bureau, was stabbed in the back of the leg during a robbery on the streets of the city's Finglas area.

Gardaí said on Sunday the victim had been attacked while on his way to work at a nearby petrol station. He was stabbed multiple times and his attacker fled the scene on foot.

The assailant, believed to be a member of the Dublin Brigade, is said to have attempted to stab his own victim on his way to work, but was unsuccessful.

"The garda who was at the scene immediately after the attack has been taken to hospital for treatment," it has been claimed.

The alleged assailant is a man who is not known to the gardaí, a source told the Irish Examiner.

The Garda Press Office said it was unable to confirm or deny the details in the article.

"The Garda Press Office does not comment on the personal details of the victims of garda investigations," a spokesperson said.

"Our thoughts are with the family and friends of the garda who was seriously injured in this incident."

A spokesman for the Irish Government confirmed that the Garda had "assessed the matter" in relation to the incident.

"The Garda Commissioner has also issued advice to gardaí regarding the circumstances of the attack and any possible threats to any member of the public," the spokesman said.

"We are appealing to the public to remain vigilant and report any suspicious activity to gardaí."

A spokesman for the Minister for Public Expenditure and Reform confirmed that a minister of the State had been in contact with gardaí.

"This was an incident which is now being assessed by the Gardaí and the Minister," the spokesman said.

"The Minister for Public Expenditure and Reform is in constant contact with the gardaí."
headline: Ireland’s first Islamist-inspired knife attack raises urgent questions about extremist threats

"This is an incredibly grave situation," said Mr Johnson, noting the "biggest spike ever" at the Cabinet, with 10 cases from September, including five women and five men.

He also wants the Irish government to create a dedicated department for tracking the cases and establish a national register of the victims.

Johnson noted that there are other cases in the Northern Ireland court system "but I believe that these cases need to be handled by a different body or a different mechanism".

He is also demanding that the Government take immediate action to deal with the issue and bring all of the perpetrators of crimes against women and girls to justice.

"I have been working with the Justice Minister to develop the possibility of introducing a new law in the Northern Ireland Assembly to deal with the issue of women and girls being abused," he said.

The HSE has launched a new app aimed at patients who suffer from mental health issues.

The app, called Healthlink, allows patients to view data regarding their health status and to request information about their mental health.

In addition, patients are encouraged to log their health conditions so that an emergency contact can be made should something go wrong.

A spokesperson for the Health Service Executive said that the app is intended to assist people who suffer from mental health issues.

"We know that having access to their health data is an important part of dealing with mental health issues," she said.

"Our app gives patients the opportunity to get in touch with their GP and see their health data. We want to make sure that as many people as possible can access this data and that we do not miss any individuals with a mental health issue."

In terms of the app, patients have access to a number of different screens to view their health data. These include an alert if they have suffered a mental health attack, a personal care assistant, a support worker, and a personal support assistant for the person with the mental health condition.

The app is available for download on the Apple App Store in Ireland for free, or can be purchased for €4.99.

Healthlink will be available from 15 July 2017 and is available in English and Spanish. It is available on the Apple App Store here in Ireland.

The app is the brainchild of Dr Paul Kelly and Dr Stephen O'Malley.

The duo launched Healthlink at the end of last year.

In response to the launch of Healthlink, the HSE launched a consultation on the app, and received responses from a number of mental health service users.

Healthlink was designed to meet the needs of the growing number of people who suffer from mental health problems.
headline: HSE launches app allowing patients access to their health data

The Israeli army on Monday shot dead a Palestinian attacker in the West Bank city of Hebron. The soldier killed the attacker as he tried to flee, the military said.

More than 100 Palestinians, most of them attackers, have been killed since the start of the year in Israeli military operations in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.

Russian-backed hackers, a group which claimed responsibility for a cyber attack on the Democratic National Committee, have now announced an attack on a top US political party.

The new effort follows an earlier attempt to infiltrate the Democratic National Committee in July.

The group, dubbed "Guccifer 2.0" (pronounced "GOO-kay", so it sounds like a "Guccifer"), claims it has obtained information from a hacker who is said to be a senior official of the Ukrainian presidential administration.

The group says it was able to take control of the DNC email server, which is the primary source for a trove of leaked emails that led to the resignation of the DNC chair.

It says it has released the emails because it believes it is "important to expose the truth behind the actions of the US government and the DNC".

According to the group, "there's evidence that the DNC and the Clinton campaign were involved in a network hack, with an aim to influence the election results".

It says it did not release information "in the interest of political expediency" or to "show American people what is the real reason of their discontent".

The group claims it is targeting US political parties "with their own agents".

"Our goal is to make public the whole truth about the so called 'Russia-Trump campaign'. We'll be exposing every single fact related to this," it says.

In July, the hacker, who goes by the alias "Guccifer 2.0", released a trove of emails stolen from the DNC.

The leaks suggested that DNC staffers favoured Hillary Clinton over rival Bernie Sanders during the presidential primaries.

The DNC eventually suspended the operations of the email server which had been hacked by the hacker.

The hack, however, appears to have only caused temporary disruptions.

The emails from June showed that the DNC favored Clinton, but that it then decided against holding an open primary in favour of a more democratic process.

The leak followed the resignation of the DNC's chairwoman, Debbie Wasserman Schultz.

In March, the hacker claimed to have stolen documents from the Clinton campaign, as well as from the Democratic National Committee (DNC) and from a separate group of hackers called Cozy Bear.

"The campaign hack may be a smokescreen for additional operations against the Democratic Party and to prepare for an even more difficult scenario", the hacker claimed.

"We have already released a file of stolen documents and we can say that we have gained access to the entire network of the Clinton campaign, which can be used to send a message to the Democratic National Committee and the Democratic Party leadership as a whole".

However, the hacker has only provided the names of the Democratic candidates who have been targeted by the attack.

It's unclear if the hacker, who is said to be linked to Russian intelligence agencies, has been involved in hacking attacks against other countries.

It's also unclear whether the hacker is directly linked to the Russian government, or if the group is an offshoot of the Russian intelligence services, or if the hackers are part of a wider hacking attack.

The US intelligence agencies have been investigating the hacks, but have not publicly linked them to Russia.
headline: Russian group blamed for hacking Democrats in 2016 ‘attempting new intrusions’

Fw de Klerk, the man who brought apartheid to South Africa and served as its first president, has died at 85.

Mr de Klerk, who won his first election in 1948 and served as president from 1961 to 1975, died on Monday at a government-run hospital in Pretoria.

South African media say he had been in a coma since November last year after suffering a stroke.

"South Africa's last president dies in a hospice in Pretoria, a month after suffering a stroke," the Express Tribune (iretribune.co.za) reported.

Mr de Klerk was born in Johannesburg and was educated in England, before becoming president in 1967.

The Mirror reported the death of Mr de Klerk to South African media with a headline reading "The Last of the Blondes".

The Mirror reported he had been suffering from Alzheimer's disease and was the only president to be diagnosed with this disease.

A memorial service was held for him at the Nelson Mandela Bayfront Stadium, Soweto, on Tuesday evening.

South African President Jacob Zuma paid tribute to Mr de Klerk.

He said: "He was the last of the blondes, a legend who brought South Africa into the world. He would be greatly missed".

Mr de Klerk was elected in 1948 as a member of the Alliance Party and served as president for five years, from 1961 to 1975.

He had previously served as justice minister and minister for communications.

Mr de Klerk was the son of a jeweller from KwaZulu-Natal province.

He was the first president to visit apartheid-era Pretoria, where he made a speech in support of the African National Congress in October 1963.

He also toured the country during the struggle and spoke to thousands in the capital.

Mr de Klerk told the Guardian he was "totally against the regime" and would not have supported it.

But he said the regime would have to be overthrown through constitutional means, such as elections and popular protests.

He added that he was concerned about the future of the country and the future of his son, who has Parkinson's disease.

He is the only surviving head of state to have undergone a regime change.

In 2009, then President Thabo Mbeki announced Mr de Klerk would be the country's honorary president, a post which was bestowed upon him in 1994.

At the time, the ANC president said he had felt a "sense of relief" when he received the honour.

South Africa was once the most powerful and prosperous country on Earth, with millions of people living in poverty.

However, the economy deteriorated significantly in the 1990s, leading to a series of economic crises which hit the ruling ANC hard.

The end of apartheid, which ended the racial oppression of black South Africans, began in 1994.

During his life, Mr de Klerk was a passionate advocate of social justice and equal opportunities, making him a hero of the South African black community.

The president made a number of speeches and was known for his colourful and colorful language.

He was a close friend of Nelson Mandela.
headline: South Africa’s last apartheid president FW de Klerk dies at 85

"I'm worried I'll end up as a carer for my mother-in-law," says the Dáithí, a member of the Labour party who said he is being treated for depression after the publication of the Daily Mail's report that he and his wife are planning to have their second child.

Dáithí, who has been a councillor in Galway for the last 18 months, is described in the Sunday People as "a great guy".

It says he is "in his late 20s, has a wife and child and his illness is not life-threatening".

Dáithí said he was feeling "terrible". "This is the last thing I need. It's going to get worse," he said.

He has been attending AA meetings for two years and he was going to have a couple of sessions to deal with his illness before "everything blew up".

His wife, who works in IT, is suffering from depression too. "I think I might get a couple more sessions but I can't take the risk. I'm very tired and I want to stop because I've been working very hard and my health has suffered."

Dáithí said he wanted to have a second child "after I get through this".

"It's hard to see what's happening. I don't know if it's my illness but things aren't going as I'd hoped," he said.

"I'm really unhappy, upset. It seems I'm not a very good person. I don't know how I'm going to cope with this. I've been going to AA meetings for two years. I get up in the morning and I'm worried.

"The day I get the diagnosis of depression is the day I want to have a baby. I don't know what to do about it.

"My family and I are in a state of shock. The family have put me through a lot and we just want to help. It's been very difficult."

He said he was in the UK with his wife when the story broke. "We were staying with a friend in London. She was upset with me. She was getting on with her life but I was getting frustrated and upset about something."

He said they had a drink and she told him she had been drinking. She had been feeling guilty about that and was upset about her illness. "I thought this could work out and it could be a good thing. But I've seen the way it has gone. I've been really concerned."

The couple had been to AA meetings in London and he was "taking care of me", he said. "It was a little bit of a shock. I had no idea it would escalate. I just wanted to know what was going on."

He has been contacted by friends and family of people who have had similar experiences.

He has sent a message to Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and TD Aodhán Ó Ríordáin urging him to intervene, saying "it is not a personal attack on you".

"I really do feel for Dáithí, it's his health. I am very concerned about the impact of my illness on my family and friends and the impact on his wife and child.
headline: Dear Dáithí: I'm worried I'll end up as a carer for my mother-in-law

By Aileen O'Doherty

The Irish Examiner

Aileen O'Doherty

January 20th 2015

In the first chapter of her debut novel, Sara Ochs tells the story of an Irish girl growing up in England, with her father still away from home and with the family struggling to cope with her growing up.

In this first chapter, Sara is only able to read the first few lines. Her father doesn't tell her where he is in England. She has no idea what is going on around her. As she spends her time reading and thinking about the story she is about to tell, her feelings towards her father rise and fall. As we move towards the end of the book, we can see a small glimpse of her father as he reads a newspaper about a recent court case involving him and the man who he claims raped her.

One of the best aspects of this book is that the author's voice is so easy to read. We don't need to ask her questions about what she is experiencing. And it is always so easy to relate to her. While it was hard to find anyone else in Dublin speaking English when the book was first released in Ireland, there were a lot of people who wanted to talk to Sara. Sara has found her voice and it is well-written and engaging. It was very hard for me to try and keep up with Sara Ochs reading this book, but it was very well written. In fact, I would go as far as saying this was my favourite book in this book series.

I was expecting a lot more of this book from O'Doherty than I got. She does not seem to have a huge following. The book was released in 2012 and was picked up by a few English publications. So I am not sure how many people know her, but I believe that there is quite a lot of people who do know her and still love her book. And that's a good thing. It seems that Sara Ochs has the ability to write a book that is relatable to everyone. I hope this is the case and, therefore, I have high hopes for Sara Ochs' book.

I would like to say that I enjoyed this book. In fact, I thought it was pretty good. But I think that I would have liked it more if Sara Ochs had written it in Irish. That would have made it much easier for me to connect to it. And then there is another aspect that bothers me a lot when I read stories in English, is the fact that I don't really get to read the Irish language. Most of the time I just get the English language version. I know that the Irish language has many different forms, but I get used to hearing English in my head. Maybe it is time that the author decided to tell this story in Irish.

The most interesting element of Sara Ochs' debut is the fact that her story is so easy to read. O'Doherty writes a very engaging, very engaging story. It is so relatable to everyone in the book. That is a good thing. And if you like a good story, this is certainly one you will love.

The next chapter is where the book really shines. It is very easy to see how Sara and her father are coming to terms with her growing up.
headline: Book Review: Sara Ochs' debut is strikingly assured and accomplished

Tuesday 19 January 2015

The judge who sentenced Jerry Harris to 12 years in prison for an attempt to blow up the Irish parliament has described the former IRA man as 'evil'.

Speaking to the media on Monday, the judge said the former IRA man acted out of a 'lack of understanding of the human being'.

The 46-year-old, who will be eligible for parole in five years time, was convicted last August of the attempted murder of three people during a campaign of violence in Dublin in 2012.

It was his second conviction.

While in prison the convicted murderer spent a lot of time in solitary confinement, often for extended periods at a time.

He claimed the confinement had a 'moody, disconcerting effect' on him.

'He does have a sense of anger, of frustration, of despair at not being able to control himself.

'And he certainly was in a state of mind on occasions to do something that would have been very difficult to control in a normal situation,' said Judge Colm McCarthy at sentencing, according to the Irish Examiner.

The judge added: 'I have to say that a lot of the time you behaved in a very cold, very calculating, very calculating and deliberate way.'

Mr Harris was also convicted of possession of an offensive weapon, unlawful possession of a weapon and attempted murder of two Garda detectives, Stephen McCartan and Eoghan O'Mahony.

He was sentenced to 12 years in prison in May and then told he would be eligible for parole in five years time.

However Mr Harris's lawyer Patrick McGrath said: 'He will not be released until he serves a full sentence and he doesn't want to get the hang of parole until then.'

The former IRA member was first handed a 12-year sentence in August 2012.

A second conviction followed in February 2014, which was handed down under Section 5 of the HSE Act.

In October 2014, the State sought to have Mr Harris's sentence reduced to one year after he was found guilty of possessing an offensive weapon, unlawful possession of a weapon and attempting to commit, or threatening to commit, an offence.

The State claimed that in addition to the previous two convictions, the 'length of his incarceration' had made it too difficult to grant Mr Harris parole, the Irish Examiner has reported.
headline: Jerry Harris says ‘I am not an evil person’ as he receives 12-year sentence

Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov has warned Ukraine against using force in eastern Ukraine, according to a Russian news report.

Lavrov told his German counterpart Frank-Walter Steinmeier in Moscow on Friday that Russia was prepared to support the right of Ukraine's people to self-determination, but that the right of self-determination did not mean that Ukrainian soldiers had the right to open fire and kill civilians, the Interfax news agency reported.

My new friends and I were on a family holiday, and when we got to the airport to board the Eurostar train to London, we were surprised to find out that we were not entitled to a return ticket. We were still staying in the same hotel, we were still living there.

When I was told about the policy, I was incredulous that we were not entitled to a return ticket because our host family hadn't booked one for us.

I asked my boyfriend, one of the other Irish travellers, if he thought it was odd. He told me to take a closer look at the rules, and he seemed surprised, but agreed we weren't entitled.

I have been working in Ireland for more than 10 years and have never experienced this. I was stunned and confused. What happened to our right to travel back home?

When I returned home, I wrote an email to the European Commission to ask what was going on. I received a reply from the UK's Immigration Minister James Brokenshire, who said:

"We will be looking at the letter you are writing and will give further advice on how to check your entitlement to re-entry."

The fact that we are still living in the same hotel as our host family is not sufficient to give us rights. We are still a new EU citizen. So, I am asking for the EU to take a closer look at the situation and to update its rules in light of changing legal circumstances.

We still can't go back to the US, and neither can our friends in Ireland.

'The Insurance Compensation Committee has reported that over the past five years, the average amount of money payable for a family health insurance policy has risen from €7,861 to €10,168, and an increase of 42 percent compared to the previous year.

'The increases have been attributed to rising premiums and the fact that some people can no longer afford their health insurance. The committee states that the average premium payment of €3,037 is now more than seven times the amount paid by the average worker for health insurance in 2010.

'The average increase over five years was 42%, up from €1,944 to €6,743.

'The average cost for a family of four has increased by €1,000.

'This is in addition to the general rate increase of 11.1% for the health insurance sector and the average rate increase of 12.9% for all forms of insurance.

'The Insurance Compensation Committee (ICC) has also identified that many people who are unable to afford the full cost of their health insurance have reduced their expenditure to reduce their premiums.

'The most common reason for reducing spending in this way is to get more coverage, particularly in areas where there is no competition for the policy.

'Some individuals will be able to get a discount on their premiums, so that they can afford more treatment, or they will buy the cheapest policy available at a lower rate.

'While these measures may result in individuals saving money, these measures are expensive and represent a transfer of wealth from those in good health to those in poor health.

'The Insurance Compensation Committee has recommended that all insurance policies should contain a provision where a person's policy does not cover certain types of treatments, or in areas where there is no insurance, where the premium is only for one type of treatment.

'A person in good health can access the full cost of their health insurance without spending more than the equivalent of a €500 annual insurance premium.

'If a person has reduced their spending in an area due to an increase in their expenses, they should not receive any additional benefit, except in the case of an increase in their premiums.

'When they are in need of care, they should have access to the full cost of their insurance.

'The Insurance Compensation Committee has advised that this recommendation should be followed in the form of a separate policy, where the only part of the policy covering the treatment is for a specific type of treatment.

'The Insurance Compensation Committee recommends that the Department of Health should introduce a cap on the amount of money that can be paid for any individual health insurance policy.

'If such a cap is introduced, insurers would have to offer a discount on the full cost of the health insurance policy for all services to be covered in future.

'This would mean that all people who have a health insurance policy would be able to avail of the full cost of their policies in the future.

'The Insurance Compensation Committee also recommends that insurers should be required to offer individuals the option to purchase the maximum quantity of health insurance coverage and to give the full cost of their policy in advance.

'If an individual's policy covers only certain services, they should be able to obtain the maximum amount of coverage without spending more than the maximum amount of money they are allowed under their policy.
headline: Over 65s pay 43% more for health insurance, watchdog finds

Investigators from the Bureau of Alcohol Tobacco Firearms and Explosives (ATF) were called to the governor's Mansion at 1225 S. Third St. around 11:15 a.m. Tuesday on reports of a fire.

Firefighters arrived at the mansion and found a large amount of smoke in the building.

Officials with the Pennsylvania Fire Marshal's Office later said the building had suffered extensive fire damage.

The man, identified as 31-year-old Christopher John E. Anderson, surrendered to police Tuesday afternoon.

Rendell died in 2010, and his wife, former state Supreme Court Justice Janet Rendell, later filed for divorce.

The governor's mansion is located about 25 miles south of Harrisburg.

Donald Trump: Iran "totally in control of [the US] by the way".

Donald Trump on Friday called on Iran to "completely shutdown" the country's nuclear program and warned it would "pay a big price" if the US moves against Tehran's military leaders, according to senior administration officials.

The president-elect had a phone call with Iranian President Hassan Rouhani on Wednesday, but did not announce the outcome of the conversation.

Trump, who was elected US president on Tuesday, has pledged to aggressively challenge Iran's nuclear program to put it on notice that it risks isolation and economic sanctions. He has also suggested the US might use military force against the regime.

The president-elect's warning came the same day as he met with Secretary of State John Kerry, who warned Tehran the US is prepared to take military action against Iran if it fails to halt its nuclear ambitions.

Trump told Rouhani: "You have to give me a signal," and called on Iran to "come to the table" with the US to negotiate in good faith, according to a senior US official who was briefed on the call.

Trump said he has been "very tough" with Iran on its nuclear program in the past, but that Iran will have to make a "much larger payment" and "must respect" a deal reached with the Obama administration in December 2013 on curbing Iran's nuclear activities.

The official said Trump also said the US wants to "get tough" on Iran and will not hesitate to put "our military assets in the region" if necessary.

"The president-elect called for a fundamental shift in US policy and we are looking forward to working with the new administration," said State Department spokeswoman Marie Harf.

"The United States will continue to press the Iranian regime to live up to its end of the bargain, to stop isolating itself, to cease providing material support to terrorist groups and to respect all agreements on Iran's nuclear program."

Iran's supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, has vowed to pursue a nuclear weapons capability in response to the lifting of sanctions on Tehran, which followed the landmark 2015 deal with world powers over Tehran's disputed nuclear program.

In December 2015 the Islamic Republic agreed to a long-term framework deal that was designed to curb Iran's nuclear program in exchange for lifting some sanctions. Iran says its nuclear program is peaceful but fears Washington and its allies could use it to develop missiles.

Iran's nuclear program is under international pressure because the West suspects Tehran is seeking nuclear weapons capacity.

The Trump administration also plans to step up US and Israeli attacks against Iran's nuclear infrastructure to deter Tehran from developing atomic weapons, a senior US official told Reuters on condition of anonymity.

The official said the US was expected to intensify "multiple waves" of attacks against Iran's nuclear facilities, including "chemical, biological and radiological", which would "increase the threat to civilians".

The official also said the US was preparing a new military option in case of a potential Iranian attack on a US naval vessel operating in the Persian Gulf.

In the call with Rouhani, Trump said, "You've been a great friend for many years. We're going to do great things for you. Thank you for your hospitality," according to a senior Trump administration official.
headline: ‘Watch what happens’ – Donald Trump issues new threat to Iran

Seth Rosenfeld and Michael Wessels review The Terror Factory: Inside the New World Order's Electronic Spying Machine (W.W. Norton).

I asked them to respond to a question I posed about why no reputable news organization would publish the book. Here's what they had to say about it:

"The book is a comprehensive, highly detailed account of how the CIA built an electronic spying machine that could secretly monitor and hack any computer on the planet. It was created to counter the threat of terrorism and, more importantly, to enable the agency to spy on its own citizens."

–Michael Wessels, Author of The Terror Factory and Editor-in-Chief, the Review of International Affairs


"The book is the first comprehensive study to examine the worldwide, electronic surveillance network the CIA constructed during the 1990s and launched as part of its campaign to defeat the Soviet Union and its allies. It is a compelling and deeply personal account of the CIA's global war on terrorism. It is also a crucial book for anyone considering the future of American politics and national security."

–Seth Rosenfeld, Editor-in-Chief, the Review of International Affairs


"The Terror Factory is a sweeping, insightful book that sets the stage for a new generation of thinking about the U.S. intelligence community and its role in bringing down a major global superpower."

–Seth Rosenfeld, Editor-in-Chief, the Review of International Affairs


The title of the book is a play on the CIA's old motto "In God We Trust."

The book contains very high level information, including:

A full description of the CIA's "Operation Mockingbird" and its ongoing operations.

A detailed account of how the CIA was able to monitor the lives of tens of thousands of people in the US and around the world using nothing more than their cell phone records.

Details of the massive data gathering operations the CIA conducted, such as the infamous "Stuxnet" malware, and a detailed look at how the CIA was able to "hack back."

How the CIA created "back doors" in all the popular computer operating systems that could be hacked into, which were then used to install and operate a massive collection of malware, including Stuxnet.

How the CIA was able to track cell phone communications from Russia, China, and Iran by exploiting the "back door" vulnerabilities in the software that most computers use.

How the CIA was able to obtain a list of all cell phone numbers in France, England, and Germany. The NSA was also able to obtain the same list of cell phone numbers in the US from the French, German, Russian, Iranian, and Chinese embassies in Washington, DC and other embassies worldwide.

A detailed discussion of how the US has "lost the plot" and is now "spying" on its own people.

Detailed information on the worldwide global electronic surveillance network run by the CIA that was set up to counter the Soviet Union. This network was built around the "New World Order" and included an electronic spy agency, "Echelon" and a massive network of command centers around the world, which were designed to monitor the communications of any person in the world who was a potential threat to the global agenda.

The book is not a simple one, and contains much more than I anticipated.
headline: Book Review: Big profits in the global spying game

UN Secretary General Ban Ki-moon says people are looking for leaders to lead them out of a "mess" of domestic and international crises.

The United Nations chief said the public is becoming disillusioned with governments in a number of countries and they are looking for leaders to "lead the way in trying to find solutions".

Speaking to the Irish Examiner during a visit to Ireland, Mr Ban said: "People look for leaders who are willing to lead them in trying to find solutions for the things that they see on the ground."

He said the people of Ireland, like many others, are "not satisfied with the way things are" and are looking for leaders "who are willing to lead the way in trying to find solutions for the things they see on the ground".

He added that a good number of people were looking to a "new type of leadership".

"They look for leaders who are willing to lead the way in trying to find solutions. "People are looking for leaders who are willing to come out and talk to people who are looking for a new kind of leadership," he said.

Mr Ban said people are looking for leaders who are willing to come out and talk to people who are looking for a new kind of leadership.

He said that many of the countries in the world are struggling with a number of issues including rising living standards, population growth, poverty, terrorism, climate change and social unrest.

"A lot of the people, who are looking for leadership, want leaders who are willing to listen to them," he said. "When it comes to the issues of the future, they want leaders who are willing to lead in trying to find solutions."

Mr Ban said many of the issues in the world that people are concerned about are "not new".

"There have always been crises, there always will be crises. What has changed recently is the level of intensity, the pace of it, the pace of change, the impact that it has had on people," he said. "But, for the most part, what has changed recently is the scale of the crisis. It is like it is a continuous and ongoing thing and that it is very hard to put a finger on the scale of the crisis."

He said he hopes the issue of terrorism will not be allowed to "take off" and will be tackled in a "different way".

"If you look at some of the things that have happened recently in the world, the levels of terror attacks, the level of conflict in Africa. How can you take it off?" he asked.

Mr Ban said that one of the challenges is how to deal with the issue of terrorism.

"How can you deal with terrorism? People say to me 'How can you not deal with terrorism?' What's it gonna take to deal with terrorism? How many countries can we keep out of the conflict, how many countries can we keep out of the conflict and where do we start to try to do that? How do we bring some order back into the world?" he asked.

He said the world has to be on "high alert" to deal with the situation.

"When we look at the terrorist threat, it is growing more and more dangerous," he said.

"We have to be on high alert.
headline: UN chief says people are looking to leaders for way out of ‘mess’

"The artist responsible for the controversial artwork at the top of a high rise in London must be arrested immediately," she said.

The artwork, the "Banksy" was erected in March on the roof of a building on the Canary Wharf luxury residential development.

Sinn Féin Westminster group chairman Martin McGuinness described it as a "disgusting" act and an insult to the memory of John Lennon who died of a heroin overdose in 1980.

The work was described as a tribute to the late Beatle and his band The Beatles and depicted a man standing on a ladder and holding a "B" and a "G" sign.

A statement from Sinn Féin Westminster said Mr McGuinness had requested that the London Borough of Kensington and Chelsea Police Service arrest the artist responsible for the artwork.

Mr McGuinness said: "Sinn Féin Westminster will be raising the matter with the Metropolitan Police at the earliest opportunity.

"Mr McGuinness believes that this act has no place in the 21st century and a further arrest should take place at the earliest opportunity.

"If we cannot get the artist under control we will move to the High Court to seek a judicial review of the arrest."

A Kensington and Chelsea Police spokesman said: "Police at Kensington and Chelsea have been in contact with the artist and will continue to investigate.

"We continue to appreciate the public's support and are very grateful for their patience while investigations continue."

The "Banksy" painting has caused a stir in the UK with its use by members of the anarchist group Anarchist-Communist Party in a campaign to reclaim the "Graffiti Bank" on the city's South Bank.

The group recently sprayed the "Graffiti Bank" and replaced it with a different Banksy artwork, depicting two men holding a swastika.

Turkey to extend hand of friendship to Greece: PM

Ankara has given Greece an extra six months to reach a political solution to its decades-long dispute with the Turkish Republic, the Turkish president announced on Monday, in a move that puts Greece and Turkey on a collision course.

"Greece must immediately and fully address its financial obligations. There has been no delay in fulfilling the obligations so far, and the Greek side must be more cooperative," said President Abdullah Gül.

"I call on all parties to respect the Greek position and abide by the principles of the European Union," the president said, reiterating his position on the issue during his recent visit to Vienna.

Greece is currently unable to pay the 3 billion euro debt, while the Turkish government continues to deny any political pressure on Ankara, despite recent claims made by Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.

"The Greek side should be more cooperative, otherwise this will be a major blow for Turkey," he said.

Gül also reiterated his firm stance on the Cyprus issue, saying it is clear to him that Turkey, along with all the countries in the EU, was "guilty in the end of their actions" when they tried to change the Cyprus issue to a referendum on reunification, which would have broken up the country.

"The issue of Cyprus has no solution, and it should never have had," he said.
headline: Greek PM willing to extend ‘hand of friendship’ to long-time rival Turkey

More than one hundred years on from that tumultuous day, a young Dubliner, who lives and works in Ireland, said he was proud of his country today.

Irish immigrant to Ireland

The man, who is from the United Kingdom, said that while he was not in a hurry to emigrate from the Republic of Ireland, he wished to be there to spend a few days with friends and family.

Marking milestones

'A warm welcome'

He said that he had spent the day relaxing and enjoying his surroundings.

The death of a Poet Michael Longley at the age of 76 has left many in the poetry community devastated by the passing of one of Ireland's most talented writers and poet-activists.

Mr Longley had previously been employed by the Irish Examiner and by the National Youth Council.

He had published two collections, The Migrant, published by the National Youth Council and a collection of poetry called The Traveller.

Mr Longley was one of the founders of Dublin's Literary Theatre and the co-founder of the literary journal The Dublin Post, among other positions.

The Poet's Voice will pay tribute to Mr Longley at a reception on Thursday.

Ciarán Lynch, chairman of the Irish Examiner, said the death had left many poets and art lovers in mourning.

"At the funeral in Tallaght on Friday morning the world of poetry was in shock," he said.

"Michael was a poet who left an indelible mark on the field of Irish poetry, and on its reputation.

"The funeral will serve to mark the end of his life."

Mr Longley is survived by his wife, Susan, and his two children from his marriage to a Dublin teacher.

A funeral will be held at 10am on Thursday at St Patrick's Cathedral.

A member of the public came forward to say he mistook an escaped squirrel for a rat in Dublin's Parnell Square this morning.

The unidentified male was walking along the pavement when he spotted the rodent, which was carrying a paper bag.

"I was in the middle of a conversation with the lady next to me and my first reaction was that I thought it was a squirrel," he said.

"Then I thought it was a rat, but then I thought I should probably get to know it better, so I asked her what it was.

"She said she thought it was a rat and I thought 'okay, that's what I thought, I should ask them'.

"So, I approached a couple of police and the gardaí and said to them 'where is this rat?'

"They said 'oh, it's a rat, it's in Parnell Square'.

"I thought 'what?'.

"Then I saw a little rat-looking thing about 4in from my right and I said 'oh, that's not a rat, that's a squirrel'.

"Then I saw the man and said 'is that a rat?'

"He said 'that is a rat' and I said 'do you know how to pronounce it?'

"He said 'I don't know, it's a name I've heard somewhere before'.

"He said 'and it looks like it's just about to go'.

"So I just walked away, and then this thing just sort of walked off.

"It was a little bit of a surprise."

The gardaí have sent a photo of the animal to the European Commission which says the rat is a cross between a squirrel and a rat.

In an email to the EU's wildlife crime centre, it said the squirrel/rat hybrid is one of about 40 species of hybrids between squirrels and rats.

"We have received this photograph from the gardaí of a squirrel-rat hybrid at Parnell Square," it said.

"The gardaí are currently collecting information from the public as to whether the animal is a cross of a squirrel and a rat.

"We would like to ensure that we are as cautious as possible with this species."
headline: Friday's Evening Round-Up: EU summit, Good Friday Agreement and mistaken identity of rodent

'If you can't beat them here, then beat them at home'

By Mairin Hughes

A car ban which has been in place in Cork city centre since 2010 appears to have had little effect on the number of people driving.

An online survey of 1,000 people found that only 13 per cent said they had been arrested for driving in Cork city centre in the past 12 months. This number had fallen by 10 per cent on last year's level.

On a similar survey last year, 18 per cent of Cork's population said they had been caught driving in the city centre.

The findings come at a time of concern that people are not being held responsible for their actions by the law.

As reported in The Irish Examiner yesterday, a new campaign has begun calling for tougher enforcement of the city centre's 'car ban' – the ban which was introduced in July 2010.

In the past, a Garda press release has revealed that there has been an increase in the number of people who have been stopped for driving offences in the city centre in the past 12 months, but the Garda press officer told The Irish Examiner yesterday that his agency had only seen an increase in the number of people stopped in Cork city centre.

He added: "When the car ban was introduced, there was a concern about the number of people driving. A Garda sergeant was on duty at the time. He confirmed that there was an increase in people being stopped, but that was at the time there was no other policing activity."

Last year, a garda spokesperson said that there was no reason for Garda attention to be drawn away from other priorities, such as criminal justice, and that the campaign was "merely a demonstration to bring to the attention of our friends in other parts of the country a similar situation in the city centre".

However, the garda press officer told The Irish Examiner that there was a concern that the campaign had "got a bit out of hand", given the Garda's "relentless" efforts to combat serious crimes such as serious assaults, burglaries and car thefts. He added: "We are quite clear on what we are after: the prevention of crime. We are not talking about a campaign."

The campaign includes a website, which is available to view here. It also includes a questionnaire.

In the past, the Cork City Council has stated that it is "committed to keeping cars off the road". It has stated that if a car is not "passable" to a person, their driver should be notified to pick it up. The council has been accused of being too lenient in its enforcement of the ban.
headline: Calls for more enforcement of Cork's Patrick St car ban

text:
"Education Minister Eoghan Murphy has announced a €1 million fund to provide free books in primary schools across Ireland.

The announcement came at a Cabinet meeting today in Dublin.

The money will be used to provide up to 80,000 primary school children with free books, including titles like 'The Little Prince', 'Fifty Shades of Grey', and 'The Hunger Games' which will be made available in the schools' libraries for free.

"I also want to reassure parents that as long as they are registered in their child's primary school, they will be able to access free books on their bookshelf," the minister said.

"These free books will be available in primary schools across Ireland and will be available in their libraries on a first come, first served basis."

This announcement follows similar announcements by other Ministers, including Education Minister Ruairi Quinn, who has announced a €3 million programme for disadvantaged children and Young Life Minister Eoghan Murphy, who has announced a €2 million fund for free books.

All these announcements are part of a wider initiative to offer children with learning difficulties the opportunity to learn in a free environment.

"We've always said that children with learning difficulties need to be in school to learn," said Mr Murphy.

"They are entitled to quality access to books. They should not be in school just to learn.

"Our aim is to ensure that every child in every school can access quality access to books, including the books from the library."

This announcement is part of the new 'Irish Access' programme, which is a cross-border initiative to promote, encourage and improve the availability of the best available free books to schoolchildren.

"This is a huge amount of money to spend on children's books, but we have already seen the success of this initiative in schools in different parts of Ireland," said Mr Murphy.

"And we want to see it replicated across the rest of the country and across the world."
headline: Education Minister announces €1m fund for free books in primary schools
