text:
"A couple of days ago, we wrote about a worrying increase in the number of people not answering calls from contact tracers.

The article noted that in Dublin, the figure was around 10 per cent and in Cork it was about 20 per cent.

It also reported on a case in the Republic of Ireland, where a woman was sent a text message from a contact tracer when she left work, while a man in the Republic of Ireland received a text message when he left work.

We also spoke to John O'Rourke from the Irish Examiner who commented on the issue of the increasing number of people not answering calls from tracers.

He said: "People have called the Tracing Agency on many occasions during the night. In fact, the calls in Dublin have actually been even higher this evening.

"While the call volume is down across the country, the percentage of calls that don't answer is increasing as more and more people are using these devices.

"We've found that some people are using them to avoid their phones ringing, which would only increase the burden on the call centre staff.

"As many as one in four of our calls are from tracer calls, and a substantial proportion of calls are from people who are out of the area they are in.

"The number of people who do not answer calls from tracers is not surprising; it is a consequence of the technology.

"If people were using the technology in a way that was more sensible, they would be more helpful and answer the calls, but they are not. They are a cost issue for the agency as they have to ensure that they are paid for the use of their equipment."

Cars

The article also pointed out that people are avoiding their cars when the tracer light is red, which is an expensive method of avoiding them ringing.

The article concluded: "Despite the trend towards using contact tracers in the modern age, there is no evidence that they are any more dangerous or that any accidents have resulted from them."

The article quoted a member of the public who spoke to the Irish Examiner about the issue: "It is getting to be like a car accident in the street.

"A couple of weeks ago I went to the bank to withdraw money and the tracer light was red. I went out to the car park and waited for the car to arrive.

"I was in the car with my kids and couldn't find my son. I was going to leave for the shop when I heard his voice call out. It was him.

"I had to give him my money back. I was really annoyed.

"The tracer light is red when you have got a message from the tracer.

"I felt so sorry for him. I had a lovely dinner with my family and got back home and had to wait for the tracer to stop.

"That's why he was so angry. If he had been out to get the money, it would have been so much easier for him.

"It is getting to be like a car accident in the street."

The article quoted another person who said: "The tracer lights are red when you are using the device and red when you have not been using it."
headline: Covid-19: 'Concerning' trend of some people not answering calls from contact tracers

text:
A report from the Environment Protection Agency (EPA) has said that a firm from West Cork is being fined €2,000 and ordered to pay €5,000 in costs and €2,000 in damages for breaching its emissions regulations.

The company, which is known as Eurelectric, is the subject of the first environmental prosecution for its environmental footprint and had to pay the €2,000 fine in addition to the legal costs imposed on it by the Environmental Protection Agency.

Eurelectric was fined €2,000 for six breaches of its emissions regulations.

A case of this nature is highly unusual. Environmental prosecutions are rare and environmental charges are extremely rare for a company in this field. It is also the first environmental case involving an Irish company and the first environmental action under the Clean Air Act.

Eurelectric is the latest environmental case under the Clean Air Act, which was introduced in 2000. This Act was introduced after Environment Minister Michael Hartnett said that environmental and social pollution should be dealt with in a way that was "fair, consistent and proportionate".

Environment Action Ireland said in a statement: "This is a significant step forward in Ireland's environmental enforcement regime.

"However, there is still a lot of work ahead.

"Eurelectric is being fined for a case that was closed in 2005 and we have a long way to go before we are able to enforce the regulations effectively and we urge people to help us in this regard.

"The Environmental Protection Agency has a range of enforcement tools available to it and we will continue to take all appropriate action to ensure the protection of the environment and our environment."

The Environmental Protection Agency said that the fines were brought under the Clean Air Act, which was introduced in 2000 to give the agency a stronger hand in enforcing emissions controls.

The agency said it was aware of the case and the EPA had advised that the fine was appropriate.

The EPA had earlier issued an interim order against Eurelectric for failing to fulfil its emission obligations.

The agency said that the company's failure to meet emission limits was a matter of public interest, and it had asked the court for the interim order.
headline: West Cork company fined for six breaches of emissions regulations

text:
"Kathleen MacMahon's latest book is an account of her mother and daughter's relationship," the article begins. "It is a love story in the making. In the first paragraph of the book, we find the writer on the phone with her mother to wish her well on a recent holiday.

"What began as a family affair, has blossomed into a series of adventures. We see her parents engaged in something of an affair before the daughter even has a chance to ask."

The Irish Examiner, Ireland's oldest paper, has an excellent review of the book and its author. It is also a good example of how some of these stories are told in the literary world, as the writer's family is "unusually close" and her mother is "the most un-American of women".

Some of the things she recounts in her mother's voice in this book are not exactly "imaginative". For example, a woman has a "dilatory" affair with her father, only to go back to him a few years later. And how about her mother's claim that she was raped, as if that's any indication of the kind of relationship that exists between a mother and daughter?

Her mother has made such comments before and has been widely criticised as "inaccurate", with many asking why she was doing so. But the Irish Examiner's review is a good example of how her mother's words are not merely "accurate" but also "amusing".

The Irish Examiner's review shows some of the "un-American" traits that sometimes accompany the kind of family relations portrayed in the Irish literary world.

As for the author, it is hard to say. The interview begins with a long, lengthy, and often repetitive description of how the author came to write this book. It then goes on to describe how she got to know her mother, how she developed a "relationship" with her mother, and how they became "close" and "romantic".

The end of the interview, though, is when the author describes her mother saying, "I don't believe any woman would ever do this". It is this that sets the tone for the entire book.

The author is well aware that this description is likely to make her detractors uncomfortable. As she says at the start of the book,

"I've never felt like I'm selling out because of the personal experience of my mother's life. But I'd rather my mother's life is a kind of secret to be kept hidden."

A book that is all about the author's mother and how she deals with life, death, and sex is a book that many will find hard to swallow.

This book is one of those books that many people will find hard to swallow. And with the author's mother in the background, it is almost impossible to read this book and not find yourself wanting to weep.

That is why it is so hard to resist the temptation of finding a copy of this book on your local bookshop's shelves.

When I first read it in 2012, I was so taken by this story that I ended up reading the book again after I had completed it. I was so fascinated by how a story about an incestuous affair between a mother and daughter could end up in this book that I made a mental note of it.
headline: Kathleen MacMahon on missing journalism, the mother/daughter relationship and her latest novel

An agreement was signed today in the hope that the beef protests will stop, but farmers from the South Armagh area claim they still are protesting.

One farmer, who asked not to be named, said: "All we want to do is bring some peace. But we are still going on protesting."

The protest is being led by the Solidarity Economy group in the South Armagh area and the Southern Cross Farmers Union.

The farmers want the EU to remove an EU regulation which allows them to refuse to sell their cattle to the U.K.

The restriction was introduced under the Irish Free Trade Agreement (IFTA) with the U.K.

Last week, the farmers, led by Steve Gough of the Solidarity Economy group, launched a protest against EU Trade Commissioner Karel De Gucht, who is seeking to prevent the restriction from being lifted on beef imports.

The farmers want the EU to re-negotiate the rule to ensure that European beef can be sold across the EU if it meets minimum quality standards.

Mr Gough said that under the current rules, EU beef cannot be sold unless it meets the same standards as beef from a third country – or under the same conditions as beef grown on the Continent.

"We have had some success with the U.K. and we want them to do the same thing here. They should make a deal to allow a good quality cow to be exported to the U.K.," he said.

Mr Gough said it had been very difficult to persuade the farmers to agree to end the beef protests, but said it was now "up to the ministers to say 'yes' to trade."
headline: Beef price protests escalate in some areas despite agreement to remove legal threat

Ronan Keating, who was found dead in his Dublin home, has been described by friends as an "icon".

The 27-year-old's parents and sister are believed to have recently been in a long-term relationship.

His sister, Tara, had been with Ronan's long-term partner, Michael McConville.

His brother, Paul, described the family's relationship as being "terrific".

"Our relationships are great. It's the best," he told the Irish Examiner.

"It's a really, really good relationship."

Mr Keating's body was found in his kitchen on the night of December 4.

His family had been informed on Monday.

Family: †We are in the dark on what happened,‖ said the family yesterday.

They have been told that his body was discovered by friends of Ms McConville.

A spokesman for the Gardaí said yesterday that the investigation into the death is ongoing.

The Irish Examiner reports that Ronan Keating was born on March 11, 1976, and his mother is from Northern Ireland.

A post-mortem examination is due in February and toxicology reports should be available before then.

Mr Keating was an academic at University College Dublin before moving to Dublin to study for a PhD at Imperial College London.

He had been on a short-term work placement in Mexico with his father.

His brother, Paul, told the Examiner that their father met Ms McConville through an acquaintance.

"We were both on holiday in Mexico for a few weeks so it was quite a short-lived relationship."

"He just said he was going to talk to his father about something and he didn't get back," Mr Keating said.

In his own words: †Words: †Ronan wrote that he was "so sorry for the loss of his brother," and expressed gratitude for the support he had received from the community.

"The High Court of Justice has allowed garda whistleblower Denis O'Brien to be named as the man arrested in a sexual assault case.

Judge Mr Justice Paul Butler in the High Court said "given the serious nature of the allegations made by Mr O'Brien that he should not be named in any case".

He said: "Given the nature of the allegations, I would not be giving anyone a fair trial and I would give it to my conscience".

"The defendant has been arrested in relation to a sexual assault case. His identity has not been disclosed as he is a whistleblower in relation to Garda Síochána.

"On a number of occasions I have been asked for reasons why a particular person should not be named. The garda whistleblower cannot be named for a number of reasons, including his identity has not been disclosed.

"It is a matter for him to defend against these allegations. In the meantime, his identity cannot be disclosed as he has not been charged."

Judge Butler said that the garda should be given no right to counsel.

He said "the case before you concerns the accused's identity. In my judgment it should not be disclosed to anyone other than the prosecutor or the court."

"It is a matter for him to defend against these allegations. In the meantime, his identity cannot be disclosed as he has not been charged."

He said the defendant, who has worked with gardaí for more than 25 years, must have a right to be represented by counsel.

"If he can be granted this right, and I have no doubt that he can, it is my duty to give him counsel so that he can be heard and can present his case to the court."

Judge Butler said there was no reason that gardaí should have to "go to all the trouble" and expense to identify the defendant.

"They can identify him and identify the accused if they wish to do so and I have no doubt that they will do so".

"I would ask all concerned to respect that in the interests of justice, the garda whistleblowers should be named and allowed to defend their case.

"He has been arrested in connection with a sexual assault case. His identity has not been disclosed as he is a whistleblower in relation to Garda Síochána."
headline: Judge allows garda accused of false imprisonment and sexual assault to be named

"A mental health author has been blackmailed online and told to withdraw from an online book giveaway.

Dr. Pat Kelly (right) said it was a 'cyber-stalking' incident that has left him "sick of being bullied online".

"I was contacted via the social media network Twitter in March of this year, by a male Twitter user who sent me an email saying that I would be the winner of an anonymous book deal," said Dr Kelly, the CEO of The Irish Examiner.

"At the time I assumed it was a prank or an attempt at harassment because I am known in the mental health industry, but then I received the message and it turned out to be a blackmail letter containing the details of the author's address and telephone number."

"The author also included links to a website that featured a list of book deal offers which he had been to," said Dr Kelly.

"He also included a number of photographs of me and my family and asked me for the reason why I had chosen to participate.

"I told him about my blog where I talk about the problems that affect our mental health."

Dr Kelly said he contacted the author via email and they both agreed to meet in person in order to resolve the matter and to clarify some of the issues and make things right.

However, on March 25th, the author went to Dr Kelly's home and he was told he was being blackmailed.

"The author was also told by him that if he didn't get the book out by April 21st, he would be 'disappointed in me'. The author then stated that he would be "disappointed in me" if he didn't release the book," said Dr Kelly.

"The author also said, 'I don't want the name of the book out because it was my idea to set it up but you said you would do it and I am glad you did.'

"I stated, 'We talked in person and I agreed to meet you. I was very clear from the start that if you were not going to help me I was going to take the book down."

"Dr Kelly has been contacting the author on twitter to help resolve the matter."

Dr Kelly said he has since been contacted by two other people who have received similar emails.

"I am a mental health therapist and I have been a victim of cyber-stalking for many years," Dr Kelly said.

"I have had my name and address published for the past 15 years on several occasions, even in major publications."

"People are not aware that there is such a thing as cyber-stalking, which is a very serious crime. It is a form of stalking which is carried out by using technology to harass, bully or threaten someone who has done no harm or injury to themselves."

Dr Kelly said that if the person who contacted him was a professional or a member of the media he would have a legal obligation to contact police and report the crime.

"I am now in contact with the author of the email to ensure that he is aware of the situation and to ensure that he is being investigated for cyber-stalking."
headline: Cork mental health author blackmailed online 'disappointed by victim-blaming'

text:
I am a 40-year-old woman with a 4.3% lifetime risk of breast cancer, and am currently undergoing treatment for it.

This morning, I woke up to a letter from the Royal College of General Practitioners (RCGP) advising me that my risk of developing the cancer in the future was "substantially increased" because of my aunt's cancer diagnosis.

I have no idea why they thought this, but I was not surprised, since my aunt, Margaret Cunliffe (aka Margaret Mary Cunliffe), was a consultant general practitioner and a consultant at the National Cancer Centre until she retired in May 2014. Her condition makes her immune to the effects of chemotherapy and radiation, so the letter is likely to be a direct result of her cancer diagnosis.

My aunt was diagnosed with "primary advanced ductal carcinoma in situ" at the age of 61 in 2012. She did a radiographic chest scan in November 2011 which revealed two small lesions on her left breast. She had been told she had stage 4 breast cancer and had four to six months to live, and that she would be in her 70s or 80s, but she had been told that she would be able to do nothing about it.

However, in the course of the following year the two small lesions progressed to a much bigger one on the left side, and when she was in hospital she was advised by a radiographer to start chemo treatment.

Her next follow-up in June 2014 showed that the smaller lesion was no longer there, and she was also told by a radiologist that she would be at risk of developing breast cancer again.

In the meantime she has been using anti-depressants and has taken anti-psychotic medication for five months. She has been told by her GP that she needs to be on anti-psychotics for a year or more. She also has to stop her anti-depressants.

So, why did the RCGP say she has a risk of developing a new cancer?

Apparently the RCGP did not investigate the facts surrounding her cancer diagnosis.

Firstly, there is no evidence that my aunt had a low risk of developing breast cancer. Her symptoms included a very lightening in the colour of her skin and the development of dark patches on her skin. She also developed a cold for the first time in nine years which she attributed to the cancer.

She has never smoked, and her hair is now growing again, and she does not have any type of diabetes or heart disease or high blood pressure. She is a very fit, fit, fit woman who has had a very healthy pregnancy.

On the day she was diagnosed with the cancer the doctors had no reason to expect any problems. My aunt has been diagnosed with this condition only once before in her career, in 1989 when she had a large tumour removed from her arm. This was because she had had a flare up of her illness in the summer of 1984.

The RCGP did not investigate the evidence that this cancer was not of the "normal" type. There is no reason to suppose that this cancer is any more benign than any other type of cancer.

Secondly, the RCGP did not investigate the evidence that my aunt had a lower risk of developing other types of cancer.
headline: My aunt's breast cancer diagnosis saved me

"Caught in the web of the fashion industry, I was stunned that fashion bloggers and fashion designers seemed to be in league with the fashion industry when it came to condemning the fashion industry.

They were calling the fashion industry 'the ugly sisters' and that all the fashion industries 'douches' were in the same league as fashion, or worse, as the French and the French are always saying.

This is a shame, because fashion bloggers are so powerful. Fashion bloggers are in the same league as fashion designers and they know that the fashion industry is in the way.

So now they are looking to the fashion industry for help.

I am all for fashion for all – but it is time to stop the hypocrisy and call the fashion industry on its hypocrisy. The fashion industry has become so powerful that it has become the fashion industry.

If you are an editor at the fashion magazine, you need to start getting together with the fashion bloggers and ask them for their input. You have to ask them.

It is not the fashion industry, it is the fashion bloggers.

text:
Progressive rock singer Jennifer Horgan has called for a "massive march for the children" in the city of Belfast on Saturday following the death of her partner, Liam Horgan.

Speaking to journalists during a press conference, Horgan said that she believes it's time for Belfast to "turn its back" on the "scourge of drug addiction and mental illness".

"When you go through the night, you go through the days and the nights, you see young people just begging for food and love and support and you think about the kids that are suffering with mental illness, with drug addiction and addiction that is so devastating to them, they are dying in their sleep," she added.

"My partner was like a little brother to me – he was a great friend. I think that if we take a moment to step back and remember that, the kids that are suffering so much, why can't we turn our back on the scourge of drug addiction and mental illness? We don't need to walk into a meeting of the drug addiction commission to ask them about it."

Horgan's comments come on the heels of the news that Liam Horgan died of a suspected drug overdose in June.

The singer, who also performs with The 1975, is due to perform at the Glastonbury Festival in the UK this week (June 16).

He was due to tour the US later this year (November to March) before returning to Ireland for a special Glastonbury gig in Dublin in September.

During her press conference, Horgan said that she had spoken to her partner's friend John O'Connor about her concerns and "he said, 'We're going to need an army of marchers, we're going to need thousands, and you're going to need the army of children'. It was great advice and it's not just me, it's so many people, I want to bring it to everyone. I want to make sure that this is something that people are talking about."
headline: Jennifer Horgan: For the sake of Ireland's children, let's march in solidarity with their carers

text:
A total of 13 Israeli hostages were released during the night by the Palestinian Authority as the Israeli military continued its unilateral operation in Gaza in a bid to free an additional five Israeli hostages held by Hamas militants.

Two Israelis and two Palestinians were released by the Palestinian Authority after six days of talks between the Palestinian Authority and Israel.

The latest announcement was made by the PA President Mahmoud Abbas and Prime Minister Rami Hamdallah at the PA headquarters in Ramallah.

As the Israeli military began its military operation in the Gaza Strip, seven Palestinians died in Israeli airstrikes.

Eight Israelis and two Palestinians were killed in Israeli airstrikes on the Gaza Strip, and two Palestinians were killed in Israeli airstrikes on the Israeli side of the border with Israel.

Israeli Defence Minister Moshe Yaalon said early Tuesday that a total of 13 Palestinian detainees were freed in the overnight operation and the Palestinian Prisoner's Society said it received word that a fourth hostage was being released.

The announcement comes amid an intense round of negotiations between the Israeli and Palestinian authorities.

Following the latest round of talks, an Israeli delegation entered the PA offices in Ramallah, the Palestinian Authority's capital, and began negotiations with the Fatah leadership.

A PA spokesman said the talks "will continue with a view to reaching an agreement".

The Israeli army released the first group of seven hostages in a bid to break the latest round of hostilities between the two sides.

The second group of six was released on Sunday after being held by Hamas for five days.

They were the son of Mohammed al-Hamad, a top Hamas official killed in a January car bombing in Gaza City, and Ahmed Hamad, a top Hamas commander in Gaza City.

The third group of three hostages were released on Sunday evening after Israeli forces took control of a bridge in Gaza and the three were transported to a hospital.

Israel's military said it had struck 17 targets in and around the Gaza Strip during the overnight operation that left Hamas leader and military commander Mohammed Deif, a top Hamas military commander, dead.

One of the three killed was Ismail al-Qasr, Hamas spokesman, who is now serving as a foreign minister in the Palestinian Authority.

"We know these are the first prisoner releases by the Israeli military in this operation. We are hopeful that this operation will lead to a full resolution of the Palestinian issue and the opening of a political process in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip," the Palestinian prisoners' society said in a statement.

"Our priority is to ensure the safety and well-being of the kidnapped families and that they are allowed to visit their loved ones. The families of the kidnapped are greatly distressed," it said.

"We are confident that they will see the families of the three freed on Sunday evening," the statement added.

The study, based on the Economic and Social Research Council's National Survey of Employment and Support (ESRC), also found the rate of working-age people having a job was higher in Dublin than in the rest of the country.

The study shows that while the Irish national rate of working-age unemployment was 5.6% in the year to June 2013, the overall rate was 6.1%.

The report states that while there were "significant" differences between the different local areas, Dublin experienced a higher working-age unemployment rate than the rest of Ireland.

Among the findings of the report are:

The unemployment rate of workers aged 25 to 54 was 5.1% in Dublin compared with 5.8% across all local areas.

Over one in four workers employed by private businesses were not in employment in the year to June 2013 compared to one in four in the entire sample.

In Dublin there were 1,600 people who were not in employment in the year to June 2013 compared to 1,900 in the whole population.

A total of 728,000 people in the country aged from 15 to 64 had never worked in their lives.

Employment rate

There was also a significant difference between the employment rates of men and women.

A total of 52.7% of men employed in private businesses were employed to a job or looking for work, compared to just 48.2% of women.

In the year to June 2013, men had a higher employment rate than women for all ages, while women had a lower employment rate than men for all ages but 16 to 24.

However, there were significant variations within Dublin, with the employment rate of people under 25 in Dublin increasing in the year to June 2013 compared with 2012.

The employment rate of people aged 25 to 54 was also slightly higher in the year to June 2013 compared with the full sample.

The employment rate of people aged 45 to 54 was slightly higher in the year to June 2013 compared with the full sample, and the employment rate of those aged 55 to 64 was slightly higher than the year to June 2012.

The report also found that the proportion of people working for the first time was higher in Dublin than in the rest of the country.

The majority of people aged from 16 to 64 were employed in full-time work. The rate was slightly higher for people working part-time, but not significantly so, compared with the full sample.

The Employment Rate for people with no qualifications (i.e. the most experienced in their field of employment) was higher in Dublin than elsewhere.

More people (34%) who were unemployed in the year to June 2013 were in work in the year to June 2013 than the total population.

More people were unemployed than unemployed in the year to June 2013 (21.1% vs 16.2%)

In terms of the composition of the unemployed, around 42% of people with no qualifications were unemployed at the end of the year to June 2013, up from just 24% in the year to June 2012.

The report's findings are based on the responses to the ESRC's National Survey of Employment and Support (ESRC). It is the only nationally representative survey of employment and social welfare and is conducted by ESRI and the Social Protection Agency.

The Irish Examiner reports that the head-mounted display (HMD) company Oculus Rift has been fined €25,000 by the European Union for having unsafe, unauthorised and unapproved materials on its website.

According to the Irish Examiner, the European Commission has asked for the €25,000 in fines to be paid to Oculus Rift.

The company has been accused of failing to ensure that it complies with all relevant regulations including those relating to EU, EU-funded research projects.

Oculus Rift's website refers to the head-mounted display (HMD) as "Oculus Rift," and the company's main page on the EU website says: "We're excited to be bringing this groundbreaking technology to Europe."

The company is due to release its first consumer HMD this autumn.

Oculus Rift, which employs over 50 people, says it uses a customised version of the Oculus Rift head-mounted display (HMD) that it developed and which it believes "could potentially revolutionise the way we interact with the virtual world".

According to the company, Oculus Rift is based on the Samsung Gear VR headset and is powered by a customised version of the Oculus Rift HMD.

The EU Commission has fined Oculus Rift for failing to comply with a list of regulations pertaining to human experimental subjects and research.

In a statement, the Commission said: "Oculus Rift's website does not contain sufficient information on how the user may be protected during the experimental procedures carried out on the virtual reality headset, which could lead to serious risks of bodily harm or damage to health."

The agency added that the company's website also does not clearly explain that the HMD is "not intended for prolonged use in a virtual environment."

It went on: "These findings suggest that Oculus Rift must take further steps to ensure its website complies with EU regulations."

The company says it will review the commission's decision.

In a statement it said: "We're pleased that the Commission has taken note of the concerns raised by the Commission and is taking further steps to ensure that all research participants, including those undergoing clinical trials, are aware of the risks associated with the use of the Oculus Rift."

The City of Cork recently commissioned a detailed study of the viability of different schemes to improve bus and tram services in the city.

The study has been commissioned by the city and published in the local paper The Herald on Sunday.

The main findings, according to the Herald, are:

Transport investment in Cork is critical for the city's economic growth and wellbeing. The city is currently operating with a net deficit of €60million. The research has identified an estimated €20m of investment is required annually to ensure Cork meets its targets for growth and sustainability.

The study has identified a lack of suitable infrastructure as a major barrier to investment in the city.

The study has identified a need for better transport links for people to reach their destinations in the city.

The study identifies a number of key transport priorities that can be implemented to improve connectivity to and from Cork city.

The recommendations for improvement include:

A dedicated bus lane on either side of the city's main arterial roads (A1/A6) and the junction with A6. This could be converted into a tram lane, bus lane or pedestrian lane. The existing bus lane on A6 at the Junction with A6 is currently the only link between Cork city and Dublin and it is currently the subject of ongoing discussions.

A new tram stop on A6 between the A6 and A6/A9 junction. The existing tram stop on A6/A6 at the junction with A6/A9 is currently the only link between Cork city and Dublin.

An extension of the existing bus lane on A6 from the A6/A9 junction to the junction with A6/A16. It would be ideal to widen this link as it currently is.

An extension of the existing tram stop on A6/A6 to include both the route to Dublin and the route to Cork city. Currently there is only an extension of one car park on both sides of the road.

The report also states that the city has over 300,000 fewer car trips than the average Dublin city centre resident, and that it is vital that more people are able to commute by foot or by bike to their jobs in the city centre.

The report recommends that more bus stops be built in Cork city centre to give people who live and work in the city the best possible access to transport.

The report states that it is not desirable to run bus services outside of main arterial roads because:

The buses are crowded and slow, and their speed is restricted. Bus journeys require stopping on the main arterial road (A1/A6) and on the road to Dublin. This means that these bus services must stop for other people in the city and that they have a delay when they get to Dublin.

The buses often carry less people than they could at a bus stop further away from the city centre.

The bus stops are not designed to be fully wheelchair accessible, and many bus stops are not connected to other bus stops.

She performed the first scene of 'Elektra' (1899) before a audience in London, and since then she has played 'The Tempest' (1905) and a number of other musicals. In this interview, she opens up about her role in 'The Tempest', and speaks on her love of music and theatre.

She talks on the stage:

'The Tempest' was the first operatic opera I ever did. I'd started out by doing musicals and then I read 'The Tempest' and just went 'Oh. Well, that's nice.'

After hearing it, I was hooked.

But I'd been through a lot of musicals, and 'The Tempest' was the first one I actually loved. I remember doing it twice. I was 14 at the time.

I don't think I had any intention of becoming an opera singer. When I read the script I was totally in love with it.

The story of 'The Tempest' is so very funny, but I think there's a very dark underside to it as well. I had a difficult time being a virgin and making it to the musical.

What's it like working with Strauss?

He was a very lovely man. He knew me very well and we had many, many conversations. In fact, I was his first choice to play 'Elektra' because he was already busy with his other work at the time.

It's quite amazing that he chose me as his first choice. He knew I'd been to London and he liked the look of me. I'd even done my hair in the style of the time.

It's one of the most unusual roles I've played, and I've done it twice.

There's a little bit of a rivalry between the two of them in the book, but I've not really got to know him. But he is always generous to me.

When you have a role that's so famous, how does it make you feel?

I'm really happy about the role. I've been working so hard for it. It's a real honour to play her.

There's a great scene with the cast and the audience in the opera, as well as all the beautiful orchestral music.

The audience has to listen to the opera three times. The first time in a cinema is an extraordinary moment. It gives you a really strong sense of what you're going to experience.

It's exciting and I think it's one of the great things about being a performer is when you know what you're doing and then it's really fun.

When I read the script I thought 'Oh God, the words are so strange and so strange.' But I thought they were brilliant.

It's one of those things that makes you feel a certain way in a moment. It's like you're in your own little world.

The stage was the best thing to do.

Why did you choose the title of 'Elektra'?

That's one of the questions I always get. I'm not really sure. I think that's the most famous name ever given to an Irish opera singer, so I think that's the right one.

Why do you think 'Elektra' has such an iconic status?
headline: Máire Flavin: Irish soprano on her role in Elektra, Strauss's famously dark opera

(The Irish Examiner)

By John O'Hanlon, Irish Examiner

On a recent Saturday afternoon, I met up with Emilie Pine in Cork city centre. She was the author of her debut novel, The Broken House, and we discussed the novel, her work as an interpreter, the role that books, and the internet, play in our lives.

In the summer of 2012, I met up with her at a book launch event for her debut novel in Cork city centre. "I feel like the author of my book has read my book," she said. "I've made a statement that I don't want to put down and that it's not about me."

She had just finished a week of writing a new novel and said that she wanted to be "the author of my book", rather than just an "interpreter".

"My book," she said, "is really about the lives of these two women, the two women who live in their basement, who I've chosen to depict as being the women of my book. It's not about me. I'm not like the author of the book."

She was just 22 at the time and had just finished an academic degree at the University of Limerick, and she had just recently won a number of awards: the Independent Irish Book Award, the Royal Irish Academy Young Author of the Year and the National Book Awards.

Her book has been a long time in the making. "I've been writing my book since I was 12," she said. "I've been writing about what I'm going through and what my life is about. I've been writing about the fact that I'm going through a divorce and a struggle with depression. I've been writing about the fact that my mother has died and I'm the sole breadwinner. I've been writing about my life without my mother and my life without my mother is very tough."

Her memoir, The Broken House, was published in 2008 and has since been translated into over 30 languages. "It's been on sale since 2009 and I've had a massive amount of international attention," she said.

She's had book festivals all over the world, and she's had book clubs in cities all over the world. The success of her book has been phenomenal. "I think it's something that I didn't really think I was ever going to get," she said.

This was her first book that she didn't write herself. She met up with a friend who was a publisher and she said, "How do you know that person is a good editor?" "He was a wonderful editor for me. He read the book in my language, he knew what I was talking about, and he gave me advice."

He gave her the script for The Broken House, which she read, liked and gave the book to him, as a gift, because she thought he'd love it.

"He gave me the script for a whole year and I did a book club on it and I read it in three weeks and I liked it," she said. "I loved the way he edited. I thought it was brilliant and I used it in my book and I think there's a lot of people who are inspired by his editing.
headline: Book review: Emilie Pine's debut novel reinforces her reputation as an empathetic writer

The Irish Examiner

Thursday September 6, 2007

Vice President Joseph Biden will have backing of the Irish by a wide margin on Thursday as the Irish presidential election gets underway, a new survey suggests.

A new poll from the Irish Examiner finds that 44pc of Irish people believe the former Delaware senator from Delaware will be able to win the presidency.

The poll also has former US Vice President Al Gore on the top of the list of candidates with 31pc support.

Another candidate, former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani, is second at 16pc.

But just 1pc of people said they would be more likely to vote for someone else for the presidency if Biden was the Republican candidate.

However, just 5pc said they would be more likely to vote for a third candidate if Biden were their party's candidate.

The poll also found that just 6pc of people said they thought Kerry was better prepared for the presidency than Biden, although he is currently the leading candidate in the polls for the nomination.

There was a wide-spread disapproval of both President Bush and former Massachusetts Governor Romney for their handling of the US economy in the last month, the poll says.

Some 35pc of people said they were more likely to vote for Kerry if he was the Republican candidate in the election, but just 23pc thought he was the better candidate.

However, just 20pc said they were more likely to vote for the former Massachusetts Governor if he was the Democratic candidate in the election.

And 8pc said they would be more likely to vote for Romney if he was the Republican candidate.

However, while 44pc of people think the election will be a "hurdle" for the Democrats, just 15pc think it will be a "race-to-the-bottom" for the Republicans.

There were also huge differences between age groups.

The poll found that 49pc of those aged 55 to 64 think the election will be a "hurdle" for Democrats, compared to just 31pc for those aged 65 and older.

Only 16pc of those aged between 18 to 29 think the race will be a "hurdle" for the Republicans.

Donation day: The only donation day where the whole population is actually there and involved

By Ian Kelly

The Daily IORexaminer

A huge turnout is expected at Irish charity Donor Day, which has its first ever 'Donation Day' in Dublin.

Organisers are hoping the event will be a success with a massive crowd of around 5,000 people expected.

The event will take place from 11am on Thursday at the Connolly Art Gallery in Dublin.

Many are expected to line up in the morning for a free hour-long admission time to a range of arts and crafts.

After lunch, groups will gather for two hours in the afternoon to listen to talks by the charities involved.

And the evening sees a series of talks by prominent figures, including former Taoiseach Bertie Ahern and former President Mary Robinson, who also founded the event in 2001.

Donation Day was launched by Mary Robinson in 2000 as a way to recognise the generosity of the public and ensure that all the money raised was used to help the vulnerable.

It was eventually expanded to be a national event in 2011.

The event is organised by the Department of Arts and Heritage, and it takes place under the auspices of the Irish National Art Gallery.

However, the event has come under scrutiny in recent years.

In 2011, an audit by Auditor General Seamus Donohoe raised concerns about the integrity of the event.

He found that the event was not properly managed, with the DHE failing to follow up on complaints about the cost of the tickets, as well as the quality of the talks.

In 2013 the auditor general criticised DHE's management of the event after it emerged that they had billed €4,500 to the event's organisers for their time.

The audit was also critical of the role of a DHE employee, who received €2,000 in payments between June 2009 and December 2011.

He also found that the DHE failed to ensure that staff were properly trained.

The DHE did not respond to requests for comment on the auditor general's findings.

Other reports have criticised the way the DHE dealt with the complaints raised by the auditor general in 2013.

One, by the National Board of Review, said that the DHE "failed to follow up and take action on" around 50 complaints, including the case of an employee who had been paid €4,000 in three years.

A similar audit by the Office of the Auditor General in 2013 was also critical of the DHE's management of the event.

It found that "the DHE did not implement any effective internal review processes to ensure the quality of the speakers' performances".

It also said that the DHE "did not adequately investigate or take action when there was information that speakers were not following the instructions".

In a desperate plea to help the grieving families and neighbours of those killed in the east of Libya, the Irish Examiner has launched a massive fundraising appeal.

The appeal has raised more than €6,000 in just a couple of days from 1,000 people, including 100 solicitors and several high-profile Irish figures, including former Irish president Mary McAleese.

The appeal, which runs until Thursday, was launched on the eve of the first anniversary of the devastating March 26th 2011 storm which engulfed the capital, Tripoli, and forced the evacuation of more than half of the population of the Libyan state.

A group of Irish people have been helping the families of those who lost their homes in the disaster.

Many of those in Libya were not evacuated during the disaster, and many of those who fled the country had not returned home, either as refugees or asylum seekers.

It is feared that around 5,000 people have lost their homes.

Many have been staying in temporary camps while awaiting help from the European Union.

The majority of the Irish people involved are from the north of the country.

The Examiner has learned that the Irish Association of Rescue Workers, founded in 2006 to help in disasters and to support the Irish government's response, has provided the bulk of the funds for the campaign to assist the relatives of the victims.

Its president, Dr Alan O'Higgins, said the group had been working hard to make sure the funds were being used appropriately, and they had received no less than €4,000 from people around the world to help with the appeal.

Last month, the newspaper launched a crowdfunding campaign to help with the crisis. The total raised to date is less than €1,000.

"We are incredibly grateful to the Irish community and we look forward to helping bring those families and relatives who have lost their homes and property back on to their feet," Dr O'Higgins said.
headline: Fundraising appeal launched as 5,300 feared dead in flood-hit eastern Libya

The play was presented at the New Theater Society's production of The Winter's Tale in Dublin last week. The play follows a young man in his late teens who arrives at the small seaside town of Huddersfield to find that it has been wiped off the map.

"He meets the headmistress of a school for displaced children, and the story follows his gradual descent into despair, as he witnesses the horrors of war and becomes increasingly ill at ease in his new surroundings."

Article:

http://www.irishexaminer.com/news/theatre-review-emma-donoghue-the-winter-s-tale-has-a-resounding-prescience/

"The play's most memorable scene is the final scene in which Emma Donoghue plays a character that is clearly inspired by an Irish Catholic church worker or priest, a member of the Catholic Church. She is on the road, and stops and asks a priest if he can help her, a gesture that can only be interpreted as an apology for the world. But when he leaves, the man says, 'I wish I could have stayed longer, but I was just getting warmed up.'

"It's a scene with which any decent person should feel uncomfortable; in a play that is often as much about how the world works as it is about the horrors of war. There is something about the way this scene plays out that feels deeply disturbing. Donoghue is not afraid to put a character in such an uncomfortable position, particularly when she makes him have to suffer this very uncomfortable fate as punishment for being an ignorant, cruel and dangerous man.

"But there's more. Throughout the play, Donoghue has to work through the question 'Why did he do it?' and I think the play does a good job of answering that."

Donald Trump will address a meeting of the top military leaders in Washington next week, a senior White House official says.

The meeting, which is to take place at Camp David next Monday, has been organised by General John Kelly, the top US military commander, and is aimed at addressing the fallout from President Donald Trump's decision to fire the country's top military official, James Mattis.

Speaking to reporters in the White House briefing room on Friday, Kelly said Trump was in constant contact with Mattis and other military leaders and would have a "thorough discussion" with them.

"He has a number of things that he wants to look at, many things," Kelly said. "He's also going to have a thorough discussion with us about what's gone on in the world with respect to our defence capabilities and what they need to be improved."

A senior White House official said Trump's meetings would be a follow-up to meetings he had previously held with top generals, and that they would involve Trump "sharing some of his ideas about defence matters".

The official added that the meeting would be held between Mr Trump and Mattis and would come after the president has "had a good chance to talk to other people" at the gathering in the secure Eisenhower Executive Office Building (EEOB).

In a statement issued on Thursday, Kelly said the meeting would "generally cover a range of topics, including how the military integrates with civilian life, improving military readiness and capability, and how to best improve interoperability".

The statement continued: "The president and his administration are committed to ensuring our military is ready to deal with any potential threats to our nation, including the need to maintain operational readiness to ensure that the military can meet the threats posed by Iran, Russia, North Korea and other adversaries."

He said Trump and the leaders of the Army, Navy and Air Force, as well as civilian and military leadership, would meet to "address the need for greater cohesion among the services, particularly with respect to their joint training and exercises".

The official said the meeting could be followed by a dinner for military leaders at the White House, but said that the menu, which is yet to be set, would be "a reflection of the priorities of the president".

The official said he expected the meeting would not involve Trump speaking to any of the generals directly but said the president and the generals would discuss "how to make sure that the forces are ready to protect American interests and values around the world".

The official said Trump and Mattis would "be talking about a number of issues including Afghanistan, Iraq and Syria".

Mr Trump will also be meeting with military leaders in South Korea later on Friday, and will then travel to Japan on Saturday.

The official said Mr Trump would return to Washington on Monday to attend a Nato summit in Brussels and to attend a working lunch at the White House.

Mr Kelly has been serving as the White House chief of staff since Mr Trump took office. He is the second highest ranking military officer to serve in the White House in as many years.

According to reports, Mr Mattis is expected to return to the Pentagon as soon as Friday. He was sworn in as the Pentagon chief as Mr Trump took office in January and was confirmed to serve as defense secretary by the Senate on 27 January.
headline: Donald Trump to speak at hastily called meeting of top military leaders, says official

Government auctioneers say Ireland must allow all new homebuyers to access the same level of mortgage relief as those buying with existing homes.

They also suggest that as the housing market recovers, the average taxpayer might be allowed to take advantage of the same loans-to-value relief as owners of existing homes.

The auctioneers say it would be in the best interests of society if the Government, in co-ordinated action, allows all new homebuyers to access the same level of mortgage relief as those buying with existing homes.

Ministers have repeatedly refused to give permission for the sale of new homes to people who buy homes with existing mortgages.

The Government has introduced legislation to limit the maximum amount that can be bought to €150,000 in the new year, but these limits are being challenged in the courts.

The auctioneers suggest that as Ireland recovers from the crash of the financial crisis, and the average taxpayer is allowed to take advantage of the same loans-to-value relief as owners of existing homes, it would be in the best interests of society to allow all new homebuyers to have the same assistance.

"The Government must provide the same level of mortgage relief to all new homebuyers as is available to the ordinary taxpayer."

"This is particularly important given that, as the housing market recovers and average tax payers can access the same rate of loan-to-value relief as those buying with existing homes, the average taxpayer may well be granted some of that loan-to-value relief.

The auctioneers say the maximum amount that can be bought is currently limited to €150,000.

"So as the housing market recovers, and the average taxpayer is allowed to access the same rate of loan-to-value relief as those buying with existing homes, the average taxpayer may well be granted some of that loan-to-value relief," they say.

"This is because the banks will be expected to lend to the new homebuyers. In this way, there is an opportunity for more people to have access to the same level of loan-to-value relief as those buying with existing homes.

"This would allow the banks to lend more than they would otherwise be able to.

"To address the problem of over-indebtedness in the housing market, the government should allow all new homebuyers to access the same level of loan-to-value relief as those buying with existing homes.

"This would be in the best interests of society and the economy.

"The Government must therefore allow all new homebuyers to access the same level of mortgage relief as those buying with existing homes.

"As the housing market recovers, and the average taxpayer is allowed to access the same rate of loan-to-value relief as those buying with existing homes, the average taxpayer may well be granted some of that loan-to-value relief."

Published: Tuesday, 3 March 2007

Cork has made an offer to the Government as it seeks a more than 10 per cent pay rise to protect the livelihoods of 3,000 fishing workers and 1,000 boat workers, who were warned last month that their jobs will be at risk.

The fishing industry, which accounts for half of all fishing jobs in the Republic, is lobbying the Government for a 10 per cent pay rise and an end to the current €250,000 cap on payments, which they believe will harm the industry, and threaten the livelihoods of 1,000 boat workers.

Cork-based fishing operator Finn McAteer said the Government had ignored the industry's concerns over the new €250,000 cap on pay for boat workers.

"We're not talking about a small increase in the wage bill. We're talking about a 10 per cent rise, which if we put that on the €250,000 cap, it will kill our industry and thousands of people's jobs. What we're saying to them is that you've got a choice: pay the wages that you've been paying them for the last 20 years, or you've got to pay the wages that you've been paying them for 20 years."

The Government has until March 30th to accept the offer.

Mr McAteer said there had been concerns raised with the Government last month by the fishing industry about the impact of the current €250,000 cap on pay and the threat to jobs.

He said it was the only way to avert a "massive job loss" and a possible EU ban on the export of Irish-farmed lobster.

Fisheries Minister John Bruton said the Government had accepted the proposal from Finn McAteer to pay an extra €10 million to compensate boat workers, but said the Government would not accept the offer from the fishing industry.

Mr Bruton added: "The Government will not accept a new EU fishing directive unless the fishing industry is protected and I am satisfied that that is the case."

The Government has been urged to support the fishing industry, which employs about 3,000 people, to protect the job security of thousands of fishermen.

Ireland's pension auto-enrolment is a turning point for women

Editorial:

Women are on the verge of achieving a significant advance in their access to pensions, but it won't be a full-blown revolution until the next generation is fully covered.

In Ireland the state pension fund is currently paying out around €1,000 a year to every woman over 60. That is around half the average salary paid to male workers and well below the national average of €2,200.

The auto-enrolment system is also one of the best in the world.

But the progress in women's pensions is being held back by a legacy of ingrained biases and a failure to tackle the structural issues that have been holding back women's access to pensions for decades.

Women have had to wait until they turned 60 to start collecting the state pension because they had to wait until they turned 62 to start taking out private pension schemes. It was only in 2015 that the state pension age was raised to 67.

The new pensions system is designed to ease the burden on women but many of its key components are still in place.

Women are still not fully covered for pensions because of a legacy of entrenched and systemic sexist attitudes.

The problem starts at the top: Ireland's pension system is set up so that there is only one pension scheme for every four working-age women. It means there are very few women contributing to the system.

This is not an accident. It has been the result of decades of policies aimed at making women's pensions more attractive.

For decades, senior women in many industries have been subjected to discriminatory attitudes that make it difficult for them to receive the full benefits of their jobs.

A series of initiatives have been developed to address these barriers and to increase women's access to pensions.

These have ranged from pension audits to the introduction of a new pension scheme for senior women called the "triple lock", a guarantee that the next pension will be funded by the first two.

However the triple lock only covers women over the age of 62, but not their grandchildren.

It was introduced last year and is being challenged in the Supreme Court.

In addition, the government has introduced measures to address the pay gap between men and women.

In its submission to the Supreme Court, the government is arguing that it is not appropriate to treat women as a separate group from men when they have a right to equal protection under the constitution.

That is an argument that many women in Ireland find hard to accept.

The system also still needs addressing because there is no specific provision for women to access auto-enrolment.

This means that women are forced to rely on a third party to cover their pension needs because the state pension fund cannot do this for them.

The only way to increase women's pensions is through the creation of a fully-fledged pension scheme.

The Government has promised a review of the auto-enrolment system.

This would include the possibility of creating a fully-fledged pension scheme and ensuring that women were fully covered from the moment they turned 60.

But it appears that the government has no intention of doing this at the moment.
headline: Ireland’s pension auto-enrolment is a turning point for women but it's not the whole story

THE Irish Examiner can reveal that the Department of Justice has recently been consulting the Department of Finance on the future of the Immigration Directive, the law that gives immigration authorities powers to deport people suspected of serious crimes.

The Department of Justice and Equality is said to be consulting with the Department of Finance to decide whether to make changes to the Immigration Directive that were introduced by the last government.

The department said it had not made a final decision but will "provide a definitive response in due course".

The directive was introduced in 2009 by the Labour-led government, when it inherited a system with a large number of people who were either deported back to their home countries or granted permission to remain in the country in order to work.

It is said to have been designed as a way of protecting Irish expats living in countries where the death penalty is applied or where people are subjected to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment.

The rules were introduced following a landmark High Court ruling in 2008 which found that EU laws relating to the right to work were incompatible with Irish law and had to be scrapped.

However, the directive has not been scrapped, as the Government believes it has to respect the judgments of the High Court, which it says would not have been enforceable against other countries.

The directive was brought in under the last Coalition government, but was not updated during the period between 2010 and 2013.

It has now been updated, but the department has failed to inform the public about it and have not made a full consultation open to the public.

The department's advice is that the directives are no longer fit for purpose and that the Minister for Justice and Equality, Frances Fitzgerald, should consider changing the law to bring them into compliance with EU law.

Minister for Justice, Charlie Flanagan, has previously said that the directive had "not been fit for purpose" and was "not in accordance with international law".

The change would mean that any new legislation could affect the rights of people living in Ireland who hold EU nationality as well as Irish nationals who hold EU citizenship.

Last year, the Department of Justice revealed that it has been advised by the department's legal adviser on the application of the new Directive, that the Directive does not need to be re-written, as the rules were not in conflict with EU law, and as the legislation in question is not currently enforceable in other jurisdictions.

The Department of Justice has been advised that the Directive is a fundamental law and that it will be difficult to reinterpret its provisions to conform to EU law.

In the absence of any statutory change of the law, a Minister could issue an interim directive by way of notice to the Department of Finance which would then be used to give effect to the new law.

However, the Irish Examiner understands that the Department of Justice has not yet taken such a step.

A Minister could issue an interim directive by way of notice to the Department of Finance which would then be used to give effect to the new law. However, the Irish Examiner understands that the Department of Justice has not yet taken such a step.

The Department of Justice has also been informed by the department's legal adviser that the Directive should not be updated.

Last October, the department made it clear that it was not in the interests of the department, or for the State, to revise the directive.

The State Government is to provide €456 million for the construction of a motorway from Ringaskiddy to Cork, to replace the Cork to Roscommon motorway (Ringaskiddy to Ringwood), which opened in 1995.

The motorway, which connects Ringaskiddy to Cork Airport via the Ringwood Tunnel, was originally intended to carry 478,000 vehicles a day.

The project will include two new lanes of traffic on Ringaskiddy Road between the M6 and Ringwood.

"This new road provides an important additional access point to the airport and will provide significant additional capacity and capacity improvements for the Airport which will greatly benefit tourism and the wider area," Minister for Transport Simon Coveney said.

"It will also provide significant benefits to the rural economy and the region around the Ringaskiddy/Ringwood Junction by increasing the capacity of the main transport links in and out of the area."

Construction of the motorway was first proposed by former AAA leader Paul Kehoe in 1995.

The government was forced to scrap the project after the AAA's membership voted it down, in protest at the cost, in particular to the AAA's financial support of the Government during the election of 1997.

The AAA did not attend a meeting in Dromore and the AAA did not vote in any of the two referendums on the issue.

However, the Government did not give up.

In 2008 it proposed to install a second ring-tunnel to Ringwood.

The second tunnel is now under construction.

Mr Kehoe, who is now part of the AAA, said the government's proposal was "an amazing vision".

He said it would link Cork Airport and Ringaskiddy as well as "providing great regional connectivity in the West-Central region".

He said the government would have "an obligation to provide access to all people who want to travel from the east end of the West-Central region to Cork".
headline: Cabinet approves €456m M28 Cork to Ringaskiddy motorway project

The article is written by Michael McGrath of Irish Farmers and supported by John O'Callaghan of the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) Ireland. It was written as part of a series of articles by the two TDs in support of the Irish Farmers' Statement of Rights (FSR) and the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) to be delivered to the EU Commission.

http://www.ireland.com/articles/news/ireland/184078-headlines/against-the-grain-what-s-the-latest-with-the-unimplemented-agriculture-deal.html

The FSR and the CAP were intended to make agriculture fairer for farmers and consumers. However, the fact that they have not been fully implemented in Ireland has caused outrage among Ireland's farmers.

The EU has confirmed that the Commission will consider its response to the FSR in order to approve a final decision on the legislation, due to be implemented on 1 July 2013.

http://www.newsweek.com/agriculture-and-food/un-agriculture-fraud-farmers-sigh-20130608

The FSF was first created in 1973 and has been implemented on a rotating basis by the Irish government. It stipulates that the Republic of Ireland shall not receive any preferential treatment in the distribution of the EU's food, drink and agricultural products.

The FSF was set up as a direct result of the Treaty of Rome. Article 23 of that treaty states that the rights of EU Member States, including the European Union (EU), are determined by the Community and the Member States shall not be deprived of their rights and obligations in respect of the Community's activities by reason of being members of the Community, without the consent of the European Parliament and without the consent of the Council of the European Union.

It was designed as a means of ensuring that Ireland, as one of the poorest member states of the EU, would not be treated differently from other member states.

The FSF states that it "will not be amended in any way with the aim of reducing the proportion of agricultural products that are produced, bought or sold by Irish farmers".

An Irish Examiner investigation has found that at least 20 nurses are being offered incentives worth €110 a day to take on part-time jobs as part of the Government's childcare scheme.

The payment has been made to nurses at a cost of €1m, despite the fact that the scheme was scrapped in 2011.

A senior nurse at the HSE's maternity and maternity hospital in Cavan, who did not wish to be named, confirmed to the Examiner that nurses were being offered payment worth €110 per day as part of the scheme.

The nurse said that this incentive was to be "in the form of a day's work". The nurse said that when there was a lot of work and the nurse is offered to work more than 10 hours a day, then she will take the extra pay.

The nursing assistant said that the incentive had been offered since last October. The nurse has been working part-time since December 2012, and has one child.

The senior nurse said that the incentive payments have not been approved by senior staff at the HSE, but that there has been an increased emphasis on offering incentives to nurses.

This appears to be a move to increase the number of nurses who are offered incentives to take on part-time jobs, and to increase the number of nurses offering them.

The incentive payments, worth €110 a day are being paid to nurses from December 2011. This means that over a four-month period, the nurse would have received €110 per day as part of the scheme.

The mother of the nurse, who works part-time at the HSE maternity hospital in Cavan, told the Irish Examiner that the nurse offered her the incentive was paid on top of her normal working earnings.

The nurse said that she was "not averse to taking the extra money", as it would have a positive impact on her future career.

The mother of the nurse, who did not wish to be named, told the Examiner: "We are not against incentives for nurses, we just don't like the way the money was being offered."

The mother of the nurse said that she was not aware that the nurse was eligible for the incentive payments, as the HSE "made it clear that you have to be a nurse".

The nurse also said that the HSE had told her that the payments were not being offered to the nurses in full-time positions.

In response to this allegation, the HSE said that the payments "were made to a limited number of eligible workers who are actively involved in the HSE scheme".

"They are not being offered money for the privilege of working in part-time roles," the HSE said.

The HSE has said that while it is "committed to supporting staff, we must ensure that the most effective use of incentives in the HSE system is being met", and that it is "committed to supporting our staff in this regard".

"We will continue to look at how we can support staff through the transition into new roles and new careers."
headline: INMO: Some nurses paying €110 per day for childcare as govt scheme scrapped

The first case of the deadly illness, known locally as "mumps", has been confirmed as a local girl.

The girl was at a school function when she was diagnosed and then taken to hospital by ambulance, where she died later that night.

Health officials are currently working on identifying the case and how many others may have been infected, and are urging parents to be on the lookout for symptoms and inform the gardaí if their child is exhibiting any symptoms.

The case was reported by a student at the Dublin National School of Music and Drama, who was at the concert, which was attended by some 70,000 people.

The 16-year-old from Dublin was diagnosed with measles on Friday and taken to hospital by ambulance.

The girl's family and friends have been questioned, but so far there has been no new information received.

Health officials said at the weekend that they are trying to locate all those in the event that more cases are diagnosed and that they want to provide them with as much information as possible.

The latest case occurred during the festival period of the Gaeltacht Celtic festival, which ran from the weekend of Saturday 28 August through Sunday 29 August.

On Monday, the health department informed the families of the new case via the social media website Facebook.

"The case is being investigated by Dublin's Garda Síochána and the case will be referred to the National Health Service (NHS) for further assessment," the department said in the statement.

The department has advised the parents to have their children vaccinated before leaving the country.

The Health Service Executive (HSE) said in a statement that the department "is aware of an additional case of mumps confirmed in Ireland in the last 24 hours.

"This case is being assessed by the NHP and, as a precautionary measure, members of the public are being asked to ensure that any children under the age of 12 have been vaccinated. There is no risk to the general public."

Gardaí have been in contact with the family and the department has advised it to contact the hospital if any children under the age of 12 are seen at the hospital and if they display any symptoms.

It is believed that the girl has been exposed to the virus during the Gaeltacht festival.

There are currently no cases in Ireland of mumps, which is generally an infection caused by the mumps virus, causing high fever and rash which sometimes includes swollen glands in the mouth and throat, but no rash.

There is no specific vaccination available for the mumps virus and in the case of any infection, it is recommended that everyone in a child's immunisation line be tested for the mumps.

The Health Protection Authority (HPA) said that there have been 14 new confirmed cases of measles in Ireland since the start of this year.

"It's been a difficult few days for public health, and the HPA is committed to working with health professionals and community organisations in an effort to ensure that those affected have the information and support they need to get through this difficult time," said Dr Michelle O'Toole, HPA's Minister for Health.

The cases of measles are not linked to the Gaeltacht festival, but Health Minister Simon Harris said the new cases would not be excluded.
headline: Covid-19: 53 additional cases with no new deaths recorded

Micheál Martin has said that he will not support the continuation of the student fees freeze, while Education Minister Michael Ring has said he is not in favour of more tuition fees, after a row broke out over a change in the composition of the Cabinet last night.

Martin said today that he and Ring had had a "constructive discussion" and that he would not support the continuation of the freeze.

However, while saying that the discussion between the two ministers had focused "entirely" on the issue of tuition fees, Martin also said that it was important to "ensure that the Government's priorities are clear and to ensure that our agenda for the future is clear".

Speaking at a press conference after his meeting with Education Minister Michael Ring, Martin told reporters: "I think we have, in fact, a constructive discussion with the Minister. There has been no discussion with me. I think it is important that we ensure that the Government's priorities are clear and to ensure that our agenda for the future is clear."

Ring, speaking on RTE Radio 1's Today with Sean O'Rourke, told the programme that he was not in favour of a further cut in the student fee. "I am not in favour of a further student fees cut," said Ring.

On Tuesday, the Cabinet met at Stormont to discuss the government's post-election programme. Ring, along with Martin, the SDLP leader Colum Eastwood and the Social Democratic and Labour Party leader Colum Eastwood, was unable to reach an agreement after a long marathon session.

After the meeting, a spokesperson for the Education Minister told Independent.ie that the talks had taken place "in a constructive spirit" and that both ministers were "very confident about the direction" of the future Government.

However, following the meeting, the spokesperson said that it would be inappropriate for the Cabinet to comment on the meeting.

Speaking on RTE Radio 1's This Week programme, Ring said that he was "totally in favour" of continuing the freeze. "I think the issue in the Cabinet meeting yesterday is that everybody understood that this is the last chance to get this programme back on track," said Ring. "I think we would agree that we have been able to do that for the last four months, to get this programme back on track. I think that is the responsibility of the Minister for Education, but I think that we are in a constructive spirit, we are in a way in agreement as to how we should move forward."

When asked about the comments from Martin and Ring about the possible future of the student fees freeze, Ring said: "I think that is what the Cabinet is going to be looking at tomorrow night. The Cabinet meeting yesterday is, I think, the most important point at which we can come together in the long run. I think we all recognise the need to get the programme back on track, but we also want to make sure that it is the best deal for students, for the taxpayer."

Yesterday, Independent.ie published an opinion piece from a former pupil who said he would be "devastated" if the freeze continued.
headline: Government split as minister casts doubt on further student fee cut

"The figures revealed that 5,700 of the 17,000 cases of domestic abuse reported to the police each year involved a property transaction, according to figures from the General Household Survey (GHS).

The most common source of the abuse was a mortgage.

An average of 20% of the cases, or 3,600 cases, involved a mortgage. The cases that were a breach of mortgage terms were almost three times as frequent as breach of other terms.

"The figures for mortgage-related violence is nearly double those for domestic abuse," said a spokesman for the Department of Social Protection.

"This is due to the wider nature of the mortgage market. A mortgage is a formal document that allows individuals to take out a mortgage and purchase property.

"Mortgages can be structured in a way that can give rise to a risk of abuse. They can also be structured to allow individuals to take on more debt to pay off the mortgage and increase their home ownership.

"These are known as 'hidden loans' and many people are unable to raise the money to repay them. These mortgages are commonly used by families to buy up expensive properties, sometimes at a very high price.

"This increases the risk of people being taken advantage of. These mortgages, and the debt that is associated with them, can also cause people to fall back on the criminal justice system.

"It also means that victims can be left with expensive legal expenses, the loss of dignity and the mental toll of repeated stress and anxiety.

"It also means that people who have not suffered from violence can have an extremely high risk of violence."

Source: Ireland Examiner (irishexaminer.com).
headline: Domestic abuse victims 'trapped' in dangerous homes by mortgages
