Fertiliser is a £45 billion industry and a major contributor to the UK's economic output.

It has been one of the UK's fastest growing industries in recent years.

The industry employs a workforce of some 4 million people and generates about £45 billion for the economy.

But with fertiliser prices having peaked in 2011, it is now on the verge of a major downturn that could damage exports and job losses.

In a bid to boost exports and boost confidence, some companies are now making fertiliser in the US, South Africa and elsewhere.

But it could spell trouble for British farmers and the North's own producers if prices start to fall, which could mean higher prices for local growers and the closure of a large proportion of the £1.5 billion business in the North.

The government's investment arm, Invest in Ulster, is leading a series of schemes aimed at encouraging the industry to expand, as there is a growing market for it.

The government has pledged £20 million for a new plant in Enniskillen to boost the local plant.

"This is not a new idea and is being driven by the business community in the North of England. It is about attracting fertiliser manufacturers and farmers to the area," said a spokesman for Invest in Ulster.

"This is the latest phase in Invest in Ulster's plan to attract fertiliser manufacturers and farmers to the North. The programme is designed to attract the best and most innovative fertiliser manufacturers to the area and help make the UK a globally competitive fertiliser industry."

The South African plant is expected to employ 100 people.

Some of the other firms involved in the programme are: Alpena, a fertiliser manufacturer based in South Africa; Fonterra, a UK-based company.

Alpena also has an EU licence for its fertilisers, and is expected to employ some 60 people, while Fonterra employs about 500 in its factory in Enniskillen.

In 2010, Enniskillen was named one of the UK's most important food processing centres by the National Farmers Union.

The local plant was among the most favoured locations for fertiliser companies as it was near the ports and on the main road to Newcastle and Sheffield.

In 2005 the government spent £15 million upgrading the plant, which is the first investment in the North of England to include the provision of a plant.

It has also been in the news because the UK is the world's biggest exporter of fertilisers.

In January 2010 the US Department of Agriculture, which sets export quotas for fertiliser, ordered the plant to sell its fertiliser on the world market.

The plants that it has ordered so far have been shipped to places such as Chile, China, Mexico and India, and the UK has yet to receive any.

However, the Northern Ireland Department of Agriculture has been involved in the project, and it is now expected to receive several fertiliser plants over the next two years.

"Fertiliser is the UK's top export for fertilizer, with exports growing by more than 30 per cent in the last five years," said a spokesman for the Department of Agriculture.

The Department is seeking more firms to come to the area, he added.
headline: Global success beckons for North Yorkshire fertiliser

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) on Thursday urged international donors to make aid deliveries to the Palestinians to end the blockade, as activists reported a dramatic increase in the number of boats smuggling in food, medicines and other supplies.

The Israeli military said it shot down a rubber boat carrying some 500 tons of food, medicine, clothes, medical supplies and other aid in the Mediterranean on Wednesday, and has since fired on hundreds more to block off the waterway.

"The blockade will have a devastating impact on Palestinian civilians and will have a disastrous impact on the quality of life in Gaza," ICRC head of operations, Martin Bujold, said.

A total of 1,600 people were killed in Gaza by Israel's military strikes this year, in addition to 1,350 injured.

Bujold also called for an end to the "unconstitutional, discriminatory, arbitrary and unlawful" blockade on Gaza, which he described as "collective punishment, enforced by the occupying power against a civilian population".

The ICRC released a statement warning that "the situation in Gaza is deteriorating" and that aid is now being sent through tunnels that are being used to smuggle weapons and weapons components into Gaza.

"The situation is also very bad at the moment, because of the escalation in rocket attacks from Gaza, and there are still a number of wounded," Bujold said.

Israel is also blockading the al-Aqsa Mosque, which Muslims refer to as the Noble Sanctuary, an ancient site where Islam's prophet was born and where more than two millennia of Muslims' history took place.

The mosque is an important shrine in Jerusalem, and is considered to be the third-holiest in Islam.

"The blockade of Gaza must end. Our main goal is the end of the blockade," said Bujold.

He called for the "immediate lifting of the blockade to allow for an immediate and unconditional humanitarian ceasefire," adding that aid supplies needed to be delivered to Gaza "not because they are needed, but because they are there".

The ICRC has been operating in Gaza since June 2009 and has been involved in a number of aid operations.

Dr Mary MacCallum, a senior expert on infectious diseases at the National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) has confirmed the fourth new case of the coronavirus in west Ireland.

This follows the first two confirmed cases in the south of the island last week and the third confirmed case last Wednesday.

"We are not surprised by this latest update," said Dr MacCallum. "The NICE teams are working hard to investigate the potential links between the new cases and outbreaks of the disease which have occurred in the south of the island.

"They are still assessing the situation at the moment and it is too early to make any conclusions about the causes, but all four cases are believed to be related to exposure to the virus."

The four new cases have all been reported in counties Mayo, Fingal, Westmeath, Tipperary and Wexford.

The NICE teams will continue to work to establish the full extent of the disease, the origins of those infected and whether there are links between the virus and other illnesses, such as measles.

The virus is highly contagious and it is believed that all the infected people are from outside the country.

The latest outbreak of the coronavirus began on 1 August in counties Sligo, Wexford and Monaghan, where a total of five people in all have been diagnosed.

The NICE experts will continue to look at any possible link between the virus and other illnesses and the outbreak will continue to be monitored closely.

The previous cases in west Ireland were reported on 21 July, 22 July, 23 July and 26 July.

The virus, which is spread by airborne droplets of virus, is transmitted by a wide range of animals and through human contact with infected animals.

The first case of the coronavirus was reported on 7 August 2009 in a man who was at the centre of the Sahanu-Kerry outbreak.

Dr MacCallum also confirmed the case of a young man who had been in hospital with a fever for several days. He was released on 5 September.

NICE said the latest coronavirus cases were all reported in west of Ireland, where the last case was reported on 15 September.

The NICE teams will continue to monitor the situation, liaising with local health authorities and other international partners who are providing assistance to the island.

Dr MacCallum said: "We are not yet able to draw any conclusions about the cause of the latest cases, but they are all believed to be linked to exposure to the virus in the south of Ireland.

"We are working closely with the NCDRC on this case, and we will continue to do so in the coming days."

The first case was confirmed in a woman who was admitted to hospital on 1 August in Wexford and was the first to be reported in west Ireland.

The woman had travelled to Ireland from Greece on 18 July. She was a passenger on a train from Ireland to Italy and she had no symptoms when she arrived in Italy.

However, she returned to Ireland on 4 August, where she stayed with relatives in Wexford for the next seven days.

The victim was stabbed in the neck during the attack at the end of a night out.

The victim was taken to hospital with serious injuries to his neck and is currently in a critical condition.
headline: Dear Dáithí: A relative left our parents' lovely holiday home in an awful state

text:
There are few things in the world that attract more attention than the use of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in resolving trade disputes between countries.

The latest example of this is a recent development in the WTO as it appears that the US has made an attempt to win a dispute against Ireland and Ireland's foreign minister has responded in the strongest possible terms.

The Irish Examiner reports that the United States has filed an objection to Ireland's application to join the EU's Customs Union. The Irish government has indicated it is willing to be a party to this dispute and wants to join the European Union Customs Union.

The Irish government has indicated that the WTO is the best avenue to resolve the dispute. It was also indicated that the Irish government would fight the case. However, it has since been made clear that Ireland is not going to be a party to this dispute and therefore will not be participating in the proceedings.

The Irish government's response to this has caused a huge amount of dismay. The government has stated that it is a 'bad idea' for Ireland to be a party to this dispute as it will 'harm its interests'.

The Irish government is now looking at what it will do to challenge this position. The Irish Examiner reports that it will 'do its utmost to ensure that its position is not taken at any stage of the dispute'.

"The government's position is a negative and dangerous one, threatening Irish interests and it is wrong for any member state to do this," a statement from the Irish government said. "Any member state that believes it can use the WTO as a vehicle to undermine Irish commercial interests must be judged by the court."

In this instance, the Irish government is not just fighting against the United States but also other governments. If the Irish government is successful in its battle, it will send a very clear message to other governments in the world that the Irish government will not accept any attempts to use the WTO to undermine Irish commercial interests.
headline: The Irish Examiner View: Hogan’s hat in the WTO ring?

text:
The Health Ministry has ordered all hospitals in Gaza to be vaccinated against polio by Monday.

The campaign will be accompanied by a media campaign, which is being coordinated by the Ministry of Health and has the support of WHO.

The campaign aims to reduce the number of people exposed to the polio virus from about 5,000 annually to around 2,500 annually.

It follows the successful eradication campaign in Pakistan in the 2000s.

The campaign is supported by the United Nations, the United States and other international organisations, including the World Health Organisation.

A total of 5,000 people in Gaza are already vaccinated against polio, mostly in the north.

It will be a month before all the vaccines are distributed to the south.

The vaccination campaign is being executed with help from the World Health Organisation and the UN.

The programme is funded by a €35,000 grant from the European Union.
headline: Massive polio vaccination campaign begins in Gaza

text:
The new technology that promises to offer a solution to Ireland's crippling air pollution problem could be within reach within years, according to a major environmental group.

Clover is the first major new source of bio-fuel, and by far the biggest in Ireland.

It promises to be a major source of energy in Ireland's future, according to the Irish Examiner.

It will be available in the form of bio-fuel from clover, which is a flowering plant native to the UK, the Netherlands and Germany.

The technique will provide energy in a more sustainable form than coal and oil.

If it does become a significant economic driver for the country, it will represent a major win for the country and its environment.

According to the Examiner, a recent study suggested Ireland could produce about 100,000 tonnes of biofuel annually.

It was said that bio-fuel could generate €2.5 billion for the Irish economy.

However, the study concluded that the bio-fuel production would still require between €13 and €20 billion, depending on the technology used.

Clover has been proven to be a more environmentally friendly alternative to oil.

It is a single-celled plant, which means the plant's roots don't need to be polluting the environment.

This means there is no need to increase the amount of land that needs to be set aside for clover farming, which can be done through reforestation.

Clover is said to be a key driver of conservation measures in the North Sea, where it is used to treat oil spills.

In 2013, Ireland was awarded a renewable fuels research and development programme (R&D), which will be funded by the European Commission and the European Investment Bank.

The research and development programme will be aimed at developing new bio-fuels from clover.

The Irish Examiner said the research would start with the research of the environmental benefits of clover and then develop techniques to convert the bio-fuelled fuel into more environmentally friendly forms.

It would also focus on using clover as a substitute for diesel and fossil fuel.

Clover is a fast-growing part of the Irish economy, accounting for around €9 billion of the €32 billion turnover.

It accounts for about 20 percent of Irish agricultural production.

For the Irish Examiner, the research into the environmental benefits of clover was sparked by an R&D study conducted in 2012 by a German research institute.

The report said that clover was a renewable source of energy that could replace diesel in a large amount of the Irish economy.
headline: Signpost: Incorporating clover offers a 'win win' for economic and environmental sustainability

text:
Transgender teen's father gives emotional testimony at Dublin hearing

(INTELLIHUB) — The father of a trans teen whose life was ruined when he was forced to undergo a sex change operation told his story to a Dublin judge at the end of a hearing today.

"I am a mother of two daughters," said Robert De Niro. "One of them is a transgender girl. She's a very happy girl. She goes to school just fine, loves everybody and is a happy girl and a joy to be with."

The former professional boxer who has spoken openly about his personal struggles with depression and anxiety has been speaking publicly about his daughter to raise awareness of the transgender community.

"She is a very happy, joyful child who is very close to home. She goes to school just fine. She loves everybody and is a joy to be with."

De Niro was also speaking out to raise awareness of the devastating effects the irreversible treatment has on the developing brain.

De Niro said the surgery has caused the girl to develop severe seizures that have been affecting her ability to learn, to communicate, to function.

She had to have her heart bypassed and also had the surgery to remove her breasts because the procedure is irreversible and irreversible.

"She has never learned to be a normal person and she's not supposed to be," said De Niro. "She's not supposed to be happy or be a normal child or a loving child. All her life she's been a freak.

"She's never been a good child. She never had any friends and she is always hated because of this."

De Niro was introduced to the judge by a concerned father whose daughter has been diagnosed with gender identity disorder.

"The mother asked me to share that her daughter has not learned to interact with the opposite sex and that she can't live as a girl, for the last eight years," De Niro said.

The judge questioned the father why he felt it was necessary to have a sex change operation on his daughter when he was able to provide for her for free on a "no strings attached" basis.

"I don't understand why you would have done this for your daughter but not for your son," he said.

De Niro insisted that he had been a good father but was devastated that his daughter, now a young woman, had been made to undergo a sex change operation.

The judge noted that his daughter had a "mature mind" and was able to make a decision as to how to act.

"She has matured and she's able to make a decision," De Niro said. "There are other options for her. She can choose not to have surgery or to have it done, if she feels she doesn't want to do it, but she does have another option that she can take.

De Niro's lawyer, Peter Dunne BL, said that De Niro could not afford a "lifetime" of treatment that would be "horrific" and that De Niro's daughter could have left home, never had to experience the operation, and never had to go through it all.

In December 2013, De Niro was forced to undergo a sex change operation on his own medical advice to save his daughter's life.
headline: Robert De Niro expresses ‘love and support’ for transgender daughter

text:
A woman in Cork has been raped by a stranger who approached her as she walked to work, a court has heard.

Eoin O'Sullivan, 42, of Kilmacruk, Co Cork, was given a 21-year suspended sentence by Cork Circuit Criminal Court at Limerick, Co Limerick.

The court heard that on March 17th, 2016, at 3.16am, a man, believed to be of Irish descent, approached O'Sullivan and said: "I'm going to take you to my house."

O'Sullivan asked why he was there, and he replied that he had taken an "old lady" to the local pub.

He then proceeded to have intercourse with her, which caused her to suffer serious injuries.

A statement of facts in the case said that, when the woman reported the offence at the police station, the officer in charge told her that there was a possibility that she may have been involved in a sexual offence.

In the statement of facts, the officer said that she did not believe the woman to be at fault, but rather her abuser.

The officer said that O'Sullivan had also engaged in "significant damage" to the victim's property, including the brickwork, and had left a note with her identifying information.

He said that the victim had asked for the note to be taken away from her.

O'Sullivan had been living in Cork at the time of the incident, the officer told the court.

The officer said that O'Sullivan had told gardaí that he had carried out the attack on the woman as a result of his drug use.

However, he denied that he had taken drugs and denied sexually abusing the woman as she approached him in the pub.

O'Sullivan, who pleaded guilty, will be sentenced on October 13th at Limerick Circuit Criminal Court.
headline: Woman who was sexually abused as child attacked by stranger in Cork city

Juanita Browne, the actress who made headlines last week by claiming that she is a lesbian and was forced to wear male clothing, has finally given a rare interview.

"I am very glad to be here today as my lawyers are ready to get going, so hopefully I can get my voice back on this issue, as I want to talk about the issue of women in the public eye who do not want to talk about it, but if you are gay, you have to talk about it."

The Irish Examiner says Browne has finally spoken out, and she was also asked why she claims to be a lesbian.

This is what she had to say:

"I am an actress, I am a mother of two beautiful daughters. I am a proud gay woman and I'm happy to be out and proud of it.

"I believe the rights of men and women are one and the same. I don't want to be seen as someone that is trying to get in the way of people. I'm a proud lesbian.

"I can't change who I am, I can only change how I am perceived."

"I have spent the last 25 years working with wonderful men and women, that have shaped me as an actor and a mother. All of the men I have been involved with have been absolutely wonderful to work with. I love that this story of an actress with two beautiful girls, that you all know, and I am proud to be out and proud of it, because it's an issue that affects women in the public eye and that is something we need to talk about.

"For me, it is not a problem of who is in the public eye, it's a problem of what people have in their lives."
headline: Juanita Browne: Give some really wild Christmas gifts this year

text:
WSJ journalists are being "unfairly" denied credentials to cover a trade conference, the Beijing-based Global Times newspaper said Wednesday.

It said the three WSJ reporters, one of whom is a US citizen, would be refused credentials for their upcoming trip to China, as would two WSJ correspondents and another correspondent from Reuters, who is also a US citizen.

The Beijing-based Global Times called the decision "unprecedented".

"The Chinese government's move is an extraordinary and unacceptable way of demonstrating its displeasure with WSJ reporters' coverage of the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP)," it said.

"It is tantamount to a ban on the publication of 'unbiased' news."

The WSJ is reporting that the three journalists — Peter Wallsten, Eileen Sullivan and Andrew Marr – are being denied entry to Beijing on the grounds that their reporting could damage China's "national interest".

The three correspondents were on a fact-finding mission with the WSJ and the Associated Press (AP) and were due to visit China later this month.

The WSJ said it had made "no specific threats" to the three journalists.

"Our editors, journalists and reporters will take a different stance, but we do not expect any significant impact on the quality of our reporting on the TPP or China-US relations," the publisher said in a statement.

"There will be no impact on our coverage of US political and economic matters, including the President's trip to China in April."

The WSJ and AP said in a statement: "We are disappointed that the Beijing Bureau has chosen to impose its will on these three journalists, even at the risk of limiting their ability to report news in China."

The Global Times said: "The WSJ reporters have been denied entry to China and are now considering their legal options."

The paper said it would be "very surprised" if the WSJ journalists' visa applications were approved.

"However, our lawyers will decide whether or not the journalists should be permitted to enter China for their visit to China."

The Global Times said the decision to deny the WSJ correspondents access to China was "an obvious provocation" that would "damage China's national interest".

It urged Beijing to "make clear its concerns" to the three journalists about their coverage of the TPP.

"If the two journalists and reporter from Reuters are not granted visas to report, we will send a joint letter to the WSJ's editors, the AP and the AP's editor-in-chief, Philip Lacey, demanding the journalists' visas be revoked."

The Global Times editorial said: "For more than a decade, the US press and its American partners have been making noise about China's 'revolving door' policies whereby American journalists and academics are regularly recruited as part of a government-sponsored program to influence China's foreign policy.

"We are worried that this is a new stage of a very old strategy of influencing China's foreign policy. In this situation, the US press has decided to impose its will on the WSJ, AP and Reuters in order to keep its silence on this issue.
headline: China revokes press credentials of three WSJ reporters

text:
Gardaí are to carry out post-election checks to ensure no political interference in a matter which would normally be dealt with by the State-appointed Oireachtas Commission.

The Taoiseach, Enda Kenny, has said he is keen to avoid another general election, while the leaders of Fine Gael and Fianna Fail are expected to follow suit.

Earlier this week, Minister for Foreign Affairs Charlie Flanagan and Taoiseach Enda Kenny attended a meeting of the Public Accounts Committee, which is investigating the extent to which the Government is meddling in the way public service funding is allocated to the local authorities.

The Oireachtas Commission, headed by Public Expenditure Minister Brendan Howlin, was established in 1996. Its remit is to investigate spending in public bodies, including the local authorities.

The report into the spending on the county council elections in 2006 and 2007 will be delivered to the public accounts committee on Wednesday.

That inquiry is expected to be conducted by former Labour TD Patrick O'Donovan, who will also be looking at whether any political interference was occurring in the area.

The Oireachtas Commission, which is made up of the Taoiseach, the Chief Minister, the Minister for Jobs and Enterprise, the Taoiseach's TD, and a number of independent commissioners, is now investigating the use of public money to encourage candidates to contest local elections, particularly in Dublin.

The inquiry is examining whether the Public Expenditure Minister, Brendan Howlin, failed to carry out his duties as public servant in overseeing the use of public money.

The committee is examining the use of public money in favour of local candidates for the 2006 county council elections and the 2007 local authority elections. The Government was accused of using local authority spending money to promote the Labour Party during the elections.

A report on this will be delivered on Wednesday, a week after the general election. The Taoiseach said he would be urging Mr O'Donovan to complete his investigation and publish his findings by the end of the year.

However, Mr Flanagan was quick to dismiss suggestions of political interference.

"I am not going to comment on a report I have received on the conduct of the commission when it is looking at the conduct of the commission itself. I'm not going to comment on the commission and all the various aspects of that," he said.

Mr Flanagan said he would not be commenting on the contents of the report itself.

"If it was political interference, if there was political interference then the Oireachtas would be looking into that."

In a written answer to questions from Mr O'Donovan he said he was not aware of any political interference by the Government in the way local authority spending was being used.

Mr O'Donovan said that he would like to see any findings delivered to the public accounts committee by October next year.

He said the report would also seek to determine whether the allocation of public money to local authorities had led to any improper payments or kickbacks.

"I'm not sure whether that can be said in the context of the commission or whatever. I would be interested to see what the findings of the commission are. I'm not sure if there will be an opportunity for anybody to make a submission," he said.
headline: FF and FG leaders keen to avoid post Covid-19 austerity

text:
A new report by the Irish Medical Association has revealed that nearly one in 10 patients with a cancer diagnosis were contacted by their doctors before the results were known.

The study has been criticised for its focus on contact between doctors and patients and not the tests themselves.

The paper also claims the study shows a need for an improved protocol for handling patients who have received the results.

The study is based on a voluntary survey of 5,000 cancer patients, conducted between October and January last year.

The survey asked:

On which day did you contact your doctor before the results were known?

On which day did you contact your doctor before the results were known? Which clinic (hospital, general practitioner, specialist, etc) did you visit to make a decision about treatment?

On which day did you visit your doctor to make a decision about treatment? When did you leave the clinic to contact your doctor to make a decision about treatment?

On which day did you leave the clinic to contact your doctor to make a decision about treatment? What was the type of procedure, for example, radiotherapy or chemotherapy, and why?

The paper notes that the most common reason for the doctor-patient contact was having a "disease that you can't do anything about".

It says:

"A significant proportion of patients were concerned about the results – in particular about the radiotherapy results."

It claims:

"A significant proportion of patients had a fear of failure."

However, in a statement to the Irish Times, the medical fraternity argued that the study was flawed and used a "low number of patients".

It said:

"The report uses low number of patients for most results, and includes a few cases where patients have refused treatment due to poor results."

The statement went on to say that only a small number of patients were referred to other clinics and clinics were not involved in the survey.

It added:

"The majority of patients were contacted by their doctors, and in cases where the doctors were not involved, the results were reported to other medical departments and clinics."

The statement concluded:

"The report does not speak to the merits of a clinical practice that will refer to the hospital and the relevant clinical unit for advice and information."
headline: Who contacts patients with the test results?

The number of people admitted to hospital with suspected or confirmed measles cases has risen to 53, up from 53 on Monday (28 January).

The number of those admitted for suspected measles cases has increased from 14 on Monday to 13 on Tuesday, with a further 2,380 cases identified.

It means the number of confirmed cases of measles in Ireland is now just over 400.

The increase in cases is the highest for any Irish State.

The health department say it is still too early to say if this is the start of a wider trend.

Dr John Cooney, the head of the measles programme at the Irish Health Service, said a large number of confirmed cases were occurring in some areas of the State, with the highest number in Cork, Dublin, Galway and Shannon.

He said the high rate of cases was "the result of a number of factors, including, as we have said previously, the increasing number of unvaccinated children in the country".

There are 3,700 suspected or confirmed measles cases in Ireland, although many of these were not identified during the initial outbreak of the disease which affected the Republic of Ireland.

The health department says, however, the situation in the Republic of Ireland is much more complicated, in part due to the high number of unvaccinated children in the country.

Dr Cooney said the number of cases was a "cause for concern" and urged all parents to get their children immunised.

"Although there is still a significant number of unvaccinated children in our society, we can't be complacent," he said.

"We need to make sure that this is not a long term problem and continue to work with parents to get their children vaccinated."

He said more work was needed and said it was possible that cases were not being identified in all areas of the State.

However, Dr Cooney said there was an increasing trend in measles cases in certain communities in some areas of the country.

He said it was still too early to tell whether this was a sign of a wider trend.

He said the health department would continue to monitor the situation and make sure all cases were confirmed before putting any warnings in place.

Measles, the virus that causes an illness with a headache, sneezing, runny nose and cough in a small proportion of people, can cause severe damage to the body's immune system.

It is common in the UK and in Ireland since last year, but the measles outbreak is the largest in Ireland in more than 25 years.

The virus was eradicated in Ireland in 1998 and there is no evidence to suggest that it is reintroducing itself in the Republic.

The virus can be spread through coughing or sneezing.

In January a measles outbreak also hit the Republic of Ireland and health officials confirmed at least three people had been sickened and six had died.

In January the virus spread to the UK, with 1,300 cases being reported to the Health Protection Agency.
headline: 53 more people in hospital with Covid, 1,380 new cases

The gardaí have been attacked by masked people during disturbances in the city centre, a senior police source has confirmed.

The source said a man and a woman who had been arrested on suspicion of serious assaults on two gardaí were "beaten and punched and set on fire" as they were being transferred to custody in the city.

Meanwhile, a garda suffered a suspected stab wound in the leg, the source said.

"We have a small group of people who are acting erratically and in an irrational manner," he said.

"It is not just the police. It is the general public who have been attacked."

The garda injured was taken to St James's Hospital for treatment.

"This is the first time in my 40 years of policing that I have been attacked by masked people," a senior Garda source told the Irish Examiner.

"I have never seen anything like it."

The garda's injuries are not believed to be life-threatening.

The Garda Bureau of Criminal Investigation is investigating.

Sinn Féin councillor Kevin Humphreys condemned the violence and called on the protesters to "leave our city centre".

"This violence must end," he said.

"We must get rid of the anger and leave our city centre and people who are still angry with our Government.

"It is important to remember that these are not ordinary protesters. They have the support of the vast majority of people in our city.

"They are not protesting because they want to turn the clock back to 1990.

"They are protesting against austerity and the Government's failure to ensure we get a better deal for our people."

A spokesperson for the Garda Commissioner has issued a statement condemning the attacks.

"While it is unfortunate that there have been disturbances in the city centre, it would be inaccurate to suggest that we have not seen this type of behaviour before," it said.

"Our officers are doing a very good job and are working hard to keep our city safe."

"We have a long way to go in tackling the issues of crime and disorder in the city but I am extremely proud of the work of the Gardaí and the support they provide to our communities."

Earlier on Friday, RTÉ News reported that two of its journalists had been assaulted in a major city centre centre, with one injured.

Gardaí on the ground on Saturday reported that two officers had been attacked in the city centre, in what appeared to be a similar manner to the incident at Dublin Port earlier in the day.

The attack was said to have occurred near the Irish Times office in a pub on Spaghetti Warehouse Street, where the Irish Times is based.

The Garda sources said that the two gardaí were both assaulted and had a minor cut on their face.

The officers have been taken to the station, which is on the corner of Spaghetti Warehouse Street and Ballyfermot Street, and will undergo a medical examination.

Gardaí in the city have set up a command post in an area at the foot of the Castlereagh Hill Road, while gardaí from the Garda Emergency Response Unit have set up a command post on the Castlereagh Hill Road near to the Castlereagh Hotel.
headline: Gardaí attacked during violent unrest after stabbing

text:
A hijacker has been shot dead after an armed hijacking in the Indian Ocean.

The terrorist group Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL) launched the attack in the Red Sea resort of Hurghada early on Monday, a senior police source said.

The terrorist group took control of the aircraft from a ground-based base in the area of Kullu in the Arabian Sea, the source said.

The source said that three people who were members of the armed group who were with the aircraft were shot dead after attempting to bring it down.

There were no casualties on the ground at the time.

An RAF Typhoon armed with two air-to-air missiles fired two missiles into the cockpit of the aircraft before it crashed, according to the source.

The aircraft, which had been flying for about 30 minutes, crashed at 10.15am after an hour-and-a-half flight from Abu Dhabi.

The aircraft was carrying more than 200 passengers, according to the source.

The hijacker, believed to be from Yemen, was identified as Omar al-Kurdi, who is also suspected of being on the radar of the National Security Agency (NSA) and of having contact with an American pilot named Thomas Eric Duncan.

Duncan, the first American doctor to die in Iraq in 2003, had been in touch with the FBI shortly before he took to the air in a Liberian Airlines plane that crashed in 2003 into the Atlantic Ocean.

Duncan had contacted the FBI in early April before he flew to Saudi Arabia and stayed in a hotel there. He also had contact with the NSA, but the FBI's interest was then focused on Duncan, not al-Kurdi, the source said.

A senior UK intelligence source told the Irish Times that the hijacker could have been the first "lone wolf" to attack an aircraft in the Middle East.

However, the US Government has condemned the hijacking as "reprehensible", saying the "vast majority" of attacks on US planes involve group-related terrorists, although they have also been carried out by "individuals who have no connection whatsoever to terrorism" or have been trained in Syria or Iraq.

The FBI is now reviewing surveillance footage from the airport and surrounding areas before deciding whether to bring charges against the hijacker and the other people who assisted him.

The US National Security Agency has been working with the British authorities to trace the whereabouts of the other suspected hijacker on the flight, it has been reported.

Earlier on Monday, the UK Foreign Office had issued a travel warning to UK nationals in the Middle East, warning them of a possible attack.

It said there was "considerable" risk to British nationals in areas where ISIL had a presence and urged them to exercise vigilance when travelling in areas of Syria and Iraq where ISIL may be operating.

Britain has also urged its nationals in the Middle East to monitor the media and their personal communications, and report any suspicious behaviour to the security services.

The warning said: "There is a risk to British nationals in the Middle East, particularly those with strong links to the UK, and where ISIL has a presence.

"ISIL may conduct suicide bombings to target British nationals and may be planning to target US and Western interests in the region.
headline: Hijacking ends in Arabian Sea, says UK agency

text:
The Pompidou Centre at Paris' Notre Dame Cathedral will close for renovation for five years.

The centre's opening in 1998 was greeted with the most lavish opening ever given a French cathedral.

The interior design by architect Philippe Starck will be a stark contrast to the iconic grandeur that greeted visitors as they entered the building.

The iconic Pompidou Centre's interior design, which is to be altered for the fifth time, was designed by Philippe Starck, who has a reputation for elegant interiors.

It was built to celebrate the 400th anniversary of the arrival of Napoleon in Paris.

A new Pompidou Centre will open in 2017, with all current services maintained.

The centre will be open at all hours during daylight hours.

It will still have its classical interiors, but they will include a number of new features.

It will be an extension of the existing Pompidou Centre, but with a number of features designed especially for Paris.

One of the new features will be the Pompidou Centre's first-ever bar, the Bar Le Clos.

The bar will serve drinks made with local, organic ingredients and will provide a space for the Centre's staff to interact with visitors.

Another feature will be a gallery at the entrance, which will be open on Saturdays and Sundays.

And there will be a public art gallery with up to 200 works for public view.
headline: Pompidou Centre in Paris to close for 5-year renovation

text:
Renewable energy sources are growing at a faster rate.

A new report says that Ireland is on course to overtake the UK as the world's biggest market for green energy.

It predicts that Ireland's power demand will grow at an annual rate of almost 7% by 2030.

It says that by 2030, all power generated in Ireland will be wind power.

The report, from Renewable Energy Agency, says that the country could be on track for a total of 200 gigawatts of wind and solar by 2025.

It says that the sector will be almost completely decarbonised by 2050.

Its findings are based on analyses of the total supply and demand of wind and solar power in Ireland, as well as projections of the amount of renewable energy in the grid and the generation of energy from renewable resources such as water, biomass, waste and biomass.

The agency says that Ireland has some of the cheapest wind and solar resources in Europe, with both types costing around $100 per megawatt hour.

It says that, to meet the country's climate change targets, Ireland needs to increase renewable energy generation from 25% by 2020 to 50% by 2030.

Wind power

The report says that wind power is expected to generate around 2% of Ireland's electricity by 2030. It projects that more than half the electricity that will be generated in the country will come from wind power.

It says that wind turbines will be installed on all of the country's major roads by 2017, providing about 1.8 gigawatts of electricity annually.

The report says that there are plans to install 2.5 gigawatts of wind turbines in Ireland by 2018, which will provide around 7% of Ireland's electricity.
headline: Renewable energy sources growing at faster rate

text:
A team of 12 engineers have made a new head-mounted device which can move an injured boy from hospital to hospital.

The device was developed by scientists from the NUI Maynooth School of Technology in Co Wexford.

It moves an injured child from hospital to hospital, and has been developed as a treatment for people with spinal injuries.

Dr James O'Connor, of the NUI Maynooth School of Technology, said the device, known as the Dino-Cart, could save the lives of children who would otherwise have died.

"If you can help an injured child to be a child, to be self-reliant and to be able to feel a lot less pain, that's a benefit to the children that are injured," he said.

The researchers have developed the Dino-Cart device after developing a similar device for quadriplegics, known as the Robo-Carter.

The new device uses sensors, motors and computer algorithms to move a child's head, body and neck as he or she walks and runs.

The researchers have also developed a system that can control the body and head movements.

"The device can be used by a wide range of people, particularly children with spinal injuries. It can also be used for the benefit of children with more serious injuries, which includes stroke and spinal cord injury," said Dr O'Connor.

The device can be used on its own or in conjunction with other devices.

The researchers have developed the device with the support of Irish Paralympics Team and Ireland's Royal College of Surgeons.

Dr O'Connor said the device was being developed to help children who have not received the spinal cord injury treatment they need to recover.

The research was undertaken at NUI Maynooth.

They have published the work in the Journal of Biomechanics.

Read more here.
headline: Dino-cart invention helps boy 'to be a child'

text:
School meal scheme will continue for the duration of the mid-term break, with a new offer to parents.

The National Meal Scheme (NMS) for the 2014-15 school year will provide an extra two days of meals for all children between the ages of 3-5 at local primary, secondary and higher education institutions. This is being extended until the summer break in September 2014.

The programme is currently under review. It is expected that the programme will be reviewed and enhanced in coming months.

A new offer will be made to parents, following consultation with the NMS Board and the Department of Education.

The National Council for Education will be informed of the new offer, which will be reviewed and enhanced at a future date. The NMS Board has been told that parents will not be charged for this additional meal.

The NMS Board, which has responsibility for the scheme, has met today with primary and secondary teachers and has endorsed the offer.

Teachers from primary and secondary schools will have their current lunch deals, which contain up to a day's worth of meals, extended until the mid-term break. This will mean that children can eat more breakfast, lunch, and dinner during the summer break.

The Department of Education will be consulted on the extension and enhancements to the scheme.

The Department has also announced that up to 12,000 children across Ireland will be able to participate in the National Meals Scheme for the summer break.

The Department has also announced that up to 2,600 children will be eligible for free school meals.

The Department is currently conducting a review of the NMS, which has already begun.

Details of the review will be announced later this year.
headline: School meal scheme to continue during mid-term break

Ireland has paid out more than €1.6m in unclaimed Lotto tickets since it started the lottery in 2008, but in a bid to find the winner there's been a significant surge in the number of tickets being sold online, it has been revealed.

The latest figures, obtained by RTÉ News, show that from the first three months of 2013, more than 8,800 people in Ireland have claimed tickets from the lottery, a 35 per cent increase on the same period last year.

text:
It is understood that up to 2,500 firefighters are battling a wild fire in the Fanad Peninsula.

The fire has spread to a number of properties in the area, which have been evacuated.

It is also expected to spread to several residential properties in Limerick.

The fire is burning in the open fields, along the coastal road towards the village of Muckmuck, and has spread to five properties on the Fanad Peninsula.

Firefighters are currently monitoring the fire.

It is unknown how many homes are affected.

Fire Service Commissioner, Mick Barry, has arrived in the area and is expected to visit the affected properties.

The fire is now in the second stage of containment.

The fire is now estimated to be 50% contained.

The fire is burning on the open fields, with a number of buildings on fire.

A number of crews have been dispatched to the scene, including six fire engines, three water tankers and one aerial vehicle.

A total of 150 firefighters are on the scene.

There has been a number of reports of injuries and damage to buildings.

The fire will continue to be monitored in the coming days, and crews will remain on site.

The Chief Fire Officer, Mick Barry, also arrived in the area to speak to people, including members of the public.

All of the properties affected are in the area of the fire.

The Chief Fire Officer, Mick Barry, will be visiting the affected properties to assess the situation.

This is not an evacuation order for the residents, the Chief Fire Officer has told RTÉ News.

The Chief Fire Officer will continue to monitor the situation.

All residents in the area have been evacuated.
headline: Firefighters tackling wildfire on Fanad Peninsula

text:
Experimental drug fails in human trials

Last year, the World Health Organisation (WHO) declared the virus-resistant EBOV virus to be "endemic" in Europe.

The latest attempt to stop it from spreading came in January this year.

The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control has launched a trial to see if an experimental drug, called Zmapp, works as a vaccine against the virus.

Researchers in the US have also been attempting to develop an experimental vaccine for the virus.

They discovered the drug works against Ebola virus, but it also had to be given in a very specific way.

The researchers wanted to see if it would also work in the other two viruses in the Ebola family, EBOV and Marburg.

This week, they successfully tested the effectiveness of the drug.

The trial started on 14 January in Sierra Leone, where more than 3,000 people have already died from Ebola virus disease.

It is estimated that around 1,000 people have already died in Guinea, Liberia, Nigeria and Sierra Leone.

Ebola virus

Ebola virus is named after a village in the central African country of Zaire.

It causes severe, often fatal, internal and external bleeding.

It is spread by direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person.

It's a highly contagious disease which can spread easily, especially through the air.

In West Africa, there have been more than 3,000 confirmed cases, and nearly 5,000 deaths, in 2014.

The disease has been transmitted in rural areas, but is still very much a problem in densely populated cities, such as Kailahun, Sierra Leone, and Freetown, Sierra Leone.

In both cities, the health service is struggling to deal with the disease.

Health Minister Kent Austin is visiting the affected areas and has called for more help in treating the epidemic.

However, he has said that despite the epidemic's scale, it is "relatively tame" compared to previous outbreaks.

The WHO has said the number of cases of Ebola virus disease has more than doubled to 11,000 in 2015, compared with 6,000 in 2014.
headline: Experimental virus drug fails in human trials

text:
Man dies in Mayo collision while cycling

A 28-year-old man has died in an accident while cycling in Mayo.

He was riding at a speed of around 10-15km/h when he was hit by a car in Kilmallock Road, about 2.45pm on Thursday.

The crash happened on a section of road known as the Old Kilmallock Road.

The Garda Traffic Branch are investigating.

The driver of the car is understood to have stopped at the scene, but witnesses reported hearing an argument shortly before the collision.

The cyclist was later taken to Mayo Hospital by ambulance.

He died shortly after being taken to the hospital.
headline: Man who died in Mayo collision was 'lovely guy'

text:
The new 'Task Force on the Seafood Industry' has been set up to help the sector in the wake of Brexit.

Speaking at the launch today, Minister for Agriculture Simon Coveney said:

"The food and drink sector has faced the biggest change in its history in the last 40 years and this is a national priority that must be protected.

"We are seeing a lot of investment coming in from all sectors. We must work together to maintain the strength and vibrancy of the sector.

"The key question is how do we ensure that this investment and all the jobs associated with it is in the right place and in the right time."

It is anticipated that the taskforce will be able to create an economic boost of around €200 million over the next five years.

The Task Force will consist of representatives from across the food and drink industry, from the private sector to the public sector and will report back to Minister for Agriculture Simon Coveney.

Tasks to be tackled

Minister Coveney said a number of challenges faced the sector.

"There are huge opportunities for the food and drink sector. We need to ensure that this investment is in the right place and in the right time."

Minister Coveney said the task force would be tackling three major issues:

• How do we protect the jobs in the food and drink sector from Brexit?

• How do we create the right conditions for the food and drink sector to expand?

• How do we preserve the great heritage of the Irish food and drink industry?

"The Task Force will be working hard to ensure that our food and drink sector remains strong and healthy."

How does the taskforce work?

A task force is an administrative body for a number of government departments or agencies.
headline: Seafood Sector Taskforce launched in wake of Brexit

text:
"Hussein Nasrallah has expressed his shock and disappointment that the Lebanese media today reported the trial of Hasan Nasrallah, the man accused in the 2005 assassination of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri.

The Lebanese politician was convicted of the murder of Hariri, who was killed in a mysterious car bomb. Nasrallah denied the charges.

Nasrallah, a senior Hezbollah operative, was jailed in 2006 in the northern Lebanese city of Tripoli for life on charges of masterminding the assassination.

He was also sentenced to death in absentia.

The court heard from the prosecution that Nasrallah, his wife, his three sons and two friends, all from Lebanon's Christian minority, plotted the murder.

Nasrallah was also convicted of the 2006 murder of Lebanese MP Ali Mohsen Taha.

At the time of the killings, Nasrallah was a key member of Lebanon's Hezbollah movement.

He was arrested in January 2005 and jailed for life. He escaped in 2006 and has been trying to return to Lebanon.

In an interview to RTÉ News, Nasrallah said: "I'm disappointed by the media, that the prime minister was killed in my home.

"The people in Lebanon, who are our brothers, the Lebanese people, did not forget, or I do not know why did not forget him.

"That was a crime, and it has been proven with evidence, the murder of Hariri."

Nasrallah denied he and his men were involved in the murder. He said: "I do not, today, know anybody else who had any part in it."

He said it was "a big lie" that Hezbollah was behind the assassination.

Earlier in the day, Nasrallah was freed from prison.

He spent more than eight years in jail in the 1990s and was later convicted of murder.

On Sunday, Nasrallah had been convicted of involvement in three assassination attempts - all failed - in the 1980s.

He was jailed for life in 2006.
headline: Hezbollah suspect found guilty of 2005 Hariri murder

text:
There is some good news for Sinn Fein. While others were left with nothing to do, Fine Gael and Fianna Fáil have been busy in the run-up to the European Parliamentary Elections.

The two main parties will now be back to square one before the next general election, where Fianna Fáil is expected to take a substantial lead.

However, it has been a bad start for the Greens, whose vote is collapsing rapidly. They are now polling around 2% in some European countries.

In Europe, they have suffered from a lacklustre campaign and are struggling to gain support in general. Their first MEP has resigned and their candidate for the Brussels-based European Parliament is already campaigning for a seat in the European Parliament.

The Greens have been polling very low on the main parties' lists, and have not won any seats in the European Parliament since 2003.

The Green MEPs have been unable to raise the funds to campaign on the European election ticket for the first time since they took power in 2011.

The two main parties have both lost seats since their 2011 election victories. Sinn Fein has lost its four MEPs, and Fianna Fáil lost a total of seven MEPs after a referendum campaign in Ireland.

Despite this setback, both major parties have shown signs of recovery in the recent polls. Fine Gael, which has been struggling to recover its fortunes after a decade in opposition, has polled above five per cent in the polls in most European countries.

Fine Gael has been on track to win over 10 MEPs in the first round of the European Parliament elections. Fianna Fáil, on the other hand, is not far behind with nine.

The Greens' campaign for European elections has been underwhelming, with a disappointing fundraising effort.

Earlier this year, the party was forced to cut back its activities in Europe after the collapse of the Socialist MEPs' campaign in Germany.

There has also been a dramatic decline in the Green MEPs' support in the run-up to the European elections, with just one Green in every 20 votes counted.

Sinn Féin's campaign director for Europe, Gerry Adams, told the Irish Independent his party was well positioned to win the Euro elections.

"We're actually well placed to win the election. We've got a strong presence in Europe and have been since the 2011 election. Our message to voters across Europe is that no-one can stop the Irish Republic coming back – our economy is the fastest growing in Europe, and the country is the strongest in Europe in terms of its resilience and the strength of its social cohesion," he said.

The next European election is not until May 2015.
headline: Candidates jostle for position ahead of Euro Parl vote

text:
Man jailed for seven years for fatally shooting Ballymun father of seven

A man was jailed today (Monday, 4 July) for seven years for shooting dead father of seven Paul Dolan in Ballymun, Dublin.

Paul Dolan, a father of three, was shot and killed by a gunman on 5 May 2014. A 31-year-old man was charged with his murder. The man was sentenced to seven years jail and a community order for his offence, the court was told today.

Paul Dolan was shot dead by a young man on his way home after having dinner with his family at the time of his death.

Dolan, who was a father of three, had walked to the house on 5 May last year and met up with family members. He returned home when a masked man knocked at his front door and demanded he hand over his mobile phone.

Paul Dolan refused and the man opened fire. One of Paul Dolan's daughters managed to escape but Paul Dolan's son was also shot in the leg.

A short time later, Paul Dolan and his wife were taken to the Ballymun district hospital with life-threatening injuries. His wife died in a later hospital stay.

The defendant, who is from a disadvantaged background and who suffers from mental health issues, had been in a relationship with the deceased's sister for four months.

The court heard the incident was not a random attack and the man who fired the shot had a history of mental health problems.

The court heard the defendant had been drinking before his family left home.

Judge Martin Nolan told the defendant "he was a very nice man. He was one of the kindest people you could meet."

"He was a dad of three and he was a good father. He was an ordinary father who was not a psychopath," he said.

In a victim impact statement read to the court by his daughter, Paul Dolan said the shooting had been very difficult. He said he was "shattered", and felt angry, sad and isolated.

"I don't know how we came to this. I wish I could go back and be a normal father. I wish I could give back to society. I wish I could go back and give back to my family. I would still be there. I would still love them," he said.

He said he didn't know what to do. He did not want to be in prison for what happened.

Paul Dolan told the court he would never again have to face the day he would shoot his son, and that he would try to forgive the man who killed him.

"I hope in my heart that there is some redemption in his heart that he will recognise that it was wrong," he said.

He thanked the gardai and the community for their support.

The case was adjourned to Dublin Circuit Court on 8 July for a report on the outcome of the investigation.
headline: Man jailed for seven years over fatal Ballymun shooting

text:

RTE's investigative team has now obtained the results of a series of experiments performed at the National Centre for Bioinformatics in Ireland.

The work was carried out on live virus samples for a new vaccine, developed by scientists at ECDC.

In the experiments, they were shown that an enzyme called V1 protein can be created from the viral DNA. This means that the ECDC vaccine could have a potential to reduce the number of cases of vaccine-preventable diseases, especially measles and chicken pox, and may also help reduce the incidence of other infectious diseases.

The research was presented to an ECDC meeting last night (Sunday 24 October) and this was published in the journal Nature Immunology last week.

The research team was headed by Prof James Ryan, head of the Centre for Cellular and Molecular Medicine at the University of Cambridge.

The laboratory in which the experiments were conducted is at the ECDC and has been funded by the Department of Health and the UK Science and Technology Facilities Council. The laboratory has been operating since 2008.

Professor James Ryan said: "The discovery that an enzyme can be created from the virus DNA has significant potential in clinical trials for preventing vaccine-preventable diseases.

"We are also developing a vaccine for herpes, which is an increasing problem in countries such as India.

"If the vaccine is successful, it could be a game changer in areas such as measles and chicken pox."

He said the enzyme would have to be produced in a laboratory, and would need to be tested for safety in people before being produced commercially.

"The virus would need to be transformed to make the protein, and then injected intravenously.

"It is quite a complicated process but it is an exciting step forward."

He added: "The ECDC experiment was carried out in an environment that was very well controlled, with a safety monitor around the laboratory every night.

"There were no complications reported during the study. The safety monitor was very strict. The laboratory has been accredited for this by the Irish Biomedical and Health Research Council."

The study was published in the journal Nature Immunology, which is published by the British journal Cell.
headline: ECDC: Virus mutation could hamper vaccine effectiveness

text:
A US military plane plummets from the skies into the sea off the Kuwaiti island of Kuwait at the height of rush hour, the US military confirmed.

The US Central Command said the flight had a "sustained climb rate of 12,000 feet" and a final descent rate of about 200 feet.

It said the plane, based at Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, had been on a training mission.

The Kuwaiti air force said the jet was destroyed by a cannon and that two troops were rescued.

"The crew was safely recovered and the mission is over. We do not have any further details as to how the crew managed to remain airborne for so long and with such precision," US Central Command said in a statement.

It said the aircraft had been on an operational exercise "as part of a demonstration of readiness of air assets to respond to contingencies."

US military aircraft have been in action in the Gulf since September 11, 2001, and are part of an effort to provide security for US military operations and support for US diplomats abroad.

The incident comes weeks after the Pentagon revealed it had temporarily grounded one of its F-16 fighter jets in Kuwait, which the Defense Department said was not related to last year's attacks on the US consulate in Libya.
headline: Watch: US military plane plummets from sky in Kuwait

text:
The Government has been told by the health service regulator that the prospect of another strike vote is not on the cards.

A new health dispute is in the offing after doctors voted overwhelmingly in favour of a one-day strike tomorrow.

Union leaders had said they could call another one-day walkout this Wednesday after they failed to reach agreement on a deal with the Government on new contracts for their members.

A spokesman for the Health Service Executive (HSE) said the deal struck on Thursday by the Health Minister Simon Harris is "an excellent outcome" and the agreement is "a clear demonstration of the HSE's willingness to put our health at the heart of the health service".

He said the deal "offers a level of protection and access to services which is in line with the previous agreements".

The agreement also provides a four-month deferral to a new contract, which will take effect in September.

Minister for Health Simon Harris said it was a "win for the health service and patients".

Talks had progressed well and a new contract is "a clear demonstration of the HSE's willingness to put our health at the heart of the health service", he said.

"It ensures patients have secure, quality and competitive healthcare wherever they choose to receive care.

"I am confident that this agreement will lead to the safest and most affordable health service in Ireland.

"The HSE is committed to the health and wellbeing of all people, and continues to work to ensure that all our patients have access to high quality, safe and cost-effective healthcare that is delivered and delivered efficiently and effectively."

He said the HSE will also continue to work "across all healthcare issues, including in relation to the contract negotiations, to ensure that we can deliver the best possible care for all our patients, wherever they are located".

"The HSE will also be seeking to bring forward the deadline for the commencement of the new contract, to give the health services providers time to make sure they can deliver the best possible care for all of our patients."

Dr Sean Coughlan, President of the Association of Irish Medical Colleges, said there was "no room for complacency".

"We now have the best possible agreement for all patients and we are looking forward to the announcement of the new contract this week," he said.

"In order to provide the best possible healthcare to all patients we have been forced to impose a number of cuts, which will affect patient care in the short and long term, with impacts on the delivery of care for some patients on a daily basis."

Dr Coughlan said it was "hardly surprising" that "a significant proportion of doctors" want to strike.

He said he had been in discussions with the HSE and other health bodies which "expect the issue to be resolved" and to the best of their knowledge no doctor had so far taken the opportunity to withdraw from the strike.

He said while the HSE was "slightly disappointed" that the deal was not as long as it had hoped, it was "encouraged by the very high level of health service workers involved".
headline: Govt will not entertain talk of pausing hospital build

text:
Ken Starr died at the age of 76 this morning after a long illness.

The legendary US president died in the grounds of his home at his home in suburban Chicago.

He is survived by his wife, Kaye Starr, and his two sons.

A statement from the Starr family said: "Ken Starr will always be an important part of our family.

"He made huge contributions to the world through his work on the Clinton impeachment and was a brilliant man.

"We would like to express our deepest sorrow at the loss of Ken. He was one of the most kind, compassionate and compassionate people I have ever met."

Ken Starr was a prolific writer who wrote a number of books on the Clintons, including one called Clinton's War: The Continuing Costs of the Clinton Presidency and How Hillary's Justice Department Could Prosecute Bill and Hillary Clinton.

He also wrote The Way to Glory: How Ronald Reagan and His Team Stopped the Soviet Empire from Dominating Europe.

He served as general counsel to the Clinton Administration in the 1990s and, in 2005, he became a senior adviser to President Bush's re-election campaign.

He had an illustrious career in politics and law.

His first term as the US Attorney General was marked by the Monica Lewinsky affair. The scandal led to the impeachment of President Bill Clinton.

He was also one of the three co-chairs of the Clinton impeachment trial.

In 1992, he served as a special prosecutor investigating the assassination of the former president's Democratic rival, George H.W. Bush, which was the first case of its kind.

Mr Starr was also the special prosecutor during the trial of former President Bill Clinton's former Secretary of State, Hillary Clinton, who was impeached in 1997.

In 2005, he became the second Republican to win the presidency after President George W. Bush.

In a statement, the Starr family said: "It is with great sadness that we announce that Ken Starr's wife and daughters, Kaye and Kendall, have passed away.

"Ken is survived by his wife Kaye, sons Kent and Todd, and daughter Kaylie.

"Ken and his family will be sorely missed.

"Ken will be remembered as a wonderful father and husband who worked tirelessly to be a champion for children and an advocate for the rule of law, both in his personal and professional lives.

"His passing leaves a profound void that no child can fill, but we ask that you join us in prayers for the Starr family.

"We also ask that you join us in thanking Ken for all that he had done."

In 2006, Starr and the Clinton Administration were involved in a controversy when it was revealed that the Clinton Library had failed to release to the public the "missing" 52 hours of Clinton's videotaped deposition.

The depositions were originally due to be made public in 2003.

In 2009, an expert on impeachment, who had previously assessed the legal ramifications of Clinton's affair with Monica Lewinsky, declared that the case against Clinton was not strong enough.

However, a federal judge overturned the ruling and ordered the remaining depositions to be made public.

Ireland is the second EU country in which the threat of climate change is set to become the country's top national security issue, according to the Secretary General of the United Nations, Ban Ki-moon.

On Wednesday, Ban said he had also raised the issue of climate change with his Irish counterparts during a meeting in Dublin.

"This is a significant issue for Ireland," he told the Irish Parliament. "It is an issue of security, of the health of our people and also of the environment."

Read the full article here.

RTÉ has obtained a copy of a memo from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Móir Air) to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade outlining its proposed measures to reduce the impacts of climate change on Ireland.

The document has been obtained under the Freedom of Information Act by RTÉ under the Official Information Act.

The document outlines the need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from power generation. The Móir Air memo said that, of the 100,000 units of power generated, 60,000 must come from renewable sources by 2020.

This is down from the 72,000 units of power that would have been generated with renewable sources in 2005.

The Móir Air memo said that the government aims to install 1.1 gigawatts (GW) of renewable energy generation capacity by 2020. This would be achieved through "the installation of up to 50% of new wind, solar, hydropower and geothermal capacity within the electricity grid".

The memo said that "Ireland is already well placed to take advantage of renewable energy, and will need to take even greater action on climate change, to keep its energy bills affordable for its citizens."

The Móir Air memo said that €150 million will be spent on climate change adaptation efforts by 2020. This is down from the €400 million allocated in 2008.

It said that €110 million would be spent on renewable energy generation; €90 million on energy efficiency and €50 million on the production of renewable energy.

The Móir Air memo says that the government's commitment to achieving a carbon-neutral economy in 2020 will require investment in public transport, the building of more green housing and energy-efficient vehicles.

The memo says that a commitment to renewable energy will "help drive down energy costs and enhance the country's competitiveness".

It also says that "Ireland must continue to lead the world in climate change mitigation and adaptation actions".

The Móir Air memo says that the Irish government will consult with the European Commission in 2014 on how Ireland can help build a Europe-wide agreement.

The memo says that "to maintain Ireland's strong position at the international table in tackling climate change we must ensure that Ireland's policies and actions are more ambitious than other countries".

It notes that Ireland "must act quickly" to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in line with its commitments to the Paris agreement, the EU Climate Change Summit and the Kyoto Protocol.

It is likely that the EU will not accept Ireland's commitments to reduce its emissions on the Kyoto Protocol, the memo says.

"Ireland must demonstrate a strong ambition to meet its international climate change commitments, regardless of the outcome of negotiations with the EU."

The judge gave a judgement in the case of a couple who were married in France but were living in Ireland with their son.

They had the right to apply for Irish citizenship and the court concluded that they were legal parents of the child.

"The main reason we wanted to do this is to really understand how the moons work and also to look at their shape. It's great to have these new images," Dr Robert Aitken, lead astronomer at the European Space Agency's Space Science Institute said.

The inquiry would examine the relationship between the local authorities and the two families and the reasons for the killings.

'My daughter loved her town'

'Fatal mistake'

"Because a person with an egg allergy has a greater risk of developing an allergic reaction to foods than a person without an allergy to foods, California's egg labeling system denies consumers with egg allergies access to a wide range of nutritious products," the Justice Department says.

The suit was filed in a San Francisco federal court yesterday, and is likely to be the first of its kind.

The lawsuit says: "This complaint was brought by the US government, and is a civil rights action. It is an action for damages, not a civil rights claim.

"In fact, the defendant's claim is a non-suit because the complaint alleges only that the defendant has engaged in alleged unlawful discrimination in the sale and distribution of products."

This is the last chance to get a legal framework in place that is comprehensive in its protection of women, is comprehensive in its protection of children and has the safeguards that are appropriate for people in prostitution.

She added that the review would seek to "ensure the protection of the victims".

There is a growing number of people in the sex industry and their clients are often the people who need support. There are other individuals who may find themselves in situations where they need professional help.

"We have to be able to provide them with the support that is right for them," she said.

The report is entitled: 'Working for Change: The State's Role in the Development of Irish Prostitution Legislation'.

According to Fitzgerald, the issue of prostitution in Ireland remains a "complex one" that requires considerable "work to be done".

"There is no silver bullet or magic bullet," she said.

She added that Ireland was "very much committed" to working towards a country in which all prostitutes had the opportunity to fulfil their profession in a safe environment, with "no violence".

This is also the reason why she has proposed legislation that would require anyone who is suspected of being in an "incident" or "being involved in prostitution" to report to gardaí, who would then investigate the matter and decide on appropriate action.

Fitzgerald has also proposed making it an offence for anyone who is in an "incident" to "harass" a prostitute, and she has also said that "the criminalisation of prostitution should be abolished".

According to Fitzgerald, the Government should also consider introducing a mandatory life sentence in cases where a prostitute suffers "significant harm", and she has said that "the Government should introduce legislation that would give the Secretary of State power to impose a compulsory life sentence on anyone who knowingly aids or abets a prostitute".

The Minister said that "the Irish criminal justice system has not worked for the vast majority of women who have entered into a relationship with an individual involved in prostitution".

Fitzgerald said that legislation was needed to protect people who have "already been harmed".

She added that her review had been prompted by the 2014 case of an Irish sex worker being forced into prostitution on the streets of Dublin.

Fitzgerald said that in 2014, her own inquiry had identified a "growing problem of women exploited by people in prostitution," and she said that she wanted to tackle that issue head-on.

"I felt it was my duty as a minister to set out my thoughts on this in a clear and comprehensive way," she said.

'Significantly improved'

The Irish government has launched a review of the laws on prostitution in Ireland. The review will examine whether all of the existing laws are adequate.

The review is being conducted by Frances Fitzgerald.
headline: Minister to publish review of sex work legislation

text:
Four local businesses in Dublin are selling sweets using their own ingredients, after a social media campaign to raise awareness about the issue.

The initiative, which has been ongoing for three weeks, sees people buying a product and baking it in the open air for public consumption.

People can then choose the flavour that they want to make their own.

Business owners from Drogheda, Cork, Galway and Ennis, have been handing out sweets to those who buy them for their own parties and celebrations.

And that's good news for Ireland's artisan producers

"I've always been a fan of chocolate. I love it, but I think it's an under-utilised tool in the business," said the owner of Drogheda's Chocolate & Candy.

"People are always asking me: do I make my own? We have the capacity to make chocolate, but I think that the best way of using that product is as a gift."

However, he admitted that selling it directly to a buyer has its challenges.

"It can be difficult to meet with a buyer. It's not the easiest thing in the world," he said.

"It's like a traditional chocolate. It's a shame that it's not an option for people who want it. I do think there's a niche market for it."

He said that the business is growing, as it has been a "trend" with other local businesses.

He said: "It's going really well. People are coming in. We're not seeing a lot of demand, so people are happy to buy it."

The owners have donated some of the proceeds from the sale to charities including the National Poetry Foundation and Irish Cancer Hospitals.

The shop is located in Drogheda and also on Galway's South Circular Road.
headline: Four business owners spreading some joy with their sweet treats
