Sydney's police operation to quell a "stubborn" outbreak of the Ebola virus is being tightened as the federal government orders a full review into whether any public health officials who are not Australian nationals were in contact with anyone who may have been exposed.

"It's frustrating to hear the same old story of people coming forward who think they have been infected, only to discover that they were not and they never had a chance to ask for help," Minister for Health Peter Dutton said in a statement.

"I want to emphasise the vital importance of the public health system, both at national and local levels.

"We are urgently reviewing whether there have been any mistakes in our screening process and whether any individuals may have been exposed to anyone who may have been infected with Ebola virus disease."

READ MORE:

* Expert says Sydney's quarantine is not working

* Sydney quarantine 'totally inadequate'

* Ebola outbreak: How did we get here?

* Police in Sydney put on alert following Ebola scare

* State of emergency in the Australian Ebola response

The statement did not say how many people have been quarantined, but some people have reported to The Guardian that they were.

The New South Wales Health Department said on Wednesday it would introduce a strict "prophylactic screening" regime across the state as a precaution in response to a "stubborn" outbreak of the Ebola virus in the Australian capital.

The department said it would put in place "enhanced" protocols and put in place more information on what symptoms to look out for in the case of a possible Ebola infection.

The announcement came hours after the Federal Health Minister, Sussan Ley, said the authorities were taking every precaution to ensure a safe and controlled quarantine of the entire population in Australia.

The department said the "prophylactic screening" would take place at ports, airports and seaports, where people arriving from affected countries or returning from the region were likely to be affected.

Sydney airport spokesman Tony Bartlett said: "We have been working closely with the Australian health authorities to ensure the screening is implemented properly and in a manner which is most effective in reducing the risk of spread of the virus.

"In addition, all passengers arriving to Sydney will be required to have their fever tested against a standard of fever considered to be 'stubborn' in humans.

"This means that the testing will not be undertaken on passengers whose fever is below the 'stubborn' threshold."

The move follows the arrival on Monday of a Liberian man who had tested positive for Ebola in New York but has since been declared free of the deadly disease.

The Ebola outbreak in West Africa has killed nearly 11,000 people and is the deadliest in recorded history.

It has prompted the United States to launch its own quarantine on its airports and seaports.

Sydney health authority chief executive Dr Peter Dutton said it was up to individual health workers to decide what precautions to take when they came into contact with anyone who may have been exposed to Ebola virus disease in the country.

"We will look at the appropriate protocol for the health workers at each point of contact," Dr Dutton said.
headline: Sydney tightens lockdown amid 'stubborn' outbreak

Thousands of protesters took to the streets of Budapest Saturday in a rally against Hungary's newly-imposed law banning gay pride parades.

The march, which was organised in support of President Viktor Orbán, attracted around half a million participants.

Some participants wore the rainbow flag, a symbol of pride for many LGBTQ people in Hungary, while others carried a large rainbow flag.

"We are marching on the streets in protest of the ban on the parade and the government's refusal to listen to our voices," said Szabolcs Zoltai, one of the organisers of Saturday's march.

"Today, we march against the ban on the parade, against the government's refusal to listen to the voices of the people, on its failure to protect the freedom of speech and to act in accordance with international law."

READ MORE:

* Rainbow flags fly high in Budapest Pride parade

* Pride in Budapest: Hungary bans gay pride parade

* Gay pride in Budapest: 'Our rights are not a choice'

The controversial law has been criticised as discriminatory to the LGBTQ community, who say it is discriminatory towards lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people.

The president of Hungary's ruling Fidesz party, which has been heavily criticised for its perceived discrimination against the LGBT community, said earlier this week that he supports the "right to protest" but that the ban was not in line with his government's stated beliefs.

Erol Onder, a member of parliament from Orbán's Fidesz party, told reporters that he supported a repeal of the law.

"It is important that we are saying that this law does not represent our beliefs," he said.

Onder, who also has close ties to the ruling party, said that the government's stance has nothing to do with its support for the gay community, saying that the ruling party does not share the views of Orbán.

"We don't have any problems with Mr Orbán and he is in no way our enemy," he said.

Onder also said he supports a move towards normalising relations with Russia, which he called a "very close neighbour" of Hungary and a "stable neighbour".

"We are talking about an alliance with Russia and I think this is a very important step for the future of Europe."

Roughly 200 members of the LGBTQI community demonstrated in the capital's main square during the march, with some wearing a large rainbow flag in support of the parade.

Other participants said they were worried about the law's possible impact on their lives and their own freedom to express themselves.

"I am worried that the law may make it so much harder for me to do my job," said a police officer, who would only give his first name as Marios. "I am not free to come to work, to go to school, or to go to church."

The parade, which was organised by the Pride in Budapest group and organised by the LGBT+ organisation Liggyi, was part of a campaign by the Hungarian LGBTQI community to counter the upcoming pride parade in St Petersburg, Russia, at the end of September.

"This year's march is organised on the ground and will be much bigger.
headline: Thousands march in banned Budapest Pride parade

A man who was caught carrying around €268,000 worth of gold bullion hidden in his attic is to plead guilty to the theft, and will face a charge of hiding a secret property.

Joseph Michael Collins, 28, who was born in Ireland but had travelled to the US two years ago, has been sentenced to six months in jail after he pleaded guilty to hiding the hidden gold in a basement.

Collins was convicted in May of hiding and concealing three cars worth an estimated €1.15 million. The cars, a white van, a black SUV and a grey Range Rover were stolen from a luxury car dealership in Dublin, and recovered in the US.

Collins also pleaded guilty to possession of the gold bullion, which he had not given his address to gardaí.

In mitigation, Collins' lawyer, Richard O'Sullivan, said Collins, who was born in Dublin, had travelled to the US for work last year.

The barrister said he was in the US working on a property in his hometown of West Point, New York, while his wife, Michelle, is pregnant.

The gold was stolen from a home on Cottage Street in Castlereagh. The Irish Independent reported that when the gardaí arrived at the scene, they found two metal boxes in a basement that were missing the gold.

Collins was living at his parents' home in Castlereagh at the time, and had travelled to the US for work.

The gardaí had been trying to track him down ever since.

Collins was arrested on May 11, 2015, after the theft of the three cars.

Collins was convicted of the theft at Castlereagh District Court on May 20, 2015.

In the sentencing, Judge James Cahill said Collins had been living in his parents' home, and had not been living in a rented apartment in Castlereagh.

He was being held in custody at the Donegal jail where he will be sentenced on June 22.
headline: Gang member pleads guilty to hiding €268k cash in attic

The American dairy industry has threatened the European Union with a tariff on cheese and wine, with an American delegation visiting Brussels to try and pressure the European Commission to make these products subject to import tariffs.

The US dairy industry has been lobbying for a 15 per cent import tariff on European cheese and wine.

The US state department, according to a diplomat, is also proposing to introduce a 15 per cent tariff on US pork and whiskey to be applied immediately on products that have undergone testing in the EU.

But European food companies have called the proposals 'unprecedented' and 'silly'.

Speaking at the World Milk Congress in the Belgian capital, Belgium on Wednesday, dairy association CEO Jean-Baptiste Lefebvre said: "This is absolutely unprecedented. We have never heard such threats before.

"If there was a serious question about the quality of European cheese, there would have been a huge outcry. It is just ridiculous, totally ridiculous."

This is the latest in a string of challenges to the European Union's food rules that have been levelled at the US since the Paris attacks in November.

US officials have been warning for months that Brussels would be unable to meet its goals of keeping import tariffs low.

The US is the second largest consumer of EU products in Europe after Germany.

President Donald Trump has also proposed a trade war with the EU, which would be aimed at punishing companies that move jobs to other countries.

However, Mr Lefebvre said the US was the largest consumer of EU products in Europe, so the US should not be treated worse than the rest of the EU.

He said: "We have the fourth largest market for US cheeses and that's why we are being singled out by the US. But no more. We can be at the table with the other 27 countries of the world.

"The US is the number one consumer of cheeses, and they have threatened us with a trade war against us."

'We are not going to get a free trade agreement'

Mr Lefebvre said the US was threatening to cut the number of cheeses that could be bought from EU manufacturers by as much as half, although that was not the case.

"This is crazy," he said. "It is not going to happen.

"We are not going to get a free trade agreement. We will have to get back to the WTO, which is going to be difficult, unless we negotiate a different trade agreement."

The US dairy lobby group, the US Dairy Export Council, claims the EU is pushing for the introduction of a "de facto tariff" on EU-made cheese and wine that could be as high as 15 per cent.

Dairy products are the biggest single industry in the US, accounting for more than 40 per cent of the $24bn (£18.3bn) annual market for frozen and fresh foods.

The European Commission has been accused of giving in to the threat of higher dairy prices and is currently holding discussions with the US over food safety regulations that could cause a spike in prices.
headline: US threatens tariffs on EU cheese, pork and whiskey

As part of the Housing Strategy for the Northern Area, the Housing Executive is recommending a review of the housing stock in the northern region to help achieve the Government's ambition of creating 2.5 million new homes by 2023.

That review has been set to last at least three years.

The review is an important step in ensuring that we continue to grow our housing stock while maintaining the standards necessary to ensure affordable housing and social housing.

We are considering the recommendations of the review and are in the process of preparing our Action Plan for Northern Ireland (APNIC).

We are also reviewing the existing programme of housing stock build (including for the public sector), a review of the delivery of new social and affordable housing (including the public sector) and the implementation of the government's National Housing Strategy.

The housing stock review will also consider how to address the needs and impacts of the changing housing sector.

In its report, the Housing Executive will consider the evidence base from the two recent Housing Supply Surveys (HSBSs) and the recent Housing Demand Survey (HDS), which were carried out in March and April, respectively.

This includes information about the proportion of homes in the public sector, private sector and social sector housing, the availability of social homes, the types of homes needed, and the impact that different planning and construction decisions have had on the housing stock in the Northern Region.

It will also consider how to deal with the shortage of affordable housing and social homes in the Northern Region.

The report will be submitted to Government on October 14. It is being shared widely and the response from the Northern Ireland Assembly and the Department of Finance will be published in the coming weeks.

There will be a meeting of the Northern Ireland Housing Executive on Wednesday, October 19, to discuss the report and to discuss the various areas of focus.

To ensure a thorough and careful process, the Housing Executive is also asking the Northern Ireland Executive to support its assessment by carrying out a review of the housing stock.

The Housing Executive has also established a number of review committees, including the Northern Ireland Housing Enterprise Review committee, the Northern Ireland Housing Strategy committee, the Housing Supply Advisory Committee, and the Northern Ireland Housing and Planning Advisory Committee.

Housing Enterprise Review Committee:

In its report, the Housing Enterprise Review Committee will consider whether the scheme is in the public interest.

There will be a discussion on the review's findings and recommendations on Tuesday, October 22.

A public session will be held on Monday, October 23.

Housing Strategy for the Northern Area:

The Housing Strategy for the Northern Area will be published on Thursday, October 24.

The report will consider the objectives of the Housing Strategy, including the objectives of affordable housing, social housing, social enterprise, and social housing in the Northern Region and in Northern Ireland as a whole.

It will also cover the Northern Ireland Housing Supply Survey, the Housing Supply Advisory Committee, and the Northern Ireland Housing and Planning Advisory Committee.

The Housing Supply Survey and Housing Supply Advisory Committee have both agreed to publish a report by the end of November.

The Housing Supply Survey is a survey of social housing supply across Northern Ireland. It will be carried out every two years.

More than three million EU citizens have applied to the United Kingdom to live for up to two years after the UK leaves the EU.

The number of new applications is up substantially on the 3.6 million EU citizens who applied to live in the UK in 2016.

The total number of applicants is up from 1.1 million people in 2015 and 1.7 million people in 2014, and is the highest number of new applications since the EU referendum.

The Office of National Statistics reported that the number of people seeking to live in the UK will increase by 3.1 million in the next two years, after figures from Eurostat revealed that the UK population is expected to grow by 6.8 million people over the next 20 years.

EU citizens wishing to stay in the UK for up to two years after Brexit can obtain an authorisation letter (AMA) by writing to the Home Office. The letter is valid for one year and is sent to the applicant's current and prospective employer at the address on the form, and to the Home Office address on the form.
headline: Over three million EU citizens apply to stay in UK

The bodies of four people and one child were found at the scene. The two bodies recovered were that of a woman, her two children and two men.

The bodies of the men were recovered from a boat and the body of the woman was recovered from the sea, according to the Coastguard.

The body of the man was recovered from the sea around 7.30pm, it said.

The bodies of the two men were recovered at around 9.30pm.

The bodies of the two women were found on the seafront.

The bodies of the two children were found at the scene in the water.

Local residents have told the media that the men were in their late teens to early 20s and lived on the highlands around the area.

The incident happened in the early hours of this morning near a resort on the north coast of Co Down.

A man was recovered from the water near a beach on the south coast of Co Down.

The incident happened in the early hours of this morning near a resort on the north coast of Co Down.

The woman, in her 40s, was discovered by a member of the public at the water's edge.

The man was also recovered from the water at the resort on the north coast of Co Down.

The area of the resort is on land owned by the Co Down & Mourne Coastguard and is closed to public entry.

The water, around 60m wide, is about 7.5m deep and is littered with debris.

One of the bodies has not yet been recovered, however it is understood that they were not the two men found earlier.

The incident is the second in the week in Co Down. A man was found dead in the River Gorman in a shallow grave on Saturday.

The body was found near a body of water, known as the Gorman, which flows through the area, around 1am on Saturday.

US warships sail towards Venezuelan waters off Florida

Sunday, 28 February 2013, 12:04 GMT (17:04 CET, 00:04 GMT)

A US naval strike group sailed south of Florida, amid fears that Venezuela's government is preparing a military conflict with the US.

US warships USS Michigan and USS Florida are based in the waters of the Gulf of Mexico.

The US warships are in the area in the wake of Venezuela's decision to withdraw from a regional pact of powers known as the US-Caribbean Partnership Organization (Carapro).

The Carapro pact allows members states to sign free trade agreements with other states, but it comes into effect on 31 December.

In a statement, the White House said the US was "committed to working with the Government of Venezuela on all international issues, including regional security and stability".

It said that "while the United States will not seek military intervention in Venezuela, we urge all parties to engage in a constructive dialogue, and to refrain from any provocative actions that could escalate tensions".

The US has been in talks with the Venezuelan opposition, which it calls the "Chavista" movement, since President Nicolas Maduro announced in February the US would suspend the participation of Venezuela's ambassador to Washington, and the country's vice president, for political reasons.

The US ambassador to Venezuela, Jaime Ortega, was also suspended.
headline: US deploys warships amid fears of Venezuela conflict

Locum GP in south Dublin has been questioned by the Medical Council over his care of a patient who died from injuries suffered during a horse riding accident.

The council has confirmed it received a complaint from the medical director of an independent hospital, Dr Martin Heffernan, on October 24.

The complaint was made in relation to a series of incidents which occurred between November 19 and 30, 2016, involving a young male patient in a medical facility at the Dublin University Hospitals (DUH) who died after being treated in a locum GP's surgery in north Dublin.

Dr Heffernan stated that the patient had been admitted to the hospital on December 11 and admitted to the locum GP surgery on December 19. He then died on January 8.

The hospital has been contacted and asked for comment.

Locum GP at Dublin University Hospital (DUH) said he had been unaware of the complaint at the time of the deaths of the patient and others treated at the facility.

"The complaints were made by a medical director and were handled accordingly," he said.

"They were passed to the appropriate authorities, the Medical Council. I was unaware at the time of the complaints in relation to the young patient.

"The decision of the Medical Council was that all investigations were concluded and the matter dealt with."

'I've never seen anything like it'

Dr Heffernan said he had been aware that in Ireland the medical director of a hospital can lodge complaints with the Medical Council.

"I've never seen anything like it and I never expected to see anything like it," he said.

"I've seen complaints lodged by the medical director of a hospital in England and it's a real issue that happens.

"I thought it was something that would be dealt with by the Irish authorities."

He said the patient had a long history of injuries to his spine.

"I don't think it would have occurred to him to ask me if he was in good health."

Dr Heffernan said the young patient had suffered a traumatic brain injury and was on a ventilator while under treatment at the clinic.

He said the young man had sustained minor injuries.

"He was put on a ventilator for a few minutes because he was going into cardiac arrest.

"He had a fracture of his tibia and he was still breathing on ventilator. He was in a wheelchair at the time.

"He was in a serious condition.

"He was having to be helped up. He was still in a severe condition and there was an opportunity to have a bowel movement."

Dr Heffernan said the hospital had no records of the young patient having problems in the past, but the medical director, Dr Tony Dunne, had been in contact with the patient's family to determine if he needed further treatment.

The young man's father, David Dunne, said he was shocked by the latest developments.

"My son was very well and his condition was much better. I was told by a nurse that his blood pressure was normal.

"He was on a ventilator and he was on a respirator as well."
headline: Locum GP before Medical Council over care of patient

The head of the Irish Defence Forces (DoF), General (ret) Stephen Donnelly has condemned the recent escalation in violence in Gaza.

Dublin protesters are calling for an end to the violence in Gaza.

In a statement to RTÉ News, the general says that the military has to respect the will of people on both sides, but at the same time he condemns all acts of violence.

It is "quite apparent" that the IDF is losing the ground battle against Hamas, he said.

The general said that what is happening in Gaza is an effort by Hamas to derail the peace process.

"There is a real danger that that is what they are doing by pushing back against the ceasefire agreement, the two state solution and the process that we are engaged in in the Middle East, and making the world realise just how serious the situation is," he said.

"It is an effort to derail the possibility of a two state solution to the conflict. They are continuing to fire rocket rockets at Israel, and this is an effort to derail the possibility of a two state solution."

Dublin demonstrators say they want an end to violence and for the military to respect the will of people on both sides.

Speaking to RTÉ News, Dublin protester, Seamus McMahon, said that they are "not here to bring peace to the Middle East".

"We are here to bring an end to the violence and the aggression that is being committed by the Israelis to Palestinians".

The Dublin protesters also say that they are here to "stop the Israeli occupation".

"We are here to stop the Israeli occupation and to end the occupation of Palestinians and stop the aggression being committed on the Palestinian people by the Israelis".

"We are here to change the way the world deals with Israel and Palestinian people so that they are free, safe and sound and that they are not subjected to the kind of acts of violence that have been carried out by the Israelis."

The DoF chief says that what the international community is saying is the wrong message.

"What they're saying is the message of peace, but it is not the message that we need to hear," he said.

"The message that the international community is sending is that they would like the Israeli-Palestinian conflict to be resolved, but they don't want peace."

"They are saying that they will support a two state solution, but the only problem is that they haven't got a plan for what happens if the Palestinians don't agree."

Dublin protesters will be demonstrating on Wednesday at 10am outside the Israeli embassy.

A spokesman for the Israeli Embassy in Dublin said that the embassy has not yet received a request to protest in Dublin.

A spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade in Dublin said that it was a matter for the DoF to assess.
headline: Dublin protesters call for end to Gaza conflict

A rare Roman coin featuring Brutus, the ancient Roman general and son of Julius Caesar, is up for auction in Geneva after being bought in a private sale at the International Numismatic Exhibition (Inumismatica).

The Roman Victory Victory Coin featuring Brutus (VICTORII SENHALI) is a gold and silver coin featuring a head of the king of Rome, Caesar.

The coin was purchased in a private sale of Roman coins in Geneva by a collector who wished to remain anonymous.

The coin is described in the catalogue as:

The Victory Victory coin, Nero's coinage (Augustan Era) is known as the 'brazen bull' coinage, and it was a huge success in the Roman world, selling over 10,000,000,000 of them in the period of Augustus to Antoninus Pius. It became the most commonly used coinage in the Roman empire.

The coin is a gold and silver coin, showing a head of Nero. The head is a Roman lion, with one eye in the form of a snub nose, and the other is of a lion with a lion's head.

The coin features the legend ROMANVS PP AVG for the date of 1st April, in the Roman alphabet.

The coin weighs 2.5 grams.

The sale includes two other Roman coins, two Roman coins with Nero's reign and one with an inscription, 'THE LESBIAN EMPEROR IMPERATOR,' for Nero's reign in 65 BC.

The coin with Nero's reign is a bronze coin with the inscription VIRGINIA AVG (Victory). The coins with Nero's reign in the inscription include a silver coin with the inscription VIRGINIA AVG (Victory) and a bronze coin with the inscription VIRGINIA AVG (Victory) and a coin with the inscription VIRGINIA AVG (Victory) for Nero's reign in the 1st year of Domitian in AD 49, in Roman script.

The seller is a Swiss collector who is keen to establish his interest in Rome and other European cities in his home country.

The Roman coinage is not very well known to collectors and this will be a first auction sale for this type of coin.

The auctioneer is the dealer, Antonella Pianetti.

The buyer is a Swiss collector who wishes to establish his interest in Rome and other European cities in his home country.
headline: Rare Roman coin featuring Brutus up for auction in Geneva

text:
Tourists in Ireland who are heading to the United States this weekend will be able to return home as the US Travel Ban is lifted.

While the US government announced it was temporarily halting all travel to the country after the executive order, it has since lifted the ban.

READ MORE:

* President Trump to veto travel ban

* US travel ban 'not needed'

* Travel ban to be 'temporary', Irish ministers tell PM

* Travel ban 'not needed' and 'unnecessary'

The US Embassy in Dublin has confirmed that people travelling to the US can now enter the US again.

"We will be issuing an update to you as soon as we can. There is no travel ban," the embassy tweeted.

The announcement follows a press conference held by US Ambassador to Ireland Terry Kramer.

Kramer said the US is open to improving relations with Ireland.

"We are open to continuing to work with Ireland, but we don't want to see anything that goes beyond a process that is fair to both sides," he said.

He said the US Government has been very cooperative and open, but added: "We are open to a good relationship with a country that is a good neighbour and ally of ours."

Asked if the US had been "extremely cooperative and open" towards Ireland, Kramer said: "There is a lot of good that's happened as a result of a lot of good will and collaboration between the US and Ireland."

Kramer said the US "will continue to work with Ireland, a country that is a good neighbour and ally of ours".

The State Department said it was "in contact" with Dublin and that the State Department "remains committed to restoring full and safe travel to the United States for all".

"We look forward to working with the Irish government to ensure that travelers affected by this executive order are able to travel to the United States once they are cleared by immigration authorities," it said.

"We expect all countries to work together to ensure that the United States is able to fulfil its global responsibilities."

The State Department said it was "working with the Department of Homeland Security to review these recommendations, and we look forward to working with the State Department and other agencies to address any additional deficiencies that may arise".

Kramer said the decision to lift the travel ban was not a political decision but a matter for the US government.

"It was a matter of practical action to allow the people of the United States to travel to the United States and we are extremely thankful for the opportunity to work closely with the Irish government and with our friends and allies in Ireland," he said.

Kramer said he was pleased by the way in which the Irish government had handled the travel ban and wished them well.

The Irish Embassy in Washington and the State Department in Dublin did not respond to calls from RTE.
headline: Tourists prepare to return to US as travel ban lifted

text:
Cian O'Reilly is a proud breeder of pups born from his "puppy farm" in Co. Galway, where he has been since the late 1980s.

In 2006, he and his family took a gamble in investing in a breeder who was selling the stock of his offspring to the lowest bidder.

The breeder's name was Tony O'Rourke who had just sold a stock of 5,000 pups for €100.

"That was an awful deal," Mr O'Rourke told RTÉ News.

"I was thinking, 'Is it fair to take on this risk of investing €100 to keep a small amount of my stock in my breeding programme in case a better breeder comes along?

"The thought of losing the pups was very worrying. I was very careful with the pups. If they are good then maybe I'll keep them but I knew I had to invest a little bit in them to make sure I got the best out of them."

Mr O'Rourke said his own two sons had also been taken in by him and his sons. "We took the gamble and thought we could have a good outcome."

The O'Robsons invested a lot of money in a breeding programme of their own, including several million euros in loans from the State, along with a large grant from the Department of Agriculture.

"In hindsight, the risk was worth taking. We went into this with the expectation of having a good result," Mr O'Rourke said.

"There have been a number of cases in Ireland of people that have bought a puppy from somebody who had no previous knowledge of the breed or were not familiar with it.

"We did our best to be very thorough with our own breeding and testing of our stock. When the pups turned out to be healthy we had very good results.

"With the exception of one pup we did not have any further success with the breeder's stock. In retrospect, we could have found a much better breeder and kept all of them."

The O'Robsons spent a great deal of money in the early 1990s getting their breeder registered with the Irish Kennel Club. The club then helped them organise their breeding programmes, which is now at its peak.

"We have had more than 1,000 pups bred here in the last four years from our breeding programme," Mr O'Rourke said.

"We had a lot of luck with the first four kids. We started in 1992 and we are now at over 2,000 pups. Some of those pups have bred and produced healthy dogs.

"We have seen dogs that were bred from broken or deformed pups have grown into healthy dogs."

A number of other breeders have now come forward to share their experience and success.

"We have had three dogs that have grown into healthy pups here. I have a couple of other pups that have bred and produced healthy pups. That is the kind of thing that makes you get up in arms."

The Irish Kennel Club's secretary, Dr Ronan O'Brien, said it is encouraging to see a number of pups getting back into the breeder's care.
headline: Cian's Kennels reunites sick children with their pets

The Irish Chamber of Commerce has been told it is not included in discussions on the future of the Government's pay deal.

The group is believed to have been asked to make concessions in their dispute over the pay deal with the Government.

Earlier this week, the Irish Chamber of Commerce was given an opportunity to attend an independent expert's meeting on the pay deal and other key issues.

The chamber claimed it was not invited and was not consulted about the dispute.

The chamber alleges this was in breach of its contract with the Government in which it would not be a party to the negotiations.

The chamber says it has a very small business client base.

It has alleged it has been treated unfairly by the Government and its payment is not competitive with that of other sectors.

It also claims it has been unable to access critical information and has been subject to a huge amount of publicity over a dispute with the Department of Finance over the amount of money that the chamber was paid last year.

Last month, the Irish Government was criticised for using taxpayer money to pay a controversial lawyer for an "unprecedented" sum of €20,000 in a dispute over payments to business clients in a dispute over a dispute with the Irish Bank Resolution Corporation (IBRC).

The Irish Government's own pay deal with the Irish Chamber of Commerce is a controversial affair as it gives its members a guaranteed 6.5 per cent pay rise in 2015.

In December, the Government announced it was considering changes to the deal and a new one was being negotiated.

Ahead of last month's meeting with the chamber, the government said the contract would provide an increase in pay for members "in line with that of the rest of the workforce".

The meeting was held to discuss a range of key issues including the future of the new contract, the Government's proposed changes to the deal and any proposals to reduce the amount of money the chamber is paid.

However, the chamber has said it is not consulted about any of the Government's proposed changes.

The chamber said its participation in the negotiation process was "unprecedented" and its members were "appalled" by the way the Government has handled the matter.

It also said the new contract was designed to "save costs by providing more certainty and accountability".

The chamber's executive director, John O'Mahony, said the dispute over the deal was "unacceptable".

text:
Fiona Naughton from the Department of Chemistry at UCD has been working on microplastics in dolphin breath for a number of years.

In 2014, she published the results of a study she carried out on the potential effects of marine plastics on the water environment.

The results were published in the journal PLOS ONE.

"This is the first study to show how microplastics can influence the marine environment," said Naughton, "this work is important because it identifies a potential cause of the 'Great Pacific Garbage Patch'."

Microplastics are plastics in the form of tiny pieces of plastic that can break down into tiny particles of other materials – sometimes referred to as microbeads – before settling on land.

Microplastic pollution can be damaging to marine life including whales, dolphins and turtles, as they absorb plastic particles from the water and then ingest them.

Although microplastics are not banned in Ireland, they are known to be present in most European nations, including Ireland, and are considered a serious environmental concern.

"Our results suggest that microplastics may also be present in marine environments, and this suggests that they may have significant effects on marine species," she said.

"It's an area of scientific research which is only just beginning to get underway, and if we can reduce our microplastic pollution, it could have a big impact on marine animals and ecosystems."

In the past, scientists have speculated that the microplastics in marine life could be toxic to marine animals, but these recent findings provide evidence that microplastics are capable of causing effects on marine wildlife, including seabirds and animals.

Naughton's research involved sampling the waters in which the dolphins were found to consume plastic.

"It is the first time we've seen this concentration of microplastics in dolphin breath, and it suggests that microplastics in the breath may be making its way back into the environment," she said.

"We haven't seen it in this study because samples were taken from the water in the Bahamas, where dolphins do not usually consume plastic. It suggests that microplastics may be contaminating other parts of the marine environment, and this is what we want to be learning from this."

She said that previous research has shown that the majority of microplastics found in the oceans are derived from plastics manufacturing in North America.

"These findings suggest that microplastics from industrial processing may be contaminating the waters of the world," she said. "We need to continue to monitor and investigate marine microplastics to determine their potential impacts."

Naughton noted that it has not been possible to study the biological effects of microplastics in wildlife so far. She is currently studying the effects of microplastics on the fish food web in New Zealand.
headline: Microplastics discovered in dolphin breath

The use of the "bloody Sunday" image of a soldier being killed on Bloody Sunday to justify the IRA's activities during that very day has been condemned by politicians on both sides of the border.

Taoiseach Enda Kenny has said he would prefer "to forget" the footage, but would not be "disappointed" in the use of it.

Mr Kenny said he would not be "disappointed" by the use of the image, but would be "disappointed with their use of it".

However, he said it was "not necessary that we have to look back at that image in every situation".

Speaking in the Dáil yesterday, Senator Brian Hayes told the House of Representatives he had spoken to Tánaiste Joan Burton and Senator Michael Ring over the matter of the images of soldiers being gunned down by the IRA on Bloody Sunday.

Senator Hayes asked Ms Burton if she would look at the footage in light of recent events, and she responded she would "look at it".

He told the Dáil:

The use of that footage in relation to the IRA activities, and the use of that footage in relation to the deaths of the six members of the Shankill Road Army Regiment (SHAR) in Londonderry in 1972, makes me sick.

Senator Hayes said he had spoken to the Taoiseach and the Tánaiste about the issue, and that he was "not disappointed".

Senator Hayes said:

These people used that image, and they used it to justify what they were doing at the time. It is sickening to me.

Mr Kenny today said that he would not be "disappointed" in the use of the image, but that it was "not necessary" to do so.

The Taoiseach made the comments after Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams said the use of the image was "disgusting" and "shameful".

Mr Kenny said:

I would prefer to forget this image, but if I have to, it will be done. I am not disappointed with what they have done, I am just very sad with what they have done.

Mr Kenny said he had asked for the Taoiseach's approval for the use of the image in the event it came up in a future interview.

Mr Kenny said that the image should not be used "for political purposes" because "that is against the spirit of the Bill".

Mr Kenny said:

It was a terrible image for all the soldiers and their families, so we should not have to look at it.

Mr Kenny said he had spoken to the Tánaiste and Senator about the issue, and that he was "not disappointed".

He said:

I asked them to look at it and they looked at it.

The Dáil today was told that Mr Kenny had already directed that a parliamentary committee be convened to review the use of the image during the Troubles.

However, in the last few hours, Sinn Fein have said that they will be asking that the inquiry be put back to today.

Mr Hayes also spoke out against the "bloody Sunday" image yesterday.

RTE News's coverage of the release of Roald Dahl's famous children's books 'Charlie and the Chocolate Factory' and 'The BFG' has raised eyebrows as some viewers have suggested he should be arrested for 'inciting racial hatred' in his works.

Headline:

'Silly child', a schoolboy has been given a new chapter in his life after he enjoyed a reading book that includes a picture of a Roald Dahl book.

A number of viewers have said they found it "silly" to suggest the boy should be arrested for having read a book containing a picture of a Roald Dahl book.

He was reading a book called Charlie and the Chocolate Factory.

It contains a picture of a Roald Dahl book.

Some viewers have said the image was offensive.

"There are children who will hate this lad for this one thing – his reading of a Roald Dahl book," one viewer said.

An investigation by the Department of Justice into the seizures uncovered several cases where drugs were seized for the amount of €6.5m.

Ireland's Finance Minister Michael Noonan has reached an agreement in principle with the European Commission on how the European Central Bank will use its emergency bailout fund in Ireland.

European Commission President Jose Manuel Barroso is expected to approve the framework in a meeting on Monday (8 November).

As outlined in a statement issued by the Government, the European Commission has agreed that Ireland will not require a bailout from the EU's emergency fund, the EFSF.

"The European Commission has agreed in principle that the ESM will contribute to the recapitalisation of the national central banks in the euro area and that the ESM may also use the EFSF to recapitalise banks in euro area member states in the event of national insolvency", said a Government statement.

The Irish Prime Minister, Enda Kenny, said the agreement was an important step towards getting the country back on its feet.

"We now have a very clear programme and in return for this, the Commission has confirmed that Ireland will not require a bailout", said Mr Kenny.

"This is the first step in a long and difficult road ahead," he said.

"I welcome today's announcement as it is the first step in a long journey, not only to ensure recovery but to help the Irish economy recovery.

"I believe today's agreement with the European Commission is a great step forward. It represents the European Commission's willingness to ensure a smooth transition for the Irish economy.

"I will continue to make sure that this is implemented properly by the Irish authorities".
headline: Eurozone 'agrees in principle' to use bailout mechanism

A record 28.6C (86F) was reached at Shannon, Ireland yesterday, breaking the world record for the highest temperature set in the area in 2014.

According to the Meteorological Service of Ireland, the highest temperature ever recorded on this island was 32.5C (97F) on 15th June 2006, while the highest temperature ever recorded in Ireland was 40.9C (106F) on 15th June 1990.

The record day was recorded at Shannon in west County Kerry between 6am and 6pm, with temperatures reaching 29.6C (86.1F) with a maximum temperature of 30.8C (86.9F).

The current record of 30.8C (86.9F) has been set twice previously, on 14th and 15th June 2006.

The highest recorded temperature ever recorded in Ireland is 24C (77.2F) on 28th December 1997 at Dublin City Airport, while the previous high was 27C (81.3F) on 15th April 2003, when it was recorded as high as 30.7C (86.9F)

An official of the Meteorological Service of Ireland said that the record is only one of a number of records set at Shannon in the past year.

Shannon was also one of the centres for an intense winter storm, which caused disruption and cancellations across the country in December.
headline: 28.6C reached at Shannon, breaking May temperature record

text:
The Curlew conservation scheme has made a breakthrough in the Curlew National Park of Northern Ireland. The aim of the scheme is to restore an area of the Curlew with a long history of wildlife conservation.

The area of the land has been under threat from the development of the Curlew National Park and development of a major rail line from the west to the east of the park.

The project is being carried out by the Curlew Conservation Trust with the involvement of the Department of the Environment.

The project is costing in excess of €2.5 million and is the first ever project in Ireland to be supported by the European Commission's Community Environmental Aid scheme.

The project is also the largest programme of conservation to be undertaken by a local authority in a national park.

The first phase of the Curlew Conservation Trust's Curlew Conservation Management Plan, has been completed with a range of environmental and social goals achieved. The first five year plan included a series of milestones, such as establishing a Wildlife Research Centre to investigate the impact of livestock on the Curlew's wildlife, the establishment of the Curlew Wildlife Conservancy, the creation of a new Nature Reserve, a new Wildlife Habitat Reserve, and the re-establishment of a Curlew Conservation Centre.

The second phase includes the establishment of the Curlew Conservancy to manage a range of natural areas within the Curlew National Park. This will consist of a natural reserve, a Nature Reserve and a Wildlife Habitat Reserve.
headline: Curlew conservation scheme makes breakthrough

All five of the Department of Finance's five main departments will take cash payments over the next two years, the Irish Examiner can reveal today.

Department of Finance, Department of Finance and Department of Finance and the Revenue Commissioners are taking cash payments over next two years under the new financial strategy.

The five departments all agreed to the cash payments following a Cabinet meeting yesterday, where Finance Minister Michael Noonan said that the Government was making the "best possible use of the fiscal space" available in order to balance the books in 2015/16.

The move follows a Government review that recommended taking cash payments in a number of sectors, including those affecting the transport system, pensions, education, health, education and the environment.

Minister Noonan has previously said that the Government is "proposing to take cash payments to the five departmental heads this year".

Department of Health will take cash payments over next two years

The Finance Department was also said to be taking cash payments over next two years.

Today, a number of sources told the Irish Examiner that the Department of Finance is paying €30 million over the next two years to the Department of Health.

The Department of Revenue Commissioners are also receiving cash payments over the next two years.

The Revenue Commissioners had previously asked the Government for the "cost of the remuneration of the Chief Executives of the Revenue Commissioners to be recognised on a cost basis".

The Government refused to do this and will instead adopt the cost of services formula which it said was "excellent".

In 2014, the Department of Finance and Revenue Commissioners agreed to a €2.5 billion pension deficit over the next two years to prevent any pensioner from going bankrupt if he or she retired.

This decision has been criticised by unions as well as TDs in opposition and it is understood that a number of the TDs are now considering legal action.

Meanwhile, Taoiseach Enda Kenny has said that he "loves" a number of the staff at the Revenue Commissioners.

He said that the tax collector has been a long-time and valued member of the Department of Finance and that he is "very proud of the contribution" that he and his team have made to Ireland's economy.

The Cabinet meeting yesterday saw Finance Minister Michael Noonan saying that the Government was making the best possible use of the fiscal space available in order to balance the books in 2015/16.

Mr Noonan said that the Government was "proposing to take cash payments in a number of sectors, including those affecting the transport system, pensions, education, health, education and the environment".

He said the Government had also been asking the Revenue Commissioners to increase the amount they were paying to workers in the sector, but they had declined to do so.

The Cabinet meeting also saw the Deputy Prime Minister, Eamon Gilmore, and Minister for Public Expenditure and Reform, Paschal Donohoe, and Minister for the Environment, Richard Bruton, join Taoiseach Kenny in voting "present" for the proposals.

text:
A team of Irish investigators have been trying to establish the truth of an eight-month period in which the gang ran a fake police station in Co. Mayo.

The gang of gangsters had the control of a local police station in Cappagh since 2007, and were able to maintain control of the business until they were busted in 2011.

The gang used a fake police station in the county, on a site owned by two businessmen, to stage a number of false robberies and robberies, including a break and enter on a woman's home in October 2011.

In December 2011, a team of Irish investigators were tipped off by the Irish police that the gang were operating a fake police station in Cappagh, in which they would stage a number of fake robberies.

The gang ran the fake police station for eight months from January to July 2012, and they also had a number of false arrests made.

Irish investigators were able to capture three people – one from the gang, a second who worked on the premises and a third who rented out the premises.

In addition to the fake police station in Cappagh, the gang operated a fake court in Tralee from October 2012 to August 2013, and one in a village in Co. Meath between April 2012 and August 2013.

The gang also had a fake prison in Dublin, as well as fake prisons and real prison cells in Cork, Galway and Cork.

In August 2012, the gang broke into the house of a local businessman named Daniel Pádraig.

It was believed that this was a ransom payment to his wife, for whom the gang were also looking for money.

However, the gang failed to break into the house and arrested the couple on a charge of robbery.

After that, the gang moved onto stealing a number of cars and then they moved onto other vehicles.

In the end, the gang went bankrupt in 2011.
headline: Indian gang ran fake police station for eight months

text:
Belfast has been the site of numerous terrorist attacks over the years and last Sunday marked the first time that a suicide bomber had been able to detonate his explosives.

A suicide attack is when a person deliberately tries to kill or injure members of the public using a weapon.

At least 39 people were injured and more than 50 were taken to hospital, with a further 35 being treated for minor injuries.

The blast has been attributed to a suicide bomber, as had a number of similar attempts during recent years. The bomber detonated his bomb during an attack on a van load of people at the junction of the M2 and M5 on the morning of Sunday, July 24.

The explosion took place near the O'Connell Street exit of the M25 around 2am and left a crater measuring about 40 x 100ft.

A bomb disposal unit was called and a sniffer dog was brought into the area to search. There were no survivors.

A short while later a second bomb was detonated at a busy junction at a busy junction. It was detonated near the same time. The explosion took place at around 6.20am and the death toll is thought to have risen to four.

The victims have been identified as John Anthony, 41, from West Yorkshire; Neil Aspinall, 34, from Coventry; Patrick McEleney, 33, from Luton; Stephen Wilson, 23, from Nottinghamshire; and two men from Cheshire, both aged in their 20s.

The three men were taken to the Royal London Hospital where they are being treated for injuries sustained during the attack. McEleney is currently in a critical condition with head injuries.

Aspinall died in hospital and Wilson, from Coventry, remains in a critical condition. They are said to be in a stable condition.

The three men are all believed to have been wearing identical white jumpsuits but only McEleney's was recovered by the police.
headline: Birmingham bombing inquests start with minute's silence

text:
Dr James McKeown is professor of epidemiology at University College Dublin.

Is it possible to be very worried about Ebola and not be a bit worried about your own health? Not only do you get sick, you get infected. Is that true?

No, it is not true. There is an enormous amount of controversy and controversy about the Ebola virus and its origin. We are dealing with viruses which have the ability to change the DNA in cells of the body, so that they can cause disease. The Ebola virus seems to do that. And it has the ability to be transmitted in the blood stream, by contact with the bodily fluids, by skin contact, by a sneeze, and it can be transmitted by coughing up blood. This is not an entirely novel concept, and it's very difficult for people to understand how this virus is capable of causing disease.

But it's not very surprising, because the virus changes. It changes so quickly, it changes so often that the viruses which cause the disease are no longer useful as a means of transmission. So we are dealing with a virus which has become a vector for other viruses. We are dealing with a virus that we have never seen before. It's not that we have never seen this virus before, but we have never seen it in this form. The first time we ever encountered it was in 1976, when a couple of US doctors got it through a gentleman with whom they were working at the time, and they infected one of the other doctors, a British doctor.

That was the first time we had a human virus in the blood stream. That's a fact.

This virus is not like influenza or measles.

Not exactly. It's a very different virus from either of them. It's not influenza or measles in that we have a respiratory disease, we have the flu. It's not measles in that you can catch it by coughing or sneezing or by sharing a cup of coffee with someone who has measles. It's not even a measles virus, but it's a very different form of the virus, one which does cause disease and it does spread.

I was reading somewhere that if you have a cold, you get a cold virus. You put it into your nose, you sniff it out, and you get a little fever, which would probably be the influenza virus, but it doesn't spread. It can cause some kind of infection in a person and it does spread.

Can you tell us why?

That's one of the things that is very difficult for people to understand. There are many people who are very worried that if they do not get some kind of vaccination for the flu, they are going to get the influenza virus, and if that happens then they are going to develop the disease. People don't realise that the flu virus, like influenza, is a very different virus. It has an immune system and it's very different in its behaviour to the influenza virus in terms of how it spreads.

The flu virus does not spread.

Well, it is different. It can spread. It is very easily spread, especially in the summer. I have spoken to people who have got the flu virus in the summer, who have got the influenza virus and then got the flu. It just sort of goes out and does its thing. The flu virus has the capacity to do that.
headline: Explained: WHO's high-risk Ebola emergency

text:
Hospitals welcomed by baby boom

"New Year's Eve celebrations for mothers and babies, has turned into the start of the birth of the baby boom in Ireland," a report published in Wednesday's Sunday Independent said.

The report by The Irish Times says that more than 5,000 babies were born in hospitals in Ireland in the space of a single night on New Year's Eve.

This compares to 3,500 on December 31, 2010.

"The number of births is well ahead of other major European countries, despite the fact that the birth rate among women aged 20-44 in Ireland is still at the lowest level in a quarter of a century," said the report.

"A baby boom appears to be taking hold across Ireland, with the country's birth rate at a record high and the number of births expected to increase from 3,500 in 2010 to 5,000 by 2018."

This, the report says, is due to the fact that "the baby boom has been driven largely by women in their 30s and 40s, and also by the changing demographics in Ireland."

The baby boom is being seen across the board in a range of industries, it said. The highest number of births in the sector is in retail, followed by professional services and finance.

However, the report noted that "this new baby-boom is likely to be at a relative low point in the years to come, with the likelihood of a low-growth rate as the baby boom continues into the future," it said.

"This is not good news for the economy at all."

The report pointed to the fact that "the Irish economy is likely to grow by only 1.2% this year, compared with the consensus expectation of 1.3%.

"Ireland's economy has stagnated over recent years and has struggled to keep pace with the rapid growth in the population."
headline: Hospitals welcome first babies of the New Year

text:
A 30-year-old man from Sligo has appeared in court charged with human trafficking.

Bart Jiggins, of Castlebridge Drive in Sligo, appeared before Cork District Court on Monday morning charged with the commission of an offence under the Trafficking in Persons Act, 1989.

Judge Pat O'Sullivan heard from gardai that Jiggins has a criminal record and was arrested for the offence in October last year.

Judge O'Sullivan adjourned the case for a year.

Speaking after the hearing, Detective Inspector Mary Boyle said gardai were satisfied that the man was the person arrested for the offence.

She said the man was charged on a variety of charges including trafficking of persons.

The court heard that the man is expected to plead guilty in the coming days.

The man has been bailed.
headline: Man due in court in human trafficking investigation

text:
13 people are believed to have died of a mysterious virus in Dublin's disability services and care homes in a week, the Irish Times has learned.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health confirmed a total of 13 people died in the last week and that the number of cases is expected to rise as people begin to come forward.

A total of seven of the deaths were in the capital's disability services and care homes, but the number of people who were not currently in employment is estimated to be around 100.

The deaths are not being investigated as a potential case of flu, the spokesperson said.

The spokesman confirmed all the deaths took place in hospitals, clinics and community facilities, but did not indicate how the people were infected, what the circumstances were or what causes caused the illness.

It was too early to tell how long it could take to identify the cause and treat the people who died, or what they may have been exposed to.

"There's been a small amount of deaths, but what you have is a pattern of very high deaths," said the spokesperson.

"This is the highest number of deaths in the entire history of the Dublin region and, frankly, it's very hard for me to see a reason why this is the case."

The spokesman added the number of deaths and the amount of people affected is still being assessed.

Last week, the Health Protection Agency warned that the level of bacteria present in the bodies of the deceased individuals can make it difficult to trace the cause of death.

In February, a man died from a mysterious illness in the Republic of Ireland, which caused a public health scare.
headline: 14 virus deaths among people in disability services

text:
The Minister for Transport is pleased that 80 driving test applicants have completed their testing.

He also welcomes the participation of the 80 applicants in the project.

The participants will be given the opportunity to demonstrate the effectiveness of their driving skills by having a car driven around the town of Ballymun.

The drivers will be given a few days' practice driving on the motorway and then they will test their skill in real driving conditions.

They will then be given the opportunity to attend a private driving course at a local hotel.

They will then have their driving test, which will be a two-mile run around the town of Ballymun, assessed by the State Transport Authority.

The driving test will take place next year and is expected to be completed by early November 2017.

He said the project is a direct response to the Government's new €2.7 billion road building plan.

"The new roads are an investment and it is a road that will see the State get a better return on that investment and the road to deliver that investment will be through this programme," Mr Kenny said.

The property is located opposite the offices of the Press Ombudsman.

A Garda spokeswoman told RTE News that the celebrity was not arrested but was taken to garda headquarters for questioning.

She said the property in Castlemore Place was searched after reports of an intruder being at the home.

She said the celebrity had not been arrested and is not in custody at this time.

The spokeswoman said the property was searched after gardaí received a number of reports of a burglary. She said the gardaí were not seeking any further suspects or persons of interest.

A number of journalists and celebrities have spoken out about their privacy and the importance of protecting their communications.

Sean Penn, who is also known as actor Will Smith, had his mobile phones and computer seized from his home in Beverly Hills in February.

He was not charged.

He was released without charge following an investigation.

text:
A fire at a US steel plant that exploded early today has claimed at least eight lives, four of whom were in hospital.

The fire broke out at the Lawrenceburg, Indiana, plant that employs 1,300 workers, shortly after 6am in the facility's production yard.

The explosion shattered glass windows, burned through steel frames and threw debris around 500 metres away.

The local fire chief told reporters that the fire was not "direct" and that the cause was unclear.

He said that no injuries were reported but that the fire "probably began in the production area."

The fire took the lives of a 23-year-old worker and two other men, who died in hospital.

The plant had operated for the last 30 years.

It is the latest industrial disaster to hit the US since 2010.

The US Environmental Protection Agency said it would work with local authorities and the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration to determine how the blaze was started, and whether it could be prevented in the future.

The plant, which was constructed in the 1950s, produces steel used in the construction of bridges and skyscrapers.
headline: Two dead, 10 hospitalised after US steel plant explosions

text:
Archbishop of Canterbury Justin Welby has been urged by the Lord Bishop of Belfast to resign over revelations of a cover up of sexual abuse by Catholic clergy.

In an open letter to the Lord Bishop, the Archbishop's office has accused the Diocese of Belfast of "grossly mis-reporting" a 2012 inquiry into a sexual abuse scandal in the wake of the abuse scandal at the Boston Archdiocese in Massachusetts.

The letter said that the Diocese of Belfast "should not be allowed to continue to lie in order to cover-up the serious failings that are rife in its own administration".

In the letter to the Lord Bishop, Archbishop Welby said he was "profoundly shocked" by the "deeply disturbing" report into the Boston Archdiocese.

"The circumstances of the Boston Archdiocese are deeply troubling and I am profoundly shocked at the serious failings that are rife in its own administration and in the conduct of Catholic clergy and other parishioners," Archbishop Welby said in the letter published on the Diocese of Belfast website.

"I am not convinced that any of the findings of the Boston Archdiocese report accurately reflect the seriousness of what has occurred within our diocese and in our diocese and, indeed, I cannot accept that the Church in the Diocese of Belfast is able to continue to lie in order to cover-up the serious failings that are rife in its own administration and in the conduct of Catholic clergy and other parishioners."

The Bishop said it was "deeply troubling" that the Catholic Church in Belfast had failed to cooperate with the Boston Archdiocese inquiry.

"In the course of the Boston Archdiocese inquiry, the diocese provided, and continues to provide, all necessary resources to the Boston Archdiocese inquiry," Archbishop Welby said.

"The diocese is able and willing to cooperate fully with the investigation and has made an excellent service of it to the diocese.

"However, despite these resources, there have been failures within the diocese to cooperate fully with the Boston Archdiocese inquiry. This cannot continue. The diocese has a special responsibility to assist the Boston Archdiocese inquiry and to ensure its thoroughness.

"The diocese is determined to act promptly and effectively and will do so. The diocese will also cooperate fully with the diocese of Boston in its work as it relates to the investigation."

'The Diocese of Belfast should not be allowed to continue to lie in order to cover-up the serious failings that are rife in its own administration and in the conduct of Catholic clergy and other parishioners'

The Archbishop said in the letter: "I have been shocked to learn that the diocese of Belfast in 2012 reported the events surrounding the sexual abuse of children by clergy to the Boston Archdiocese and that the diocese has failed to fully cooperate with the investigation.

"I am deeply shocked and deeply disappointed in this failure to cooperate.

"As the Lord Bishop, the diocese of Belfast has a special responsibility to act swiftly and effectively and will do so. The diocese will also cooperate fully with the diocese of Boston in its work as it relates to the investigation."

The letter said the Catholic Church had lost trust in its own hierarchy and in Catholic institutions.
headline: Archbishop of Canterbury urged to resign over scandal

An anonymous caller reportedly spotted the figure on the grounds of the property on October 1 and alerted gardai.

An investigation was launched at the scene after gardai and representatives from the State Pathological Institute were called to the scene.

The report claims that a number of images were found.

In the report, an anonymous source describes seeing a figure and a "glowing" beam on the ground, as well as several large holes on the ground and trees.

In the image, the figure is standing on a mound of earth.

It is not clear when the apparition took place.

An investigation is ongoing.

"The matter is not a serious one. The matter is being investigated and there is no threat to anyone," they said.
headline: Leinster House visited by Ghost of Christmas Past

text:
"UN special envoy to Lebanon warns of possible reprisals"

"UN Security Council has demanded that a UN-backed investigation into a deadly strike near a Beirut hospital be expedited, the UN chief of staff has said.

The statement came as US and EU ambassadors meet in Geneva on the eve of an expected meeting of world leaders in New York to discuss the crisis, which began after a group of pro-Houthi Hezbollah gunmen overran two hospitals in the southern Lebanese city of Tripoli on Monday.

UN human rights chief Navi Pillay said on Tuesday that the UN could not conduct an impartial investigation into the "tragic" attack that left at least nine people dead and scores wounded.

She described the "tragic" strike as a "clear violation of international humanitarian law" and called for prompt intervention by the UN, which could be deployed to the area to help negotiate a safe evacuation of the wounded.

"The death toll could easily reach more than 100 and it is too soon for us to say whether or not the incident is the result of a mistake, or was a deliberate act," she said in Geneva. "The world should not rest until the perpetrators are held accountable for the crimes they committed."

Rescue workers said on Tuesday that the wounded had been buried by Tuesday afternoon.

Pillay said the UN security council should be "given the necessary resources" to conduct an investigation, and the Security Council should condemn the attack without delay.

The Security Council met on Tuesday morning to discuss the crisis and to discuss the possibility of sending UN peacekeepers into the southern city of Tripoli, where the attack took place. The 15-member council has been looking to send a peacekeeping force into Syria in recent days.

The Security Council's special envoy to Syria, Staffan de Mistura, will also present his conclusions of a visit to the country on Tuesday, diplomats said.

"At this stage there has been no reaction from the government of President Bashar al-Assad to the statements that he made about the incident, but it is clear from his statements that he considers the attack to be a criminal act," a council diplomat said.

The UN has said that the Lebanese Hezbollah group and the Iranian Revolutionary Guards was behind the attack and that it was part of a deliberate effort to gain control of hospitals and other medical facilities in a number of rebel-held areas.

The UN says that it has no indication that the bombing was conducted by the Syrian government, and that the Lebanese group did not use chemical weapons. The Syrian government has denied responsibility for the attack, describing it as a "terrorist" attack.

According to a report by the UN, the UN security council is set to hold an emergency meeting on Tuesday to discuss the crisis.

The Security Council is expected to discuss the humanitarian situation in the city of Tripoli with the aim of seeking "enhanced coordination" to resolve the crisis and to help "avoid further suffering", the report said.
headline: UN demand 'prompt' probe into strike near Beirut hospital

text:
SUSI IT's €6.1 million cost overrun at its Irish headquarters is a major blow to the company's management team.

A confidential report from the Independent Commission Against Corruption, which investigated the issue, said the overspend was "particularly concerning" given SUSI had been assured it would be able to recoup the investment.

The report, released on Wednesday, said the overspend was caused by "unwarranted and unreasonable" cost increases to the IT project.

The report said SUSI's chief executive, Eamonn O'Sullivan, had not shown any indication the costs of the project would be recouped or any desire to, even at the time.

The Commission said the "suspected" overspend was the reason for the audit in the first place, and found no evidence to support the suggestion that any of the SUSI staff involved had done anything illegal.

The report also found SUSI management had failed to make adequate preparations for a company-wide review of the project, which resulted in the overspend being recorded by SUSI as part of the project.

It also said an internal audit conducted by SUSI's auditing department found "no indication that it was appropriate or required" to record the overspend as part of the project.

The SUSI chief executive, who is also the company's European head of IT, told the Commission that "the accounting system used by the company for financial reporting of projects is completely different from that used by other companies".

The report said the overspend was caused by "unwarranted and unreasonable" cost increases to the project, but also "inappropriate management decision making".

It also found that there had been no evidence that there had been any financial loss incurred by SUSI as a result of the overspend.

The investigation was launched in January 2014, when former SUSI board member Sean Connolly raised concerns with the organisation's then general manager, Sean O'Malley.

The investigation found that the overspend was the "first instance of audit findings in a project to come to the attention of the IBAC".

It said that during the course of the inquiry, SUSI had been assured that "the costs of the project would be recouped or recovered as it moved through the IT service provider's management and procurement processes".

The Commission said that there were "no indications of any misconduct" on the part of SUSI management, and that it had no evidence to support the suggestion that any staff had done anything illegal or criminal.

However, the Commission said that the overspend had "contributed significantly to SUSI's poor financial position".

It said the overspend would have been rectified if SUSI had been able to recoup the overspend, but that "it appears as if SUSI's management and governance structure do not allow this to occur".

The report said that "in its absence, the business case for the project would likely have been substantially improved".

It said that a "potential for a future failure" was "real" and that "as a result of the overspend, SUSI would have faced significantly more costs and challenges in the future.
headline: Significant overspend in cost for SUSI IT system

text:
A Norwegian-flagged submarine has been discovered submerged in waters off the coast of Papua New Guinea. The vessel was last sighted on a surveillance radar.

The Norwegian Maritime Safety Authority (MSHA) has confirmed the presence of a small submarine in the area. The discovery was made on Tuesday afternoon (1 April).

MSHA told media that the vessel was not a conventional submarine but was actually a "small diesel submersible". It had a crew of seven, two of whom were Norwegian citizens. The vessel was located in the vicinity of the Rote Tuin Naval Base.

MSHA told press that the vessel is under tow at the moment and will be lowered to the surface when the tow is complete. The submarine is in excellent condition, according to MSHA, but there is no indication at this stage of any equipment or any illegal activities taking place.

The Norwegian authorities have confirmed that the vessel was last seen leaving the base in a hurry, before taking a turn around the island. The vessel was seen on CCTV footage leaving the base at 6.37pm, and on radar returning to the base by 12.02am.

The Norwegian authorities will be in contact with MSHA. The area will remain a precautionary area until the vessel can be retrieved.
headline: Sunken Indonesian submarine found broken in three

Managing Director of Shannon Airport John O'Leary is to step down from his role, which is being held in a special capacity.

Mr O'Leary said he had taken on the role as Managing Director on the basis that he would not be able to continue in the role at a later date.

He said he had taken on the role as a special position and that he would be seeking new employment elsewhere.

Mr O'Leary was appointed Managing Director of Shannon Airport on November 1, 2014.
