headline: Shannon Airport Managing Director is to leave his role

text:
Bomb disposal experts have defused an improvised explosive device found at a bar in Cavan in the north of Co Down.

The device was found at around 10.30am this morning in a doorway on a balcony of the Bar in the town. It was reported that there had been a "scuffle" with police, after which the device was defused at about 1.45am.

The emergency services are also involved in the investigation.

A spokesman for the Irish Fire and Rescue Service says the bomb squad was called by the local ambulance service.

"The fire service were alerted at 10.30am this morning by the ambulance service," he said.

"There has been a scuffle with police in the area at this time and then the device was disarmed at about 1.45am this morning and it was removed safely to the nearest forensics team for examination."

The spokesman said that at this stage, nothing has been discovered on the premises which prompted the ambulance service to make the call for help.
headline: Pipe bomb defused after being found in Co Down

text:
Defense Minister Ehud Barak yesterday threatened to annex parts of the Gaza Strip to Israel if Israel is prevented from establishing a "security corridor" over the border.

The minister said Israel must not permit any other country to "unilaterally and unilaterally" enter Israeli-occupied lands.

He said Israel was prepared to send troops into the Gaza Strip, if needed, and to continue shelling the territory until its people are free from the rocket attacks launched by Hamas.

"If (Israel) is unable to establish a secure corridor, the IDF will use all means at its disposal," he said in an interview.

The Defence Minister did not specify what actions Israel might take to secure the border, but said that it would "take all steps necessary in order to ensure that Israel's security cannot be threatened."

"If it is necessary to secure the Gaza Strip as a sovereign state, there will be a state of affairs where we would be prepared to annex parts of the Gaza Strip to Israel."

Barak said that Israel's right to self defence must be respected and that Israel would not allow anyone to threaten it with force.

The minister said the Iron Dome anti-rocket missile system is working and the IDF will defend itself if there is an attack.

Barak said that if necessary, the government would consider military action to force Hamas to withdraw from the Gaza Strip.

He said he was prepared to meet with any group to negotiate a truce.

He said it was unacceptable for Hamas to fire rockets at Israeli civilians.

"We will not allow it to happen. If we were to open a new front, there would be no limits to what we could do."

On Sunday, Barak said there would be no daylight between Israel and Hamas and that Hamas was not interested in dialogue, but he insisted there would be no daylight between the two sides.

A day after meeting with President Shimon Peres, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said there was no chance of a ceasefire in Gaza.

"I am ready to say that Israel will not accept a ceasefire that does not guarantee Israel's security," he said.

"The only way for us to protect our people and preserve our existence is to take on Hamas and its allies."

Mr Netanyahu said Israel would only accept a ceasefire after the security situation had been restored.

"I have no doubt that we have the means to restore security in Gaza, after we have restored it to its pre- Operation Cast Lead status."
headline: Israeli defence minister threatens to annex parts of Gaza

text:
Two men were jailed for up to 26 years yesterday for tax evasion, in the biggest tax fraud case ever to be tried in the North-west.

The sentences were handed down in the trial of Maurice Costello and his partner Pat O'Sullivan, who were convicted of a total of £8,000.

The defendants are the first to be convicted in Northern Ireland for tax fraud.

The trial in Belfast heard how they exploited loopholes to illegally transfer almost £25m from a corporation into a trust account for themselves.

The trial heard that Costello and his partner had set up a company in a small village in County Tyrone in 2011, but its profits were lost to the tax office.

They had then transferred the money into a Trust account in a bank account belonging to O'Sullivan.

The pair were each given a 10-year suspended sentence and ordered to pay the Revenue Commissioners £1.9m for breach of trust.

The pair's legal team will appeal against the sentences.

In May, a jury took less than nine hours to convict O'Sullivan of fraud and breach of trust in a similar case, which has already cost £2.6m to the Revenue.

However, she will also have to pay £1.6m in costs in the ongoing trial in Northern Ireland.

Costello, who was also accused of theft, was found guilty of breach of trust by a majority verdict at the high court in Belfast.

The jury heard how the pair had to pay tax on a series of sales from their corporation, the Revenue Service, which they falsely declared on their invoices.

They took about £5,000 from each sales and spent the money in an Isle of Man savings account.

The Revenue Service is not being prosecuted for the sales made by the corporation, and instead the two men have pleaded guilty to offences including fraud and false accounting.

The trial was told that the money from the sale of the corporation's sales was transferred into a trust account for Costello and O'Sullivan, who lived together in a rented house, to the tune of £5,000.

They also transferred about £3,000 to the Isle of Man's Revenue Service account in the name of the Trust.

The trial heard that the money was taken from accounts held by several corporations, including the Revenue Service.

It also heard how they were unable to pay the tax due on the sales.

They also diverted the money to their own personal account, with the proceeds of the fraud going on their mortgage, car insurance and other bills.

Judge William Geddes heard that the Revenue Service has launched an investigation in the wake of the trial, and that the defendants' behaviour is likely to be investigated further.

He added: "It is a very complex matter. In the absence of any other proof of criminality, I cannot find any mitigating factors that would enable me to suspend your sentence."

O'Sullivan's barrister, Patrick Dineen, said his client had no previous convictions.

Mr Dineen added that his client had been a long-term unemployed person, had had difficulty in the job market, and had received no support from the courts.

The trial in Belfast, in which the men appeared together, lasted less than nine hours.
headline: 27 people sentenced in biggest tax fraud case in NI

A migrant family rescued

text:
Government to expand free contraception scheme

Government will expand the free contraceptive provision in some cases, in response to growing concern from individuals. The announcement in yesterday's Budget will expand the free contraception benefit from €15 a month, to €20 for the first three years of the scheme and €30 thereafter.

The Government will also extend the duration of the scheme so that it will continue until December 31st 2016, even if no new member is registered for the scheme.

The Government is also committing to make free contraception available to women from up to age 27 who have had a hysterectomy, or who have had a termination of pregnancy.

This includes those who had a hysterectomy when under 18 years of age or had a pregnancy terminated when under 18 years of age.

The Government is announcing that the total number of Free Contraception (FC) recipients will increase from 26,000 to 30,000 by 2017 – a figure of up to 4,500 additional free contraception recipients.

The Minister for Health, Simon Harris TD, said this would provide more women in Ireland with the benefit that they so desperately need.

"This is a particularly important step in the right direction, as we continue to see an increase in the number of women in Ireland who are using free contraception.

"I also want to thank women throughout the country who have contacted me, concerned about the fact that while many women in this country have access to free contraception, they are unable to use it.

"In Ireland it is also important to recognise that we are a country of choice for contraception. It is important that we continue to give women the right to make their own decisions about their fertility and about their reproductive health.

"I believe that this is a very positive step forward in providing more women with access to contraception.

"It is important that we continue to support women who are choosing not to use contraception.

"Over the last couple of weeks I have met with a number of women who were concerned about their fertility and how this will affect them should they decide to take on more children."

The Government will also make free contraception available in all institutions, including the NHS, from 2016.

For more information on the Free Contraception Scheme, visit www.ec.gov.ie/faq/contraception/free_contraception.htm.
headline: Government expands free contraception scheme

Children are increasingly at risk of homelessness, according to a report by charity ActionAid.

Nearly 9,000 children under the age of 18 are experiencing homelessness in Ireland. While an estimated 50,000 children sleep rough in Ireland every year, fewer than 3,000 are unaccompanied and around 250 unaccompanied children are homeless, according to the latest figures from the Department of Social Protection.

ActionAid's report entitled 'Homeless Children: A Call to Action' identifies five critical areas where ActionAid is calling for urgent action.

The first is the impact of the recession on child poverty, as the recession has caused widespread family breakdown. As a result, there are more children being placed in care.

Second, the impact of the recession on family breakdown has been compounded by an economic downturn that has caused more family breakdowns, as families are increasingly isolated and are unable to access support.

Third, the impact of the recession on child homelessness, particularly the number of unaccompanied children in crisis, is also serious.

Fourth, the impact of homelessness on children is exacerbated by the fact that children in crisis have a very low chance of gaining access to school and there is a real risk of them ending up in care.

Fifth, children are at risk of becoming homeless if their families become too stressed and they are unable to access housing.

The report concludes that ActionAid must continue to address the housing crisis and that they must work with the government to ensure that children are not being placed in crisis homes and that their lives are not at risk.
headline: Major concern over pace of child homelessness

The Irish Employers' Federation (IEF) has condemned a new tax rule that has caused SMEs to lose billions of euro in tax savings.

The new tax rules, which were introduced by the Government last month, will be introduced next year to replace the so-called Covid-19, which has seen SMEs lose billions of euro in revenue through increased costs and reduced tax receipts, despite the Government's own economic forecasts suggesting a loss of around €1 billion a year.

The tax rule will see the tax base of the tax base which includes the VAT component of a business tax base shrink from 20% to 8.5%, while the tax base that includes the tax paid on investment income will shrink from 30% to 15%.

The tax rule has caused SMEs to pay higher tax rates in some areas. In many cases this means that SMEs cannot access tax reliefs, and have been forced to lower their taxable profits, leading to higher costs and reduced tax receipts.

The Government has been forced to change the rules following a report from the Irish Tax Payers' Alliance (ITPA), which said that it was unfair that SMEs were paying lower tax rates in some parts of the State while paying high tax rates in other parts.

The ITPA said that the Government should consider lowering the tax base to allow the tax base to reflect the economic conditions in every area of the State, rather than having 'special treatment' for one section of the State or for certain industries.

The ITPA, who represent the small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Ireland, said that the Government's proposed change would lead to higher tax rates for SMEs in certain areas of the State, and would result in SMEs paying higher tax rates.

The ITPA urged the Government to reconsider its decision to introduce the new tax rule, and for the State's Revenue Commissioners to continue to work with the ITPA to see how the new rules can be implemented in a way that does not favour certain industries.

The ITPA said that the current arrangements are unfair to SMEs, as it is unlikely that SMEs will be able to claim relief for VAT in every State where they operate.

The ITPA said that the current arrangements will lead to higher tax rates for SMEs in certain areas of the State, and will result in higher costs to SMEs, in particular for SMEs that are in the construction industry.

It said that the tax rules were unfair as the tax base of the tax base includes the VAT component of a business tax base and the tax paid on investment income, while the tax base that includes the tax paid on VAT cannot be reduced.

The ITPA said that the proposed change to the tax rules will see SMEs pay higher tax rates in certain areas of the State, and will lead to higher costs to SMEs, in particular for SMEs that are in the construction industry.

However, it said that any change to the tax base should not be made unless the Government is able to demonstrate that the change will deliver a benefit to SMEs.

The Irish Employers' Federation said that the tax rules should not have been introduced in the first place and that the Government should reconsider its decision to introduce the tax rules.
headline: SMEs lose billions due to Covid-19 restrictions

EU member states will ease a crackdown on foreign care workers by allowing them to stay permanently in the UK if they have skills that would help employers to fill job vacancies, the European Parliament has said.

The Parliament's rapporteur on human rights, Martin Schulz, said in a statement that the new rules will make it easier for EU citizens who work in the UK to stay in their home country.

Currently, EU nationals can work in the UK up to the amount they can earn in the EU in a year. However, EU nationals can only stay if they have a job offer from a British employer that meets their skills requirements.

In a statement, Schulz said that with the UK's "generous" benefits system, the restrictions could affect millions of EU citizens who work in the UK in areas that are not currently considered to be a "job market" – such as social welfare and social care, he said.

"The new rules will allow people to stay in the UK permanently if they have a job offer from an employer that meets their skills requirements," Schulz said.

"Employers will have the option of offering those people a job offer as a permanent resident, regardless of their nationality, after they have completed an English language test and completed the national insurance card. This means they will not have to apply for citizenship on arrival and may also have their residency permit renewed, at the individual's request," he said.

"The EU should not be discriminating against its citizens in such a way as to discriminate against EU citizens working in Britain and, in the end, this should be the objective of EU law," Schulz added.

Schulz said that EU citizens who work in the UK can still apply for permanent residence after they have completed the language test and National Insurance cards. The MEP said the new rules should also apply to citizens who work in the NHS or other public services or have been trained in the UK.

The MEP said that there had been growing concerns about the treatment of EU citizens working in the UK who have skills or qualifications which would have an impact on their ability to find jobs in the UK.

"The government should take action to address this situation as the EU citizens have a duty to their country," he said.

"The government should set up a commission to look at the need for reform in this area and implement a new immigration system that ensures that EU citizens do not have a discriminatory effect on British workers."

Schulz said that there had been some evidence to suggest that EU citizens who have taken training and worked in the UK could be employed by British companies in fields that do not currently attract a high proportion of EU talent.

"However, this type of evidence is hard to find and we need to see further evidence to support this and that is why we should set up a commission to look at the impact of EU nationals' working here. This commission will look at the labour market impact of EU citizens in the UK and how we can adjust the law to protect them and their families in the UK," he added.

However, the MEP said that it was "important to put the responsibility for this to the employers who recruit people and we also need to improve the quality of the workforce.

"It is also important that employers can employ the best people and that the legal framework is not used as a tool to restrict employment opportunities for EU citizens."
headline: UK to ease immigration rules for care workers

The Government intends to buy an additional 450 million kilowatt hours of electricity in the next 12 months.

This will be achieved by purchasing an additional 4,100MW of wind power, 1,300MW of rooftop solar and 1,100MW of hydropower.

The extra electricity will be supplied through a variety of schemes.

For example, the Government will invest €1 billion in upgrading the HSE's electricity network and another €200 million in the National Grid's electricity distribution network.

The two-year Energy Supply Plan will also see a reduction of the current rate of renewable energy certificates (RECs). The Government will reduce the renewable energy certificates from 7% to 5.5% from 2015.

This will ensure that electricity bills in the State are not increased by any undue amount.

The Government will also spend €200 million on expanding and modernising the National Grid.

The Budget statement will also see the extension of the national electricity network to include electricity sold in the State as a whole and to include all the electricity sold to consumers.

The Government will also make further investments to make the electricity network more secure and secure-like.

The Minister for Transport and Tourism, Shane Ross TD, said:

"I am pleased that the Government has set out plans to deliver electricity to all its citizens, as well as the provision of a more secure and secure electricity network.

"The Government is also investing in new renewable power stations, bringing down costs for consumers and reducing emissions.

"Electricity is essential to the State's economy and we have taken steps to ensure that it remains a high-performing and affordable electricity supply.

"The increased investment in renewables, along with the decision to phase out carbon taxes, mean that consumers in Ireland will continue to receive electricity that is lower in cost than in other countries."
headline: Govt to purchase extra 450mw of electricity next year

Huge news from Amsterdam – a mammoth meatball has been unveiled.

The mammoth has been discovered in the zoo, and scientists claim it is the oldest preserved mammoth meatball ever discovered.

The meatball, called The Mammoth, is made of mammoth DNA, and has been described as the oldest preserved meatball from anywhere in the world.

Scientists say it was discovered in an elephant zoo in Amsterdam by a team led by Prof Mark Williams.

The scientists say the meatball was made with elephant and bison hair, and was discovered in the Elephant Conservation Centre in Amsterdam. The meatball was given to the zoo by a member of the public who was interested in the meatball and also wanted to donate it.

It was found by a member of the public when they were checking out the Elephant Conservation Centre when the lab's doors were locked. It was taken to the museum and exhibited. The meatball has been named The Mammoth after Professor Williams and is now on display in the zoo.

Prof Mark Williams, curator of the Mammoth Center told RTÉ News: "This is a very exciting find, and it is exciting because it is a piece of meat which has a provenance which is very unusual."

He said there are a lot of mammoth meatballs out there, but only a few are known to have been made in the past, and this is one of the few where there is an element of provenance.

Prof Mark Williams said he was impressed by the mammoth meatball because it is the earliest preserved meatball discovered.

He said: "That's a massive find, it's really something new, and it's something that we haven't seen before."

He said the meatball was first displayed in the zoo in 2008 in a small exhibit and has since been moved in to an exhibit in the Elephant Conservation Centre, where it is now displayed.

Prof Mark Williams said the meatball was found in an elephant zoo in Amsterdam and has now been given to the museum.
headline: Meatball made with mammoth DNA unveiled in Amsterdam

The Commission's investigative team investigating the controversial investment deal between Argentina and the European Union may not be able to determine its full implications, a senior official of the European Union's trade union federation told The Irish Times.

"The probe in the Argentine case, involving €4 billion in bonds which are held in a European depositary institution, seems to have stalled – there is currently no information on how much the probe has cost, whether it has resulted in an indictment or not," said the official, who has been involved in the probe since its inception.

The official added that the probe "is also undermining a very important investment deal between the EU and Mercosur, which will ultimately lead to free trade between Europe and Mercosur".

The decision to suspend the investigation had been taken by the Commission on Wednesday after the two-month deadline, the official said.

The probe centres around a group of Argentinian investors, some of whom are EU citizens and others who were EU residents when they bought their bonds in 2005 and 2006.

According to the Commission, the investment deal would have brought more than €6 billion to the EU, while the Argentine investors have claimed the debt is their property.

The commission investigation has been going on for several years and was launched after the European Commission asked Argentina to explain why the investors had not been paid the €4 billion they had been promised.

The official said the probe would not delay the European Union's efforts to get a trade deal inked with Argentina, which is currently negotiating with the EU on a free trade agreement.

"The Argentine investors have shown a good example of how the trade deal should work: on the one hand, all sides must be fully aware of the benefits of trade, and they need to be ready to pay the money. On the other hand, they need to be able to prove their investments, so that investors can invest in their future," said the official.

"As long as the Commission keeps on putting pressure, the Argentinians are sure to delay the conclusion of the deal," the official said.

Last month, Argentina's foreign minister, Susana Malcorra, said the country had offered to hand over €1.9 billion to the EU and said she would be willing to negotiate on the issue.
headline: IFJ probe 'undermines' EU-Mercosur trade deal, says IFA

The outcome of the talks between the European Commission and the United States over the Transatlantic Trade and Investment Partnership (TTIP) is uncertain, a senior EU source told RTE News.

"We have had no progress on a few items, but at the moment that is not certain, and there is still some detail that needs to be worked out," the source said.

However, it is understood that the EU will attempt to conclude talks on a free-trade agreement with the US this month in a bid to end a stalemate with the US over intellectual property.

The EU has refused to include a clause in the TTIP that would require a minimum level of protection for intellectual property in trade deals, but the US has refused to go that far.

The EU source stressed that the talks between the US and the EU were being conducted in the open, so no one was negotiating behind closed doors.

It is not just about trade but also about protecting public health. We can't afford for medicines and healthcare to go out of date. Dr Brian Keel, Chief Executive of the UK's Royal College of Physicians

He said the EU was trying to negotiate a deal that addresses public health issues, such as access to cheap medicines and a more open Internet.

"We don't have any definitive timeline but there is a certain amount of progress and some things that could be done that we would be pleased to see happen," the source said.

However, he said it was difficult to say whether the US's concerns with regard to copyright policy in the agreement were acceptable.

"If we start talking about patents and IP policy, then I think it's something which will be controversial," he said.

"There are elements that are pretty radical in some of the areas that we are talking about, so it's difficult to see how we can work out if they are acceptable."

Dr Brian Keel, chief executive of the British Medical Association, said the EU had failed to offer a new free-trade agreement with the US since 1994.

"We can't afford for medicines and healthcare to go out of date," he said. "We need a new free-trade agreement with the United States."

He added that it was a "major embarrassment" that the EU had agreed to a deal which would allow US companies to sue EU states which did not meet their demands for public procurement or environmental standards.

"It is unacceptable for the EU to allow foreign investors to sue European governments if those governments do not comply with their demands."

Dr Keel said that there was also a need for more protection for patients in the EU, including the possibility of a public health system for Europe.

"When you look at what we now have, the NHS is being pushed out to the private sector," he said. "We are not doing enough to prevent that."

"We need a national health service for Europe which protects people from private healthcare companies."
headline: Outcome of EU-US tariff talks 'not certain'

The number of fraud cases in the Republic of Ireland increased by a staggering 24 per cent last year, and the number of those in which the defendant was convicted increased by 27 per cent.

This was the first time in the Republic of Ireland's 20-year history that the number of fraud cases had increased by 24 per cent.

The Government says the rise in fraud cases is because of improved technology, better reporting systems and a better understanding of who is a fraudster.

The figures also show that the number of people who reported being victims of fraud to the fraud investigations unit increased by 2,000 in the period to June this year.

Meanwhile, the fraud and cyber crime unit has recorded an increase of 10 per cent in the number of people it has spoken to after the launch of Operation Ring.

Fraud is the third biggest category of crime in the Republic of Ireland and the latest figures show that fraud cases have increased by 24 per cent over the past year, with 3,857 fraud cases being reported in 2015.

Between July 2015 and June this year, the fraud unit was contacted by almost 20,000 people who were victims of fraud.

The fraud unit said it has received a high number of reports of fraud in recent years, with the number of fraud cases increasing each year.

The data, released by the Department of Justice and Equality, shows that there has been a 21 per cent increase in the number of people receiving a conviction in the last five years.

In the last five years, the number of people receiving a conviction of fraud rose by 9% (9,838) compared to the period 2009-2014.

The most common type of fraud was financial fraud, which was the most commonly reported offence and accounted for 24 per cent of the total fraud offences.

In addition to financial fraud, the top five types of fraud that were reported include:

• Property crime: 4,838 cases

• Social welfare fraud: 4,835

• National health care fraud: 4,929

• Personal injury fraud: 4,894

The top five offences for which those who received a conviction were subject to a monetary fine were:

• Fraud by an organ donor: 5,037 cases

• Fraud by a health care worker: 4,638

• Fraud by a financial institution: 4,635

• Fraud by an employee: 4,547

• Fraud by a third party: 4,447

A spokesperson for the Department of Justice and Equality said:

"We're committed to tackling fraud in all its forms – which is why we are increasing the number of staff working in the fraud and cyber crime units.

"These units have been a vital part of our efforts to tackle fraud and to protect the public from fraud and the criminals who commit it."

There has also been an increase in the number of people involved in the use of encryption software, which has resulted in an increase in the number of financial crimes.

The Fraudster's Guide to Cyber Crime has been updated in response to the increase in fraud cases.

The guide outlines how to spot a scam, warns about phishing scams, and provides tips on how to protect yourself from identity theft.
headline: Large increase in fraud cases in year to June

Children's hospice care unit at Maghaberry Hospital in Dublin will be put under a new management system after an inspection report.

The Children's Hospice Trust's new management structure includes a new chief executive officer, appointed by the Minister for Health.

In a decision accepted by the Minister, the trust's chief executive, Dr Patrick O'Sullivan will be put in charge of the trust's new business.

The report, which was issued by the Irish Hospice Organisation, said: "The trust will continue to provide inpatient care to children with life-threatening conditions, and will continue to provide services for those with less serious conditions.

"The trust will also provide services for adults in the care of the National Life Skills Institute."

The report said the trust is committed to "making sure that patients are cared for in a way that minimises waiting times".

It said it would continue to provide services for children with life-threatening conditions, and it would continue to provide services for those with less serious conditions.

The report said the trust had "exemplified the best practice of caring for children with life-threatening conditions" and had been recognised by the trust's own board as the best in the country.

The report said the trust will not enter a new contract with the state but will continue to provide services to children with life-threatening conditions until their needs can be addressed by the Department of Health.

The report said that the trust had been "working towards this long-term outcome" since the establishment of the hospice in 1982.

It said the trust had "been a model hospice provider and has been valued for its work".

"Our new management structure and the work of the trust's board are aimed at continuing to provide quality healthcare, and to ensure that our new management structure addresses the changes in the way that children's hospice care is delivered," said Dr O'Sullivan.

The report, which was published today, said the children's hospice had a "high degree of autonomy" and is "capable of leading from the front in many aspects of care".

It said that the trust's approach to the management of its patients had been "driven by long-standing practices which have been recognised by the trust's own board".

In an interview to RTÉ News, the Minister for Health James Reilly said he will "keep this issue in the front of the Minister's mind" as he considers the findings of the report.

"We accept the recommendations of the report, and we're going to look at those with particular focus on how the care that is provided is done better and for longer-term needs for children," he said.

He said he was looking forward to receiving the report and will keep it in his thoughts.

"But the Minister's position remains the same, as I understand it, that the Children's Hospice Trust will continue to provide inpatient care to children with life-threatening conditions until their needs can be addressed by the Department of Health," he said.

The report said that after three years of "constant improvement", the children's hospice was "a very successful hospice service in relation to the goals it had been set in terms of quality and in terms of care of the patients".
headline: Six children waiting for special care unit place

We have heard from thousands of people in support of the people of Northern Ireland since last year's general election. The support for the people of Northern Ireland has been extraordinary, and I want to thank everyone who has contributed.

James Watson, a British genetics pioneer, is believed to have died in his sleep at his home in Cambridge on Monday (May 22) evening, aged 97.

He had been a vocal critic of the 'diseases of civilisation' which, he believed, were the result of genetic mutations.

Watson's contribution to science had been to show how mutations in the human genome could influence the risk of diseases like cancer and cardiovascular disease.

His theory of evolution was first proposed in 1950, and in the early 1960s Watson published the landmark research that showed the structure of DNA, and subsequently his theory of genetic inheritance.

Watson, who married American mathematician Ada Lovelace in 1952, was considered to be an inspiration to many in the field of science and an essential figure in the field of biotechnology.

In 2012, Watson and his wife Anne were knighted in the New Year's Honours list for their work in genetics.

His work was recognised by the New York Times in their year-end issue in 2012, as well as being honoured as one of the "World's 100 Most Influential People in Science" in his honour by The Guardian in 2014.

Watson was also the first person to be awarded the Nobel Prize in physics in 1962 for his contribution to the understanding of particle physics. He was awarded the prize for his work on DNA's molecular structure in 1986.

In 2001, Watson was appointed the first director of the Human Genome Project, which has resulted in the sequencing of almost 90,000 human genomes.

His achievements and the impact he had on our lives are as remarkable as the science he discovered.

He was regarded as one of the world's leading scientists, and his impact on science, society and the wider world is immeasurable.

I would like to dedicate this to our friend and colleague Professor Stephen Hawking, whose passing this morning was very sad.

Professor Hawking was an important figure in the history of science and a scientist himself. I was fortunate to have a wonderful relationship with him, and to learn more about him on this occasion is extremely sad.

He was the creator of the term "The Theory of Everything" and, as he described it, "was responsible for the most important scientific advance of our time".

Professor Hawking is survived by his wife, Ann Druyan.

I would also like to pay tribute to the many others who have helped to make the scientific world better through their work.

I would like to express my sorrow at the passing of a man who inspired me, and I am sure many others, with his great insight and generosity.

The cause of death has been registered at the London General Hospital.

The family request privacy at this time.

Editorial note: The Irish Examiner regrets the inadvertent use of the word "goddess" in this article.
headline: DNA pioneer James Watson dies aged 97

The letter was sent to German Chancellor Angela Merkel, UK Foreign Secretary Philip Hammond and US President Barack Obama, as well as to the secretary of the US department for disarmament, the deputy secretary of the department for disarmament and global security, and the director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency.

The ambassador's letter, which was circulated to news organisations across the world, urged a global ban on the use of nuclear weapons and the end of nuclear arms as an instrument of national policy.

The ambassador urged the German government "to accept an arms race in a world without nuclear weapons, which could lead to a nuclear arms race between the US and Russia and between China and Iran", adding: "The world is much safer when the weapons are eliminated."

An anonymous Japanese envoy, who has not been named, wrote the letter to the German government, the UK and the US.

The ambassador appealed for action to eliminate nuclear weapons and for the US to join the efforts to end nuclear weapons.

"We are not alone in seeing the threat posed by nuclear weapons. In the past, when all options were on the table, such as nuclear weapons, missile defence and a new arms race, we always managed to stop them. That was a good example," the letter said.

"Now, it appears that we are once again facing a nuclear arms race with the United States and with Russia, which are the only major nuclear weapons states. In the end, this might lead to a nuclear arms race, because it will not lead to a world without nuclear weapons."

The ambassador called on "all states to commit themselves to the abolition of nuclear weapons in the interest of peace, security and development, and the safety of the people of the world".

"We are aware that in the past the world has done a lot to eliminate nuclear weapons and that we cannot count on this to change. However, we are confident that the international community will do all it can to eliminate nuclear weapons."

He said that the US and other nuclear weapons states must "respect the international law" and "take responsible responsibility for the future peace and security of the world".

"We believe that the main way to achieve this goal is through the abolition of nuclear weapons. We call on all states to accept an arms race in a world without nuclear weapons, which could lead to a nuclear arms race between the US and Russia and between China and Iran."
headline: Japanese ambassador appeals for end to nuclear weapons

It's a busy day in the car industry. A Ford executive has been quoted saying that sales of the new, low-cost EcoSport hatchback have dropped "like a rock" and that sales of the new, cheaper and more capable Ford Focus hatchback will also suffer a "significant" drop "as a result of the move to a hybrid system".

The article also reports that the Ford Focus will "now be available in the same trim range as its competitors" including the Ford Fiesta, Ford Focus ST and Ford Focus Electric – and it'll also now come with a "compact hatchback" and a larger, "full-sized" Focus.

The article goes on to say that Ford, "as usual", doesn't want to sell a large car – it wants to sell the cheapest car, because a large car is the only way of making money in the car industry. It's a great way of getting people to buy Ford cars in the first place, but the cost of a large car is going down, and the company is happy to make money by selling smaller cars.

So, it's looking like the next big announcement from Apple on the car front is that it won't bring CarPlay to other car manufacturers (Apple has sold over a million cars in Ireland) and that the next big feature from Apple on the iPhone/iPad side will be a "full-size" car.

Advertisement

The article then goes on to report that Ford Focus sales have been "stagnant" and that the company is "now looking at a large refresh of the Focus line this year".

The headline and the article are both accurate in their assessment of what's happened. The only part that is incorrect is the assertion that Ford sold 2,000 fewer cars in June than it did in June 2013. The 1,000-car figure is more or less correct.

What was wrong with Ford sales in June was that it didn't have the new Focus hatchback in stock at all.

Advertisement

The problem with that claim, according to the report is that Ford doesn't actually sell more cars than it can sell.

The strike has been called by drivers from the Midland Trains and Southern Rail.

March 11th, 2005

By

Dr. Patrick D. McManus

Chairman and Editor

The

Journal of Hospital Medicine

Source: The Irish Times

March 10, 2005


There are still over 4,000 beds in the Republic of Ireland (RI) hospitals.

Most of these are in emergency departments and are used by the elderly, young people and people with physical disabilities.

The average age of the hospital beds in Ireland is 53 with the average age of patients over 60 in the emergency departments.

The most frequent reason for admitting a patient to hospital is "heart failure or cardiac arrest".

The Republic of Ireland has not met its targets for bed occupancy for the last 15 years, despite a sustained effort to increase this by increasing the number of beds by 10%.

The reasons for this are:

1. The number of beds (in emergency departments) is kept down by the fact that the majority of patients are admitted in the early morning.

2. The cost of maintaining hospital beds is not paid for by the patients, but by the Government.

3. Patients have to be referred to hospital or be discharged from hospital, rather than discharged on the same day.

4. The proportion of beds in the population which is over 65 is only 30%.

5. The hospitals in the Republic of Ireland have a lower average age than Ireland as a whole, the average age of the population is 66, compared to 75% of the population in Ireland as a whole.

6. The proportion of patients admitted for non-medical reasons is much lower than that in other parts of Europe.

The Ministry of Health has tried for many years to increase bed occupancy.

The Minister for Health in the last five years has had a number of meetings with nurses, doctors, hospital managers and the Department of Health to discuss the problem.

There is a considerable increase in beds in the emergency departments.

It would be wrong to conclude that more beds are needed.

The majority of beds in the population are over 65 years old and in many cases are very old.

The problem is that the majority of people who require hospitalisation are over 60 years of age.

The Minister for Health has asked that beds in the hospitals be extended for people who are at high risk of hospitalisation such as those with cancer.

The number of beds in the emergency departments in Ireland will increase as the number of seniors increases.

However, this is unlikely to improve the situation in the long run.

The Ministry of Health must consider the problem of bed occupancy and make sure that it is not causing long-term harm.

In the meantime, the Minister for Health should ensure that there are sufficient beds in the hospitals.

The Minister for Health may also wish to consider proposals that could be made to allow for the use of bed occupancy management.

The Minister for Health may consider the possibility of the sale of certain areas of hospital property.

The Minister for Health may also wish to consider the sale of hospital properties to reduce the current stock of hospital beds.

The Minister for Health may consider the possibility of the sale of large numbers of hospital properties to increase the stock of hospital beds.
headline: Patients will continue to suffer unless bed capacity increases, says expert doctor

China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has ordered all three chip giants – Nvidia and AMD – to stop selling their products in China immediately. The move comes after the companies signed a memorandum of understanding that would see Nvidia sell their processing power for use in Chinese military and police applications.

The companies have until May 10 to produce products, but the notice states:

"This notice is based on the fact that the companies do not intend to sell the technology used in the production of these products, which have been used in the production of these products."

This does not mean that the products are being removed from the market, but rather that the products will be restricted to a certain level in the local market. The notice is expected to be complied with by the end of the week.

The notice goes on to state that Nvidia and AMD must also stop selling other technologies from the company, namely their high-speed PCI Express and DDR3 PCI Express (M.2) memory modules.

It also states that Nvidia and AMD must stop using any of their chips in the manufacture of other products.

The reason for the order is the apparent rise of counterfeit chips. The notice says that Nvidia and AMD have been able to detect "a significant amount" of counterfeit components in the market.

The two companies are not the only ones accused of selling counterfeit products in China. A report from KSN (China's top internet portal) recently states that in April 2013, more than 700,000 Chinese companies received a warning from a state regulator for using counterfeit components in their products, according to the China Daily.

The warning was issued because of the high rate of counterfeit chips that are in circulation.
headline: US orders Nvidia and AMD to stop selling technology to China immediately

The protesters are said to have been holding a large banner that said "We are Americans and we want to live in peace," and to have waved flags and banners in support of President Bashar al-Assad in Syria.

The fighters were said to be fighters of the Popular Mobilization Forces, a group that has operated in northern Iraq since 2006 but has not yet been officially recognised by Baghdad.

"We were hit in the outskirts of Mosul with US warplanes and Iraqi forces and we killed 25 fighters from this militia," Iraqi government spokesman Saad Maan said.

The Iraqi minister of defence, Yahya Rasool, accused the militia of "using civilians as human shields" and said "the terrorist group behind this aggression is not an Iraqi militia".

"It is an Iraqi group which has been attacking the Iraqi army and the Popular Mobilization Forces."

The militias were behind two deadly suicide bombings in Baghdad last year that killed more than 100 people.

US aircraft reportedly attacked Iraqi positions across northern Iraq in recent days as the US-led coalition prepares to leave the country, the New York Times reported.

They are part of a campaign against Isis, which controls large areas of Iraq and Syria, but the US has insisted the air strikes have not been aimed at Isis itself.

He said: "A lot of parents don't want their children to have a jab or a cough shot, so why shouldn't we take the same approach?"

The Government has said there will be no exemptions for children under the age of five, but this has angered parents, who want to vaccinate them.

Mr Ó Broin, who is a GP, has argued that a five-year-old should be immunised.

The Irish Independent understands that the proposal has not gone down well with some parents, but that a final decision will be made later in the year.

However, the headteacher said that parents could also opt to have their child vaccinated if they felt a certain level of risk, but did not want to be known as a "no jab, no pay" school.

He also argued that children who are immunised were more likely to have a good immune system, and were less likely to have a cold or flu.

He said: "You can't have a vaccine that can protect against a serious disease, that can protect against cancer or infectious diseases, and that is not right."

The headteacher said that parents needed to be informed of the risks and benefits of vaccination.

He said: "In the end, it's all up to the parents."

The papal train will arrive at the Santa Cruz di Tardio train station at noon, from where it will reach the Church of Santa Maria Maggiore, near the site of his funeral mass. The train will then leave again at about 2pm and will reach the Santa Cruz di Tardio in about an hour.

They said that the trains of previous Pope's funerals were not "like this", and would not be held at the same time, but they said the train could be expected to leave at about 2pm.

The Irish Council for Agriculture, Food and the Feed Industry (IcaFFI) said it was sending out a team of experts to help treat sick birds in one of the country's most isolated regions.

In a statement, IcaFFI said the disease, known as Emerald Ash Borer, was "extremely distressing to the people of the Emerald Coast" where the emerald ash borer has devastated the Emerald Coast forestry industry.

The Emerald Ash Borer, also known as ash-oak borer, has been eradicated in many parts of Europe over the past decade. But the disease continues to cause significant damage across Ireland.

While it was initially thought that the disease was spread by eating the infected leaves or wood of ash trees, the disease is now being spread by beetles. It has also spread to a number of other countries, including the US, and can cause serious illness.

The Court of Appeal has awarded a family of a 14-month-old girl in Galway the largest award in history in the ongoing case of a baby who got scalded on a Ryanair flight from Dublin to London.

The award will be paid to the family of the child, who was brought to hospital on a Ryanair flight from Dublin to London last August as a result of being scalded by the mother's coffee.

It is the largest award of its kind in Irish legal history and represents more than €19,000 in compensation, including costs and legal fees.

The family will also receive a €100,000 "bonus".

In addition to the award, the court has awarded the mother €5,500 in costs.

The mother's solicitor said it was a "proud day for the family" and she was "overjoyed with this result".

The mother, who cannot be named for legal reasons, had sought compensation following her 15-month pregnancy, after she experienced a severe infection that affected her blood pressure and caused a liver infection.

The mother had flown from Dublin to London with her child to visit friends in Spain, then travelled to London on the Ryanair flight from Dublin and then to her friends' holiday homes in Spain.

The child was returned to her in Ireland and the mother suffered a long period of sickness, requiring specialist treatment in the UK.

The baby became a major focus of the family's attention and their concern was raised when the hospital in London told the family they were unable to meet the baby's medical treatment costs.

They had to move the baby to a specialised child hospital, which was able to meet their costs and provided the child with the best possible care.

The family asked for a determination to be made on their claim for compensation and an order for the mother to return to Ireland so the baby could receive full treatment, as this could have been a life-saving treatment for her condition.

The court ruled in favour of them in November 2015 and the matter was referred to the Court of Appeal in 2015, which ruled in favour of them in February 2017.

The case was heard by a three-judge panel of the Court of Appeal in Galway.

The mother will receive a lump sum payment of around €4,000, the court has ruled. The award amounts to more than €19,000 in compensation, including costs and legal fees.

The mother will also receive a €100,000 "bonus" in addition to the lump sum.

The judge presiding over the case said that her findings were based on the evidence from witnesses, including the nurse who treated the mother at hospital, the hospital staff, and the family doctor, and a medical expert who visited the mother in hospital and gave evidence.

A statement released by the court said: "As the mother has been able to establish that she did not have any other illness on the day the incident occurred, the Court is of the opinion that her claim was not viable.

"The Court therefore makes a finding of fact that the mother had suffered a substantial loss of blood and a substantial reduction in her blood pressure during the short time she was in hospital."

The court also ruled that the mother has no chance of winning in court and that the claim should be declared void.
headline: Toddler who got scalded by hot coffee on Ryanair flight wins close to €19,000 as court hears she sat in agony for more than three hours

The Department of Justice has released Enoch Burke from Mountjoy Prison following a long battle in the Irish supreme court. Burke was arrested for contempt of court for refusing to comply with a court order to return to a pre-removal order.

The Department of Justice have now released Mr Burke on bail. He will be on a strict bail condition prohibiting him from associating with those who contravene the court order. The condition will not prevent him from attending court or making a statement.

Mr Burke, who is now in his mid-20s, will be monitored by the state's Probation Service over the next few weeks. His bail condition will be renewed and extended if any further breaches of the court order occur.

His release was granted following a judgment of the Court of Appeal in 2014.

Mr Burke was sentenced to seven years imprisonment in July 2014 for contempt of court relating to a case that arose out of his refusal to comply with a pre-removal order which required him to comply with the orders of the High Court and Supreme Court.

Mr Burke was also ordered to pay a fine of €1,000 and to pay €7,000 costs.

He was released on parole in December 2014 but was found in breach of his parole in May 2015. He was immediately arrested and released pending appeal. He was again released pending appeal and was sentenced to a total of seven years imprisonment in July 2016.

The appeal against his sentence was refused by the Court of Appeal on the grounds that he had not been in breach of any of the conditions of his parole. This was contrary to provisions of the Parole Act 2013.

The decision of the High Court in 2014 in the case of Burke v Mountjoy Prison has been upheld.

After being released from Mountjoy, Mr Burke applied to the Irish supreme court for permission to appeal.

The supreme court dismissed Mr Burke's application on the grounds that it had no jurisdiction to hear the appeal as it had been brought before a lower court. Mr Burke appealed to the Irish Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction.

The supreme court also dismissed Mr Burke's claim that the High Court order was an invalid exercise of judicial power.

The appeal is now on appeal in the High Court.

Mr Burke was sentenced in July 2014 for contempt of court.

He was later sent back to Mountjoy after a review of his case by a tribunal in Dublin.

The minister told reporters that he didn't have the exact details of the allegations, but added: "We are trying our best to get to the bottom of it." The minister added that he will be bringing the matter to the attention of the country's chief prosecutor.

THE HAGUE, 31 October 2016 – The head of the International Criminal Court, Ms. Fatou Bensouda, has said that it is premature to speculate on the outcome of the post mortem examination of Nora Quoirin. Ms Bensouda, who was recently re-elected as head of the court, explained this to the Irish Times. "It may be premature to make any predictions on the outcome of the examination," she said. Ms Quoirin, the head of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, has been in hospital since 24 August.

The article goes on to say that Ms Bensouda was "very upbeat" about her appointment to the role.

Headline: Prosecutor says she was upbeat about her appointment to role

Article:

IT'S not clear how long the head of the International Criminal Court, Ms Fatou Bensouda, will be in hospital. Yesterday, after several days of hospitalisation, Ms Bensouda flew into Dublin for a special meeting with a group of Irish officials to discuss her upcoming mandate. Ms Bensouda is due to start her new role on 1 November, just over two years after her last one.

The following is a news article from The Sunday Times (thetimes.com.au).

The former prosecutor to the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, Ms Fatou Bensouda has been in hospital since 24 August.

The Independent has been told that Ms Bensouda's condition had deteriorated dramatically after returning from a trip to Belgrade.

She was discharged from hospital yesterday afternoon. A source said she had been discharged in the early hours of the morning on Friday and had flown to Dublin from a private hospital in Belgrade for her appointment at the Irish embassy.

"Her condition had deteriorated dramatically since she arrived in Dublin last night," an Irish official said.

"She is now on a drip and in a stable condition at the National Maternity Hospital. Her condition is stable."

A source said Ms Bensouda had been flown from Belgrade after suffering a "major stroke" on her return from the trip and doctors were still assessing her condition. Ms Bensouda's medical records showed she had suffered a stroke while visiting Yugoslavia.

The source said she was "extremely upbeat" about her appointment and was "not worried". Ms Bensouda was appointed by the UN Human Rights Council in September.

A spokesman for the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in The Hague said: "The head of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, Ms Fatou Bensouda, has been admitted to hospital and will be transferred for further treatment in the coming days."

The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) is a special court established by the UN in the Hague in 1998 to try crimes committed during the former Yugoslavia's 1992-95 war for independence and then, during the NATO military occupation of the former Yugoslavia from 1999 to 2003, crimes committed during the war against Yugoslavia's own people.

In 1999 the ICC's first justice of the peace was appointed. She was succeeded in that role in 2001 by Judge Juan Dato' Soliman.

Italian officials have confirmed that the death toll from the deadly Coronavirus outbreak in the country has reached more than 400 people.

The virus, which has infected at least 200 people in Sicily, has spread to more than two dozen other parts of the country, including the southern port of Naples, where a health scare last weekend claimed the lives of eight people.

Last Saturday, health officials warned that the country would not be free of the disease until next summer. However, earlier this week, the country's chief health official admitted that the outbreak has only been able to expand because of the lack of surveillance.

"It is not only that there are so many people who are infected, but also because the number of people who are infected is not increasing," Giancarlo Paolini told a press conference.

"A lot of people were exposed to people infected with this virus while they were working or went to school," he added.

In recent days, some 40 people have been diagnosed with the virus and 10 have died, according to local authorities. The virus affects people between the ages of 5 and 80, but can affect children as young as three or teenagers. It has a similar symptoms to the highly-fatal dengue virus, which kills up to 40% of those infected.

In all cases, the virus is fatal within 21 days.

Read more

Some have called on Italy's Prime Minister Matteo Renzi to resign after a health scare last weekend which claimed the lives of eight people.

The Italian minister said on Friday that the country will not be free of the Coronavirus until next summer, while the country's chief health official admitted that the outbreak has only been able to expand because of the lack of surveillance.

A spokesman for the Ministry of Health told the Italian Press Agency (itap) on Monday that the number of confirmed cases of the virus had risen to 400.

"We cannot deny that the situation is dire, given that we have not had a serious outbreak in Italy in the last 60 years," Giovanni Calenda said.

"In the coming days and weeks there will be a very, very high number of new cases reported. The situation is very grave," he added.

The Italian Health Ministry will soon hold a meeting with the Italian President Giorgio Napolitano. According to reports, the Italian leader will call on the authorities to speed up the preparation for the outbreak.

While many Italian health officials have been quick to call for the resignation of Renzi, others have called for his resignation in the hope that he will try to resolve the situation on his own.
headline: Coronavirus: Disaster in Italy as death toll surpasses China’s, where the Covid-19 virus was first detected

Posted: Fri, 25 Jul 2016 07:59:42 +0000

"Supermacs boss John Lyons is demanding an increase in wages for Irish beef farmers in the region as he claims the current system of payments to beef farmers is unfair and not being adequately reflected in the market," a statement from the Supermacs boss said.

"The Irish beef sector is extremely vulnerable to an increase in commodity prices and I'm calling on the Government to support these important farmers in their campaign for fair market prices."

Mr Lyons is calling for the Irish government to increase its contribution to the supermacs fund from the current 1% of gross sales.

This is in stark contrast to the 1.5% currently paid out to Irish farmers, which is well below the 3% currently paid to all other Irish industries.

Mr Lyons wants the Irish government to match the UK's contributions as the rest of the European Union (EU) is not contributing sufficient to the fund.

"Irish farmers are paid less than €1 for every £1 they sell in the market. This does not reflect the reality of what Irish beef farmers are actually making and that is a very low cost product," he said.

"Supermacs have been lobbying heavily for a fair contribution to the fund, and it is time we did, so that we can ensure our farmers are paid more for the hard work they do."

Mr Lyons said he would be looking at all options to ensure the supermacs fund meets its full potential and that the fund is sustainable for the future.

"We are doing everything we can to raise the contribution from the current 1% of gross sales and the other markets we're in, and it's my hope that this can be achieved," he said.

The Irish beef industry is highly sensitive to the impact of competition and increased costs. We need the Government to support the continued development of our industry to ensure the future is well worth living in.

Irish Beef Industry Chairman David O'Reilly said: "Supermacs are the only part of the market that actually pays them for their performance. There are many other Irish farmers who work hard, and are getting paid too little.

"With Supermacs funding being cut and the other markets being starved of funds, the entire industry is in an unprecedented situation. Supermacs are the only market that actually pays them the cost of doing business, and it is unacceptable that farmers are not paid for the hard work they do."
headline: Supermacs boss says Irish beef farmers are not being paid enough

To ensure there is a constant supply of floor space in rooms, the Irish Housing Executive in the year 2011 released a national strategy, 'How to Ensure Floor Space in Rooms.'

The strategy was developed following the experience of the Housing Executive in Dublin, in particular that the supply of floor space was not maintained for the duration of the period of the Strategy.

The Strategy sets out a framework to help ensure that the needs of individuals and businesses are met, and ensure that demand for floor space is maintained for the duration of the Strategy.

The Strategy sets out two key outcomes for the provision of floor space:

1) The supply of floor space in rooms and the supply of floor space in businesses is improved.

2) The demand for floor space is maintained.

1) The supply of floor space in rooms is improved.

According to the strategy, the need for floor space can be met by:

- Increasing the number of individuals and businesses that qualify for rent allowance,

- Creating more social housing accommodation,

- Creating more social housing accommodation in multi-unit homes and

- Providing additional and better quality floor space for businesses.

In 2011, the Irish Housing Executive undertook the following:

To improve the efficiency of the supply of floor space.

To encourage the use of efficient and proven materials and equipment in the preparation of floor space in rooms and in business premises.

To create a supply of floor space in rooms.

To improve the efficiency of the supply of floor space for homes and businesses.

In the year 2011, the Irish Housing Executive commissioned a survey of the availability of floor space in rooms.

In October 2011, the survey was completed by the Irish Housing Executive in the Dublin region. The results of the survey were:

• There were an estimated 1,500,000 square feet of floor space available for residential purposes in rooms, of which 2,000,000 square feet are vacant.

• The vacancy rate was 26% and the average age of the rooms was 33 years and 2 months.

• The supply of floor space in rooms was 26% and the supply of floor space for business premises was 38%.

• The vacancy rate was 34% and the average age of the rooms was 31 years and 4 months.

• The supply of floor space for homes and businesses was 35% and 43% respectively.

• There was a shortage of floor space in the Dublin region with the supply of floor space in homes falling from 21,000 to 17,000 square feet between 2006 and 2011.

• The supply of floor space in shops and the supply of floor space in business premises are affected by the supply of vacant rooms and the supply of vacant shops and the supply of vacant businesses.

The Irish Housing Executive will continue to be involved in the planning and development of floor space in rooms in the Dublin region.

2) The demand for floor space is maintained.

The strategy also set out the following outcomes:

• The demand for floor space in rooms and the supply of floor space in businesses are maintained.

• The demand for floor space in homes and the supply of floor space in business premises are maintained.

• The demand for floor space in shops and the supply of floor space in business premises are maintained.

Spain's head of the National Health Service has said that unvaccinated children can enter the country for holidays for the first time since 2000, after a report found that up to 500 children had been given the "unnecessary" vaccinations in the past decade.

Dr Rafael Marín, head of the National Health Service, said the new policy would only affect children who were unable to attend schools due to illness.

He said there had been a "huge problem" with unvaccinated children entering the country.

The new policy, which was approved by the health minister, follows a report by the health service's inspector general in Spain that found that up to 500 children have been given the "unnecessary" vaccinations.

Dr Marín said it was up to individual health authorities to decide if children could go to holidays.

A spokesperson for the Health Service, which oversees the country's health service, said the new policy would apply to "children who cannot attend school because of their illness".

The spokesperson said: "There was no specific request or guideline that these children must receive immunisations. It is up to individual health authorities to determine if children can come to the holidays."

Spain has seen a massive increase in the numbers of unvaccinated children since 1998, when the country introduced a mandatory vaccination programme for school children.

It is the first time the government has imposed a blanket ban on vaccinations in a public place, in this case on an island in the west of the country.

An outbreak of measles among children in the region last year was blamed on the outbreak of the highly infectious disease.

The outbreak is thought to have involved three children who did not receive the vaccination for measles, mumps and rubella, which has been blamed for several deaths in Spain in recent years.

Dr Marín said in a statement: "For two years we have had a huge problem with unvaccinated children entering the country.

"I am going to propose that at the moment when they enter the country, children are vaccinated against measles, mumps and rubella.

"This is also a measure to prevent them from coming back to the country again.

"For some of them, the treatment will be similar to what is used for healthy children, so they can return to school."

He added that the new measure would apply to children who were unable to attend schools because of illness.

Some local health authorities have already been asked to implement the measure as part of a national plan to combat the spread of the infectious disease.

There have been warnings from health experts and parents that a vaccination ban could lead to a resurgence of the disease in Spain, which is already reeling from a measles outbreak that caused at least 25 deaths in the past two years.

Dr Marín said: "It was necessary to ban the vaccination, but it is also essential for people to understand the consequences.

"People who do not have the vaccination are going to be at risk and that is a risk for the country."

More than 10,000 children have been diagnosed in Spain with measles in the past two years, many of them under the age of 12.

Many of the cases have been linked to outbreaks in the Canary Islands and in the southern province of Galicia.
headline: Finally a bit of sanity returns to Spain as unvaccinated can now enter the country for holidays

By John Murphy

Irish national news site The Liberal have published a lengthy story today on a case where the prosecution has tried to keep a teenager out of prison for a €16,000 Snapchat scam.

The article is the best summary of the story available on the internet and a little bit more than what the newspapers themselves are publishing. It seems that the teenager in question has been prosecuted for selling his "stolen" camera to a local person in the hope that he would sell it to a member of the public.

The teen has been caught by police as he was attempting to sell the camera, in order for him to make a profit off the sale of the camera, to a new owner. But while the camera was being sold to a new owner, it turned out that the device was not the product of a genuine digital theft in itself, but that it was the work of a hacker.

In particular, the hacker had managed to steal the camera's address data which included his home address. He did this by using a program called "FindMyDevice" which is part of iOS.

The program allows someone to find out all sorts of personal information about a device, from its manufacturer to its unique serial number. This is usually done so that it is possible to contact the owner and demand a refund.

The hacker, being an amateur, managed to trick the police officer in question into believing that he wanted to speak with the hacker for a chat. While this is clearly an attempt to obtain a chat log to assist in his own prosecution, it turns out that the conversation did not take place, and so the investigation has now been handed to the US Marshals service (USMS).

The USMS have been given the task of determining whether there is enough evidence to prove a case.

The story of the €16,000 scam is still a matter of interest to the Irish media. We have had reports that it has been going on for almost a year. We have also been told that in addition to the jail time, the teenager has also been put on a strict supervision order which will be imposed for a period of nine months.

The story of the case is now more than a bit of a dark cloud hanging over the Irish student's head.

Further Reading

We have a link to a story in the Irish Independent on the story of the teenager who was found guilty by a criminal court in Ireland after selling a smartphone to a young person in the hope of finding a job, in particular to a young woman who was employed in a restaurant.

The story is in Irish, but it is published in The Irish Independent as "Irish man sentenced to jail for selling stolen iPhone in selfie scam".

Our original story is here.

A Department of Education (DoE) directive has banned the use of electric vehicles on Ireland's roads after the European Commission declared them to be a danger to public health, safety and road safety.

The directive, dated September 20, 2016, was issued by the European Commission, with a decision that it is not appropriate to allow electric cars on roadways with the sound emitted by the vehicles.

The directive states:

"Electric vehicles are not allowed on roads with the sound emitted from their motors and generators."

As a result, electric vehicles will be prohibited from being used on roads throughout the entire country, except for those areas where exemptions are provided.

The directive states that the ban will remain in place until 1 June, 2017, with a period of three months for each year of the ban to be implemented.

It then says:

"The prohibition shall continue until the end of the three-month period beginning on the day following the date on which the directive is notified."

However, DoE Minister for Communications Pat Rabbitte said the directive does not mean an end to electric vehicle use on roads.

He said the directive "simply sets an end date for the use of electric vehicles on roads in Ireland, which is three months from the date that the directive was issued. We will continue to monitor the situation and monitor how the ban is implemented in the various areas and in accordance with the EU rules."

A spokesperson for the Department of Transport said the directive did not mean that the ban would be withdrawn immediately, and said the Department's transport departments were still in discussion on whether to continue with electric vehicles on roads.

In October last year, Minister Rabbitte said there would be a three month period for the prohibition to be implemented but at the time he did not rule out that electric vehicles would be allowed to be used in areas that were exempted.

The ban follows on from the commission's decision to classify electric vehicles as a threat to public health, safety and road safety. The EC was prompted to write the directive after a study by its Office for the Protection of the Environment (OPE) concluded that electric vehicles emit noise similar to that from a diesel engine at lower speeds.

Electric vehicles have been banned in the UK and Ireland since October 2016. The European Commission has also imposed stricter emissions tests on the vehicles.

Electric vehicles are not allowed on roads in the UK as a result of the European directive.

The European Commission has also adopted a list of criteria for classifying electric vehicles as a risk to public health, safety and road safety. The criteria include sound level measurements, vehicle operation characteristics and vehicle emissions data.

Electric vehicles also need to meet a minimum amount of fuel economy when compared with petrol-powered cars, and they also must have a higher energy efficiency than the average diesel vehicle.

However, the commission found that electric vehicles emit noise comparable to that from a diesel engine and that a review of the current EU rules into electric vehicles would be necessary.

The EC said that the use of electric vehicles could pose a risk to road safety and public health.

"As a result, the EU Commission considers that the use of electric vehicles on roads with the sound emitted from their motors and generators is not appropriate in the European Union," it stated.
headline: Electric vehicles to be fitted with noise emitting devices from today onwards

Mr McGuinness, who has not ruled out a future return to politics, made the comments as he was speaking at a forum hosted by the Irish Centre for Political Studies at the University of Limerick on Wednesday.

Mr McGuinness said Mr Collins and Mr Adams, whose candidacies are underlined by a poll indicating Mr Adams may have made significant gains in the last month, could "bring people together" if they were able to do so as part of a coalition.

He claimed that if they did so, the resulting coalition would be "more stable and effective than any other coalition we have seen before".

Mr McGuinness said it was "not a question of if", but when Mr Collins and Mr Adams would be in a position to form a coalition.

He said the issue of coalition had come to the fore as a result of the "very clear divide within the two main parties".

Mr McGuinness added: "It is not in any way a question of whether they [Gerry Adams and Michael Collins] would be able to bring people together or not.

"It is more an issue of how they will bring people together and how stable and effective they can be in making the sort of coalition that would bring the best of all worlds."

The former Irish ambassador to the US, who has served in a number of positions with the Irish State over the years, said that the party in government "cannot have a leader who seems to have no understanding" of the country and that the leadership would have to be "more flexible" in its dealings.

Mr McGuinness said the Green Party had not been seen as an option for the presidency as it was perceived to be a threat to the existing arrangement between Fine Gael and Fianna Fail.

The Green Party's current leader, Senator Patrick Kavanagh, is expected to be part of a coalition, he said.

Speaking on the issues surrounding the current government, Mr McGuinness said: "One of the issues you've had to deal with recently is the possibility of the Green Party being the dominant force in Irish politics – whether that is going to be because we are the political force or because we are not."

Mr McGuinness also said that while he was personally committed to supporting a referendum on the issue of marriage equality, he recognised that the "only way to guarantee equal marriage in Ireland" would be if a majority of people in Ireland supported a vote.

He said that as a result of the election of the new Irish president, he was now "open to the possibility of a partnership" between Sinn Féin and the Greens.

Mr McGuinness said his views on gay marriage were "in line with those of Sinn Féin and those of many others" but that he hoped to see a resolution in the referendum.

"I am open to the possibility of a partnership with the Green Party. We will see how the two parties come together.

She told Independent.ie: "We are concerned that this is a very premature step, that the ban will go ahead and that people with epilepsy will be unable to use this technology because of this.

"We have concerns that people with epilepsy will be affected and may not be able to use it."

Ms O'Neill said the current device cost €60, but that it would be up to the manufacturer, a new company called TikTok, to change it to make it less expensive.

"It was a very expensive, non-invasive, non-invasive device," she said.

"It should not be used for this, as we don't know what this technology is going to do to people's health."

"It is a medical device that is used to treat epilepsy," she said.

"It was the only use of this technology that we could find from the data that we had."
