McCafferty wrote that FDLE has been communicating with the federal agency and with the department's design engineers to determine whether any safety issues exist related to the collapse.

As this latest incident happened last month, Tallahassee Mayor Andrew Gillum is expected to announce a citywide safety improvement program that includes a $150 million upgrade to the city's fire apparatus. He also is expected to announce that Tallahassee is moving forward with the $150 million upgrade of Tallahassee's water and sewer system.
headline: Miami tower block collapse: Engineers demolish the remains of the Champlain Tower South block

Ireland's youth unemployment rate is at its highest level for more than 20 years, with just under 40pc of the unemployed (aged 18-24) in some of the most deprived areas.

The most deprived areas in Ireland are Kilkenny in County Cork and Tipperary in County Mayo.

Irish youth unemployment is at its highest level for more than 20 years and the Irish government is on course to make no effort to reduce it, according to the latest census.

The most deprived areas in Ireland are Kilkenny in County Cork and Tipperary in County Mayo.

The census found that just over half (56pc) of the unemployed in the area were unemployed by the time they completed the census.

While just over one in five (22pc) of the unemployed were unemployed for more than a year in the most deprived areas, just 10pc of the unemployed in the most affluent areas were unemployed for more than a year.

It comes just three years after the Irish government, then led by Enda Kenny, began to make an effort to make it easier to get into the workforce.

While the unemployment rate for young people is still at its highest level since the 1960s, it is expected to fall in the coming years, according to the census.

The latest figures showed that while the jobless rate for 17-24 year-olds stood at 24pc, it was down from 28pc a year ago.

Almost half (47pc) of the unemployed were aged between 25 and 34, the latest figures show.

"We are all a little bit concerned as to what might be going on," said Dermot O'Leary, a member of the National Youth Employment Council.

"The youth unemployment figures are not good and it is a concern.

"It is a huge problem and the Government needs to make sure that they do something about it."

Last week, it was revealed that the young people who take up a part-time job in order to get into a job as a trainee carpenter would only be allowed to leave the job at the end of a two-year contract.

"We don't know what is going to happen. We know that we are experiencing a very high level of youth unemployment," said Dermot O'Leary.

"We don't know what is going to happen. We know that we are experiencing a very high level of youth unemployment."

The government has been under pressure to show it is making an effort to reduce youth unemployment, since a number of studies have shown that while the number of young people out of work is on the decrease, the levels of youth unemployment remain high.

The statistics come as Taoiseach Enda Kenny and Minister of State for Employment Michael Healy-Rae signalled this week that a new employment guarantee is being considered.

The Minister, who has called on young people to be in employment, said that the government was "in touch with youth".

Mr Healy-Rae was responding to the findings of a report by the National Youth Employment Council which found that between 2010 and 2014, there was an increase in the number of young people out of work, but a decrease in the number of young people in employment.
headline: Gone for good? Ireland’s youth exodus accelerates as record numbers emigrated in 2025 as homeownership remains a pipe dream

text:
36 people have lost their lives as a result of a train crash in Greece with many more injured.

A driver lost control of the train at the railway station in Piraeus after the derailment at around 4.30pm. Witnesses say there was a loud explosion as the train derailed, but the full extent of the tragedy is not yet clear.

Six people are dead and 20 are injured according to reports. Emergency services are working hard to treat the injured. The injured are being taken to hospitals in the town of Vratsa.

According to preliminary reports, the train derailed as it was turning left from the western edge of the town on to the main road from the city.

The train was carrying around 40 passengers.

Greece's Transport Minister Zografos Fotakis told state television: "At around 4.30pm, the train derailed. At the moment, no one is in a position to give more details.

"We don't know if there are fatalities, but it's a tragedy of the worst kind."

The crash was caused by the driver apparently leaving the tracks, which are closed to traffic, Fotakis said.

A rescue helicopter has been sent to the scene to support the search and recovery efforts.

The accident happened at around 4.30pm as the train was travelling towards the outskirts of the capital Athens.

A spokesman for the police said the driver did not obey the conditions of the road and that he was not able to control the train, according to Agence France-Presse.

The crash happened near the town of Vratsa, 80km (50 miles) from the city centre, and close to the city's railway station, which is connected to the main road that leads to the city from the south.

The crash happened after a driver left the tracks at the Piraeus railway station and the train travelled towards the city, according to witnesses.

An initial police statement said that 37 passengers were on board the train. The exact number of people on board has not yet been confirmed, though one person died in the incident.

The crash happened in a country where some of the country's deadliest road accidents and accidents have occurred in recent years.

On 19 March 2015, a man lost his life when a train travelling from the northern port of Piraeus to Athens derailed near Vratsa. Five people were injured.

The same year, a driver lost control of a train in the southern city of Thessaloniki and crashed into a bridge.

There has been a recent spate of derailments in Greece, including an incident in November 2015 which resulted in four deaths and dozens of injuries.

Greece has seen high levels of the number of fatal road accidents in recent years, according to statistics released by the national statistics office.

A total of 584 people have been killed in road accidents in Greece in 2015, according to the statistics office.
headline: No fewer than 36 people dead following train collision in Greece

Irish doctors, whose numbers have dwindled in recent years, are now taking on the highest number of patients in Britain, a new report has said.

Headline: Dr Glynn: Ireland is in a precarious position as R number is between 1.2 and 1.8

Article:

The number of patients seen by Irish doctors has slumped by over one-third in five years as a result of underfunding, says a report by the Royal College of General Practitioners (RCGP).

Headline: Dr Glynn says Ireland is in a precarious position as R number is between 1.2 and 1.8

Article:

Rural Ireland is also becoming more disadvantaged than urban areas, according to a report by the College of General Practitioners (CGP), which says the number of residents in rural areas in Ireland has increased by one-third since 2004.

Headline: Dr Glynn: Rural Ireland is also becoming more disadvantaged than urban areas

Article:

One of the most worrying developments, according to the report, is the decline in general practices in rural areas. This is due to a rise in non-practitioners seeking care in the health service, as well as a reduction in the number of specialists.

Headline: Dr Glynn says Ireland is in a precarious position as R number is between 1.2 and 1.8

Article:

The study, published on Monday, found that there are a record number of GP practices in rural Ireland but the number of specialists has fallen by a quarter.

Headline: Dr Glynn says Ireland is in a precarious position as R number is between 1.2 and 1.8

Article:

The report suggests that the number of specialist GPs will go up again in the next few years as more practice spaces are created in rural areas.

Headline: Dr Glynn says Ireland is in a precarious position as R number is between 1.2 and 1.8

Article:

The report was commissioned by the RCSI, the Association of Specialists in Ireland (ASI). It found that over the next decade Ireland will have to take on a total of 4.2 GP practices, compared with 3.5 currently.

Headline: Dr Glynn says Ireland is in a precarious position as R number is between 1.2 and 1.8

Article:

Dr Glynn said: "The report highlights the critical need to increase numbers of general practitioners so that they can meet the ever increasing demand for primary health care."

Headline: Dr Glynn says Ireland is in a precarious position as R number is between 1.2 and 1.8

Article:

The report also suggests that as the rate of patients who are seen by general practitioners in rural areas continues to decline, so will the number of specialists who will be needed to provide the service.

text:
Today, a massive protest is planned against the East Wall, which will see the removal of thousands of migrants from the area.

The protest will take place at 10am at the Ballsbridge Park and Ride. This will be the largest protest of its kind to take place in the city this year.

On Wednesday 12th August, around 2,000 people marched across the city to a local pub. The group began the march by shouting anti-immigrant slogans, which were echoed by a group of around 30 people carrying banners reading 'Stop the East Wall'.

Around two dozen people attempted to enter the pub and were met by police.

The protest then moved to the Ballbridge Park and Ride, where there were several arrests.

A report from The Times (via theliberal.ie) quotes an anti-migrant protester as saying that the "mass removal of migrants from the East Wall is a bad outcome for people of East London and the wider area."

As the headline points out, the anti-migrant protest is designed to "equal the score" with affluent communities. The demonstration's organisers say that the area's population is "unfit to live here" and that the "community in East London is not worthy of being treated as a community. These people do not respect the human rights of others and, instead, seek to impose their culture and their needs on others."

The report notes that "the East Wall is a very well regarded area which is recognised and respected in the area." But it also notes that it is "one of the largest communities in East London".

On the same day, around 1000 people demonstrated at Finsbury Park to "resist the Muslim ban", according to The Sun. The protest, which was organised by the Stop the Mosque Action group, began peacefully but quickly turned violent, according to the report.

A local newspaper, The Sun, reports that the protest was attended by thousands of protesters from across the country and "some from as far away as New York, Philadelphia and Los Angeles".

"The protest started peacefully but quickly turned violent with the mob setting fire to cars, destroying a police car and attacking police officers."

The Sun adds that "The mob then descended upon the area to attack any Muslims they saw."

The Sun reports that "Police officers and stewards were pelted with bottles and bricks by a hostile crowd".

It notes that "one cop was left with serious injuries to his head and neck, he was taken to hospital."

As well as Finsbury Park, around 1,000 protesters gathered in nearby London Bridge in solidarity with the refugees.

The Guardian reported that "The Metropolitan Police said it was assisting the authorities at Finsbury Park to deal with the disorder".

In response to the mass protests, the Home Office announced that asylum seekers would be detained in the borough "for the duration of their stay at the detention centre".

Speaking at a press conference today, Home Secretary Amber Rudd announced that new guidance would be issued "to ensure that the protection of the asylum seekers and migrants is not at risk".
headline: Today’s the day! Huge anti-migrant protest to take place in Ballsbridge today for #EastWall to “equal the score” with affluent communities

The Irish Freedom Party, an Irish political party founded in 2010, today launched a campaign in the European Parliament to oppose the practice of requiring medical vaccination for all non-EU staff and visitors and to put an end to the current situation whereby EU staff who have a measles or mumps vaccine but have not undergone an 'Covid-19' vaccination certificate are entitled to free entry into the EU without a problem.

In the wake of the announcement by the European Parliament to allow vaccines for mumps and measles to be offered in school classes without a certificate, the Irish Freedom Party is calling on European authorities to introduce a 'one-size-fits-all' standard that is incompatible with Ireland's laws.

The Irish Freedom Party claims that the current system is 'too complicated' and 'has led to unqualified children being offered immunisation when there is no medical need for it'.

The party also wants the EU to take measures to make it 'more sensible for the EU to require a medical certificate' rather than require parental consent for inoculations against diseases.

The Irish Freedom Party believes that vaccines are 'harmful and unnecessary', and that 'medical intervention' is unnecessary.
headline: Leader of Irish Freedom Party spearheads campaign in EU Parliament to oppose MEPs, staff and visitors having to produce a Covid-19 vaccination certificate

The Queen's Award for Distinguished Public Service has been presented to two people whose work has made them iconic and influential in Ireland.

The Oireachtas has awarded the Order of Merit to U2 lead singer Bono and Mary Robinson, who has spearheaded the campaign for a referendum on marriage equality in Ireland.

The Order is an honour granted by the Queen to individuals who have demonstrated outstanding public service in their field and who have made significant contributions to the public good.

The Queen will award the award to Mr Bono and Ms Robinson at a ceremony in Dublin on Saturday (July 9).

The Queen and the President of the Republic have accepted the Award and it will be presented by the President in Dublin.

Both awards were presented by the President in June.

Bono, a former Bono Foundation board member who founded the charity in 1991, has been a champion for gender equality and in March, he will become the first person to be made a Master of the Order of Merit in the same year.

The singer was the subject of a landmark landmark ruling by the Supreme Court of Ireland that said gay people could marry.

Ireland's most famous singer and political icon has campaigned against same-sex marriage for the last 25 years.

Mr Bono's long-term partner is his partner of 17 years, actress Bono's partner and daughter Tessa is also married to Mr Bono.

'A remarkable achievement'

Speaking during the ceremony, Ms Robinson said she had been "delighted" by the Queen's award and said she was honoured to have been awarded the award.

"I feel incredibly grateful," she said. "It is an honour and privilege to be associated with a group of people who have set such an example for equality. It has been a remarkable achievement for me to be associated with them.

"When I think of Irish people I think of a lot of the hard-working and courageous people who work to ensure that our communities are at the forefront of all that we do. They have achieved such an incredible achievement in terms of their work and I think that is really wonderful."

Ms Robinson and Mr Bono have been together for the last seven years after meeting in the 1980s through a mutual friend.

He also has a daughter from a previous relationship.

Mr Bono, who rose to fame as the lead singer of Bono & Friends and now runs a charity to help disadvantaged children, was born in West Belfast.

The couple married in 1980 and have two daughters.

Their two-year-old daughter, Tessa, lives in London.

Mr Bono was awarded the honour after winning the European Union's Sakharov Prize for Peace in 2015.

The award was given by the president of the European Council Donald Tusk on behalf of the European Parliament, where Mr Bono is vice-president.

In June, Ms Robinson announced that she was to hold a referendum on a referendum on marriage equality.
headline: Two has-beens? Mary Robinson and U2 are being awarded European Order of Merit

THE DEAL has finally been announced and the EU has accepted the British withdrawal treaty, leaving the British government at last able to give a clear signal to its citizens in other European countries.

"The Prime Minister said it was 'difficult to see how we can negotiate with ourselves' while the EU confirmed the agreement was signed by Prime Minister Theresa May."

EU negotiators gave the British a clear indication that there is no longer a need for Article 50, the formal mechanism for leaving the EU and the UK will not need a special legislative process of exit.

The British government had insisted that Article 50 was still required to trigger the divorce process, but EU negotiators said the agreement makes no distinction between Britain leaving on Article 50 or withdrawing after the end of this two year transition period.

This agreement means Britain will leave the EU on January 31, 2020, on the day after the date when the negotiations with the EU officially end.

The Prime Minister announced the agreement at 5pm last night and said:

"The terms of the United Kingdom's withdrawal from the European Union are clear.

"The British people voted to leave the EU and we are delivering on our commitments.

"Today we have secured a deal for Britain to leave the European Union.

"For Britain, the EU is an immense economic, social and cultural strength and an important part of our national identity.

"The agreement we have reached today is the outcome of months of hard work and we look forward to a strong and ambitious partnership with our European partners moving forward."

It is estimated that some 800,000 EU citizens currently living in the UK will be able to apply to leave the EU on January 31, 2020.
headline: Brexit Withdrawal Agreement breezes through Parliament, meaning Britain will likely leave the EU for good on January 31, 2020

The Fine Gael party has been ordered to pay €50,000 in damages to the man who accused them of a 'dirty game' at the 2011 general election when they were in opposition.

Former Fianna Fail leader Eamonn McCann says the party's 'wholly inappropriate conduct' contributed to his eventual loss of the party leadership to Mr Varadkar.

Mr McCann said he was vindicated in his complaint by the High Court in Dublin last week, which ordered the party to pay him €50,000 in damages for the incident, on the grounds of reputational damage.

Mr McCann said the allegations made during the 2011 election were 'not only extremely serious, but extremely damaging' and could have led to the party's collapse in the general election.

He said he had been subjected to an unprecedented campaign of 'disgraceful, humiliating and degrading' behaviour by party staff during the campaign. He said he had suffered 'a campaign of intimidation' and 'sabotage'.

Mr McCann told the court he was a party member during the 2011 election campaign and had been involved in the decision to suspend the Fine Gael leadership of the party.

He said he had been asked to vote for one of the two candidates and was asked to vote against another of the candidates, with his name never disclosed. He said he was then told by party staff members to remove his ID card and sign a blank piece of paper which stated that he had been suspended as a candidate for the party. He said the staff members were told by party officers that he was a member of the party and had to abide by party rules.

Mr McCann said he was then asked to sign a document which he found to be unfair to him. He said he was then forced to sign a document which he was asked to sign which he believed was untrue and had not been signed by him. He said he was then told that Mr Varadkar had the power to suspend him.

Mr McCann said he was then told he would be barred from holding office in the party. He said he was also told that he was under investigation by gardaí.

Mr McCann said he had never been part of any illegal activity and said he had nothing to hide.

The suit was filed by Mr McCann in 2011, but his case was eventually dropped by the High Court due to an application from Mr Varadkar's legal team that the lawsuit could damage Mr Varadkar's reputation as the Fine Gael leader.

The suit, launched in the courts in May 2011, alleged that a campaign of 'disgraceful, humiliating and degrading' behaviour was carried out on Mr McCann's behalf by party officers during the campaign.

Mr McCann said the party breached its rules and regulations and that it had a duty to protect its members and supporters.
headline: Taoiseach says Bailey case did cause reputational damage to the Fine Gael party

text:
The World Health Organization has warned that the number of people infected with the virus in South-east Asia has more than doubled to 2m, according to the latest figures.

The WHO said the figure represents the majority of new infections that have been reported globally in 2014.

As of 11 June the WHO reported to WHO headquarters in Geneva the number of infections in South-east Asia has reached 2m, with nearly 120,000 deaths as a result.

"These numbers are alarming and highlight the urgent need to halt transmission of the highly pathogenic virus," WHO Director-General Margaret Chan said in a statement.

"South-east Asia is the primary centre of transmission for the virus and we strongly urge countries to work together to control the outbreak."

The virus has been detected in Pakistan, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Nepal since it first emerged in India in March 2011.

The latest figures show that Pakistan accounted for 58% of all cases, followed by Afghanistan (36%), Sri Lanka (10%), Thailand (6%) and India (2%).

One in four (24%) of cases in Pakistan was in children under the age of five, according to the WHO.

South Asia is the major region for the transmission of the virus but some countries, including India and Nigeria, are also thought to be at risk.

The WHO said many countries – including Pakistan, Afghanistan and the Philippines – have inadequate surveillance and response systems to detect and manage outbreaks.

More than half the infections were among patients with very high-risk conditions, including pregnant women.

The virus causes severe vomiting, diarrhoea, pneumonia, respiratory failure and even death.

The most common symptoms are bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever and vomiting.

"The virus has a very high mortality rate and is difficult to treat if it spreads to other areas," Dr Marie-Paule Kieny, director general of the WHO, said in a statement.

"We urge all countries to work together to control the outbreak."

Last month the WHO announced that the World Bank had agreed to a $1.9m loan to fund a health crisis management initiative for the region.

The aim is to increase access to health care and reduce the risk of further outbreaks.

The region is a critical source of funding for the bulk of WHO programmes in Africa and Asia, and has a $600m budget earmarked to tackle the outbreak.

There has been a dramatic rise in deaths as well, with the disease often spreading in a matter of hours.
headline: Coronavirus: Global number of infections reaches 2m, with over 120,000 deaths so far

Green party TDs Roderic O'Gorman and Kevin 'Kev' O'Higgins have written to the Department of the Environment in an apparent warning to voters about independents who could push the Government into a "cliff edge" exit from the EU.

"These are desperate times and the Government should be in a position to make its position very clear," said O'Gorman, who was among more than 50 TDs, including Fianna Fáil's Brian Cowen, who submitted their own letter to Minister for the Environment Alan Kelly.

"At present it seems certain that the Government will not be able to secure a majority in the next Dáil and so it is vital that a clear and unequivocal position is taken immediately on the future direction of Ireland within the EU.

"At present the Government seems to be in a position to maintain its current arrangements, with a very narrow majority in the Dáil, if it is prepared to enter into a transitional period to secure a majority."

His letter says that under the terms of the Lisbon Treaty the Government is required to seek the endorsement of the European Council (which is currently meeting) on the direction it wants to take in Ireland.

"In the event of a vote of the European Council rejecting a proposed Government position, the Government should, under EU rules, be entitled to invoke Article 44 of the Treaty, which provides for the appointment of the European Commission's 'Special Representative' to negotiate a new government in Ireland," he said.

"Such an appointment would be subject to the approval of the European Council and to a ratification by the European Parliament."

O'Gorman said he was "appalled" by the suggestion that independents, or even people who were not members of the Dáil, could help the Government achieve a majority.

"It seems very strange and not at all plausible, to me at least," he said. "These are desperate times and the Government should be in a position to make its position very clear.

"We are dealing with a Government, for the first time in decades, that is not in a position to secure a majority in the next Dáil."

O'Gorman said he would "rather see a government of the people, by the people, for the people".

He added: "This would be a government of the people, by the people for the people, and not a government of the parties or of the independents."

O'Gorman said the Department of the Environment should be asked "to make public in their own words the position that is under discussion and to make a public statement of that position".

He said he would be "extremely surprised" if the Government did not make its position clear soon.

"I am calling on the Department of the Environment to make a statement that clearly says that no government can be in a position to secure a majority and that the only way to ensure the stability of the country is to accept the EU referendum result."

The Irish Independent contacted the Department of the Environment for comment.
headline: Please don’t do it! Green’s Roderic O’Gorman warns public against independents propping up coalition

text:
It is time for a much more robust, comprehensive and accurate study on the impact of online gaming. In order to do this the National Statistics Office (NOS) must be allowed to conduct a systematic study of the effect of online gaming in the Irish economy.

The NOS have been very open about their plan to carry out such an analysis. Unfortunately they have not yet published the results of their study so we don't know the actual impact of online gambling.

The following is the headline of the article:

Online Gaming in Ireland is a $100 billion industry, says new report

Summary

Online gaming was worth €5.9 billion in 2005. The average gambling experience has been estimated to last 2.4 hours.

Since January 2006 there has been a 2.2% increase in the gambling turnover for online operators (excluding sportsbook operators). This is equivalent to €8.7 billion. This is an increase of €5 billion in just over 4 years.

These figures include money earned from online gambling, the sale of goods and services (including goods and services associated with the playing of slot machines), sponsorship and advertising and sales tax.

The growth in online gambling revenue in the past year (2005) is the highest since the introduction of the online gambling sector in 2006.

Source: National Statistics Office, The Irish Gamblers' Association, The Irish Gamblers Association, the Irish Gaming Industry Group

Analysis: The impact of online casinos on the Irish economy

The Irish gamblers' association is the largest of its kind in the world, representing over 5,000 members across the country. Its report "Casino Games on the Internet" has been commissioned by the Department of Finance (DoF) to examine the impact of online gaming on the Irish economy.

The report provides a comprehensive overview of the industry and its impact on the Irish economy. The author of the report is Brian Lynch, who is also the chairperson of the NOS. He is a former Director of the DoF, and is currently a senior adviser with the Ministry of Finance.

The report also provides a comprehensive survey of the Irish gambling industry. As a first step towards addressing the question of the impact of online gambling on the Irish economy, the NOS has commissioned the following research:

A statistical study of the Irish gambling industry, based on data from the NOS

An analysis of the gaming industry, including the online gambling sector

An analysis of the Irish gaming industry through the lens of the NOS report

An analysis of the Irish gaming sector through the lens of the Department of Finance

The findings of the report will be used by the DoF to develop a strategy for the sector, and for the government to make changes to the gambling regulations.

The report will also be used by the Irish Gaming Industry Group (IGIG), to inform their report on the state of the Irish gaming industry. The IGGG will present the results of the report, together with a set of recommendations, at the second NOS conference, which is expected to take place in Dublin in April.

The impact of online gambling on the Irish economy

Online gaming has a negative impact on the Irish economy, according to the report. The total losses attributable to online gaming are estimated to be €5.9 billion.
headline: The Impact of Online Casinos on the Irish Economy: Analysis and Prospects

A newbie Garda has been found dead after abandoning his car on a M1 motorway.

The Garda spokesman confirmed a body had been recovered and was taken to hospital.

The scene of the incident on the northbound side of the M1 at the A68 junctions near Carrigaline, Co. Meath, is now a crime scene.

The Garda who found the dead Garda, Sean Keating, was still in hospital.

He was taken to Hospital Galway and later moved to Kilmainham Hospital.

He had suffered a head injury and was initially listed in critical condition, but has now been discharged.

The incident marks the second time a new garda has been found dead this year.

A new garda was found dead on the night of June 2, and a third was found dead on the night of October 28.

In a judgment handed down on the 12th of October 2014, the County Court in Dublin ruled that a woman and her sister-in-law were wrongfully dismissed from a claim for damages arising out of a taxi accident in 2009, which resulted in a broken leg and two concussions.

The Court ruled that the women had failed to state a claim for personal injury or damages, and that they had breached section 37 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Act 2004 which provides for a statutory claim procedure.

This procedure is specifically intended to ensure that claimants do not simply "drop" their claims, and that all evidence and claims are submitted to a full hearing before a judge, as required by the Law of Evidence.

The court has also ruled that the insurance company was under no obligation to compensate the family for any claims, and that the claims made by the women were false, as they relied on "false information" provided to them by the driver.

The Court ruled that the decision of the insurance company to terminate the claims is invalid, and that there is no remedy available to the family against the insurers. The judgement, however, does not hold up to the test of section 37 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Act 2004.

There have been further appeals of the judgment to the Court of Appeal, and, while the first three appeals failed to reach the higher courts, the judgment was unanimously upheld by the Court of Appeal in the case of Hamer v. Garda Síochána, Case No. 517/06 of 2014.

Background information

The case in question was the action brought by a family in Co Clare against a taxi driver for damages for a taxi crash that left their sister-in-law with a broken leg and two concussions and their father with permanent disability.

The sister-in-law had sought compensation under the Insolvency Act 2004, which provided for a statutory claim procedure.

The insurance company, which operated a taxi service in Co Clare, claimed that the woman and her sister-in-law, who both live in Clare town, had been negligent, and that the accident had occurred as a result of a dangerous driving condition in the taxi driver's car, the cause of which was not disclosed to the passengers in the cab.

The taxi driver did not disclose the dangerous condition, and, when contacted by a passenger, said that he had nothing to say about the accident.

The insurance company then sought to have the case heard before a full hearing before a judge, and the woman and her sister-in-law were found by the Court of Appeal to have been wrongfully dismissed from the claim.

The case of Hamer v. Garda Síochána, Case No. 517/06 of 2014 concerned the issue of the extent to which the Insolvency Act 2004 operates in relation to the cancellation of a statutory claim for damages arising out of a private incident.

The case was heard before Mr Justice Maurice Greally, who dismissed the appeal in the case of Hamer v. Garda Síochána, Case No. 517/06 of 2014, and which resulted in a judgement against the insurance company.
headline: Angered judge throws out ‘fraudulent’ insurance claims from Co Clare women against Dublin taxi driver

Ireland's largest city Cork is facing an average of 14,000 reported pothole complaints a day, according to figures released by the city's transport authority (Cork City Council).

The highest number of complaints was recorded at 7,700 in Cork city centre, compared to 6,700 in the inner city and 2,600 in the wider south county and west county regions.

A total of 1,900 complaints were made in the Cork city region, compared with 2,200 in the south county, and 1,500 in the west county.

Cork City Council said that the figures, which were compiled over a four-month period from May to September last year, showed a 40pc increase compared with the same period last year.

Cork city councillor David O'Hagan said: "The Cork city region has experienced a 35pc increase in the number of pothole complaints made to the council.

"The Cork city region has witnessed an average of 14,000 reported pothole complaints a day this year, which is more than double the previous year and more than double the 10,000 recorded in 2009."

Mr O'Hagan said the increase was because of a number of factors including a rise in the number of vehicles travelling through the city centre.

He added: "As a result of that, the complaints are being sent to the council as a whole and this is where we make a difference."

He said that the council was seeking a number of initiatives to tackle the problem, including the installation of temporary barriers in designated areas.

"We are also working to identify ways to improve the signage around our streets in order to provide a quick and easy way for citizens to report potholes."

He said that the council had also taken action to improve the condition of a number of routes.

"Potholes are not new to Cork City Council. We have dealt with pothole complaints as far back as 2001."

Mr O'Hagan said that the council's overall budget to tackle potholes in Cork, which has seen the construction of a new bridge and the installation of new pothole barriers, had increased from €13.2million in 2012 to €15.8million in 2015.

He said that there were two major initiatives underway to tackle the issue.

"In Cork we are working on a new bridge with a major focus on reducing the number of potholes by introducing permanent pothole barriers in places such as the Cork River.

"This new bridge was opened in May and is now being used by pedestrians to cross the river. In addition, we are developing a new pothole barrier on a number of existing bridges in the city centre and are working with the authorities to see whether they could be retrofitted in future years.

"The second issue is the installation of a major maintenance and rehabilitation programme to address the condition of a number of pothole-prone roads in the city centre, including the city's main thoroughfare, the Gardiner Expressway, as well as major road junctions around the city.
headline: Pothole complaints surge around Ireland with 14,000 reports in Cork alone

text:
In Ireland we have been for quite some time a nation-state, with the Irish state being composed of two nations, the Irish Republic and the British Isles.

If we are to make any real changes to our national identity, then we need to think through a series of questions that are pertinent to us all.

Firstly, what is our definition of Ireland as a nation-state? The answer to this question means that the State of Ireland must have a coherent and effective political unit, with all people of the Irish state being members of the same political group.

Secondly, the State of Ireland has to have the means of co-operation with the European Union. The State of Ireland must not be subject to the jurisdiction of the European Court of Justice.

As regards the first question, the Irish state is composed of two nations. The Irish Republic, as it stands, has been ruled by the Irish Parliament for nearly 300 years.

It has a parliament and a government, but the constitution of the Irish Republic is largely irrelevant. In fact, the majority of the laws in the Irish state are not in force.

The people of the Republic are essentially Irish, although we don't have an official language.

The Irish language, and many other things, have been part of our national identity for over 250 years.

The Irish constitution does not give the government of the Republic the right to impose its laws on the people of Ireland. However, the Irish state does have the right to give guidance on how the people of the Republic must behave.

The Irish state has a special status which is dependent upon the existence of a separate Irish national identity.

The Irish state has a long and proud history of being an independent nation-state. There is nothing in our constitution that gives the Irish government power over the Irish people.

The British Isles have been part of the Irish state since the 14th century, in fact the British Isles and Ireland are two separate nations, although the Irish Republic and the British Isles are both part of the same nation-state.

The Irish language is an important part of the Irish national identity and is something that all Irish people should be able to read, speak and write.

The people of the Irish Republic, as is the case with all Irish people, are entitled to vote in elections for the Irish parliament.

The Irish parliament has a role as an elected body in the Irish state to give advice on all matters pertaining to the state of Ireland.

It is also a right to the Irish state to legislate on matters of policy and legislation in the Irish parliament.

Article:

In Ireland, it is recognised that the State of Ireland is not a nation-state and that its government does not have any responsibility for the welfare of its people.

It is recognised that the State of Ireland has a separate and independent legal system as defined by the Constitution of the Republic of Ireland.

It is also recognised that the State of Ireland, in relation to the Irish nation-state, is the exclusive representative of the Irish nation and, to that extent, the State of Ireland is autonomous in matters of foreign policy.

Article:

In Ireland, all citizens of the State of Ireland are citizens of the Republic of Ireland.

All Irish citizens are citizens of the Irish State.

LIVING WEREAHS

DIGGING THE EAR,

THE DOUBLE-FIST CHOPPER

I know, I know, no one ever wants to talk about their crippling anxiety disorder or the fear of a mental illness.

It's not a life to be spent in constant fear and isolation, the kind that can leave you feeling like you can't do the simplest things, like brushing your teeth.

I'm not talking about that.

I'm talking about the kind of terrifying reality that haunts so many women and puts them off work, their family life and their relationships.

Women are told to go home every day and be more gentle and less emotional when they are in the workplace.

One woman I know has been told to "toughen up".

If you think that sounds harsh, you're not alone.

Women told that they need to be "emotional" or they'll get hurt.

Or they'll get sacked.

I know because I was the target of such abuse.

I didn't know any of this at the time.

It was the 1990s.

I worked for a charity I was so proud of, and I enjoyed my job so much.

But, when I was in my thirties, I felt like I had to step back and let a man who was working for me do most of the work.

I started to feel like I was losing my way.

I felt like I was missing out on some big life goals that I could never live up to.

I could have been a better mum, more ambitious at work, more confident in my career.

I didn't know what was wrong with me.

I felt like I had failed.

I felt like I was missing out on a life that I had so much potential to have.

So, I turned to the nearest medical professional, who told me to go home, rest and try to make myself less anxious.

And then, she gave me a little pamphlet about how to make myself feel better.

It started with just taking a little chilli.

She told me that it would relax me, calm me down and even put some light to my life.

It's a simple, and very effective, medication.

I'm now on it six times a day.

I think I'd be a lot less worried if I'd been told that I had to brush my teeth every night.

I don't think that was in the cards for me.

But, when I was a junior officer with the PSNI, I was put in charge of a new unit that would deal with the victims of sexual assault and exploitation.

I got to work and the day started.

As I walked through the door of the victim support unit, I was greeted by a group of women.

They were waiting in a long line for a toilet.

I had never experienced anything like that before in my life.

I felt so overwhelmed with emotions.

They looked at me and I just wanted to cry.

I felt so ashamed.

But the policy is being misused, with the sale price of some houses soaring to around €1.5m – more than double what it would have been.

Some buyers are paying far more than the market value.

The Irish Times examined the sale prices of 865 homes in Dublin and the three main commuter counties, and found that some sellers are paying more than the market value.

This is despite the fact that many of the houses are listed and advertised as being available for short term letting.

For example:

* There is a three bedroom home for sale for €5,000 under a short term letting contract. The listing says it is available for one year, but there is no contract to confirm it.

* A three bedroom property listed in Dublin for €1,000 under a short term letting contract is being advertised as being available for seven months. There is no contract to confirm it.

There is even a three bedroom home listed for sale for €3,500 under a short term letting contract that is advertised as being available for one year. There is no contract to confirm it.

* A three bedroom house in Clontarf for sale with a two year contract is advertised as being available for nine months. No contract to confirm it.

* A four bedroom property listed on Facebook for €1,500 under a short term letting contract is advertised as being available for a year. No contract to confirm it.

The Government is now trying to stop the selling of these properties. The government is set to make short term letting rules permanent when it introduces legislation in the coming months.

An expert group appointed by the Minister for Justice has also recommended that the current rules be modified so that they are enforced.

The expert group was set up to give a greater degree of certainty to the long term letting market so that people are not forced to sell their homes at a discount.

The expert group is recommending the following changes:

* A one year rental contract should be required for short term letting contracts.

* A three month fixed term should be required for short term letting contracts.

* A two year fixed term contract should be required for short term letting contracts.

* Rent should be calculated at the market rate, not the minimum cost, which is £2,500.

This article was written by The Irish Times. Follow us on Twitter: @IrishTimesMag

Irish Times staff contributed to this story.
headline: We know best: Govt is restricting short term letting in larger towns

The new Irish Times poll for the Sunday Times gives the party its biggest result for 40 years, and the biggest swing to the Fine Gael side since the 1980s, according to the polls.

Read about Brendan Howlin

Fine Gael could well go into opposition with a large majority of seats. The party is likely to lose as many as 30 seats but, as this article pointed out, that is still a good place to be in.

As for Labour, it is possible to imagine a second election, particularly if the party can make gains in the south.

That would be the best result possible for Labour, as it would allow it to try to regain the party's former glory.

Read more about Labour's prospects

The Fine Gael leadership's position will be determined by the vote – even in the short term – as they will have to form a government in the event of a hung parliament.

The Taoiseach has made it clear that he intends to lead a government and it is important that he does.

Read more about the Taoiseach's position in a hung parliament

"We are not the only organisation that's making redundancies at the moment," he said.

text:
Gatwick Airport ranks second-worst European airport for delays

By Andrew MacCormick

The Independent, January 21st, 2017

A survey conducted by transport consultants the ITA last week has found that the UK's third largest airport is a disgrace and does not deserve its status as Europe's second worst.

The ITA's airport delay index was launched in 2014 with the intention of putting together a comprehensive list of the UK's worst airports.

The index was designed to help airports improve their performance in the face of rising passenger numbers.

Its methodology is based on data from the International Air Transport Association (IATA) and the UK Office of Rail Regulation (ORR).

The index has included some surprises, including the likes of Madrid's main airport and Heathrow.

But in the end, the worst airports on the list are found to be Gatwick and Stansted in the UK and Munich and Frankfurt in Germany.

The ITA's findings on the UK's third largest airport are based on the amount of time that a plane has to arrive at Gatwick – or at least be cleared through the security lines and onto the runway.

This amount is divided by the number of flights that were delayed by one hour or more.

The worst airport for delays in 2016/17 was found to be Gatwick with an average delay time of 4:58 hours, followed by Stansted with 4:49 hours, and Manchester Airport with 4:41 hours.

In contrast, the ITA's worst city airport, Amsterdam's main airport Eegertal, had a 3:02 average delay time in 2016/17.

* British Airways warns of delays for holidaymakers in the UK

* British Airways warns of delays for holidaymakers in the UK

* Gatwick Airport 'scare list' to be used to advise travellers

* British Airways warns of delays for holidaymakers in the UK

The UK's second worst airport was found to be Madrid's main airport. It had a total delay time of 6:02 hours.

The ITA's worst airport for delays in 2015/16 was found to be Frankfurt with 4:41 hours, followed by Manchester Airport with 4:38 hours, and Amsterdam's main airport with 4:14 hours.

The ITA's worst airport for delays in 2014/15 was found to be Paris' main airport Charles de Gaulle and it had a total delay time of 6:16 hours.

headline: Gatwick Airport earns dubious honor of second-worst European airport for delays

"This is not an easy situation for us," he said.

"We've got four or five people working in the station and we are trying to look after the people who have come to work.

"They were very upset and felt they were made to feel they were not welcome.

"We are trying to deal with that and find out what went wrong and make sure that people are treated fairly and with the respect that they need to be treated."

Sgt O'Mahony said he did not have further details on the case as of yet.

He said it was not about whether or not the message was offensive or not. "It was the context of that post that made it more serious.

"The message was posted in the early hours and it was made more serious as people who were coming to work in the early hours of the morning got to their shift in the station and were made to feel they were not welcome."

Meanwhile, Superintendent O'Mahony has thanked the public for their support.

"I know it has been very distressing for the individuals involved and I would encourage people to come forward.

"It would be very nice if that information was given to the gardaí.

"I would encourage people to come forward and speak to the gardaí or the investigation team.

"I am working with an external organisation to try and support the individuals and the investigation team in terms of what the implications are and what steps that need to be taken in terms of the legal process.

"We are still trying to make sure that the appropriate procedure is followed in terms of the disciplinary process."

Sgt O'Mahony said he was also trying to find out who was responsible for posting the original Facebook post.

He added that the PSNI had recently received an anonymous tip about the post and wanted to know who had posted it.

"We are not going to stand by and let people feel they are not welcome in the workplace.

"It's important that the gardaí are able to work and that's what we're about."
headline: Five trainee gardaí dismissed over ‘Prank’ that saw another garda handcuffed and thrown into a cold shower

President Donald Trump declared the US government of the USA a national emergency on Wednesday afternoon, and ordered the Department of Health and Human Services to develop a plan to counter the rapidly spreading outbreak of the potentially fatal viral disease, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said in a statement.

The declaration comes after a woman in California reportedly contracted the infection after she was bitten by a bat while at a bat house in an abandoned house.

In the U.S., people are encouraged to check the CDC's advice for how to manage the outbreak.

The outbreak has been widely reported in Texas, Illinois, New York, Florida and Georgia. In California, a person was infected and four other people were confirmed to be infected.

Read the full statement:

President Donald J. Trump declared the current epidemic of Ebola to be a national health emergency on the third full day of his administration. The declaration provides enhanced resources for response to the Ebola outbreak. The declaration also directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to issue a final plan to prevent, prepare for, and manage the spread of Ebola to all Americans who come into contact with infected patients. This plan must address public health risks posed by the disease and protect all Americans, including those living with infected relatives. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said it was responding to an outbreak that has killed at least 15 people and infected at least 1,300 others in the west African countries of Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone. The CDC said in a statement that since the beginning of the outbreak in West Africa, more than 10,000 people have been infected and at least 2,400 people have died.

CDC to be prepared to fight Ebola in the U.S.: CDC official

New Ebola risk levels to be published ahead of U.S. declaration of emergency: CDC

U.S. government declares national emergency on Ebola outbreak: CDC

In an open letter to the president, Secretary of State Rex Tillerson stated the following:

The US Department of Homeland Security will help facilitate the safe transport of medical teams and supplies to West Africa."

The Government is considering a major psychological assessment of Mohammad Al-Shaker Al Tamimi, the Labour Party's candidate for Dublin North West.

In the last week, it has emerged that the State will pay Al-Shaker Al Tamimi €40,000 for a full psychiatric assessment.

Mr Al-Shaker Al Tamimi was released from prison in November 2011 after serving a year in prison for his involvement in a car bomb in 2002.

He was later given permission to travel back to England.

His legal team alleges that the Government will use the €40,000 to fund the psychiatric assessment.

Mr Al-Shaker Al Tamimi has said he does not believe he will be questioned over the car bomb.

However, his legal team claim they will raise it as an issue in the next general election.

"The Government should investigate Mr Al-Shaker Al Tamimi's medical history," said his legal team.

"There is a concern that he may be subjected to undue and unnecessary psychiatric screening, which could result in a denial of him entry to the State and/or place him in a condition of permanent disability."

The full psychiatric assessment will take place between January and March 2016.

Under the Mental Health Act, the assessment must be considered a "medical necessity".

But the Government has said that it has no legal obligation to pay for the assessment.

Last year, an inquiry into the matter into Mr Al-Shaker Al Tamimi revealed that no such assessment had ever been conducted in the State.
headline: Public not happy that Mohammad Al Shaker Al Tamimi is getting taxpayer-funded full psychological assessment

text:
Crowds of young people from the West End and elsewhere are flocking to the South of the city, and some are now making off with children from the city's troubled families.

The number of kids from the West End who have gone missing has doubled in the past three months, with a number of cases of children being taken into care.

According to the Dublin Metro Child Protection Committee, the number of kids reported missing in the city is higher this year than last.

They say there is a worrying trend of young people from the West End heading to the city's troubled families, with the number of cases having doubled in the past three months.

In the first three months of this year, there were 23 cases of missing children from the West End – 10 of those from the West End and three from the South of the city.

In the first three months of last year, there were 14 cases of missing children from the West End – nine of those from the West End and three from the South of the city.

The committee say their information came from three police forces and one social worker who have expressed concerns about the cases.

The committee has now issued warnings to local authorities across the city and Dublin Metro Child Protection Committee chairman Pat Sheehan said the committee had received "a lot of concern".

"The issue of young people going missing in the West End has been a problem for quite some time. There have been at least two reports in the past few months of young people going missing from the West End and that is a really worrying trend," he said.

He said the most recent cases, in the last two months of the year, were a repeat of the 2009 disappearance of three boys from the West End.

Mr Sheehan said the children in these cases had been taken into care as a result of a number of cases in the last year.

"The children are getting into trouble in different ways and at various times they have ended up in foster care and at different times they have ended up in the care of child protection agencies," he said.

The committee chairman said if the trend persists it could pose a risk to the social safety of the child who is missing.

In the past the problem was addressed through social workers or a combination of social workers and social workers working together, he said.

"If they go missing in different ways or different times, we're worried that this could be a repeat of what happened in 2009 with three boys, who were taken into foster care," he said.

The committee chairman said this week's spate of missing kids is "a real concern".

"These cases are very worrying and we are not sure what is going to happen to them, but there are other problems that are coming to light which is causing alarm," he said.

It is understood that the police have issued new appeals in recent weeks and that new child protection guidelines have been issued.

The new guidelines now include a focus on identifying the risk factors among those who are reported missing and where they are likely to be taking place.

Earlier this year, reports suggested that there were 10 cases of children going missing in the West End in the month of October – two in the West End, three in the South and three in the North, with a number of cases involving boys.
headline: Kildare, Offaly and Laois warned to be on alert following rise in Covid-19 cases

A woman has died after she got into difficulty in a waterhole in Co. Tipperary.

Gillian Hickey, a woman in her 70s, was rescued by the Coast Guard when she fell into the waterhole at Loch Hilda, Co. Tipperary.

Gillian had been on the beach looking for her dog, he told BBC Radio Ulster, when she slipped and fell into the waterhole.

Gillian's husband was called and she was taken to hospital.

She had been missing since the evening of Friday and had not been heard from since.

Gillian's husband, Stephen, said: "Gillian was on the beach at 5pm, she went back to the house around 6pm, then she went into the waterhole.

"The dog has been searched, the gardaí are there, the local people, all the local authorities have been contacted.

"She is still missing and we are doing everything that we can."

The Coast Guard confirmed they had recovered a woman on Saturday morning at Loch Hilda.

A spokesman said: "Gillian Hickey, 70, from Creggan in Tipperary, was rescued by the Coast Guard after falling into the waterhole at Loch Hilda at 9.08pm last Friday.

"She was airlifted to hospital for treatment.

text:
'He surrendered and then he shot himself'


A gunman has surrendered to police in a shooting incident at a Florida bank and a man who was shot in the face is in a critical condition.


It's understood a man armed with a handgun burst into the First National Bank in Vero Beach, Florida, in the early hours of Friday morning with a "large knife" before firing a shot at a receptionist and two other employees.


The receptionist was shot in the face but survived. She was transferred to St. Mary's Hospital in Daytona Beach.


A colleague of the receptionist was also shot in the arm, but sustained only a graze wound.


The gunman then fired at the receptionist as she came down from the bank and then two other people, a customer and a bank teller.


They were shot and died at the scene.


Police have arrested the man in connection with the shooting.


One of the victims, an employee, had surgery on Friday afternoon and remains in a critical but stable condition. A woman who was shot in the arm has since been released from hospital.


At a news conference at Vero Beach police station, police said the man had a large knife and a long firearm in his possession.


Officers said they were not seeking any further suspects but were looking for additional information about the case.


One employee, who was not wounded, said he came out of the bank holding a pistol and heard what he thought was two gunshots.


"I thought it was something really loud," said the employee. "I ran back in the office and started calling my colleagues."


A bank teller was shot in the shoulder and was in a critical condition. A receptionist suffered a graze wound to the left arm and a colleague received multiple gunshot wounds to the left arm and abdomen.

The suspect reportedly yelled, "Help me, they're dead, I did it."

The incident comes two weeks after a gunman opened fire on a Fort Lauderdale nightclub, leaving five people dead and 20 injured.

Gunman says he was 'going to kill people'


The shooting came shortly after a gunman opened fire in a Fort Lauderdale strip club, injuring five people.

Police say it is the first time an active shooter has struck Florida.

The Vero Beach police chief said the man's actions were an act of terror.


"We know that the suspect was motivated by hatred," chief Robert D'Andrea said. "He said he was going to kill people and he was going to do it in a way that would inflict the most suffering and the most harm."

The suspect was arrested at the scene. He was identified by witnesses as 26-year-old Michael Stephen Loughner.

He had a lengthy criminal history in the state and was charged with assault with a deadly weapon and possession of a firearm by a felon in 2012, according to court records.

He was in jail in North Carolina at the time of the shooting and had been convicted of carrying a concealed weapon in 2011.

ABC News' Brian Ross, Matthew Perrone and Emily Shapiro contributed to this report.
headline: Gunman surrenders to police after shooting five people dead at a Florida bank

"The Government will tomorrow call a meeting of its junior ministers in Dublin, after more than 6 weeks of strikes by teachers.

The talks are expected to be a reprise of last year's action which followed months of strikes by staff over issues like pay, pensions and conditions.

As well as the strike, teachers have been locked out on a day-to-day basis for a further 4 weeks as part of the ongoing education reform process.

A number of schools have been locked out since May 2 in order to allow the implementation of the new pay structure to take place.

"Today's meeting of the junior ministers will aim to determine whether or not the Irish public are to be locked down again for another 6 weeks.

The decision will be made at a meeting of the Government's executive committee on Thursday morning, following the announcement of the new pay structure.

"The new pay structure will mean that teachers will receive less money than they did last time out – as the current system of pay is based on earnings over €25,000, but the new system will be based on earnings over €24,500.

The change will mean that if teachers receive €20,000 a year they will not be paid more than the €23,500 they are currently paid, while teachers in the mid €25,000 category will get around €18,500 and those in the €24,500 category will get around €16,500.

These figures are expected to be a major blow to the economy and public confidence, and the Government has announced an extra €10 million in funding for schools to help tackle the crisis."

"We are determined to get back to work, we have set a tough timetable but we cannot afford to be taken for a ride again."

I would have thought that a Government with a "hard" stance on education would know that it should be working with the teachers and that they have the right to strike.

It is an attack on teachers and it is not an attack on any person, but it is an attack on the state.

The Government has put teachers' pay out of reach and it has done this in order to "mend" the relationship between the State and the teachers.

It is not a real reform. It is the same old crap that is being put out every year.

The Government has no business telling us what to do and that is why it is the best place for the State to put the blame for all this on teachers.
headline: Government trio to meet today to decide whether or not the Irish public get locked down again for another 6 weeks

An "early bird" payment of €300 would be introduced to help families with families with children living in Dublin, with a payment of €300 to be paid on the first of the month.

It is hoped that the initiative will encourage a return to work and will not lead to any families losing out financially.

The Government has been consulting on the concept of a Child Benefit for some time as the cost of living has increased in recent years.

The payment to be paid on the first of the month, and €300 per child, would be available to families with children living in Dublin from January 1st, 2016.

The first payment would be paid in two equal payments of €300. The cost of the payment to be paid out would be based on a person's disposable income from both earnings and expenses. The first payment would be for one child, and the two payments would be paid in equal instalments.

A payment for two children would not be offered if the family's income fell below €300 per month.

The Government said the Child Benefit policy was not the first time this had been raised as it was previously discussed in the Social Welfare and Welfare Committee, and was also discussed at the recent Fiscal Commission, and the Minister for Social Protection Joan Burton said she did not see any reason why it should not be considered.

However, the Government noted that there is a cost to the Government of having to pay the benefits at the beginning of the month, as it is a once-off payment.

Deputy Prime Minister, Fianna Fáil leader Micheál Martin said a similar measure was already in place in the United Kingdom. He told TheJournal.ie the Government should also consider a similar measure in the Republic.

"I'm sure that we will see that the Government has the political will to take this action, if it will help families like ours that face financial difficulties," Mr Martin said.

"I am sure that our colleagues in the European Commission and elsewhere will be keen to look at this and work with the Government to see if this could be part of a package of measures that will be more effective in solving this very serious challenge we all face in dealing with the rising cost of living."
headline: Government considering a once-off double Child Benefit payment to help with rising cost of living

The shocking footage obtained by a priest has been published on a Facebook page run by the Diocese of Clogher.

The footage, which has been posted in the past 24 hours, has been released just hours after a priest was attacked at the same Church of the Holy Family in the town of Westmeath.

A video shot at the Cathedral of the Holy Family in the town of Westmeath, County Clare, reveals the moment a group of men, aged between 18 and 30, entered the church and attacked a bishop during a service.

“This is absolute madness,” said Diocese of Clogher (DC), Diocese of the Rock, Diocese of the Lanes and Diocese of Killaloe, in a statement. “Our faith teaches us that we are not to harm others and that the life of the church is for the benefit of all, so the behaviour of these men is deeply shocking and deeply disturbing.”

The group had arrived at the church to celebrate Mass, and as they arrived they were met by a member of the clergy who was there as a volunteer and he asked them to leave. The group then shouted at a male member of the clergy who was not involved in the service, before demanding the priest leave.

When the male member of the clergy attempted to intervene to stop the abuse, the group attacked the bishop, punching and kicking him and pulling out a knife.

They then attacked the priest in the same manner.

“The male cleric, who was the victim’s friend, came to his aid and tried to help him, as did the male cleric who had been the victim’s victim,” reads the statement. “The female cleric was also present, and attempted to intervene. The male priest was injured as he attempted to stop the attack and he sustained a cut on his arm.

“The male cleric was attended by a member of the clerical staff member who also attempted to intervene.

“The male cleric who was attacked and the female cleric who was involved in the event were assisted by members of the clerical staff, and also by a member of the clergy who tried to assist.

“The male cleric who was the victim’s friend was also present at the scene and attempted to intervene.

“Members of the clerical staff member then tried to assist. They were assisted by the male cleric who was the victim’s victim, as well as a member of the clergy who was the victim’s victim.”

The attack happened during a service and the bishop was immediately rushed to hospital by the church secretary, who was able to stop the bleeding from the priest’s injury.

The National Radio and Television Office (NRTO) is proposing a new ‘Internet Protocol for a New Era’ in the context of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit scheduled for 2019 in Taipei. It suggests to develop a new communication framework that is consistent with international standards for global information dissemination.

NRTO’s initiative is aimed at fostering innovation in telecommunication policy, such as a new Internet Protocol for a New Era, or IP4NA, a new communication standard that is based on the IPv6 and IPv4 protocols.

The proposal for the new Internet Protocol is based on three pillars. The first pillar is that it is consistent with international standards, which means that the same protocols will not be used for the Internet Protocol. The second pillar is that it is not a replacement of the existing Internet Protocol (IP) but a fundamental new framework for information exchange, which enables communication between different parts of the world. The third pillar is that it is a more flexible protocol that can be used to facilitate innovation in information provision.

The new Internet Protocol would replace the current Internet Protocol, which is an application of the Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (TCP/IP), a well-known protocol, with a new communication protocol. The new Internet Protocol will be compatible with the existing Internet Protocols and be compatible with the Internet Protocols of other countries.

The current Internet Protocol is the most popular protocol, being the most widely used Internet protocol, and it is based on the Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (TCP/IP). This is because the current Internet Protocol uses the TCP/IP protocol, and the Internet Protocols of other countries are based on the TCP/IP protocol. The new Internet Protocol will be compatible with the existing Internet Protocols, and is based on the IPv4 and the IPv6 protocols.

According to the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), the current Internet Protocol can be summarized as follows:

As an Internet Protocol, the current Internet Protocol consists of the Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (TCP/IP) and the Internet Protocol Version 4 (IPv4) and the Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6).

The current Internet Protocol is based on the TCP/IP protocol, which provides transmission, network management, and data dissemination features. The TCP/IP protocol is based on the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), and it uses IP addresses. The TCP/IP protocol has been widely adopted by the Internet communities, such as the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). The IETF describes the TCP/IP protocol as follows:

The TCP/IP protocol uses IP addresses, which are 32-bit binary numbers. A TCP/IP network uses IP addresses for addressing IP traffic. It uses IP addresses when the IPv4 or IPv6 addresses have no meaning for TCP/IP or when the addresses are dynamic.

The current Internet Protocol is a protocol that is based on the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP). TCP uses IP addresses for the transmission and network management of IP traffic. The TCP uses IP addresses when the IPv4 or IPv6 addresses have no meaning for TCP. The TCP uses IP addresses when the addresses are dynamic. The TCP uses IPv4 or IPv6 addresses. The IPv4 addresses are 32-bit binary numbers.
headline: Taiwan’s participation can strengthen international cooperation to fight transnational telecommunication fraud in the postpandemic era

Sitting on the steps of a building with a very large
white stone column, a man and his son are contemplating a
painting. It depicts a seated figure, with a robe, hair
covering his shoulders, and wearing a hat. To the right
are seated two figures, one with a plump white beard, the
other with a beard nearly as long as his hair. The painting
is of a well-known figure in Chinese history, Confucius,
who in the past served as the ‘de facto’ leader of the
people of China. The son, whose head is bowed, is
attempting to lift the robe, so as to make an offering
to Confucius’ feet. He is having difficulty, and turns
away in embarrassment. The father stands and lifts
up the robe. He turns to his son, who is not able to
make the offering, and says: “You should make an offering
to my feet and say something.” The boy then asks his
father, who says “This time he has to do a hundred
times more than before.” Confucius then says, “It is
only the man in the robe that is worthy of such an
offering.” The son then asks Confucius: “If you do
this, what will happen to you?” Confucius responds: “I
would be punished.” The son then offers his own robe,
which Confucius accepts and then rises from the
platform. The man in the robe is then led away as he
was previously, and his son is left alone on the steps.

The painting is a representation of the idea of Confucius as the leader
of the people. He is seated on a platform, with a
long white beard, in his robe. He has his feet on a
low platform, and his robe is hanging to his side.

He is being praised by two figures who are standing on either side
of him, who hold out their hands to him in an offering.
His robes are being opened and he is being offered a
full meal. He is a member of the people, and therefore
he is worthy of being offered a meal, and a place to
sit. He is also being honoured as the “de facto”
leader of the people.

In the painting, there is a symbolic representation of the power of
Confucius, and his role as the de facto leader of the
people. When one person is honoured and honoured, the
other person, or the ‘de facto’ leader, is
celebrated.

It is a way to represent that the whole Chinese people (the
people of China) should be honoured, and should not be
deceived by their leader. It is an acknowledgement of
the role of the whole of the Chinese people in the
society and government of China. This was the role of
Confucius, which has been carried out by him since his
birth.

It is an expression of the fact that if anyone is honoured and
honoured, it is not only the “de facto” leader of the
people, but the whole Chinese people.
headline: The lasting relevance of Confucius

text:
A new study has suggested that many economic worries about societies in the developing world are overly exaggerated.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) published an expert report this week on the economic situation of developing countries, based on a survey of experts at 28 countries. The experts are all members of the Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).

The study concluded that, for the first time, the OECD survey had found no correlation between the economic well-being of countries and the level of political development.

In addition, the report found that the poorest countries had lower life expectancy than richer countries, while the average wealth of countries at the bottom of the ladder was the same as the average wealth of the top half of countries.

The study, published by the OECD at its spring meeting, also found that countries were becoming more like wealthy countries in the quality of their social safety nets. For example, the OECD countries are on average better off now than in 1973 when they were first surveyed, and have better social protection than they did in the last survey.

‘The study is not about economic growth’

It also found that countries were becoming more like wealthy countries in the quality of their social safety nets. For example, the OECD countries are on average better off now than in 1973 when they were first surveyed, and have better social protection than they did in the last survey.

‘I would be surprised if we had a better standard of living than we enjoyed in the mid-20th century,’ OECD chief economist, Klaus Wurst, said in a press release accompanying the report. ‘It would be good news, but I would not be surprised if we saw a modest improvement.’

Wurst is one of four senior economists who wrote an initial draft of the OECD report but whose work was not chosen for the final version.

Economists and the media were furious when the report was published on Wednesday.

‘It is deeply concerning that OECD economists are trying to make the case that poor countries are getting richer, when the reality is the opposite,’ said Michael Hewson, head of the International Trade Policy Centre and a former senior adviser to the British Treasury.

Hewson said the report’s main findings were based on a survey of experts at 28 countries, many of which are members of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

The survey was undertaken by the OECD in late 2006, and it is a second survey, this time of economists and researchers from the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development. The OECD has a large database of experts, and the survey is designed to capture the views of a wide cross-section of experts on different subjects.

The OECD says that it has contacted each of the 28 OECD member states’ institutions to request a copy of the report and to gain an estimate of the total number of experts involved.

‘It would be very unusual for a country with a population of over a billion people to have no experts involved in economic policy,’ said Dr Michael Pettis, an economist who worked on the survey team, in an interview.
headline: Study: Economic fears of ageing societies overblown
