By Fergus Mullett,

The Irish Times

THE worst years in the Irish economy have been the past few years.

For the creative, the best are behind the worst.

The Irish economy has been in freefall for the past three years and the worst of times have been the best of times.

When it comes to the creative industry in Ireland it is now the best year of the year for the Irish economy.

In 2016 the number of jobs created in the creative sector was a record 40,000 jobs, the highest ever. In addition the number of jobs created in the IT sector was a record high.

The figures show a continuation of the recent progress made by the Irish economy in the past three years.

It is clear that Ireland’s creative industries are making a remarkable recovery since the global financial crisis.

The Irish Government will be looking to see how the creative industries and services can be harnessed to grow the economy in the future.

A spokesperson for the Office of the Taoiseach said: “The economic and employment crisis in Ireland has been a long time coming.

“The number of jobs created in the creative sector in the past three years, coupled with the increasing number of Irish people who have jobs in the creative sector is a clear indicator that we are working with our partners in the creative industries to grow the Irish economy.

“The creative industry sector is responsible for over a third of the total number of jobs in the Irish economy.

“We want to ensure the sectors contribute to our long-term economic growth by creating new jobs, increasing investment in the sector and strengthening our global reputation for innovation and excellence.”

The Irish Government is currently in the process of reviewing existing legislation and is also setting up a new industry group, The Creative Industries Group.

The group will provide advice, guidance and information on the economic and employment trends affecting Ireland’s creative industry sector.

It will also support the development of new creative industries and services in Ireland and support the growth of the Irish creative sector through training and research.

The Creative Industries Group will be led by Chief Executive Martin Shanahan, who is also chairman of the Irish Creative Council.

The group’s board includes representatives from the leading Irish creative and arts organisations including: The Abbey Theatre, the National Theatre, Arts Council of Ireland, Irish Theatre, Irish Arts Council, Irish Arts Council for Film & Television and Film Ireland.

In 2015 there were 50,000 Irish people working in the creative sector and an estimated 7,000 Irish people are now employed in the sector.

The Irish Government is also looking to see how the sector can be harnessed to grow the economy.

A spokesperson said: “We have a long way to go in terms of increasing the number of jobs created in the Irish creative economy, but we are making good progress in the right direction.

“Since last year we have seen a sustained recovery in the Irish creative economy.

“It’s a significant increase in the number of jobs created in the sector since the global financial crisis.

“That growth is due to the sustained recovery in the Irish economy.

Dermot Ahern has been criticised for not having the necessary information, a spokesperson said.

RUSSIA, the latest state to join the ‘new’ NATO alliance, is threatening to deploy nuclear weapons if Sweden and Finland join that alliance.

On Wednesday, the Russian Foreign Ministry said in a statement that if Sweden and Finland do not join NATO, the Russian Federation would deploy nuclear weapons at ‘our disposal’.

The move comes just days after Russia warned Finland that it would respond to an attempted Swedish-Finland joint air attack on Moscow by launching nuclear strikes in Finland. Russia has also accused Sweden of ignoring security threats on its borders.

Finnish President Sauli Niinisto, speaking at the NATO summit in Brussels, told his Finnish counterpart that Finland “would not hesitate to use nuclear weapons” if Sweden and Finland did not join NATO.

The Baltic countries are close to joining the EU’s newly reformed European Defence Union, which has seen them pledge to make their own defense arrangements.

The Kremlin’s threat came after a Finnish foreign ministry official told Russian media that Finland “is preparing the deployment of nuclear weapons in response to the Finnish-Russian conflict,” according to the Moscow Times.

RFE/RL’s Russian Service reported:

On Wednesday, the Finnish foreign ministry said it had received Russian official documents that called for the deployment of nuclear weapons in the Nordic region.

The documents were allegedly written by the deputy chief of the foreign-affairs committee of the National Defense Council in the Finnish parliament.

The Finnish foreign ministry official told RFE/RL on Thursday: “We receive information from the Finnish foreign ministry,” referring to the documents.

The official said that Finland should not be “bluffing” about the Russian documents. “I don’t understand why Finland says it wants to use nuclear weapons,” the official said, adding, “We are talking about NATO.”

The official noted that, while Finland has long been a NATO member, Finland has not joined NATO’s new “new alliance” of 18 European countries.

Finland also rejected Russia’s ultimatum, and said it would not respond to the Russian declaration with any more nuclear threats.

“The Russian Federation should be ashamed of itself,” the Finnish foreign ministry official said. “This is not a real discussion of the question, but a statement of a provocation and blackmail.”

On Wednesday, a joint statement by the Russian Foreign Ministry and the Finnish Foreign Ministry called for “the use of nuclear weapons to protect regional and global security” and accused Sweden and Finland of ignoring Russian security threats.

The Russian government also called for the European Union to increase the number of NATO members to 20 or even 25 by 2015.

The Finnish Foreign Ministry said that Russia’s accusations were “unacceptable” and that they “are based on lies.” It also denied that Finland was seeking to play the “nuclear card.”

It added that “any nuclear threats [by Finland] would be the direct consequence of Sweden and Finland’s decision to join the NATO alliance.”

Teenage girls’ suicides are now the “number one cause of deaths by suicide” in the UK, according to a new government report.

The warning comes after the UK Government introduced a ban on puberty blockers last year after a teenage girl in Hampshire died by suicide after taking testosterone.

In the new report, published today, the Office for National Statistics said the number of suicides by 17 year-olds in 2015 was the highest in a decade. In 2013, the number was the lowest.

The new figures show that the UK suicide rate among teenage girls fell by 24% in the year to August 2015, which was “a huge improvement” from the year before.

The number of suicides by 17 year-old girls rose by 4% in the same period.

The latest figures came from the Office for National Statistics, which found a significant rise in the suicide rate among teenage girls between 2010 and 2015.

The rise was “clearly driven by a rise in the number of teenagers in the UK who were in care,” said Caroline Pidcock, who is leading the Office for National Statistics’s gender-based violence and sexual health working group.

“The number of female-to-male transgender people is likely to have increased during this period, as more transgender people in care are likely to have come out.”

The figure is similar to figures showing the rise in suicide rates among young adults over the last five years. In 2014, there were 25,000 suicides in England and Wales, and the number is now 22,000.

In 2012, there were 12,000 suicides in England and Wales, and the number is now 10,000.

In Scotland, there are 12,000 suicides in the year to August 2016.

But the Government’s statistics show an even bigger rise. Between 2011 and 2015, the number of suicides among young people aged 15–24 went up by 21%.

Pidcock said that while the rise in suicide among young people is alarming, more than two decades of research has found that there is no evidence of a link between puberty blockers and a heightened risk of suicide.

“Puberty blockers are not a causal factor in the increased number of suicides among teenage girls,” she said. “They are not a direct cause of the increase in suicides.”

Pidcock said it is “dangerous” to “speculate” about the increased suicide rates among young people.

“It is only safe to point out that the suicide rate among girls in the UK is the highest ever seen in recent history,” she said. “The government’s figures show the suicide rate in Scotland is the highest recorded in a decade. We are clearly at a tipping point.”

She said there is “no doubt” that more than 1,000 teenage girls have taken to their deaths by suicide.

“We must protect these young women from the dangers of a life of silence, by addressing the causes of their suicide, and by taking steps to ensure their lives are better supported and saved.”

Suicide rates among teenage girls rose by 9% in the year to August 2015 compared to the same period in 2014.
headline: Claim puberty blocker ban causing suicide in children unfounded and “dangerous”

I was delighted to see that Ireland had, for the first time ever, voted to repeal the eighth amendment.

The repeal campaign was a two-pronged effort. First, it was a referendum on the abortion referendum; the eight amendment was also a referendum on the abortion referendum. The referendum was held on October 21, 2014. The eighth amendment referendum was held on December 15, 2015. That’s why I was pleased when the Irish electorate voted to repeal the eighth amendment.

The second reason I was pleased is because I was pleased that the Irish electorate voted to repeal the eighth amendment, because I see it as a watershed moment. The eighth amendment was a law passed by Parliament in 1916 and signed into law by King George V. This was a law that was passed with the consent of the Irish people. It was a law that was passed with the consent of the people who were the soldiers of the Great War. The Eighth Amendment was passed with the consent of the soldiers who were serving in the Great War, and it’s part of their legacy as a war to remember.

The Irish people did not ask for this law. The Irish people did not ask for the eight amendment. The Irish people did not ask for these laws to be repealed. The eight amendment was passed with the consent of the Irish people and the consent of the men and women of the Great War. The men and women who were the soldiers of the Great War were the men and women who were going to fight and die in the Great War. The men and women who were soldiers of the Great War knew that the eighth amendment was a law that should be repealed.

But the Irish people did not demand that they repeal it. The Irish people did not demand that they repeal it in 2016. They did not demand that they repeal it now. The Irish people voted to repeal it, and that’s why I’m happy that the Irish electorate voted to repeal the eighth amendment in 2016.

If we did not repeal it, if we did not repeal it for the Irish people to have the opportunity to vote, I think that we would be in a much more dangerous situation. There would be no chance of our being able to protect, to protect women and children and elderly people. We would be less safe. The Irish people did not repeal it. We have had years now, a very long period of time that have been devoted to trying to repeal it, and in that time we have been beaten back every time.

Headline: Government Jet has flown for 125 hours this year, costing half a million

Date Published: Saturday, 07 May, 2019

In what may be a sign of things to come for Ireland’s “last” Air Corps jet, the Government’s Aeronautic Administration and Jet (AAJ) has been able to operate over 250 flights this year, costing half a million euros.

That is despite the fact that the new airline has been established only in February, with no operating licences or crew until the end of the year.

The Aeronautic Administration and Jet will launch on the 21st May on what they claim is the “first commercial flight to be made by a non-Air Corps aircraft”.

This is the first time in the airline’s history that a non-Air Corps airline has flown. However, it is not the only one. In the first half of the year, they have been able to operate flights on six jets – four Air Corps jets and two “private” jets.

However, in this first half, the AAJ has been able to book more than 450 flights from one plane – a Boeing 737-800 – than any other operator.

According to the AAJ, this is the biggest number of flights it has ever flown from one aircraft.

“We have now started the commercial operation of a jet aircraft. The first flight was made on a single aircraft and has flown 125 hours over the last six weeks. This makes a total of half a million euros in income from the last two weeks of the year,” a spokesperson for the AAJ told The Irish Times.

They said that the 737-800, which cost €400,000 for the operation, will be flown twice a day at peak traffic.

“The aircraft will make up the first commercial flight to be made by a non-Air Corps aircraft,” the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson added that the airline will be “operated as an Air Corps operator”, and will continue to be so in future.

The AAJ said that the airline currently has a full complement of 24 flight crew, 10 pilots and 10 cabin crew.

However, the spokesperson said that it will be operating from one plane for the foreseeable future.

The spokesperson said that there are “many” issues that need to be solved before the airline can be flown commercially.

“We need the new aircraft and crew to be available by the end of May to start the commercial flight. We have been working towards this day since January 2018,” the spokesperson added.

They said that the airline will have its own identity when it is launched, which is why it is being operated by a separate company.

“The AAJ is committed to providing a safe and reliable flight for its customers. We will be operating one of our own aircraft with a full complement of crew from the start,” the spokesperson said.

The airline is not the first of its kind.

On 14 November 2010, the DSP and the High Court issued a warrant for Pound’s arrest.

Following evidence from the prosecution, Pound pleaded guilty to the offences under the Animal Health Act 2006 and the Control of Cruelty to Animals Act 2007.

Boiling the water for the day in Ireland is a controversial practice that is carried out only in cases where a company is suffering losses.

This is the case for 22,000 customers of Wexford Water, who received a notice from the Irish state-owned utility warning them that their water will be boiled at certain times to ensure the quality of the product is good enough to satisfy customers, Gript reports.

The notice, dated January 13, gives customers the option to boil the water or not boil, on a day-to-day basis.

This follows a similar warning issued in August 2014, when 15,000 Wexford customers were given the option to boil their water or not, in order to ensure that the water did not become unfit for use and also to make sure that the water was boiled at a minimum temperature of 46 degrees Celsius.

The notice also warns them that if they do not boil their water, they may be prosecuted under the Environmental Protection Act 2002 for carrying out the act without a licence.

The notice gives a number of possible reasons that water might be boiling:

To ensure the quality of the product, to make sure that there is enough water and that there is not water that has gone off the water line

To ensure that the water is sufficiently hot

To ensure the water is sufficiently fresh, or alternatively is boiling to destroy any bacteria present in the water

To ensure that the water has been boiled for a sufficient period of time

The notice makes no mention of any particular chemicals that might be contained in the water.

"Allowing our customers to choose whether or not they boil their water, as they have the opportunity to do, is a prudent step," said Gript CEO, Michael W. O'Brien.

He pointed out that this notice has been put in place by the company to provide customers with a safer and more reasonable method of controlling the quality of their drinking water.

The utility, which owns and operates more than 20 water treatment plants in the region, is aware that it has been using boiling for a very long time, to which it has not responded.

"Our customers are now faced with a situation where they can either choose to boil or not boil their water. I think it’s prudent for the company to make the necessary preparations to allow the customers to make their choices," Mr O'Brien said.

The Irish Water Authority has been in regular communication with the company since the notice was issued.

"The Irish Water Authority has a responsibility to ensure that all customers are provided with the information necessary to make a smart choice, based on the company’s own internal information, and that we have an appropriate monitoring capability to ensure that this kind of issue is being addressed," Mr O'Brien said.

The Irish Water Authority will be liaising with the company to ensure that the water is boiled as quickly as possible and will be monitoring the boiling to ensure it is not happening again.

"I would encourage the water company to do the right thing by its customers and to ensure that the water is boiled as quickly as possible."

“We are in the midst of a ‘rebirth’ in Dublin,” said John Hughes, who chairs the Gript Rent Advisory Committee, which reviews the data. “While the average monthly rent has stayed stable, it’s very different from the time when I was looking at the data in the early part of the decade. The recent rent changes are a big change for all renters in Dublin.”

“This is a very significant change and, given the size of the tenant market in Dublin, it is a significant change for the rental market in general. A significant increase in the average monthly rent was, in all likelihood, driven by a lot of people looking for a change in lifestyle. We expect the next phase will be a significant increase in the number of landlords willing to sign up to rent to more than €2,000 per month.”

The data comes to light with the publication of the Dublin Tenancy (GDP) Report – The Annual Economic Report for 2015. It also comes at a time when there are now 2,000+ tenant applications for a lease in Dublin.

Since 2011, the number of tenant applications for a rental licence has increased by 1,500%.

Gript.ie has launched a new website to help tenants in Dublin find the right landlord to rent to. It will also link with other Gript sites around the world and with its sister site of Renting.ie.

The website includes a guide to help tenants find their local landlord who will rent to them. It also includes a list of companies that offer €2,000 or more a month to rent.
headline: Average rent now almost €2,000 per month in Dublin

Home ownership

Growth and stability

Home ownership

Home ownership rates among the Irish population has fallen from 63% to 46% since 2011.

The number of home ownership loans outstanding increased from 40,000 in 2011 to over 200,000 in 2012, with more than 50% of these loans being from individuals and families.

In December 2013, the Central Statistics Office reported that the average price of a house in Ireland was over €200,000. This represents the average price of a house in the Republic.

The number of people living in rented housing increased from 29,000 in 2011 to over 43,000 in 2013.

The number of people living in houses with over 5 bedrooms grew from under 100,000 to over 2 million.

For every person that moved to Ireland, only 1.6 people were moving back.

This figure, which is the highest such number for any European Union country since Statistics Ireland was established in 1999, shows the importance of a housing strategy.

However, as the Central Statistics Office notes, it does not provide enough detail to give an indication of the impact on Ireland of this increase in housing demand.

An increasing number of housing units are needed

The Central Statistics Office suggests that the number of housing units in Ireland needed to house the population will increase from 7.9 million in 2012 to 8.9 million in 2016.

However, the Central Statistics Office also notes that there are limits to what the Government can achieve. It indicates that even if housing demand increased by 100% as predicted, it would still not meet the demand from the Irish public.

For example, it notes that only 8.8% of the Irish population had a mortgage in 2012.

This number is based on the Mortgage Interest Deduction (MID) of 5% on mortgages.

If this figure was applied on a yearly basis it would require about 5.4 million new homes to be built over the life of the forecast period.

The Central Statistics Office suggests that the Government needs to act quickly to address this issue.

The Central Statistics Office says that a housing strategy is needed to address housing supply constraints and to achieve a more sustainable supply of housing.

It also says that this strategy should also be complemented by a more active land market and new forms of development, including a more flexible land use policy, public participation in design and planning decisions, and a greater focus on affordable housing.

It notes that the Government has a duty to provide housing for all at a price that is sustainable in the long run.

It suggests that a more sustainable housing supply would improve Ireland’s economy, increase economic activity and improve the wellbeing of the Irish people.

The Government must act to secure a better housing market, which would allow new homes to be built, and should act to address the lack of affordable housing that is a particular problem in rural areas.

It says that this would allow more people to move to better housing, and would increase tax receipts and the overall welfare of the Irish people.

The Central Statistics Office also highlights the need to increase investment in and the availability of land in order to create new housing and to achieve an increase in housing supply.

It says that the Government must also take a more active role in setting standards for new housing.
headline: The housing crisis threatening An Ghaeltacht

Irish Times -
Monday 30th of February, 2018

The Dáil last night voted to accept a report of the joint parliamentary committee on medical treatment in the dying process, recommending that the Government introduce legislation into the Penal Laws to permit the assisted suicide of patients with serious life threatening illness or injuries.

The report recommended that such legislation should not be subject to the provisions of the Medical Research Council (MRC) and the European Convention on Human Rights, as these are not compatible with the law in force in Ireland. The report was tabled by the Dáil’s public health spokesperson, Dr Michael McGrath.

The report, ‘Assisted Suicide in Ireland’ was tabled by the joint parliamentary committee on medical treatment in the dying process. It recommends that assisted suicide be permitted under the MRC and ECHR.

The report contains a range of recommendations, including the following:

• A special legislative instrument would be required to authorise a decision to take a patient’s life by means of any of the three types of assisted suicide permitted by Irish law. This instrument could only be used in cases where a person is terminally ill, suffering from a terminal illness or where the person has had a terminal illness for less than 12 months.

• This legislative instrument should be subject to the approval of the Minister for Health who would have to have regard to a number of factors including the impact on public health, on the functioning of the healthcare system and on the economic costs involved.

• This legislation should not be subject to the provisions of the Medical Research Council (MRC) and the European Convention on Human Rights. It should not be applicable to anyone dying under Irish law, where a medical practitioner can diagnose a disease and treat it, or where a patient may have been terminally ill for more than 12 months.

It also recommends that the legislation should not be subject to the provisions of the Irish Courts Act and the Irish Courts Code.

The report states that the MRC and ECHR were not applicable in Ireland because they did not recognise a right to self-determination. The report recommends that the MRC and ECHR should be incorporated in the legislation as it would be consistent with the Irish Constitution.

Dr Michael McGrath of the Dáil said:

“We welcome the report which sets out the reasons why it is important that the Irish legal system should have protection against assisted suicide. It is our obligation as legislators to look at what can be done to protect the right to self-determination from abuse in the provision of healthcare and assisted suicide.

It’s important to note that the report does not represent a determination to enact this legislation. It’s up to the Minister to set it in the form he prefers.”

The public response to the report has been overwhelmingly positive. There were over 1,700 messages of support.

The Irish Medical Organisation, the Irish College of Anaesthetists, the Irish General Practitioners Association and the Irish College of General Practitioners issued a statement, following the Dáil vote, saying that they welcomed the report and would be seeking its co-sponsorship.
headline: Dáil votes to accept report recommending legislating for assisted suicide

Kanye West’s new album is “more gospel than pop” and “more black than white”, and it comes with a rap verse by Kanye West himself. The artist who is now known as Yeezy, West has a gospel album in his future, but that doesn’t mean he’s trying to be a black icon in the same way that his mentor, Bob Dylan, is. In the interview he gave on Good Morning America, West talked about his gospel influences, religion, and his new album ‘Jesus Is King’.

Jesus Is King is definitely more gospel than pop

“I’m trying to make this record the best gospel album ever,” said Kanye West. “There’s some gospel stuff that’s on my album that I want to keep because it’s gospel, but there’s also a gospel-influenced hip-hop track on Jesus Is King that I’ve been talking about.” “If I had a lot of time I would do a gospel album, but I’m trying to make it more gospel than pop,” he added.

“It’s more gospel than pop. I mean, that’s not saying there isn’t a pop element. It’s just there’s more gospel on Jesus Is King than there is on most pop records, and if you take that gospel from a gospel album and put it on a pop album it will sound completely different.” “A lot of the rap stuff is gospel and I want to incorporate that into my music,” West continued. “I do not want to try to copy the whole gospel sound like the gospel artist, the artist that uses gospel that was on Bob Dylan’s first album. That’s the same thing I do on Jesus Is King. When I rap on Jesus Is King I don’t want to be the same Bob Dylan that uses the gospel that’s on his first album.”

Kanye West has been making music since he was nine years old, he said, when he was “listening to gospel records”. “I was listening to gospel music,” he said. “I grew up in South Central, I was born in the United States, I was raised a Christian, and the church had a big influence on my life.” “I grew up listening to gospel music. I was raised a Christian, I grew up in the church, but when I was a kid I was listening to gospel records, and now I’m a grown man and I have my own opinions on what my faith is,” he said.

He said he grew up wanting to be a rapper, which he says he began doing at the age of 14. “I want to be an artist. If I had to make one record right now, that would be my gospel album,” West said. “It’s more gospel than pop, but I will keep that rap element in there.” “It’s more gospel than pop.” “It’s more gospel than pop.”
headline: Kanye West says “Jesus Is King”. Here’s why that matters

In a conversation with a journalist from The Times of London, Elon Musk said that Twitter has played a role in the U.S. election campaign.

The exchange took place between Musk and The Times’s James Risen, at the Tesla tech conference in Los Angeles.

Read full article below:

A conversation with James Risen, the reporter from The Times of London, was interrupted by a question from Elon Musk.

It started with a discussion of a tweet by @elonmusk: “Twitter is basically a big data dump of all the data coming from my Twitter account, including the data from my iPhone. I just got a new iPhone a few weeks ago. So I thought I’d see if it was really as bad as I thought.”

Risen pressed the argument that the “data dump” was really a searchable database on the site: “So if it doesn’t really reflect the activity of my Twitter account, is it as accurate as I think it is?”

“Well I think it’s absolutely accurate,” Musk said. “But the real question is how accurate is Twitter?”

“How accurate are they?” Risen countered.

Musk replied: “I don’t really care that you’re trying to give me the answer, but the reality is that if you actually look at my Twitter feeds, you would find that I’ve been saying about the election for a year and a half now.”

“I can’t argue with that,” Risen replied.

“Well that’s actually what the whole thing is,” Musk replied. “It’s really an ongoing series of posts that are really being shared on Twitter. So it’s an ongoing search.”

“This is not a search,” Risen said. “This is an ongoing series of posts that are being shared on Twitter.”

“Well, that’s an honest point, but the truth is that the amount of information that is being shared on Twitter is so minute and so small that it really doesn’t reflect the activity of my Twitter feed. So the truth is, this is an ongoing series of posts that are being shared on Twitter.”

“I can’t argue with that,” Risen said.

“This is an ongoing series of posts that are being shared on Twitter,” Musk said, “which is absolutely accurate.”

Risen said he tried to ask about his own posts, and received no response.

“The reality is,” Musk said, “the more I say about it, the less I can answer.”

Musk said he’d been looking at how many people were tweeting at him and how many tweets he could see for himself.

“And I was actually surprised at how many people didn’t have any Twitter accounts at all,” Musk said. “And I thought that this was really going to be some kind of weird thing that I was seeing.”
headline: Musk says Twitter interfered in elections

In the weeks following the shocking defeat of the All Blacks in the last-minute Super 8s, Tom McDonnell’s journey up the Newbridge rugby field has led him to the spotlight.

Now, with the Super Rugby tournament in progress, the former Springboks flanker, who plays a key role in the scrum, has emerged as a contender for the best player in Super Rugby.

McDonnell, who was named as Super Rugby’s best player in the competition’s inaugural year, has been out in front of the media since the contest against the All Blacks and has been the subject of many a social media hashtag and internet post, but his rise to the top of the Super Rugby pecking order has taken a huge leap in the last week.

The man he is chasing is none other than the All Blacks’ captain and a man who has been on the field in action for New Zealand at all three Grand Slam tournaments.

Having arrived in Auckland for the last two Super Rugby tournaments, McDonnell said this morning that there is no one he is more looking forward to meeting in the Super Rugby competition.

“It’s an incredible honour to be chosen as best in the competition, but as I have always said, I can’t wait to be a part of this great and exciting world game.

“The challenge from the moment I arrived in Auckland has been huge, but for myself and the rest of the backline to do their best, the All Blacks will be there.”

Having captained the All Blacks to two World Cup quarter-finals and a semi-final in New Zealand, there is a real feeling of respect and admiration that comes with McDonnell and his No.8 jersey.

“It’s an honour to be picked to be Captain, and I’m not the only one in that group. There are a lot of great players in that group. I can’t wait to be a part of it.

“They are all incredibly good rugby players and deserve their opportunity.”

And so it is with a sense of anticipation that McDonnell has emerged as the player to be chosen in the most important position in the game.

The All Blacks will also be determined to find a way past the All Blacks’ defensive unit in Newbridge, and McDonnell is one of the few players capable of doing exactly that.

“They are the most defensive team, and they make you work for everything in those games,” he explained.

“If they are playing to the high balls, it’s not easy to play. They know this and they make you work for it, so there are a few times I have come out to challenge for it.

“I am trying to make sure I am doing my best for the team, and hopefully I am able to do that this year.”

The All Blacks’ new coach, Steve Hansen, believes that the New Zealand backline is set to be the biggest strength in Super Rugby.

With the competition due to continue until the end of the next season, there is a real feeling of excitement around New Zealand that there will be a new era in the game.

Sweden’s lockdown is showing us the flaws in our own government’s over-reach.

In an article for BBC News, Anna Moberg and Johanna Koskova look at the Swedish lockdown. They explain that Sweden’s new lockdown was not the result of any real ‘scare’. Instead, it has been a response to the government’s own overreach.

The new lock-down was not as simple as turning the power off – it required that the entire country was locked down.

Sweden has become the biggest exporter of ‘food and medicine’ to the rest of the world, and the country has lost about 12,000 businesses in the process.

The lockdown was intended to be a means to protect all the residents of Sweden – not just the wealthy.

Many Swedes did not even realise that this was a lockdown.

The lockdown in Sweden has been criticised for the fact that it has made the lockdown even more of a burden on the people of the country.

According to a survey conducted by Ipsos, only 4% of respondents said they were in favour of the lockdown, which is a far smaller percentage than the 7% who were against the lockdown.

The fact that the government is being forced to act is even more of a problem for the politicians who have been making a lot of money off people’s fears.

The lockdown has also created a lot of uncertainty as to when the lockdown will be lifted.

Sweden’s lockdown has shown us the flaws in our own government’s over-reach and the fact that the government has not yet realised that the lockdown has become an unnecessary burden on the people of the country.

The lockdown in Sweden has shown us that when we lock ourselves out of our homes, we can’t expect society to be any less vulnerable.

What do you think? Do you think Sweden’s lockdown is a good thing for society? Are you in favour of a lockdown? Let us know in the comments below.

I am so sorry you had to witness that and feel like you were there. But as I am sure you are well aware, such a lockdown would put even more pressure on the economy. In a situation like that, no one wants to see the economy drop.

The economy of a country is dependent on the economy of a neighbor. They do not work together, they do not get along with each other, they do not spend together.

Sweden has no problems with the economic cooperation between the two countries. It’s the fact that the economy of one country depends on that of the other that has become a problem.

It’s true that the economy of Sweden depends on the economy of other countries, but the economy of Sweden depends on the economy of other countries because this way everyone can get a good price on Swedish goods.

When goods are not priced properly, then people buy cheaper products from other countries. This then has a knock on effect for the economic growth of the countries which buy the goods from Sweden. This is the reason for Sweden’s problem with the economy.

We should all realize that the lockdown in Sweden did not happen in a sudden crisis. The country’s economy has grown slowly since the lockdown began.
headline: Does Sweden show we need a lockdown against the spread of government over-reach?

MOSCOW, October 28, 2013 (RIA Novosti) – Ukrainian police have arrested a woman who was allegedly involved in a brutal assault on a man in the country’s main refugee center near the city of Kherson.

The suspect, Olena Khvostenko, 20, of Kiev, appeared in a Kherson court on October 25 on charges of murder and aggravated assault. She has confessed to the crime and was sentenced to eight years in jail.

According to the prosecution, Olena and a group of her friends, who were visiting the city’s main refugee center, were taking part in a drunken party when they were confronted by a man who had been seeking asylum at the center. As a result, the suspects were forced to flee the scene and then attacked the person.

As an explanation for the brutal attack, the prosecution said that Olena “decided to throw a punch in the face of the man as a signal that she did not want to have a conversation with him, and the man reacted and hit her.”

The prosecution alleged that Khvostenko also committed aggravated assault on the victim and tried to strangle him, which is why she was arrested on October 25.

According to the prosecution, Khvostenko had a long criminal history of violence, including assault and robbery, and was arrested after the incident.

“I was born in Ukraine and was brought here as a child and didn’t see this,” a 20-year-old refugee from Kherson told RIA Novosti. “I did not know that such things happen. The authorities should stop to help.”

The victim of the assault, who is still in a critical condition, has been identified by the International Organization for Migration as Dmytro Pachonetski, of Kharkiv, who was robbed, beaten and dragged along the street in the Kherson district.

The refugee center in Kherson is also called the International Refugee Centre, which is home to about 5,000 asylum seekers in various stages of the application process.

The International Organization for Migration says that the center receives thousands of asylum seekers every year.

A special team from the Kherson Prosecutor’s Office will investigate the case.

Preliminary information shows that the suspect arrived at the center on September 19 and applied for asylum, the local newspaper Krasnaya Pravda reported, quoting the police.

The investigation is ongoing and there is no mention about the suspect having had anything to do with the violent attack, Krasnaya Pravda said.

“It is a strange case because it is not clear what the suspect was doing in the center,” a source from the office of the Russian prosecutor in Ukraine said.

The source said that the case has been closed due to lack of evidence.

The suspect is a 40-year-old woman from the Dnipro region who is in court for the first time. She has only one prior conviction from 2003. The other arrests were made during the investigation of a different case.

Khvostenko was also arrested in Kiev, and has a criminal history dating back to 2008.
headline: Ukrainian charged in connection with fatal assault on man in asylum centre

Ireland is not a haven from the consequences of human rights abuse and it certainly won’t be a haven for refugees.

However, it is a haven for asylum seekers, who are fleeing from Syria and other Middle Eastern states.

An IHREC ruling last month that refugee families should be granted the same protection as British residents – and are therefore not entitled to housing rights – is a landmark judgment that will be hard to overturn by the courts.

A group of civil society groups is calling for the case to be re-opened.

IHREC is Ireland’s refugee resettlement scheme and the charity says it has a “moral and legal duty” to “ensure that those affected are treated in accordance with human rights and in the circumstances in which they have been put in, and that there are no unintended consequences.”

The case has been criticised by a number of human rights groups who have called for the courts to throw the case out.

“The IHREC case is an outlier,” said Niamh Ni Dheargains.

“It is a court of law in Ireland which has found a precedent to apply and it is now set to be followed elsewhere,” she added.

“This is not a refugee situation in which it is possible to ‘throw out’ the principle of a right to housing.”

It has been suggested that the case is being used to justify the closure of the so-called “Right To Housing” scheme (RTH).

RTH was launched in 2009 by then Labour Party leader Brendan Howlin.

It was set up in the wake of the Syrian crisis as an alternative to the “welcoming centres” set up in cities such as Birmingham.

The policy aimed to stop the arrival of refugees into “welcoming centres” which were “inherently abusive”.

It was created to protect the rights of those seeking asylum in Europe, including families in Dublin, who were being pushed out in the Mediterranean on a weekly basis.

The main aim was to ensure that refugees were not being placed “in an environment where their basic human rights and entitlements are violated,” according to the IHREC website.

Since its inception, the RTH scheme has received almost €3 billion from the European Union.

However, in 2014, following a legal challenge by the Legal Aid Board, the Dublin city council agreed to the closure of all the centres in order to reduce waiting lists for housing in Dublin city.

But while the IHREC case is still before the courts, it has raised concerns that some of the centres have since been reopened.

The legal battle between the IHREC and Legal Aid Board began in 2014, when the IHREC won a landmark case in the High Court which found that some of the Dublin centres were in breach of the Human Rights Act.

In the wake of that ruling, the Dublin city council agreed to the closure of the centres, but in November 2015, the EU issued a new ruling which said that centres located on the outskirts of the capital were not “welcoming centres” as the EU said.
headline: IHREC refugee case shows why “Right To Housing” would end badly

The Labour Party has just lost a parliamentary debate and its leader has resigned, just weeks after calling for the party to distance itself from the Irish-Caribbean community.

The resignation of Fianna Fáil’s Cllr John deignan (pictured) as Taoiseach ends a parliamentary debate on the issue of immigration. Fianna Fáil voted against the motion.

The party’s deputy leader, who is in charge of the party’s parliamentary party, also resigned, saying it was “detached from ordinary person.”

The party is due to hold its annual general meeting on Tuesday, where it may choose another party leader.

“I’m not going to sit down for the sake of it,” Cllr Deignan told the Irish Times. “The party is detached from ordinary person. We need to move on and focus on policies and the direction our country is heading.”

He added: “I would not want this to be my legacy. I would want to be seen to be an ordinary person, not a politician.”

The Taoiseach was reacting to the Fianna Fáil motion tabled by Cllr Deignan on Wednesday, in which he called for the party to “re-focus on policies and the direction our country is heading”.

Speaking during a committee meeting, Cllr Deignan said that the Fianna Fáil parliamentary party’s position on the issue had “not changed.”

He said the party had voted against the motion but he added that he “wouldn’t want to resign” in the wake of the party’s loss.

Cllr Deignan also criticised the party’s “overly public” position on the issue of immigration.

“This debate that happened recently has created a lot of divisions and caused the party to lose members,” he said. “I feel a need to point out that the majority of the people who voted against this motion are not ordinary members of the party.”

In response, Cllr Deignan said that his party had “no issues with the current arrangements of immigration.”

The issue of immigration has been on the party’s agenda since 2006, he added, saying it had always been in the “party’s long-term strategy to reduce the number of immigrants coming to this country.”

On Wednesday night, Fianna Fáil said that it had also voted against the motion, adding that it was concerned by the extent to which this issue was being politicised.

The party also said that it had opposed the motion because it was “not the right time to be discussing this issue at the moment.”

“We have not been able to get enough members for the party to be able to take part in the debate,” Cllr Deignan said.

“I do feel the debate is not the right time and we will not take part in it.”
headline: Fianna Fáil Cllr who criticised immigration policy resigns, says party “detached from ordinary person”

The European Union (EU) has today (Friday, 21 March) adopted a resolution to amend the Copyright Directive to include provisions for online censorship. The resolution states that the Directive “shall not prevent the collection, storage, storage of information on the Internet, as well as the distribution of that information by Internet service providers,” and “does not constitute an infringement of the freedom of expression, which, as defined in article 16(4) of the European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, does not extend to information concerning illegal activities of public authorities.” The report from the Committee on Civil Liberties of the European Parliament (ECL) on the adoption of the resolution (which is here) explains why the EU decided to go along with the proposed amendments to the Copyright Directive and the Directive on the Protection of Copyrights and Related Rights. The Committee on Civil Liberties has now been asked to “consider how best to ensure that, on the basis of the Directive, online platforms which have the right to use the content of communications are not in a position of being able to block access to information they have the right to use,” as well as to “study the use of internet filtering and the implementation of the proposed measures” and “provide advice to Member States.” The ECL Committee on Civil Liberties was first to propose a measure against online filtering by Internet service providers (ISPs) in a resolution (see here).

The news report also provides links to a short article on the Committee on Civil Liberties website, and to the ECL Committee’s web page.

The Committee on Civil Liberties is an advisory body to the Committee on Fundamental Rights of the EU parliament. Members of the Committee on Civil Liberties can be contacted by e-mail: civil-liberties@parliament.eu.

To find out more about this topic, please see this summary.

This summary was updated on 30 April 2020.

The Copyright Directive and the Directive on the Protection of Copyrights and Related Rights (the “CD/DR” Directive) were adopted by the European Parliament on 3 November 2017. The Directive aims to improve online copyright protection. One aspect of the Directive is the prohibition of filtering by Internet service providers (ISPs). The Directive requires that ISPs are to have “access to a complete set of metadata” for all traffic that they send out. It is not clear whether this is in fact the case, and it is not stated clearly whether this means that ISPs should have access to the entire IP-address database of every website they serve. The Directive also creates a number of new rights and obligations for Internet platforms, which means that ISPs must not block access to websites (i.e., the ‘blocking’ of content). The Directive applies to providers of the Internet, and therefore to ISPs. It was adopted in an extremely short period of time after the adoption of the Digital Single Market directive in the EU in 2004.

It is estimated that there are about 25,000 companies operating as ISPs in the EU, and their number is expected to grow. The adoption of the Directive represents a major step in the EU towards the creation of a single legal market for online content. However, the Directive is not without criticism.
headline: EU to Use COVID Pass Sequel for Online Censorship

The UK population is still ageing rapidly. So is the economy, and if the growth rate is not increasing, it is falling. So are the wages of the young and the middle class. In fact, the number of people in work is falling.

But the question of what’s happening to the UK’s population is far from being settled. The last census was in 2011 and revealed that the number of people living in the UK was falling by an astounding 25.1%.

The decline in the number of UK nationals has been particularly marked among the young, with a drop of almost 20% between the 2001 and 2011 censuses. That decline is due to an ageing population that is growing rapidly, with a fall of over 10% between 2011 and 2015. That drop is even more marked among the elderly, with a fall of 17% over the same time period.

Even the latest census showed that the working age population is shrinking. In 2017, the number of people aged 16 or over living in the UK was just 7.7 million, or 2.4% of the population. That is the lowest number since the official 2010 Census, which was the first to ask about people aged 65 and over.

With the population ageing, there is also a corresponding fall in the birth rate, which has been falling steadily since the 1970s. Since 2012, the average number of births per woman has fallen from about 26.9 to 22.3. That falls from the mid 1990s, when it averaged 32.1 births per woman.

As a result of these trends, the number of children born in the UK is expected to fall by another 10% by 2030. That is the same as the annual reduction in the number of children born in the UK since the second half of the 20th century.

The decline in the UK birth rate is not the only factor affecting the number of children born in the UK, however. The ageing population is also contributing to an increase in the number of people with a low social status, such as those on benefits or in paid employment, or those on low pay.

The number of people with a low social status is also expected to rise in future, as the Government is introducing “workfare” to tackle the problem of low pay and high unemployment among this group.

The number of people on low pay has been rising steadily in recent years, as has the number of people on benefits. The number of people on benefit fell from 7.2 million in the autumn of 2016 to 7.1 million in the spring of 2017, then grew again to 8.2 million in the autumn of 2017. By 2020, however, this number will be about 6.5 million, as benefit claimants move into private sector employment.

In the past year, the number of people on low pay has risen by 8.2% to 8.5 million. The number of people on benefits has increased by 10.5% to 12.2 million. The number of people with low social status has increased by 6.2% to 6.8 million.

However, even as the number of people on low pay and benefits grows, there is also a fall in the number of people in work. The number of people in work fell by 2.4% over the period 2013 to 2016.
headline: Are we entering an age of decay as birth rates fall?

China reportedly has slapped the Vatican in the face, as it tries to put into effect a controversial agreement that would let the Vatican pay a portion of its debt to the government.

According to a leaked internal document, China’s central bank has approved the move. The document, dated February 11, 2016, was seen by the Vatican’s envoy to China, Monsignor Pietro Parolin, who is the Vatican’s representative in China. The document was obtained and published by CNA earlier this week.

It said the Beijing central bank “exerted a degree of pressure” on the Vatican to accept the “deal”.

The document also said China would not “reward” the Vatican for paying off the Vatican’s debts by making the Vatican a “favourable partner”.

The agreement would mean that the Chinese central bank would issue a bond, called a “tender”, for up to 50 billion renminbi (US$15 billion) of “tribute”, at par with its own borrowing.

The document says the “tender” is issued by the central bank for the Vatican’s debt.

The document also says that the Vatican could have to accept the tender if it does not agree to reduce its debt to the Chinese government.

The Vatican has been under pressure to accept the deal for some time, and is seeking to show that it can pay off its debts.

On January 9, the Chinese government announced that it had reached an agreement with the Vatican, under which the Vatican would pay a certain percentage of its debt, and China would buy the remaining 60% of the debt.

The deal would make the Vatican a “favourable partner”, but would not be a “reward”.

The Vatican has insisted that it would not accept the deal unless it also agreed to make the Vatican a “favourable partner”.

This is because China has stated that it believes the Vatican is not a partner.

The Vatican has also expressed fears that accepting the deal may result in a major break with the Vatican’s traditional support for the Vatican’s Catholic Church in the fight against the Falun Gong movement.

The deal has been controversial in the past for the fact that it would require the Vatican to pay up the Vatican’s debt of more than $1.9 billion.

It is widely believed that China’s central bank is acting in an attempt to cut the Vatican out of its budget and thus ensure that China does not feel the impact of the debt.

The Vatican’s debt is currently around $7 billion.

If the debt is not paid off before the end of 2018, the Vatican may have to give up the right to appoint a papal consul in China, and also its right to nominate two bishops who are in China on official visits.

The deal has prompted anger from Catholic officials and groups in China, as well as concern from many observers in the U.S. and internationally.

11 Dec, 2016

by JONATHAN WICKHAM

A 17-year-old schoolgirl assaulted by a black classmate has been called to account by an Irish judge who is expected to decide the issue within weeks.

The student, whose identity is not being revealed, was attacked by the classmate, who punched the girl on the back of the head, knocking her unconscious, before running away. The girl’s friends were arrested but have now been released.

Last Tuesday, a High Court judge called the boy a “lout” and said the girl’s parents had asked for an apology. The school has said it will hold a discussion with the boy and the girl’s parents.

Last month, the boy had posted a Snapchat message under the name “Kai” that he called “a racist cunt”, and said “I need to be removed” on another message that appeared to include racial abuse. The boy had also sent a Facebook message that read “This is not how I thought my life would end”.

Judge John O’Neill told the boy he needed to apologise to the girl’s family as well as to the girl. “If the girl’s family had apologised to you and you apologised to her family, then I think you would have been forgiven. But what is not acceptable is what the girl’s family has done to her,” the judge said.

Mr Justice O’Neill said he was in no doubt the school had behaved badly but had not behaved badly enough.

“The school has apologised to the school’s principal, the police, the girl’s family, and the girl herself,” he said. “I don’t know why the girl’s family have not apologised to the girl and the boy to the boy.”

He said there was evidence the school would “never be safe for the girl” and that the school needed to be reformed. The school must “act to improve its behaviour in the future and, if necessary, put itself out of business by changing its policies”, he said.

He said “behaviour is not what the school is about. Behaviour is the behaviour of everyone in the school”.

“The school’s behaviour is not the behaviour of the girl’s family. They are being rude and disrespectful but they are not behaving in an inappropriate way”.

He said “one of the school’s members came in and told the girl’s father the girl’s behaviour was unacceptable”. “This member of the school’s administration should also come and apologise to the girl’s family,” the judge said.

He said the boy’s actions were “more likely than not” to have resulted in the girl being punched unconscious. “What would have happened had there been no incident would have been much more serious,” he said.

He said the school had been put on notice about “the seriousness of the incidents”.
headline: School asked student (13) if she had said anything racist after she was assaulted by black classmate

“The Russian Defence Ministry, in a statement published online on Sunday, claimed the aerial attack on the Romanian village of Ghencea. According to the ministry, it targeted a residential building on the site of the local police station,” the Romanian site, RENTEFONTE, reports.

“The Russian Defence Ministry’s statement is an effort to portray the incident as being an act of aggression carried out by the Russian Armed Forces in violation of international law, and is in fact a distortion of the facts by the ‘Russian media’,” the article continues.

The site adds that Romanian sources deny the ministry’s claim.

“On Sunday, the Russian Ministry of Defence released a statement which denied that it had any involvement in the ‘provocation’. It also claimed that the ‘attack’ was a technical and professional one carried out by a Russian Helicopter Company and was not intended to harm the civilian population.”

“The statement was published in a Russian-language news website, The RIA Novosti, which was also the first to report the fact that the Russian military had launched a large-scale strike on the village.”

According to RENTEFONTE, the incident occurred at around 10am local time on Sunday.

The Russian military told RENTEFONTE that the assault was in response to a request by the local police station to install electronic devices in the village.

“The Russian Air Force is involved in a complex military operation in the region of the Ghencea, which has become an area of tension in the region between Russia and the NATO member countries.”

“The Russian military claims that it responded to a request from the local police station to install electronic devices in Ghencea, a small village in the region of the Black Sea, after the military had warned the police station that it would be responsible for any threats to its safety.”

“The Russian military and the local authorities in the village agreed to make the necessary arrangements to protect the police station’s staff and residents from harm,” the Russian military says.

RENTEFONTE adds that the site has also confirmed that the Russian military “conducted a training exercise near the area of the incident.”

“This type of exercise is conducted to determine if there are any technical errors or other mistakes that could have led to the loss of life.”

According to the site, the Russian military said that the military command received an alert, which was then followed by an “aerial strike” by a helicopter.

“In a statement, the Russian military said the helicopter was carrying three to five bombs. The military said the helicopter landed on the roof of a nearby building, which it claimed was a residence belonging to the chief of a small town in the region.”

“The Russian military added that the operation began as a search-and-rescue operation and then took over as a military exercise, ‘for the purpose of learning about the combat capabilities and equipment of the Russian Armed Forces in the area.

The fourth largest cocaine consumption country in the world is Ireland, which is also the second largest cocaine user in the world, with the third highest per capita consumption rate.

The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) has drawn up a new report on cocaine consumption and addiction which found that most people from the European Union (EU) and the Nordic countries use cocaine in the same way as they do in Ireland.

A major reason for this is that most cocaine users are young people between 15 and 35 years of age, who are not yet in the position to buy large amounts of the drug.

Another factor that affects cocaine consumption in the EU and the Nordic countries is that many young people are now using synthetic cocaine (a mixture of cocaine and additives like caffeine or ephedrine, which do not affect the psychoactive properties of the drug), which is cheaper than the cocaine that the young people are used to.

While in Europe and Scandinavia, cocaine was first produced in the 1970s, cocaine use and addiction has been on the rise since the 1990s, with most users coming from the former Soviet Union, China, and the Middle East.

The UNODC said it was not aware of any European country that has not reported significant increase in cocaine consumption in recent years.

The report, published on 26 February, says the drug has become a major problem in many African and Latin American countries.

It said that the consumption of cocaine in the EU has increased by 6.5 per cent in 2014, the third largest increase in the past five years. In the EU, cocaine was the second most consumed drug in 2014 after cannabis, followed by ecstasy.

The report said that consumption has increased in the Nordic countries, particularly in the Nordic countries of Denmark, Norway and Sweden.

In Denmark, consumption has increased for both males and females by 22.2 per cent, while consumption among women increased by 14.6 per cent.

In Norway, consumption has increased for both males and females by 17.7 per cent, while consumption among women increased by 13.2 per cent.

In Sweden, consumption has increased for both males and females by 26.8 per cent, while consumption among women increased by 24.5 per cent.

The report said that the consumption of cocaine has increased in the Nordic countries because of the “increasingly prominent use of cocaine among young adults, with increased usage particularly among young males and females.”

The report said that there was also a significant rise in cocaine use among young people in the EU, particularly in Greece, Italy and France.

It said that the use of cocaine in Greece had increased by 33.3 per cent, and that consumption had increased by 40 per cent in Italy.

The report says that consumption of cocaine in France is among the highest in Europe, with consumption increasing by 27 per cent in 2014.

The report says the drugs are highly addictive and that the high level of use among young people means that more people are trying them.

The report also says that there was an increase in cocaine use in Finland in 2014, although it did not specify where this was.

While cocaine consumption in Italy has declined in the past five years, it increased by 20.1 per cent in the year to 2014.

“An external review of a claim of wrongful termination is being carried out by the Health Service Executive.”

In a press release sent out late on Friday, the HSE confirmed that external reviews will be carried out in relation to three separate cases of terminations where the claims have been made by women who were wrongly given the wrong diagnosis for terminations. The HSE has been working with the Women’s Health Trust to ensure that all appropriate procedures have been carried out in relation to these cases.

The HSE is fully aware of the complex and complex nature of a medical matter involving multiple conditions. This is why it is taking the time to undertake this external review and review procedures. The review, which is also being conducted in partnership with the Women’s Health Trust, is being carried out with the full and free consent of the parties concerned – that is, the women affected.

The HSE has always been a champion of women’s rights, and has for decades ensured that those who would attempt to obtain a termination of pregnancy should have the correct medical diagnosis. Indeed, the HSE’s Code of Practice on the use of its services allows for the use of alternative diagnoses in cases where the proper diagnosis has been obtained.

The review of each of the three cases involves a medical professional who is undertaking a review of a case. This medical professional has no involvement whatsoever in the case itself. The review itself will examine the medical case in question, as well as any evidence gathered from the patient, including any notes and notes that may have been made by the patient.

The HSE has been working with the Women’s Health Trust throughout the review process. The review will not have any impact on either party’s work or activity within the health sector, nor on their own work or work activities.

We have no doubt that the external review will be carried out with the full and free consent of the parties concerned. It is important to remember that the process is being undertaken in partnership, and that the HSE and the Women’s Health Trust will not be part of this external review.

The HSE has received a number of submissions regarding the review process and it is important that these be received as soon as possible. The review is being carried out in full cooperation with the Women’s Health Trust, and therefore we would urge all concerned to take this opportunity to read and consider what the HSE has said.

A separate consultation is being carried out by the Women’s Health Trust in relation to the case of an 18-year-old woman who was misdiagnosed as suffering from a terminal illness before her abortion was carried out. It is important that all of the women affected by this case, as well as the appropriate medical professionals involved, are consulted. It would also be helpful to hear from people who are directly involved in this particular case.

Women’s health professionals will be provided with all of the relevant information in the review process, and the appropriate HSE services are available to all involved.

As the HSE recognises, the process of carrying out external reviews is time-consuming and difficult. We are doing our utmost to make sure that we provide the highest standard of health care, and to provide the greatest level of patient privacy possible.

GRAINS, IRAN – The Palestinian Authority’s political leader, As’ad Abu Khalil, is reportedly being held in Iranian custody.

The PA’s official website reports:

“On the orders of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) and the Quds Force, Asad Abu Khalil has been detained in Iran and is currently in custody.”

The PA’s website further states:

“Iranian and Quds Force Qassim Soleimani, who is under the IRGC, ordered the IRGC to carry out the assassination of Asad Abu Khalil.”

The Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) is an arm of Iran’s Intelligence Ministry (MOI). It was established in 1961 by the Islamic Republic of Iran to carry out clandestine intelligence operations against foreign countries and individuals. It has been known since the 1980s as ‘the main force of national terrorism’.

Soleimani is a commander of Iran’s Quds Force.

The news of Abu Khalil’s arrest comes amidst ongoing tensions between Iran and the West.

In April of this year, Iran shot down a US surveillance drone.

In July, Iran attacked a military parade in Tehran.

In August, Iran blocked the UN from investigating an alleged gas attack in Syria.

In October, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it killed several top Iranian security personnel in Syria after a botched suicide bomb attack.

As such, the arrest of Abu Khalil comes at a time when many observers believe that the situation in Iran is on a knife-edge.

This is evidenced by an article published by the BBC this week:

“Iran’s president has reportedly made a decision to release political prisoners in the run-up to presidential elections next month in the latest sign of escalating tensions with the West.”

BBC reports that President Hassan Rouhani has said his government will release some political prisoners “in the run-up to upcoming elections”.

An Iran-funded news agency, Press TV, reported that Rouhani’s order came in a letter from his office, citing an unnamed official.

Iran is currently at war with the US-backed Lebanese Hezbollah. This week, Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commander Adel-Abbas Quds Force, who is also the president’s brother-in-law, was killed in an airstrike in Syria.

According to a report from the UK’s Daily Telegraph:

“Hezbollah has called for revenge and Iranian state media has warned of further attacks against the group. Iran has warned of further attacks against the group after an alleged chemical weapons attack in Syria last week.”

The Telegraph article goes on to note that this is the first time that Iranian President Hassan Rouhani has publicly expressed support for Hezbollah.

As such, the news that Iran is releasing Abu Khalil adds to the growing perception that Iran is pursuing political objectives in the Middle East.

Furthermore, Iran’s recent actions against the Syrian regime suggest that Iran is not averse to the use of proxy states. This may further increase the tension with the West.
headline: Political leader of Hamas, Ishmail Haniyah, killed in Iran missile strike

A new Irish Health Protection Agency (HPA) helpline will now be opened for calls about coronavirus and information on the COVID-19 pandemic.

The new helpline, helpline.irish.gov.uk, is operated by the Irish Mental Health Commission and is open for all emergencies on a 24/7 basis, with a dedicated team to respond 24 hours.

In a statement, the HPA said it’s been running the helpline as part of the government’s efforts to reduce coronavirus-related deaths, and that volunteers and callers are welcome to join.

The helpline is staffed by a dedicated team of mental health professionals from the HPA, the Department of Health and the Department of Education, and is run through a partnership with mental health charity Crisis Support Ireland. The helpline is open to all calls, however, it is not accessible to the general public.

The HPA has previously extended its opening hours to accommodate the pandemic.

By GARY O’DONNELL (GAA) The latest in a series of reports from women whose stories of abuse are being ignored by the Irish judiciary.

Last month, Judge Richard Ahern rejected the appeals of two women who claimed to have been victims of domestic violence by a man they thought they could trust. One woman, who cannot be named, wrote to the Irish Court of Justice (ICJ) in June 2017 after being repeatedly told by a judge that she has no authority to speak on her own behalf.

The second woman, who cannot be named, appealed against the decisions made against her by Judge Richard Ahern last year, stating that she had been subjected to “unlawful treatment” by a partner and her then-boyfriend.

The appeal was rejected by Judge Ahern on the grounds that the law does not allow for judicial review over the ICJ’s decision-making processes, although Ms Justice O’Driscoll agreed that the process should have included “clarification and clarification”.

“I have no hesitation in coming forward and testifying in my own defence. I know that my evidence would be credible and that I would be able to establish the truth of my allegations, even if this is not the preferred outcome.”

Another woman has called for an inquiry into what she claims are serious failings in the way that domestic violence cases are dealt with in the Irish courts.

The pay gap myth is one of the most common criticisms of feminist work. In the past, feminists have been accused of using “pay-as-you-go” models as a way of attacking women’s earnings and living standards.

That’s what has been happening for years now, even though recent figures have shown a small pay gap between women and men.

That’s despite the fact that the feminist movement has never been very successful in reducing the gap. For decades, feminists have tried to convince everyone that women earn less in comparison to men.

One of the most common myths among feminists is that the gender pay gap exists because men are paid less than women.

A recent study by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) published in the latest edition of the World Economic Outlook (WEO) shows that the gap in the world economy is actually lower in 2018 than it was in 2013.

This means that the gender pay gap has actually narrowed.

The report also revealed that the gender pay gap is now at its lowest level in the past 10 years.

The Gender Pay Gap in the World Economy (PDF) is the first study to present the data on the gender pay gap in the world.

The study was compiled by the International Monetary Fund with the help of more than a thousand economists and policy analysts, as well as women, men and other stakeholders who use the report in various different ways.

The researchers looked at how women’s average pay in several sectors changed over time. The report, which provides the latest data on the gender pay gap in the world, also presents the gender wage gap in the world.

In most of the countries examined, the gender wage gap has narrowed since 2013. This is the first time the gender pay gap in the world has been examined in a decade, and it confirms the general trend of narrowing the gender gap over the past years.

The study also includes the global gender wage gap, the ratio of women’s wages to men’s wages, the gender unemployment gap, and the gender pay gap in developing countries.

These figures show that the gender pay gap has also narrowed in many developing countries since 2013, as well as in most of the countries where the gender pay gap is smaller than 1 percent.

The study also shows that the gender pay gap continues to be much smaller in the advanced economies than it is in the developing countries.

This is also the first time that the gender pay gap in the advanced economies has been assessed since the World Economic Outlook started in 2000.

Women’s Economic Empowerment

The gender pay gap is one of the most popular topics among feminists in the recent years, partly because of the debate surrounding inequality in the workplace.

As a result, a lot of feminists have been working on ways of achieving gender equality.

One of the most popular methods of achieving gender equality is women’s economic empowerment. In this context, the gender pay gap is often viewed as the cost of having no paid work for women.

For example, some women are employed full-time but unable to afford a home, or earn a small salary, even though they are able to pay for their children’s education.
headline: Regina Doherty revives feminist pay gap myth

Today, the European Commission launched its “Democracy Shield”, an attempt to promote political parties with an opposition or independent platform. The goal is to ensure that opposition parties can get more support from voters and increase their participation.

The Commission also intends to increase the pressure on Member States to provide more space and space for independent parties. The Commission will also discuss a new EU-wide data protection regime and the possibilities to ensure that digital information does not remain private.

The Commission’s Democracy Shield programme was launched at the EU Parliament in Strasbourg, where EU ministers participated in a video conference about the EU’s work for the upcoming European elections in 2014. The programme is expected to last for the next two weeks, and will be updated regularly.

Democracy Shield is a new initiative by the European Commission that aims to help parties rise to the political forefront. The European Parliament and the Commission are working closely together to help the EU gain support for its work to ensure that citizens’ rights are protected. The Democracy Shield initiative aims to create a more active and visible EU-wide framework for political parties and ensure that these parties have the necessary space and funds to grow and attract voters.

In order to be successful, EU political parties will need to demonstrate that they are independent or have an opposition platform. Independent or opposition parties could become the second largest party in the country’s parliament (for example, in Sweden, they are the largest party in the Riksdag). A party could also become the second largest party in a European Parliament district (for example, in the Netherlands, they are the largest party in the Dutch parliament).

Democracy Shield has five tasks, which are:

A new financial mechanism will allow opposition parties to be financially independent.

A new online tool will help political parties to find voters and spread their message.

An online platform will be created that allows political parties to register and raise funds.

A project to increase the use of digital information and the development of a European data protection regime.

A strategy to increase the importance of independent political parties in Europe and Europe-wide and in all European political structures.

It is important to note that the EU has a different conception of democracy than that of the US. While the European Commission, the European Parliament, and EU member states have a clear goal of democracy, in the US and other Western democracies it is more important that politicians who are elected are seen to represent the majority views of the people.

The Democracy Shield programme also has an eye on the world beyond Europe. The Commission has a vision of a global European network of independent political parties.
headline: European Commission announces ‘Democracy Shield’
