An abortion doctor who faced harassment allegations last year has provided no tangible evidence of being victimised, despite the allegation made in the police statement.

The Irish Independent can now reveal that at the start of November 2015, Dr Michelle Fitzgerald, a specialist abortion provider, sent two of her own medical documents – a letter of resignation and a letter of resignation as a doctor – to Dr Michael O’Reilly, the Irish Minister for Health.

The letter of resignation – sent by email – stated:

“In accordance with the Department’s policy on sexual harassment and discrimination, I wish to resign as a qualified medical doctor from the Irish College of GPs. I have been contacted by various media organisations and am happy to comply.

I have no intention of rehashing the details of the complaints I lodged against Michael O’Reilly, Minister for Health in October 2015. All that I am doing is simply resigning my Irish College of GPs position in order to focus on my health and wellbeing.

I would ask to be removed as a witness in any future proceedings and that the case against me is withdrawn.”

The resignation letter was sent to the Minister in November 2015 and sent to her with an attached medical file, which also stated: “I have no intention of rehashing the details of the complaints I lodged against Michael O’Reilly, Minister for Health in October 2015.”

The letter was then emailed to the then Minister for Health in Ireland, Fianna Fáil, which she then signed.

This letter was sent in relation to the complaint lodged against the Minister by the Irish GPs’ Association, an umbrella organisation set up in March 2014.

This complaint was a response to a Freedom of Information request from the Irish GPs’ Association in 2014.

The letter stated that Dr Michael O’Reilly’s position as Minister for Health was a matter of “public interest” and asked to be removed from the complaint against him as a doctor.

It also stated: “I am sure that you will not wish to withdraw the complaint against the Minister, Michael O’Reilly. I would simply like to resign my position as a member of the Irish College of GPs.

I would like to ask that you remove me as a witness in any future proceedings, and that the complaint against the Minister, Michael O’Reilly, be withdrawn.”

The Irish GPs’ Association had then requested that Dr Michael O’Reilly provide them with a letter confirming his resignation as a Member of the College. The letter was received in November 2015 and sent in November 2015 to the Irish College. It stated:

“Dear Dr O’Reilly.

I am writing to confirm my resignation from the Irish College of GPs as a Member of the Irish College of GPs.

I have been informed that you are currently the Minister for Health in Ireland. I have been asked by the Irish GPs’ Association to resign my membership of the Irish College of GPs in order to focus on my health and wellbeing. I believe it is in the interests of my health to have a private and confidential medical practice.

The ICCL has called for the implementation of ‘human rights’ principles for people living with COVID-19, including a review of lockdown measures including the ban on non-essential travel and the restrictions on gatherings.

The ICCL, a human rights NGO, said that these human rights principles must be incorporated into the decision-making process from the earliest stages of the pandemic.

The ICCL has called for “human rights review” of the Covid lockdown measures as an essential part of the pandemic response, as well as for the government to provide “adequate, reliable and timely information to the public on the latest developments” on the pandemic.

The ICCL said that the Covid lockdown measures should not be considered as a ‘bail-in’ policy and that the people living with the virus should not ‘bond out’ to a specific community, a geographical area, or a specific group of people in the community.

The ICCL pointed to the lack of access to the health care system in many countries, which has resulted in the large scale mortality and morbidity of Covid-19, as well as the lack of public awareness.

The ICCL also called on the international community, governments and the international community’s partners to ensure that the people living with the virus “can live with a sense of dignity and without fear”.

The ICCL said that the “human rights of those in vulnerable situations, including the poor, the elderly and people with compromised immune systems” must be respected.

“The ICCL is calling for the international community to work with local people, and governments, in an effort to ensure that the people living with the virus can live with a sense of dignity and without fear.”

The ICCL said that “a review of Covid-19 lockdown measures is a vital part of the response” and that “a comprehensive review of the Covid-19 lockdown measures is essential, and must be an integral part of the international response”.

“These human rights principles must be incorporated into the decision-making process from the earliest stages of the pandemic.”

The ICCL said that the Covid-19 lockdown measures must be implemented “humanely, promptly and accurately”.

The ICCL also said that the Covid-19 lockdown measures should be implemented “by the time they are reviewed”, “with a public health emergency declared and a risk to public health in place”.

“The Covid-19 lockdown measures should not be considered a ‘bail-in’ policy and that the people living with the virus should not ‘bond out’ to a specific community, a geographical area, or a specific group of people in the community.”

“The Covid-19 lockdown measures should be implemented by the time they are reviewed,” said Ms. Toni Pienaar, Executive Director of the ICCL. “They must be implemented humanely, promptly and accurately”.

The ICCL said that the Covid-19 lockdown measures should be implemented “in a way that will preserve the human rights of the people in vulnerable situations”.
headline: ICCL calls for “human rights review” of Covid lockdown

Despite climate hysteria, it's a car-free country.

The latest news in Ireland's green agenda is that a new survey by car-sharing company Giro.ie shows that, for the first time ever, the country has fewer cars than it did a decade ago.

To be exact, the survey found that in 2013 there were 9.4 million vehicles on Ireland’s roads. This year there are 8.7 million vehicles, a decline of 1.1 million vehicles on the roads.

The figures are significant because, according to the latest statistics published by the Department of Transport, the Irish car ownership rate is just 8.3%. Of the 8.7 million cars on Irish roads, only 5.7% of these are owned by the public. The rest are private car ownership.

Giro.ie president Michael O’Neill told The Irish Times that there is a huge gulf between the current situation in Ireland and the “fantastic success” of the climate change movement.

“We have had a low car ownership rate for over 10 years,” O’Neill told the newspaper. “If you don’t drive a car, you’re still not in the car-free country.

“For the last 10 years, there has been a massive increase in public transport.

“When the transport minister announced that he was going to put money into public transport, nobody believed him and nobody understood why the minister was doing it.

“He then announced we will put $4 billion into public transport and the fact that he has put so much money into it, nobody understood.”

O’Neill said Giro.ie is now pushing for a public consultation on the matter and is calling for Ireland’s government to introduce a cap on the amount of vehicles on Irish roads.

“We are also calling for a cap on the car ownership rate to keep up with the rate we are seeing in the US,” he said.

The Irish Times (Ireland) contacted the Department of Transport for comment but was referred to the Department of Finance’s office in Dublin.

The Department of Transport said it does not comment on the views of its stakeholders.

“We are delighted to see that the car ownership rate in Ireland has returned to levels that were 10 years ago.

“When the Department of Transport published its latest statistics, the Irish car ownership rate was 8.3% of the total number of cars on Irish roads in 2013, which is well below the rate found in the first decade of the 21st century.

“Ireland’s car ownership rate, when compared with that of other EU countries, was also one of the lowest in the OECD countries.”

Giro.ie president Michael O’Neill, on the road, Dublin. Image: Giro.ie

“At Giro.ie, our focus is on the car-free country. The car-free policy is already in place in Ireland, where every car will be re-registered and taxed on its return to road.

“Giro.ie members will be able to use their own cars and take them wherever they want.
headline: Despite Climate Hysteria, figures show Ireland has low car ownership rate

Green taxes, renewable energies and EU emissions trading schemes have combined to create an unprecedented spike in fuel prices across Europe.

It is the most expensive year for Europe’s fuel supply, and it comes amid the biggest price rise in history. It also follows a decade of price spikes and falls, which has highlighted the importance of energy efficiency across Europe.

The energy crisis is not only affecting household consumers. As the price of oil keeps increasing and carbon emissions continue to rise, the EU has a responsibility to address the issue. But there is only so much energy efficiency that can be done with the EU’s limited resource and technology.

The energy market is now being transformed in a way that will reduce emissions and, crucially, price fuel at a level that can be sustained for generations. With its low-emissions strategy, the EU is trying to help make a difference.

The price of gas is now the most expensive in Europe’s history and is also rising rapidly in some countries, most notably the UK, where a one-cent rise in price a week results in a one-third increase in prices.

The gas price rise comes on the heels of a decade of price spikes and falls, which has highlighted the importance of energy efficiency across Europe.

In 2009 and 2010, the price of gas increased by more than three and one-half times the price of oil, respectively, during the crisis. The average price of gas in 2012 (the latest data available) was $1.36 per UK litre. In London, it rose to $1.68.

That’s an increase of nearly 70 per cent – a fivefold increase.

The government’s response has been to spend billions of pounds on infrastructure, such as new pipelines, to transport gas to Europe. But these will only reduce demand for petrol. As the price of gas increases, the energy industry will need to find other ways to generate electricity.

In 2011, the EU agreed the first phase of the Electricity Market Operator’s (EMO) ESM project. The objective of the project was to create a single European market for electricity. The ESM project is being overseen by the European Commission, but it has been supported by the EU’s European Investment Bank (EIB).

Over the last decade, the EU has made it a priority to reduce emissions by creating a single energy market. The European Parliament has also passed legislation (the Emission Trading Scheme) that allows for the use of carbon prices to limit emissions in the European Union.

But the ESM’s impact on the European economy has been mixed. The ESM has been praised for its impact on emissions, but it has not been able to deliver on its emissions reduction goals.

As the price of gas increases, it is now becoming harder to meet these emission reduction goals.

“The ESM has not been a success,” said Toni Calvarese, chief economist at the think tank Ecofin. “What we would like is a carbon price that is based on the real-world cost, rather than the price we paid during the crisis.”

The EU is under pressure to do more to cut emissions.
headline: How European green policies caused the energy crisis

For the first time, political leaders face the dilemma of how to advance a pro-European agenda without being seen as ‘anti-Europe’. There are a lot of different things people are looking at and what people are saying about Brexit is a lot different from what the political elite is saying about Brexit. This is because political leaders are getting more and more concerned with what people think than what people are thinking.

The new Government now has a clear mandate and is committed to delivering a new package of Government reforms. The aim of the new package is to make the Irish economy more flexible, to take advantage of the current opportunities and to reduce our reliance on the Euro.

My vision of the new package is to deliver a new relationship between business and government that makes sense for Ireland, and is capable of being successfully implemented. The Government of Ireland has made a commitment to improve the quality of public services and to reduce the impact of inequalities. We will increase the funding available for essential public services and the level of investment in education and research.

On April 9, hundreds of farmers across Ireland demonstrated in support of their rural communities, as a protest action taken by the Irish Farmers’ Union (IFAU) continues in Dublin. It is a continuation of a protest action which had been launched a day earlier. This time, the actions have also attracted the support of a number of leading farmers’ organisations, including the Irish Farmers’ Federation and the National Farmers’ Federation. The IFAU’s protest actions are scheduled to take place in the coming weeks in other rural communities across Ireland, while this week the farmers will also host a public protest at their national conference at Liffey Park on May 22nd.

The protest actions today were carried out by farmers from across the country who are seeking to ensure that they are well represented on the European market. The farmers gathered this morning in the city to protest the Government’s decision to bring in new rules to bring the market under the EU Directives. The new rules are coming into force from 1 May 2016. These rules are designed to force Irish farmers to sell their products on the EU market.

“These new rules are designed to force Irish farmers to sell their products on the EU market. This is simply a government attempt to make us part of the EU,” said IFAU President, Peter Fitzpatrick. “These rules are clearly a back door to the EU and they should not be implemented. The government should not introduce these new rules in Ireland without consulting the people of Ireland.”

The protestors today met at the IFAU’s Dublin headquarters to discuss their concerns with the Minister for Agriculture, Simon Coveney.

The Minister for Agriculture, Simon Coveney was informed of the protest actions on April 9th. He was also informed of the protesters today and he told the protestors that he had spoken to the Minister and there had been no further comment from the government.

In a statement, Coveney said: “I have had a meeting with our farmers yesterday. I have no intention of taking any further action on this matter. However, I have assured them that I am very clear in my position about the need to consult the people of Ireland. I am fully supportive of their concerns and will continue to do so,” said the Minister.

“The government has been making it very clear that the rules that will be brought in to force Irish farmers to sell their products on the EU market are a back door to the EU. The rules are being introduced just before we are about to embark on the autumnal harvest in Ireland. I have met with our farmers and they have raised very strong concerns about what is happening and I want to do everything I can to ensure that they understand that I have the full support of the government.”

“I am very clear that farmers are not going to be forced to sell their products on the EU market. We have a range of agricultural products in Ireland and we are going to sell them there.”

“I have met with the farmers yesterday and I have assured them that I am very clear in my position. I am very clear about the need to consult the people of Ireland and I will continue to do so.

“A new study has found evidence that the link between Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s may be a viral infection, but the results are still preliminary and need to be confirmed by further studies.”

The researchers carried out the study in the Netherlands, which is one of the top five Alzheimer’s research centers in the world.

“They have discovered a link between the two diseases and found that the genes in the Alzheimer’s gene cluster, which was found to be over-expressed in Alzheimer’s, are also present in Parkinson’s.”

“The findings of this study point to the possible role of infections in both disorders,” says Dr. Pieter Vermeer from the University Medical Center Utrecht in the Netherlands, who led the research team.

“This may open up new possibilities for treatment of both disorders,” he adds.

The scientists looked at a population of 3,300 people, which were all of Dutch descent, who were all over the age of 50.

“After a thorough medical examination, about half of the participants, or 1,500, were diagnosed with Alzheimer’s and the other half were diagnosed with Parkinson’s.”

The researchers analyzed the brains of the individuals using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which allows the researchers to look at the structure of the brain.

“We saw a link between the two conditions.”

“The scientists compared the brains of people with Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s to those of people with a control group.

“They also compared the brains of people with Alzheimer’s with those of people with Parkinson’s and found that the Parkinson’s brain had more cells, as well as more areas that showed areas of increased intensity.”

“In Alzheimer’s, areas of the brain showed increased intensity that corresponded to the loss of dopaminergic cells – the brain cells responsible for the movement of the nerves that transmit signals between the brain and the muscles of the body – compared with Parkinson’s.”

“However, the Parkinson’s brain did not show any areas of increased intensity compared with Alzheimer’s,” he adds.

These differences could be linked to a viral infection, says Vermeer.

“The idea is that the genes of Parkinson’s are linked to the genes of Alzheimer’s, which in turn may be linked to a viral infection, and that’s what this study is suggesting,” says Vermeer.

“This study also provides new insights into the molecular pathways involved,” he adds.

“But at this stage, we have no idea of the biological mechanisms behind the different types of brain changes.”

“The findings need to be confirmed with additional research and it will be important to understand the association between the virus and the two conditions.”

Description:

A few minutes walk from The Grove in Cherry Orchard this is a residential street with a small cluster of detached houses. There is very little in terms of amenities here and the whole street is very rundown. The main building is only a single storey and the gardens have only four or five tilling options, one of which is in a field in the gardens.

To quote from the article: “The street is in serious need of a major makeover to add more attractive facilities that will attract the local population to live in this area.

Residents’ feedback

There has been a high level of residents’ feedback to the street. The majority of the feedback was positive on the overall state of the street. There was one complaint that there was too much noise from the traffic in the street. This was down to the construction and demolition of the former supermarket close to the street.

The main concern here is the lack of a community centre, there are no toilets within the street, and no access to any community facilities. This is down to the lack of funding from the local Council to maintain the street and the lack of any community facilities in the street.

In the future it is hoped that the Council will look into creating a community centre and a sports field at Cherry Orchard High School, the main building is not large enough and will cost a lot of money to build. This will not only provide the space for people to live but will provide a community hub that will draw people from all over the area.”

The article goes on to mention a few of the other amenities that the street has to offer but there are few in terms of the street being in a good state.

Comments

I’m a resident of the area. My issue with the residents is the noise from the road and from the shops. I think it is a shame that a local school (I believe it is Cherry Orchard High School) is so close to the street. The noise from the shops is so loud at night that it is difficult to sleep at night. It also causes a lot of traffic on the road, especially at night.

The road is not really wide enough for cars. It seems that the road itself is getting wider every year.

I can’t really see it any improvement to the street, if I have to see a major development that will bring people from all over the area.

I wish that the Council had invested in a community centre. It is a shame that it is not a community centre. This is where the shops will be and there will be parking.

There is also the issue of access to the centre. If you are a local it is a very small area. There are no community facilities in this area. There is only one toilet at the high school and the toilets are situated on a very small area. It is very hard to get somewhere.

I would love a community centre if it had a football pitch and a gym. Also a park where the local community can have picnics and things to do.

For this area to be an attractive street is very important, for the residents of the area this is one of the most important issues.

We think we live in an age of over-diagnosis, but do we really?

For the last few years, we have been asked to participate in a two-week study, designed to measure the impact of the “new evidence-based treatments” on the quality of life of people with Parkinson’s disease (PD) and other progressive neurological diseases.

The results of this survey are available here, and are considered a key component of any effective patient-centred approach to the management of these diseases. We are grateful for the opportunity to be involved in this ongoing and important study.

However, there has been a recent “breakthrough”, which is currently being explored by two groups of researchers who are aiming to determine whether certain new treatments are more likely to be effective for people with these diseases. This has been called the “Therapy Culture” phenomenon, and it is interesting that this phenomenon is being investigated in Parkinson’s Disease.

In a recent paper from one of these groups, the researchers found that one new treatment is already being used on a large scale in the UK for people with PD – Botulinum Toxin-A (BTA) Dose-Increasing Therapy (BTA-DIT). The treatment is being used at over a thousand sites in the UK and the treatment is being used as part of an existing service model. These results are presented in the paper below.

This therapy is being offered for two years, and for the first two years patients are given a “trial” of BTA-DIT every other day, and are also given a BTA pump to be used for a further two years. The BTA pump is a small, battery-operated device that delivers small doses of BTA in the small-volume of an MRI-compatible, small bore (3.5 T) scanner. This means that patients can be “locked” into a specific dose of BTA for a number of weeks, before having it progressively increased in steps, or “titrated”. Once they have been titrated for over three months, they are then free to switch back to the BTA pump.

BTA-DIT works by attaching the BTA to a small reservoir of concentrated botulinum toxin. The toxin is pumped into the muscles of the muscle group affected by the symptoms of the disease. This leads to muscle paralysis, which helps to relieve the symptoms of the disease, and helps to reduce the symptoms of the disease.

The effects of BTA-DIT are well documented, with the majority of participants reporting an improvement in both their motor and non-motor symptoms of PD. The treatment has been used in many different countries, including the UK.

The results of the study are very interesting, and provide strong support to the idea that BTA-DIT is an effective treatment. The question then becomes, could this work also be used for people with other progressive diseases, such as ALS?

There are some important caveats, however. Firstly, there is some evidence to suggest that BTA does not work for people with ALS, and that the effects are less than those seen in people with PD.

“The eviction is not a criminal case or one arising out of a tort or breach of contract,” Chief Judge O’Neill said. “It is a public order eviction and any potential damages are in the public interest.”

The judgement is also a blow to the Council, which hopes the court would find it immune from civil claims as it had argued before.

The judgment will be appealed by the Council to the Court of Appeal.

The Council said it would continue to take legal action against the City of Dublin. “There has been no suggestion the judgment is unfair,” the Council said.

However, in response to the High Court ruling, the Council has decided to drop its appeal and to bring the matter again to the Court of Appeal.

“We have been extremely disappointed by today’s decision, and we look forward to bringing the matter once again to the Court of Appeal.”

The Council was ordered to pay €4.6m to the families affected by the eviction.

A spokesman for the Council said that the “good reasons” judgment did not mean that “other agencies” would be exempted from liability.

“The Council is pleased that the court decided that the Council is not liable for damages arising from the eviction of the homeless families,” he added. “The Council had no involvement in, or control over, the eviction of the homeless families.”

In a statement, the Council said that the High Court ruling is a “very important and significant judgment in the process of dealing with the case”.

The village of Karpas, Meath, is planning to oppose a planned refugee settlement of an unknown number of people in an area of the village that is under the jurisdiction of the Irish National Bureau of Statistics.

However, at a meeting last night, residents voted down the proposal to oppose the planned development of the Karpas village on the grounds that it would threaten their culture, their way of life, their identity, and their livelihood.

“We have a special relationship with Ireland,” said Pat Cairns, chair of the Meath Branch of the Irish Refugee Network. “We have been here for 500 years and we have the same beliefs and culture that our forefathers had – we just have different language and customs. It was announced back in 2015 that the Iranian government had already decided to end their water subsidies, and that the “solution” was to create a new water tariff – but this was not popular and it was not until the new year that the subsidy was dropped.

The new incentive is the third in this type of incentive that Iran has introduced this year and the second type of incentive to be introduced that year. This is the first incentive from the government to the farmers to help them with their water problems and with the drought. This new incentive is the only one that was introduced since the “Water Market Reform” came into effect in 2016.

The new incentive is called ‘Asef-e e-Mujtaeh’ in Persian. (As far as I can understand it, it is pronounced “Ah-Sef-e mujtaeh”). This new incentive is called the “Asef-e” because it was meant to be a “tax” on water. The government gave farmers a new incentive for them to help them deal with the drought by paying them a new tax.

It may sound like the solution to the problem of a dry water supply, but it’s not. It is a new, and a very, very small, incentive, and the government only really hopes that by giving it to the farmers it will help them get through this drought. It’s very unlikely that it will, and if it does, they may be getting the money by other means.

“Asef-e e-Mujtaeh” does not mean a “tax” on water, but it does mean an incentive for the farmer to help with the water shortage. Nowhere in the announcement did the government say that it would give farmers a tax break on water, but the words have been there for a long time.

The announcement says that the government will now give a tax break on water to the farmers and that they will have a better chance of getting water when it becomes cheaper to get it.
headline: Baby drought fears prompt introduction of pro-family incentives in Iran

An Irish-registered asylum centre for refugees will be demolished and its land will be sold off in a drive to make money. The Government says the €60 million centre, which has been based at a derelict building in Kildare, will be demolished after plans for a new development are approved. But local residents are furious that plans to tear down the building are still being drawn up despite its ongoing development. Kildare County Council is working on the plans which would see the former asylum centre being torn down and the land on which it is situated sold off. The new planned development on the site, which is at the bottom of a valley overlooking the Liffey river and is on an access road to the Dublin Airport, would see the site of the old asylum centre being redeveloped. The project is to take around ten years and could involve the demolition of the current building. Mr O’Toole and the other applicants for the development are currently seeking planning permission from the local council which is to be granted next year. Mr O’Toole claims the new development will increase the number of refugees coming to Ireland, with a spokesman for the Department of Social Protection (DSP) saying that the plans are to build a number of residential buildings in the area which would meet the needs of the asylum seekers. “The development is not just about accommodation and new social housing. The development is about a new town centre, a new development on the land where the old asylum centre is situated,” he said.

The Irish Independent reports:

Dublin County Council is looking to build housing and commercial space on land on which the Irish centre for asylum seekers, Kildare House, is located, a spokesman said. The plans were announced by the DSP on Tuesday and would see the property being redeveloped, according to the latest information on the plan which was submitted to the council last week. It would involve the demolition of the current asylum centre and the sale of the land on which it is situated, the spokesman said. The new development is to take around ten years and could include the demolition of the current asylum centre. In the early 1990s, the Government allowed a development of 600 houses to be built on the site of the old asylum centre.

“We are looking at this development with great interest,” said the spokesman. “We want to make sure that we have the necessary resources to build on the site of the former asylum centre. The site has been vacant for the last ten years. There have been no planning applications for the site. We want to move quickly to get planning permission for the new development.” Mr O’Toole has previously said that if the plans were approved they would “tear down the building, tear it down and put it back up on the site”. He has also warned that if the government decided that the building should be demolished, that a number of other buildings which were erected on the site in the 1990s would also have to be demolished. The land on which the asylum centre is situated is on a minor access road which leads to the Dublin Airport. The site is currently occupied by a property developer, the developer building company, who plans to develop a mixed-use development on the land. The former asylum centre at Kildare House, a converted mansion in a picturesque setting, is not a significant site.

The medical profession in Ireland seems to be in for some major upheaval when it comes to plastic surgery, as an increasing number of Irish people have opted to become plastic surgery patients.

Dr J.J. O’Leary of the Dublin Eye Hospital said that the average age at which Irish women have undergone surgery to reduce their breast size is just 23. That’s an increase of almost six years over the past seven years.

Dr J.J. O’Leary, who has performed more breast reduction procedures than anyone else in the world, told Newsbeat that the reason for the increase in the number of breast reductions is a combination of increasing awareness of how women’s bodies work, and the desire of women to be able to look ‘as pretty as possible’.

“The increase in the number of women opting to have plastic surgery is probably because they’ve seen more articles in magazines and on the internet, in particular, ‘Celebrity Rehab’ and the like, that talk about how the bodies of women have changed, that the breasts are getting bigger and more spherical. There was a survey in 2013 that showed that 30% of the Irish population considered themselves to be extremely overweight,” Dr O’Leary said.

“What we’ve seen in the last decade is that if you’ve ever walked down a street, you will see women in heels and heels, and we’ve come to the point now where you don’t need to wear heels any more,” he added.

“We’ve changed the way that women can look, we’ve got them to be more attractive, and we’ve had women opting to have smaller breasts,” Dr O’Leary said.

Dr O’Leary said that there has been a huge change in the way women are viewed. “There was a time where most of the people that you would see in magazines would be pretty slim, and people used to think they were very attractive,” he said.

“There was a time where women were considered to be the centre of attention, that they were the image of society, and now that’s not the case.”

Dr O’Leary said that there is now a significant minority who are “very, very unattractive”, and he thinks that this is a combination of the increased awareness and the increased interest in surgery.

“Some of the women that I have seen who are quite unattractive, who have had surgery, are women that were in their teens when they had surgery,” he added.

“There are two types of surgery – the traditional, which is to change the shape of the breasts, and the minimally invasive surgery. The minimally invasive surgery is to use incisions to take out the fat from the inside.”

Dr O’Leary said that the majority of the women who choose to have their breasts reduced by surgery are women who have been obese for a long time, and he believes that there is an increased interest in surgery because of the desire of women to have a more spherical shape.

European countries have seen a steady rise in the number of people claiming asylum after fleeing war-torn places in the Middle East, the latest official figures from the European Asylum Support Office (EASO) show.

But the number of asylum claims in the 28 European Union nations fell by 12% in the year to the end of August 2018, according to figures from the office's EASO database.

Refugees from Syria and Afghanistan made up the biggest share of the total number of asylum claims in the region, with the number of claims in the country surpassing 50,000 by the end of August, with the numbers coming from several European countries.

As a result of the fall in numbers, the number of asylum applications in the EASO database dropped from 14,818 in the previous year to 14,062 in 2017, the EASO said.

The number of applications for political asylum in 2018 fell by 11% to 1,871, while the number of applications for protection of families and relatives fell by 8% to 1,401.

The number of applications from asylum seekers in 2017 was highest in Greece, while there were fewer applications from asylum seekers in Romania and Poland than in 2017.

The fall in applications in 2018 was partly offset by a rise in applications for protection of children in 2018, as well as a small rise in the number of applications for family reunification.

The data also shows that the number of applications for refugee status in 2018 was highest in Estonia (25,456), followed by Lithuania (23,912), Spain (20,906) and Portugal (18,822).

The data is based on the EASO database of asylum claims for the 28 European Union countries and is provided by the European Asylum Support Office for the purpose of EU Member States’ decision making on requests for asylum.

Refugees are seeking protection in countries where they are fleeing a conflict and persecution. The EU aims to provide protection for as many refugees as possible, with countries agreeing on a system of quotas for those fleeing from conflict that is based on the number of people living in a country.

In addition to the number of applications, the EASO also has information about the duration and circumstances of the asylum seeker’s claim.

The number of people who have been granted refugee status fell by 26% in 2018 to 7,812, as many people had applied for asylum for the first time, rather than renewing their claim and for a different reason.

The number of asylum seekers granted refugee status was the lowest in Greece and Turkey, with the highest in Serbia, Albania and Croatia.

Overall, 1,721 people have been granted refugee status in the EASO database for 2018.

The number of those granted refugee status was the highest in Serbia (2,738), followed by Albania (1,811), Albania (1,848) and Croatia (1,607).

The highest number of people granted refugee status in 2018 was in Romania (4,094), followed by Greece (3,639), Spain (3,501) and Poland (2,921).

The highest proportion of people applying for asylum in 2018 was in Lithuania (33.9%) and in Poland (31.5%), the EASO data shows.

The Government has long had to defend a variety of cases that it has been accused of wrongly and repeatedly labelling “misinformation”. The latest example concerns the “Papers” programme which is the first of three new government services in the area of child protection that it has recently launched.

In this case we are told that “the Government had no role in preparing the papers”. This is in reference to the fact that the Department of Social Protection only produced three of the papers, which were put in the public domain in January 2009.

The press release goes on to state that “in the course of implementing the new arrangements, the Department of Social Protection has been given an opportunity to revise all documents and make them clear.” This is true in part, since the Department is now responsible for the production of the papers. But this is also true in part because the Department has already produced the papers which was already set out in the press release.

So while the Department is currently in charge of the production of papers that are only now being revised, the Department has already produced those papers in the past and was told by the Department that it was “the Department of Social Protection” that “produced” those papers.

A year ago, this was not the case. The Department told us that the documents were produced by the Department of Social Protection, it had “the right to revise them and make them clear” and that “the Department has a responsibility to make them clear and clear as well.”

The press release also states that the new Department of Social Protection is “not responsible for the accuracy of the papers” but “the Department is responsible for their production”. This is not true.

The press release says that “the Department of Social Protection” is now responsible for the production of the papers and that “the Department is responsible for ensuring they are accurate”. This is true, but the Department is still responsible for the papers’ content and the fact that they are “the papers produced by the Department of Social Protection”. It is the responsibility of the Department of Social Protection, not that of the Department of Social Protection.

The Department of Social Protection is now responsible for the “revision of all documents and the making of them clear” and that this is “the responsibility of the Department of Social Protection”. But is it the responsibility of the Department of Social Protection to make sure that the documents are accurate?

It is the responsibility of the Department of Social Protection, not the Department of Social Protection.

This is a classic instance of a “misinformation defence”, but a defence that appears to have been invented by the Department of Social Protection itself.

The press release goes on to say that “the Department of Social Protection has also established a task team that will be tasked with the production of the papers.” This is a ludicrous claim.

The Department of Social Protection did not establish this task team. It was established by a Department of Social Protection official – Dr Michael McGlinchey – in September 2011. This official was then appointed by the Department of Social Protection.
headline: The Government’s “misinformation” defence is utter waffle

In the last 5 years the number of dog bites in Ireland has more than doubled and there are now over 50,000 dog bite cases a year. There are no statistics to support this, but I would like to believe that dog bites are a public health issue. If a person gets a dog bite, should that person go to the emergency department and have his dog removed? I don't think so. Dogs are so innocent, they deserve to be treated with kindness, courtesy and dignity.

The Irish Times has some statistics to back up my contention that this is a public health issue. It states:

“A single dog bite in Ireland costs the Irish economy at least €1.3 million. A single bite in the Republic of Ireland costs the Irish economy at least €5.9 million.

This means that dog bite injuries are the third most expensive public health crisis in the world, after malaria and tuberculosis.”

The Irish Times have also reported that one in 20 cases is recorded as a serious case of dog bites and injuries in Ireland, compared to 1 in 50 in the Republic of Ireland.

“The figures come from the Central Statistics Office, an independent authority, which said that in 2007, the average cost of a serious dog bite in Ireland was €200,000. In 2007, an average dog bite cost the Irish economy the equivalent of €7,976.”

“The figures are shocking,” Dr. John Donaghue, the chief medical officer, said. “They underline that a simple dog bite can be life-threatening, especially for children.”

“As a doctor in a major hospital, the risk is too great. There are patients who may die waiting to be seen, and it is unfair to leave that part of the health system to people who, for the most part, are not fit or willing to go to the hospital.”

“It is not about the amount of money that the individual is paying for the dog, it is about their humanity and the pain of the people they are leaving behind.”

And if you have children, would you like to know that you can reduce the risk of serious injuries by getting dogs neutered before they leave home?

You can now get your dog spayed or neutered, but before you do, you need to find out what your local pet sterilisation service is offering.

The Irish Times article states:

“The average annual cost for a dog and cat sterilization is about €4,300, and the cost could be as much as €6,000,” said Dr. John Donaghue, the chief medical officer in the Cork university hospital.

“The most expensive procedures are the same as for any pet - spaying and neutering.

“The sterilization is cheaper because it involves surgery. The cost of a simple spay and neuter can vary between €75 and €120, which is not much.”

“In Ireland, the cost for neutering a dog is around €400, for a cat €200 and for a rabbit €1,200.”

“This means that in the short term, neutering is about 50 per cent cheaper than sterilizing the animal.”

In a dramatic court appearance last night, the 85-year-old man charged with the murder of his wife, Patricia Aust, appeared in a court in Bangor at the request of his solicitor and pleaded not guilty.

Mr Moore, who appeared in a blue shirt, blue jeans, light blue socks and black shoes, appeared in a black suit, green trousers and a blue shirt.

He was escorted to the courthouse by a black-and-white-coloured female officer.

When he arrived at the courthouse Mr Moore pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder.

He was remanded to Cloverhill Crown Court to be arraigned at 9pm on Friday.

Ms Aust, a retired teacher, was a resident of the Mount St Bernard community in the town centre on the eastern outskirts of the city.

At the time of her murder Ms Aust’s husband was the only person known to have been in her flat on the night in March last year when she was shot as she lay on the floor with her head on a pile of cushions.

The two-month-long murder investigation was led by Detective Sergeant Michael McCrone, from the Bangor Policing Command’s Special Crime Branch, who was assisted by Detective Constable Sean Gribble of Bangor City Policing.

Detective Sergeant McCrone described the murder as a “cold-blooded and vicious killing”.

The investigation began after Ms Aust, her husband and other neighbours were called to the scene on March 26th last year to find her badly wounded.

The murder weapon was later found in the flat and DNA analysis connected Mr Aust with the scene.

Detectives said they were investigating a number of theories about the murder including that the woman was killed by a burglar, a man who was looking for the family after a visit from a relative and a member of the local drug-dealing gang.

Mr Moore had been in custody on other charges, including possession of cannabis and possessing a firearm without a licence, at the time of the murder.

The investigation into the murder is continuing.

A judge is expected to make an order in relation to the sentence that Mr Moore must serve, which was not disclosed.

A post mortem report into the cause of death will also be made.

The Crown will argue that the murder was racially motivated.

The judge at the trial will be the respected Judge Brian Murphy.

Mrs Aust’s stepfather, Robert Aust, who was present at the time of the murder and at the murder scene, is a retired teacher and a former principal.

Mr Aust is a member of the Church of Ireland, the Church of Ireland National Youth Assembly and the Catholic Teachers’ Training Organisation.

He served as the Church of Ireland Chaplain to the British Army during the Troubles and was the chaplain of the RAF Regiment in Northern Ireland.

He was also the Catholic chaplain for the British Army’s 1st Battalion, The Royal Regiment of Fusiliers.

Mr Aust was also a member of the Ulster Unionist Party.

He was a member of the Royal Anglian Regiment and served in the Coldstream Guards, the Royal Sussex Regiment and the Duke of Lancaster’s Regiment.

Irish Independent - 16 December 2019

By Brendan McDermott

The €50 million will be spent to develop a model of health service that will enable the Irish public to be better protected against the spread of Covid-19.

This announcement from the Irish Government is an indication of its determination to create a better world. Health and Social Protection Minister Simon Coveney has made it clear that Ireland is now in the position to lead the world in its fight against COVID-19 by working with Europe, the United Nations, and other partners to develop a strong and efficient response.

The €50 million will be spent to develop a model of health service that will enable the Irish public to be better protected against the spread of Covid-19.

This is a significant milestone for Ireland and we now have a chance to become the first country in the world to adopt a universal approach to the development and implementation of a national health service. This is the first stage in our plan to make this country the leader in the fight against COVID-19.

The first step to transforming health services in Ireland began with the creation of the health and social services department in late 2017. This department was created to ensure that the health and social security of the Irish population was recognised and that the health and social needs of people with special needs were provided with the best possible care, with the knowledge and skills that they deserved.

The department’s mandate is to manage the delivery of health and social protection services, and to facilitate the provision of services for persons with disabilities and persons with intellectual and developmental disabilities, the elderly, the homeless, the disadvantaged, asylum seekers, vulnerable children, and asylum-seeking people.

The department also provides services for persons with mental health issues and supports vulnerable adults and children.

The department will work to develop models for the delivery of health and social protection services and is committed to supporting other stakeholders to adopt a similar approach.

This is the second stage of the plan to transform the delivery of health and social services in Ireland.

This new approach to health and social protection services is a significant departure from the current health and social services model in Ireland and other European countries, where the emphasis is on an individualist approach to healthcare and where services are provided on the basis of need.

Instead of promoting the notion of health and social security as a continuum, the approach of the department is to promote a more differentiated model, which aims to promote the needs and rights of a more diverse population.

This approach to health and social protection services is based on the notion that the health and social services of the Irish population is a product of the people, the environment and the institutions, and that services must be delivered in a manner that is responsive to the needs of the population as a whole.

This is a departure from the current approach to health and social protection services in Ireland and other European countries. The current health and social protection service model is a highly fragmented, fragmented, fragmented service delivery model, where each service is provided in isolation without co-ordination and coordination.

This is a departure from the current health and social protection service delivery model in Ireland and other European countries.

The department’s approach is to provide health and social protection services in a way that creates an inclusive system, where the needs of the whole population is taken into account.

The man who was born a man, the man who was born an angel, a born and raised male, and became a member of the royal priesthood of Jesus Christ of the Latter-day Saints, a man who was born with a penis.

This man lived in a time when the world was filled with a great deal of suffering. He lived in a time of poverty, when people had none to eat, when people were dying and there was no one who could help, and in a time when Jesus had gone to the cross and died for our sins.

The man who was born a man, the man who was born an angel, a man who was born and raised male, and became a member of the royal priesthood of Jesus Christ of the Latter-day Saints, a man who was born with a penis.

And what happened to this man that caused him to live like this?

The man became an apostle, a very special man. He was called by name, and he was called by purpose, and his mission was to build his people.

“To build his people.” That is the very key phrase in this gospel, the key to success, and this has been the key to happiness, happiness for many of us since that moment when our son was conceived and born. It is the key to his priesthood sealing, his ordination, his temple rites, his temple ordinances, his wedding, his funeral, and everything else that you see and hear about him. The key to his life, his joy, and all of his greatness.

The man of the prophet and the apostles who called Jesus to the cross, who called the Christ from the dead and who baptized and raised the man from the dead. It was the man of the prophet and the apostles who told Jesus to take the man from the cross and hold him.

And it was this man of the prophet and the apostles who told Jesus to put his hands on Jesus, and Jesus said to him, “I am not the one who will father this child, but the woman whom you saw was not my mother, but my disciples.”

And this was the man of the prophet and the apostles who told Jesus to forgive his brother. The man of the prophet and the apostles who took Jesus from the cross and gave him his brother to be with him and Jesus gave him his brother’s name, “Father.”

And this man of the prophet and the apostles who told Jesus to take the man from the cross and hold him, and Jesus was a man of sorrows and acquainted with suffering. He was suffering because his mother died and the angel Gabriel gave him life, because his mother’s spirit had been broken, and he was born and raised in a place where people had none, and he suffered because of this and he was born with a penis.

What has been called the “Newman era” in Irish politics is under way, as an era of progressive politics is taking root across the world’s second largest European Union country.

The Irish government is planning to launch a series of new government structures, bringing together a range of political parties across the political spectrum. This is the first step in the process of taking the country from the status quo of power sharing with the United Kingdom, to a government that is led by an Irish political party.

The government is planning to set up a new political party, which it plans to call the Irish Progressive Party (IPP). There has been some discussion in the past about the need for a new party to represent Irish political aspirations, but the question has remained open as to whether an Irish political party would have a seat in the European parliament.

The Irish government intends to launch a new political party, which it plans to call the Irish Progressive Party (IPP).

A statement by the government, issued on Saturday, said:

“The IPP is a political party dedicated to representing and representing the aspirations of all people in the 21st century and beyond. In the Irish context this aspiration may be the desire to have a political party that is inclusive, non-partisan and representative of the nation, of its values and beliefs and of the aspirations of all its citizens.”

In order to bring about that change, the new party is to be launched with an event at Dublin Castle on February 2.

The announcement comes as the government has been discussing the future of the Irish presidency for almost a year. It is a joint responsibility of the Taoiseach and his deputy, the deputy first minister and Taoiseach, the minister for justice.

The Irish presidency was first mooted by Bertie Ahern, the first Taoiseach in 1979. It was revived by John Bruton, the current Taoiseach, in 1993, in an attempt to give the Irish presidency a new mandate.

“The IPP believes that to have a European Parliament seat or, ideally, to lead the EU in a new direction, it needs to be led by an Irish party,” the government said in its statement.

The IPP will be seeking to become the first Irish political party to be represented in the European parliament.

The Irish party must be non-partisan.

The IPP’s mission is to ensure that it represents the full range of Irish aspirations and aspirations of all its citizens.

The IPP’s primary purpose and mission is to advance the progressive values of Irish society.

The IPP will seek to make Ireland a world leader in the areas of economic policy, trade, and social rights.

The IPP has agreed to hold itself accountable for its actions and to reflect the wider Irish electorate.

The Great Barrier Reef (GBR) has a record high level of coral cover, according to a new coral survey carried out by the British Geological Survey (BGS).

The survey of 16 sites on the GBR by the BGS found that 92% of the reefs surveyed are covered with at least one of the three main coral species: Acropora, Porites and Pocillopora.

The survey, carried out in 2013, showed that 92% of the sites surveyed had coral cover above the threshold of 95%, with the highest levels found at the Lizard Island and Lizard Island Reefs in the Great Barrier Reef, and the Wreck Reefs on the southern GBR.

The sites covered in the survey are all on the north side of the reef, with the highest levels found in the Lizard Island Reefs, which are located between Lizard Island and Cairns.

The survey also found that the total number of species and genera found in the surveyed reefs has increased by 11% from 2013.

The survey was carried out by the BGS, which is a joint research partnership between the University of Queensland and the University of the Sunshine Coast, and is part of a wider global collaborative effort to understand how the global coral reef ecosystem is changing.

The results were announced to the public on Monday morning and the results were released ahead of the reef’s annual general meeting later this month.

BGS Senior Scientist, Professor Michael Taylor, said, “The coral cover in the Great Barrier Reef is on a record high.

“It’s not a fluke. The rate of coral loss is accelerating, and the corals are getting damaged more quickly than ever before.”

The survey also found that the levels of corals at the Lizard Island Reef are up to five times higher than the previous year.

Professor Taylor said it’s important that the public, politicians and industry get involved in understanding the coral cover and rate of decline.

“This is a good time to be keeping an eye on what’s happening to coral and how much of a rate of change we see over the next 12 to 24 months.”

Brigitte Macpherson, CEO of the BGS said, “We would like to thank the public, the media and the government, which have all played their part in making the Great Barrier Reef a place we all love to visit and explore.

“This new survey is a great start, and now we need to work with stakeholders and local communities to get this work up and running.”

In an article published in the journal Nature last week, a team of scientists from the University of Melbourne in Australia, the University of Manchester in the UK and the National Oceanography Centre in Southampton in UK showed that the GBR’s coral reefs face unprecedented threats from climate change, specifically in areas of the Great Barrier Reef where reefs are already highly vulnerable to warming and ocean acidification.

They found that the rate of change in coral cover in the GBR’s most recently measured study area has been accelerating, and it is now at a level that is a threat to coral survival.
headline: Great Barrier Reef has record levels of coral, says survey

There is something about the political right that has always made me a little uneasy.

Sure, there’s the political right of my generation; the white, working-class, libertarian, or libertarianish wing of the political right (which is where I belong anyway). These are my people; these are the people who want to preserve the institutions of the free market that are part of their life-style. In the case of the left, the political right has always been there to support the free-market institutions that their supporters have always loved (the police, the schools, the welfare state). The political right, in essence, has always been there to preserve these institutions that the left’s supporters love, no matter how much we disagree with the left on other issues.

But then there’s the left. The left is not there to support the free-market institutions that we love. The left is there to oppose them. The left’s core message is that the institutions of free market capitalism, which they claim are necessary to the functioning of the free market, are not enough to be truly free. They need government control. They need the state to monitor and control what happens to those institutions of capitalism, which they claim are necessary to the functioning of the market. The state is always the enemy. We need our own institutions. But if the state is the enemy, who are the left to tell us that we need to control the state? The left is not there to support the free market.

The state has always seemed to me to be an institution that the left is more than happy to put in place. We all know that the state will be there to protect us from those who would harm us. That’s just the way things are, as we know well. But I have never really believed that it was necessary to put the state in place. I have always seen the state, in some form, as a necessary institution to protect us. Now, as a progressive, I have always assumed that the free-market institutions that we enjoy are important enough to deserve protection from the state. In that sense, I don’t think the left is as anti-state as I’ve always assumed.

But that’s the left. When I see the left acting in such a negative way towards the state, I can’t help but wonder if they just aren’t paying attention to what they’re doing. They are acting in a way that makes it look like the state is the enemy. And they’re not just talking about the state. When they speak about the state, they’re also talking about the police. And they’re talking about the military. They’re talking about the government. And then, of course, the government does what it does. And the people who would destroy the state aren’t exactly the kind of people to do that. But I’m starting to believe that there is a small, vocal group within the left that is against the state. And I’m wondering if they just don’t notice what they’re doing, or if they just haven’t realized they’re doing it.

It’s not just the left that is acting this way.

How the vaccine passport is making vaccine trials far less secure

Where is the evidence that vaccine passports make vaccine trials far less secure?

How the vaccine passport is making vaccine trials far less secure

In the autumn of 2015, Professor Sir David King, Head of the School of Public Health at the University of East Anglia, was interviewed by Sky News for a special report on vaccine science and public health. Dr King’s comments were particularly controversial as they were made before he had published any papers regarding vaccine effectiveness, immunogenicity or protection.

His comments and the report led to widespread controversy and accusations of bias. In April 2016, King stepped down from his post as Head of the School of Public Health at the University of East Anglia.

In the summer of 2016, Dr King’s former research assistant, Dr Elizabeth Huxley, was found guilty of misconduct in two separate incidents at the University of East Anglia. The events are detailed in the 2016 UK Inquiry into the Vaccination Record. Dr King’s former research assistant has been charged under the Misuse of Drugs Act (MDA), which is an act of the UK’s General Medical Council. Dr King and Dr Huxley were both charged in a single indictment.

The charges were upheld by the General Medical Council and the university issued a press statement explaining that ‘it is not possible for a person to act against the Code of Conduct of the University of East Anglia without being guilty of an offence.’ (‘Vaccination records made public: UK Inquiry into the Vaccination Record,’ The Times, 29 April 2016).

Dr King has been very clear about his position on vaccine passport arrangements:

‘I can confirm that in the event of my departure from the University of East Anglia I will have to sign a non-disclosure agreement to protect myself and my research team from any legal action or inquiry in relation to my work with the vaccine passport and other vaccine issues. The university has taken this action in consultation with the Faculty of Public Health. It is important that individuals in our position, who are not employed by the university and do not have access to confidential information about research, are aware that this is a key element in safeguarding research integrity.’ (‘Vaccination records made public: UK Inquiry into the Vaccination Record,’ The Times, 29 April 2016)

Dr King’s role at the University of East Anglia has also been questioned by many on the right. In June 2016, former Conservative MP and UKIP parliamentary candidate for Eastleigh and St Helier, Michael Fabricant, appeared on Sky News to describe Dr King’s position on vaccine passports as ‘absurd’ and ‘anti-vaccine’. In July 2016, Professor King appeared on Channel 4’s Q and A to respond to the accusation and call for more evidence to be made public. In the same interview, he said:

‘What I will not allow is anyone to use my name in a deliberate attempt to defame or harm anyone.’ (‘Michael Fabricant, Vaccination Record: Former Tory MP, Says Vaccine Passports Are ‘Absurd’,’ Channel 4 News, 7 July 2016).
headline: Where is the evidence that vaccine passports work?

“Big Gay” may have a new name.

by A. A. M. Mc GUIRK

The year 2013 has seen a resurgence of the biggish of Irish sport. In the absence of the biggish’s traditional name, the acronym “Big Gay” has emerged.

The biggest sport in Ireland is, of course, soccer. But in recent years the most controversial sports in the country have been the bantam and junior titles in hurling, and the hurling-only championship in football. The latter is now joined by a few more senior Gaelic Games titles.

The Gaelic Games is one of the only sports in which fans are genuinely interested in watching the games. Yet the “biggest” sport in Ireland, the one with the most fans, the one that gives the most publicity, has a long history of being the least interesting to watch.

In the early years of the game there was a tendency for the biggish, and Irish players with biggish names, to be dismissed for being part of the “big” Irish middle class and for being a poor reflection of what the Irish are actually like as a people.

The story is told of the great hurler O’Neill, who went to Paris in the 1950s and came out as a gay man, after years of hiding his sexuality in the hurling club at which he was a member. In his obituary he was described as “a great hurling player and a great homosexual,” by a writer who described his greatest moment as the game which ended with his side losing to the French team.

The story of Brian O’Nolan is the story of how the biggish became the big. It was not until 1998 that the biggish was introduced as a new name for the big Irish game. The official name, and the name which is used to this day, has a very strange history. It began as a pejorative term for “gay”.

The O’Nolan story was, of course, not the only one of this kind. It has been told of several big Irish names: James Keaney, who was the Irish rugby player from a big, gregarious family, and who went to a big school in Australia and came out as gay; the great Eamonn DeValera, the ex-footballer who became a great Irish politician and the ex-rugby player; the great Irish boxer, Martin O’Sullivan, who died at the age of 24 of an AIDS-related infection; and the great Irish author, Seamus Heaney, who died in the late 2000s of a heart condition.

The Irish were also biggish in their attitude to the big game. The Irish sports writers, both before and after the 1980s, were the only people who made any real political or sports comment. They were the only people who showed the public the difference between being Irish and being Irish as a sport. They were the only people who wrote about the Irish attitude to a game.
headline: MCGUIRK: It’s time to stand up to “Big Gay”

In a major boost for the environment, the European Commission is set to allow Ireland to go carbon neutral in the coming years, putting it on a par with the UK and Finland.

This could be a major step forward in addressing one of the most serious problems affecting climate change.

The €375 billion annual cost of implementing a carbon tax on global greenhouse gases could now be made up of three elements: the first is an income tax on carbon; the second is a charge on emissions from small enterprises; and the third is a carbon tax on the cars, buildings and machinery that power the Irish economy.

The move by the European Commission is one of the most ambitious carbon price plans the bloc has ever launched, and could finally put Ireland on the path to being carbon neutral in the next few years.

The Irish economy would benefit hugely from the carbon tax if it were passed. In fact, Ireland’s economy would be hit with €370 billion in extra tax revenue. The main sources of income would be from carbon emissions and the costs of carbon-intensive activities.

The costs of an Irish carbon tax would be much lower than those of the UK, where the government set a price for carbon dioxide of £37 a tonne. A carbon tax on €4 trillion in annual global emissions by 2030 would reduce the annual cost of energy by 40%, and reduce emissions by up to 9.8 gigatonnes, and take the annual carbon dioxide emissions of the UK economy, which would increase from 20.4 billion tonnes in 2017 to around 33.6 billion tonnes by 2030.

The carbon tax could also be implemented without the need for a subsidy, thus removing the economic barrier to an Ireland becoming a leader in the field of climate change adaptation and mitigation.

But the carbon tax would have to be paid into a fund that would then be spent on research and energy efficiency. This fund would need to be spent without using money from any other source, which is particularly important in a time of austerity.

Carbon neutral Ireland would also need to develop a new energy infrastructure, which is estimated to cost €40 billion over the next decade, but which could save the government money.

A €375 billion carbon tax would create significant growth for the Irish economy over the coming years. It would reduce the number of vehicles sold by around 1.1 million per year, creating an additional annual investment of €400 million. The carbon tax would also increase the electricity generated by the Irish power grid by around €10 billion over the coming years.

To pay for the new infrastructure, Ireland’s tax revenue would have to be spent on new buildings, which are estimated to cost €60 billion over the next decade, while the investment would generate €300 million in new jobs.

A new carbon tax would also help address the need for Ireland to invest heavily in renewables as part of its climate change adaptation strategy.

In fact, the carbon tax would make the transition to a more sustainable economy much easier, and would free up the government to put other policies in place to boost the economy and tackle climate change.

A carbon tax would also put an end to the EU’s carbon trading scheme.
headline: TD: Ireland going carbon neutral could cost €375 billion

A year of getting it wrong

By
Catherine Böker, Greet Verstappen, Marko Ražnatović,
and Marko Stubbins

The last few weeks have brought the news of a Ukrainian army’s attack on a key Russian airbase. The base is located in Ukraine’s Ternopil region, a strategic position along the eastern frontlines with Russia and NATO. This is a significant blow for the Kremlin. This attack is being carried out by a group of pro-Russian separatists who have been fighting for several months against the Ukrainian government.

The attack comes just one year after the Russian government, acting on the orders of President Vladimir Putin, announced the removal of the Ukrainian government from power, the ousting of the elected president, and the declaration of a general election to be held on February 21, 2014. In late January 2014, the Russian Federation declared that “the current situation is not acceptable.”

In order to understand the nature of the Russia-Ukraine crisis, we need to understand what a conflict of this size and scale would mean to the international community. Russia does not want a conflict with Ukraine as part of the “near-east” strategy. But Russia’s interests are not limited to Ukraine’s western borders, and Russia is not averse to seeing conflict in Eastern Europe. There are already tensions in Ukraine over Ukraine’s intentions to join the Customs Union, and Russia’s desire for more influence there.

As the Russian government’s position is clearly and increasingly clear, the international community is now at a crossroads. A year of getting it wrong.

The war in Ukraine has already begun. As of November 2014, the Russian military has been involved in actions on several fronts. The Russian military has been involved in the Ukrainian conflict since the day after the Russian-Ukrainian war broke out in March 2014. This war began as a war between pro-Russian separatists and Ukrainian soldiers in a village named Debaltseve in eastern Ukraine. The battle was joined on April 6, 2014, in the town of Debaltseve, which was about twenty-four miles south of the Ukrainian city of Mariupol.

On April 8, 2014, Ukrainian artillery fire on Debaltseve reportedly killed hundreds of Ukrainian soldiers and residents. This was not a battle of choice, but an inevitable result of the ongoing war.

On the evening of April 8, at 8 p.m., Russian President Vladimir Putin made a televised statement in which he said that Russia would “continue to provide armed support to the Ukrainian people, and [would] defend Russian sovereignty, as the legitimate government of Ukraine.” This statement came as a response to a statement made by Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko the day before by saying that Russia would not interfere with the Ukrainian people’s ability to govern themselves.

This statement by Putin was a direct challenge to Poroshenko. Poroshenko, who had recently been elected to succeed Viktor Yanukovych and who was seen as pro-Russia, decided to back down from the offensive in Debaltseve. Poroshenko was defeated in the election in Ukraine’s presidential election on March 31, 2014.
headline: A year of getting it wrong. A review of the Russia-Ukraine War

The British journalist John M. Smith was interviewed for the British Broadcasting Company (BBC) by Canadian MP Pierre Poilievre and a group of Canadian MPs in the Commons on December 28, 2014, as part of the ongoing debate around the United Nations Economic and Social Council (UNESC)’s proposed changes to the WEF.

In the course of the interview, Smith had the opportunity to comment on the proposal for the WEF to be stripped of its powers to create independent public oversight to allow for more “local” decision-making, in particular a stronger role for the provinces, which would have the authority to intervene in UNESC-decreed and implemented rules and regulations.

MP Poilievre asked Smith, “Can you tell us what you think is the right way to go about this proposal and what we could do about it in the near future?”

Smith replied, “The way you’re proposing is basically a wholesale transfer of our responsibilities over to some sort of centralised entity, to the Canadian Department of Foreign Affairs, that will be basically making the decisions, not us. The whole proposal is a very, very dangerous one.”

MP Poilievre replied, “You are not in a position to answer that, Mr. Smith. In the first place, I am not aware of anything in the plan that would allow for the Canadian government to be involved in this type of governance.”

Smith replied, “I didn’t say that.”

MP Poilievre then asked, “I’m sorry, I know you’re trying to be careful and try to be sensitive, but you’re going to have to say, ‘I’m sorry, but I don’t think this is the way to proceed.’ Is that fair to say?”

Smith replied, “Yeah, it’s fair, I’m sorry, it’s just the way it is.”

MP Poilievre said, “I understand. Can you give us an example of what you mean by a centralised entity?”

Smith replied, “A centralised entity would be someone like the International Institute for Environment and Development, and I suppose they’ve got their own problems of course, they could do with a little bit of a shake-up.”

MP Poilievre replied, “Mr. Smith, you are not in a position to answer that question. In the first place, I am not aware of anything in the plan that would allow for the Canadian government to be involved in this type of governance.”

MP Poilievre replied, “I’m sure that there will be no difficulty in finding out what the plan is and how it is being implemented.”

MP Poilievre then said to Smith, “Can you give us an example of what you mean by a centralised entity?”

Smith replied, “It would be a government that actually would have a lot of power.”

A mother from Dublin has become the first person to apply for residence in the UK for a mother who lost her child in a car crash.

Hannah Smith, 29, is hoping the lottery will help her find temporary housing for her seven-month-old daughter.

She has been living with her partner, who is also from Dublin, and said it was her first time living outside the capital.

She has also written to the Garda Siochana, claiming her child has been in an accident that led to her being left in the care of an elderly relative.

Hannah’s partner has already spent €1,000 on her accommodation for the month.

Garda spokesperson Noel Malone said: “A mother claiming temporary residence in the United Kingdom is not considered a homeless person as per current legislation and is not required to pay a tax on the cost of her accommodation.

“It is the responsibility of the parents to arrange the provision of accommodation for their children.”

Hannah, from the New Ross area, has applied for temporary housing in Britain and has spent €1,000 on her accommodation. (PA)

It is the responsibility of the parents to arrange the provision of accommodation for their children. It is therefore the Garda Siochana’s responsibility to ensure that Hannah receives housing for her child.

Garda spokesperson Noel Malone said: “This is a unique situation, which must be treated as such.

“In line with the Government’s commitment to reduce the number of people sleeping on the streets, all those who are homeless must be provided with accommodation.”

“I know he’s been in contact with his mother and his social worker and I want to send him some money.”

“I’m worried about my partner, but I know he’s not going to take the money. I’ve spent a few days in bed with a lump in my throat,” she said.

This leaked document from AstraZeneca's UK subsidiary, AstraZeneca, outlines plans for a no-profit trust with its own board and endowment fund.

The leaked document outlines the endowment fund will be made up of an income from the company's existing assets, as well as an investment of the company's own.

The board will be appointed by a trustee with the power to nominate a successor from the existing group of directors who are appointed by the company's shareholders.

The trust will be managed and funded by a trustee appointed by the company itself, and not by an external fiduciary.

The company will also continue to use the AstraZeneca UK brand, which will still be owned by the company as a whole.

The trust will only become a fully operational company, and no board meetings or meetings of shareholders are to be held, as with the AstraZeneca UK brand.

It is claimed that the fund is to be "independent" and is not to be linked with AstraZeneca as a whole.
