A national organisation which aims to help marginalised and under-represented leaders to support systemic reforms is launching a new scheme to provide funding and other support services which help these leaders to deliver the outcomes they need.

The new fund, to be run by the Irish Council for Global Affairs, is offering funding for the launch of a new programme of services designed to support marginalised leaders to support systemic reforms.

The new fund’s aim is to “aid and advise” under-represented leaders on “complex policy challenges and problems”. The fund will also provide “information and assistance to those leaders” who are looking to use public and private sector services.

This is the second fund of its kind launched to support people in government, and the first to be launched by the Irish Council for Global Affairs.

This new fund is funded by a new investment which will see the fund raise an additional €3 million.

The fund is run by the Irish Council for Global Affairs (ICGA), which was set up in 2013 as a not-for-profit foundation.

This year’s fund-raising will be facilitated by the ICGA, and will include a series of consultations with a number of under-represented leaders.

The consultation period begins on July 20, with a public launch expected in October.

The fund’s launch is set to coincide with the launch of ICGA’s new policy framework for government in Ireland.

Gail McHugh, ICGA’s chairwoman and former president of the European Commission, said: “The consultation has been very comprehensive, with a wide range of views and perspectives from leaders, civil society and the public.

“It is clear that the consultation has been very useful and constructive, and we are therefore delighted to be able to launch the fund,” she said.

The launch of the fund is part of the ICGA’s efforts to “build bridges” between the government and the public, and to help the public to have a better idea of the types of problems that government must address.

Gail McHugh said: “Our aim is to make government work better and more transparent, and to be able to provide leaders with the support they need to do this.

“Our new fund will be crucial in enabling us to do just this, because it will ensure that the government takes ownership of its work.”

The funding will be used to carry out a series of consultation events for under-represented leaders on issues such as the new social protection legislation, the public service and the devolution of economic policy in Ireland.

The consultation period will culminate in a public launch of the new fund on October 12.

Gail McHugh said: “As we begin the consultation process we are very pleased to hear that ICGA is seeking to build bridges between government and the public. The fund will allow our leaders to have the support they need to work better for all.
headline: New fund aims to help “marginalised” leaders to “support systemic reforms”

GEO-Ireland is seeking €8M to bring academics to Ireland for a one-year fellowship scheme.

Headline: €8 million to be spent bringing academics to Ireland

The new scheme was launched last week at a presentation to the Irish Academic Network in Cork. The €8 million funding will be used to train the first cohort of graduates from an emerging discipline in Irish universities, with the support of academic disciplines such as geography, economics, psychology, medicine, and engineering.

The first cohort of graduates will be trained in a one-year fellowship. These include full, part-time and part-time part-time students.

The funding will be spent on two-year study courses at Irish universities, with three years of full-time study offered at Trinity College Dublin, and four years of part-time study at the University of Limerick.

The scheme will be funded with a combination of €1M from the Irish Research Council (IRC), €1M from the National University of Ireland (NUI) and €500K from the Government.

The funding will be available to the academic discipline that is being trained. The research project could be of any nature, however the project will cover the costs of travel and accommodation, as well as the cost of books, and the cost of courses.

To be eligible for the scheme, the project has to be an innovative research project. The project must be conducted in collaboration with institutions in the academic disciplines that the project is aimed at.

The project must be submitted in a format that allows for the publication of the research in an Irish journal, if the academic institution grants it.

The project must also include research publications on the subject matter of the research, and the project must be presented at conferences or national events.

The research project should be designed to benefit the international community, and to generate a significant and valuable publication from the research.

The research project should be considered for approval in collaboration with the academic institution that sponsors the project. The funding application should include a plan to ensure that this funding is used to support a national research programme.

The application should be sent to the Research Council for the proposal to be considered by the Research Council’s Research Review and Approval Committee.

This should include a full copy of the proposal and the proposal should be considered in collaboration with the academic institution that sponsors the project. The Application for Funding should not contain any financial support for a commercial organisation.

Once accepted, the application for funding should be submitted to the Research Review and Approval Committee by the beginning of the next academic year. The deadline for the project proposal and the application for funding is January 30.

Funding from the Irish Research Council will be available to the academic disciplines that are being trained by the project, in order to support an emerging and innovative research programme.

The research project will be conducted in collaboration with institutions in the academic disciplines that the project is aimed at. The academic institutions may choose to sponsor the project, or they may choose to co-sponsor the project with the funding body.

The funding will be used to support students, post-graduates, and research projects. The project will also cover the costs of travel and accommodation, as well as the cost of books, and the cost of courses.

When people tell me that the Irish government is run by a bunch of grumpy old men with no vision or energy, I always wonder how true that claim is. In any case, I feel the Irish government is a great place to be. It’s in a good place. I’m not saying that people won’t be in power for a very long time. I’m saying that they won’t be as bad as they were before, that they will be in a much better place.

It’s an excellent environment to work and live in. In Ireland, I’m never stuck in traffic or in a traffic jam. People who are not Irish are treated with respect and with care. We do get the feeling that things are being made to order and we don’t have to do a great deal of the work ourselves.

A lot of the other things that people say, I think, is rubbish. When you’re in a small country, you start to see other countries where they’ve made a lot of the decisions, and you think, “That sounds a bit like me.” I think that if you start to see the Irish government doing a bit of the stuff that’s being done in other countries, it may not be as bad as it was before, and that’s one of the things that makes it a good place to be.

There is some evidence that there are problems within the Irish government. There is this issue with the fact that they want to send people to other countries and put them in positions where they’re not being paid properly and they’re not properly trained. I know there’s an argument that that’s to cut spending, but it’s also to cut expenditure. When you look at a country that’s doing badly economically, you look at some of these decisions and ask, “Is there a reason why they’re making the decisions that they’re making, and then doing them on a whim?” And that’s the thing that’s going on with the Irish government, that’s why they’re doing it.

That’s one of the things that I don’t like. I don’t like that they’ve gone from being such a nice place to have a government that’s run by a small group of very intelligent people to become a gerontocracy. Because there’s some other countries where they have more power. It’s a bit like the idea that we need to leave the EU to be able to have our own countries, that’s not the way it works. We all need to be able to make our own decisions.

The second thing that people say is, “Why is it going on?” Well, the problem is that because the Irish government is doing a bit of the things that other countries are doing, there are people who are getting a lot of the money that are getting from the EU, but then they’re getting less because there’s a bit of a problem within the Irish government.

When you look at the Irish government, the whole system has changed.

A recent scientific study has found that “in Denmark, the vaccine used by public health authorities is not available for children over 18 years old. The vaccine was developed by a Danish vaccine manufacturer and was distributed without a license in 2014.” The article continues:

Danish health authorities have halted distribution of the vaccines to the elderly, in accordance with Danish law. The vaccines, manufactured by the Danish National Vaccine Center, were given out by the government’s health department from June 2013.

The article goes on to point out that the “children” referred to are not “those 18 years and over.” Rather, it is referring to children under the age of 18 who are “under the age of 18 years,” i.e., under the age of 19.

Salman Rushdie’s execution sparked a wave of protest, with thousands of Iranians taking to the streets and hundreds of thousands of people gathering in Tehran to protest the act. The death of Rushdie’s “Satanic Verses” characterised the protests as a protest against censorship of literature. It also led to the Iranian government’s release of the book, which triggered another wave of criticism in Iran. Critics say that Rushdie’s execution was a violation of a freedom of speech. They accuse Iran of arresting and prosecuting people for reading and publishing satirical works. The book had been banned since its publication in the 1990s. But it was published in the Persian Gulf countries as it was a new literary form and a new medium, with a different audience.

They have shown their anger against the regime and they have expressed their fear and hatred for the regime.”

The Irish Examiner’s “In Focus” feature this week is the stunning gallery collection of Hugh Crawford. A former member of the British army and former director of the American National Gallery of Art, Hugh Crawford is at the centre of a very Irish story.

He is the first black director of any American national museum in the past century.

The exhibit at the Crawford Gallery, a former bank in the historic city of Dublin, is a collection of his life’s work – and it is a great show of the man.

The Crawford Gallery is a testimony to the strength of the Irish people. But for the Crawford family – Hugh’s father – it is also the symbol of their loss.

The Crawford Collection is a memorial to his father, who died in 2009.

Hugh Crawford

The exhibition was in his father’s family vault, in the family’s home in Dublin. The vault had been broken into and robbed several years earlier. Hugh Crawford had been in Ireland on business and, after a long discussion with his family, he said he decided to donate the collection to the Crawford Gallery. “When I heard the story of the vault robbery and its destruction, I was shocked,” said Mr Crawford, in a statement released by the gallery on Friday.

The collection, which was made up of works from his lifetime, is now a much more powerful, much more poignant display.

“The collection is a part of history,” said Hugh Crawford.

“It is an incredible story. It’s a story of the strength of the Irish people, a story of an art that was never supposed to exist and a story of a man who believed in his people, a man who took a chance and gave it to the Irish people.”

Hugh Crawford said that the exhibition was also a tribute to his father, who died shortly after his son took on the gallery.

“I have always said that I want my father to be the one to carry on and show what he did,” said Hugh Crawford.

“My father was passionate about what he did and it took a lot of courage for him to be the one to carry on the legacy of what he did.”

For Hugh Crawford, the collection is an object of pride. He said that “the power of an object is to reflect the strength and courage of the people who have the power to hold it,” and that it is “the power of the people who put that collection together that I’m most proud of”.

The Crawford family

Hugh Crawford’s father, William Crawford, was born in 1890 and emigrated to America in 1900. He started a grocery business in the United States and eventually moved to Dublin.

William Crawford was an avid collector of Irish art. In the years following his son’s departure for the gallery, his son Hugh was busy with his own career. He spent the 1980s as a director of the National Gallery of Art and was president of the National Council of Irish Life and Issues.

In 2004, Hugh Crawford joined his father’s family vault in Ireland.

'America is a nation of immigrants. It’s not a racist nation. It’s a country with a high degree of tolerance for people of all ethnicities, creeds, genders and sexual preferences. In Ireland, we don’t accept people who come here with the intention of being a racist.’

Jennifer Horgan and her family came to the U.S. in 1989 and came to an American state where they still live. She says her family has been welcomed in the U.S. without the discrimination, bigotry and racism she experienced in Ireland.

‘I believe, if you have the same background as a person, you’re going to have the same level of expectation that that person would have of you,’ Ms Horgan told The Irish Examiner.

‘I believe it’s fair. I think it’s fair for me to be treated like I’m a citizen. I have to prove that, I have to prove to myself that I’m not some strange, weird or alien. I have to prove that I’m a citizen because that’s what I am.’

The Horgan family also grew up speaking Irish. ‘We all spoke that language’, Jennifer Horgan said.

‘It was just as it is now, except that when we went to America it was all different. It wasn’t the same as what it was in Ireland, even though Ireland is known for its diversity, it was different. But when we came to America it was different.’

Jennifer said her family is not anti-immigrant, they are just against the type of immigration that many of her fellow Irish people have supported.

‘It just comes down to racism. It comes down to prejudice. That’s it. That’s the only way it can go.’

Jennifer said she has not received any personal or professional advice to stop her children from growing up in Ireland.

The mother of two said she believes that if the U.S. can offer opportunities to immigrants, she would do the same.

‘What I see is that in the United States you have different opportunities,’ Jennifer said. ‘I see a lot of people who come here who have no skills, no skills for the jobs that they want to have.

‘I don’t see anyone coming here and going to school, or doing anything. Why don’t they want to go and get the opportunity to go to college, or do the things they want to do?’

But she said she would have never taken a holiday in Ireland.

‘I would have never taken a holiday to go to the U.S. if my children didn’t have the chance,’ Jennifer said.

‘They have to come and work in the U.S. to get an education.’

Ms Horgan said she has supported her children’s immigration.

‘They have had it for so many years that we’ve been doing it, I think they have learned their lesson,’ she said.

Cork City FC beat Cork United for first time at home this season, with the crowd gathering to watch a rare double.

The match itself went well. The first goal was a header from a corner, with the second one a corner into the box. It was the second goal of the game that was the most eye-catching. This was the first time that City’s home crowd, many of whom are city workers, had an opportunity to watch a competitive game at a venue other than the City Ground.

The second goal was a free-kick that was taken by Mark O’Hare and was deflected into the path of the keeper for a goal kick by James Doolan. City had the better of the chances in the first half, but it was the efforts of the United’s defenders that proved to be the most noteworthy.

O’Hare was the first to touch the ball. A close-range header from a corner by Michael Nevin was met by Doolan in the box and then the ball was played to Mark O’Hare at the back post.

With the game being played in the second half, it seemed as if the home fans were ready to give the game their all for a second half. The crowd were not short of encouragement, with O’Hare’s header going into the wall. However, there was no second half.

The score was a draw, so why was there a goal kick awarded?

It was decided that the goal should be awarded as a penalty kick. It was also decided that the goal kick had to be awarded after the two teams had scored one goal. This meant that there had to be two teams with one goal. This created a very odd situation.

The two teams had been awarded a goal kick, but one of those teams had to be the winner of the penalty shootout.

This meant that a team who had already been eliminated from a tournament for the first time in their career was the one who had to take the penalty.

In the end, City had to settle for the penalty, though it had taken a while to get there. It was a very poor goal kick that didn’t go in the goal for Cork. This meant that the best goal kick was in fact from James O’Meara.

Cork United manager John Horan said that his team would have been happy with just the goal kick. Horan was aware of the need for both teams to go into the penalty shoot-out with a goal.

This is not the first time this week that City have had to play without their best player. This was the case the day after City played UCD in a qualifier. The game was a difficult one for City, as the City fans were hoping for a win. However, it came down to the last minute of the game, with City taking an early lead.

The first goal was scored by Tomáš Petřík. The second was a strike from Michael O’Loughlin. It was this second goal that was the most remarkable, as it was scored in the last minute of the game after the game had already been decided.

In the end, City won the game, though this was only because they were the first team to score an away goal.
headline: Beat goes on for busy weekend in Cork

THE TOP 8 – SUPERMARKET CEDDARS HAVE BEEN TASTE TESTED, AND THEY’RE QUITE GOOD

In a world of supermarkets, supermarkets are a rarity.

The only supermarkets that come to mind are the ones that sell a range of produce and foodstuffs, such as in Tesco in the UK, Co-op in Ireland, and Waitrose in the UK and Ireland.

So, what on earth is a supermarket?

A supermarket has two words in common with any large supermarket – a “supermarket”.

It is usually a large building – often a building designed with the aim of creating a great atmosphere – that is divided into sections with a series of shelves, each of which is dedicated to a different product.

A supermarket is the equivalent of a market stall, except that supermarkets are generally much more organised and in many cases very much more efficient.

It may not be called a “supermarket” because it does not have a large display or a variety of goods, but it is a supermarket in a very different sense from the rest of the supermarket world.

In fact, you may be the only person in the supermarket and indeed the entire supermarket network who does not know exactly what is in the shelves of the supermarket nearest you.

The supermarket is not only about the goods that are sold in the front of the building – it is also about the atmosphere created by the different product types that you can buy.

So, there is a real shopping experience at the supermarket; customers can look round and explore the different sections, or talk to staff who are in the store.

But as well as being a place where people can buy food and other products, a supermarket also provides a place for you to do a variety of things.

Food may be the most familiar part of a supermarket, but there are many other services that are offered, from the supermarket’s shops to the café, the canteen and the information point.

It is worth noting that a supermarket is not just about what is sold in the store – it is also about the atmosphere and the shopping experience it creates.

One of the most important things you can do when you first start out as a supermarket customer is to try and find out what is available, what is different from what you are used to, and what is on offer.

This is where some supermarkets are different from other supermarkets, such as Tesco.

The food that is sold in Tesco is very much aimed at the working person. It is designed for those who are looking for a good food budget as a part-time job, not to do part of their day-to-day shopping.

Some of the things that are available in Tesco that are different from what you are used to are the range of produce, as Tesco is not exclusively about food.

There are many items that are available, ranging from breakfast cereals to meat and poultry. There is a wide choice of items available on the shelves, and people are able to choose from a range of products to suit their needs.

Tesco is also a very busy place, and the food that is sold in Tesco is also very busy.

Food can be quite a moving experience at Tesco.
headline: Top 8: Supermarket cheddars put to the taste test for school lunches

Article:

RICHMOND, June 12 (Reuters) – A Limerick dairy farm bought for an accumulated sum of over three million euro ($3.8 million) has been sold to the European Commission.

A statement released by the Irish Farmers’ Association (IFA) on Tuesday said the “unexpected” sale of the farm to the EU body, which has been under investigation since 2017 for using EU money to finance a campaign to promote the agri-food sector, was a “positive development for the farming industry”.

The sale, which includes the farm itself, its 20 buildings, and its assets, was worth a total of almost three million euro.

The IFA said the sale was made under the same rules as other agricultural enterprises, in which the farm’s assets and properties can be sold in certain circumstances.

In a statement the commission said: “The sale of these properties and farms is a positive development for the farming industry.”

It added that the sale was made as the IFA had been informed that the farm would be used for the commission’s monitoring and to address “the concerns of farmers and consumers”.

The commission said it was not able to say when this sale would take place, and it was a “work in progress”.

The sale was part of a wider sale of assets and properties of farm companies for a total price of about three million euro, including the sale of the farm.

The IFA said the sale of the farm was for the commission’s purposes, and not to satisfy any conditions imposed by any state authority.

It added that the sale would only be used to provide the IFA with the ability to verify the identity of the company’s owner and assess the risk of possible conflicts of interest.

The commission is reviewing the sale and could make further comments at a later date.
headline: Limerick farm sold for accumulated sum of over €3.8m

Johnnie Depp has been sentenced to 11 years in jail in connection with a murder case.

The actor and the director of “Thelma and Louise” was found guilty at Dublin High Court of a charge of “perverting the course of justice” after he was found to have shot a rival with a .45-calibre gun in 1993.

He was originally charged with unlawful killing with intent to cause grievous bodily harm after shooting John McBride at the Grand Hotel on the banks of the River Liffey at the age of 43.

On Monday, the court heard that in December 1994, Mr Depp went to a courthouse in Londonderry to answer a charge of murder.

During a brief court appearance he made a number of controversial statements, saying he had been in a car when he was shot by the man he was pursuing.

Judge John Boyle QC told him: “I am satisfied there is a reasonable suspicion you shot John McBride because you believed he was in your car.”

“Mr McBride died of a bullet to the chest,” the judge said.

“He is dead now. I am satisfied you shot him because you believed he was in your car.”

The judge told the judge that Mr Depp had not taken the court into his mind when he stated: “I don’t know whether I was in a car, but I think I was in a car, and I shot him.”

“That was a statement which, if you are prepared to accept it, I think is highly objectionable,” said Judge Boyle.

“The jury have got to be satisfied that it was a very serious crime in the circumstances.”

The judge said he accepted that Mr Depp believed he had been driving and when he saw someone he believed was in the car he was pursuing shooting at, he had pulled out his gun and shot at the man.

“You were prepared to kill a man,” the judge said.

“The defendant’s statement that he did not know whether he had been in a car, that he did not know whether he was in a car, is extremely objectionable.”

“This is not an indictment against the defendant of a murder. It is an indictment against his character.”

Judge Boyle said that he accepted Mr Depp did not realise when he shot the man that he had shot at a rival, and that there was no question of his intention.

However, he said he had to accept that Mr Depp did not take the court into his mind when he made the statement: “I don’t know whether I was in a car, but I think I was in a car, and I shot him.”

“You were prepared to kill a man. The defendant’s statement that he did not know whether he had been in a car, that he did not know whether he was in a car, is extremely objectionable.”

“This is not an indictment against the defendant of a murder. It is an indictment against his character.”
headline: Johnny Depp ‘did not receive a fair trial’, lawyers to tell Court of Appeal

The Irish Examiner

The headteacher of a primary school in Cork has called for a fleet safety audit after a teacher was seriously injured when a school bus driver crashed into him on Monday.

Sinn Féin’s Education Spokesperson, James Brokenshire, said the school’s school management and the Transport Authority are “urgently” looking into the incident.

However, Brokenshire called for drivers to be trained and “have a minimum 2-year minimum” training to avoid similar situations in future.

Mr Brokenshire said that the driver was not under the influence of alcohol or drugs and was not injured seriously.

“It’s important to remember that this accident did not take place in a vehicle,” he said.

“There’s a number of aspects of the school bus driver’s behaviour that are of paramount concern.

“However, I would like to reassure everyone that the driver involved in this incident has now passed his police driving test. He has been employed by the Transport Authority as a bus driver for more than four years.”

Mr Brokenshire said the driver will now be suspended with pay.

“The Transport Authority has undertaken a thorough investigation into the circumstances of the accident and is in the process of sharing its findings with the school,” he added.

“The school has agreed to this decision, which was taken at the request of the Transport Authority, as an appropriate result of this accident.

“The Transport Authority is now taking steps to ensure there will be no repeat incidents of this nature.”

Sinn Féin Senator Michelle O’Neill has called for a national review of school drivers to reduce “unacceptable” incidents.

Ms O’Neill said the situation was “unacceptable” and that the incident must be investigated properly.

“The Cork school bus driver involved in Monday’s accident was not under the influence of alcohol or drugs and did not injure anyone seriously,” she added.

“The Transport Authority has done a full investigation and it has been a very serious accident. I am sure that it will be a matter of urgency for the Transport Authority to find out why the driver of the bus was involved in this accident.

“This needs to be looked at as soon as possible as we know that the Transport Authority will have to take immediate and serious steps to ensure no more similar incidents occur.

“The Transport Authority needs to ensure that drivers are adequately trained and there will be a minimum two-year minimum. I would like to see the Transport Authority’s management, the school management and the school authorities involved in this incident do something about it now.”

Sinn Féin Senator Michelle O’Neill said it was “unacceptable” that a school bus driver injured a teacher and the Transport Authority had been slow to respond.

“I am calling on the Transport Authority to immediately carry out a review of school bus driver training and to take immediate action to ensure the safety of children in schools.
headline: Parents call for fleet safety audit after Cork school bus driver injured

A former president of the University of Limerick (UoL), Pat Hegarty, has lost his appeal against the university’s decision to reject his re-appointment for the position of president of UoL College.

Mr Hegarty, the former president of UoL College (1991-95), was appointed as president of the college in January 1995.

The college’s governing council, which included the president of UoL College, John O’Brien, and the vice-chancellor, the Honourable James Byrne, made a formal decision to reject his reappointment.

The UoL College Council subsequently made a formal decision to accept Mr Hegarty’s reappointment.

After the college’s formal decision to accept Mr Hegarty’s reappointment was made public, Mr Hegarty asked the college’s executive committee to consider his ‘claim that the college was not informed of any alleged procedural irregularity in the application process’.

The executive committee of the college’s governing council, which included Mr Hegarty and Mr Byrne, declined to consider Mr Hegarty’s appeal against the college’s decision to reject his reappointment.

A tribunal was appointed by the College Council to consider Mr Hegarty’s ‘claim that the college was not informed of any alleged procedural irregularity in the application process’.

In making the college’s decision to accept Mr Hegarty’s reappointment, the College Council also accepted that the college had not been notified by the university of any alleged procedural irregularity in the application process and the college had accepted the fact that it had received Mr Hegarty’s application.

The tribunal unanimously confirmed that, in its formal decision, the college had ‘carefully considered’ and had acted ‘within the limits of the college’s discretion’ and had not acted improperly, as Mr Hegarty alleged.

The College Council of the College has subsequently asked the tribunal to confirm its ‘decision’.

In the formal decision of the tribunal, the college has agreed that the college had ‘carefully considered’ and had acted ‘within the limits of the college’s discretion’.

It was found that the college had ‘acted within the limits of its discretion’ because ‘the college had the power to reject any applicant’.

In its decision, the tribunal noted that Mr Hegarty’s re-appointment was ‘not an extraordinary event’ which had caused the college ‘to be more sensitive to any procedural irregularities’.

The tribunal found that it had ‘carefully considered’ the college’s decision to reject Mr Hegarty’s re-appointment.

The tribunal accepted the college’s conclusion that Mr Hegarty’s re-appointment would not be in the best interests of the college, the university and the students at UoL.

The tribunal noted that the college had ‘acted within its discretion’ in accepting Mr Hegarty’s reappointment.
headline: Former WIT president loses High Court action over college's decision not to reappoint him

A letter from Mary Lowry’s attorney, who is also her father-in-law, outlines “concerns” about Patrick Quirke’s use of the land he bought in 2007 for €100,000 for a €500,000 mortgage.

The land was purchased for the then-Irish Labour Party leader’s son Patrick’s own personal use.

The letter obtained by the Irish Examiner was sent to the High Court in Limerick in May.

It said that while the judge found that the mortgage was used for “heritable” purposes, it did not affect the ruling that the land should be sold.

The land, known as the Cavan Hill, was purchased at €1.5m when Patrick Quirke was 23, and had been in the family for generations.

However, the legal letter says that “he is in possession” of the land since his father was living in Ireland.

The land has been used for years by the Quirke family, the letter says.

Quirke bought it at the time when the Irish economy was suffering from the recession.

Mary Lowry, Patrick’s sister, who is a barrister, says her brother “is a very private person”, and does not want anyone to know about his income.

Quirke bought the land with the intention to build a house on it.

“The whole thing is a fraud and a complete lie,” she said.

She said the land was part of a scheme by Patrick Quirke and his family to buy a large parcel of land cheaply for his own use.

The letter also states that Patrick Quirke used the land for a period of about 12 years.

“He used it for his private development and nothing else,” the letter says.

“The land was not cultivated.

“He did not develop the land.

“I am not the one who gave the land to him.”

The letter also states that the Quirke family were responsible for paying no taxes on the property.

The land is not in the Quirke family name.

It is in his wife’s name, who used the title “Lady”.

The letter also says that the court does not need to know the precise location of the land, because the letter shows that the land was “used” on the day before it was purchased.

The letter says the property is a “stranger” to the Quirke family and that the land was never under their direct or control.

It also says there were “circumstances that required Patrick Quirke to act” to prevent anyone knowing about the property.

The letter says that the Quirkes have also not sought any compensation for the land.

The letter says the couple live in a house on the property.

It says that “the courts can only consider the legal and factual evidence presented by the plaintiff”.

“There is no evidence before the court that the land was actually the subject of an agreement”.
headline: Love triangle trial: Letter from Mary Lowry's lawyer outlined 'concerns' over Patrick Quirke's lease on her land

The world is coming to an end, according to a leading Irish journalist, and with the rise of the internet, the media, and social media, he says, we're going to see the end of newspapers.

Irish Examiner, September 2nd, 2007

It's no secret that there has been much speculation about the demise of the UK's Sunday newspaper.

Some say the days of the tabloid are numbered and newspapers will cease to exist in Ireland.

Others see an opportunity to revive the print edition.

And the public have no doubt that the demise of the Sunday Times is imminent.

And how would that be possible?

One of the few things that makes this newspaper unique is its sheer ambition - to reach every part of the country, to bring the whole of Ireland to life.

The paper has never had anything close to a financial crisis.

Its editor is no slacker - but the rest of the board is very much in the same boat as him.

It's no surprise then that so many people are interested in becoming a reporter for The Sunday Times.

There are some very talented people in the paper - they are a mixture of the finest talent and the most brilliant minds in the country.

It's a newspaper that will be the envy of the whole world.

So what would it take to make The Sunday Times a reality?

As it is, it's a newspaper with an even more ambitious agenda to realise the dream that this newspaper has so passionately championed for so many years.

For many newspapers, the newspaper business is all about producing more stories, more analysis, more news.

But for The Sunday Times, it's about the power of the words.

When you read The Sunday Times, you will be reading for both the news and the words.

The words will do the talking for you.

And the stories will do the telling.

The newspaper will be a powerful agent of change in the world of news.

But it's the ability to convey ideas in a compelling way that is what will make The Sunday Times - and what will make it truly special.

The Sunday Times believes that the power of words is much greater than the power of the paper it was printed on.

It's the power of words that will propel the newspaper into new, and perhaps even extraordinary, places.

And that's why it's so important for The Sunday Times to find a new editor, a new chairman, and a new management team to take over its troubled and often failing operation.

And the only way it can do that is to get the best person in the business on board.

The paper needs someone who has the passion, the knowledge, and the determination to keep the papers on the right track.

The newspaper is, after all, an independent enterprise that is owned by a handful of people, the most valuable media in the country, and there is no doubt about who that is.

But what is the man who will be running the paper and who will be in charge of it?

And what is it that makes the man who has the power to take the papers to the next level?

The name that will ring through every newspaper in Ireland will be that of one Mr. Brendan Murphy.
headline: 'What is the world coming to?'

The Irish medical profession’s growing frustrations with the rising cost of healthcare – compounded by the fact that many patients do not know they have a problem – are likely to continue to be a factor in the ongoing conflict between health ministers, who are increasingly concerned about the high costs, and doctors, many of whom believe the situation is being exacerbated by cuts to public health budgets.

This week, the Department of Health said it would not be issuing any more guidance on the issue, in the face of growing criticism.

The growing criticism is unlikely to have ended any time soon. The Irish Medical Organisation and the Medical Council, which have issued statements criticising the department, are likely to press for the issue to be dealt with swiftly and on the basis that it should be dealt with in the budget process.

The government is likely to demand a review of the growing number of patients being forced to wait for weeks or months for the results of the latest cancer screening.

The doctors’ organisation AIE said: “The pressure on NHS resources is having a serious impact on the health of patients in the region.”

The doctor group said that while the number of cancers that can be detected has continued to grow, there has been a “noticeable decrease in cancer cases and a significant increase in the numbers of patients being referred and found to be free from cancer symptoms and therefore waiting until their test results come back.”

It added: “This is having a significant impact on the availability and utilisation of hospital services.”

The AIE also said that while it was not the intention of the health secretary to increase the rate of cancer screening, the increase was “likely to be substantial, particularly in certain areas.”

The AIE said that while it understood that cancer screening programmes “should be delivered more efficiently and equitably for patients, the recent changes in the policy and practice of cancer screening could undermine the effectiveness of the existing programmes and lead to unnecessary delays in diagnosis.”

It added that while patients did not necessarily need to see a doctor to have their test results returned, they would “increasingly consider seeing a doctor to discuss these issues”.

The health minister’s office issued a statement criticising the comments and said: “The Minister is aware of the recent news reports in Ireland and around the world.

“He is aware that this is an area of significant controversy and one which has been the subject of intense and heated discussions amongst his colleagues in the department.”

The statement continued: “The Minister has repeatedly emphasised his commitment to improving the quality of care and improving the standard of care across the country.

“The Minister has been extremely clear that it is his intention to improve the standard of care across the country and to ensure that as many as possible have the care they need.

“These initiatives will not be compromised by the comments made by the AIE and it is the Minister’s intention to continue to put the health of our people at the heart of government policy.”

But the Department of Health has no intention of changing its position and said it was not in the public interest for the issue to be dealt with further or on the basis of any new ‘guidance’ being issued.
headline: Department of Health and hospital doctors at odds over growing waiting lists

In an escalating series of attacks in the Gaza Strip, Palestinian security officials say the death toll has risen to 32, with more than 60 Palestinians injured. In the latest incident, Palestinians were killed during clashes between Palestinians and Israeli troops in the city of Khan Younis, east of Gaza City, and in a number of smaller incidents in the Shati refugee camp, a few kilometres south of the city.

The Israeli military said it had deployed a force to protect the coastal enclave, which has a population of about 1.7 million people.

“The number of Palestinians injured is now more than 60,” an Israeli military spokesman said. “Three-quarters of the people injured are civilians, with many of them being children. We are trying to control the situation so that we don’t have to call in troops.”

In Shati camp, Israeli soldiers and riot police fired tear gas and rubber bullets to quell the protests, injuring many Palestinians and damaging homes and property, which are now sealed off by the military. The soldiers also used live ammunition and rubber-coated bullets.

The situation escalated last night when Israeli aircraft launched an air raid over Khan Younis. The army said the strikes targeted a “terrorist hide-out” but did not name the attackers.

Khan Younis is close to the Israeli border.

A spokesman for the Israeli military said there were “no indications of a terrorist attack”.

Israeli forces said they had shot down a drone in the area but the Israeli military was not able to identify the aircraft or to claim responsibility for the strike.

The Israeli military had earlier used rubber-coated bullets, tear gas and stun grenades to disperse Palestinian protests.

Palestinian medics say they have treated around 150 Palestinians over the last few days and are at a loss to explain what is happening.

The Israeli army says it is not prepared to negotiate with the Palestinians, and that it will not allow the two sides to hold talks. It added that, so far, it has not targeted any military facilities.

Israeli forces said they had shot down a drone in the area but the Israeli military was not able to identify the aircraft or to claim responsibility for the strike.

The Israeli military said it was targeting a “terrorist hide-out”.

A spokesman for the Israeli army said there were no indications of a terrorist attack.

He did not rule out the possibility that the drone was part of a larger operation.

But the spokesman said it was too early to say whether or not the aircraft was a military aircraft, and that it was “a regrettable incident”.

Israel was forced to apologise after a video of the strike was leaked last week, showing soldiers shooting a dog in the head as it ran over them.

The video was then quickly made public by a senior officer in the army’s military intelligence unit.

The officer, Major General Erez, said on Facebook that the strike, which took place on the Israeli side of the border, was a mistake, and that it had been meant to hit a “terrorist hide-out”.
headline: 32 Palestinians killed ‘while trying to reach food distribution sites in Gaza’

By FRANCIS WHITE

Theresa May is determined to deliver a credible alternative to the government’s backstop, despite warnings from Labour that it would be politically toxic for the party to back the plan to keep Northern Ireland in the EU.

During Prime Minister’s Questions on Tuesday, May said she would not compromise on the issue, and a backstop was “not good enough” for the Good Friday Agreement.

Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn has repeatedly said the backstop was a “no go” for Labour, and suggested the party’s support for it was a “betrayal” of the union.

However, during the Prime Minister’s Questions, he said the Government’s own proposals for a replacement to the backstop would not be acceptable to Labour, while a senior government minister was “sceptical” about Labour backing the plan.

On Tuesday, the Independent Parliamentary Standards Authority (Ipsa) upheld the Government’s decision to reject an amendment which would have limited the scope of the backstop to cover “a limited number of the economic elements of the Withdrawal Agreement”.

This decision was based on the fact that the Government had previously refused to give the green light for a no-deal Brexit.

The Ipsa also ruled that the Department for Exiting the European Union (DExEU) had been given sufficient time to prepare for a no-deal outcome, rejecting a request to extend the period for the DExEU to prepare.

In addition, the Ipsa found the Prime Minister’s failure to produce a new plan to replace the backstop did not undermine her efforts to get the final deal approved by Parliament, as she had claimed.

“The backstop is a binding constraint,” said Ipsa Chair, Andrew Tyrie.

“We need to move on and get a deal that works, and that’s what the Government are working towards.

“But I think the Government has made a very strong case that this backstop should not be allowed to remain in place.”

The Ipsa’s findings were released as the Government continued to seek to avoid a damaging backstop.

With the announcement of the new customs arrangement, the Government has been able to make it clear that the backstop would be “subject to the regulatory checks, checks and controls that we have set out in the Withdrawal Agreement”.

In a move which may be seen as a victory for Labour, the Ipsa ruled that the Government had not been given sufficient time for the DExEU to prepare for a no deal outcome, despite the Prime Minister stating that the “difficult decision” of how long the DExEU was required to prepare for no deal had been “put forward”.

“I was pleased that the DExEU was given additional time,” said the Prime Minister.

“I have always argued for a two-year transition period.”

This new ruling is a victory for Labour.

The Ipsa’s findings do not appear to contradict the Government’s position that the DExEU had to be prepared for no deal.
headline: Coveney tells Raab to produce viable alternatives to backstop

Author:

The Irish Examiner

DUBLIN, Nov 25 (Reuters) – Officers would not recommend the Defence Forces career to their close friends or family, a survey carried out by the Irish Examiner on Sunday said.

The survey found 95.3 percent of soldiers surveyed would not recommend a career in the Irish Army to friends or family. This is despite the Irish army being the only military in the world where the majority of officers have not been in contact with their troops.

The findings are the first since the Defence Forces introduced a new programme of career support for its officer cadre in 2016.

“In his eight years as president, he led a country to the brink of collapse, fought against all odds to hold on to its independence and became an icon of the struggle for freedom and human rights,” said the statement issued by the government.

De Klerk, a former head of state who was president between 1986 and 1994 and again between 1999 and 2001, was in charge when the country was at the height of its apartheid system. De Klerk was born in Natal in 1948 to a middle-class father who became a policeman and a mother who had a series of spells in nursing school.

De Klerk left school aged 16 and joined the African National Congress (ANC) in 1964. He worked first in the South African Railways Corporation and then as a driver in a factory.

In the 1980s de Klerk became president of the ANC and was elected in 1986. His first act in power was to declare “no political parties or non-racial organisations” in government departments. De Klerk was elected the ANC’s national leader in 1994, but resigned in 2001 in the face of corruption charges that he denied.

De Klerk was acquitted of all charges in 2004 and was re-elected as ANC leader in 2004 but resigned again in September 2006 in protest at government policies. The following year, he was convicted of fraud and corruption but was pardoned by President Thabo Mbeki and was replaced by Nelson Mandela.

He was elected as South Africa’s first black president in 1994 and became South Africa’s first black prime minister in 2008.

The last time de Klerk was president was in March 2001, shortly after the end of his presidency, when he had to abandon the ANC in a dispute over a plan to take over the South African Reserve Bank (SARB).

De Klerk was first elected to parliament as an ANC MP in 1989 and was re-elected to Parliament in 1994. He became deputy prime minister for foreign affairs in 1993 and held that position until 2001.
headline: South Africa’s last apartheid president FW de Klerk dies at 85

A year on from the Japanese bombing of Pearl Harbor, the Japanese people marked the anniversary in a powerful display of patriotism.

Ahead of the 76th anniversary of the atomic bombing of Japan by the US Air Force on 7 December 1945, a commemorative plinth was unveiled at Nihonbashi in Tokyo. The plinth bears the signatures of the survivors of the bombing, whose remains lie in a cemetery in the north of Tokyo, and those who attended the ceremony.

A similar tribute to the atomic bombing of Hiroshima, which occurred the same year as the Nagasaki blast, was held in Hiroshima in February 1945.

It was also a year when the number of civilian victims was at its lowest, but that did not stop the Japanese government from giving an annual commemoration of the event.

The ceremonies in Nagasaki and Hiroshima were conducted by the US Air Force, a service that, under US civilian control at the time, is considered the sole authority for Japan’s commemoration of the atomic bombing.

The US Air Force established the Air Force Museum in the city of Nagasaki in 1954, and has since maintained the museum in the city of Yasukuni in the south of the city, with the main building housing the museum being located in the former US Army barracks of the Yokota Air Base.

The ceremony in Nagasaki was held on 21 and 22 November, the same day that the US Naval Air Station at Oomori was bombed to pieces, and the ceremony in Hiroshima took place on 24 and 25 January, the day the atomic bombing of Hiroshima took place.

As the last ceremony of the two dates, it marked the end of an era.

The event, which was called the Remembrance Year, is organised by the US Air Force, and is an annual event to honour the bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The two cities have been designated as the only cities in Japan that have been declared World War II war-crimes sites, but the names of the cities have not been used.

The ceremonies were attended by senior officials from the US Air Force and other nations.

Ahead of the ceremony, the US Air Force released a statement of condolences to the families of the Japanese victims and members of the US armed forces.

“We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families of the victims of the atomic bombing in Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Our people, our Government, and our entire military, air force, and national defence structure have sustained the effects of the attack for seven long, hard years.”

A US Air Force statement said that the Air Force’s mission is to ensure the safety of all Americans.

“The Air Force and other US Armed Forces personnel are in the midst of an unprecedented humanitarian effort to help the people of the United States recover from the effects of the atomic bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. We are confident that all of us are working to ensure that the survivors of these twin attacks are able to fully recover and re-enter the life of society as soon as possible,” the statement said.

The statement continued: “We have no illusions about the difficulty of such a task, particularly in the post-holocaust period. The suffering of the victims is hard to bear.
headline: Nagasaki marks 76th anniversary of US atomic bombing

Dáithí – I'm worried I'll end up as a carer for my mother-in-law

“I’m worried that when I have kids it might change my whole lifestyle.” This is a message that has been put out there by a man called Daithí, a well known young Catholic in his 30s who has a teenage son and daughter in the States and a baby granddaughter in the UK. “I’m not the kind of person who takes care of myself,” he said. “I’m a very busy person.”

The idea of being a mother-in-law to someone who has three children of her own isn’t something that Daithí had in mind. But after giving birth to the third child, his life took a twist when his wife, who was already living with them in the US, had an abortion. “She called me up and said: ‘Are you ready to have a baby?’” he said.

Daithí’s mother-in-law had died from a brain haemorrhage, leaving a child-less man with a daughter and a granddaughter. Daithí’s father had died from cancer, leaving his family without a wage to care for their three young children. “It’s a very different situation,” Daithí said, “but I’m ready to do whatever it takes to get a job, and I’m prepared to work myself to death”.

He was offered a job at an Irish company in Chicago, and after a few weeks’ training he was offered a job with a company that provides childcare services to the US military, but has since been told that they are looking for a new manager.

“But I’m worried that I’ll end up a housewife, not working,” he said. “When I’m not there to provide for the kids, they can do what they want. They can put them to work. If I’m not there I can say: ‘I’m not there, my daughter is not there, I’m not there for you’. And you know what, I’ll be doing exactly the same thing for my kids.”

He said he was ready to give up his job, but his boss at the company had said they would take him on. “The man said: ‘I think you’d be great for the place’. And I said: ‘OK, I’ll do it for one month’. Then I said: ‘OK, I can do that for six months’. And I went on to give up everything and just work full-time, but I’m still going to look after the kids.”

At the moment his youngest child is in school, Daithí is staying home, but he said it is likely that he will take on an assistant. “I’ve got all these skills,” he said. “I know how to take care of these kids and I can deal with the housework. I can cook, I can clean.
headline: Dear Dáithí: I'm worried I'll end up as a carer for my mother-in-law

Ahead of the Estonian-based Russian military lawyer Sergei Skripal on Thursday (12 November), it is expected that he will challenge the request to extradite him to Russia, which will likely be opposed by the UK.

Sergei Skripal was poisoned in Salisbury in March last year.

The Skripals, who lived in Britain, were later found on a train.

The Salisbury attack was linked to Russian President Vladimir Putin's alleged efforts to influence the 2016 presidential election in the UK.

The UK's extradition request, which the EU has yet to comment on, has been subject to considerable scrutiny since the poisoning was made public in March last year.

It is expected the request to extradite Skripal to Russia will be opposed by the UK in October of this year.

Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia are believed to have been targeted by a Russian nerve agent.

Russian lawyer Sergei Skripal arrives at a court in Salisbury, Britain, on 9 March 2018 (AFP/Getty Images)

The court was unable to hear the defence arguments due to the disruption of the trial, but defence lawyer Sergei Skripal appeared before the court for one hour.

He was accused of committing the crime of "attempted murder" for allegedly selling nerve agents to the Russian state.

He was charged with the following offences:

Two counts of attempted murder

Two counts of attempted grievous bodily harm

One count of causing an explosion with intent

One count of attempting to cause the explosion by detonating an explosive device

One count of attempting to use a weapon with intent

The judge at the court hearing, David Cairns QC, will rule on the defence arguments of the Russian lawyer.

The Russian lawyer, Sergei Skripal, poses with his daughter, Yulia. He is escorted out of the court by the Judge, David Cairns QC, on a hearing in Salisbury, Britain. (PA)

The trial is being held behind closed doors, which will keep the hearing from public view, but it has been covered by the media.

It is likely to be the third hearing in the trial that will not be open to the media.

The court heard from the Russian lawyer before the court hearing began on Thursday morning.

The Russian lawyer, Sergei Skripal, is escorted out of the court by the Judge, David Cairns QC, on a hearing in Salisbury, Britain, on 12 November 2018. (PA)

In the court room, Mr Skripal said: "As I am now being questioned by the court and I am being heard I am very disappointed. The court is very clearly doing its work very well and I am very disappointed that it cannot hear my defence properly."

He added that he felt sorry for the "victims who have suffered this awful tragedy".

He said: "I was in Salisbury myself. I have seen the devastation this has caused. There were bodies lying on the roads and I just can't understand how the public can allow this to happen and how it can happen to innocent people.

"I have seen the Russian intelligence agents there, all in black uniforms, they have the same equipment as the ones who committed this crime."
headline: Estonian Kinahan hitman will challenge extradition bid in October

Sara Ochs on "The End of the Rainbow"

On Wednesday, we look at the remarkable novel "The End of the Rainbow", which is the first in a new series by Sara Ochs, one of Ireland’s most acclaimed young novelists, who is now writing under her own name.

The novel’s title, the only real clue to Ochs’s identity, is taken from the book’s title: ‘The End of the Rainbow’.

The ‘rainbow’ is a concept that has haunted Ochs since she was a child. She’s an artist who has been drawn into this kind of work because of her fascination with the natural world and the way it relates to people. The story is set on a day when her father, Irish novelist, author and Nobel laureate Seamus Heaney is due to fly off to Canada, from where he will go on to travel the world for a new book.

Ochs was 12 when she started writing this book – a book that has had an impact on her life and will continue to affect hers for years to come.

In the beginning of the book, when she is 13 and living in a small town on the western seaboard of Ireland, Ochs, a teenager, begins to go through her father’s possessions to see what he has collected over the years. This includes paintings that he has left behind. She also begins to draw inspiration from some of these paintings, as she watches her father’s life – from before he went to Canada to after he returned to Ireland – come to life on the pages of her notebook.

The work that Ochs did is to make a book that makes a living, and a beautiful living at that. ‘The End of the Rainbow’ was released by Picador last year and quickly became the subject of the international attention it attracted. It was a great success, not only because it was an amazing debut novel from one of Ireland’s foremost novelists, but also because it was a stunning example of what Ochs could achieve in her art.

‘The End of the Rainbow’ is a deeply personal story about the artist and her family. The story is set in her own town and is told in her own words, which is very different to the kind of language that she has previously used, in her short stories.

The story follows her father as he starts his life again, in his new, quiet and private life in New York. She also follows him as he travels back to Ireland with new ideas and feelings, and has the opportunity to share them with his wife, and with his mother.

The novel’s ending is a remarkable testament to Ochs’s strength and ability to write a novel that has a lasting impact.

The book, in its entirety, was only three months old at the time of the release of the film ‘The End of the Rainbow’. It was published in November, when the book was still a new book, and quickly became one of the most widely reviewed books of the year.
headline: Book Review: Sara Ochs' debut is strikingly assured and accomplished

Irish Examiner

By John Joyce

The High Court has ruled that the Irish Government cannot block the appointment of a Minister in the next Government, if a candidate is not on the official shortlist.

Paul Murphy, a Minister in the Dáil for the first time in 35 years, is seeking a Court injunction to block the appointment of an ex-minister, Dara Calleary, who sits in the Government in the Dáil for the first time in 28 years.

In the High Court yesterday (16 April), Mr Justice Barry Kennedy upheld the State's argument that the appointment of Mr Calleary would undermine the Government and the Office of the Deputy First Minister, the position that he had been appointed by the Government.

Mr Calleary had been the member of the Government for the whole of 2011 but was first appointed as an independent in 2005. He was elected a Senator in the Dáil in 2006.

Mr Murphy’s suit was brought by the Irish People’s Alliance Against Austerity and the Irish Republican Socialist Party, who say the appointment of Mr Calleary would damage their interests in their quest for a government.

The Department of Justice was represented by Michael McDowell, the chief legal counsel to the Department. Lawyers for Mr Calleary were represented by Geoffrey McLaughlin of the Irish Law Society.

Mr Calleary is a barrister in the European Parliament and was appointed in 2009 to the Dáil, after which he was an independent for a further 12 months.

Mr Calleary is now a member of the Government and was appointed Deputy First Minister. Mr Murphy was appointed Minister for Transport, Communications, Culture and Sport in the Dáil after the first general election in 2005 and was subsequently appointed Minister for Tourism in the Dáil, which he held until he was appointed to the Dáil in 2011.

The Irish People's Alliance Against Austerity are represented by John Healy, while the Irish People’s Alliance Against Austerity and the Irish Republican Socialist Party are represented by John Curran.

Mr Murphy’s barrister, Alan McChesney, told the court that a Minister cannot block a candidate’s appointment.

“It is not within the competence of the Dáil to prevent the appointment of a Minister in the Government if a candidate is not on the shortlist,” he said.

“An important purpose of the Dáil is to provide a platform for Government and Opposition Ministers to provide a platform for the public, the press and other stakeholders.

“But the Dáil’s role is not to be a platform for the Government. It is to provide Government with a political forum in which Ministers can seek to seek answers to the Government’s and Opposition’s policies. The Government’s role is to provide a platform to the Government’s proposals.”

Mr McChesney submitted the case to the High Court in response to the Government’s application for an injunction to prevent Mr Calleary’s appointment.
headline: Paul Murphy takes High Court case to block super junior ministers from Cabinet meetings

The Irish Examiner

Leo Varadkar said that he did not think he would be here without the work done by US President Donald Trump and his allies on the issue of LGBT rights.

“I think I would not be here without all of the work done in this field,” Varadkar said on RTÉ’s The Late Late Show on Saturday.

Varadkar told the interviewer he thought that in the coming months the Trump administration would be “trying to make it very difficult, if not impossible” for him to hold his position in the Dáil.

Varadkar was speaking on RTÉ’s Late Late Show after he was asked on Friday whether he was “disappointed” with the way the new president has conducted himself since taking office.

When the interviewer told him that he would not have the opportunity to work for the new administration if he did not support gay rights, he said he would “take the blame for the work done, and not the blame for the work not done”.

He later told the interviewer that he did not have much to say to the new president.

“I was surprised [Trump] said he was going to make gay marriage illegal,” he said, referring to an interview last week in which the president said he wanted to impose “some kind of guidelines” for state marriage laws.

Varadkar also said he “was surprised that, at the very end of the interview, the interviewer got very serious.”

He said he had been “taken aback that I would be the first Dáil member to have to answer [questions] in a press conference,” but also that he had no idea whether he would do so.

Varadkar also said he found it “very interesting” that “the president did not seem to think that the Irish Government would have any power” over the US border with the US.

He said that his “political advisers” told him that, if he were in the Dáil, he would not have a problem voting to repeal the Eighth Amendment, which allows for civil unions.

“I’m not sure what the government’s position would be on this, but I am sure it would be something I would have a problem with,” he said.

In the same interview, Varadkar also said that he was “worried” by the “lack of progress” on LGBT rights by the new Irish government.

He said he was also concerned about the “lack of commitment” shown by the new Irish government in relation to the issue of sexual orientation.

PHILADELPHIA – Authorities have charged a man with arson after a fire gutted the mansion of the governor of Pennsylvania and two firefighters.

Firefighters found the house on Thursday, the paper said.

The mansion’s exterior of logs was burned in the fire, and the interior was destroyed, the Inquirer said.

“Our state is not a place that needs a flashover,” Gov. Tom Wolf told reporters at a press conference Monday.

“It’s important that we move swiftly to prevent any further damage,” Wolf said.

The state fire marshal said the fire was not contained.

“The cause of this fire remains undetermined at this time,” the fire marshal said in a statement.

A Dublin man has launched a legal challenge over his €30 million claim to EBS and Ulster Bank to the €50m that he says he lost after being sued by the two banks for not forwarding payments to his former partner.

David Harkin has been pursuing the claims of breach of contract against EBS and Ulster Bank for more than two years.

The case has been settled in favour of EBS in May 2013, but Mr Harkin has not been paid.

Mr Harkin has since been seeking legal clarification from EBS, arguing that the bank failed to inform him about a payment he had received from the bank’s former office in the Republic.

He is also suing Ulster Bank for a breach of the parties’ agreement in relation to the payment.

The Irish Examiner understands that Mr Harkin has been unable to confirm the exact amount he claims he was due for when the bank failed to forward the payment.

Mr Harkin is also seeking to recover a £10m sum that the bank failed to inform him about from the time he took over the bank’s former branch in the Republic from 2009 to 2012.

Mr Harkin said: “I’ve had two years’ worth of work and we have been able to get close to the settlement.

“The issue of my claim was resolved.”

A statement released on the bank’s behalf by Mr Harkin’s counsel said: “The matter is now closed.”

However, the statement does not explain the legal status of the payment or say how Mr Harkin has been left with no money.

The bank also declined to say whether the settlement is final, saying that it could take some time.

A spokesperson for the bank said: “The settlement is final and all disputes have been settled.”

Mr Harkin said he was “very, very happy” with the resolution and added: “I am very happy that the settlement is final.”

He said he does not accept that the bank’s legal position has been affected by its legal fees. “I am not complaining and it has been paid in full,” he said.

Mr Harkin has not received any further payments since he commenced the legal action.

The bank said it has received no complaints about its handling of Mr Harkin’s business.

Mr Harkin said he has been receiving money from his Irish lawyer. He added that the money will be used to settle the case and to assist his legal costs.

EBS said that, because it is a separate company from the bank, it had no obligation to forward payments to Mr Harkin.

The bank also said that it did not have a policy or procedure that led to the loss of Mr Harkin’s €30m claim.

EBS said it would continue to deal with Mr Harkin in accordance with its normal procedures and practices.

The Culture of Disruption

Pat Shortt was, for most of his life, a man of action. He was the mayor of Dublin city, and he was also the Labour party leader in the Irish parliament for many years. But he had never been an activist. In fact he was only in politics for seven years: he was elected as the leader of the Irish Labour party, in 1969, and he held that post until 1997. He served as deputy prime minister from 1978 until 1985. When he became Labour party leader, he was not an activist. There was a period when he was a leading member of the Labour party, but this was nothing more than a leadership role. It was during this leadership tenure that he started to develop a new style, a style which did not involve a lot of activity. In his last two years as Labour party leader, he had the opportunity to do a lot of what he had done during the leadership of the Irish Labour party. His style at that time was to work and work and work.

This style, at one point, made Shortt, the leader of the Irish Labour party, look like a saint. This was because in a way, it had been a style in the past.

The first time this style was used in the Irish parliament was when the Fine Gael party, the Irish Labour party and the Irish Labour party all sat together in the Irish parliament. The idea was that it would be interesting to see how the different groups would react to the proposals that the Labour party had put forward. The Fine Gael party wanted to put forward a proposal. The Labour party wanted to put forward a proposal. And the Labour party had no idea what the Fine Gael party was proposing, so they sat around and started talking about the problems that the Labour party was going to have with the Fine Gael party.

The Labour party, after that, started to use a style of work and work and work which was quite different from the style that Shortt had previously used in the Labour party.

The Labour party used this style to make the Fine Gael party look terrible. The Fine Gael party did not have a particularly good record when it came to the way it dealt with the Irish electorate. The Fine Gael party made many proposals which were very negative towards the Irish electorate. The Fine Gael party tried to make it look like it was the Irish party that was responsible for all the problems the Fine Gael party had and had no idea what the Fine Gael party was proposing. The Fine Gael party was the party which came out as the voice for the interests of Irish people. And it used that as an excuse for its failings.

But when Shortt became Labour party leader, he did not revert to his previous style. He continued to use that style. And that style came to mean that there were all sorts of things that the Fine Gael party should have done that he did not do. The Fine Gael party made very negative proposals, and he said, “No, no, no.” He said, “We are the party of the people, we are the party of the Irish people, we are the party of the Irish electorate.” So the Fine Gael party was the party of the Fine Gael party.

And he made the Fine Gael party look very bad.

But he did not go back to the style that he had used before he was in politics.
headline: Culture that made me: Pat Shortt

The man whose name was at the centre of a war of words between the United Kingdom and Turkey before and after the March 2014 referendum is now considering making a generous gesture to his country.

Ioannis Metaxas, the Greek prime minister who led the country out of the euro zone and into the EU, made it clear that he would not be satisfied with just his country’s EU membership. His “hand of friendship” is to Turkey, Mr Metaxas’s office said yesterday.

As well as “an opening of relations between the two countries”, Mr Metaxas’s office said his “efforts for a peaceful solution of the Cyprus problem” had reached a level “where the two countries are interested in resolving the issues at hand”.

A Turkish government spokesperson told The Telegraph yesterday that Mr Metaxas’s “efforts for a peaceful solution of the Cyprus problem” were being hampered by the Greek Cypriot leader’s “strong commitment” to the island’s reunification. “He said that, although he cannot force the issue, his country would continue to support the ‘normalization’ process,” the spokesperson said.

Meanwhile, British Prime Minister David Cameron said he was worried about the increasing number of “misinterpretations” of his government’s position by Turkey’s president, Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Turkey has been one of the European Union’s most intransigent critics of the EU, and is now a major exporter of illegal drugs. In a speech yesterday, Mr Erdogan made clear that he had “come to the conclusion” that the UK “had betrayed the people of this country and this region”.

“The Turks’ position is clear,” Mr Cameron said. “The UK cannot be perceived as being so hostile to Turkey that it is willing to do anything at all that will have an impact in a way that we can’t reverse.”

He added: “I feel I have to say that the prime minister is absolutely right about that.”

Mr Cameron suggested there were “two options” on the table in dealing with Turkey:

Either Turkey will be expelled from the EU or it will be forced to agree to more stringent conditions on its visa policy.

He pointed to the “very clear message” Turkey had been given by the United Nations that it “should be allowed to continue its membership”.

But a Downing Street spokesman said the UK would not be “giving up on the whole question of Cyprus” and would “always be ready to talk to anyone in the international community”.

Asked if Mr Cameron had made up his mind, Mr Metaxas’s office said: “We have no intention of giving up on the whole question of Cyprus and we will continue our efforts for a peaceful solution of the Cyprus problem.”

The Greek prime minister has said he would not be satisfied with his country being given EU membership for free. In a speech yesterday, he described Turkey as “a major state-sponsor of terrorism” and as “an enemy to Europe”.

DUBLIN - The woman who was kidnapped by Irish gangs and held captive for a week was located safe and well on Monday after she escaped from a car and ran for her life to the remote countryside in Co. Kerry.

Serena Ryan was discovered near a car with her brother and her sister, both suffering from broken bones in the head and other wounds, on Sunday.

The couple, who were travelling from Co. Cork to London, were abducted along with seven other people on a motorway on December 31.

The woman said she had walked from Co. Clare to Belfast with her brother to visit a friend and she believed they had been taken for money.

She said she had been in bed and when the gang found her at her home in Co. Clare, they forced her to kneel on the floor before dragging her to the back of the car, where they beat her and told her they would kill her if she spoke.

“They said that they would kill me but I didn’t ask to die,” she said.

She said she was “terrified” but kept quiet as the men in the car repeatedly hit her and she had no idea what was happening.

She said the men then took her to the car where they tried to force her out.

“My brother opened the door and he grabbed me to try to keep me quiet so they could drive us to England,” she said.

She was found by her brother near the car and taken to the hospital where she was reunited with her family.

The gang, she said, had taken her brother and sister as they did not have identification or a way to get back to their home.

She said she had broken her left arm in a fall after being beaten and that her brother had broken a leg.

When she arrived at the hospital she was told by the doctor that she had been beaten “very hard”.

She added: “They had a cut on my cheek that they had to take out. I was in a coma and I was not allowed to go to Ireland for four weeks.”

She said she had been beaten and had lost a lot of blood.

She was taken to Cork University Hospital where she was diagnosed with a broken skull and broken arm.

She was released from Cork University Hospital on Sunday and admitted to hospital again on Monday after being admitted for two days.
