In a country of 1.6 million people, every person is a potential subject for the next genetic test, a prospect that keeps the news coming in Irish circles.

One woman who knows all too well how she can benefit from such a tool is a 40-year-old mother of two from Galway City.

“I’ve been through a few genetic tests myself,” says Mrs McCarthy, “and it’s something I’ve used for more than a decade now.”

“I know what my children are like, my children are very good-looking, and I know how they’ll turn out,” she says. “My husband and I are both teachers, so I’m going to see a lot more of my children, and I hope they’re very healthy.”

She is also thinking of her next child, who she hopes will look more like her than his siblings do.

“I have a 12-year-old son, and we have a 13-year-old daughter. We’re hoping that one of them will look more like me than our children do,” she says.

While the tests are not as widespread as they are in Europe, they can be invaluable for parents with children who have an uncertain future.

“The information we have is priceless. I know my daughter will have a better future because she’ll have an older brother. If she has a brother who’s 18, she’ll have another brother,” Mrs McCarthy says.

But one woman who is looking at her next child’s results is from the same county as Mrs McCarthy.

Sara Tarr, a 32-year-old mother of two from Dublin, says she doesn’t want to think of having to think of next generation and that there’s no guarantee that her eldest daughter will have the same features as her brother.

“I think that we’ll see her as an adult,” she says. “I don’t want her to be a girl, I want her to look more like me. She’ll probably have a slight difference, a tiny bit, but we’re not that worried.”

Sara Tarr and her husband have two daughters aged 12 and 16, the oldest of whom has not yet turned 18.

In the meantime, they are looking at next generation information and are “very, very excited” about having a fourth child.

“We’ve had our third, and we’re so excited about having another,” Sara Tarr says.

She’s also had a 12-year-old boy, her daughter’s older brother, but he now has a girlfriend and is “a very happy and loving boy”.

“So I think that’s what our children will look like as adults,” she says. “I know how the kids will turn out, and I think it’s going to be a good thing.”

There are no guarantees, of course, and the test can never guarantee a healthy baby in the mother.

"Our assessment is that this is an international crisis, and therefore we need to be prepared for the worst," she said.

The Department of Health also said this morning that it will be "open to proposals for a second lockdown".

McEntee told the audience in Londonderry that she was very concerned about the economic impact of the virus, which has already resulted in large-scale unemployment and a drop in the value of the Pound since the beginning of March.

The Londonderry and Strabane hospital, which is home to more than 300 patients, has been closed since Easter week.

Since then, the number of patients treated for the virus in the hospital has dropped from almost 10,000 to nearly 3,000, and that has led to a "substantial deterioration in our clinical services".

The hospital is among the only facilities offering all necessary tests and advice, including the isolation of patients who are unwell, the medical officer warned.

She also said that the government was "urgently seeking further information about what is happening" in the United States and New York.

"We also need to see whether or not there is any reason to be concerned that the situation has become more severe in the United Kingdom and whether there are any specific recommendations or plans that need to be put in place to deal with the situation," she said.

Michael Longley, who died last week after a long illness, was considered a national treasure and a man of few words.

The Dublin-born poet was born in Limerick in 1929 and was always fond of making poetry. His son, Kevin, describes his father’s love of poetry in his own words: “My dad was a wonderful poet, and it was always a joy to hear him talk of his work.”

Born in a large family of nine children, Longley grew up in a large house and was taught to read from an early age. He attended Limerick Senior School and Limerick Grammar School before going to Trinity College in Dublin and graduating from Dublin University.

Longley’s work has been described as lyrical and philosophical and his poetry is well-known. His work often reflected on Ireland’s history and the past. One of his most famous poems, ‘The Dream’s on Me’ was set to music by Rolf Harris.

Longley’s work was published throughout Europe and it was in Ireland that he published his first collection of poems, The River Flows by Moonlight in 1969. He wrote: “My first poems were poems of Ireland.”

Longley married his second wife, Elaine, in 1957 and was married until his death. They had five children and five grandchildren.

A memorial service was held at Limerick City Cemetery on June 26, 2010 and the funeral was held at the National Cathedral on July 9, 2010.

Michael Longley was remembered as a man with a deep love of words and a passion for Ireland and her history. He leaves two children and five grandchildren.

The EU’s latest summit in Brussels on Thursday, the day after Good Friday’s 20th anniversary, was a typically dull and boring affair. The leaders of the 28 EU member states appeared to do the same. The leaders met with the same platitudes, with little in the way of new ideas for making the EU a more efficient and effective body. The summit also failed to agree on anything important, as the EU’s decision to create a European Space Agency (ESA) has been called into question. The EU had initially hoped to create this new agency in 2017. The Commission, the EU’s executive body, rejected the idea on the grounds that it would lead to a lack of co-operation between member states on a number of issues. However, the European Parliament has voted to reject the idea, citing the need to protect public interests. If the Parliament is correct, the ESA will remain an independent body in a reformed European Space Agency. The EU will, of course, continue to meet and debate and debate the subject of the ESA. The EU is not averse to a debate on the ESA issue, but it has not been in the mood to debate the ESA question in any detail.

So what has the EU got for Good Friday? This week’s headlines would not be complete without mentioning the so-called “Good Friday Agreement” (or, more specifically, the so-called “Ferry Agreement”) as well as the controversial “European Arrest Warrant” which was approved by the European Parliament on January 20th.

The “Good Friday Agreement” was first signed by the UK and Ireland on the eve of Good Friday (the day after the crucifixion of Jesus Christ) in the early hours of that fateful holiday. It was to have enabled the Irish government to enter Britain's European Union (EU) territory in exchange for the right to negotiate the accession of the two countries to the EU. At the time of the signing, the two governments were concerned about the consequences of a vote by the UK parliament to reject a non-member state's bid to join the EU in a referendum. The agreement was then drawn up by the Irish government, but only became a reality after the Brexit process was underway. A vote in the UK parliament to accept the agreement was held on the Friday evening of Good Friday, and the two governments, led by Tony Blair and Gordon Brown, signed on the next morning.

In Ireland, the “Ferry Agreement” was introduced by then Taoiseach, Bertie Ahern, on the eve of Good Friday. However, the agreement was criticised by the then government of Fine Gael and the opposition coalition Fine, who suggested the agreement did not conform to the requirements of EU law. However, the agreement was then signed in the late afternoon, and the “Ferry Agreement” became an EU law. Although a “binding” agreement, the agreement only enabled the Irish government to enter the British territory with the understanding that it would negotiate the accession of the two countries to the EU.

The EU and the UK agreed that the “Ferry Agreement” was a legally binding, binding and irreversible agreement.
headline: Friday's Evening Round-Up: EU summit, Good Friday Agreement and mistaken identity of rodent

A letter from an HSE worker to the Irish Examiner on the role of the HSE: “We were very surprised to read your article and are particularly disappointed that you have not spoken to us about the serious issue of safety for our colleagues working in the healthcare sector.”

An HSE worker in the area to which we refer in the letter sent to you, wrote the following: “I am pleased to have the opportunity to tell you that the healthcare worker is being targeted and is on a ‘list’ which will be published and will detail any of the actions taken by the HSE staff.”

The issue of safety at the HSE is a very serious and grave matter and has been for a number of years. We are confident that we could find the right people who would be able to provide a more detailed and comprehensive answer than the one given to the Irish Examiner.

In response to the Irish Examiner’s request for more information, the HSE has sent us a statement, dated 30 June 2016, which is attached. It confirms that an HSE worker who is on a “list” will be targeted on 4th July 2016. The HSE is concerned for the safety of other HSE workers on the list and is taking all the steps that are required to protect them.

In response to the Irish Examiner’s request for more information, the HSE has sent us a statement, dated 30 June 2016, which is attached. It confirms that the HSE is not involved in the list as the HSE is not involved in the operation of the list. In order to protect other HSE workers, the HSE has developed a process to help ensure that other HSE workers are treated and protected in the same way as the ones on the list.

The process has been fully rolled out and is now being used for all of the list. There will be a written procedure to be followed and, where possible, you will be informed of any actions that the HSE is taking in order to protect other staff on the list.

It is possible that the process may change to include other HSE staff. As well as this, we have been asked to inform you in any case of any incidents involving any of the staff on the list.

It is important that these steps are implemented immediately. The HSE has already received a complaint from one of the doctors concerned and is working closely with the doctor to ensure that the process is followed as far as it is possible to do so.

It is important to note that the HSE has not been asked to do anything which we would find objectionable or to take any decisions which would put other staff at risk. The HSE is just following a process which has been developed through a number of meetings with the HSE staff on this list and has been taken to a ‘proof of concept’ stage. This process has already been fully rolled out to all the workers on the list and is being used to protect all other HSE staff.

We understand that you are very interested in the process and are very much aware of the steps that have already been put in place. We are confident that this process will be followed in the same way, and with the same respect, to all staff working at the HSE.

Please let us know your thoughts on this.

Education Minister Leo Varadkar has announced a new scheme to help primary and secondary school children buy books that they can read at home.

€1m fund for free books in primary schools

Sinn Féin Education spokesman John O’Dowd said the fund would be used to buy 10,000 books in €750,000 over four years.

It is hoped the fund would also help promote books and reading at school.

In a speech in the Dáil on Tuesday, Mr Varadkar said the €1m funding was part of a €2.5m package of new initiatives for primary schools and secondary schools in the coming financial year.

“The scheme will focus on teaching reading through the reading curriculum,” he said.

The initiative will be run by a commission of inquiry to be set up by the Department of Education, he added.

“It will be an independent group of experts who will report back in the coming months on the feasibility of the scheme and how best to implement it.

“We have no specific dates for implementation but the first phase of the scheme, which is intended to launch in September, will begin in the schools next September and will last for four years.”

In the Dáil, Mr O’Dowd said the scheme would work in tandem with the €1.2m scheme announced on Wednesday to help schools with special needs children get access to a range of books and learning materials.

“The commission of inquiry will also look at ways of providing more access to education for children with special needs in primary schools,” he said.

“The new scheme will enable some students to buy books at home. The commission of inquiry will also look at how we can work more closely with schools to ensure they have access to books and learning resources.

“We will also examine the impact of having a wider range of books in primary schools, such as biographies of political leaders, biographies of famous people and novels, as well as how it might impact on students’ ability to read at school.”

Mr O’Dowd added that parents and pupils would be consulted on how to organise the scheme.

“In the future, we plan to provide a number of ways for parents to be involved in the scheme.”

The minister’s announcement followed calls from the Tánaiste, Mary Mitchell O’Connor, and Fianna Fáil Fine Gael TD Richard Boyd Barrett, who both said that there was a need for more resources for schools to help children with special needs.

Mr Varadkar said schools across the country will have to increase their levels of teaching and learning to prepare pupils for the new curriculum.

“We are determined to ensure that we create an environment in schools where pupils are encouraged to study the new curriculum.”

Mr Varadkar said the new scheme would be led by an independent expert commission, with the Department of Education having final responsibility for ensuring the scheme is feasible, effective and financially sustainable.

In June this year, the Department of Education said more than 500 schools had signed up to the scheme.
headline: Education Minister announces €1m fund for free books in primary schools

In this week's Irish Examiner, we are talking about Joanna Fortune. Joanna is a woman who has pulled other people's hair. She has had to deal with it, and she has talked about it, but she hasn't told anyone about it because it is embarrassing. This is Joanna, she says.

“I have a bad hair day, a hair day, a hair day… a hair day,” says Joanna.

That’s what Joanna, who is 33, tells us about her condition.

She is a mother of two, a young Irish mother with an online dating career, a full-time university student and a part-time journalist. She’s also a wife.

The Irish Examiner spoke to Joanna about her experience pulling other people’s hair, how it feels, what she thinks her hair has done to her and where she is now.

Is this the first time that you have had this problem?

Joanna: I am really, really, really bad at picking my own hair. I am like 90 per cent Irish and I think that means that my hair is like an Irish person’s hair. I never had this problem growing up. I always had a lot of hair.

I never thought I would ever be able to have a bad hair day, but I think I am really bad at doing it myself. I was at a wedding and they were like, “Let’s show you.” I had this terrible, terrible hair day, because I didn’t do anything with it. I used to have to wash my hair every day.

I like to think that my hair is just really good, but I do know my hair is not that good.

Do you think your hair is doing other people’s hair, like yours, or is it just that you’ve just got really thick, thick hair?

I had to go to the salon and the hairdresser. I tried not to look like I was pulling my own hair. I tried not to have to say, “Hair day,” but that was the hardest thing in the world to try to hide.

I would look at my hair and I just knew that it wasn’t my hair, I knew that it was someone else’s. It was just the way I look, but it wasn’t my hair. I just looked at it and I was like, “Oh my god. My hair is not my hair!”

What has happened, what has caused this hair problem?

My daughter started doing that thing. She got into the habit of pulling other people’s hair and that started in the third grade. She started doing it in the second grade.

She was doing it in the third grade, she was doing it in the second grade. She would grab it, grab other people’s hair and she would start pulling it.

I think it has been hard for me, because I never would have thought it would come this far. I thought I would just get better at it. But I think when she started, it was hard for her. And then my sister, and then my mum and then my mum’s sister started doing it.
headline: Joanna Fortune: My baby keeps pulling other people's hair

"Concerning" trend of some people not answering calls from contact tracers: Some people don’t even have a contact tracing history

By Nia Griffiths and Brendan O'Neill, Express & Star, London

LONDON, Nov 1 (Reuters) - Some people just aren’t bothered by contact tracing, and in some cases they may not even have a contact tracing history.

That’s the finding of an Express & Star investigation, commissioned by the Irish Council for Civil Liberties (ICCL) and carried out in collaboration with Public Health England (PHE) and the British Government.

Contact tracing is a process whereby people who have come into contact with someone who has or had the disease can be traced to see if they are at risk of infection or, in some cases, to monitor their health for signs of an acute flare-up.

This is in line with the government's strategy, but does not apply in all cases. It’s designed to help people who may not have had direct contact with someone who has the illness.

“People who don’t have an official contact tracing history and do not have a phone number or address will not be traced,” said Michael Gannon, PHE’s head of epidemiology.

“PHE will continue to work with key contacts to help people who do not have contact tracing histories to access their records and access the information required to help them better understand their own risk and the risk they pose to others,” Gannon told the Express & Star.

“If people do not have contact tracing records, PHE will work with them to help them access these records for research, to access health information, and to help them understand the implications of their decisions.”

PHE has more than 12,000 people registered as having contact histories on its public health website.

About three-quarters of those have contact tracing records, the agency said.

PHE found a total of 981 people in the Irish Republic and Northern Ireland who have not yet responded to any contact tracing request.

“We would like to see these people connected so we can learn from their experiences,” Gannon said.

The majority of people don’t have an address or phone number linked to them.

“This would suggest they are in a situation where they are self-isolating and are at high risk,” Gannon said.

“We are providing help to these people to access these services, but we also need to work with them to ensure people’s privacy and confidentiality is protected.”

A total of 8,967 people in the EU have contact tracing records, which were updated by PHE in July, with the vast majority having their last known contact date and place.

“People who have had contact with a coronavirus-infected person have an increased risk of infection with coronavirus and may be advised to self-isolate,” PHE said.

The Irish Council for Civil Liberties said this information is not enough to ensure privacy and confidentiality.
headline: Covid-19: 'Concerning' trend of some people not answering calls from contact tracers

The head of the Cork mental health charity, the Cork Youth Mental Health Authority, Michael McCarthy, has been blackmailed via online message, the Irish Examiner has learned.

In a message sent through the agency's online portal last night, McCarthy wrote: “The situation is unfortunate, but I cannot imagine how you can be so quick to dismiss the person whose plight you have been placed in.

“I understand and empathise with how you feel but I don’t wish to be the one to take a more personal interest in what is going on.

“I will continue to be the same person I am now.”

Cork Youth Mental Health Authority staff were also warned about the message.

A senior source, who has asked to remain anonymous, said the message was sent to McCarthy’s email address and his mobile phone number by the hacker.

The source also said that the hacker was well-known to the agency’s staff.

Another source, who has been briefed on the matter, said the message was from a hacker who had been involved in multiple cyber attacks in the past year.

“It’s not just the one [email address] that was hacked; it’s the whole system,” the source said. “It’s a massive database.”

“It’s definitely not something you will ever recover from but it’s a massive database, it’s going to remain.”

The source said the agency had been contacted by the police who are “very confident” that the identity of the hacker was known.

The email was emailed to the agency’s staff this morning, and then delivered to McCarthy’s home yesterday morning, the source said.

Cork Youth Mental Health Authority chief executive Simon O’Neill has said he was “shocked” to hear about the message from a hacker.

He said: “This is something that you would expect to find in the news. It is not something we would tolerate and something we would not expect to happen.

“I am really surprised that this kind of thing would be happening at all and I was really quite shocked.”

The source said the agency was already under a threat from criminals, with no less than five threats in the past year.

The source said there were “numerous” attacks on the agency’s websites in the past year. “There was also an attack that took place on the agency’s phone,” the source said.

The source said there was an “all-party email committee” of the government which “always takes the security of the agency very seriously”, but was not aware of the threat.

The agency had been given assurances that the email had been intercepted by the hacker. “It was obviously just a matter of time before it was. We are not aware of this email being sent,” the source said.
headline: Cork mental health author blackmailed online 'disappointed by victim-blaming'

"I'm only a few months into my 30s but I'm already in the most intense phase of my life. I'd never been so happy to be diagnosed with breast cancer," says one of the most unlikely people to have a breast cancer diagnosis.

The 30-year-old, who works part time as a freelance editor in the city, is the first person to have her cancer diagnosed at the age of 33, and the first person to be diagnosed in the United States. "It's something I would never have expected," she says.

This week she found out she had breast cancer in one of the worst possible ways.

"It happened in the middle of an interview, right in the middle of it. You're sitting there and the doctor is talking and then I just burst out crying. There was no way I was going to do it - I was crying so hard I couldn't breathe, I was so embarrassed. I wasn't sure what to do. I was so upset. I was just so upset about it."

And it was just one of a string of illnesses that she has had in the past couple of years that she has had to overcome. This week, while working on a story for a local newspaper, she went into an exam room and was diagnosed with diabetes.

"It was a big mistake - I should have stayed in bed."

The fact that she is the first person to have her cancer diagnosis in her 30s was not the end of the road. The next day she was told that she had cancer in her breast.

When she asked for an operation, she was told by a doctor that a lump was found in her breast and had to be removed surgically.

"I couldn't believe it. I wanted to say it was a mistake - that they should have taken a biopsy," she says. "But that wasn't even in the conversation."

And so she had her cancer taken out. "I know I'm not going to have the surgery done again and I'm not going to have to go through chemo. But I'm so relieved that I know there's nothing that can go wrong."

She has never known anything about her family history, but she has researched and written about it in order to give the general public an idea of the different conditions and diseases that can come with her condition.

She and her sister had a history of high blood pressure problems and had been treated for a rare cancer in their brother, which had eventually gone into remission.

But her aunt is a heavy smoker and has had trouble with her blood pressure. Her aunt is in her late 70s and lives alone, but she lives close to her sister and her brother.

"My aunt's life is just so hard, you know, not having any support. My aunt lives with her daughter and grandaughter and she goes out and about every day. I think she really relies on her family. I feel like my mother's generation used to be like that, but now people don't really care. It's so hard."

But that did not stop her from going for her operation. She was on the phone with a breast cancer specialist. He told her that it was stage three and so, if she wanted a mastectomy, it would be in her 40s.
headline: My aunt's breast cancer diagnosis saved me

Israeli and Palestinian negotiators continued to push for a renewed truce Wednesday, as the body responsible for negotiating the accord, the Israeli prime minister’s office, said it had received a “new round of information” on the status of five Palestinian prisoners.

The releases of the remaining five prisoners would bring the number of Palestinian prisoners to 11, a number the Israeli government has repeatedly denied is true.

The release of a “new round of information” is seen as a significant milestone in the Palestinian-Israeli peace process, and is likely to provide an opportunity for Palestinians to try to extend the ceasefire deal they signed with Israel in August.

As Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat said Tuesday, the Israeli government had released its latest information about prisoners held in Israeli jails before the deadline of 4 p.m. Tuesday. “The Israeli government has released a new round of information in the past several days regarding the prisoners,” Erekat said in a statement. “This is a very important day for the Palestinian side and for the Palestinian leadership.”

The news came a day after the Palestinian Liberation Organization announced that Erekat had met Israeli negotiators and discussed plans for a renewed ceasefire deal. “We discussed a ceasefire agreement, but I cannot disclose any details about it,” Erekat said in a statement.

Erekat said he had told the Israelis that he would be willing to put up a list of prisoners who “are suitable” for release. The group, also known as Fatah, has been at odds with the Israeli leadership on how to handle the prisoners.

“I have made it clear in the past that we would like to extend the ceasefire until the end of the year, but I have also informed them that our position is that we are ready to sign an agreement only when the prisoners are released,” Erekat said. “Therefore, in my view, the fact that the prisoners have been released, as they say, is an important step.”

The Israeli government said it also had “confirmed” the release of another prisoner on Wednesday. “The Palestinian Authority has received a new round of information regarding the status of the remaining four prisoners in Israeli prisons,” an Israeli government spokesperson said.

The spokesperson was not speaking on behalf of the PA, who issued a statement late Wednesday saying that it was “pleased” by the “new information.”

The Israeli army declined to comment on the release. However, in a statement to the Israeli parliament, the chief of staff, Maj.-Gen. Gadi Eisenkot, said the army was still examining the prisoner’s situation and whether they were suitable for release.

The Israeli ambassador to the United Nations in Geneva, Ron Prosor, said the news of the release of the prisoners “is significant and is a clear indication that the Palestinian side wants a ceasefire and an end to the occupation.”

The Israeli envoy also called for a “pause” in the continuation of the talks. “The Palestinian Authority has not changed its position on the status of the prisoners.”

Prosor said he was “optimistic” that the two sides would be able to reach an agreement, but that he would not support continued talks.
headline: Hopes for extension of Israel-Hamas truce as more hostages released

The play about one year of the Easter Rising in Northern Ireland had its run in this year’s Edinburgh Fringe, as did a play from the same era called The Easter Plot.

The plays were not, perhaps, quite the same as those of the past; but the similarities are striking. They are a reminder that something, at least, has changed.

If you are not familiar with these plays, they are all based on real events in Northern Ireland. One of the most famous is by the writer Mary Norton, Emma Donoghue’s play. The most recent play, in fact, was written almost exactly a year after The Easter Plot, the play which was first performed. The plays of Mary Norton and her contemporaries are based on one, or more, real events. In the case of the other plays, it is not hard to draw similarities. The themes were the same; in the case of the later play, the events were all over again. The events and the actors were all different; but they all shared one thing in common: the people who were affected by them.

What is more, the characters, and the themes of the plays, are as much part of our history as are the events and the actors. Both the events and the plays of the past are part of our history. They are all part of our Irish and British history. But in a more recent, less conscious way, those are now part of our English and British history, as much as the events of the past.

The Irish and Scottish Revolutions are part of the story of modern times in our British and English history. The Irish revolution was the second in the British history of Ireland, the first was the English one. But it was the second which affected the English. The same for the Scottish, and for the French Revolution in France.

It was the French revolution which brought down Charles X. And it was the British Revolution which brought down Charles III. And it was the British Revolution which brought down King George III. And it was the French Revolution which brought down King Louis XVI and King Louis XVIII. And it was the French Revolution which brought down King Louis XVIII. And it was the French Revolution which brought down King Louis XVIII. And it was the French Revolution which brought down King Louis XVIII.

So that history is part of our English and British history. The French revolution, and the British revolution are part of our history and part of our modern history. It is part of the story of the period we live in. But the same is not true of the Irish and Scottish Revolutions. And so it is a reminder of something else. The Irish and Scottish Revolutions are not part of our history and part of our modern history. They are part of the British and English history. They are part of our history and part of our modern history, but not part of our history. It is not part of the history of us.

US President Donald Trump will call for the meeting of the US military chiefs in the wake of a deadly military raid in Yemen, a statement on Wednesday read by White House press secretary Sarah Sanders said.

The meeting was initially due to be held this month at the White House, but the White House has said the date has been changed to Tuesday.

The statement, which Sanders read from on the White House’s website, said “this morning (Wednesday) Vice President Mike Pence sent out the following text message:

‘The US military leaders will convene a meeting in the coming days.”

A senior official told the Times that there had been “miscommunication” with the White House over the scheduling of the meeting.

A military official told Reuters that the Trump administration was still attempting to work out a date.

The raid in question was conducted by special forces in a military vessel operated by the Saudi-led coalition on 18 April.

Saudi Arabia and its allies have been at odds with Yemen’s Houthi militia, which controls the capital and has been conducting a civil war with the support of Iran.

Saudi-backed forces, who are backed by a US-led coalition, have launched hundreds of air strikes in Yemen since March 2018, including on hospitals and schools in the country.

The Saudi military began a large-scale offensive against Houthi positions in March to fight the Iranian-backed group.

The US has been one of the main countries supporting Saudi Arabia’s campaign, with more than half of the roughly $1 billion a month US military support goes to the Saudi coalition.

The Saudi-led coalition, which includes US-allied militaries from Britain, France and Germany, is leading a military campaign in Yemen.

A Saudi-led coalition in Yemen (Getty)

A Saudi coalition official had earlier told the UK Telegraph that the US was considering the possibility of “satellite operations”, which are also possible in Yemen.

The US has been in talks with Saudi Arabia and the UAE to agree to direct combat air raids on the Yemenis, but these have not yet been implemented.

Trump has called on the country to stop supporting Yemen’s Houthi rebels, who control the capital Sanaa, and is calling for the establishment of “true” Yemen.

The statement from the White House press secretary did not say when the US military chiefs’ meeting was to take place.

A senior Saudi official told Reuters on Thursday that Trump’s speech could only be considered “if all parties work together to find a date”.

US President Donald Trump speaks (AP)

The meeting has become one of the biggest foreign policy failures in the Trump administration, with Trump repeatedly contradicting his own statements and statements from senior military leaders.

Trump has come under pressure to meet Saudi Arabia’s emir, a key ally, as he seeks to cut off funding for the coalition. The Saudi regime has denied that it is funding the Houthis.

The Houthis said in a statement late on Wednesday that they had asked Trump to give “decisive and unqualified support” to the coalition.

Headlines

Government must help average earners overcome 'impediments' to homebuying, say auctioneers

“The government must do more to help those in need”, has become a mantra for the Irish tax industry.

Despite the increasing number of housing starts registered by the Irish Government over the past year, a recent report from the Irish Independent shows an acute shortage of low-cost homes in the country.

The report has highlighted how the auction market could have to face a downturn unless the government does more to help homebuyers overcome “impediments” to obtaining a home.

The report’s head economist, Dr Nial O’Sullivan, explained that there is “limited supply and high demand for low-cost properties in the Irish market”. He said that the government needs to do more to help homebuyers overcome the “limitations of the Irish housing market”.

“While the market can still recover over the next few years, it is likely to do so by using the same strategy as was deployed after the crisis in 2006, which was to use the ‘one-stop’ system of the Irish housing market,” the report says. “This has been successful for a number of years, particularly when compared with a market which has been left uncompetitive for a number of years.”

“Houses for sale in Ireland are sold through an auction process, and this is an important part of the market, but it can be difficult for people to secure properties for sale. There has been an increase in the number of new auctions for the past few years, and with this increase has come a decrease in supply”, the report says.

“In 2011, there was an average of three auctions per month, but this dropped to one in 2014 and only two in 2015. In 2016, there were only two auctions per month.”

“The price in these auctions is set by the auctioneer and is based on the ‘standard’, ‘average’ price for a similar property in the auctioneers’ book of sold and advertised homes. There are currently around 500 auctions across the country, but the number is expected to double over the next few years,” the report says.

“Auctioneers in Ireland sell homes through a number of different methods including private sales, auction and buy-to-let markets, and the auction market, which has been a very important part of the Irish property market over the past few years, is now seen as being inadequate.”

“While the auction market can still recover over the next few years, it is likely to do so by using the same strategy as was deployed after the crisis in 2006, which was to use the ‘one-stop’ system of the Irish housing market.”

The report also stated that a number of other housing providers have been working in partnership with the Irish government on helping people purchase homes.

“The biggest example is the Housing Enterprise Fund, an initiative by the Department of Housing and Local Government which was set up in 2013 and covers housing providers, both private and public, to improve and expand supply in the private market.”

Crowe was sacked in October this year after leaving the company.

“Irish businesses are looking to invest and to gain market share in the short term, but the long-term outlook remains uncertain,” it said.

The report, which is based on detailed surveys of business leaders across the country, shows the economy is “facing a set of challenges”. It says uncertainty over Brexit, together with a “sinking stock of skilled workers and business leaders”, will force “a period of investment fatigue”.

The introduction of auto-enrolment for pensioners in Ireland will start from July 1. It has been called a “turning point” in the battle for pension rights for the millions of older people in the country.

The change came after years of campaigning by women and young people including former Taoiseach Liam Cosgrave who has been credited for bringing the issue of pensions to the attention of Irish society.

The introduction of the scheme to pensioners will be for those aged 50 to 59.

Auto-enrolment is a measure that allows an already well-off person to pay lower monthly pension rates and also have their full pension pot paid for the time being until they get a pension.

The Government estimates the cost of the scheme to be €11 million a year in additional costs for the state, but the cost to the taxpayer is around €7 million.

Colin Sheridan has described the recent reform of the Immigration Act (the Bill) as a “catastrophic mistake”, but said it is necessary to modernise and restore the system of immigration.

Ahead of the Bill’s first reading on Saturday night, Mr Sheridan said it was necessary to modernise the system in order to combat terrorism in the wake of the murder of an Indian man by gunmen in the city of Newmarket, Co Cork in June.

Mr Sheridan said that, while the Bill contains many positive points, it also raises significant challenges, including that it is in the nature of an emergency legislation.

“It is a catastrophic mistake because it is such an untested law in so many aspects,” Mr Sheridan said.

“But there are a number of significant positives to this new law.

“I have to say I am really impressed with the fact that you can get a visa here.

“But you cannot apply for a visa and have a family, that is simply not how immigration works.

“We need a system that is efficient and fair in the sense that a vast majority of the people come here to live and that is the way the system is structured today.”

Mr Sheridan’s comments, in his first public speech in the House of the Oireachtas following the Bill’s passage through the Oireachtas and being debated in the Dáil, have been welcomed by those in the country who are concerned with the impact of the Bill on their rights and opportunities and the impact it may have on the economic growth it will bring to the country.

“It is very important in the debate I am having now that the focus is on the people of this country,” Mr Sheridan said.

“There is a massive economic recession right across the country, and in the Oireachtas there is a huge focus on how we tackle it and how we deal with it.

“But the point of view I am having now is that the point of view of the people who are affected by these changes is not to be about that recession.

“Their point of view is how can we create the conditions where people can move into their own homes, their own business and their own work so they can have the opportunity to make a contribution to society and to the economy.

“That is my focus.

“What is very important for me in these debates, which are very important for the future of this nation, is that we are talking about the right to move, the right to be part of our economy and our society.”

Mr Sheridan said the debate should take place in the Dáil rather than the Oireachtas.

“What we have here is a bill that will affect everybody in this country but the House of the Oireachtas,” he said.

“It is an emergency bill.

“People are very concerned about the future of this nation and we have to be focussed on that.

“We need to focus on the job that we are doing.”
headline: Colin Sheridan: New reforms risk transforming what it means to be an immigrant in Ireland

Talks on the €456 million M28 Cork to Ringaskiddy motorway project have begun and cabinet has given its backing for the project.

The Cabinet agreed that the €456 million M28 Cork to Ringaskiddy scheme is a good one, says a statement.

The M28 is Ireland’s largest road and rail project, which was unveiled in 2013. It will create an eight-lane, eight-kilometre-long motorway running along the Cork and Kerry Coasts in the west of Ireland.

Work is already underway on the motorway and work is expected to begin later this year.

Construction works on the M28 will be in two phases. Phase one is scheduled to begin in late 2016 and run for a few years, while the phase two is expected to begin in 2017 and last for about a decade.

The project involves the construction of two roads: the M8 and the M32, and the reconstruction of the M1 between the M1 and the Ringaskiddy Road.

The M28 will be opened as a toll road in 2019. The toll charges on the M28 will be as follows:

M8 Tolling: €3.70 – €5.70 (one way)

M32 Tolling: €6.70 – €10.50 (one way)

M1 Tolling: €2.70 – €3.70 (one way)

It’s estimated that the M28 will create 100,000 jobs, and create a total investment of €1.1 billion.

Cork County Councillor James Dillon said that the project “is an exciting opportunity for the city of Cork to grow with the new route opening this year”.

“This project will provide much needed jobs, will create opportunities for the people of Cork to develop their communities, and create more investment in our city,” he said.

Dillon said the decision on the M28 was made by the government as part of the ongoing and accelerated phase 1 of the M1 Motorway.

Cork County Councillor Noel Power said that the decision is in the best interests of the people of Cork and the economic opportunities it creates.

“This is a great news for Cork, we have had a long discussion with the Department of Transport to see if it was the right project for Cork and the people of Cork who are going to have a huge investment in this motorway that will create jobs and growth,” said Power.

“This is a fantastic opportunity for Cork and we are very pleased that the Cabinet has agreed that the scheme is good for the people of Cork and for the economy,” said Power.

The M28 will open on the new Cork–Corkbeg Road in 2019.

The M28 will be opened as a toll road in 2019.

The Irish grain industry is under siege, writes the Irish Examiner

For the Irish food industry, the latest crisis comes as a great relief. While the global food supply chain has become highly automated, there is not much competition to drive down costs.

This has had the effect of driving up prices.

But for the Irish grain industry, a recent spate of bad news has come as a great relief.

A major global organisation announced its latest global grain deal last month. This announcement was accompanied by a pledge to improve the quality of Irish grains. The Irish Grain Trade Association said that all the new grain contracts would be in the first 100 per cent Irish-bred seed variety, with the Irish National Seed Exchange (INSENEX) expected to introduce its Irish seed contract to the market in 2013.

This latest agreement, with the Irish government, aims to bring down costs and improve the quality of Irish grains. But there is some disappointment amongst Irish farmers and trade groups that this has not brought about a similar reduction in price volatility.

One Irish farmer who is frustrated by the change of course is Patrick McCall. The 62-year-old says the “bunch of new contracts” is still too few, which means he is “still paying a lot of money for low-quality, highly volatile stuff.”

Patrick McCall, who is one of the owners of two dairy farms in the Clare region, is one of many farmers in the country who believe there is little competition in the Irish grain market.

“Irish grain is still the king of the world and you have to be in the top five countries to get it,” he said. “I could have got it if I put my hands in the ground, but that doesn’t make it any better.

“We are selling to people all over the world, and I know it’s going to be hard to compete against the other major countries.”

Patrick McCall says his two farms, which produce milk and butter, face being squeezed out of the market by smaller competitors. The farmers are now worried about being forced into the “bunch of new contracts” as the industry looks for ways to improve the quality of the grain supply.

But with the EU’s new grain deal, the Irish grain industry is looking to change the economics of the industry by making it more profitable.

A report by the Irish Grain Trade Association said that the current deal was only one element of a wider package of reform.

“The main aim is to improve the quality of Irish grains and to bring down the volatility of pricing,” said a spokesman for the trade association, who added that the industry’s new grain deal, which the trade association is calling the “Next Grain Deal,” would also provide a “strong foundation” for improving the supply chain in the future.

The New Grain Deal aims to improve the quality of the Irish grain supply by introducing the Irish National Seed Exchange (INSENEX) to the market, and improving its Irish grain contracts to the standard required by the industry.
headline: Against the grain: What's the latest with the UN's grain deal?

The former Congressman told federal agents he had sex with a 12-year-old girl in Washington, D.C. on a bed in a hotel room in June 2011 and then another underage girl in New York. He will have to register as a sex offender.

Gaetz’s attorney, Jonathan Turley, told Judge Richard Sullivan that Gaetz’s cooperation with the government in the investigation and the guilty plea was limited to the hotel room in Washington, D.C. and that he would not be offering any statements to the media.

Turley did not release a list of the victims, saying Gaetz was “very reluctant to be interviewed and not willing to say anything about the crimes.”

Gaetz, a Republican from New York, faces a maximum prison sentence of 10 years and a $250,000 fine if convicted of all counts. The plea comes at the end of a two-week trial in which he and the government presented the testimony of more than a dozen witnesses, including two former law enforcement officers and two former employees at his Capitol Hill office.

He is one of at least a dozen people facing sex trafficking charges for selling minors for sex. The largest is former New York Congressman Anthony Weiner, who was charged with 13 counts of sex trafficking last year and pleaded guilty to one count in March.

In a statement, Turley said:

“We believe it is essential for our elected officials to speak out and to be held accountable for their actions and that this guilty plea is in the best interest of the government and for the victims.”

“We are extremely grateful for the cooperation of Matt Gaetz and his team and we wish him the very best.”

Gaetz will appear in federal court in Manhattan on Sept. 24.

The plea deal was negotiated by Assistant U.S. Attorney Mary Ann Pignataro.

RISE: Minister blames cuts on lack of student numbers

Cuts to higher education by the government will cause “significant difficulties” for students in coming years, the Minister for Education, Simon Coveney, has conceded.

Speaking to the Independent newspaper last night, he said that the “cuts we are making are going to have a significant impact on our students.”

“You’re going to have lower-cost higher education institutions shutting down,” he said. “That will have a major impact on students at all levels.”

He also denied that students are being told to stay at home because the number of students in Ireland has been falling since the 2008 recession.

“No, we haven’t got this one going yet,” he said.

“We’ve got this coming back and a couple of years from now and we’re going to be doing the same things again.”

Mr Coveney, who is in his first stint as a minister in the Irish government, said the government was not prepared to cut student allowances from current levels in order to tackle what he called an “entrenched problem”.

“I do not think that we’re going to get anywhere near to what we are dealing with today by cutting student allowances,” he told the Independent. “This has to be the absolute starting point in tackling this problem.”

The minister’s comments come as he is due to publish a set of proposals to the Oireachtas Housing and Public Finance Committee, which will be debated by ministers tomorrow.

Mr Coveney said the proposals would form part of an “overarching” plan to address the current “inefficient” state of higher education in Ireland.

In an interview with the Irish Times, the minister conceded that “student numbers are still not up to snuff”, but noted that the “scaling back” of higher education would cause difficulties for students in coming years.

“You’re going to have lower-cost higher education institutions shutting down,” he said. “That will have a major impact on students at all levels.”

The education minister said students who were “scattered across the world” were facing difficulties as there were fewer places to put them in.

“There are going to be problems there, there are going to be challenges, and you don’t want to see students coming to Ireland having to do that because they are in the middle of it,” he said.

“It’s the challenge for all of us to make sure there is a system that makes sense for students.”

The minister also suggested that students had become resigned to the fact that there would be no way out of the current funding crisis.

“I think the whole situation is starting to get pretty hopeless for students,” he said. “There are no obvious solutions to this problem.”

“The government is not about to get to the point where we can sort out the funding problem by cutting the amount of money that we put into higher education.”

As such, a temporary €1.1m fund has been set up to help offset the loss of revenue, while it awaits a long-term plan to secure future income from the zoo and flower show.

The money will be set up over a two-year period, with a one-off payment of €500,000 in June 2020, and a further two payments in 2023 and 2024.

The Irish Examiner understands that the €1.1m was agreed in principle between the zoo’s board of management and the director of the zoo, and will be presented to the board for approval next month.

The €1.1m fund will be divided between the zoo’s directors, the zoo’s chief executive, Pat Byrne, and Pat Byrne and the museum’s director, Mary Ryan, while a number of staff will also be provided with additional funds.

The zoo will also pay the zoo’s rent and board payments as usual.

The zoo’s board of management has been working with the museum to reach a solution to the current financial problems, and the issue will be formally discussed at the next board meeting, which is in May.

The success of the world’s largest-ever synthetic-fertiliser plant in
North Yorkshire has led to a boom of similar projects all over Europe.

It may seem hard to believe that such a small plant could be so
successful. But the answer is simple and it’s being achieved with very
little taxpayer subsidy.

The plant is now able to turn a single 1,000-tonne truck, which was
used in the first stage of the plant, into a 50-tonne tanker that can
supply the equivalent of an entire city. The facility was built at the
former Tarmac site in Harrogate, north of Sheffield.

This week, the European Commission’s chief executive, Karel De Gucht,
said: “The UK is a major international player, a world leader in the
development of large-scale renewable resources that can be used to
generate energy in new ways. The UK’s industrial capacity makes it an
important place to invest.”

The North Yorkshire plant was the world’s largest and most advanced
fertiliser operation when it opened in May 2009. Since then, it has
been expanded and doubled its capacity, employing more than 2,500
people. This means the North Yorkshire plant is capable of supplying
the equivalent of an entire city to the EU.

The UK’s success in developing large-scale renewable resources, which
are more environmentally friendly and cost-effective than conventional
fuels, has been a major factor behind the expansion of North Yorkshire
fertiliser. However, the world’s largest and most advanced synthetic-
fertiliser plant in North Yorkshire has been built at a cost of just
£15 million.

The plant is now capable of turning a single 1,000-tonne truck, which
was used in the first stage of the plant, into a 50-tonne tanker that
can supply the equivalent of an entire city.

The £15 million plant has been built by North Yorkshire
Fertiliser, part of the world’s largest plant development company,
Dow Jones.

The facility was built at the former Tarmac site in Harrogate, north
of Sheffield. (Photo: Hulton Archive/Getty Images)

In the first year of operation, the plant employed 8,200 people,
producing 13 million tonnes of nitrogen gas per annum. Total economic
benefits for the UK were about £2.7 billion, the company said.

The plant is a success story for North Yorkshire Fertiliser,
considered to be one of the UK’s most efficient fertilisers.

North Yorkshire Fertiliser, which is owned by the world’s largest
fertiliser company, Syngenta, said it is the world’s largest
nursery-fertiliser producer. The plant produces a mixture of nitrogen
and phosphorus, which is then combined with hydrogen sulphide and
hydrochloric acid to create ammonium sulphate.

The fertiliser, which can be used for agriculture, animal husbandry
and forestry, has also been found to help grow crops in the Arctic
region.
headline: Global success beckons for North Yorkshire fertiliser

The Irish Examiner looks at how a new US trade deal may affect Ireland’s WTO accession and the EU’s membership of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

The agreement between the US and the European Union (EU) was signed in Washington on Friday by US Secretary of State John Kerry and EU Trade Commissioner Cecilia Malmstrom.

This follows on the heels of the US and EU signing the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) which will be a key part of the Transatlantic Trade and Investment Partnership (TTIP). The European Commission has also confirmed that it is preparing a draft TTTIP with the US.

The agreement will provide for increased access for the US and EU for goods and services from developing countries to the US market, as well as increased access for the US and EU for goods and services from developed countries to the EU market.

It does not address the issues surrounding the Irish WTO accession which the US and EU have agreed to negotiate, but will include an article which sets out in detail how the EU will “consider and respond to any request from a State party for a WTO membership application and review”.

There has been concern within Ireland that this agreement, which will take the form of the “EU-US Trade and Investment Partnership” could affect Ireland’s WTO accession and membership of the WTO, but no details have been given of what this would mean.

However, the Irish Examiner has received a clarification from the EU negotiator that there will be no change to Ireland’s WTO membership, which will remain as of the next agreement in November next year.

This was confirmed by Cecilia Malmstrom, EU Trade Commissioner, who stated: “The negotiations are still going ahead. We are negotiating with the US, and we are negotiating with the European Commission on the TTTIP. We have not changed our position on the status of the WTO.

“These negotiations are ongoing and we will continue to discuss the TTTIP and what it means to the EU and the US. The EU-US Trade and Investment Partnership will be based on the TTTIP agreements, and the EU is working closely with the US on the TTTIP and the EU-US Trade and Investment Partnership will have the same framework as the TTTIP.

“The EU-US Trade and Investment Partnership will have a very strong commitment from the US that the EU cannot enter into any new trade or investment deals that undermine the rules of the WTO. This is an important element in the agreement. The same commitment exists from the EU.

“In the case of Ireland, the EU is not changing its position on the status of WTO membership. The EU-US Trade and Investment Partnership will not change this and is not part of the TTTIP. It is a complementary element.

“The WTO membership requirement is a very important element in the agreement. The US has agreed that it will not pursue a WTO membership application for Ireland.

“The EU will continue to negotiate and implement the EU-US Trade and Investment Partnership, and Ireland will continue to negotiate its accession to the WTO, and it will be subject to the same WTO rules as other WTO members.
headline: The Irish Examiner View: Hogan’s hat in the WTO ring?

A massive polio vaccination campaign began in Gaza in 2012. The virus is still circulating in the region. It could take a decade to completely eradicate polio in the region.

The campaign, part of the government’s effort to eradicate polio in the Middle East region, will continue to run over the coming months and years. It is one of the most ambitious and important programmes in the world.

A large vaccination campaign was held in July 2012, in Gaza City. According to a report from the International Commission for Control of Small Arms, Nocks campaign, an estimated 1.5 million people were vaccinated with the new vaccine.

As part of the campaign, the European Parliament and the European Commission issued a joint statement about the benefits of polio vaccination.

As part of the campaign, the European Union issued a statement on how polio eradication is linked to economic development and is a key factor in creating jobs. In addition, the statement said that vaccination of children is also linked to the “recovery of a healthy society and a healthy environment.”

The UK has also been a vocal supporter of the vaccination campaign, and has supported the European Union’s statements.

As part of the campaign, the UNRWA agency that oversees the Gaza Strip launched a campaign against polio in July 2012. UNRWA says that vaccination campaigns can provide much needed health care to the Gaza Strip’s 3.5 million people.

“A polio vaccination campaign has the potential to make a significant impact on the health of the people in Gaza as well as the wider Middle East region,” UNRWA Chief Executive Officer John Ging said in a statement.

“This is important because the region is home to an estimated 1.5 million people with polio.”

“We know that it can be very expensive for a health programme like this to run across the whole of Gaza, and so we aim to take every possible action that we can to ensure that polio eradication can continue,” he said.

In August 2012, a WHO expert team visited Gaza to provide technical advice on polio eradication.

In September 2012, UNICEF launched an initiative called “Polio Is Life” to increase support for polio vaccination in the Gaza Strip.

“UNICEF launched the initiative, called Polio Is Life, with the goal of providing up-to-date information on the challenges that polio eradication can pose for children in Gaza,” UNICEF’s executive director Anthony Lake said in a statement.

“UNICEF hopes that by educating, informing and informing, it can be part of the health sector’s overall commitment to polio eradication and to the health of the people of Gaza and the whole of the Middle East region.”

The campaign is an example of the importance of polio eradication and of UNRWA’s role in this endeavour, according to UNICEF’s Lake.

“UNICEF is working closely with other partners to ensure that polio is never again a priority health challenge in Gaza,” he said.

“We also recognise the critical role that polio vaccination plays in ensuring that every child has the opportunity to be protected against polio.”

For those who want to see Ireland take the green step, the Department of Communications has come up with a smart idea.

The Dáil is considering introducing a clover-based certificate scheme for solar photovoltaic (PV) projects which have been certified by Irish Photovoltaic Standards, or IPVS.

The scheme, which is being considered by the Dáil in the autumn, would be the first in the European Union to incorporate clover, a green crop, into a standard for environmental sustainability and energy use.

"This is a win win for the Irish people," said James O’Loughlin, Dáil deputy spokesperson for communications and communications strategy.

The Department of Communications has proposed introducing a clover-based certificate scheme for solar photovoltaic (PV) projects which have been certified by the Irish Photovoltaic Standards. Photograph: Eamonn O'Brien

"This is a win win for the Irish people. This is a move from a green policy perspective to an economic one, which is the key benefit," he said.

He said the clover certification scheme would be introduced alongside the green power scheme, which was due to start in September. It will include the planting of clover on solar farms which have received green certification from IPVS.

"It is an environmentally friendly way of building solar farms but we know that it will also drive business in this area,” Mr O’Loughlin said.

“This is a win win for the Irish people and we are looking at what other renewable sources we can offer to the market,” he added.

Clover is planted in large quantities throughout Ireland, and it has been used for a number of applications including biofuel and for animal feed. The department is also considering whether to allow clover to be used on other applications such as the use of the crop in construction, or for biofarming.

The Dáil is due to consider introducing a green power scheme in the autumn. Photograph: Eamonn O'Brien

Last year, the department announced its green power scheme to help the solar industry. It plans to invest €2.5bn in wind, wave and biomass projects to help the industry generate enough electricity to meet demand and help reduce CO2 emissions.

The green power scheme is aimed at assisting the solar industry to develop new technologies, build and build green infrastructure and to establish a new market for renewable energy.

The department has been trialling clover for five years, and Mr O’Loughlin said it had been a success in that it had encouraged the farming community to plant more clover.

He said the department had been exploring the possibility of using clover in the green power scheme.

The department is also looking at whether to introduce the clover-based certificate scheme for solar photovoltaic (PV) projects which have been certified by the Irish Photovoltaic Standards, or IPVS.

He said that had been put in place in the past, but that there had been no major changes in the scheme since.

“There has been no major changes in the scheme since the previous green certificate scheme was put in place,” he said.

She has proposed the creation of a “Special Delivery Service” that allows shoppers to purchase products directly from companies such as Wal-Mart.

“I think that the idea of a special delivery service is the best way that we can give back to the community,” says Ms. Browne, who has proposed creating the service since April. “I think that it would help with the economic situation because everyone is trying to get everything at once.”

Ms. Browne has also proposed the creation of a “Kids’ Choice Program,” similar to the “Best Choice Awards” that are given out during the summer to high-achieving students.

“The idea of a toy box is one that I think we should create in every town in the country,” she says.

Maryland joins several other states, including Pennsylvania, Delaware and Oregon, in developing the “Special Delivery Service” program.

China revoked three of its journalists’ press credentials on Monday in a rare move by a major country.

The three editors and reporters of the Wall Street Journal were expelled from the party-controlled newspaper for critical coverage of Beijing’s economic and political policies. The editors are in China to write a book about their experiences.

China has a long history of censoring information that it finds inconvenient, and the move comes at a sensitive time. The US is debating the potential effects of a so-called “One China” policy on its own South China Sea disputes with Beijing.

The WSJ is also involved in a high-profile dispute with China over the rights to the North China Sea. That story has received a lot of attention in the US, which has criticised the paper for its coverage.

The Chinese government has been cracking down on the media in recent years, with a series of amendments to the state media’s code of ethics. The latest amendment to the Code of Ethics for Publishing Media, for example, bans newsrooms from reporting on “conflict of interest” in their coverage.

The decision to expel the editors from the Chinese government newspaper comes at a time when President Barack Obama is in China to discuss the US role in the world’s second biggest economy.

The editors have written a scathing book, which includes interviews with hundreds of people in China’s Communist Party.

Mr Baddeley has called the experience in China “embarrassing” and said the country’s press freedoms were being systematically eroded.

“I would hope that anyone that holds a reporter’s job in China would be extremely concerned about the effect that this decision is having on their personal safety,” he said.

The editor in Beijing, Ben Hurd, said the suspension was a “welcome step”.

“However, the actions of this decision have done little to address the fundamental issues that we have raised over the last four years,” he said.

The editors had been due to report on “China’s relentless crackdown on press freedom and online freedom of speech”.

They will also “reveal details of the government’s response to the protests that have been ongoing since 2008”.

Their book, China Confidential: The Making of the C.R.C.’s Rise to Global prominence, will be launched on Thursday at a press conference in Beijing.

China’s move to expel the WSJ was “an embarrassing step” that the newspaper will not take lightly, Mr Hurd said.

“China’s media landscape is changing drastically and our lives and journalism are being affected,” he said. “They have been working to tell the truth about what’s happening in China for many years.”

She says that she lost her consciousness and her vision when she was hit by a bullet train at Kilmainham Junction in Dublin on Thursday morning.

In this image released by RTÉ, a passenger who is no stranger to the Irish rail system says she had to be transferred from a train in Dublin to a wheelchair after she was hit by a bullet train at Kilmainham Junction in Dublin on Thursday morning.

The woman, who was in a wheelchair, was injured when the bullet train driver slammed it into her head, causing the bullet to ricochet around and strike her on the left side of her face.

She was rushed to University Hospital Limerick for emergency treatment. The bullet travelled into her head and exited at a right angle. It then came back, hitting her face. She has since been given a CT scan to determine the extent of her injury.

The woman, who asked to be referred to as ‘D’, described the incident as “like a scene out of a bad movie”, saying that the bullet, which came from a train, was “dangling” out of the right side of her face.

“The train driver came towards me. He had a gun on his belt, he was wearing a vest. He told me to get off. I couldn’t and I was hit with the bullet that was hanging out of my face,” she said. “The bullet was stuck in my face. I was screaming. I was screaming and crying.”

She was taken to the Royal Victoria Hospital in central Dublin, where her injuries were assessed.

Speaking to RTÉ News, D said she was injured so badly that doctors told her she was “dead”. She says the bullet train driver was “so mad, he was shaking me up like I was a piece of meat”. She says she was eventually taken to University Hospital Limerick.

The incident occurred shortly before 8pm on Thursday, just after the new trains which are being replaced by a fleet of bullet trains entered service this year.

“It was like watching a horror movie,” said D. She says the bullet that struck her “didn’t feel real”.

The female passenger had just entered the building, before the incident, when she says that she turned her head and saw a bullet train driver, holding a gun.

She says that when she looked down and saw the bullet train driver he was shaking his head back and forth like he was trying to say “no”.

“He was walking around, going from one end of the building to the other, not saying anything,” said D.
headline: Bullet train driver abandoned controls for toilet dash

A former Irish Football Association (IFA) senior player has revealed that the organisation has apologised after it was revealed that female former players were not given support after they had spoken out against sexism in Irish football.

In a piece for the Independent, Julie White, the former Féile na nGael senior player who was involved in the Dubliners squad that won a Champions League title in 2002, spoke of a period when she was a young player who experienced sexism in the game and was not supported by Fianna Fáil.

“I had played a number of seasons before in Ireland but my first year with the team was when I was 21, I was 21 and I was still a young player. We played the Champions League final, and a lot of the women there didn’t wear the dress I was playing in and they didn’t come to the game. I didn’t get the support I would have expected,” she said.

“In the weeks after the game there was an article written in the national newspaper. It said that women’s football is no longer the province of Irish women’s players, so that’s how it was in Ireland.

“I thought I had got away with it until we all sat down and talked about what was going on. We agreed that we didn’t want to go back to being victims of sexism and that was that. I had to leave the Fianna Fáil team at the end of the season and I didn’t get a call from them.”

Julie said she was the only woman in the squad that had played in the dress at the Champions League final but, after that, she and the rest of the squad were never invited to be part of the dressing room or the team bus.

“The fact is there were all these clubs who would say, ‘Well, we will just get her to come out in the dress,’ but there were no women on the teams. I think it was all a big secret for some players in Fianna Fáil as well as the IFA to get some of the players on the teams to wear dresses.

“There was a point in time when I remember we said to each other, ‘We won the Champions League in 2002 and we won it playing in a dress.’ So we thought, ‘Well, let’s go to the dress as well,’ but as time went on, I got used to being treated differently and people said to me, ‘This is how things are in the sport and you’ve got to start respecting it.’

“I think, in the end, there was nothing I could do. I felt so upset and frustrated because I thought I had got away with it. I was left feeling so frustrated because it wasn’t just me that was doing that but everyone else.

“I had the courage to speak out and speak up for myself. I am still here and I will always be here because I just never felt the people in the IFA were listening to me and didn’t support me.”
headline: FAI apologises to female former players who have spoken out

After a series of clashes on the island of Ireland, gardaí have been attacked by protesters.

An officer with the Garda Síochána has been attacked in the early hours of this morning by a man who tried to run him through a gate. A further officer was attacked in the early hours of this morning, while at a petrol station in the town of Kells, Co Louth.

A source with the Garda said that the attackers were armed with knives.

Gardaí are not allowing people in to take photos or video of the incident at this stage.

As well as the Gardaí, some businesses and schools in the town have closed due to the violence.

It is not known if more attacks are planned.

The incident comes just a day after clashes also took place in the Co Tipperary area of Ireland.

In the early hours of this morning, members of the Gardaí were attacked by members of the Irish Defence Forces as they attempted to enter one of the communities which have been affected by a large number of protests across the country.

A number of Gardaí were injured in the clash with people throwing bottles, rocks and petrol bombs.

The injured gardaí were moved to a nearby hospital for treatment. A gardaí spokesperson said that this was a peaceful protest in one of the more deprived communities in Co Tipperary. The spokesperson did not say how many people were involved in the attack.

The attack came as part of protests across the country protesting the handling of Gardaí by both the Irish Government and the British Government, and the treatment of the Gardaí in the last few weeks.

Last week, Gardaí arrested a man in Co Tipperary after he was caught trying to burn a car at a petrol station. The man was charged with public order offences and remains in custody.

Also last week, Gardaí on the island of La Mancha were attacked by members of the Irish Defence Forces, after a group of demonstrators threw rocks, petrol bombs and other objects at them.

In September, during another protest in the town of Ennistymon, Co Laois, one man was stabbed to death after he was caught trying to attack a Gardaí member in the town.

On September 29th, there was another incident involving Gardaí and members of the Irish Defence Forces. A Gardaí member was stabbed to death after a man allegedly attempted to attack another member of the Irish Defence Forces. The man who was killed is believed to have been a member of the Gardaí's Special Support Group. A man in his 60s was arrested on the suspicion that he was involved in the attack.
headline: Gardaí attacked during violent unrest after stabbing

Green energy is growing at a pace of 15% every year, an annual figure that’s far outpacing the rate at which it is replacing conventional energy sources.

A report produced by the Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency Alliance for Ireland (REEMA) shows that renewable energy in the country is growing at a pace of 15% every year.

A total of 8,600MW of renewable energy capacity was installed across Ireland in 2014, an increase of 3,000MW on the previous year. This was up from 7,700MW in 2013.

REEMA chief executive, Andrew Fenton, said that the growth in renewable energy is “a significant driver of the national economy” and “a further step towards the goal of a decarbonised economy by 2045.”

“Green energy is the cleanest, most cost-effective and least harmful energy source for Ireland. It’s now well established across the country and is playing a pivotal role in the efforts to decarbonise our energy sector.”

“With the rapid growth in the renewable energy sector, it’s clear that Ireland has one of the strongest and most sustainable supply of renewable energy in the world.”

“Renewable energy sources are more competitive than other forms of energy and save energy in the long term. The benefits for customers are huge as well – it makes Ireland a leading supplier of energy to the EU and supports thousands of jobs.”

“The growth in renewable energy in Ireland over the last six years has been enormous. In 2013, Irish customers paid €4.3 billion for renewable energy while the industry itself saved €4.3 billion in energy costs.

The Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency Alliance for Ireland (REEMA) reports that Ireland is on track for the highest annual renewable energy growth in the world, with a 12% growth forecast in 2014.

The figures, published in the 2014 Renewable Energy Outlook report, show that Ireland, along with Sweden and the US, is on track for the highest annual growth of renewable energy in the world in the coming years.

“RTE will be celebrating the record for the most renewable energy installations in a single year for the second year running,” said REEMA Chief Executive Andrew Fenton.

“These increases in renewable energy are helping to put Ireland on a trajectory towards the decarbonised energy economy by 2045. This is in line with the European Union’s vision for decarbonising Ireland’s energy sector.”

“Ireland’s green energy sector is driving an increase in renewable energy demand and, in turn, contributing to the decarbonised economy that has been a key part of the EU’s Renewable Energy Directive. The EU goal to decarbonise Ireland by 2030, is now within reach.”

“This momentum towards the decarbonised energy future is creating new jobs, providing incentives for businesses and helping consumers with electricity bills.
