RTÉ News report:

‘The death toll from the COVID-19 pandemic will soar beyond 4,000 before the health system is prepared to cope with the crisis’

15 February 2020

On the second day of the government’s first National Symposium on the COVID-19 pandemic (S2/COVID19) in Galway City, the number of deaths linked to the disease increased to 14, while 16 people were in a critical condition.

While the two-day event was initially intended to review the disease, and to assess the impact on the public health system, the two-day “convenor’s briefing” turned into a major political event as it was attended by over 1,500 people and the chief medical officer of the Department of Health, an expert panel and senior health executives from across the country.

However, the real focus of the event, which began on the eve of the World Environment Day, was on the crisis that has left the Irish population with over 2,000 cases of infection – a figure that is set to skyrocket in the coming days and weeks.

There were no new deaths linked to the COVID-19 pandemic on the second day of the S2/COVID19 meeting on Sunday as the total number of cases across the country had risen to 2,076, with 3,161 people across the country receiving support from the Irish Emergency Service.

“I am pleased that the figures we have are in line with our estimates of the expected increase over the next 24 to 48 hours,” Dr John Connolly, the country’s chief medical officer, said.

The COVID-19 crisis in Ireland has come to a peak on Thursday, with 7,845 cases confirmed as of late Friday, and a further 4,000 cases expected to be confirmed over the coming weeks.

With the increase in cases continuing, officials on Thursday announced that 14 people had died from the virus, a figure that is expected to increase to 16 after the number of cases is assessed.

Speaking on the second day of the S2/COVID19 meeting in Galway City, Dr John Connolly, the country’s chief medical officer, said the figures would be in line with their estimates for the increase in cases over the next 24 to 48 hours.

Dr Connolly said while the Irish population has no immunity in the short term, he was confident that the country would be able to cope in the short term.

“We are moving fast because the numbers are rising very quickly, and because the numbers are going to increase much faster than we can control them.

“We are in a situation where we cannot see the numbers of new cases, because they are going to rise very quickly.”

He said while the Irish health system was functioning, its capacity to deal with the COVID-19 outbreak had not been tested properly and there had been no system in place to monitor the epidemic.

“This is not a situation in which we will be able to get out of, because we have a massive outbreak of the disease in a population. We have to have a system in place to manage this. We cannot do this in isolation,” he said.
headline: 14 virus deaths among people in disability services

An Irish man has been hospitalised with burns after a suspected petrol bomb was thrown at his car in northern Dublin.

The 31-year-old man was injured in the incident, which happened around 12.30am at the Bridge Road in the south inner city in what the National Roads Authority said was a serious assault.

A Garda bomb squad officer at the scene said the device had been thrown from a passing car and a number of objects had been hurled from it.

The victim was treated at the scene before being taken to a hospital in Dublin for burns, the authority said.

The man's car was damaged and is still being assessed by gardaí.

A Garda spokesman said it is believed the man had been walking in the area when the man in the car started to follow him.

A Garda bomb disposal officer said the man was targeted because he had been travelling to or from the capital. He said a man was stopped by a man who followed him and assaulted him.

The man is reported to be in stable condition.

The man was taken to Tallaght University Hospital for treatment.

The National Roads Authority said no-one has yet been arrested in relation to the incident.

The Dublin Circuit Road will be closed between the Grafton and Bridge Roads, where the suspect was arrested, and will be reopened once the investigation is complete.
headline: Man uninjured after suspected petrol bomb attack

'Non-recent' allegations made against Brand to police

The police have been asked to conduct a thorough investigation into allegations made to them by a female who was allegedly sexually assaulted by a Brand executive.

In a letter to the Garda Ombudsman, dated May 13 this year, the garda commissioner said the gardaí were also asked to investigate allegations made by a number of other people.

In the letter, the commissioner said it would be up to a committee to decide whether an investigation should be held.

He also noted that it was not a crime to make false allegations to the Garda Ombudsman.

The garda commissioner's letter to the Garda Ombudsman is dated on May 13. Source: RTÉ News

The garda commissioner's letter to the Garda Ombudsman says that they have been asked to investigate claims made to them by a female who was allegedly sexually assaulted by a Brand executive.

The allegations were made by a woman who works in an HR department in Ireland, with the aim of 'providing information to the public' concerning a 'lack of women in high office' in Brand Ireland.

'The woman who made the allegations provided information to the Garda Ombudsman concerning the gender balance in the senior management ranks of the company,' the letter says.

'As a result of her information, the Ombudsman’s staff were sent a request for information from the company which the woman provided. This inquiry is ongoing.'

'The Ombudsman’s staff was also provided with a copy of the internal report on the women from the company. The Ombudsman staff then provided the material to the Garda Ombudsman.'

'As part of the Garda Ombudsman’s investigation, a number of interviews with senior executives were conducted. There is a possibility the company may have engaged in conduct which is against the law. In such circumstances it is expected that the garda commissioner will be required to take remedial action.'

The garda commissioner wrote in the letter: 'The matter is not a criminal matter, as the woman did not commit a criminal offence.

'It is believed that the complainant was acting on information that was made available to her and/or the company. The company is now aware of this information, and the matter is being investigated.'

He also said 'there is a possibility the company may have engaged in conduct which is against the law'.

'In such circumstances it is expected that the garda commissioner will be required to take remedial action.'

The garda commissioner's letter to the Garda Ombudsman also states that the allegations are being referred to a Garda Ombudsman committee, who will decide whether an investigation is necessary.

The garda commissioner's letter to the Garda Ombudsman dated on May 13

The Garda Ombudsman is a Garda Ombudsman committee, appointed by the Minister to investigate alleged incidents of professional misconduct in the garda profession and to make recommendations to the Minister on these matters.

The Garda Ombudsman's remit includes assessing the conduct of gardaí, their senior leadership and other individuals or organisations in matters affecting the profession.

In relation to allegations made by a woman to the garda commissioner in relation to a Brand Ireland executive, it is understood that the committee will make its decision by this evening.
headline: 'Non-recent' allegations against Brand made to police

Two people are dead and 10 are injured after two explosions shook a US steel company. Two days after a gas explosion killed three and left another injured, a man died at a hospital in New York City, and the FBI and US Secret Service are investigating.

The first explosion occurred on Monday, May 12, in a US steel plant near Taos, New Mexico. The second occurred on Wednesday, May 15, at a steel plant in Alabama, where workers were told to prepare for another gas explosion. The explosion at the Alabama plant left 11 people injured, but two people were confirmed dead as a result of the blast.

The US steel industry is a highly lucrative business, accounting for roughly half of the country’s GDP.

In the last three years, it has been the subject of a series of deadly explosions and gas attacks.

On March 25, 2013, a gas leak at the Alcan steelworks in China killed more than 200 people, and a month later, two Chinese-made gas cylinders exploded at a factory in the Chinese city of Wenzhou.

The explosion at the Wenzhou factory was the largest of the three incidents. Three men were also killed in the explosion. The Wenzhou incident has been the subject of a number of investigations, including by the Chinese government. A month later, an explosion at the Blyth steelworks in Scotland in April 2013 killed 14 people, and another explosion at the Grangemouth steelworks in the UK on the same day claimed the lives of 32 people. The Grangemouth explosion was the biggest explosion in UK steel industry history, and the death toll was estimated to be up to 1,600.

These events brought the US steel industry into global headlines, prompting major companies to introduce new safety measures. At the same time, the industry has been undergoing a difficult period with a series of deadly explosions and a loss of profits.

The Wenzhou incident raised awareness of the dangers of using toxic gas. In the US steel industry, a toxic gas, helium, is often used as a de-mineralising agent. It can lead to many health and safety issues and is suspected to be involved in the deaths of two workers who died in 2009.

This was also the first time a steel plant in the US has ever experienced a gas leak, and it was also the first time a US steel company had ever suffered an explosion.

The US steel industry is highly profitable. In 2009, the US steel industry produced approximately $35 billion in revenue. This has continued to grow, and now, US steel companies are making $50 billion in profits every year.

While there are many issues that can lead to an explosion, one of the key points that should be considered is the size of the blast. Gas leaks, such as that at the Wenzhou plant and the Grangemouth plant, can cause very large explosions, which can lead to the death of as many as a hundred or more people. The death toll is, however, very low. This is because the steel blast can occur so rapidly, and is often so powerful that it is difficult to detect.

The size of the explosion can also make it difficult to predict who will die as a result.

A new Washington has emerged for America’s new president-elect, with Democrats saying he is a “lonely” and “self-serving” leader who is “destroying” the country.

Mr Trump’s America is “self-serving” and an “insecure place”, said Kamala Harris, the California senator who has been a prominent presence in the presidential race, but is not likely to be the first 2020 Democratic candidate to campaign in the state.

“As long as the self-serving president-elect is winning, the American people will be in a very difficult position,” she said.

“I am not sure that that will get better,” she added, describing how the president-elect is “trying to get everything he can in an attempt to have his way with the Congress and the courts”.

“And he’s destroying us as a country,” she said. “And the last thing we need is to be a country that is not good for America.”

The president-elect is “trying to undermine” the judiciary, she said, “and we should be very concerned about that”.

“We are not going to be able to do the job that the people of America expect us to be able to do. The American people expect us to be able to go to war,” she said.

“And when you start a war, there’s no end to the violence,” she added. “I think it’s time for our country to be much more aware that war should not be the answer.”

The president-elect has “no desire to do what he promised to do”, she said.

Ms Harris said the American people did not want “this president” who “will not only be destroying the economy, but the country itself”.

She added: “Our Constitution is designed for the American people to come together, to be in agreement, and it is designed to be a great nation of freedom. And it’s not a great nation if there is one person that doesn’t feel free to be who he wants to be and we have people who are trying to undermine that.”

Mr Trump “has made it clear he is a man who is self-serving, and that he will not listen to the people of America,” she said.

“He’s made it clear, and he’s trying to make it very clear that he will not listen to the people of America,” she added.

“I don’t think he will listen to the people of America,” she said. “I think we’ll have to do this all on our own and it may not be pretty.”

“And there’s a lot of pain,” she said. “We can’t just let him continue to do this and continue to say what he’s saying.”
headline: Trump's America is 'self-serving', says Kamala Harris

Archbishop of Canterbury Geoffrey Fisher has called on the country’s church leaders to resign over a series of sexual abuse claims.

Fisher, 76, said his decision to quit his post was in response to the “unacceptable” behaviour of senior figures and he had no choice but to go.

The Archbishops of York and Canterbury issued their letter of resignation on Wednesday. The statement said a meeting of senior Church leaders had been held on Thursday to discuss the findings and recommendations of an independent review.

“The findings show the Church’s response has been grossly inadequate and unacceptable,” the statement said. “The response of the Church has been too lenient when dealing with allegations of sexual abuse and is no longer appropriate.

“Our actions have failed the victims who have been referred for support and assistance. We need to work with people across the Church and within our schools, colleges and charities.

“The Church’s leadership must demonstrate the necessary sensitivity and care to the victims in this case and the wider abuse situation.”

The Archbishop also urged “all those with a part in this abuse situation” to have their say on the issue.

“The abuse must be recognised and treated in the same way by all those who have a part in it,” he added.

The statement from the church leadership also says the leadership of the Church of Ireland has been “inappropriate in recent years.”

“There has been an unacceptable failure to deal with allegations of sexual abuse in Ireland. It is in no one’s interests to let that continue.

“All those who have a part in this must be held to account for their actions or lack of action and in no other situation should their actions be seen as acceptable.”

The Independent Alliance (IA) leader, who has been the subject of widespread allegations of sexual abuse by clergy and others, said the Church of Ireland leadership had not responded to “any serious allegations” of abuse.

“There has been no serious response to any serious allegations that I have made and there should be a serious response,” said the IA. “The most obvious and serious problem in the Irish Church is that of leadership.

“This is not acceptable and the leadership in the Church of Ireland must be challenged to change their approach.”

The Church of Ireland’s senior clergy said they were “deeply saddened” by the announcement and were reviewing their handling of the abuse crisis, but declined to respond directly.

A spokesman said: “This is a deeply sad time for the Church of Ireland. We have been working closely with the leadership and the Church of Ireland Council in this matter. We will be reviewing the way in which we respond to abuse allegations and the way we are working with other church leaders.”

A statement issued by the church says: “These are not only difficult questions for the Church of Ireland, they are equally difficult for the wider community. The church has been and continues to be a caring, caring place where people are welcomed.

“However, we are deeply concerned about the way the Church has treated victims of abuse.
headline: Archbishop of Canterbury urged to resign over scandal

Headline: UN demand 'prompt' probe into strike near Beirut hospital

New York: A UN human rights chief is calling for an independent probe into the deaths of more than 2,000 people injured by a strike near the Lebanese capital Beirut on Monday.

Speaking to a UN group of experts in Geneva, Zeid Ra’ad al-Hussein said the incident should be investigated by an international panel, including France, as it relates to the Syrian conflict.

He also said the UN has to continue to monitor the situation in Lebanon and Syria and continue to support the government of President Bashar Al-Assad.

Mr Zeid called for international involvement in a resolution that could be adopted at the United Nations General Assembly this month to demand a global investigation into the strike that has killed over 100 people, most of them civilians.

He said the UN was in an urgent need to find out exactly what occurred at the hospital.

“If a UN commission is required, it must be an independent investigation carried out by a qualified and independent group of experts and with due regard for human rights,” he said.

Mr Zeid also noted that the Lebanese Government was “working on the implementation of a National Security Law and taking all necessary measures” to protect the country’s borders.

“We have to respect the rule of law and ensure that there are no violations of international humanitarian law that can be used as a weapon in the hands of terrorists,” he said.

He said the UN human rights chief was meeting officials in Lebanon and Jordan to discuss the situation.

The UN said the strike was “an attack on a UN hospital” which left at least 100 people dead, including dozens of children, many of whom were on the same operating table as the doctors treating them.

An international investigation into the strike, the deadliest in Lebanon since the war began in neighbouring Syria in 2011, is needed to verify claims of responsibility and to establish the full circumstances surrounding the strike, UN human rights spokeswoman Ravina Shamdasani said.

“We can confirm that over 100 people have been killed and over 100 have been injured in an attack on a UN hospital,” she said.

“The medical staff and hospital staff, along with their colleagues in the hospital, were conducting operations when the attack took place.”

She said the hospital was not in the control of the Syrian government but the hospital was in the control of an unnamed group based in Syria.

“We are aware that the hospital is in the control of an unnamed group,” she said.

“It is imperative that an international investigation be carried out into the events that took place and determine who is responsible for them.”

The UN said it was also working with the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) to “ensure that all necessary precautions are taken and that no further loss of life occurs”.

She said the Red Cross had also been in contact with local authorities and the medical staff of the hospital.

The ICRC spokeswoman said the hospital was not in the control of the Syrian government and that it was an “unnamed group” based in Syria which was “not recognised by any international organisations”.
headline: UN demand 'prompt' probe into strike near Beirut hospital

By Claire Daly

A new initiative is in the pipeline to increase the availability of free contraception to young women in Ireland.

Last year, Minister for Health Simon Harris announced the introduction of a €4.4 million scheme, aimed at ensuring that young women have access to information, advice and contraceptive support, as well as free family planning services in Ireland, from the age of 15.

Now that the scheme is in place, it has the potential to dramatically increase access to contraception in this country, as well as encourage greater use.

It is a great opportunity to make a huge change in the lives of young women – to encourage them to seek out a contraception provider, rather than go to an over-night pregnancy clinic, as is the case with many of our young women.

For Ireland, this could be the opportunity to put some money in the hands of young women who don’t have the opportunity to avail of free contraception from the age of 15, and help to change their lives for the better.

The new scheme is called Access to Compulsory Contraception and Information (ACCIN), and is part of a nationwide rollout of the free family planning service which was introduced by the Minister in November 2014.

It is a programme that is aimed at ensuring that young women have access to information and advice on contraception, and this will include the provision of free contraception, and in some cases, the opportunity for young women to be referred to a free clinic or family planning service, should they be unwell.

The scheme, which is part of the free contraception package, will include the following:

All young women 15-19 years old will be offered the opportunity to have counselling and/or advice about contraception. It will also include access to the full range of contraception options and information, including condoms, withdrawal and intrauterine systems.

The scheme will also provide young women with a list of all the relevant contraceptives offered by contraceptive providers in Ireland and details of their cost and price.

Minister Simon Harris said: “Access to contraceptive services is one of the most important things we can do to help women in Ireland, both as individuals and as part of our families.

“That’s why I’m delighted that we’re making these changes to ACCIN.

“Through ACCIN, young women have the chance to seek help and support, and the right to know what contraception is available at their own free cost.”

Minister Simon Harris said: “We have a clear and simple message to all young people in Ireland who are considering or already using contraception.

“Family planning is a key part of my commitment to making this country a more equal place to live and work.”

“As part of ACCIN, young women have the opportunity to go online and find the best contraception services for them, wherever they live in the country, with the opportunity to find the services of an organisation which is part of the family planning scheme in Ireland.

“This means we are giving young people a choice and help them make the best choice for their own individual circumstances.”

In the last year, 1,848 children were in temporary accommodation, compared to 623 in the previous year, according to the CCIE report.

In addition, almost 50,000 children, or 13.3 per cent of the total homeless population, have been on the streets for longer than five days a week, and around 14,000 on a regular basis.

Irish Council for the Homeless chief executive Colm O’Loughlin said: “It is shocking that, in our lifetime, over one in three children living in Ireland may have slept on the streets.

“It is also a tragedy that this increase in the homeless population would be happening, when thousands more children are left sleeping rough on the streets than there are children in foster homes. This is completely unacceptable and shows a lack of leadership on the part of the government and the Irish Government’s Department of Social Protection.”

Child homelessness has been rising steadily in Ireland, according to new data from the Irish Council for the Homeless (ICH), the country’s most experienced homeless charity.

The organisation recently found that, in the three months to December 2014, the homeless population in Ireland had increased by more than 1,000 children, making up almost 1.3 million homeless people in the country.

While the overall homeless population has risen by a similar amount over the same period, the increase in homelessness has been more than double.

In the first three months to December, the homelessness increased by 1,723 children, making up approximately 2.4 million homeless people in the country.

In the same period, the number of children in crisis accommodation increased by 688 children, making up 7.6 million homeless people in the country.

‘The number of children in crisis accommodation has almost doubled in a decade’

The report from ICH also reveals that a record 15,000 children were on the streets in the 12 months to December.

The latest figures show that the number of children in crisis accommodation, the biggest of any type of accommodation, had increased by 30,000 between January and the end of December, the report says.

“While the homelessness situation has been worsening over the last number of years, the increase in the number of children sleeping rough has been particularly dramatic, with nearly 3,000 children sleeping on the streets between January and December 2014,” the report says.

The number of children in crisis accommodation has more than doubled in the last decade.

In the report, the ICH says children are often in crisis accommodation because their welfare is being addressed, they face serious health and safety problems, or they are having their own children removed from the family because of a history of neglect.
headline: Major concern over pace of child homelessness

The EU and the US are not likely to agree to a new trade deal before the end of the year, with the outcome not certain, according to senior officials in both countries.

The two largest economies in the world face a series of uncertainties over the next two months as the EU's chief negotiator, Michel Barnier, prepares to begin discussions with US trade chief Donald Trump over a trade deal that could involve a reduction in US duties on EU-made goods.

US Trade Representative Robert Lighthizer has said he will seek to keep all existing US tariffs in place.

The decision by Lighthizer to maintain tariffs is a blow to European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker's desire for an agreement before the end of the year.

"The talks will now come down to the very last minute, which will be quite chaotic because we have this new president," one EU official said.

"The two leaders have made their respective promises, and we need to show up and make sure that we get it right."

On Wednesday, Juncker said he believed the EU should agree to a deal.

"We can't say no to this new president, to a president who wants to take us to a trade agreement in the end of the year," Juncker said in Luxembourg.

"We will do everything within our power, we will do everything within our competence and within our legal framework and I think that we will get there."

Mr Trump and Mr Barnier are due to meet on Friday.

'Hard questions'

Mr Trump has previously said he is willing to "sign a deal that works for us, not for China."

Mr Barnier had said on Tuesday that he and Mr Trump had agreed to the outline of a new deal, with the possibility of additional issues to be discussed.

"It was agreed that we will not sign an agreement before Christmas, that it will be a new deal," Barnier told reporters.

"We will not sign an agreement that does not reflect the interests of the United States. The US has obligations to other countries that are much more important than the interests of a small country, such as the EU, and we will not sign an agreement that does not meet the interests of the US.

"We have put forward concrete proposals, and it will be up to the president to decide what the final text will be. But the negotiations will not be easy."

"It will cause major damage, not just for the United States, but for the entire region," Ms Malmström said.

US Trade Representative Lighthizer said in a briefing on Wednesday that the new trade agreement would "significantly reduce" existing US tariffs on EU goods.

"There will be no tariff changes for goods coming from the EU to the US," Lighthizer said.

"And we are going to negotiate to the extent that they make the US more efficient and more competitive," he said.

Mr Trump has previously described the Trans-Pacific Partnership as "not fair" and has vowed to reverse its provisions.

The Northern Ireland’s Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) has urged the UK government to come up with alternative policies to support the economy if the UK leaves the European Union.

The Dáil this afternoon also voted down an amendment calling on the government to seek support in the EU for a new treaty to help the country if it leaves the UK. The amendment was made by Labour’s Conor McGinn.

However, Taoiseach Enda Kenny said the government would not “just sit on the fence”.

Speaking in the Dáil today, the Taoiseach said the UK had to face the reality of a post-Brexit reality. “This is the reality of the country as a whole, and so this is a reality that the UK needs to take into account,” he said.

“We have to face that reality and that is that when we have the United Kingdom, we have the United Kingdom.”

The Dáil’s decision to back a Brexit amendment on a post-Brexit treaty was voted down by a significant margin by a vote of 38 to 29. This was not the first time in the Dáil that a Brexit-related amendment on an EU Treaty has been defeated.

However, the Dáil was due to debate the Brexit amendment in order to allow for a debate on the amendment itself – a debate which was eventually agreed by a narrow margin of 23 to 22.

Speaking in the Dáil, Labour TD Stephen Donnelly said the party was disappointed at the result. “I was confident we would prevail on the issue of the new treaty,” he said.

“We knew that this would be a contentious issue, and it has turned out to be as it was. The Dáil has now been thrown into the real world of Brexit and I know it will be very difficult for the government to implement this.

“In order for the Dáil to be able to say that we have a policy that will meet the needs of the country, we have to have that in place for the first time in a year. The government has put forward a new proposal which I hope will be accepted.”

“But the problem for the government is, if we do not have a new treaty, we will leave a hole that we will have to fill in, and that will be the reality of the post-Brexit reality for the country and for the people of Northern Ireland.”

“We will be facing a scenario where the economic recovery will be extremely fragile, particularly for the people of the North-east of the country, and it will be very difficult to rebuild an economy and infrastructure, with only the European Union to support the economy.”

“That will put the whole country at risk.”

The government’s proposal to seek support from the EU for a new treaty to help the country if it leaves the UK was rejected by a vote of 19 to 23.

Speaking on the House of Commons side, the prime minister was asked by Deputy Leader of the Labour Party Andrew Rosindell what would be the alternative for the UK if it left the EU.

text: MELBOURNE, April 10 (Reuters) - A fast-moving fire that broke out on Tuesday in one of the poorest parts of Greece forced hundreds of people to flee their homes as the government tried to keep the flames out, residents told Reuters. The blaze broke out in the small Greek city of Agios Panagiotaros in western Greece. "It was like a firestorm," Agios Panagiotaros resident Yiannis said, adding that many people fled in panic when they heard that the fire was coming from a building next to their house. A fire department spokesman said the blaze had been brought under control, with the cause still under investigation. "The fire started on Monday morning but it has now reached the second floor of the building," he said. The blaze caused major disruption to roads and a number of buildings were damaged, said Agios Panagiotaros resident Christos Konstantinidis, who added that it also destroyed a number of cars. The evacuation of the city in the afternoon was also due to be carried out in the afternoon because of the dangers of smoke from the fire, said Konstantinidis. The blaze spread quickly in the area, the blaze department said, but it was not known how long the blaze had been burning and how much damage had been done to the city. A man from the village of Thespiota on the Peloponnese coast was among those who fled their houses, and told Reuters that it took them more than three hours to reach the safety of a hotel. "It's been three hours, three hours and there are still fires in other buildings," said the man, who did not wish to be named, adding that the incident had a major impact on the Peloponnese. On Monday, the fire department said it had received more than 3,000 emergency calls and more than 1,000 calls to the fire department. The blaze had destroyed some 20 outbuildings and damaged some 100 buildings by the time the fire reached Agios Panagiotaros on Tuesday morning. The fire had also destroyed the local factory, said Konstantinidis, who said it took up to three hours to reach the area. More than 2,000 homes had been damaged by the fire, according to the fire department. People evacuated from the area were told to return to their homes by the end of the day, and the city was put on high alert after the incident. "The blaze had destroyed the city's main bus station and it took some 40 to 50 minutes for a bus to reach Agios Panagiotaros from the city centre," he said. "The rest of the city is on high alert and will remain on high alert for at least 48 hours," the fire department said in a statement, adding that police were looking for a potential bomber. People who had been told to evacuate from the area were told not to go until the government gave the go-ahead to the evacuation, the fire department said.

The largest ever figures on the productivity of all gardaí in the State’s Road Policing Force (RPF) are to be released today.

The Department of Justice and Equality (DOJE) has published the report entitled ‘A New Approach to Improving Road Policing. A Report of the Transport and Road Safety Steering Group (TRSSG) Report’.

The report highlights that, according to statistics and the Department’s own analysis, the RPF is one of the worst performing parts of the Garda Síochána (GS) and is “virtually non-productive” in terms of productivity and number of police staff working on the roads, particularly around traffic control.

The study shows that the RPF employs 11 fewer officers than it did in 2007, and that the number of cases resolved as a result of gardaí assistance and prosecutions in 2008 and 2009 fell by 10% and 14% respectively, the largest fall since 2002. The figure rose again in 2011, when it fell by another 10% and 19% respectively.

The report also states that “the level of collaboration and the impact of the gardaí’s use of specialist technology to the detriment of the RPF’s efficiency can only be properly assessed over a relatively long period of time”.

“The current level of productivity of the RPF was achieved in the second half of 2008. This was achieved despite a number of difficulties in the governance of this department and a large increase in workload.”

“We have identified a number of areas of potential productivity improvement, including the use of data analytics as well as an improved data quality management system.”

The report also reveals that gardaí across the State are now spending more time in traffic hotspots than they did in the previous year, and that many of the RPF’s new roles and techniques are now being used to deal with traffic-related incidents, including motor vehicle accidents.

The report also warns that the GS’s use of specialist technology for traffic offences and prosecutions is “inherently linked to the effectiveness of its Road Policing”.

“Gardaí have a responsibility to ensure that road-related enforcement is as effective as possible, but it must be acknowledged that the technologies available to the GS are not necessarily suitable for use in an RPF”, the report states.

“Road Policing is a strategic activity which must be supported and supported by a system of governance, which is often difficult to manage and to establish and maintain.”

The report concludes that “the level of productivity of road policing in the RPF is unsustainable.”

Jon Venables, author and editor of The Liberal, is planning his latest appeal for freedom.

He will be releasing a book, “Free All,” on the freedom of the individual and freedom for others.

The book will be published in January, by John F. Kennedy University Press. The first edition will contain the first chapter in Free All: The Freedom of the Individual, and the second edition will cover the same material but will contain additional chapters on the rights of the individual and the rights of others.

The aim is to provide a clear framework for anyone who has ever been imprisoned for a crime they did not commit, or for a crime against someone they did not cause harm.

“I have a vision,” says Venables, “that I want to help people move away from the trap of being imprisoned. I’m not talking about physical incarceration. It’s more like physical imprisonment of one’s spirit.

“We are getting it.”

Venables has been in jail since 2008, when he was imprisoned for two years and eight months for “public order offences”.

Venables was the co-founder of The Libertarian Republic, which published a magazine from 2002 to 2008. It was one of the few free newspapers in Ireland, which had been shut down by the government in the years following the collapse of the Irish Republic in 1998.

The libertarian republic was a reaction to the government being unable to implement some of the provisions of the Magna Carta. Many people thought that the government was not serious about these provisions, which were a legacy of an “Empire of Liberty” that had lasted almost 200 years.

The magazine, which was sold to the Irish Catholic Press in 2008, was shut down in 2008 by the government.

Venables was the sole contributor to the magazine and the only publisher of The Libertine Republic until it was published in 2008.

“I don’t regret it. I was doing what I thought I had to do to stop that from happening,” says Venables.

“In fact, I’m still doing it. I did a lot of things that made me feel very proud of that. It was the only time I ever published anything without a contract. It was the only time I ever published anything without a contract.

“I think I’ve always been a libertarian. I think there are those of us who would be described as being on the left, and you’re either on the left or you’re on the right, but I’m on the left. I’ve been on the left for a long, long time.”

He says the reason for his release is that he wants the public to understand that there is a freedom movement.

“When I was in jail I was writing my articles and things like that,” says Venables. “I was writing about a lot of things. I was writing for my family and my girlfriend.

DUBAI (May 7, 2017) – Malaysian authorities are planning to release the results of the post mortem of the missing Malaysian national, Nora Quoirin, later today.

Quoirin, 29, was last seen on April 24 when she went out for a walk in Muara Malaysia along with her sister, Aishah, 21.

Her whereabouts since has been a mystery for the last five months.

On January 10, Malaysian Prime Minister, Najib Razak, said that the results of the post mortem on Nora Quoirin would be released by tomorrow evening.

Last week, the Malaysian Federal Territories Police stated that there was no evidence of foul play in the disappearance of Nora Quoirin.

According to the Malaysian authorities, Nora’s case will be discussed at the National Police Headquarters in Kuala Lumpur by May 10.

It was said that the post mortem results will be made public in a closed session of the National Police Headquarters at about 7.30pm local time on May 10.

A message from the Malaysian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said: “The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and National Unification has been informed of the results of the post mortem which were released yesterday (May 6) by the Malaysian Federal Territories Police (MFP).

“On the basis of the findings, there is no evidence of foul play in the disappearance of Nora Quoirin. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and National Unification would like to stress that the Malaysian authorities will not be making any statements in relation to this case.”

“I have to say that I have received the results of the post mortem which were released yesterday (May 6) by the Malaysian Federal Territories Police (MFP),” he said.

“The findings are not sufficient to indicate that there is any evidence of foul play in the disappearance of Nora Quoirin.”

On Tuesday, Malaysian Prime Minister, Najib Razak, said that the government and authorities would not comment on any matters relating to the Nora Quoirin case.

“The government has nothing to say on this,” he said at an event to announce new measures to improve relations with the United States.

“We will continue to pursue the recovery of Nora Quoirin and bring her home,” he said. “I hope all of the efforts undertaken by our government will contribute to this case finding.”

By Lorna Gallagher

Refugees Welcome, a campaign of protest against the Dublin government’s proposed changes to the Dublin Act which would see the arrival of thousands of asylum seekers in the city from the UK, are in Dublin to demonstrate against the planned increase in numbers.

Last Wednesday night, the protest was organised by the Refugee Welcome campaign (RW), which has been campaigning on the issue of the mass arrival of asylum seekers into Ireland. According to the RW, Dublin city centre is one of the last safe points for refugees fleeing conflicts and civil wars in the Middle East, including Syria and Iraq.

Dublin city centre is also one of the last safe points for those fleeing war, famine and displacement in Africa. The RW say that the mass arrival of refugees is taking place as Dublin becomes more violent and chaotic as a result of the political situation in the country.

RW is an organisation of international activists and campaigners who are concerned with the consequences of the rise of political Islam in Europe and the Muslim world, the growing presence of neo-fascists and other right-wing figures in the UK and France and the general climate of hostility towards refugees and minorities in Europe.

The march

On the eve of the protest, hundreds of people – many wearing the colours of the Refugee Welcome banner – turned out for the protest, calling on the Government to do more to welcome refugees.

They marched in Dublin city centre, from Dublin University to O’Connell Street, stopping in at various sites to show solidarity with those fleeing from conflicts in countries across the Middle East and Africa. They were joined by over a thousand people, many of whom were refugees.

The protest also passed through various other areas including the former Irish Army barracks in O’Connell Street, which is currently being renovated, and in the University of Limerick, the location of the University’s new refugee accommodation.

“I want to send a message to the minister that we won’t be satisfied with a second look at Dublin’s asylum policies and the fact that Dublin is a big centre of international terrorism. We want Dublin to be the safe haven that it was meant to be for asylum seekers.”

- Mary Rose, Refugee Welcome march in Dublin

Roughly 2,000 people attended the rally, which was organised by the group, and many were carrying their banners – which had been painted with the RW’s black and orange flags.

Some people had set up camp on the steps of St Anne’s Cathedral, where the protest was organised, while others gathered on the steps of the old Irish Army Barracks in O’Connell Street.

There were also some people who travelled into the city from various other cities and towns including Cork, Waterford, Galway, Limerick, Clonmel and Tipperary, in addition to Dublin.

Refugee welcome banner on the march, on O’Connell Street, Dublin

- Mary Rose, Refugee welcome march in Dublin

Some people carrying signs reading “we welcome refugees” and “we welcome the asylum seekers” were also among the large crowd.

At the rally, there were over 200 people from different parts of the country.
headline: #RefugeesWelcome brigade protest in Dublin saying it’s the start of their campaign to buck anti-migrant trend

A new government website will help translate state warnings into English from a limited number of foreign languages (such as Spanish, Arabic, Italian and French) for health professionals and those who care for them.

The government intends to launch a new ‘covid-related’ advice site aimed at people whose English fluency is not up to the task, according to an email sent by the Department of Health to staff and those from other professions who will be working to put the information into English.

The website will launch this week at The Liberal, a branch of the Department of Health, with a new section called ‘covid related advice’.

It will be available as an online service, where you can find out about the new advice and translate it into English. There will be links to other sections of the government site which deal with other aspects of COVID-19.

The Government is making the Covid-related advice the centrepiece of its digital public service offering, which has also included, alongside the new advice, a new section called ‘Covid related advice for those in the foreign language’. The new advice, says the Department, will focus on communicating with other health professionals and those caring for them about the virus as well as being an easy way for people to keep up-to-date with the latest information and advice.

‘It is a new section of our advice website where health professionals, carers and community nurses can all keep up-to-date about the advice,’ said a spokeswoman for the Department of Health.

‘We believe that it is an important step to ensure everyone who is a part of our health services and care for vulnerable people can keep up-to-date with the advice.’

One element of the Covid-related advice which is already on the site is a section called ‘Covid Related Symptoms’, which has some general symptoms of the virus.

The Department of Health will also be offering advice in English on how best to self-isolate and ‘social distancing’, including advice on the role of self-isolation in isolation or quarantine.

‘We will be announcing advice on other types of Covid-related advice, including those for those with underlying health conditions, as well as advice on how best to keep our community safe while we carry out the best possible testing and prevention of infections,’ said the department.

The Department of Health is also encouraging all public health staff who are working for the government to work online and use the Covid-related advice as a ‘digital hub’ where they can keep up-to-date with the latest advice.

The Department will also be publishing its coronavirus website to help people find out more about the advice, including information on testing and self-isolation, but it is not yet clear whether people will be able to register to access the new advice.

Headline: Supermacs boss says Irish beef farmers are not being paid enough

Published: Tuesday, 15 May 2014

THE leader of Ireland’s largest dairy farmer group has said that Irish beef farmers are not being paid enough.

Amber Lafferty, the former chief executive of Ireland’s largest dairy group and a former Irish government minister, made the comments in an interview with the Irish Times.

“The Irish Government has promised the Irish beef industry that it will pay the Irish Government €9 million to compensate beef farmers, and I believe this is still very much on track,” Ms Lafferty said. “The Irish Government has promised that it will also pay the Irish farmer a minimum of €2.6 million for the additional cost.”

Ms Lafferty said the compensation scheme was “not too bad” and that her group received €3.6 million to meet that promise.

“We believe that we are being given a good deal,” she said. “We are the biggest group of Irish beef farmers in Europe.”

A spokeswoman for the Irish Beef Association said the beef group has made “a good faith effort to pay compensation as promised.”

“The Irish beef industry is a crucial part of the Irish economy and the Irish Government will continue to help the Irish beef industry through any compensation payments to be made,” she said.

“We are disappointed that the Irish Government has chosen not to meet its commitment and we will work with the Irish Government to find a way to make sure the compensation money is paid to Irish beef farmers.”

The beef industry has been rocked by a strike of Irish cattle farmers since November.

The farmers were protesting against the collapse of the so-called Supermacs, the largest farmers’ organisation in Ireland.
headline: Supermacs boss says Irish beef farmers are not being paid enough

Instagram is the world’s most popular social media platform with the estimated 3.8 billion users

A new report by the social media measurement company, Quantcast, shows that the social media app is the world’s largest platform with the estimated 3.8 billion users. This comes as no surprise considering that Instagram was founded on the idea of bringing together friends and strangers who enjoy sharing each other’s posts.

The Quantcast report shows that in 2018 Instagram reached a total of 1.2 billion active monthly users. This figure is on track to pass the 2 billion mark in 2019.

Of the 1.2 billion daily active users, Instagram’s most active users are between 18-34 years of age with the most active users being the youngest users. The most popular type of content on Instagram is the photos with the most comments and likes followed by the posts with the most likes.

The report also reveals that Instagram’s growth is driven by the number of its monthly active users. As of this writing, the total number of active users is at 623 million, a rise of 20 million, or a 4 percent, over the total number of users in 2018.

The report also reveals that the users of Instagram are primarily male with a male to female ratio of almost equal. The users were primarily in their teens and twenties with the highest number of users coming from the age groups of 21-34, 18-24, 18-34, and 23-39. The report also shows that the most popular user groups on Instagram are women and women only groups.

In terms of top countries where Instagram users spend the most time, Canada is the top country for Instagram users while the United States and United Kingdom are the top two.

The Instagram users were predominantly between the ages of 25-34 with the users in the 25-34 age group spending the most time on the app. The users were predominantly female with the most popular user group being women.

In terms of the most popular countries where Instagram users are from, Canada ranks number one with more than three million users in this country. The US comes in second with more than 1.3 million users followed by the United Kingdom with more than 800,000 users.

The top countries where Instagram users are least active, and the least popular user group, are in Asia (e.g. Indonesia and Malaysia) and Europe (e.g. France, Germany and the UK).

The noise mitigation scheme announced today by the Department of the Environment, Community and Local Government is a key part of the government’s ongoing policy of reducing the use of fossil fuels.

The new devices are set to be compulsory for all new electric vehicles produced in Ireland between 2010 and 2012. The current fleet of vehicles will be fitted with these new devices as part of the new “energy-efficient vehicle” regulations introduced by the European Commission in January, which will see most new vehicles sold in Ireland powered by 100% clean electricity.

The regulations also include the use of zero emissions zones, emission trading, and the development of green-friendly vehicle technologies for the future. These will make it possible to reduce the amount of harmful emissions in vehicles on Irish roads and allow the use of clean diesel and biofuels to be a cheaper alternative to petrol.

“I am absolutely delighted that we have the opportunity to introduce new regulations that will ensure electric vehicles are cleaner for everyone around the world,” said the Minister for the Environment, Community and Local Government, Peter Fitzpatrick.

“These new regulations will also make it much more affordable for everyone to buy an electric vehicle.”

A number of electric vehicle manufacturers have expressed concerns over the introduction of these devices, with some stating that the devices will not stop vehicles going faster than 250km per hour when the devices are switched on, and they will cause a drop in battery life that will put drivers at a risk of an ‘inability to brake’.

A number of the companies have pledged to undertake significant work in the next few years to ensure that the new devices are fitted correctly on all new vehicles in Ireland.

“The introduction of these new devices is part of the government’s commitment to reduce the use of fossil fuels and to make electric vehicles more available to more people,” said Ms Fitzpatrick.

“I welcome this announcement and the commitment of the industry in Ireland to make it a reality.”

The new regulations will come into effect on 01 January 2011, and will ensure that all new vehicles produced in Ireland by 2010 will be fitted with these new devices. This will allow vehicles to travel with little or no impact on their performance, and will make it easier for drivers to maintain a safe distance when needed.
headline: Electric vehicles to be fitted with noise emitting devices from today onwards

As part of the Government’s austerity measures, it will also be giving some fuel allowance payments to households from today, according to an Irish Independent report.

Minister for the Environment, Simon Coveney confirmed that the new measure would be applied to household bills paid over the next four months, in order to reduce the deficit.

“The new fuel allowance will be for a month and is paid on a weekly basis,” he said. “We are giving households that have been paying for fuel over a long period of time now the payment is there and for a very short period.”

“We are paying some of these over the next four months and the fuel allowance is there for those that need it.

“The main aim for those who need it, the main aim is to see people get into work.”

In a speech to the European Parliament on Thursday Coveney said that he was confident that the new measures would help to “make a significant contribution to the reduction of the deficit and to our economy”.

“I am certain that these new measures will have a significant impact on jobs and the economy in Ireland and the Government is working very hard to meet that objective,” he said.

The fuel allowance, worth €130 a week, was introduced under the Budget in July of this year.

A report published by the Department of Social Protection said that the allowance would apply to fuel costs incurred on an average week in September and December.

The report estimated that an average household would incur a total of €857 a week in the four months covered by the new measure, and an average household would receive €4,856. The Government’s estimate was based on an estimated population of around 150,000, and a household size of four members, of which the majority would be women.

“I am very confident in the new measures,” he said. “I think they are the right thing.”

The new measures are being introduced by the Fine Gael-led Government to support the deficit reduction plans of Taoiseach Leo Varadkar, including the tax concessions.

He said the measures would not be detrimental to the budget deficit.

“We are making sure that we are getting the best possible deal for all of us in the end and if it’s right and if it is the right thing to do, I am very confident that it will make a significant contribution to the reduction of the deficit and to our economy,” he said.

Fianna Fáil has previously criticised the Government over the new fuel allowance, claiming that it will exacerbate the deficit.

However the Finance Minister has rejected the criticisms, saying that the allowance is not designed to reduce the deficit but rather to reduce the cost of living.

“These are measures that are not designed to reduce the budget deficit,” he said. “These are measures that are designed to make a significant contribution to the reduction of the deficit and to our economy.

“I am very confident that these new measures will make a significant contribution to this.”

He added that the measures are a step towards a balanced budget and the Government is working to achieve that objective.

The Gardaí of the North County Dublin regional garda station are to cancel the use of a Covid-19 RT-Line in Donegal after 60% of calls were found not to be breaches of the country’s covid-19 laws.

The move has been made on the basis that the Gardaí are the guardians of the law and must act as “first line” to detect and prosecute breaches of the Covid-19 legislation.

The decision was made after an audit into the use of the RT-Line by the Gardaí was launched last year which found that the system was in “operational disarray”.

The RT-Line has a camera system on its system of lines that allow it to automatically record all calls made on the line. This system has been used to record a number of calls which the Gardaí say are of “no significant concern”, despite the fact that the RT-Line has been used to record an increasing number of calls by callers who do not even have a proper telephone number.

This morning, the head of the Gardaí said that the RT-Line was being used to record a disproportionate number of calls that did not have a valid telephone number and was therefore a waste of the RT-Line system.

This is in line with the Government’s guidance that RT-Lines should only be used for emergency purposes.

The head of the Gardaí said that the decision to cancel the RT-Line was taken after receiving a “request from the Public Accounts Office (PAO) to review the use of the RT-Line for the purpose of recording a disproportionate number of calls from individuals who do not have a telephone number”.

He said: “The RT-Line is being used for its primary role which is to record and monitor calls in an emergency, but unfortunately this use of the RT-Line has been inoperational and in disarray in recent months, resulting in significant call costs being incurred.

“The decision has been taken after considering the position of the RT-Line and the request made by the Public Accounts Office.

“We will therefore cancel the use of the RT-Line in the future.”

The Gardaí of the North County Dublin regional station were asked to examine the use of the RT-Line by calls made to the station by citizens who do not have a telephone number.

The audit found that it was not clear that the RT-Line was capable of recording and monitoring calls from citizens who do not have a telephone number.

The RT-Line has a camera system on its line that allows it automatically to record the call which is captured by the system and sends the video to the system. This system has been used to record a number of calls that the Gardaí say are of “no significant concern”.

This is in line with the Government’s guidance that RT-Lines should only be used for emergency purposes.

Posted:

17 February 2020

CHINA’S central government has stepped up efforts to prevent the spread of Covid-19, following the first major public health incident of the outbreak. Beijing has imposed restrictions on public transportation, including taxis, buses and other means of transportation within the city. The government announced that the city will implement a series of new measures. The government said:

“In order to ensure that all passengers are able to board and leave freely and safely, there are restrictions on the number of passengers. The passenger can only take public transportation for one round trip. The passenger may not take buses, taxis and private vehicles for one round trip. The passenger should not go to a hotel or a restaurant which is located in a city where there is a large amount of people, or where the number of people in a specific room is too large.”

The restrictions were imposed in response to a report from the People’s Daily newspaper stating that a group of more than 30 people had infected with the virus, and that several other people had recovered.

Beijing has reported more than 200 coronavirus cases, and has banned visits to its main airport, China National Space and Space Agency, as well as other areas of the city for the next 24 hours.

The first case was in Guangzhou, in southern China. The city reported four new cases in early February. The city’s health authority announced a temporary ban on all non-essential travel in the city.

China will be the world’s second biggest country by number of cases. The world’s eighth biggest country by number of deaths, the death toll in China stands at 1,743.

According to official statistics, 595 people have died from the coronavirus since the outbreak began in December.

In the meantime, a man named Zhang Jie, the chief officer of a small transport firm, said that his company had received a phone call from a city official on behalf of the government saying that if the company doesn’t stop its efforts to transport goods from Wuhan, the capital of Hubei province, to the southern city of Guangzhou, the city will shut down its operations.

The company said it was “not interested in this matter at all.”

The company said that the Chinese government had called it and asked it to stop its work.

“We were not allowed to go to the city or to transport any goods because we didn’t have a permit to be in the city,” Zhang told The Associated Press.

“So, we did not dare to work. And I was very worried,” said Zhang.

“All my customers were afraid,” he added. “It was a big challenge for the company.”

On Tuesday, a Beijing official said that the city has been “overwhelmed” by the number of coronavirus cases. The official, Wang Zhen, said the city had reported a total of 199 cases in two and a half weeks. The official added that China’s number of cases was much higher than that of the U.S.

Headline: Stop the clock on TikTok ban – US ban will go ahead tomorrow

Article By:

The US Department of Commerce and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) are set to take action today (Monday 2 September) against TikTok, the popular photo sharing app that has been the subject of a global investigation and threat from its US parent company, Y Combinator.

The FTC investigation alleges TikTok violated copyright and trademark laws by using footage and images of copyrighted works without permission, while violating the privacy rights of its users.

The FTC also accuses TikTok of engaging in deceptive conduct and unfair competition in its dealings with users of the service.

A group of prominent internet experts, including former Federal Trade Commission Chairman Joe Simons, is reportedly preparing to launch a class action lawsuit against TikTok today, which will seek to recover millions of dollars in damages.

The DOJ, meanwhile, is expected to announce today that it is bringing an investigation into the service, seeking to determine whether TikTok is in fact a platform.

As part of its investigation, the FTC is also set to take action against Y Combinator, which has received $5 billion from investors and has a vested interest in the outcome of the TikTok investigation.

While the US government's case against TikTok is expected to be the most significant case involving a major online platform in recent years, the company has previously been the subject of two high-profile investigations from the US Department of Justice, in 2011 and 2016, with both targeting its business model and use of copyright laws.

The DOJ has made clear that it will seek to prosecute companies whose conduct it considers detrimental to society and whose business models are questionable.

"We are not concerned with the legality of the business models of companies that seek to profit from infringement. We are concerned with whether or not the businesses are in fact making a meaningful contribution to society and, in particular, whether they are making a contribution to the cause of promoting free expression and innovation," said US Attorney Channing D. Phillips in a statement.

The Department of Justice has been aggressively pursuing companies that it perceives are engaged in infringing on copyright and are operating in a way that is harmful to society.

It has also brought legal action against platforms that offer users a variety of platforms to circumvent copyright. In January 2016, the Department of Justice filed a civil action against Snapchat, alleging that the company's business model was responsible for infringing copyright.

TikTok has denied the allegations, pointing out that it makes its money from advertising and user generated content. The company maintains that it is not actively engaged in infringement and that it is an "independent business" that has not violated any copyright laws.

TikTok was founded by Andrew Y. W. Chang, a Harvard University grad and Y Combinator member, and has amassed a vast collection of user videos in an effort to create the largest and most comprehensive collection of photo and video content available on the internet.

A Garda helicopter has been called out to confiscate an illegal TV set top box and several other items as part of a €10,000 reward being offered for information leading to an arrest and conviction.

The aircraft was part of a massive raid conducted last Thursday in the centre of Co Kerry.

The operation was conducted in conjunction with the Garda Criminal Investigation Command (GCCI) and involved a number of searches and seizures which have since been referred to the Criminal Assets Bureau for prosecution.

In particular, a number of the items seized from the premises in Dublin were allegedly involved in illegal set top boxes.

Gardai seized two portable storage units, a portable telephone and mobile phones, a laptop, a mobile radio and an external hard drive which is thought to be the equivalent of approximately 4,500 DVDs.

The operation is ongoing and the equipment seized has now been handed over to the Criminal Assets Bureau for further investigation.

This is not the first time Gardai have been called out to tackle the illegal use of TV set top boxes in the Republic. In December this year they launched Operation Mango which was targeting illegal TV box units in the city.

This was the largest operation carried out by the Garda in terms of the number of items seized and the number of people involved. In total more than 50 sets of illegal TV boxes were seized. The Operation Mango raid netted over €600,000 in cash and €120,000 in computer equipment.

Anyone with information about illegal set top boxes should contact the Garda National Bureau for Criminal Activity (GNBKA).

The operation is a joint operation between the GNBKA and the Garda Operations Group.

The GNBKA has been in existence for over 60 years and has been responsible for many successful operations including Operation Banner, Operation Uplink and Operation Suez.

Operation Mango was launched in December, 2016, at the behest of the Government, after a lengthy enquiry into the illegal use of illegal set top boxes in the Republic of Ireland.

The operation was launched at the request of the Department of Foreign Affairs.

In 2017, a total of 1,091 illegal set top boxes were seized in the Republic.

During the course of the operation 597 sets of illegal TV boxes were recovered from addresses in the Republic of Ireland.

In total more than €6 million was recovered from addresses in the Republic.

The operation was launched with a view to shutting down the illicit market for set top boxes.

In 2015, the Irish Press was the first media outlet to expose a criminal organisation in the Republic.

The criminal gang responsible for operating illegal set top boxes in the Republic of Ireland operated from a small, but thriving operation in Dublin.

The gang was formed by a group of Irish citizens from Dublin who set up their own illegal set top box business in Dublin.

The gang targeted the Irish market by illegally setting up shop in Ireland’s largest Irish language television set top box manufacturer and by illegally setting up shop in the Republic of Ireland.

The gang was responsible for sending at least three Irish citizens to prison in the Republic of Ireland.

The gang took delivery of a shipment of illegal set top boxes from a supplier in China and then resold them on a black market in the Republic of Ireland.

Ireland is in the grips of a prison crisis that has led to the jailing of at least a dozen prisoners, a sharp fall in prisoner numbers and a rise in the use of drugs to break the rules.

The report by the Prison Reform Trust (PRT) on the prison system in Ireland concludes that overcrowding is the major cause of the dramatic rise in prisoners.

According to the PRT report, nearly 40% of inmates in Irish prisons are held in “maximum” security. That figure has dropped significantly since 2010 and is now just 17% of all prisoners.

The report, published today, also found that overcrowding is a major issue in Irish prisons, where prisoners are being held in “very” and “max” levels of security.

The report states that prisoners are now being held in “max” security for “a third longer” than they were in 2010, while the average number of inmates per holding cell is down by 14.6% to almost 14.4.

“Prisoners are being held in a range of security levels across the country. This is despite the fact that almost 100% of inmates are held in ‘maximum security’ in prisons. It is not only an increase in the number of prisoners but a significant increase in the length of time they are held and the number of cells,” said the report.

“The PRT recommends that the authorities consider the need for the maximum security of prisoners and the number of cells they are housed in when planning and designing prisons.”

The report also recommends that the system be reviewed so that, in the future, prisoners in “maximum security” can be accommodated in “max” security.

“As well as reducing the overall length of time prisoners spend in prison and the number of cells they are housed in, the PRT recommends that the prison system be reviewed so that prisoners can be accommodated in ‘max’ security. This may be achieved through an increase in the level of security of prisons and a reduction in the number of cells,” the report states.

“This may lead to prisoners being accommodated in ‘max’ security where they may be allowed a longer period of time in security. This would not only reduce the overall amount of time prisoners spend in prison but also reduce the time they spend in prison in the ‘max’ security, which would in turn reduce overcrowding.”

The PRT’s report says that overcrowding is an issue in all prisons, but it has become a “dominant” issue in Irish prisons.

“The PRT report finds that overcrowding has become a major issue in the Irish prison system. This is because it is a major cause of the dramatic rise in the use of drugs to break the rules and for inmates to break their own rules,” said the report.

“In general, the increase in the number of inmates has been attributed to prisoners being overcrowded and therefore, there is an increase in the use of drugs. The rise in use of drugs has led to an increase in the length of time inmates spend in prison and the number of cells they are housed in.”
headline: Overcrowding is now a major issue is Irish prisons, report finds

“For us to go to court now, we have to prove to the court we did not do anything wrong,” the Taoiseach said this morning. “We had no reason to think that this case would come to court. There is no other way to bring the case to a conclusion.”

The Taoiseach was speaking on the day a High Court judge granted a temporary injunction blocking a legal case being brought by former Fine Gael Senator and party Vice-Chairman John Collins against TDs’ leader Jack Flanagan. In a ruling that could have a significant impact on the party and a number of legislators’ pensions, the court was told that Flanagan was seeking to seize the assets and pension plans of TDs and senators on the grounds they are no longer in office.

The ruling by the Judge, Mr Justice Mark Walker, came after it was argued in court that the constitutional prohibition on former TDs and senators seizing the assets of members of their parties on the basis that they are no longer in office, applies to the constitution of the party itself.

At the end of the hearing, the judge was told that Flanagan was seeking to seize assets that are in the possession of the members of the party, both in the State and the UK. In particular, Mr Justice Mark Walker noted that this is a concern in a situation where a former senator and party Vice-Chairman has accused the leader of the party, and in a case where the alleged culprit is the vice-chairman of the party.

In a written judgment, Mr Justice Mark Walker, who is currently the judge in the case, ruled that the prohibition on former TDs and senators seizing the assets of their party members applies to the party itself.

In his judgment, Mr Justice Mark Walker found that if the injunction is granted, it will “cause reputational damage to the Fine Gael party and its members”, and said it would be “irrelevant for this case to determine the question whether the former members of the party are entitled to assets and pension rights that belong to the parties themselves.”

In an interview today, the former Taoiseach said he was “disappointed” with the ruling, but pointed out that “this was not a court of law. It is a court of equity”.

The Taoiseach said: “I am disappointed by the decision. I am not surprised. In the court of law we have to prove to the court we did not do anything wrong. We have to prove to the court we did not do anything that the law would prevent.”

He said there are three elements that he wants to be able to demonstrate. “One is there is no evidence that the assets have been stolen,” he said.

“The second is that there is no evidence that there has been any breach of trust that the assets of the former members of the party have been seized or misused. The third is there is no evidence that this case will affect the relationship between the State and the party itself.”

Speaking to the media outside the Court House last night, Mr Flanagan said he “can’t understand” why a judge was taking the issue into her own hands.

In light of the footage of the mob violence that was carried out in Courtown and other parts of Wexford, the Irish Examiner wishes to highlight the following:

A video emerged in late August showing a mob violence being carried out at a number of locations in the county of Wexford where several foreign men were living. As many as 17 men were involved in the violence in Courtown town, while in Co Donegal more men joined the violence in various locations and in Co Armagh more people joined in. The violence took place at locations such as a pub, a hotel and a pub car park, as well as a pub car park in Co Down. This is not the first time that foreign men in the country have been involved in incidents of violence. In 2015, an incident of domestic violence was reported by a female victim at a hotel.

Despite attempts to contact the individuals involved in the incidents, there has been no response from them in relation to the violence they have been part of. Wexford County Council, in collaboration with the police and local authorities in the county, are seeking the views of concerned parties in relation to the incident in which foreigners are involved in an alleged assault.

“We are in the process of trying to establish who these individuals are,” said a spokesperson from the Council. “The Council is also seeking to ascertain whether they are in the country legally, but at present they cannot comment further.

“We know of an individual who resides in Wexford who is facing deportation at this stage. They have been involved in a number of incidents of violence recently. The Council continues to appeal to anyone with information in relation to the incident to contact it, in accordance with the law.”

In the aftermath of the recent violent incident, the Council has issued a number of statements, including one from the spokesperson.

“We have issued a statement to all relevant authorities, including the Gardaí, following the recent incident,” said the spokesperson. “A short statement is below. It reflects our position and that of the council.”

“The recent violence has raised further concerns,” the spokesperson continues. “It is in this regard that we have issued a statement to all relevant authorities. It was made as a direct appeal to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General on behalf of the Council and the people concerned, in which we have reiterated our call for them to cease and desist from any further violence.”

“It was only in the aftermath of this incident that the Council could ascertain the identity of the individuals involved,” the spokesperson added.

“The Council has also been contacted by the State and there are several reasons why, as well as the risk of further violence, we are unable to comment further. However, we are appealing to anyone with information or concerns about the incident in question, or anyone with information of any kind relating to the incident in question to contact us directly.”

“The Council is appealing for the welfare of all involved to be safeguarded and, in the process, we are seeking to ensure that those involved in the incident are apprehended and brought before the courts for their trial,” the spokesperson continued.

DUP Minister and SDLP TD Michael Martin called the government’s move to ease restrictions on the Republic of Ireland’s borders, “sickeningly irresponsible” and said he is increasingly concerned.

“I don’t care what the Government says or what they do. I think that they are acting in an irresponsible manner,” he added.

The airline has advised customers travelling to the airport to “be aware” of the weather conditions, and to “consider alternative routes in case of bad weather”.

The airport tweeted the following message:

“We are advising people traveling to the airport to be aware of adverse weather conditions and to consider alternative routes in case of bad weather.

– Check for flights via www.air.ie, the airline’s website.

– Ask the airlines, airports and other operators what is expected and when to expect bad weather.

– Be aware of road closures and traffic queues and consider alternative routes in the event of bad weather.
