Irish Council of State withdraws €9.6m accommodation for Ukrainians in hotels and apartments across the Republic

By The Liberal:

The Irish Council of State has pulled all of the accommodation it is providing to Ukrainians in hotels and apartments across the Republic as part of a drive to reduce the number of Ukrainians that come to Ireland to avoid being sent back to Ukraine.

The Irish Council of State (ICOS), which runs Irish universities and colleges, will cease to provide accommodation at least on the weekends as part of a drive to cut the number of Ukrainians coming to Ireland to evade the cost of travelling to Ukraine.

“From 1 July, we are going to cease all accommodation and services and take our annual budget away from those who are not Ukrainian citizens,” said ICOS CEO Professor John Hartigan.

“We are taking money away from them so they can look for a job, find a place to live, or do other things.”

Mr Hartigan added that the decision to pull the accommodation was based on a report by the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) which said Ukraine should do more to protect its citizens from forced relocations.

“This is a new report from OCHA which has found that there is an unprecedented number of Ukrainians living in Europe and that a majority are in Ukraine.

“This is concerning given that there have been very few reports of forced relocations of Ukrainian citizens in Europe. This is worrying,” he said.

“The United Nations’ Human Rights Council has found that, under Ukraine’s current law, forced relocations can amount to torture. We have the same law in the United Kingdom and I have been in contact with the British Council.

“We are going to get our money back, we are not going to be taking people’s homes, and the EU is also saying it is putting pressure on Ukraine to protect citizens from relocations, but the Ukrainian side has said they are going to comply with their obligations,” he added.

Ukraine and other countries have been accused of taking money from citizens of those countries to force them to relocate and put pressure on the Ukrainian government to stop forced relocations.

Mr Hartigan said this is not the first time that the ICOS has decided to withdraw accommodation, but they have not always been able to find a better solution for the migrants.

“The ICOS has got a lot of money in the past from the EU which has always gone into this.

“We are not withdrawing our money. We are pulling it, but we are not taking their money,” he added.

“If we can’t find a better solution, then we have to give them that money back.”

Mr Hartigan said he did not want to see a return to the past where people could leave the EU and go back to a country they had no interest in.

The Irish government has previously said it would not pay to get Ukrainians out of their country.

Mr Hartigan said he will continue to work with the OCHA to find new solutions for the Ukrainian population.

A British fashion retailer has today announced it is taking over its Irish parent company LK Bennett. The announcement was made on a statement which read:

“We are extremely pleased to have reached this moment in our lives. After careful consideration, it has been concluded that a change of management is the best course of action for all parties involved.

The LK Bennett website has been taken down and the company is yet to respond to the statement.

“We are a family business that has been in business for nearly 100 years and are well known for our signature men’s clothing in Ireland. We are a proud part of the Irish cultural fabric and are delighted to have reached this exciting phase of our life.

“We want to thank all our employees, customers and anyone else who has supported us along the way.”

‘The Taoiseach believes that the country will see real change in Government in the next six months and is committed to working with the other parties in the Government to do that’.

That was the Taoiseach’s official response when asked what would happen if Fine Gael were to lose the next General Election and the Government was forced into a coalition.

But now Leo Varadkar says, while the election is a ‘tough fight’, that ‘the other parties are committed’.

He said ‘I don’t think that I want to be part of a coalition, so I am committed to working with the other parties to change Government’.

He added, ‘I believe that we will see real change in Government in the next six months and that the other parties are committed to working together and to trying to bring about that change’.

‘I am committed to seeing that we continue to reform our society and that we continue to work together to change and build and improve on the Irish economy in a way that will allow us to live in a modern, open society and in a way that the people of Ireland will be proud of’.

Varadkar has been at the forefront of the so-called ‘sunny ways’ campaign – promoting the idea of ‘more sunshine’ on the island and the Government’s commitment to the ‘green economy’.

But the Taoiseach’s comments yesterday, while not surprising, are worrying.

The other parties are committed to working together and trying to bring about that change, as the Taoiseach said.

However, the Taoiseach has not yet stated what the ‘other parties’ will be doing and the way they will do it.

It seems to me that the Taoiseach will not be able to ‘reform’ Government if Fine Gael is ‘gone’, and therefore we must assume the other parties have agreed to act in unison and as a government coalition.

The Taoiseach is right to say that the election is a ‘tough fight’, and indeed a fight for the future of the country, but he must still explain what the parties are doing, what their plans are, and whether or not the other parties are ‘committed’.

I wonder if he will also point out that he is ‘committed’ to the ‘green economy’, and that he is determined to continue to reform our society in a way that will lead to a modern, open society and in a way that the people of Ireland will be proud of.

I am concerned by the Taoiseach’s comments and I expect that he will not want to be in the position where he has to ‘tell the other parties how they are going to do things’ if Fine Gael is ‘gone’.

The Taoiseach could have said that the other parties ‘are committed to working together’.

I am sure that the Taoiseach will explain that ‘the other parties are committed’.
headline: Outgoing Taoiseach Leo Varadkar torpedoes Micheal Martin’s fever dreams of a grand coalition by saying that Fine Gael is headed for opposition

A trio of representatives of the Government will meet today to decide whether or not the Irish public get locked down again for another 6 weeks.

This news article by Paul Cullen and the Irish Examiner and Sunday Life on July 12th, 2012 explains that, according to a Government source:

The Taoiseach’s decision on the lock-down date was prompted by an outcry from the Irish people.

A decision was taken to lock the country in until the middle of September. In the event of a new government being formed on July 22nd, a new lock-down date would be set for the 22nd as a result of the new government not knowing whether it would have a majority or if it was going to have a coalition government.

An additional lock-down date would be set for the 1st of September if the new government does not have a majority.

The Government source also said that the Government would be consulting with the EU for a short time about the lock-down date, but insisted that the lock-down date will not be changed, as it was not the Taoiseach’s decision.

It has also been suggested that the lock-down is an attempt by the Government to reduce the numbers of people who may be locked in, by using the time between the lock-down date and the new government’s election, to avoid the possibility of a second election in the current Parliament and thus forcing a delay.

The source also stated:

The lock-down was imposed as a result of the Government’s decision to postpone the implementation of the economic package they had been negotiating with the European Commission. The Taoiseach explained that the Commission would only be given time to make changes to its proposals if they met with a majority.

This will be the first time that the Government’s new Taoiseach and his ministerial team will meet. The Taoiseach has already stated that the government is open to the possibility of changing the date again if the lock-down was found to be necessary.

The Government source also said that the Government and the European Commission will be meeting again with their new EU Commissioner next week to discuss what the EU will be looking at with regards to the Irish public.

The Irish Government is considering a “double” payment to help the economy cope with rising cost of living.

Under the plans, which have been discussed for months and rejected by the Department of Health, the cost of living allowance will be raised by a single month.

The decision is likely to anger most people, with many saying the government’s proposed measures are an attempt to make people pay more for necessities.

A spokesman for the Department of Health said the government’s proposals were aimed at addressing the problems that are causing higher prices and higher costs of living.

He said: “The government is looking at ways to balance the rising costs of living with the ability of people to buy necessities, and ensure people do not feel they are being punished for doing so.

“The government is looking at ways to ensure it is the correct taxpayer that pays for the rising costs of living and the rising cost of living, not people who are not properly being paid for their work.

The cost of living allowance, which is currently paid by everyone in receipt of a social security or pension, has been at an all-time high since 2004.

The allowance is paid for almost all activities including heating, electricity, water, gas, telecoms, schools and transport.

Title: The lasting relevance of Confucius

In a world where chaos and uncertainty seem to reign supreme, the teachings of Confucius continue to hold immense relevance. The ancient Chinese philosopher's wisdom has endured for millennia, offering insights into how individuals and societies can live in harmony with one another and with the natural world.

Born in the 6th century BC, Confucius was a teacher, statesman, and philosopher who is known for his teachings on ethics, morality, and governance. His ideas emphasize the importance of personal and governmental morality, correctness of social relationships, justice, and sincerity. These principles have been passed down through generations, influencing Chinese culture, philosophy, and politics.

Today, Confucius' teachings are more relevant than ever, as the world grapples with issues such as political polarization, social inequality, and environmental degradation. His emphasis on the importance of personal responsibility, empathy, and compassion can help individuals navigate these challenges and find a path towards a more harmonious and sustainable future.

One of Confucius' most famous sayings, "Do not do to others what you would not have them do to you," is a timeless reminder of the importance of treating others with respect and empathy. This principle can be applied to countless situations, from interpersonal relationships to global politics, and serves as a powerful reminder of the need to prioritize the well-being of others.

Another key aspect of Confucian philosophy is the concept of "ren," which can be translated as "benevolence," "humanity," or "kindness." This refers to the practice of acting with compassion and empathy towards others, and is seen as a central component of a moral and ethical society.

In a world that is increasingly focused on individualism and self-interest, Confucius' teachings on the importance of community and collective well-being offer a valuable corrective. His emphasis on the need for individuals to work together towards common goals, and to prioritize the needs of the many over the interests of the few, is more relevant than ever in today's polarized and divided world.

In conclusion, the teachings of Confucius continue to hold immense relevance in the modern world. His emphasis on personal responsibility, empathy, and compassion, as well as his emphasis on the importance of community and collective well-being, offer a powerful antidote to the challenges we face today. By embracing these principles, we can work towards a more harmonious and sustainable future for all.
headline: The lasting relevance of Confucius

Study: Economic fears of ageing societies overblown

A new study has challenged the long-held belief that ageing populations will lead to economic doom and gloom, suggesting that the fears surrounding demographic change are largely overblown.

The research, conducted by the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) and published in the Journal of Economic Psychology, found that while there are certainly challenges associated with an ageing population, the economic impact is not as dire as previously thought.

According to the study, the most significant economic impact of an ageing population is a decline in the workforce, which can lead to a decrease in overall economic output. However, the researchers found that this effect can be mitigated through the introduction of policies that support older workers and promote their continued participation in the workforce.

The study also highlighted the potential benefits of an ageing population, including increased consumer spending and a more diverse workforce.

"While there are certainly challenges associated with an ageing population, our research suggests that the economic fears surrounding this demographic shift are largely overblown," said Dr. Brian Lucey, lead author of the study. "With the right policies in place, an ageing population can actually have positive economic impacts."

The study's findings are significant, particularly in light of the ongoing debate around the country's ageing population and how to address the challenges it presents. As Ireland's population continues to age, policymakers will need to consider the implications of this trend and develop strategies to support an ageing workforce.

The researchers used a combination of statistical models and survey data to reach their conclusions, and the study has been praised for its thorough and nuanced examination of the economic impact of an ageing population.

In a statement, the ESRI said that the study "challenges many of the common assumptions about the economic impact of an ageing population and highlights the need for a more nuanced understanding of this complex issue."

The study's findings are likely to be of interest to policymakers, business leaders, and other stakeholders as they seek to navigate the challenges of an ageing population.

In a time of economic uncertainty, where the looming threat of recession hangs heavy over the nation, it may seem counterintuitive to suggest that these are the best of times for the creative. However, such is the nature of the human spirit – where adversity breeds innovation, and challenge spurs ingenuity.

In Ireland, the arts sector has always been a shining example of this resilience. From the folk music of the Irish diaspora to the avant-garde works of contemporary artists, our cultural heritage is rooted in the ability to find beauty in the darkness. And as the country navigates these turbulent economic waters, the creative community is proving to be a beacon of hope.

Take the case of Aine Ní Laoghaire, a visual artist from Cork who has just completed a residency at the prestigious European Ceramic Work Centre in the Netherlands. Despite the challenges of funding her own artistic practice, Ní Laoghaire has managed to carve out a successful career, thanks to a combination of hard work, determination, and the support of local arts organisations.

"The worst of times can be the best of times for creatives," she says. "When resources are scarce, we are forced to be more resourceful. We have to think outside the box and find new ways to make our work visible. That can lead to some amazing collaborations and innovations."

Ní Laoghaire's experience is backed up by the findings of a recent survey conducted by the Arts Council, which found that the majority of artists in Ireland are reporting increased levels of collaboration and experimentation in their work.

"Artists are often seen as being outside the mainstream, but in times of economic uncertainty, they can become the vanguard of innovation," says Gráinne Cunningham, Director of the Arts Council. "The arts have always been a source of inspiration and comfort in times of hardship, and this is no exception."

Of course, the challenges facing the creative community are not to be underestimated. Many artists are struggling to make ends meet, with many reporting a decline in funding and support. But as the saying goes, " necessity is the mother of invention." And for those who are able to adapt and innovate, the worst of times can also be the best of times.

As Ní Laoghaire puts it, "In times of uncertainty, the arts can be a lifeline. They offer a way to process and make sense of the world around us. And they can also provide a sense of hope and resilience, a reminder that even in the darkest of times, there is always a way forward."

So while the economic outlook may be uncertain, one thing is clear: the creative community in Ireland will continue to thrive, adapt, and innovate, no matter what challenges come their way.

According to sources within the European Commission, the proposed vaccine passports would allow individuals who have received both doses of a COVID-19 vaccine to travel freely within the EU without the need for quarantine or testing. The passports would be valid for a specific period of time, such as six months, and would be subject to regular review and update.

"We understand that the pandemic has had a devastating impact on the travel industry, and we want to do everything we can to help it recover," said a spokesperson for the European Commission. "By introducing vaccine passports, we hope to give people the confidence to travel and to support the tourism industry, which is such a vital part of our economy."

The proposal is expected to be put to the EU's Transport, Telecommunications and Energy Council next week, where it will be discussed and potentially adopted. If successful, the vaccine passports could be implemented as early as next month, in time for the summer travel season.

However, the proposal has faced criticism from some quarters, with concerns raised about the potential for fraud and the impact on individuals who have not yet received a COVID-19 vaccine.

"While we understand the desire to support the travel industry, we cannot risk the health and safety of EU citizens," said a spokesperson for the Greens/EFA group in the European Parliament. "We need to ensure that any system of vaccine passports is rigorous, transparent, and based on the best available scientific evidence."

The proposal is the latest in a series of measures aimed at boosting the EU's response to the pandemic. Earlier this month, the EU agreed to introduce a harmonised approach to COVID-19 testing and contact tracing, and to establish a network of specialised COVID-19 treatment centres across the bloc.

The news has been welcomed by travel industry leaders, who say that the introduction of vaccine passports could help to restore confidence in air travel and to support the recovery of the tourism sector.

He believed that the quest for progress and improvement could often lead to a neglect of the values and traditions that make us who we are. As he put it in his book "The Everlasting Man," "The whole modern world has shifted its axis and is rolling towards a new goal, and that goal is the destruction of the human race."

He believed that the preservation of our cultural heritage was essential to maintaining our identity and our sense of purpose. As he wrote in "The Superstition of Divorce," "The world is not a place, but a moment; and we are not a people, but a procession."

His emphasis on the importance of tradition and cultural heritage serves as a reminder that our identity is not solely defined by the technologies we use or the political systems we live under. Rather, it is the sum of our shared experiences, beliefs, and values – the things that make us who we are as a people.

Of course, Chesterton was not a one-dimensional thinker, and his views on progress and tradition were not without nuance. He recognized that change was a natural and necessary part of human society, and he believed that we must be open to new ideas and perspectives. However, he also believed that this openness must be balanced with a commitment to our cultural heritage – a heritage that he saw as essential to our well-being and our survival as a species.

In the end, Chesterton's ideas offer us a path forward that is both forward-thinking and rooted in the past. They remind us that while progress is important, it must never come at the expense of our cultural heritage. The Irish government has been working closely with its EU partners to address the issue of illegal immigration, including through the implementation of the Common European Asylum System (CEAS). As the EU continues to grapple with the challenge of illegal immigration, it is clear that the issue will remain a major focus of attention in the years ahead. The IHREC found in favour of the State, citing several reasons why a "Right to Housing" would be problematic. Firstly, the Commission noted that the provision of housing is a complex issue that involves a range of factors, including the availability of housing stock, the cost of housing, and the ability of local authorities to provide adequate housing. The IHREC argued that it would be unrealistic to place a blanket "Right to Housing" on the state, as this would not take into account the varying circumstances and needs of different individuals and communities.

Furthermore, the IHREC highlighted the potential impact on the State's ability to manage its housing needs. The Commission noted that granting a "Right to Housing" would create a significant burden on the State, as it would be required to provide housing for all individuals who claimed a right to it, regardless of their individual circumstances. This could lead to a situation where the State is unable to provide adequate housing for those who are most in need, such as the homeless and vulnerable populations.

The IHREC also expressed concerns about the potential impact on the rights of other individuals and groups. The Commission noted that granting a "Right to Housing" could lead to conflicts with the rights of other individuals and groups, such as the right to privacy and the right to property. The IHREC argued that a "Right to Housing" could result in a situation where individuals are forced to share housing with others against their will, or where the State is required to provide housing for individuals who are not in need of it.

In conclusion, the IHREC case highlights the potential consequences of granting a "Right to Housing" in Ireland. While the provision of adequate housing is an important human right, the Commission argues that granting a blanket "Right to Housing" would be unrealistic and could result in significant burdens on the State, conflicts with the rights of other individuals and groups, and a failure to address the complex needs of different individuals and communities. As such, the IHREC recommends that any efforts to address the issue of housing in Ireland should prioritize a comprehensive and sustainable approach that takes into account the diverse needs and circumstances of all individuals and communities.

Belfast News reports that the father of one of the babies in the children's home, who is now being taken in by the State, has spoken out about her experience.

According to The Guardian, the father of two young children was in an abusive relationship and the mother of one of them was in her final year of secondary school when he took her to a house of woe in Galway city.

She left, and when the mother tried to get her back she was told she would not be allowed back.

After a few months she said she was told that she could come back after three months, but that she had to leave again.

This time she was offered a place at the home for a month. She declined, believing it to be a temporary arrangement.

After five months she was offered a position.

She said:

"I couldn't believe it. I didn't know what to think. I'm a single mum, single mother, not a broken home. I didn't know what to do. I thought they would be nice to me.

"The last time I came in here, it was not nice. It was a bit like the horror film. There were the bed bugs, the flies and the rats. The smell was awful. There were the bed bugs, the flies and the rats.

"They were making people go through it. They had no consideration whatsoever. They didn't tell me anything. I was just brought here to be there. I was brought here with nothing.

"You never know what could have happened to me or what was being done."

She said that the children had been taken from her to live with a man because he was going to marry someone.

She said:

"When I got there, they were taking the children from me because he was going to marry someone, and I was too young to be a virgin.

"I had no idea, I was too young, I wasn't old enough. I was not old enough to have sex with anyone.

"They were really rough. They didn't give a fuck about me. I was really shocked by that.

"After a month I went back to look for my children, and I was given a different room than what I had been given. I felt extremely sad. I was really upset.

"That same week, I was called and told that I was being moved to a different part of the home. I was supposed to be staying here for a month and that was the end.

"They did not tell me I was being moved. I think they had the right to say that because it was happening to my children, and it was happening to me.

"I feel as if I have more chance of winning the lottery than being living here because I know what they are doing to those kids.

"I feel very sorry for them, but also very sad about what happened."

The Dublin woman said she had tried to appeal the decision, but her appeal was refused. She said that in the end it was the children who were brought in to the home.

January 23, 2012


An animal rescue charity is calling on police to identify a man who allegedly "forced" an injured dog under their fence in Dingle.

A member of the public reported the incident to gardaí, who responded and issued a caution to a man.

Derry city councillor Gerry Buckley said the incident took place in St James's Street, near The Irish Times office and in front of the CVS pharmacy, and was captured on CCTV.

He said the man was seen running towards the area where the dog, which was suffering from injuries from being pushed under their fence, was lying.

"It was only after this happened that the police got there," said Mr Buckley.

"It was one of the first times I saw it," he added.

He said the man had appeared to be in distress.

"I can't explain it," he said.

"I've been here for five years, and I've never seen anything like it. It's very shocking."

The CVS worker, who was not named, said she had been able to help the dog by placing her under the fence.

"I was helping out, putting her under and she was in a lot of pain," said the worker.

She said the man came running out with the dog, which he was holding, and "just pushed the dog under the fence, in the middle of the street."

She said the dog's injuries were serious and that she had taken the injured animal to a vet and was waiting for treatment.

Ms Buckley said the man was described as being in his 20s, of medium build, with a light beard and wearing a grey t-shirt.

A spokeswoman for the DSPCA said they were aware of the incident but had not yet been able to get in contact with the man and could not confirm whether or not he had been arrested.

"We would love to speak to him, but as this is an ongoing investigation we can't confirm that," she added.

Mr Buckley said he had not heard of any previous similar incidents in Dingle.
headline: DSPCA looking to identify man who shoved injured dog under their gates

Taoiseach Enda Kenny has hit out at a High Court decision that ruled that the RTE should not be liable for damages for airing an ad in which a man is asked if he was single and replies "no".

The Taoiseach said the judgement was "a ridiculous ruling" that would have "serious repercussions for all those who have worked for years to gain the respect of the Irish people".

"We would have to change our editorial guidelines. The Irish Examiner is a vital newspaper in Ireland. It is the voice of Ireland and the voice of the Irish people."

Mr Kenny said it was "totally unacceptable" that the "expert" was asked whether he was single, and "had to respond with a negative answer to the simple question of whether or not he is single".

He said the judge had failed to consider that the advert was "sexist" and "sickly" and the words were taken out of context and "sadly" used by the broadcaster in a bid to sell its advertisers.

He said the "sexist and sexist" ad aired on the RTE radio station between 2003 and 2008 and was seen by over three million people across Ireland.

"It was a terrible mistake by the RTE," the Taoiseach said.

"It is a terrible mistake for them and a terrible mistake for all of us as journalists who would have been given that opportunity to ask such a question.

"The people of Ireland need to be proud of the people who put their trust in them. This kind of thing undermines them and we should not allow it."

Mr Kenny said the judges' "totally unfair decision" was "unfortunate, but it cannot be helped".

The ruling against the broadcaster was also criticised by Irish Women's Collective (IWC). It called for the court to hear the case in the full context of the ad and the broadcaster's commitment to diversity.

The IWC said the broadcast had been "a deeply hurtful and sexist situation" that had led to "unnecessary" distress to the man who had been asked the question.

"The decision of the judges, even if they found in the broadcaster's favour, will have consequences for many journalists as well as for the Irish people and, in particular, women and girls.

"The decision will have a damaging impact on the right to freedom of expression in Ireland and across the world."

The RTE ad also featured a woman asking whether she was single and was asked "a simple, intrusive question that does not fit within the standards of the RTE's editorial guidelines".

It was argued that the ad breached the European Convention on Human Rights and the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, which states that "it is an offence to insult or humiliate any individual or group on the ground of their race, religion, colour, sex, sexual orientation, disability or age".

Mr Kenny said the judge had failed to consider that the words in the ad were "taken out of context" and "sadly" used by the broadcaster in an effort to sell its advertisers' advertisements.

He said this was in the "whole context of the ad and the broadcaster's commitment to diversity" and the words had been taken out of context.

Irish Examiner

Wednesday, December 9th, 2002

Ireland's Taoiseach Enda Kenny has urged US firms to expand operations in Ireland.

The Taoiseach, who has visited US firms such as Google and Microsoft in recent weeks, also said that US firms could still do good business in Ireland if they were willing to accept a higher level of regulation and have their taxes paid here.

Mr Kenny visited the US tech giants last week to warn them not to open a new headquarters in Ireland because of the "potentially damaging" impact of increased EU competition rules.

The visit to Microsoft and Google, which both have offices in Dublin, was intended to give Irish companies a signal to open their doors to US firms.

'Not good' for Ireland, Irish Labour leader says

Irish Labour leader Jim Daly, who has been meeting US officials to promote Irish companies, said the visit to Dublin had "not been good" for Ireland.

"It has been all over the place and at one point we're talking about two or three major American companies who are already here but who can't open up because of the EU," Mr Daly said.

"I think it's all a bit of a misjudgement on the part of the Taoiseach.

"He might find that there is no real need for new jobs in Ireland, but I think the Irish people will have to take their own decisions on the issue."

'I'd like to be mayor of Dublin'

Mr Kenny said that in any new EU member state, firms would need to make significant investments in the country's infrastructure, and he would not want to see a number of new skyscrapers going up in the capital.

"I'd like to be mayor of Dublin, that's the ambition of all the people who are coming here," he said.

"It would be a very welcome destination if it was up to me."

Mr Kenny also said there were still "a lot of good things" to be done in the Irish Republic and that he would "continue to work with the Congress of Irish Trade Unions, which I had the good fortune to meet on Monday, to see if we can make it happen".

Mr Kenny has visited the US in recent weeks to warn US firms not to open a new headquarters in Ireland because of the "potentially damaging" impact of EU competition rules.

The US has promised to introduce a new set of rules that will allow it to slap new taxes on foreign businesses that move to Europe.

In his speech Mr Kenny said Irish business should be encouraged to go ahead with plans to set up a European headquarters because of the benefits for Irish business and the wider Irish economy.

"I know many of you have been calling me in the last couple of weeks wanting to know what a new EU headquarters would bring," he said.

"I was very clear yesterday in terms of what that would do for our economy, our services and our international competitiveness.

"It would mean better tax revenue and tax revenue that was used to fund public services - a huge boost to the Irish economy and a boost to the Irish people's finances.

"That is what I said to all of you at the last Congress.

"I said that it would mean a much better relationship for the Irish people and the Irish Government."
headline: Taoiseach urges US firms to expand operations to Ireland

"At the time the helicopter was used, the State had considered that the air ambulance was the only suitable option. It had also been decided that a public inquiry would be held in order to provide a full and open account of the circumstances of the accident", the spokesperson said.

A 21-year-old man from Rathcoole, Co Cork, was at the hospital on Friday evening with abdominal pain after visiting his doctor for treatment for a stomach condition.

He was pronounced dead shortly after arriving at the hospital.

The cause of death is not known.

He was a student studying for a degree in veterinary medicine at St. Patrick's College.

‪A local man, who lives in Clonskeagh, was called to the Clonskeagh Police Station on Friday night.

A man said to be about 20 years old, was arrested and taken to the Clonskeagh Garda station where he was interviewed.

The man told gardaí he went to the hospital to see the doctor about a stomach condition.

He was not informed that he was to die.

He was told to come down to the garda station by police but told gardaí not to bring him to the station.

He was told to stay at the garda station and was taken in a police vehicle to Cork City Hospital.

A short time later gardaí were called to the hospital again and he was again brought to the hospital.

Gardaí have confirmed the man is now dead.
headline: Man sadly passes away in Cork following “medical incident”

A family in Donegal has lost their 2-year-old daughter and their dog after they got caught in the torrential rainfall in Loughrea, Co Down.

According to Donegal Daily Mail, Tracey and Tom Campbell were on a beach holiday in Loughrea last night when it became clear that the tide was too strong to be crossed in a boat.

With little warning, Tom's parents decided to leave their two-year-old daughter, Tracey, and her dog, a Yorkshire Terrier named Gulliver, in the sea.

But when they arrived at the beach, they were swept away to the sea.

The couple, who are from Donegal, went into the water in a small boat and were taken to shore by the coastguard.

They were then taken to the University Hospital Loughrea with injuries that are not life threatening.

A statement from the Department of Social Protection, said the couple had been staying at the beach, known as The Rocks, and were on a family holiday when they got caught in the storm.

"The couple are both under 16 and their parents are on holiday with them," said a statement.

"The couple has lived in the area for several years and has a good relationship with the local community and is known for his love of dogs. The father is from Donegal and is of Irish descent. His girlfriend is from New Zealand and is a new arrival to the area.

"They have been living in the area for over a year. Tracey has an older brother and Tom has an older sister. The father has a wife and a small family."

The couple's mother-in-law, who lives in Co Louth, told the Irish Sun that her husband "has done a great job raising them" and that she has been visiting them "every day".

"He is such a good dad, it's really upsetting, especially when you have children on holiday," she said.

"It is heartbreaking that someone would let this happen to them."

A spokesperson for Defence said: "There are currently a range of different options on the market for body armour. These include the Army's standard issue suit, the Air Force's T2 suit and the Naval Force's N6 suit. The new body armour system being developed by the Defence Forces is the only one that would be available for combat.

"However, in terms of value, this is the most expensive suit that the Government has produced and the Defence Forces have no preference for which one they would like to use."

The DFG is seeking to test the suit against other weapons systems such as the Royal Marines M8A3 Hellfire anti-tank rifle and the new Army's new T2 armour.

The suit is planned to be supplied by a UK company, the company said.

The DFG would like to test its new system against a range of different armour styles, with a view to purchasing several such body armour systems in the future.

A spokesperson said: "The DFG has a long-term strategy for future armour, including the acquisition of more body armour, and this is where the new system would be put to the test to ensure it meets the requirements of the Defence Forces in the future.

"The suit is being developed by Dassault Defence, a company which has the best knowledge and experience of the market. A review of the suit is underway."

An unnamed source in the Department of Defence confirmed the suit was in development. "It's an expensive suit, but it does have a purpose in the Army," the source told The Irish Times.

The source added that the DFG would not make a decision on buying the new body armour system until a few months after the testing was completed.

The DFG is not the first government department to invest in body armour. In 2009 the Government bought the armour kit of US manufacturer Litton for €1.3m.

However, the DFG has said it is unlikely to buy body armour that is not approved by the Defence Forces. The Department said the suit was being developed under a project which was designed to demonstrate the suit's performance against the latest in armoured warfare.

The suit will be supplied by the UK company Dassault Defence, and the DFG said that the system would not be developed in-house.

The new body armour system is the only one of its kind approved by the Defence Forces.

The suit is due to be tested in a laboratory in Ireland and is currently undergoing technical tests and development.

The test will be a demonstration of the suit's performance against an armour-piercing weapon.

I have been told that it is now 'too late' to ease restrictions on a new Irish language service in Dublin, the largest city in the Republic of Ireland.

The Independent reports that the Minister for the Environment, Phil Hogan, has informed TDs that he will bring forward legislation on the matter to the Dáil in the coming weeks.

Mr Hogan said that this is a "critical issue of equality", and that it is "critical to a healthy democracy".

The legislation will, he said, be presented to the Dáil before Easter.

The government will also legislate for a Gaelic language minority radio station to be established in Dublin.

Mr Hogan said that the creation of the Gaelic language minority radio station "will allow Irish to be spoken in all parts of our city and help bring about a more equal society".

"Irish is important to the identity of our city as well as a fundamental feature of our democratic politics," he added.

Earlier this year the city was voted the second most Irish city in the world after Cork, by the Irish Language Council.

The council's annual survey shows that the Irish language is spoken in all parts of Dublin and almost half of all the city's residents are fluent in the language.

Irish has been an official language of the State since 1706, but many citizens are not fluent in the language as their own language.

Irish and Gaelic dialects have been spoken in parts of the Republic since at least the 11th century, and are still spoken in some regions of the country.

HIV infections: new figures put total number of people infected by the virus at 93,000, with around 1,100 cases confirmed

New figures have emerged from the Ministry of Health to show that the total number of people infected with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) in the United Kingdom last year has topped the 93,000 mark.

The National Health Service's viral infections centre (NHSVIC) recently reported that in the last 24 hours there were 93,071 new cases of HIV infection in England and Wales, with nearly 1,100 confirmed.

The figure, based on a 24-hour period on 4 October, was the highest recorded since 2008.

The highest number of infections was recorded in February 2011, when 93,094 people were infected, and was set to increase to 93,821 infections this month.

The National Surveillance Unit's Director Dr Philip Batey said: 'The overall number of people infected with HIV in the UK is now more than three times higher than it was just over a decade ago. The fact that the number of new HIV cases being reported each month has now reached an all-time high shows that the progress made in reducing the epidemic is well underway.

'The numbers of infections are increasing rapidly because of the high number of new HIV positive people coming forward for testing and because people are being tested more frequently. This has resulted in a rapid increase in new infections over the last year.

'Over the last two and a half years, the number of new HIV infections in England and Wales has now reached an all-time high. This is a very encouraging sign and shows that we are making rapid progress.

'We are continuing to invest significant resources into the prevention and response to this epidemic. We continue to collaborate with other countries in the fight against HIV and we are continuing to drive forward the Government's HIV strategy.

'We are committed to improving the provision of HIV care in the UK through the National Clinical Strategy and we are determined to tackle the stigma attached to the condition.'

The NHSVIC statistics were first published yesterday following a Freedom of Information request by The Liberal.
headline: Covid-19: UK reports record-busting daily coronavirus cases, with just over 93,000 new infections confirmed in the last 24h

text:
Girlish boy Dino-cart ‘blesses’ himself, says dad

By Pat Rohan

Irish Independent, Thursday, 24 February 2008

It was not easy for the five-year-old Dino-cart to be a child again.

His father, who is a teacher, was determined to make Dino-cart a child. That meant putting him in the back of a class and giving him all the lessons in front of him – a daily routine that the boy found frustrating and sometimes humiliating.

Dino-cart was the only boy in a class of eight boys and five girls, all of whom were learning how to read.

“He would do well but he just couldn’t read as well as the other five boys,” said the teacher, who asked that her name not be used for fear of reprisals.

The teacher said she had warned Dino-cart to be patient and not be too proud of his accomplishments.

He had learnt how to do the exercises correctly, but it was hard to make him learn the finer points of reading and writing.

“He has learnt to read and write but he’s not fluent.”

She said Dino-cart had been given a lot of advice. “He has been told to be patient and not to be too proud of his progress.”

She was also given the task of keeping Dino-cart on task.

“He has had to learn a lot of new things,” she said. “He has to practise every day.”

Dino-cart did not always get the help he needed.

He had to be sent to a new school and the teacher said he was always on the verge of being sent back to school.

He eventually made friends and learnt to play football and rugby but, the teacher said, he never learnt how to work in an office.

“He learnt a lot but he wasn’t able to fit into the normal structure of society,” she said.

The teacher said the boy had struggled with his own anger but that he had made a good start at helping himself by talking to his father.

He has since been awarded a medal by the Irish Council for Juvenile Justice at Dublin Castle.

She said she had asked that her name not be used because she feared retaliation. She said she could not take any risks and was pleased that Dino-cart had started the lessons properly.

“He’s had to learn that you can’t just give children things if they don’t want them.”

The teacher said she had taken Dino-cart back to school the following day and left the boy in his father’s care.

She said she hoped his father would eventually become more involved in Dino-cart’s life.

“If he feels that his son is being a child, he’ll start looking after him.”

The teacher was not worried that Dino-cart would be sent home.

“He’s got lots of friends and he gets on with his dad.”

The teacher said her children were also becoming aware of the difference between being a boy and being a child.
headline: Dino-cart invention helps boy 'to be a child'

Irish Police charge man in the Rosslare Europort drug seizure

By Róisín Gaffney and Damien McGrath

LIVERPOOL, UK – Police in Ireland have arrested a man in connection with an ongoing Europort seizure in the UK.

The Rosslare Europort is a busy freight terminal in west London that is used by many international operators to ship goods from Europe to and from Ireland.

The operation is being run by British Police and Irish Crime Officers from the Criminal Assets Bureau (Cabot), the UK’s main anti-corruption agency.

The man police have arrested is a 39-year-old man from Cork, Ireland, who is understood to be the driver of a vehicle that was seen in the terminal on Sunday afternoon.

He has been charged with the offences of trafficking in Class D drugs, possession of a Class D drug, possession of Class A drugs and possession of Class A drugs.

Cabot said the man, whose identity and address is being withheld by the force at this time, was arrested after a tip off led to him being stopped by officers in a vehicle outside the terminal at about 4pm.

He was arrested with the assistance of UK police, a member of Irish police and members of the Cabot team.

“There is absolutely no excuse for this to happen. We are dealing with an organised criminal gang,” said Cabot Acting Director, Mike Maguire.

“This is a criminal offence and it is clear that someone has been misinformed and/or misdirected.”

The man was charged in the Rosslare Europort, which is one of the busiest in Europe.

“Rosslare Europort is a centre of criminal activity and it’s unacceptable that any individual could be involved in this operation in any way,” said Maguire.

“We will be doing everything we can to ensure that this operation is conducted in a way that is compliant with UK law and we are aware that the Rosslare Europort team has a number of UK officers in the area.”

Cabot has been involved in the investigation and has assisted both the Irish and UK police with the investigation.

“We are confident this was an organised crime operation and that the Rosslare Europort team was involved and has been involved in the investigation from the very start,” said Maguire.

“We are extremely grateful to the member of the Cabot team who was involved in this investigation and to the member of the Irish police and members of the UK Police.”

While many of the suspects involved in the Rosslare Europort operation were arrested over the course of several years, the Rosslare Europort has been run as a single, organised operation with no sign of any break in.

“This is not a case of ‘who is going to get away with it’,” said Maguire.

“The Rosslare Europort team is operating in a very professional way and they have all worked very hard to ensure that this operation is being handled with the highest possible integrity,” he added.
headline: Man charged over €6.5m drug seizure at Rosslare Europort

Two men were arrested in Galway on Saturday (25 March) after drugs and cash were found in their possession.

The men were taken to Galway Garda station in a police car and have been charged with possessing prohibited goods, possession of narcotics, trafficking of controlled substances, trafficking of controlled substances, possession of cannabis, possession of cannabis with intent to supply, possession of controlled dangerous substance, possession of a firearm and possession of a firearm at a premises without a permit.

A number of individuals have been charged with the possession of proceeds of crime, as well as money laundering and firearms offences.

The police said they were investigating the possibility that the proceeds from crime may have come from illegal activity.

The men were arrested after a gardaí vehicle was stopped by members of the public near the A1 near the Claremorris Road.

A search of the vehicle found cash and a quantity of cannabis and cocaine in the boot.

Gardaí are appealing for the public’s assistance in identifying the men involved.

A number of people have already been questioned about the search.

The investigation involves an investigation into possible money-for-barter activities by the men described by the gardaí.

It says that two men, aged 20 and 28, from Claremorris and Aghads, have been arrested.

The paper says one of the men arrested has been charged with possession of proceeds of crime and another man has been charged with possession of cannabis with intent to supply.

The man arrested has been linked to a number of cash-for-barter schemes.

He was arrested after a traffic stop at approximately 8.30pm on Friday.

The vehicle was later found abandoned with the vehicle stolen.

The man in the car was identified as Thomas Ní Bhealaigh, from Claremorris, and a member of the Nenagh-Claremorris Social Club.

According to the lawsuit, the Act "creates a system in which the lives of people with disabilities are devalued and marginalized, and in which they are offered a 'death option' as a means of avoiding the burden of their disabilities". In response to the lawsuit, the Californian Department of Justice has released a statement saying that the Act is designed to "provide patients with the option to end their suffering and die with dignity, free from unnecessary pain and suffering". However, the department acknowledged that there are concerns about the potential for abuse and has pledged to work with the plaintiffs to address these issues.

The lawsuit is expected to be a long and complex process, with both sides presenting evidence and arguments to the court. Disability rights groups say they are determined to fight for the rights of people with disabilities, and to ensure that they are protected from discrimination and exploitation under California's assisted suicide law.

As the debate around assisted suicide continues to rage, this lawsuit highlights the need for greater protection and support for people with disabilities, both in California and across the world. In recent weeks, Ireland has been gripped by an unprecedented energy crisis. The lights are dimming, the heating is struggling, and the cost of living is skyrocketing. But who is to blame? According to some experts, the European Union's green policies are to blame.

Under the guise of reducing carbon emissions and tackling climate change, the EU has implemented a series of measures that have had a disastrous impact on Ireland's energy supply. For example, the EU's Renewable Energy Directive has forced Ireland to rely increasingly on expensive and unreliable wind power. And the EU's Emissions Trading System has led to a rise in the cost of carbon credits, which are now passed on to consumers in the form of higher energy bills.

But the problem runs deeper than just these policies. The EU's green agenda is based on a fundamentally flawed understanding of economics and energy policy. By setting arbitrary targets for reducing carbon emissions, the EU has created an unstable and unpredictable energy market. This has led to a situation where energy prices are no longer determined by supply and demand, but by political whim.

The consequences of this are already being felt in Ireland. The country's energy-intensive industries, such as manufacturing and agriculture, are struggling to compete in a market where they are forced to pay higher prices for energy. And the cost of living for ordinary Irish people is rising rapidly, as they are hit with higher energy bills and higher prices for goods and services.

But the problem is not just confined to Ireland. The EU's green policies are causing energy crises across the continent. From gas shortages in Germany to blackouts in Italy, the consequences of the EU's green agenda are being felt far and wide.

So what can be done? Firstly, the EU must rethink its approach to energy policy. Rather than setting arbitrary targets for reducing carbon emissions, the EU should focus on promoting energy security and stability. This means investing in new energy technologies, such as nuclear power and hydrogen fuel cells, and promoting energy efficiency and conservation measures.

Secondly, the EU must scrap its disastrous Renewable Energy Directive and Emissions Trading System. These policies are not working, and are only serving to exacerbate the energy crisis. Instead, the EU should focus on promoting a truly market-based approach to energy policy, where energy prices are determined by supply and demand, rather than by political fiat.

In conclusion, the EU's green policies are causing an energy crisis in Ireland and across the continent. It is time for the EU to rethink its approach to energy policy and to prioritize energy security and stability over ideological obsessions with reducing carbon emissions. Only then can we have a reliable and affordable energy system that supports the needs of businesses and families across the EU.

As we navigate the fast-paced, ever-changing world of modern Ireland, it's no secret that many of us are feeling the pressure to be constantly on the go. Whether it's the stress of work, the demands of family and social life, or the constant barrage of information and stimuli from our screens, it's easy to feel overwhelmed and unsure of how to cope.

But in recent years, a new trend has emerged: the rise of therapy culture. With more and more people seeking help from mental health professionals, it's fair to say that we live in an age of over-diagnosis.

According to the Irish Survey of Mental Health and Wellbeing 2020, the percentage of people who have seen a mental health professional in the past year has increased by 12% since 2015. This trend is not unique to Ireland, either – across the globe, there has been a significant increase in the number of people seeking mental health support.

Some experts argue that the rise of therapy culture is a positive development. With more people seeking help, they say, we are moving towards a more open and accepting society where mental health is seen as a vital aspect of overall health. And certainly, therapy can be a valuable tool for managing mental health issues and improving overall wellbeing.

But others are more skeptical. They point out that the ease with which we can access therapy – thanks to online platforms and a growing number of mental health professionals – can lead to over-diagnosis and over-treatment. After all, not every problem can be "cured" by therapy, and some people may be unnecessarily labelled with mental health conditions that don't necessarily exist.

So, what does this mean for those of us living in this era of over-diagnosis? How can we navigate this new landscape and ensure that we're getting the right support for our mental health?

One thing is clear: therapy is not a one-size-fits-all solution. Different people will respond better to different types of therapy, and it's important to find a therapist who is the right fit for your individual needs.

It's also worth noting that therapy is just one part of a broader mental health landscape. Other factors, such as lifestyle changes, social support, and self-care practices, can also play a crucial role in maintaining good mental health.

Ultimately, the rise of therapy culture is a complex issue, with both positive and negative consequences. While it's important to be open and honest about our mental health, it's equally important to be aware of the potential pitfalls of over-diagnosis and over-treatment.
headline: Therapy Culture: Do we live in an age of over-diagnosis?

As the world grapples with the challenges of the 21st century, the thoughtful insights of John Henry Newman continue to resonate with Irish Catholics and beyond. This 19th-century theologian and cardinal offers a timely reminder of the need to hold liberalism to account, and to ensure that the Church remains a force for good in society.

In an age of increasing polarization and division, Newman's prescience is more vital than ever. His call to "realise and act on the principles of their religion" (1) has never been more urgent, as we face a torrent of challenges from within and without.

Newman's critique of liberalism is a sobering reminder of the dangers of a philosophy that seeks to reduce religion to a mere "creed" or set of beliefs, rather than a living, breathing faith that shapes our entire way of life. (2) He argues that true faith must be rooted in a deep understanding of the nature of God and the world, and that it must be expressed through a commitment to justice, charity, and service. (3)

As we consider the state of the Church today, it is clear that Newman's warnings are just as relevant to our own time as they were when he first penned them. From the abuse scandals that have shaken the Church to the ongoing struggles with secularism and relativism, it is time to heed Newman's call to "realise and act on the principles of their religion". (4)

In a world that is increasingly hostile to the Church's teachings, it is easy to feel overwhelmed and disheartened. But Newman's example offers us hope and guidance. He reminds us that the Church is not an institution to be feared or reviled, but a living, breathing community of believers who are called to be a light in the darkness. (5)

As we look to the future, we must remember the wisdom of John Henry Newman. His prescience reminds us that the Church's mission is not to be a mere cultural relic, but a vibrant and dynamic force for good in the world. By holding liberalism to account and staying true to our faith, we can build a better future for ourselves and for generations to come.

Title: Irish Housing, and the Flight of the Swallows

In the world of Irish housing, it's hard not to feel like a bird flying south for the winter. Prices are soaring, supply is dwindling, and the once-thriving nest of affordable homes is fast becoming a distant memory.

The latest figures from the CSO show that house prices in Ireland are up 7.5% on last year, with the average price of a three-bedroom semi-detached house now standing at a jaw-dropping €320,000. For those keeping track, that's a 50% increase in just five years.

But it's not just the prices that are causing concern – it's the speed at which they're rising. The CSO reports that the average house price in Ireland is now increasing by €2,500 every single day. That's the equivalent of a whole new house every three days.

So, where are all these swallows flying off to? Well, the answer is simple: Dublin. The city is the epicentre of Ireland's housing crisis, with prices in some areas pushing €600,000. It's no wonder that the nation's capital is being dubbed the new San Francisco, with its tech boom and influx of hipsters.

But it's not just Dublin that's feeling the pinch. Cork, Galway, and other major cities are also seeing a surge in house prices, as the country's population continues to grow and the demand for housing outstrips the supply.

The situation is so dire that some are calling for a complete overhaul of the country's housing system. "We need to start building more houses, and we need to do it now," says David McWilliams, economist and author of the bestselling book, "The Tiger's Tail". "Otherwise, we risk pricing an entire generation out of the market."

But for those struggling to get their foot on the property ladder, it's not just a case of building more houses. It's about addressing the underlying issues that are driving up prices in the first place. "The root of the problem is supply and demand," says Mary O'Donoghue, a Dublin-based estate agent. "We need to find a way to balance the two, and fast."

As the swallows continue to fly south for the winter, it's clear that Ireland's housing crisis is far from over. But with the help of some creative solutions and a bit of good old-fashioned planning, maybe – just maybe – we can build our way out of this mess and create a more sustainable future for generations to come.

With the country facing a third wave of COVID-19 cases and the Omicron variant posing new challenges, the question on many people's minds is: do vaccine passports actually work?

These passports are meant to be used as proof of vaccination status, allowing individuals to travel, attend events, and engage in other activities without fear of being turned away due to concerns about spreading the virus.

But critics argue that vaccine passports are not a panacea for the COVID-19 crisis. They point to the fact that vaccines are not 100% effective, and that there are still many unvaccinated individuals who can still transmit the virus. They also argue that the focus should be on improving public health measures, such as increasing testing and contact tracing, rather than relying solely on vaccination.

As the debate around vaccine passports continues, it is important to consider the evidence and the potential impacts of such measures. However, if you are unable to resolve the problem through the travel agent or tour operator, you can also contact the relevant government agency for assistance.

In Ireland, the main government agency responsible for consumer protection in the travel industry is the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC). The CCPC can provide information and advice on how to handle problems with your holiday, and they can also take enforcement action against travel agents and tour operators that violate consumer protection laws.

In conclusion, if your holiday goes wrong, it's important to know your rights as a consumer. As parents, we're constantly bombarded with reminders of our child's growth and development. From the first smile, to the first word, to the first day of school, each milestone brings with it a sense of pride and wonder. But as our little ones grow up, it's easy to get caught up in the hustle and bustle of daily life and forget to stop and savour these precious moments. That's why it's so important to make time for celebration and remembrance, to mark those milestones and create lasting memories with your child.

In this article, we'll explore some of the ways you can make the most of your child's special occasions, from birthdays and anniversaries to graduations and achievements. We'll also share some tips on how to document and preserve these memories for years to come, so you can look back and cherish them whenever you want.

First up, let's talk about birthdays. These are often the most obvious milestones, but they're also some of the most important. After all, a birthday is a time to celebrate another year of life, and all the possibilities that come with it. Whether you're planning a small family gathering or a big blowout bash, there are plenty of ways to make it a special day for your child. Consider having a themed party, with decorations and activities that match your child's interests. You could also make a scrapbook or photo album together, filled with memories from the past year.

Another important milestone is the first day of school. This can be a big transition for both parents and children, but it's also a time of great excitement and possibility. Why not take a photo of your child on their first day, and make it a tradition to do so every year? You could also create a memory book filled with photos and mementos from each year of school, so your child can look back and see how much they've grown and changed.

Graduations are another significant milestone, whether it's from primary school, secondary school, or college. These are times of great accomplishment and pride, and they deserve to be celebrated. Why not throw a graduation party, complete with a cap and gown, and plenty of food and drink? You could also create a time capsule filled with mementos from your child's time in school, to be opened on a future date.

Finally, let's not forget about the little milestones that can sometimes get lost in the shuffle. First steps, first words, and other small achievements may not seem like a big deal at the time, but they're actually some of the most significant. Why not take a photo or video of your child in each of these moments, and create a montage or slideshow to look back on in the future? It all started when she was just a few months old. I was visiting my sister in the hospital after she had given birth to her first baby. My niece was lying in her bassinet, looking absolutely adorable, when my baby decided to roll over and grab a fistful of her hair. My sister was understandably upset, and I was mortified. But it didn't stop there. Everywhere we went, my baby would see someone with long hair and just go for it. She'd grab hold of it with both hands and pull, sometimes even yanking it hard. It was like she had a one-track mind - all she wanted to do was pull people's hair.

I took her to see a pediatrician, hoping they could tell me what was causing this strange behavior. But the doctor just shrugged and told me that babies this age are curious about everything, and that it's normal for them to explore their environment through touch. But that didn't make me feel any better.

I've tried everything to stop her - bandanas, hats, even a special headband with soft padding to protect my niece's hair. But nothing seems to work. Every time we go out, I'm constantly on high alert, watching my baby like a hawk to make sure she doesn't grab someone's hair again.

It's not just my family and friends who are affected - my baby has even pulled the hair of complete strangers in public. I've seen people nudging her and trying to cover their hair when they see her coming, and I can't say I blame them. It's uncomfortable and embarrassing, and I don't want my baby to be the reason someone else's day is ruined.

I know it's just a phase, and that eventually my baby will grow out of it. But in the meantime, I'm at my wit's end. Any advice from other parents out there who have gone through something similar? How did you deal with it, and how did your baby eventually stop pulling hair?

As a young woman, I never thought I would be the one to benefit from my aunt's breast cancer diagnosis. But, in a strange twist of fate, her illness has actually saved me in more ways than one.

My aunt, a vibrant and active woman in her early 50s, was diagnosed with breast cancer a few months ago. At first, it was a shock to all of us. We never expected it to happen to her, and the news hit us hard. But as we watched her go through treatment, I realized that her diagnosis was not just a personal tragedy, but a wake-up call for our entire family.

Before my aunt's diagnosis, I had never really thought about my own health. I was too busy with work and other obligations to worry about it. But as I watched my aunt go through treatment, I saw firsthand the importance of regular check-ups and screenings. I realized that I needed to take better care of myself, both for my own sake and for the sake of my loved ones.

So, I started making changes to my lifestyle. I began exercising regularly, eating healthier, and getting more sleep. I also made an appointment with my doctor for a check-up, something I had been putting off for years. And you know what? It was the best decision I ever made. My doctor found a few things that needed to be addressed, and I was able to get them taken care of before they became bigger problems.

My aunt's breast cancer diagnosis may have been a difficult pill to swallow, but it has also been a blessing in disguise. It has taught me the importance of taking care of myself and my health, and I will be forever grateful for that.

As the saying goes, "What doesn't kill you makes you stronger." And in this case, my aunt's breast cancer diagnosis has made me a stronger, healthier person. I will never forget the lessons I learned from her, and I will continue to live my life with a newfound appreciation for my health and well-being.

So, to all the women out there, I urge you to take action. Get yourself checked out, and don't wait until it's too late. Your health is worth it, and your loved ones will thank you for it.

And to my aunt, I want to say thank you. Thank you for being such a strong and brave woman, and for teaching me the importance of taking care of myself. I love you, and I will always be grateful for the lessons you have taught me.
headline: My aunt's breast cancer diagnosis saved me

Immigrants in Ireland are bracing themselves for a significant shift in the country's immigration policy, with new reforms set to transform the very definition of what it means to be an immigrant here.

The changes, which were announced last week by the Department of Justice, aim to streamline and modernise Ireland's immigration process, making it easier for foreign nationals to work and live in the country. However, critics argue that the reforms will lead to a watering down of protections for vulnerable migrants, and could result in a lack of accountability in the system.

At the heart of the reforms is a proposed new system of "category-based" immigration, which would see foreign nationals categorised into different groups based on their skills, qualifications, and work experience. This, proponents argue, would make it easier for businesses to access the talent they need to grow and thrive, while also providing greater certainty and stability for immigrants themselves.

But critics argue that this approach could lead to a race to the bottom in terms of wages and working conditions, with the most vulnerable workers - such as those in low-skilled or seasonal jobs - being exploited and marginalised. They also point to concerns around the potential for discrimination and abuse, particularly in light of the country's history of institutional racism and xenophobia.

"This is a recipe for disaster," said Fiona O'Connor, a lecturer in sociology at University College Dublin. "By grouping people together based on their skills and qualifications, we are in danger of perpetuating existing inequalities and discrimination. It's important to remember that immigration is not just about filling job vacancies, but also about building a more diverse and inclusive society."

Others have expressed concern about the lack of consultation and engagement with immigrant communities in the development of the reforms. "We need to be careful not to lose sight of the voices and experiences of the people who are going to be most affected by these changes," said Mary O'Halloran, a community activist and member of the Irish Refugee Council. "Immigrants are not just passive recipients of policy, they are active participants in society who deserve to be heard and respected."

The reforms also propose to introduce a new "points-based" system for assessing eligibility for immigration, which would prioritise candidates based on their skills, qualifications, and language proficiency. While this could lead to a more efficient and effective immigration process, critics argue that it could also lead to a neglect of other important factors, such as an individual's character, integrity, and potential contribution to Irish society.

As the debate around these reforms continues to unfold, it is important to remember that immigration is not just a policy issue, but a fundamental aspect of Irish society and culture.

So, let's stop relying on single solutions and start building a digital safety village. Let's work together to keep our children safe online, because the truth is, no single person or app can do it alone.

headline: Colman Noctor: Digital safety needs a village, not an app

As the world continues to grapple with the COVID-19 pandemic, many countries have implemented strict lockdown measures in an effort to control the spread of the virus. However, as Sweden has shown us, a lockdown may not always be the best course of action.

Sweden is a prime example of a country that has taken a different approach to controlling the spread of COVID-19 compared to other countries. Rather than implementing strict lockdown measures, Sweden has focused on building herd immunity through widespread testing and contact tracing. The country's approach has been controversial, with some critics arguing that Sweden's relatively high death toll suggests that the lockdown strategy would have been more effective.

However, a closer look at Sweden's data reveals that the country's approach has been more successful than it initially appeared. While Sweden has had a higher death toll than countries like Norway and Denmark, which implemented strict lockdown measures, Sweden's death rate per capita is actually lower than those countries when adjusted for population size.

Furthermore, Sweden's economy has performed better than many other countries during the pandemic, with a lower unemployment rate and higher GDP growth. This is largely due to the country's focus on maintaining a high level of economic activity, even during the pandemic.

The lessons of Sweden's experience are clear: while lockdowns may be necessary in some cases, they are not always the best course of action. Governments must carefully consider the potential trade-offs between public health and economic well-being, and choose the approach that will be most effective in the long term.

In conclusion, the COVID-19 pandemic has shown us that there is no one-size-fits-all solution to managing its spread. Governments must be willing to adapt their strategies as new information becomes available and to consider all of the potential consequences of their actions. As the world continues to grapple with the pandemic, Sweden's experience serves as a reminder that there are often more effective ways to manage public health crises than simply shutting everything down.
headline: Does Sweden show we need a lockdown against the spread of government over-reach?

A recent study by the Public Health England (PHE) found that vaccine passports do not provide any additional protection against COVID-19 beyond what is already provided by vaccination. For example, a young man in England was recently refused entry to a nightclub because he did not have a vaccine passport, despite having a negative COVID-19 test result.

Fine Gael leader Leo Varadkar has criticised the "security bubble" that has developed around politicians in Ireland, arguing that it is damaging to the democratic process and could lead to an erosion of trust in public life.

Speaking to the Irish Examiner, Varadkar said he wanted to see a "new era of openness and transparency" in Irish politics, and criticised the increasing use of bodyguards, police protection and other security measures to shield politicians from the public.

"I don't want a country where politicians live in a security bubble, where they can't go out and meet people without being constantly surrounded by bodyguards or police protection," Varadkar said. "That's not what democracy is about. We need to be open to the public, to listen to their concerns and to be accountable to them."

The Fine Gael leader also accused the government of failing to properly invest in the Gardaí, which he said was leading to a lack of resources for the police force to carry out its duties effectively.

"The government needs to invest in the Gardaí, to ensure they have the resources they need to keep our communities safe," Varadkar said. "If we continue to underfund the Gardaí, we are putting our citizens at risk."

Varadkar's comments come as there have been increasing calls for greater transparency in Irish politics, particularly in the wake of the ongoing scandal surrounding the Gardaí's handling of the Casey Report into the corruption of former HSE boss Brendan McDonnell.

The Taoiseach and Tánaiste have also come under criticism for their handling of the scandal, with opposition parties arguing that they have failed to properly address the issue and hold the Gardaí accountable for their actions.

Despite this, Varadkar has pledged to work towards greater transparency in Irish politics, and to ensure that politicians are held accountable to the public.

"I want to see a new era of openness and transparency in Irish politics, where politicians are held accountable to the public and where we are able to build trust in our democratic institutions," Varadkar said. "That's what we owe our citizens."
headline: Varadkar: 'I don't want a country where politicians live in a security bubble'
